items: Protein is built from a small set of chemical elements, and one of them, nitrogen, is found in no other nutrient. This is what makes protein different from carbohydrate and fat.
Every protein contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen. Some proteins also contain small amounts of sulphur, phosphorus and iron.
Protein is the only nutrient that contains nitrogen. Carbohydrate and fat contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, so they contain none. Nitrogen is the element essential for growth.
These elements are arranged into basic units called amino acids. A protein is a large molecule made of many amino acids joined together.
Nitrogen sits in the amino group (the –NH₂ part) of every amino acid, so the nitrogen in a food comes from its protein.
Sulphur is found in only some amino acids, such as cysteine and methionine, which is why only some proteins contain it.
Every amino acid has the same central carbon atom bonded to four groups. Only the side group differs between amino acids, and that difference is what makes each one unique.
An amino group, –NH₂, which carries the nitrogen. It is basic (alkaline).
A carboxyl group, –COOH, which is the acidic part of the amino acid.
A variable side group, written R. It differs between amino acids and gives each one its identity. R is a group of atoms, not an element.
The body builds its proteins from about 20 different amino acids. Different proteins are different sequences of the same 20, much as different words are made from the same letters.
Diagram: draw a central carbon bonded to H, R, –COOH and –NH₂. Label each group, naming the amino group (–NH₂), the carboxyl group (–COOH) and R as the side group that varies.
The body can make some amino acids itself but not others. Those it cannot make have to arrive in food, which is why the idea matters for diet.
Essential (indispensable) amino acids cannot be made by the body, or not in adequate amounts, so they must be supplied by the diet. Lysine is an example.
Eight amino acids are essential for adults: lysine, leucine, isoleucine, valine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine and tryptophan.

Children also need histidine and arginine, which makes ten essential amino acids for children. Give the figures of eight for adults and ten for children; if a question gives nine, accept it, since some sources count histidine as essential for adults too.
Non-essential amino acids can be made by the body from other amino acids and nitrogen-containing compounds, so food does not need to supply them.
Examples of non-essential amino acids: alanine, asparagine, aspartic acid, cysteine, glutamic acid, glutamine, glycine, proline, serine and tyrosine.
Non-essential does not mean unimportant. It means a dietary supply is not normally required, because the body can make them.
A protein's biological value (its quality as a source of amino acids) depends on whether it supplies all the essential amino acids in the right proportions.
Amino acids become proteins by being joined end to end. The link between two amino acids is called a peptide bond.
A peptide bond forms when the carboxyl group (–COOH) of one amino acid reacts with the amino group (–NH₂) of another. It is not formed between the R groups.
A molecule of water is released in this reaction, so peptide bond formation is a condensation reaction.
Two amino acids joined by one peptide bond form a dipeptide. A short chain of amino acids is a peptide, and a long chain is a polypeptide.
A protein is made of one or more polypeptide chains.
Diagram: draw two amino acids side by side, then joined. Label the –CO–NH– link and the molecule of water released.
Hydrolysis is the opposite of the reaction that builds protein. It is how long protein chains are broken back into their amino acids.
Hydrolysis breaks a peptide bond by adding a molecule of water, which reverses the condensation reaction.
Repeated hydrolysis splits a polypeptide into smaller peptides and finally into free amino acids.
In the body the enzymes pepsin (in the stomach) and trypsin (in the small intestine) do this in digestion. Acid and heat can also hydrolyse protein.

Every protein is a chain of amino acids (the small units proteins are built from). The primary structure is simply the order of those amino acids in the chain, and it decides how the chain can fold later.

Primary structure is the number and sequence (order) of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. In other words, it tells you which amino acids are present and in what order, not what shape the chain takes.
The amino acids are linked by peptide bonds (the bonds that join one amino acid to the next), which form the backbone of the chain, and the chain is called a polypeptide.
Different proteins contain different amino acids in a different order, which is why different proteins have different properties.
Primary structure determines the shape the chain can later take, so changing one amino acid in the sequence can change how the protein folds and behaves.
Settings: models made from differently coloured blocks or shapes, one colour per type of amino acid, joined in a row to represent a polypeptide.
Diagram: a row of labelled amino acid blocks, one colour per type of amino acid, linked by peptide bonds to show primary structure.
A long chain of amino acids does not stay straight. Bonds form between different parts of the chain and pull it into a local coil or fold, which gives the protein a definite shape.
The chain is further linked and folded by bonds between different parts of it, giving the protein a definite shape. This is often a spiral (coil) or a pleated sheet.
The main bond is the hydrogen bond: a hydrogen atom in one part of the chain is attracted to an oxygen atom in another part, in the same chain or a neighbouring chain.
Each hydrogen bond is weak, but there are very many of them, so together they hold the coil in shape.
Collagen is an example in which polypeptide chains are linked by hydrogen bonds.
The Irish marking schemes also name disulphide links and salt bonds as ways the chains are linked.

Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional folding of the whole polypeptide chain into one compact unit. The pattern of folding gives the protein its final shape, and several kinds of bond hold it there.

Disulphide links form between the sulphur atoms of two cysteine amino acids, each of which contains an –SH group. They can join two parts of one chain or two separate chains, and are stronger than hydrogen bonds.
Salt bonds form because oppositely charged side groups on amino acids (the parts that differ from one amino acid to another) attract each other.
Hydrogen bonds add further links between sections of the folded chain.
The folded shape may be fibrous (long, straight, coiled or zig-zag chains) or globular (the chain folded into a compact, roughly spherical shape, as in albumin).

The shape is held by many weak bonds, so heat, acid and whisking can break them. Breaking the secondary and tertiary structure unfolds the protein, which is the first step in denaturation. The peptide bonds are not broken.
Diagram: a folded polypeptide chain with the disulphide, hydrogen and salt links between sections of the chain labelled.
Protein structure builds up in three levels, each adding something to the one before. Putting them side by side shows what each level is and which bonds hold it.
Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain, joined by peptide bonds.
Secondary structure is the local coiling of the chain into a definite shape, often a spiral, held by hydrogen bonds.
Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole chain into a compact unit, held by disulphide, hydrogen and salt bonds.
There are thousands of different proteins, so they are sorted into groups by what they are made of and where they come from. The two main groups are simple proteins and conjugated proteins.
Simple proteins are made of amino acids only, while conjugated proteins are a protein part joined to a non-protein part. This is the split to use first in any classification answer.

A third group, derived proteins, is formed when chemical action or an enzyme (a biological catalyst) acts on a protein that already exists. An example is caseinogen digested by rennin to give casein, and gelatine made from collagen.
Proteins can also be classed by origin as animal proteins (high biological value) or plant proteins (low biological value). Exam schemes accept this as an alternative way to classify.
Simple proteins are the plain proteins: break one down by hydrolysis (splitting with water) and you get amino acids and nothing else. They are classed by source as animal or plant proteins.
Animal simple proteins are found in meat, fish, eggs, milk, cheese and yoghurt, so any dairy food or flesh food is a source.
Plant simple proteins are found in cereals, pulses, soya beans, nuts and seeds, so vegetarian diets get their protein from these foods.
Poster setting: give one named food example for each class of protein, for example egg white for an animal simple protein and wheat for a plant simple protein.
A conjugated protein is a protein part combined with a non-protein part, called the prosthetic group. The type of prosthetic group decides which sub-group the protein belongs to.
Lipoproteins: protein combined with a lipid (fat), found in cell membranes and egg yolk.
Phosphoproteins: protein combined with a phosphate group, such as casein in milk.
Nucleoproteins: protein combined with a nucleic acid, found in chromosomes and cell nuclei.
Chromoproteins: protein combined with a coloured non-protein part, such as haemoglobin in blood. Its prosthetic group is haem, which contains iron and gives blood its colour.
On hydrolysis a conjugated protein yields amino acids together with its non-protein part, unlike a simple protein, which yields amino acids only.
Simple animal proteins divide again according to the shape of their chains. The shape decides whether the protein is tough and structural or compact and soluble.
Fibrous animal proteins have long chains arranged in strands, which gives tough, insoluble structural tissue.
Examples of fibrous proteins: collagen in connective tissue (found in meat and fish), elastin in elastic ligaments and myosin in muscle. Keratin, in hair and nails, is also fibrous.
Globular animal proteins have compact, roughly spherical chains, and most of them dissolve in water because the folded shape suits it.
Examples of globular proteins: albumin (ovalbumin) in egg white, lactalbumin in milk and myoglobin in meat.
Simple plant proteins divide into sub-groups too, and the two to know are the main proteins of cereal grains. They are told apart by what they dissolve in.
Glutelins and prolamines are the main protein types of cereal grains such as wheat, rice and maize, and they are classed as plant simple proteins.
Glutelins dissolve in dilute acid or alkali but not in water or alcohol. They occur in wheat as glutenin and in rice as oryzenin.
Prolamines dissolve in 70 to 80 per cent alcohol but not in water. They occur in wheat as gliadin and in maize (corn) as zein.
When wheat flour is mixed with water, gliadin and glutenin together form gluten.
Protein comes from both animal and plant foods, so everyone can meet their needs whatever they eat. Exam answers earn marks for naming a variety of foods from each group.
Animal protein sources are meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, cheese and yoghurt. Cheese and yoghurt belong in the list because they are made from milk.
Plant protein sources are soya beans and soya products, pulses (lentils, peas and beans), cereals (wheat, rice, maize and oats), nuts and seeds.
Cereals such as wheat, rice and maize supply protein as well as carbohydrate, so everyday foods like wheat, bread and pasta are plant protein sources.
Potatoes and vegetables contain only small amounts of protein, so they are not counted as main protein sources.
Albumin is the protein most people meet first, in the white of an egg. It is a good example of a protein that is tied to one particular food.
Albumin is the main protein of egg white (ovalbumin), and it is also found in lean meat.
Lactalbumin, a related albumin, is found in the whey of milk, the watery part left when the casein is removed.
Albumin is a soluble globular protein. It dissolves in water and coagulates (sets) when heated, which is why raw egg white turns solid and white on cooking.
Casein is the main protein of milk, so it follows milk into every food made from milk. Cheese-making depends on changing it.
Casein (the older term is caseinogen) is the main protein of milk.
Casein is present in cheese and yoghurt, the products made from milk.
Casein is coagulated by the enzyme rennin, which is the first step in making cheese because it forms the curd. Acid also coagulates it, which is why milk curdles when it sours.
Gelatine is the protein behind jelly, but it is not found in raw meat. It is made when another protein, collagen, is heated.
Gelatine is not present in raw meat; it forms when collagen from animal bones, skin and connective tissue is heated in moisture.
Gelatine sets to a gel when it cools, so it is used in jelly, aspic, gelatine-set mousses and desserts, marshmallows and some sweets.
Gelatine comes from animal sources, so foods set with it are not vegetarian.
Gluten is the protein that gives wheat bread its structure. It does not exist in dry flour; it is formed when the flour is wet.
Gluten is the protein of wheat and wheat flour.
Gluten forms when the proteins gliadin and glutenin, both already present in the flour, are mixed with water. Flour itself contains gliadin and glutenin, not formed gluten.
Gluten is elastic and stretchy, and kneading develops it. It gives bread dough its elastic, stretchy texture and traps the carbon dioxide made by yeast, so the dough rises.
Foods that depend on wheat gluten include bread, pasta, cakes, pastry and other flour products.
Each of these proteins is tied to a food or food group. Pairing every named protein with one food is the quickest way to answer a naming question.
Albumin: found in egg white and meat, and it sets when heated.
Casein: found in milk, cheese and yoghurt, and it is coagulated by rennin.
Gelatine: found in set desserts such as jelly, and it is made from collagen.
Gluten: found in wheat flour and bread, and it traps gas in dough.
Meat and fish are made of muscle and connective tissue, and each contains its own proteins. Higher Level questions ask you to name them.
Myosin and actin are the contractile proteins of muscle, which means they contract to move the muscle. They are found in the flesh of meat and fish.
Collagen is the main protein of connective tissue and is found in meat, fish and bones.
Collagen in meat and fish is the source of gelatine when it is heated in moisture; this is why cheap tough cuts of meat tenderise on slow, moist cooking.
Elastin in meat and globulin in egg are also acceptable answers when asked for proteins in meat or egg.

Cooking and food preparation change protein in two linked steps. First the folded protein chain unfolds (denaturation), then the unfolded chains join up and set (coagulation). Both are permanent, and together they explain most of what happens to eggs, meat, fish and milk.

Denaturation is the irreversible unfolding of the secondary and tertiary structure of a protein (the folded shape of its chain), without breaking its peptide bonds (the links between amino acids), so the chain keeps its amino acids but changes shape.
Denatured chains lose the original shape and functional properties of the protein, because the function of a protein depends on its shape.
Denatured chains can then link to one another, and this linking is coagulation.
Coagulation is the setting of denatured protein into a solid or semi-solid mass, which is why a runny raw egg becomes firm when cooked.
Denaturation changes the texture and appearance of a food, and denatured protein is more digestible, so cooked protein foods are easier to digest than raw ones.
Denaturation can be caused by heat, mechanical action (such as whisking), chemicals (such as acid and salt) and enzymes.
Egg white coagulates from about 60 degrees C, turning from transparent to opaque and firm; the yolk sets at about 68 degrees C. These are approximate temperatures because eggs set over a range.
Fish flesh changes from translucent to opaque as its protein coagulates during cooking, which is how you can tell fish is cooked.
Examples of coagulation in cookery: omelette, quiche, boiled egg, meringue, soufflé and lemon meringue pie.
A foam is a mass of air bubbles held in a thin film. Egg white makes a good foam because its protein, albumen, can be stretched into a film around each bubble and then set by heat.
Whisking or beating stretches and partly denatures the albumen chains, which unfold and arrange themselves around the air bubbles. This is mechanical action, not heat, that creates the foam.
The protein film around each bubble holds the trapped air, forming a foam.
Gentle heat in cooking then coagulates the albumen around the bubbles, setting the foam permanently, which is why a baked meringue stays firm.
Over-whisking denatures the protein too far and breaks the film, so the foam becomes grainy and collapses.
Examples: meringue, pavlova, soufflé and whisked sponge cake.
A gel is a liquid held in a soft solid. Some proteins, especially gelatine, can do this: they dissolve in hot liquid and set into a network as it cools.
A gel forms when protein chains (gelatine) dissolved in a hot liquid cool and link into a network that traps the liquid, such as water.
Gelatine is the main protein used to make gels in cookery.
A firmer gel results from a higher concentration of gelatine, because more chains form a denser network.
Examples: jelly, aspic, mousses and cheesecake.
Dry heat cooks food without added liquid. It acts mainly on the surface protein, which is why roasted and grilled foods firm up and brown.
Dry heat (roasting, baking, grilling and frying) denatures and coagulates the surface protein, causing shrinkage and firmness.
Prolonged dry heat dries the muscle protein and makes meat tough and dry, so overcooked meat is chewy.
Dry heat at high temperatures produces the Maillard reaction, which browns the surface of meat, bread and biscuits.
The golden-brown crust on bread and roast meat is not caused by sugar alone or by enzymes. It comes from protein and sugar reacting together under dry heat.
The Maillard reaction is non-enzymic browning, which happens when the amino acids of protein react with a reducing sugar (a sugar such as glucose) on heating.
It needs high heat and a dry surface with little moisture; it does not need enzymes.
It produces brown colour and roasted, savoury flavour, as in a toasted bread crust, roast meat, grilled or toasted cheese and biscuits.
Moist heat cooks food in liquid or steam at lower temperatures. For meat it does something dry heat cannot: it changes the tough connective tissue into a soft jelly.
Moist heat (boiling, stewing, poaching and braising) converts the collagen (the tough protein in connective tissue) to gelatine, which tenderises meat.
Collagen conversion needs long, slow cooking in moisture, so cheaper cuts of meat, which contain a lot of connective tissue, become tender.
Prolonged high heat toughens muscle protein, so gentle moist heat is used for tender results.
Heat breaks the weak bonds that hold the folded structure, which is why heat denatures protein.
Whisking, beating and mincing physically stretch and break protein, so they change texture without any heat.
Whisking, beating and mincing unfold protein chains; whisking egg white is the example that forms a foam.
Kneading bread dough develops the gluten (the protein of wheat flour) into an elastic network that traps the carbon dioxide from yeast, so the dough rises.
Beating meat with a mallet breaks up the muscle fibres and tenderises it.
Excessive agitation denatures protein so far that it becomes tough or curdled.
Acids and salt change protein without any heating. That is why a splash of lemon juice curdles milk and a marinade softens meat.
Acids such as lemon juice and vinegar denature protein; lemon juice added to milk curdles it, which is also how milk sours.
A marinade of acid, such as vinegar, wine or lemon, tenderises meat by denaturing its surface protein.
Alkalis also denature protein and change its texture.
Cheese-making uses acid to help set the milk protein, and salt to increase the firmness of the curd (the solid part of the milk), which controls the texture of the cheese.
The acid in the stomach denatures food protein before enzymes hydrolyse (break) it, so the chains are easier for digestive enzymes to reach.
Enzymes are biological catalysts, and some of them work on protein. Cooks use them to set milk for cheese and to soften tough meat.
Rennin, traditionally from the stomach of young calves, coagulates casein (the main protein of milk) for cheese-making.
Papain, from papaya, is a proteolytic enzyme (one that breaks down protein) that tenderises tough meat.
Proteolytic enzymes hydrolyse peptide bonds, so too much enzyme action makes protein soft and mushy.
Enzymes in the digestive tract hydrolyse protein to amino acids.
Heat inactivates enzymes, which is why cooking stops enzymic tenderising.
This investigation shows denaturation in practice by comparing egg white that is left alone, heated and whisked.
Aim: to show how heat and mechanical action denature egg white protein.
Independent variable: the treatment (heating in a water bath, or whisking); dependent variable: the change in appearance and texture of the white.
Controlled variables: the same volume of egg white, the same starting temperature and the same type of dish.
Control: place an untreated sample of egg white in a labelled dish for comparison.
Method: heat a second sample gently in a water bath until it sets, then whisk a third sample until stiff.
Safety: use fresh eggs, wash hands after handling raw egg, and do not taste raw egg white, because raw egg can carry bacteria.
Expected result: the heated white turns opaque and firm, and the whisked white forms a stable foam; the untreated white stays clear and runny.
Conclusion: heat and whisking both denature the protein of egg white and change its appearance and texture.

Protein does far more in the body than most nutrients. Its jobs fall into three groups: building structures, regulating and defending the body, and supplying amino acids (the small units protein is made from).
Structural proteins build and maintain body tissues such as cells, muscle, skin and connective tissue, so they give the body its shape and strength.
Physiologically active proteins regulate body processes, acting as hormones, enzymes, antibodies and blood proteins, so they keep the body working and defend it.
Nutrient proteins are the proteins of food that supply amino acids, including the essential amino acids the body cannot make, so they are the raw material for the other two groups.
Structural proteins are the building material of the body. Cells and tissues are made largely of protein, so the amino acids in food are needed to make new tissue and to mend old tissue.
Growth and repair: amino acids from protein are used to make new body cells, for example during childhood growth and pregnancy, and to repair damaged tissue such as a wound.
Muscle: myosin and actin filaments make up muscle fibres and contract to produce movement, which is why muscle is built from protein.
Connective tissue: collagen forms the fibres of tendons (which join muscle to bone), ligaments (which join bone to bone) and skin, giving them strength.
Hair and nails: keratin, a structural protein, forms hair and nails.
Cell membranes: proteins are built into the membranes around cells, helping to control what passes in and out.
Some proteins do not build anything. They work inside the body to control reactions, fight infection and carry substances, and this is why they are called physiologically active.
Hormones: protein hormones such as insulin, made in the pancreas, control processes like blood glucose levels. Insulin is a hormone, not an enzyme.
Enzymes: protein catalysts (substances that speed up a reaction without being used up) speed up chemical reactions, for example pepsin, which breaks down protein in the stomach.
Antibodies: proteins made by white blood cells bind to invading micro-organisms and toxins as part of the immune response, so they help the body fight infection.
Blood plasma proteins: albumin keeps water within the blood vessels, helping to maintain blood volume and pressure.
Clotting proteins: fibrinogen is converted to fibrin, which forms the mesh that stops bleeding after an injury.
Haemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells, carries oxygen from the lungs to the body tissues.
Nucleoproteins are proteins combined with nucleic acid, found in chromosomes, and are listed as physiologically active proteins.
Nutrient protein means the protein in the food we eat, seen as a source of amino acids. The body digests it and rebuilds the amino acids into its own proteins.
Nutrient proteins supply the essential amino acids that the body cannot manufacture and must obtain from food.
Amino acids supplied by food are used to make the body's own structural and active proteins, so food protein ends up as muscle, enzymes, hormones and so on.
Surplus amino acids are not stored as protein and can be used for energy. There is more on this in Energy value.
A common exam layout sets the three classes against their functions, with an example of each. It is a quick way to learn the whole topic.
Structural: growth and repair of body cells, muscles and skin. Examples: collagen in skin and tendons, keratin in hair and nails.
Physiologically active: hormones, enzymes, antibodies, blood proteins and nucleoproteins. Examples: insulin, pepsin, albumin, haemoglobin.
Nutrient: provide the essential amino acids the body cannot make, with excess protein used for energy. The example is the protein in food.

Not all protein foods are equally useful to the body. Biological value (BV) measures how fully a protein food supplies the essential amino acids (the amino acids the body cannot make for itself) in the right proportions for growth and repair.
High biological value (HBV) protein, also called complete protein, contains all the essential amino acids in adequate amounts, so the body can use it to build and repair tissue.
HBV sources are mainly animal foods: meat, fish, poultry, eggs, milk, cheese and yoghurt.
Soya beans are the main plant exception: they contain all the essential amino acids, so soya beans and soya products are classed as HBV.
Low biological value (LBV) protein, also called incomplete protein, lacks one or more essential amino acids or contains them in small amounts.
LBV sources are mainly plant foods: cereals such as wheat, rice and maize, and pulses (dried peas, beans and lentils), along with nuts and seeds. Peas, beans and lentils are LBV on their own.
To sort foods quickly: eggs, fish, meat and milk are HBV; peas, rice, wheat and maize are LBV.
A low biological value food is not a dead end. Two LBV foods eaten together can supply all the essential amino acids, because each makes good what the other lacks.

This is called complementation, or supplementary value: one protein food makes up the deficiency of another, so the combined meal provides protein of high biological value. The foods are eaten in the same meal or the same day.
Beans on toast is the classic example: bread supplies methionine, which beans lack, while beans supply lysine, which bread lacks, so together they give a complete set of essential amino acids.
Hummus with pitta bread and dhal with chapatti are further complementary pairs, as are rice with lentils, lentil soup with wholemeal bread and bolognese with beans.
Adding a small amount of an HBV food such as milk, cheese or egg to a cereal or pulse also raises its value, for example in macaroni cheese, rice pudding or cereal with milk.
Complementation lets vegetarians and vegans meet their protein needs from plant foods alone, makes meals cheaper, and lets pulses stretch meat as meat extenders.

Complementation is easy to put into practice, because everyday meals can be built around a pair of foods that fill each other's gaps. When you plan a simple meal, say which two foods complement each other and why.

Pair a cereal (rice, pasta, bread or oats) with a pulse (lentils, chickpeas, beans or peas) in the same meal, for example lentil soup with wholemeal bread, because the cereal and pulse lack different essential amino acids.
Add a small amount of egg, milk, cheese or yoghurt to a plant-based meal to raise its biological value.
Soya products such as tofu and textured vegetable protein are HBV, so they can provide protein alone in a vegetarian meal.
Use pulses as meat extenders, adding them to minced meat dishes such as bolognese or chilli to stretch the meat, which makes the meal cheaper.
Protein is often a large part of a food bill, so value depends on cost per usable portion rather than the price of the pack.
Compare unit prices, such as price per kilogram or per 100 g, to judge value across different pack sizes and brands.
Allow for waste: bone, gristle, fat and cooking losses reduce the usable portion of meat and fish, so a cheap-looking pack may give less to eat.
Cheaper cuts of meat for stewing and braising are as nutritious as expensive cuts and suit slow, moist cooking.
Eggs, milk, cheese, dried or tinned pulses, tinned fish such as mackerel, tofu, textured vegetable protein and mycoprotein are low-cost sources of protein.
Fish is usually cheaper when in season, for example mackerel.
Own-brand products and special offers save money only if the extra food can be used before it spoils.
Bulk buying saves money when the food is divided into portions and frozen, so that only the amount needed is thawed.

Plan meals and use a shopping list, and use pulses or TVP to extend mince. Low-cost protein foods also fit the Food Pyramid shelf of meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans and nuts, where two servings a day are recommended.
Protein foods such as meat, fish and dairy spoil quickly and can carry bacteria, so safe buying and storing matter as much as price.
Buy from a clean, reputable retailer, and check the use-by date, and the quality assurance and traceability information on the label, before buying.
Chilled meat, fish and dairy should be kept at 5 degrees Celsius or below, so they are bought last and carried home in a cool bag.
Frozen protein foods should be solid when bought and stored at −18 °C, and packs that have thawed and refrozen should be avoided.
Packaging should be sealed and undamaged, and cans should not be bulging.
Fresh fish has firm flesh, bright eyes and red gills; fresh meat has a fresh colour and smell.
At home, refrigerate protein foods quickly, keep raw and cooked foods apart, defrost in the fridge and cook thoroughly.
Protein can be burned for energy, but its main jobs are growth and repair, so it is a supplementary (secondary) energy source rather than the body's main fuel.
Protein provides 17 kJ, or 4 kcal, of energy per gram. Energy value is measured in kilojoules (kJ) or kilocalories (kcal).
Carbohydrate provides 16 kJ, or 3.75 kcal, per gram; fat provides 37 kJ, or 9 kcal, per gram; alcohol provides 29 kJ, or 7 kcal, per gram.
Fat provides more than twice as much energy per gram as protein, so a fatty food packs far more energy into the same weight than a lean protein food.
Protein is used for energy when carbohydrate and fat intake is too low to meet the body's energy needs, because the body then has to burn protein as fuel.
Surplus protein is used for energy once the body's needs for growth, repair and body proteins are met.
Protein-sparing: when the diet has enough carbohydrate and fat to supply energy, protein is left free for growth and repair.
Eating more protein than the body needs does not build extra protein, because surplus amino acids (the units protein is made of) cannot be stored as protein.

Protein is one of the three energy-giving nutrients, alongside carbohydrate and fat (alcohol also gives energy). It supplies only part of the total energy in a day's food, and the rest comes mainly from carbohydrate and fat.
Energy from protein is calculated from the grams of protein in a food, so a food's energy value is the sum of its protein, carbohydrate, fat and alcohol energy.
Lean meat and white fish supply protein with little energy, because they contain little fat.
Full-fat milk, cheese, fatty meat and nuts supply protein together with considerable fat, and therefore more energy.
Pulses supply protein along with carbohydrate and fibre, and little fat.
For healthy eating, choose lean protein foods. Excess energy from any source, including protein foods, can lead to weight gain.
The energy a food gets from its protein is worked out from the grams of protein it contains, using the energy value per gram. The total energy of the food then adds the other energy-giving nutrients.
1. Find the grams of protein in the food or portion from its nutrition label or a food composition table.
2. Multiply the grams of protein by 17 kJ, or by 4 kcal, to find the energy in that portion.
Sample data: a portion with 25 g of protein gives 25 x 17 = 425 kJ, or 25 x 4 = 100 kcal.
3. Add the energy from protein, carbohydrate, fat and alcohol to find the total energy of the portion.

The body cannot store protein, so amino acids that are surplus to its needs are broken down in the liver. Deamination removes the nitrogen-containing part, so that what is left can be used for energy.
Amino acids cannot be stored as protein, so surplus amino acids are carried to the liver.
1. In the liver, the amino group (–NH₂) is removed from each amino acid and converted to ammonia, which is highly toxic.
2. The liver combines ammonia with carbon dioxide (CO₂) to form urea, which is much less toxic and so safe to carry in the blood.
3. Urea enters the blood, is filtered from the blood by the kidneys and leaves the body in urine.
Adequate fluid intake is needed so that the kidneys can excrete the urea.
The remaining carbon skeleton, which carries the carboxyl group (–COOH), is oxidised in respiration to release energy (heat and energy).

The three fates of the carbon skeleton after deamination are energy, glucose or fat. When energy is in surplus, carbon skeletons can be converted to glucose and stored as glycogen, or converted to fat and stored in adipose tissue (fatty tissue).
Diagram: draw a flow chart of the sequence: excess amino acids, liver, NH₂ removed, ammonia, urea, kidneys, urine; and the carbon part going to energy.

Novel (alternative) protein foods replace meat, fish or eggs in the diet. They come from two kinds of source: plants, and micro-organisms (living things too small to see without a microscope, grown in large quantities).
Soya beans are the main plant source. They are made into tofu, tempeh, textured vegetable protein (TVP), miso, soya milk, soya yoghurt and soya cheese, and also soya flour, soya sauce and soya oil.

Other plant products include seitan, which is made from wheat gluten (the protein part of wheat), and pulses such as lentils, chickpeas and beans. Nuts and seeds, quinoa, edamame and hummus also supply plant protein.
The micro-organism sources are fungi, bacteria, yeast and algae.

Mycoprotein is a protein food made from a fungus grown by fermentation (growing it in a controlled tank), so it is a micro-organism product and not a plant. It is sold as Quorn in mince, pieces, burgers and sausages. Quorn is a brand name; the general term is mycoprotein.
Nutritional yeast is a yeast product used as a flavouring in vegan cooking and, when fortified, as a source of B vitamins. It is also used as a source of protein in vegan cooking.

Soya beans are turned into several quite different foods, and the way each is made explains its texture and taste. Some are curdled or ground, others are fermented (changed by moulds, bacteria or yeast).
Tofu: soya milk is curdled and the curds are pressed into blocks. It is bland, so it takes on flavour from marinades or smoking.
Soya milk: soaked soya beans are ground with their soaking water and the mixture is strained, which removes the solid pulp.
Tempeh: cooked soya beans are fermented by a mould, giving a firm, chewy texture. Because the whole beans are used, it is not the same as tofu, which is made from curd.
Miso: soya beans are mixed with rice (or another grain), salt and water and fermented into a paste.
Soya yoghurt: soya milk is fermented in the same way as dairy yoghurt.
TVP is a meat substitute made from soya flour that has had its oil removed. The aim of the process is to turn a protein-rich flour into a fibrous, chewy product, so learn the stages in order.
1. Soya beans are cleaned and de-hulled (their outer skins are removed), and their oil is extracted.
2. The de-oiled beans are ground into flour.
3. Carbohydrate is removed, leaving a protein-rich flour.
4. Vegetable oil, flavourings, seasonings and nutritional additives such as vitamin B12, iron and methionine (an amino acid) are added, which improves the taste and nutritional value.
5. The mixture is heated and extruded (forced through a machine under pressure), which forms a textured, fibrous product.
6. The product is cut, cubed or chopped into pieces such as mince or chunks.
7. The pieces are dried, packed and labelled.
Mycoprotein is grown rather than farmed or pressed. A fungus is multiplied in tanks and then shaped into a meat-like food in a series of stages.
1. A fungus is fermented (grown) in carefully controlled conditions so that it grows in large quantities.
2. The fungal cells are harvested, filtered and drained.
3. A binder holds the fungal sheets together, and flavour and colour are added. The traditional product uses egg albumen as the binder.
4. The mass is textured to resemble meat.
5. It is sliced, cubed or shredded, steamed to set the binder, then packed and labelled.
Soya and mycoprotein products can supply protein in place of meat, but their nutritional value depends on the product.
Soya protein is high biological value (it supplies all the essential amino acids in good proportions). Soya products also supply polyunsaturated fat, fibre and B group vitamins.
Calcium and iron are present in many soya products, especially tofu set with calcium salts.
Mycoprotein is relatively high in protein and fibre and low in saturated fat. Plant alternatives contain no cholesterol.

Advantages of alternatives: they supply high biological value protein, are low in saturated fat and contain fibre. They suit vegetarians and vegans, are relatively inexpensive and versatile, need little preparation and reduce reliance on meat.
Plant foods contain no vitamin B12, so vegans need it from fortified foods or supplements.
Processed alternatives may be high in salt, sugar and additives, so their labels should be checked. Soya is a labelled allergen, and Quorn contains egg in some products.
In the Food Pyramid of the Department of Health healthy eating guidelines, these foods sit on the shelf of meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans and nuts, which supplies protein and iron.
These foods can replace meat in meals, be used as meat extenders (mixed with meat to make it go further) and be eaten in vegetarian and vegan diets.
Choosing and handling these foods well depends mostly on reading the label and following the pack, because each product keeps and prepares differently.
When selecting, read the label for ingredients, allergens, nutrition information and use-by date. Compare salt, sugar and fat in processed alternatives.

Labels must show ingredients, allergens and a nutrition declaration, under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
Dried TVP and dried pulses keep in airtight containers in a cool, dry place, which keeps moisture and pests out.
TVP must be rehydrated in hot stock or water before use, and it takes on the flavour of the liquid.
Tofu is sold chilled or in sealed packs. Once opened it should be kept under fresh water, with a lid or cover, in the refrigerator and used within the number of days on the label.
Tofu is drained and pressed before frying, so that it browns well and holds its shape.
Pulses are soaked and boiled before use, or bought tinned and ready to use.
Mycoprotein products are sold chilled or frozen and should be cooked thoroughly as the pack directs. Follow the pack instructions for all of these products.
Most alternatives have little taste or texture of their own, so processing and cooking are what make them appealing and meat-like.
Extrusion gives textured vegetable protein its fibrous, chewy texture, which resembles meat.
Marinating or smoking gives tofu flavour, as it is bland on its own. It can then be marinated and stir-fried or baked.
Fermentation by moulds or bacteria gives tempeh, miso and soya yoghurt their texture and flavour.
Mycoprotein is shaped and then steamed to set its binder, so that the pieces hold together during cooking. It must be cooked thoroughly as the pack directs.
TVP is used in dishes such as bolognese, chilli and shepherd's pie. TVP, tofu and mycoprotein take on the flavour of what they are cooked in, so seasoning and sauces matter.
Protein bars and high-protein products should be judged from the label data rather than from the words high protein on the packet. A high-protein claim does not make a product healthy.
Compare per portion the protein, energy, sugar, saturated fat, salt and fibre, not the protein claim alone.
Bars often contain added sugar, a chocolate coating, saturated fat and salt, so check these as well as the protein.

Protein bars may be made with milk (whey) protein or soya protein, which supply high biological value protein. Bars are portable, which makes them most useful where portability is needed, such as for sport.
A high-protein fruit yoghurt supplies high biological value milk protein, calcium, phosphorus and B group vitamins.
Sweetened fruit preparations raise the free sugar content of a yoghurt. Full-fat versions contain more saturated fat, and low-fat versions may contain more added sugar.
Plain yoghurt with fresh fruit is generally the less processed choice.

Under EU nutrition claims rules (Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006), a food can claim to be a source of protein if at least 12% of its energy comes from protein. It can claim to be high protein if at least 20% of its energy comes from protein.
When reading a data table, pick the product with the most protein and fibre and the least energy, sugar and salt for the person stated, for example a young person who plays sport.
Green plants make their own food. They build glucose, a carbohydrate, from carbon dioxide and water, using light energy, and this process is photosynthesis.
Plants are producers because they make their own food. Animals, including people, are consumers: they get their carbohydrate by eating plants, or animals that ate plants.
Word equation: carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of light and chlorophyll, gives glucose + oxygen.
Balanced equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, with light energy and chlorophyll written above the arrow. It is balanced because there are 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on each side.
Four things are required: light energy, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water. There are two products: glucose and oxygen.
Light energy is changed into chemical energy stored in the glucose molecule. This stored energy is what a person later releases from carbohydrate in respiration.

Chlorophyll is the green pigment (colouring substance) in the chloroplasts, the parts of leaf cells where photosynthesis takes place. It absorbs light energy, mainly red and blue light, and uses it to drive the reaction.
Chlorophyll reflects green light rather than absorbing it, which is why leaves look green.

Diagram: leaf cross-section labelled with stomata, palisade cells containing chloroplasts, xylem and phloem, with arrows showing carbon dioxide entering, oxygen leaving, water entering through the xylem and sucrose leaving through the phloem.
A leaf can only make glucose if carbon dioxide, water and light all reach its cells. Each arrives by its own route, and the oxygen made leaves by one of them.
Carbon dioxide enters the leaf from the air by diffusion (spreading from where there is more of it to where there is less) through stomata, small pores mainly on the lower surface of the leaf.
Root hair cells absorb water from the soil, and it is carried up the stem to the leaves in the xylem, the tubes that carry water.
Oxygen, the by-product of photosynthesis, diffuses out of the leaf through the stomata. Some of it is used by the plant in its own respiration.
Respiration goes on in plant cells all the time, day and night, whereas photosynthesis needs light. This is why plants do not simply breathe in carbon dioxide by day and oxygen by night.
A plant does not keep its glucose as glucose. It uses it for energy, stores it, moves it and builds with it, and each job uses a different form.
Respiration: some glucose is used immediately to release energy for growth and the plant's other processes.
Starch: surplus glucose is joined into starch, an insoluble polysaccharide (a large carbohydrate made of many glucose units) kept as a store in leaves, stems, roots and tubers such as potatoes.
Starch is insoluble, so it can be stored in large amounts without affecting the water balance of the cell.

Sucrose: glucose is converted to sucrose, which is carried in the phloem, the transport tubes for sugars, from the leaves to the other parts of the plant, such as growing tips, roots, fruits and storage organs.
Cellulose: glucose is joined into cellulose, the main structural material of plant cell walls.
Plants also make fruit sugars (glucose and fructose), pectin in their cell walls, and, with nitrogen from the soil, proteins, and from glucose, oils and other lipids.
Every carbohydrate in a person's diet starts in a plant. This link is the opening of any answer about where carbohydrates come from.
Plants make glucose by photosynthesis and join it into larger carbohydrates, so every sugar, starch and fibre in the diet was first made by a plant.
Plant foods supply carbohydrate directly, and animal foods supply it indirectly because animal feed is plant material.
Lactose in milk is made by the animal from glucose; it is not made by plants.
Fibre in the diet is cellulose, which is plant cell-wall material.
Photosynthesis also releases the oxygen that people use in aerobic respiration (respiration using oxygen).

Every carbohydrate molecule is built from just three elements (a compound is a substance made of two or more elements, and a formula shows the atoms in one molecule). This small set of elements is what separates carbohydrates from proteins.
Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. They contain no nitrogen, which is how they differ from proteins, because proteins do contain nitrogen.
In sugars the hydrogen and oxygen atoms are in a 2:1 ratio, the same as in water, which is why carbohydrates are described as hydrated carbon (carbon combined with water's elements).
The 2:1 ratio does not mean a carbohydrate contains water; it only means the hydrogen and oxygen atoms are present in the same proportion as in water.
Carbohydrates are grouped by the number of sugar units (saccharide units) in each molecule. One unit makes a monosaccharide, two make a disaccharide and many make a polysaccharide.
Monosaccharides (simple sugars) have one sugar unit: glucose, fructose and galactose, each with the formula C₆H₁₂O₆.
Disaccharides (double sugars) have two sugar units: sucrose, lactose and maltose, each with the formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁.

Polysaccharides (complex carbohydrates) have many sugar units joined in long chains: starch, glycogen, cellulose and pectin, with the general formula (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ. Pectin is a polysaccharide found in fruit.
Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all made of glucose units, so cellulose is a polysaccharide and therefore a carbohydrate even though people cannot digest it.
The three monosaccharides share one formula and the three disaccharides share one formula, so they differ in how their atoms are arranged, not in how many atoms they have.
Sugars (monosaccharides and disaccharides) are sweet and soluble, while polysaccharides are not sweet.
Dietary language uses a simpler three-way grouping: sugar, starch and fibre (cellulose). Chemical language uses monosaccharide, disaccharide and polysaccharide, so learn both.

Revision table: monosaccharide, one unit, C₆H₁₂O₆, glucose, fructose, galactose. Disaccharide, two units, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, sucrose, lactose, maltose. Polysaccharide, many units, (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ, starch, glycogen, cellulose, pectin.
A monosaccharide is the building block of all the larger carbohydrates. Knowing its formula and ring shape explains how sugar units later link together.
A monosaccharide is a single sugar unit that cannot be split by hydrolysis (breaking a bond by adding water) into a simpler sugar.
Glucose has the formula C₆H₁₂O₆, which means six carbon atoms, twelve hydrogen atoms and six oxygen atoms per molecule.
In solution, glucose forms a six-membered ring: five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom make up the ring, and the sixth carbon is a CH₂OH group above the ring.
Hydroxyl (–OH) groups are attached to the other carbon atoms of the ring; these groups take part in linking sugar units together.
Fructose and galactose have the same formula as glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, but their atoms are arranged differently (they are isomers). Fructose can form a five-membered ring, as in sucrose.
Diagram: glucose molecule drawn as a ring, with the ring oxygen, the carbon atoms numbered 1 to 6, the CH₂OH group and the hydroxyl groups labelled.
In the usual ring diagram (alpha-glucose) the –OH on carbon 1 points down, on carbon 2 down, on carbon 3 up and on carbon 4 down, with CH₂OH up on carbon 5.
A simpler ring of C, C, C, C and O with H and OH groups and a CH₂OH group is also accepted.

Sugar units are joined by a reaction that gives off water. Repeating it once makes a disaccharide, and repeating it many times makes a polysaccharide, a polymer (a long molecule built from many repeating units).
Two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction, in which one molecule of water is eliminated as the bond forms: C₆H₁₂O₆ + C₆H₁₂O₆ → C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O.
The bond between two sugar units is called a glycosidic link, the –O– bridge formed where the water is lost.
Glucose + glucose gives maltose; glucose + fructose gives sucrose; glucose + galactose gives lactose. Fructose is not in lactose or maltose.
Polysaccharides form in the same way: many monosaccharide units (glucose) join in a long chain, with a molecule of water lost at each link. Chains may be straight or branched.
Starch is a mixture of amylose, which has straight chains of glucose, and amylopectin, which has branched chains.
Glycogen is a highly branched polymer of glucose, the form in which animals store carbohydrate, in the liver and muscles.
Cellulose has straight, unbranched chains of glucose units held side by side by hydrogen bonds, forming strong fibres in plant cell walls.

Diagram: two glucose units joined by a glycosidic link, labelled with the water molecule released, and the resulting maltose molecule. For a polysaccharide, draw a longer chain of blocks, one straight and one branched.
Monosaccharides are the single-unit sugars, the simplest carbohydrates. Only some turn up in food as themselves, so it helps to know which foods supply each one.
Glucose occurs naturally in fruit, such as grapes, and in some vegetables, so everyday fruit and vegetables supply it.
Glucose syrup, a refined sugar used in sweets and processed foods, is another source of glucose in the diet.
Fructose, also called fruit sugar, occurs naturally in fruit and is the main sugar in honey. Honey contains both fructose and glucose, with fructose the larger part.
Galactose is not usually eaten free in food. It is released when lactose, the sugar in milk, is digested, which is why the marking schemes call it the sugar from digested milk.
Galactose comes from lactose, not from a plant food, so it is not a sugar you eat in quantity.
Disaccharides are double sugars, made of two sugar units joined together. Each common one has a typical food source, and much of the sugar in a modern diet is sucrose added to processed food.
Sucrose, the table sugar, is extracted from sugar beet and sugar cane and sold as white and brown sugar. It also occurs naturally in many fruit and vegetables.
Sucrose is added to biscuits, cakes, sweets, jam, fizzy drinks, breakfast cereals and other processed foods.

Lactose, the milk sugar, is found in milk and milk products such as yoghurt. If cheese is mentioned, only say that hard cheese has almost no lactose, because most of it is lost in the whey or fermented in making it; fresh and soft cheeses keep some.

Maltose, the malt sugar, is produced when starch is broken down during the germination of cereal grains, especially barley, which is the basis of malt. Malt is found in malted drinks, malt extract and malt loaf, and is used in brewing.
Added (free) sugars in processed food include those in biscuits, cakes, sweets, chocolate, jam, fizzy drinks, ice cream, breakfast cereals and sauces. Check the ingredients list to find them.
Natural sugars in whole fruit and vegetables and in milk come packaged with fibre and other nutrients. Added sugars supply energy with few other nutrients, which is why the two are not equal.
Starch is the main carbohydrate in the Irish diet and the main energy-supplying carbohydrate in staple foods (the basic foods a diet is built on). It comes mostly from cereals and from root crops.

Cereals and cereal products are rich in starch: bread, breakfast cereals, porridge oats, pasta, rice and flour. The grains themselves, such as wheat, oats, barley, maize and rice, are rich sources, and flour is made from ground grain.
Potatoes, rice, pasta and bread are the main starch foods in the Irish diet, so they are the easiest examples to give.
Potatoes and other root vegetables contain starch, and so do pulses such as peas, beans and lentils, which also contain fibre.
Porridge oats and many breakfast cereals are starch-based, so a breakfast of cereal or porridge is a starch source.
Glycogen, a polysaccharide, is present in small amounts in meat. It is not a significant dietary source.

Non-starch polysaccharides (NSP) are the plant polysaccharides, mainly cellulose and pectin, that human digestive enzymes cannot break down. Together they make up the dietary fibre of food, the part of plant food that passes through the gut undigested.

Cellulose is found in the skins of fruit and vegetables, in leafy and other vegetables, in wholegrain cereals and in bran. Wholemeal bread, brown rice, wholemeal pasta, nuts and seeds also contain it.

Pectin is found in the cell walls of fruit, especially apples and citrus fruit (the peel and pith of citrus). It is also in soft fruits such as gooseberries and blackcurrants, and unripe fruit has more.

Wholemeal and wholegrain products have more fibre than white versions because the bran, the outer layer of the grain, is kept. White flour and polished (white) rice have the bran removed in refining, so white bread has little fibre.
Seeds such as sunflower, sesame, pumpkin and linseed are high in fibre, as are nuts, and peas, beans and lentils.
Other good fibre sources are the skins of fruit and vegetables, fruit and vegetables generally, wholemeal bread, brown rice and pasta, bran, porridge oats and high-fibre breakfast cereals.
Fibre comes only from plants, so meat, fish, eggs and dairy foods contain none.
Fibre sources fall into two kinds, depending on whether the fibre dissolves in water. This sorts the foods above into two groups.
Insoluble fibre is cellulose and wheat bran. Its sources are wholemeal bread, bran and vegetable skins.
Soluble fibre is pectin, plus the soluble fibre in oats, beans and lentils. Its sources are fruit, oats and pulses.
Exam questions often ask for sugar, starch and fibre sources side by side. A summary of foods by carbohydrate makes these easy to answer, and many foods contain more than one kind.

Sugars: fruit, honey, table sugar, sweets, jam, cakes, biscuits and milk. Starch: rice, pasta, potatoes, bread, flour and cereals. Fibre: wholegrain cereals, fruit and vegetable skins, nuts, seeds and brown rice.
Bread has starch, some sugar and fibre, with more fibre in wholemeal bread. Wholemeal bread should not be called high in sugar.
Fruit has sugars, pectin and cellulose, so it supplies a sugar and fibre together.
Potatoes in their skins have starch and fibre, while milk has lactose only.

Higher Level table: glucose, fructose and galactose come from fruit, honey and digested milk. Sucrose, lactose and maltose come from table sugar, milk and barley. Starch, cellulose and pectin come from potatoes and cereals, vegetables and fruit.
Poster or collage: head a poster with the classification groups (sugars, starch, fibre) and stick pictures of foods under each group.
Sugars are the sweet, water-loving carbohydrates, and these two properties explain why they are used so widely in cooking. Starch is the contrast: it is neither sweet nor soluble in cold water.
All sugars are sweet, but to different degrees. Fructose is sweeter than sucrose (table sugar), and lactose (milk sugar) is the least sweet of the common sugars.
On a scale where sucrose scores 100, the 2017 marking scheme gives fructose 170 and lactose 15. Learn the order (fructose, then sucrose, then lactose) and use the figures only as that scale.
Sweetness is why sugar is used to sweeten cakes, desserts, drinks and sweets.
Sugars are white crystalline solids that dissolve readily in water, and solubility increases with temperature, so more sugar dissolves in hot water than in cold.
A concentrated sugar solution is a syrup. Syrups are used to sweeten drinks and sauces, to make icing and to bottle fruit.
Starch is different: it is insoluble in cold water, so it does not dissolve but settles as a cloudy suspension (tiny solid particles spread through the liquid). It is also not sweet.
Starch behaves differently from sugar: it is insoluble in cold water and must be heated with a liquid before it thickens anything. It also takes in moisture from the air.

Gelatinisation: when starch is heated in a liquid, the granules swell, burst and absorb the liquid, thickening it into a sol (a colloidal solution, where tiny particles stay spread through the liquid).
On cooling, a concentrated starch mixture may set into a gel (a solid-like network that holds the liquid), which is why a cooled custard or sauce can become firm.
Gelatinised starch thickens white sauces, custard, soups, gravies, risotto and fillings for pies and flans.
To prevent lumps, the granules must be separated before they swell. Mix the starch with a little cold liquid first (a cornflour paste), or coat it in fat as in a roux.

A roux is a mixture of fat and flour cooked together before liquid is added. The fat separates the starch granules, and the starch in the flour gelatinises as the liquid is stirred in, giving a base for white sauce.
Starch is hygroscopic: it absorbs moisture from the air, so dry starchy foods such as flour, biscuits and crackers soften or clump if stored in damp air. Store them in airtight containers.
Sugar, especially brown sugar, is also hygroscopic, so it can turn hard or lumpy if left open in damp air.
How a carbohydrate food is cooked decides what happens to it. Dry heat browns it, while moist heat softens it and thickens liquids.

Dry heat (baking, roasting, toasting, grilling) on starch makes the granules burst and absorb fat, and dextrinisation occurs: the starch breaks down into brown dextrins. This gives a brown colour and a crisp, flavoursome crust on bread and toast.
Dry heat on sugar causes caramelisation and the Maillard reaction, which brown the surface of the food and give it flavour and a crisp texture.

Moist heat (boiling, steaming, stewing, poaching) on starch causes gelatinisation: the granules swell, burst and thicken the liquid, thickening sauces and puddings. Pasta, rice and potatoes become soft and digestible.
Moist heat softens the cellulose in vegetable cell walls, so vegetables become tender and easier to digest. The vegetable keeps its fibre.
Sugar dissolves in the cooking liquid and forms a syrup, for example when fruit is stewed, so the syrup carries the flavour of the fruit. Sugar also helps the fruit keep its shape.
Enzymes (proteins that speed up chemical reactions) break complex carbohydrates down in stages until they are small enough to be absorbed.

1. Salivary amylase in the mouth begins breaking starch down into smaller polysaccharides and maltose. This enzyme stops working in the stomach acid, so no carbohydrate digestion takes place in the stomach.
2. Pancreatic amylase, in pancreatic juice released into the small intestine, completes the breakdown of the remaining starch to maltose.

3. Maltase, sucrase and lactase, made by the wall of the small intestine and found in the intestinal juice, finish the job. Maltase splits maltose into two glucose units, sucrase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose, and lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose.
Only monosaccharides (single sugar units: glucose, fructose and galactose) are small enough to pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood.
Humans have no enzyme that digests cellulose, so it passes through the intestine as dietary fibre.
Sugar does much more in the kitchen than sweeten. Each property has a use, and exam answers pair the two.
Sweetness: sweetens cakes, desserts and drinks. Solubility: dissolves to make syrups and icing and to bottle fruit.
Preservation: sugar draws water out of micro-organisms, so they cannot grow and spoilage is slowed in jam, jelly, chutney and crystallised fruit.
Fermentation: sugar is the food for yeast, which produces carbon dioxide that makes bread dough rise.
Aeration (trapping air): creamed sugar and fat trap air in cake mixtures such as sponge cakes. Whisking traps air in egg white, and the dissolved sugar keeps the foam stable, which makes meringue.

Maillard reaction: sugar reacts with amino acids (the units that make up protein) when heated, a non-enzymic browning that gives brown colour and flavour to roast meat, toast, roast potatoes and baked goods. Caramelisation is different because it involves sugar alone.
Gel formation: sugar, acid and pectin together set jam into a gel.
Caramelisation gives crème caramel and toffee, crystallisation gives confectionery, and inversion is used in jam and boiled sweets.
Caramelisation, the Maillard reaction and dextrinisation all brown food, so they are easy to confuse. What differs is what is being heated and with what.
Caramelisation is sugar alone, heated dry until it melts and browns, so it needs no protein, as in caramel sauce.
The Maillard reaction needs sugar and amino acids together, heated dry, so it browns foods that contain both, such as toast and roast meat.
Dextrinisation is starch, not sugar, broken into brown dextrins by dry heat, which is why toast browns even though bread is mostly starch.
Gelatinisation is a different change again: starch heated in a liquid (moist heat) swells and thickens it, while inversion is the hydrolysis of sucrose by acid or enzyme.
Hydrolysis is the reaction that splits big sugars into small ones, and it is the same reaction that happens in digestion. Inversion is the form of it that cooks use on sucrose.

Hydrolysis is the breakdown of a compound by reaction with water: the bond between two units is split and water is added across it. It is the reverse of condensation (joining units with the loss of water).

A disaccharide reacts with water, with enzymes or with heat and acid, and splits into its monosaccharide units. Sucrose gives glucose and fructose, lactose gives glucose and galactose, and maltose gives two glucose units.
Inversion is the hydrolysis of sucrose by heating with an acid (lemon juice, cream of tartar) or by the enzyme invertase. It produces invert sugar, a mixture of glucose and fructose.
Invert sugar is sweeter than sucrose (it contains fructose), is more soluble and is less likely to crystallise than sucrose.
This is why invert sugar is used in jam and boiled sweets, and for smooth icing and fondant. Honey and golden syrup contain invert sugar.
Heating and cooling sugar and starch changes their colour, flavour and texture in three different ways. Each is wanted in some foods and avoided in others.

Caramelisation: sugar heated strongly on its own melts, turns from colourless to golden and then brown, producing caramel with a distinctive, pleasant flavour. Overheating makes it dark and bitter and finally burnt (carbonisation).
Caramel is used in caramel sauce, crème caramel, toffee and brûlée.
Crystallisation: when more sugar is dissolved than the liquid can hold at that temperature (a saturated solution) and the mixture cools, sugar crystals form.
Controlled crystallisation gives the texture of fudge, fondant and sweets, while unwanted large crystals make jam grainy.
Crystallisation is prevented by adding acid or glucose syrup (which causes inversion) and by not stirring while the sugar dissolves.
Dextrinisation: dry heat breaks starch down into shorter chains of glucose units called dextrins, which are brown. The 2005 scheme names the brown compound pyrodextrin.
Dextrinisation gives toast and the crust of baked bread their brown colour and flavour. Browned flour used for a roux thickens less, because its starch has already been broken into shorter chains.
Dextrinisation is a property of starch, not sugar.
Jam sets because of pectin, a substance in fruit cell walls. Making jam depends on getting the pectin out of the fruit and then giving it the right conditions to set.
Pectin is extracted by simmering the chopped fruit in water until soft. Acid, such as lemon juice, helps release the pectin from the cell walls.
Fruit high in pectin includes cooking apples and crab apples, citrus fruit (especially the peel), gooseberries, redcurrants and blackcurrants. Strawberries are low in pectin.
Unripe fruit contains more pectin than ripe fruit, so under-ripe apples are a good source of pectin for jam.
A gel forms only when pectin, sugar and acid are present in the right proportions and the mixture is boiled and then cooled.
During cooling, the pectin molecules link into a network that traps the sugar solution (the liquid), so the jam sets.
Too little pectin, as in strawberries, gives a runny jam. Add lemon juice or a pectin-rich fruit to fix this.
Pectin test (optional): a little cooled pectin extract added to methylated spirits (alcohol) forms a jelly-like clot if much pectin is present.
This simple test shows that starch does not thicken a cold liquid but does thicken it when heated.
Aim: to show the effect of heat on starch mixed with a liquid.
Method: mix a spoonful of cornflour with cold water and observe that it does not dissolve and does not thicken. Then heat the mixture while stirring and observe that it thickens.
Variable: temperature is the variable that changes (cold, then heated).
Control and comparison: the unheated cornflour and cold water mixture is compared with the heated one.
Result: cold, the starch settles as a cloudy suspension and the mixture stays thin; heated, the granules swell, burst and absorb the water, and the mixture thickens into a sol.
Heating sugar on its own, with no water, shows caramelisation happening step by step.
Aim: to observe how granulated sugar changes when it is heated on its own, with no water added.
Method: place a measured quantity of granulated sugar in a dry, heavy-based pan on a low heat, stirring gently as it melts, and note the colour and smell at regular intervals.
Variables: heating time is the independent variable; colour, smell and taste are the dependent variables.
Control: a sample of the same sugar left unheated, for comparison.
Safety: molten sugar is extremely hot and causes severe burns, so use heatproof utensils and keep hands and skin away from the pan.
Expected results: the colour darkens gradually from pale to golden, then deep brown, and the caramel smell strengthens.
These two tests show a change in starch caused by dry heat and a change in sucrose caused by acid.
Dextrinisation, aim: to show that dry heat changes starch. Method: toast white bread, or brown flour in a dry pan, or compare a roux cooked for different times.
Dextrinisation, result: the browned starch is darker and thickens less than unbrowned starch, because its chains are shorter. Safety: the pan is hot.
Inversion, aim: to show that acid changes sucrose. Method: boil a sucrose solution with a little lemon juice and cool it.
Inversion, result: the invert sugar does not crystallise as readily and is sweeter.
A Benedict's test shows the invert sugar: reducing sugars give an orange-red colour, while sucrose does not.
Carbohydrate is the body's main and quickest source of energy. Sugars and starch both end up as glucose in the body, and what the body does with that glucose explains each of the functions below.

Heat and energy: glucose is oxidised in the cells (respiration, the process by which cells release energy from glucose using oxygen). This releases energy for movement and growth and heat to keep body temperature at about 37 °C.
The brain and nervous system rely on glucose as their main fuel, and red blood cells depend on it too, so the body needs a steady supply.
Protein sparing: when enough carbohydrate is eaten to supply energy, protein is kept for growth and repair rather than being used as fuel.
Glycogen store: glucose not needed at once is converted to glycogen and stored in the liver and muscles as a short-term energy reserve, which can be turned back into glucose when blood glucose falls.

Fat store: when the glycogen stores are full, surplus glucose is converted to fat and stored as adipose tissue (body fat) under the skin and around organs, where it also insulates the body and protects organs. Excess energy of any kind is stored this way.
Starch is digested to glucose in the body, so it provides the same energy as sugars, but more slowly.
Sugars give a quick supply of energy. Starch gives a slower, steadier release, along with other nutrients, in foods such as cereals and potatoes.
Dietary fibre (non-starch polysaccharide, mainly cellulose) cannot be digested by humans, so it passes through the digestive system. Its value lies in what it does on the way through the bowel.
Fibre absorbs water and adds bulk and softness to the contents of the intestine and to the stool, so waste is easier to pass.
The bulk stimulates peristalsis, the wave-like muscular contraction that moves food and waste through the intestine. Waste leaves faster, so there is less time for toxins to form in the bowel.
Regular movement of the bowel prevents constipation and reduces the straining that causes haemorrhoids (piles, swollen veins at the anus).

Low fibre intake is a risk factor for constipation, haemorrhoids, diverticular disease (small pouches forming in the bowel wall, which can become inflamed, called diverticulitis) and colon (bowel) cancer.
Fibre absorbs water and gives a feeling of fullness, which helps control appetite and body weight.
Soluble fibre, such as pectin and the soluble fibre in oats, beans and lentils, slows the release of glucose into the blood, which helps keep blood sugar steady.
Soluble fibre also helps to lower LDL cholesterol (the type of blood cholesterol that raises the risk of heart disease), so it reduces the risk of heart disease.

There are two kinds. Insoluble fibre (cellulose, wheat bran) speeds the movement of waste. Soluble fibre (pectin) slows sugar absorption and lowers LDL cholesterol. Fibre provides little or no usable energy.
A diet low in fibre and fluid slows the movement of waste through the bowel. Examiners ask for one bowel disease with an account and its symptoms, and constipation is the model answer.
Constipation: stools pass too slowly through the large intestine, so they become hard and difficult to pass, causing discomfort and straining.
Cause: a diet low in fibre and too little water, because without bulk and moisture the stool stays hard and peristalsis is weak.
Effects: hard stools, straining, bloating and discomfort, and a risk of haemorrhoids (piles) from the straining.
Prevention: eat more fibre, drink plenty of fluids and take regular exercise.
Haemorrhoids (piles) and diverticular disease are the other bowel conditions to name if asked, and both are linked to low fibre intake.
Bowel-protecting guidelines: choose wholegrain cereals, leave the skins on fruit and vegetables, snack on fresh or dried fruit, nuts and seeds, eat whole fruit rather than juice, and drink water.
Sugar does far more in the kitchen than sweeten. Each use below is something sugar does for the food, and exams ask for three or more.
Sweetening and flavouring cakes, desserts, drinks, sauces and sweets, which improves palatability (how pleasant the food is to eat).
Preserving jam, chutney, syrup and crystallised fruit: sugar in high concentration draws water out of micro-organisms, so spoilage is slowed.
Feeding yeast: fermentation of sugar by yeast produces carbon dioxide, which makes bread dough rise.
Browning and caramel flavour: caramelisation and the Maillard reaction brown the surface of baked goods, glazes and crème caramel.
Giving the texture of fudge, fondant and boiled sweets through controlled crystallisation, since sugar crystals form their structure.
Giving volume: creamed sugar and fat trap air in sponge cakes, and sugar helps egg white hold a stable foam in meringues.
Coating: syrups and icing (a solution of sugar) are used for coating, and sugar syrup stops cut fruit in a fruit salad discolouring.
Sugar holds moisture (it is hygroscopic), so cakes stay moist and keep for longer.
Starch and pectin are carbohydrates that change how food holds together. Starch mainly thickens, while pectin sets fruit into a gel.
Starch is a thickening agent: it gelatinises (swells and thickens) in a hot liquid, thickening sauces, soups, gravies, custards and pie fillings.
In a roux the fat binds with the flour and separates the starch granules, so the sauce is lump-free.
Starch binds and coats: it forms the thickening in batters and coatings and gives body to a sauce.

Starch helps structure in baking: starch in flour gelatinises as a cake, pastry or bread bakes and helps to set the crumb. The elastic structure of bread comes from gluten, a protein in wheat flour, not from starch.
Starch browns on dry heat (dextrinisation), giving crust colour and flavour to toast and baked goods.
Pectin is the gelling agent in jam, jelly and marmalade: with sugar and acid it sets the fruit mixture into a gel.
Pectin is also used in food manufacture as a gelling agent and stabiliser (additive E440) in confectionery, desserts and yoghurts, and it supports shape in cooked fruit and thickens fruit fillings.

Every nutrient releases a set amount of energy per gram, so we can work out how much energy a food supplies from its nutrient content. Carbohydrate is the main energy nutrient in most diets, so you need its figure and how to use it.
Carbohydrate provides 16 kJ (3.75 kcal) per gram. Sugars and starch have the same energy value per gram, so a gram of sugar gives no more energy than a gram of starch.
For comparison, protein provides 17 kJ (4 kcal) per gram, fat 37 kJ (9 kcal) per gram and alcohol 29 kJ (7 kcal) per gram. Fat gives more than twice the energy of carbohydrate for the same weight.
Fibre (non-starch polysaccharide) is not digested by human enzymes, so it contributes little usable energy. Say 'little', not 'none'.
To calculate the energy from a food, multiply the grams of carbohydrate by 16 to get kilojoules (kJ), or by 3.75 to get kilocalories (kcal).
Worked example: 30 g of sugar provides 30 × 16 = 480 kJ, or 30 × 3.75 = 112.5 kcal. One kilocalorie is about 4.2 kilojoules (1 kcal = 4.184 kJ), which is why the kcal figure is smaller.

Label point: the nutrition declaration on a food label states carbohydrate and, of which, sugars; fibre is an optional item. The energy figure is calculated by the manufacturer, so it may not match your own calculation exactly.

Settings, comparative study: compare two breakfast cereals, one with added sugar and one without, using the label's carbohydrate, sugar and energy per 100 g. Discuss which supplies more energy and which supplies more fibre.

Settings, activity comparison: work out the energy in a food such as a bar of chocolate and compare it with the time an activity such as walking or running takes to use it up. Use the energy values from the source given with the question.

Carbohydrate, mostly as starch, is the main source of energy in most diets, and it should supply the largest share of the energy in the diet, with fat and protein supplying the rest. The kind of carbohydrate matters, because some carries other nutrients and some does not.

Healthy eating guidelines use the Healthy Ireland Food Pyramid (Department of Health and HSE, 2016). Its base shelf is vegetables, salad and fruit, and the second shelf up is wholemeal cereals, breads, potatoes, pasta and rice.
The top shelf holds foods high in fat, sugar and salt. These are eaten in small amounts and not every day, so they should not be the main source of energy.
Choose wholemeal and wholegrain starchy foods, because they supply energy together with fibre, vitamins and minerals.
Foods with a lot of added sugar supply energy but few other nutrients, so they are described as energy-dense and nutrient-poor ('empty calories').
Replacing sugary foods and refined starchy foods with wholegrain starchy foods, fruit and vegetables raises the intake of fibre and nutrients without raising the energy intake.

Fibre is the part of plant foods that humans cannot digest, and adults are advised to eat a set amount each day. Many Irish adults do not reach it, so you should know the target and the everyday ways to meet it.
The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) recommends a daily intake of dietary fibre for adults of 25 g a day. This is its adequate intake, set in 2010 for normal bowel function.
Irish healthy eating guidance from the Department of Health and the HSE (the Healthy Ireland Food Pyramid) also advises eating wholegrain cereals, fruit and vegetables every day.
Breakfast: choose a high-fibre cereal (look for at least 3 g of fibre per 100 g on the label), porridge, bran or wholegrain bread or toast. Check the fibre per 100 g when choosing cereals.

Choose wholegrain or wholemeal bread, brown rice, wholemeal pasta and brown flour in baking in place of white versions, because the fibre is in the outer part of the grain that white versions have lost.
Add pulses such as beans, lentils, peas and chickpeas to soups, stews and salads. Half a tin of beans gives about 7.5 g of fibre, and chickpeas, kidney beans and butter beans give about 10 g.
Add two tablespoons of seeds a day, such as sunflower, sesame, pumpkin and linseed, or bran or porridge oats, to cereal, yoghurt, bread and salads.
