Eat vegetables at lunch and dinner, about a third of each meal; frozen vegetables are as good as fresh. Leave the skins on fruit and vegetables, and bake or boil potatoes in their jackets, since most of the fibre in a potato is in the skin.

Eat 2-3 pieces of fruit a day (a piece gives about 2 g of fibre), and snack on fresh fruit, dried fruit or a handful of nuts instead of biscuits or crisps. Increase fibre gradually and drink plenty of water, because fibre absorbs water.
Added sugar supplies energy with few other nutrients, so cutting it down is a main healthy eating target. Strategies fall into two groups: what you buy, and how you prepare and eat food.
Purchasing: read labels and ingredient lists, because added sugars appear under names such as sucrose, glucose syrup, fructose, honey, cane sugar, brown sugar, corn syrup and fruit juice concentrate.
Choose reduced-sugar, lower-sugar or no-added-sugar versions of drinks, jams, cereals and yoghurts, choose fruit canned in juice rather than syrup, and avoid sugar-coated cereals.
Front-of-pack colour (traffic-light) labelling, where used, shows at a glance whether a food is high, medium or low in sugars. It is voluntary, so not every product carries it.
Preparing: reduce the sugar in recipes and use spices, vanilla or ripe fruit for flavour. Pureed fruit, banana, dates or apple can sweeten recipes instead of sugar.
Do not add sugar to tea, coffee or breakfast cereals. Replace fizzy drinks with water, or with fruit juice diluted with sparkling water, which cuts the sugar per glass.

Eat whole fruit rather than fruit juice or smoothies. Juice contains little fibre, and the sugar in juices and smoothies is released from the fruit's cells so it counts as free sugar, whereas whole fruit keeps its fibre and fills you up.
Snacks and treats: limit sweets, biscuits, cakes, sweet sauces and sugary drinks, and keep fresh fruit, fruit or vegetable sticks, nuts and natural yoghurt as snacks instead.
A diet high in sugar causes harm in several ways, some directly on the teeth and others through the energy and nutrients the diet supplies. Each effect needs its reason to earn marks.
Tooth decay: bacteria in plaque (the sticky film on teeth) ferment sugar to produce acid, which dissolves the enamel of the teeth.
Weight gain and obesity: sugary foods are energy-dense and nutrient-poor, so regular intake adds to excess energy intake.
Type 2 diabetes: a diet high in sugar and energy is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, which is linked to excess body weight.

Heart disease and high blood pressure: high sugar intake is associated with a higher risk of heart disease and raised blood pressure. High fructose intake has been linked with higher blood pressure, and refined carbohydrate with excess insulin that can raise LDL cholesterol.
Nutritional deficiency: foods high in sugar displace fruit, vegetables and other nutrient-rich foods from the diet, so vitamins and minerals fall short.
Sugary foods are also low in fibre, so they do little for bowel health.
Artificial sweeteners give a sweet taste without the energy of sugar, or with less of it. They fall into two types, intense and bulk, and each has its uses and limits.
Intense sweeteners, such as aspartame and saccharin, are many times sweeter than sugar, so only tiny amounts are needed and they add almost no energy.
Bulk sweeteners, such as sorbitol, mannitol and xylitol, have a similar bulk to sugar and provide some energy, though less than sugar.
Uses in food manufacture: they sweeten and improve palatability, and they are used in low-calorie, sugar-free, slimming and reduced-sugar foods, soft drinks and confectionery.
Sorbitol and other bulk sweeteners act as humectants: they retain moisture and stop products drying out.
Bulk sweeteners are used where sugar's bulk is needed, as in confectionery and fudge. Xylitol and sorbitol do not cause tooth decay, so they are used to avoid it.
Sweeteners cannot replace all of sugar's functions: they do not provide the bulk, browning, preserving or bulk-texture roles of sugar.
Sweeteners are food additives with E numbers. Labels must say 'contains sweetener', and aspartame carries a warning for people with phenylketonuria.
Excess bulk sweeteners can have a laxative effect, so their labels carry a warning.

Fatty acids are the building blocks of fats and oils (lipids). They are sorted into three classes by the number of double bonds between carbon atoms in the chain, and that count decides how the fat behaves.
A fatty acid is a long chain of carbon atoms with hydrogen attached, made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. It has a carboxyl group (–COOH) at one end and a methyl group (–CH₃) at the other.
Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds between carbon atoms, so every carbon carries its full quota of hydrogen atoms. Saturated means saturated with hydrogen.
Monounsaturated fatty acids have one double bond (C=C) in the carbon chain, so two neighbouring carbons each hold one hydrogen fewer.
Polyunsaturated fatty acids have two or more double bonds in the carbon chain.

Saturated fats are generally solid at room temperature, while fats rich in monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids are generally liquid oils. Coconut oil and palm oil are plant oils that are rich in saturated fat.
Examples: stearic acid (or butyric acid) is saturated, oleic acid is monounsaturated, and linoleic acid (or linolenic acid) is polyunsaturated.
The shape of the carbon chain explains why some fats are solid and others are liquid. Higher Level questions ask you to describe and draw each type.
Saturated fatty acids contain only single C–C bonds and are fully saturated with hydrogen. The chain is straight and flexible, so the chains pack tightly together and the fat is solid.
Each cis C=C double bond in an unsaturated fatty acid puts a kink (bend) in the chain, so the molecules pack less tightly and the fat stays liquid.

A monounsaturated fatty acid has one double bond and so one kink. A polyunsaturated fatty acid has two or more double bonds, so it has one kink for each cis double bond and is liquid at room temperature.

Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated, with the first double bond between the third and fourth carbon atoms counted from the methyl (omega) end. Omega-6 fatty acids have their first double bond at the sixth carbon from the methyl end.

Diagram: draw a zig-zag or a simple row of carbons for a saturated, a monounsaturated and a polyunsaturated fatty acid. Label the –COOH (carboxyl) end, the –CH₃ (methyl) end and mark each C=C double bond.
A double bond can hold its two hydrogen atoms in two different arrangements. The arrangement changes the shape of the chain and how the fat acts in the body.
Cis and trans describe the hydrogen atoms at one double bond in an unsaturated fatty acid, not how many double bonds there are.
In a cis fatty acid the hydrogen atoms on either side of the double bond lie on the same side of the carbon chain (both above or both below), so the chain bends.
In a trans fatty acid the hydrogen atoms on either side of the double bond lie on opposite sides, so the chain stays nearly straight, like a saturated fatty acid.
Most naturally occurring unsaturated fatty acids are cis, for example those in plant oils such as cooking oils and in oily fish.

Trans fatty acids form when oils are partially hydrogenated in food manufacture, so they are found in some processed foods such as biscuits, pastries and fried takeaway foods. Small natural amounts occur in the fat of ruminant animals, in dairy fat and in beef and lamb fat.
Most fatty acids can be made by the body, but a few cannot. These essential fatty acids are polyunsaturated and must come from food.
Essential fatty acids are polyunsaturated fatty acids that the body cannot manufacture (or cannot make in enough quantity), so they must be obtained from food.
Linoleic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid) and linolenic acid (an omega-3 fatty acid) are the two essential fatty acids most often named.
Arachidonic acid is also counted as essential by examiners. Strictly the body forms it only from linoleic acid, when enough linoleic acid is eaten.
Essential fatty acids are needed for growth, for the structure of cell membranes, for the nervous system and brain, and for the immune response.
The body uses essential fatty acids to make prostaglandins, hormone-like compounds that regulate blood clotting, blood pressure and inflammation.
Good sources include vegetable oils such as sunflower, corn, soya and rapeseed oil, nuts and seeds, and oily fish.
Omega-3 fatty acids are a family of essential polyunsaturated fats with several health benefits. They come from a limited range of foods, so it helps to know the sources by name.
Omega-3 fatty acids help reduce the risk of heart attack, stroke, circulatory disease and the formation of blood clots, and they can help raise HDL cholesterol.
Omega-3 fatty acids are linked with healthy brain activity and reduced inflammation, and they may reduce the risk of certain cancers.
Oily fish are the main animal source: salmon, mackerel, herring, sardines and trout.
Plant sources include walnuts, flaxseed (linseed), soya beans and rapeseed (canola) oil.
Some eggs and milk are enriched with omega-3 by changing the diet of the hens or cows, and fish-oil supplements are also accepted as a source.
The type of fatty acid in the diet affects the amount of cholesterol carried in the blood. This is why the balance of saturated, unsaturated and trans fats matters for the heart.
Cholesterol travels in the blood bound to proteins, forming lipoproteins (carriers of cholesterol). LDL and HDL are these carriers, not types of cholesterol itself.

LDL (low-density lipoprotein) carries cholesterol through the blood to the tissues and can deposit it on artery walls, where it narrows the arteries (atherosclerosis) and raises the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD).
HDL (high-density lipoprotein) removes cholesterol from the circulation, carrying it away from the tissues to the liver for removal.
Saturated fatty acids raise LDL cholesterol, increasing the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD).
Unsaturated cis fatty acids, both monounsaturated and polyunsaturated, reduce LDL cholesterol and help to raise HDL cholesterol, so they are generally good for the heart.
Trans fatty acids raise LDL cholesterol and lower HDL cholesterol, increasing the risk of CHD. They are thought to do more harm than saturated fat.
Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats can lower total cholesterol when they replace saturated fats in the diet.
Essential fatty acids must be eaten because the body cannot make them, and omega-3 fatty acids add the heart and brain benefits.
Lipids are the fats and oils in our food. Most of the lipid we eat is in one form, the triglyceride, so knowing what a triglyceride is made of explains most of this topic.
Fats are solid at room temperature and oils are liquid, but both are lipids. Most dietary lipid is in the form of triglycerides.
Fats and oils (triglycerides) are made of carbon (C), hydrogen (H) and oxygen (O) only. They contain no nitrogen, so, unlike protein, they are not a source of nitrogen.
Lipids are made up of fatty acids and glycerol, which join together to form the triglyceride.
Other lipids exist, such as phospholipids like lecithin and sterols like cholesterol, but triglycerides are the lipids studied here.
In digestion the enzyme lipase, made in the pancreas and carried in pancreatic juice, breaks triglycerides down into fatty acids and glycerol.
Most fats and oils in food are triglycerides: one glycerol molecule combined with three fatty acid molecules. The name tells you this, because tri means three.
A triglyceride contains only carbon (C), hydrogen (H) and oxygen (O) atoms, with no nitrogen.
Glycerol is an alcohol, with the formula C₃H₈O₃. It carries three hydroxyl (–OH) groups, one on each of its three carbon atoms, which gives three places for a fatty acid to attach.
The three fatty acids in one triglyceride can be the same or different, and may be saturated, monounsaturated or polyunsaturated. This mixture decides whether the fat is solid or liquid.
The carboxyl group of each fatty acid joins to one hydroxyl group of glycerol, forming an ester bond (–COO–).
Each fatty acid is joined to glycerol by the same reaction, repeated three times. The result is a glycerol backbone with a fatty acid chain hanging from each of its carbons.
Each ester bond forms by condensation, a reaction in which two molecules join and one molecule of water (H₂O) is eliminated.
Three water molecules are removed when one glycerol and three fatty acids combine to form one triglyceride, because three ester bonds are made.
A triglyceride is therefore a glycerol backbone with three fatty acid chains hanging from it.
Digestion runs this in reverse: lipase breaks the ester bonds by adding water back, which is hydrolysis, releasing the fatty acids and glycerol.

Diagram: a glycerol backbone with three fatty acid chains attached by ester (–COO–) links, labelling glycerol, the fatty acid chains and the ester bonds, and marking the three water molecules released during formation.
One way to sort lipids is by where they come from. There are three classes: animal, vegetable (plant) and marine.
Animal fats come from land animals, for example butter, lard, suet, dripping, cheese, egg yolk and the fat in meat.
Vegetable (plant) oils come from seeds, nuts and fruits, for example olive, sunflower, corn, soya and rapeseed oils, and avocado oil.
Marine lipids come from fish and other sea creatures, for example the oil in oily fish such as salmon, mackerel, herring, sardines and trout, and fish-liver oils such as cod-liver oil.
Palm oil and coconut oil come from plants but are high in saturated fat, so they behave like animal fats in the diet.
The second way to sort lipids is by the type of fatty acid they contain. Every fat and oil is a mixture, so the class depends on which type is present in the largest proportion.
A lipid is classed as saturated, monounsaturated or polyunsaturated according to which type of fatty acid makes up the largest proportion of its fatty acids.
Olive oil is classed as monounsaturated because most of its fatty acids have one double bond. Rapeseed oil and avocado are also mainly monounsaturated.
Sunflower, corn and soya oils are classed as polyunsaturated because most of their fatty acids have more than one double bond. The oils of oily fish are also mainly polyunsaturated.
Butter, lard, suet, dripping, meat fat, cheese, coconut oil and palm oil are classed as saturated because saturated fatty acids form the largest proportion of their fatty acids.
Most fats contain a mixture of all three fatty acid types, so classification depends on the predominant type. Butter has some monounsaturated fat and olive oil has some saturated fat.
The fatty acid type explains the state: a lipid that is mostly saturated is a fat, solid at room temperature, while one that is mostly unsaturated is an oil.

Lipids (fats and oils) reach our diet from three kinds of source: animal, vegetable and marine. Animal sources come from the meat, milk and eggs of land animals, and some are fat in its almost pure form.

Meat fat is a major source of lipid in meat products. It includes the visible fat on bacon, the fat trimmed from beef and the fat in sausages. Fatty cuts of lamb and pork, burgers and pâtés also contain it.
Marbling, the fine streaks of fat running inside the muscle of meat, is hidden fat, so a cut can look lean and still contain fat that cannot be trimmed off.
Butter, cream, whole milk, cheese and ice cream supply fat. Milk fat also carries the fat-soluble vitamins A and D, meaning vitamins that dissolve in fat rather than water.
Egg yolk contains fat and lecithin (a fat-like substance that helps fat and water mix). The egg white contains no fat.
Lard is rendered pig fat, which means fat melted down and strained, and is used in pastry and frying.
Suet is the hard fat from around the kidneys and loins of cattle and sheep, used in suet pastry and puddings.
Dripping is the fat that collects from roasted meat, used for frying and roasting.

Visible fat can be seen and cut off or avoided, such as the fat on meat, butter, cooking oil and spreads. Hidden fat is built into foods such as cakes, pastries, biscuits, chocolate, crisps, fried foods, sausages, cheese, ready meals and takeaways.

Plants store fat in their fruits, seeds and nuts, and people press this fat out as oil or process it into spreads. Vegetable (plant) sources are the group most often named in exam answers alongside animal and marine.
Vegetable oils include olive, sunflower, corn, soya, rapeseed (canola), sesame and groundnut (peanut) oils, plus coconut oil and palm oil.
Olives and avocados are fruits that supply lipid, which is unusual because most fruits contain almost none.
Nuts such as almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, peanuts and Brazil nuts are a concentrated source of lipid. So are seeds such as sunflower, sesame and flax (linseed).
Soya beans are a legume (a bean or pea crop) rich in both fat and protein.

Cereals and cereal products supply small amounts of lipid, mainly in wheat germ and oats. Wheat germ is the embryo of the wheat grain, the part that would grow into a new plant, so it holds the grain's fat.
Chocolate contains cocoa butter, which is the plant fat in cocoa.
Margarine and vegetable spreads are made from processed plant oils, so they count as vegetable sources. Shortening is another processed plant fat.
Vegetable oils are also hidden in biscuits, pastries, crisps, fried and takeaway foods and ready meals, which is why these foods are high in fat even though no oil is visible.
Fish and other sea foods give a third group of lipid sources, quite different from the fat of land animals. How much fat a fish has, and where it keeps it, decides whether it counts as a rich source.

Oily fish such as salmon, mackerel, herring, sardines and trout store their fat in the flesh. They are a marine source of omega-3 fatty acids, a type of polyunsaturated fat, so the fat itself is the valuable part.
Fish-liver oils, such as cod-liver oil, provide polyunsaturated fat along with the fat-soluble vitamins A and D. Fish-oil supplements are another source of these.
White fish such as cod, haddock and whiting store their fat mainly in the liver, so the flesh is low in fat.
Shellfish, such as prawns and mussels, contain only small amounts of lipid.
Fats are made of fatty acids, which are saturated, monounsaturated or polyunsaturated. Each food has a pattern in which one type is largest, and that pattern decides how healthy the fat is.

Mostly saturated fats are butter, cream, cheese, lard, suet, dripping, fat on meat and hard cooking fats. Animal fats such as these are generally saturated and associated with raised LDL (the blood cholesterol that harms arteries).
Coconut oil and palm oil are high in saturated fat despite coming from plants, so a food being a plant product does not make its fat unsaturated.
Olive oil, avocado and rapeseed (canola) oil are mostly monounsaturated, as are many nuts such as almonds, hazelnuts and peanuts.

Standard sunflower oil, corn oil and soya oil are mostly polyunsaturated, as are walnuts, seeds and oily fish. Plant and nut oils are associated with HDL, the blood cholesterol that protects the heart.
Sesame oil is a mixture of mono- and polyunsaturated fat, so it does not fit a single class.

Most foods contain all three fatty acid types, and a food is named for the type with the largest share. Butter, for example, contains a substantial share of monounsaturated fat as well as saturated fat, and olive oil contains some saturated fat.
The healthy swap is saturated fat for unsaturated fat, for example butter for olive oil.

Small amounts of naturally occurring trans fat appear in dairy and in beef and lamb fat. Industrial trans fat is limited in the EU to 2 g per 100 g of fat (Regulation (EU) 2019/649, applying from 1 April 2021).
A poster turns the three groups of sources into a picture you can recall quickly in an exam. It works as revision rather than being examined itself.
Group the sources into three columns headed animal, vegetable (plant) and marine.
Give one example food for each column and the type of fatty acid that predominates in it.
Add the main health message for each food, such as the role of omega-3 in oily fish or the saturated fat in butter.
Show the source of each food with a small picture or label so the groups are clear at a glance.

As a fat is heated it passes through three different stages, each at a higher temperature than the last: it melts, then it smokes, then it can burst into flame. Knowing these temperatures explains how fats are chosen and used in cooking.

Melting point is the temperature at which a solid fat turns to liquid. Fats are mixtures of triglycerides, so they melt over a range rather than at one sharp temperature, and solid fats melt at about 30–40 °C. Oils are already liquid at room temperature.

Fats with a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids have lower melting points, because their kinked chains do not pack tightly. Fats with more saturated fatty acids, whose chains are straight and pack closely, have higher melting points.
Smoke point is the temperature at which an overheated lipid begins to decompose and gives off a continuous blue haze. Smoke points are about 200 °C for solid fats and about 250 °C for oils.
On decomposition the fat splits into glycerol and fatty acids, and the glycerol breaks down further to release acrolein, which has an acrid, irritating smell.

Free fatty acids, impurities and food particles left in the oil lower its smoke point, and repeated use builds these up, so used or dirty fat smokes at a lower temperature. This is why frying fat is strained and replaced.
A fat with a high smoke point suits frying, while butter, with a lower smoke point, burns.
Flash point is the temperature at which the vapour from an overheated lipid ignites spontaneously and bursts into flame. Flash points are about 310 °C for solid fats and about 325 °C for oils.
A fat that reaches its flash point is a serious fire hazard. Never leave a deep-fat fryer unattended, never heat fat until it smokes, and smother a fat fire with a fire blanket or lid, never water.
This practical compares how common fats and oils behave on heating, and links the results to their fatty acids and to impurities. Care is needed because the fats become very hot.
Aim: to compare the melting, smoke and flash points of common fats and oils, for example butter, lard, olive oil and sunflower oil.
1. Use a small amount of each fat or oil, so any smoke or fire is limited.
2. Heat each gently, preferably on a hot plate rather than a flame, which is safer for a class demonstration, and read the temperature with a thermometer.
3. Record the order in which the fats melt, and which fats smoke first. Do not heat beyond the smoke point.
Conclusion: link the order of melting points to how saturated the fatty acids are, and the point at which smoke appears to the fat's impurities.
Oil and water do not mix normally, but they can be forced to, and in some foods they stay mixed. This is the basis of mayonnaise, butter, milk and many sauces.
An emulsion is a mixture of two liquids that do not normally mix (immiscible), such as oil and water, with one dispersed as tiny droplets in the other.
Vigorous shaking, whisking or blending forces the liquids together by breaking one liquid into droplets that spread through the other.
A temporary emulsion, such as French dressing (oil and vinegar), separates again on standing because nothing keeps the droplets apart.
A permanent (stable) emulsion, such as mayonnaise, hollandaise sauce, ice cream, cream, milk or butter, stays mixed because an emulsifying agent coats the droplets.
An emulsifier has a hydrophilic (water-attracting) end and a hydrophobic (water-repelling) end, which sit at the boundary between the oil and the water.
In an oil-in-water emulsion, oil droplets are dispersed in water, as in mayonnaise, milk and cream.
In a water-in-oil emulsion, water droplets are dispersed in fat, as in butter, margarine and some spreads.
Making mayonnaise and a French dressing side by side shows the difference between a temporary and a permanent emulsion.
Aim: to show emulsion formation and the effect of an emulsifier, using mayonnaise (egg yolk, oil, and vinegar or lemon juice) and a French dressing (oil and vinegar).
1. Make the mayonnaise by adding the oil to the egg yolk slowly while whisking, so the droplets are small and evenly spread.
2. Shake the oil and vinegar together for the French dressing, and leave both to stand.
Result: the French dressing separates, but the mayonnaise stays stable because the egg yolk is the emulsifier. Comparing with and without an emulsifier shows this.
Two kinds of additive help keep an emulsion together, and they do different jobs. An emulsifier makes the emulsion, while a stabiliser helps it stay that way.

An emulsifying agent is a molecule with a hydrophilic (water-loving) end and a hydrophobic (water-hating, fat-loving) end. The hydrophilic end attaches to the water and the hydrophobic end to the oil, so the droplets are coated and cannot join together.

Emulsifying agents include lecithin (found in egg yolk and soya; the food additive E322), mustard, and mono- and diglycerides such as glycerol monostearate (GMS; mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids are E471).
The function of an emulsifier is to reduce the tension between oil and water so they mix, and to make and keep the emulsion stable.
Stabilisers do not form the emulsion. They thicken the water phase and stop droplets joining together (coalescing).
Examples of stabilisers are starch, pectin, gelatine and gums such as xanthan gum and guar gum. They are used in dressings, sauces, ice cream and low-fat spreads.
Some fats can be spread or shaped without being runny or rock hard. This property, called plasticity, is why butter and margarine behave so differently from oil.
Plasticity is the ability of a fat to be shaped, spread or worked (creamed, rubbed in) at a given temperature without being fully liquid or fully hard.

It is due to a mixture of solid and liquid fat within the fat: the solid fat forms a network that holds the liquid fat. The proportion of saturated fatty acids only decides how much of the fat is solid.

Butter, lard, margarine and shortening are plastic over a range of temperatures. Oils are not plastic, a very unsaturated fat is too liquid to hold its shape, and a very saturated fat is hard and brittle when cold.
Plastic fats are valued in pastry and cake making because they can be creamed, which traps air, or rubbed into flour and layered. Plasticity also gives butter and margarine their spreadability.
Liquid oils can be turned into solid fats by changing their fatty acids. This process, hydrogenation, is how margarine is made from vegetable oils.
Hydrogenation is the addition of hydrogen to the double bonds of unsaturated fatty acids, using a nickel catalyst under heat and pressure.
It converts unsaturated fatty acids to saturated ones, so a liquid oil becomes a semi-solid or solid fat.
It is used to make margarine and spreads, hard margarines, shortenings and baking fats from liquid vegetable oils. The fats are solid, plastic and more stable against oxidative rancidity.
Partial hydrogenation forms trans fatty acids, so the process is now controlled. Full hydrogenation gives a hard saturated fat.
Rancidity is the spoilage of fats and oils, which gives them an unpleasant taste and smell. It happens in two different ways, with different causes.
Oxidative rancidity: oxygen from the air reacts at the double bonds of unsaturated fatty acids, which also breaks the chain. This produces aldehydes and ketones, which cause the rancid smell.
Light, heat and traces of metal ions speed up oxidative rancidity. It affects polyunsaturated oils most because they have the most double bonds.

Hydrolytic rancidity: water, together with the enzyme lipase from the food itself or from micro-organisms such as moulds and bacteria, breaks fats down into fatty acids and glycerol. The free fatty acids, for example butyric acid in butter, give the smell.
Hydrolytic rancidity can occur in a freezer, because lipase is not destroyed by freezing. Blanching vegetables before freezing destroys these enzymes.

Fats are protected from rancidity when stored in airtight, opaque containers in a cool, dark place, kept dry, bought in small amounts and used before the date. Refrigerating or freezing, using less-unsaturated fats, adding antioxidants and not reusing frying oil repeatedly also help.
Antioxidants are the main chemical defence against oxidative rancidity. They are added to fats and oils so that they keep their flavour for longer.
An antioxidant is a substance that slows oxidation. It delays oxidative rancidity by reacting with oxygen or free radicals before they attack the double bonds.
Natural antioxidants include vitamin E (tocopherols, E306), present in some vegetable oils, and vitamin C (ascorbic acid, E300).
Synthetic antioxidants added to fats include butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA, E320) and butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT, E321).

Antioxidants are added to oils, margarines, spreads, snack foods and fried foods to keep their flavour and extend their shelf life. They appear in the ingredients list by name or E number under the additives rules (Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008).
Lipids (fats and oils) do far more in the body than provide energy. Each function below follows from where fat sits in the body or what it does as it passes through the digestive system.
Lipids are a concentrated source of energy, supplying the body with more energy per gram than carbohydrate or protein, so a small amount of fat gives a lot of energy.
Excess energy from any food is stored as adipose tissue (the body's stored fat), which is a reserve of energy for when food intake is low.
Adipose tissue lies under the skin and insulates the body against heat loss, which helps to keep body temperature constant.
Adipose tissue around organs such as the kidneys and heart cushions them against knocks and pressure, and holds them in place.
Lipids slow the emptying of the stomach, which helps to delay hunger, so meals containing fat are more satisfying.
Beyond energy and body protection, lipids carry nutrients, build cell structures and affect how food tastes.
Lipids carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K and help the body absorb them, because these vitamins dissolve in fat and not in water. Dairy fat, oily fish and egg yolk supply them.
Lipids are a source of essential fatty acids, the fatty acids the body cannot make for itself and must get from food.
Phospholipids (fat-like lipids containing phosphorus) and cholesterol form part of the structure of every cell membrane, the thin layer around each cell.
Fat also adds flavour and a smooth texture to food, although this is a cooking benefit and not a biological function.
Digestion link: the enzyme lipase digests triglycerides (the main fats in food) to fatty acids and glycerol, and any excess is stored as adipose tissue.
Cholesterol is a lipid that is often blamed for heart disease, yet the body needs it. It is different from the saturated fat in food, and students often confuse the two.

Cholesterol is a fat-like substance called a sterol, found only in animal foods such as egg yolk, offal (liver and kidney), meat, butter, cream, cheese, prawns and other shellfish. Plant foods contain none.
The liver makes cholesterol itself, in fact most of what the body has, so the amount eaten has less effect on blood cholesterol than the saturated fat in the diet.
Saturated fat in the diet raises blood LDL cholesterol more than dietary cholesterol does. A plant oil such as coconut oil is cholesterol-free but can still be high in saturated fat.

The body uses cholesterol to make cell membranes, bile salts that emulsify fat (break it into tiny droplets) for digestion, and steroid hormones such as oestrogen, progesterone, testosterone and cortisol.
Vitamin D is made in the skin from a derivative of cholesterol.

Too much cholesterol in the blood, especially LDL, builds up on artery walls and narrows them, which increases the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) and stroke. It is also a main constituent of most gallstones.

To lower blood cholesterol, eat less saturated and trans fat and more unsaturated fat, oily fish, oats, pulses, fruit and vegetables (their fibre helps). Keep to a healthy weight, be active and do not smoke.
Functional spreads containing plant stanols or sterols also help to lower blood cholesterol.
Foods high in saturated fat are energy-dense and raise blood LDL cholesterol. A diet high in them over years raises the risk of several diseases, and each has its own mechanism.
Obesity: saturated-fat foods are energy-dense, and surplus energy from them is stored as adipose tissue, which can lead to obesity.

Coronary heart disease and high blood pressure: raised LDL cholesterol narrows the arteries (atherosclerosis), increasing the risk of coronary heart disease, high blood pressure (hypertension) and stroke.
Type 2 diabetes: excess body fat reduces the effectiveness of insulin (the hormone that controls blood sugar), which is called insulin resistance, so the risk of Type 2 diabetes increases.
Gallstones: cholesterol is a main component of gallstones, which can form in the gall bladder.
Varicose veins and infertility are also linked to a high-fat diet; the first four effects carry the most weight.
Lifestyle changes recommended for someone at risk of CHD: a low-fat, low-cholesterol, low-salt diet; losing weight; not smoking; limiting alcohol; exercise; and managing stress.

Irish healthy eating guidelines from the Department of Health advise replacing saturated fats with unsaturated (mono- and polyunsaturated) fats and using fats and oils in small amounts, which is the fats, spreads and oils shelf of the Food Pyramid.
Other advice: choose lean meat and low-fat dairy, and grill, steam or bake instead of frying. Saturated fat should supply less than 10% of daily energy (HSE and Department of Health guidelines).
Energy is measured in kilojoules (kJ) or kilocalories (kcal). Fat has the highest energy value per gram of the three nutrients, which is why fatty foods are so energy-dense.

Fat provides 37 kJ or 9 kcal of energy per gram, which is more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate or protein. The true/false statement that 1 gram of fat provides 20 kilocalories is false.
Carbohydrate provides 16 kJ or 3.75 kcal per gram; protein provides 17 kJ or 4 kcal per gram; alcohol provides 29 kJ or 7 kcal per gram.
Energy from fat is calculated by multiplying the grams of fat by 37 kJ, or by 9 kcal.
Worked example (sample data): 20 g of fat gives 20 × 37 = 740 kJ, or 20 × 9 = 180 kcal.

A large part of the energy in the average Irish diet comes from fat, much of it hidden in processed and convenience foods, meat products, dairy, cakes, pastries, biscuits, chocolate, fried foods and takeaways, and much of that is saturated.

Guidance is to reduce total fat, especially saturated and trans fat, replacing them with unsaturated fat and complex carbohydrate. Over-consumption of fat leads to obesity because fat is energy-dense and stores readily.
Fats and oils are the most concentrated fat foods in the diet. Knowing what they supply, and what they leave out, explains how they should be used and chosen.

Fats and oils are almost pure fat, supplying 82–99.9% fat. Butter and margarine are about four-fifths fat or more and oils are almost pure fat, so the balance is mostly water in butter, margarine and spreads, and water varies inversely with fat.
They supply energy at 37 kJ or 9 kcal per gram, which is more than twice the energy in a gram of protein or carbohydrate, so a small amount of fat adds a lot of energy.

They supply fat-soluble vitamins (those that dissolve in fat, not water) and fatty acids. Butter has vitamins A and D naturally, vegetable oils supply vitamin E, and essential fatty acids (ones the body cannot make) come from plant oils.
Margarine and spreads are usually fortified with vitamins A and D, which are not naturally present in plant oils, so they match the vitamins that butter provides.
They supply little or no protein, carbohydrate, fibre or minerals. Butter and margarine contain traces of minerals such as calcium and sodium (from added salt).
Spreads contain water as well as fat, so a lower-fat spread contains more water than a butter or margarine of the same type.

The type of fat depends on its source. Animal fats (butter, lard, dripping) are saturated and raise LDL (the 'bad' cholesterol), olive oil is monounsaturated, and plant and nut oils are polyunsaturated.

Spreads and oils are eaten daily but in small amounts, yet much of the fat in the diet is hidden in processed, convenience and takeaway foods, meat products and dairy, so total fat intake is greater than the visible fats suggest.
In the Food Pyramid, fats, spreads and oils are used sparingly, choosing mono- or polyunsaturated types.
The three main commodities start from different raw materials. Butter comes from milk, oils from plants, and margarine from plant oils that are then hardened.
Butter is made by churning cream. The fat droplets clump together, the buttermilk is drained off, and the butter is worked and salted or left unsalted.
In the EU, butter is at least 80% and under 90% milk fat, with at most 16% water. It is an animal, saturated fat and a water-in-oil emulsion (tiny water droplets spread through the fat).

Oils are pressed or extracted from seeds, nuts and fruits such as olives, rapeseed and sunflower. They are then refined (cleaned, bleached and deodorised) to remove impurities, giving a bland oil with a higher smoke point (the temperature at which it starts to give off smoke).
Extra virgin olive oil is made from olives by mechanical pressing without chemical refining, so it keeps its flavour. It is used for dressing and gentle cooking.
Margarine and spreads are made from vegetable oils, and sometimes fish oils. Spreads are lower in fat than margarine and butter and contain more water.

The types on sale are butter, margarine, low-fat spreads, functional dairy spreads (cholesterol-lowering), blended spreads (butter with vegetable oil), oils (olive, rapeseed, sunflower, vegetable), lard, suet, dripping and cooking fat.
The right fat depends on what it is for, what the label says and your health needs. Reading the label first makes each choice easier.
Read the label for the type of fat, ingredients, energy per 100 g, total fat, saturates, salt, additives and allergens (milk, soya).
The ingredients list shows the largest ingredient first, so a spread listing water or vegetable oil first contains mainly those.
Choose by health: more mono- and polyunsaturated fat and less saturated fat. Olive or rapeseed oil are healthier choices, and low-fat or functional spreads suit people watching weight or cholesterol.

Choose spreads with few hydrogenated fats in the ingredients list when reducing trans fat (a fat formed during hydrogenation that is harmful to the heart) in the diet, and avoid partially hydrogenated fats.
Choose by use. Oils have higher smoke points than butter, so oils suit frying and butter suits spreading and baking.

Hard margarine or block fat suits pastry and creaming because it is plastic (firm yet workable) at room temperature. Low-fat spreads are unsuitable for cooking and baking because of their high water content.
Other factors are cost, taste, dietary needs (dairy-free, vegan, allergy), brand, packaging, shelf life, organic, and whether it is Irish (the Bord Bia quality mark).
Fats spoil in two ways, which is why storage advice differs. Air, light and heat make fats go rancid, while fat also soaks up smells from other foods.
Rancidity (the off smell and taste of spoiled fat) is the main storage problem. Oxidative rancidity is caused by air, light and heat, and hydrolytic rancidity by water breaking down the fat.
Store fats and oils in dark or opaque, airtight containers in a cool place, away from light and heat, to limit oxidative rancidity. Buy sensible quantities and use them before the date.
Store butter and spreads in the refrigerator, with a cover or in the original wrapper or tub, because fats absorb strong odours such as onion and fish. Freeze butter for longer storage.
Store nuts and seeds in airtight containers in a cool place, because their oils go rancid quickly.
Oily fish and fatty meat are stored in the fridge and used promptly, or frozen.
Keep used frying oil covered and strain it, so food particles do not speed up its breakdown. Do not top up old oil, and discard it when it is dark, smokes at a low temperature or foams.
Foods that contain fat, such as pastries, cakes, biscuits, crisps, nuts and whole-grain flours, are kept in airtight tins or packs.
How fat is handled in the kitchen changes both the energy in a dish and how it turns out. Some methods add almost no fat, while others depend on it for texture.

Methods that add little or no fat are grilling, steaming, poaching, microwaving and baking on a rack. Trimming visible fat from meat before cooking reduces the fat in the finished dish, as does removing skin, using a non-stick pan and cutting the fat in recipes.
Frying adds fat and therefore energy, because the food absorbs fat. Shallow frying uses a little fat and transfers heat evenly to food, giving it a golden colour.
Deep-fat frying in a deep pan at the correct, controlled temperature limits the amount of oil that food absorbs. Do not overheat the oil, and drain the food on absorbent paper.
Creaming butter or margarine with sugar traps air in the mixture, giving cakes a light texture.
Rubbing fat into flour makes shortcrust pastry. The fat coats the flour proteins and limits gluten, which shortens the pastry. Fat is layered in flaky and puff pastry.

Fat is also used for frying and roasting (heat transfer and browning), greasing tins, emulsions such as mayonnaise, hollandaise and dressings, roux and sauces, and for flavour, richness and moistness.
Fat from roasted meat collects in the tin and can be strained and used as dripping for frying.
Heat changes fat, and not always for the better. Knowing what happens when fat is overheated, and how manufacturers process fats, explains the safety rules and the labels.
Fat melts when heated, but overheating breaks it down (its smoke point is reached and acrolein, an irritant, forms). Repeated heating lowers the smoke point and produces off flavours.
Fat that reaches flash point (the temperature at which it ignites) can catch fire, so never leave a deep-fat fryer unattended.

Processing includes refining, hydrogenation (turning oil into fat), blending, emulsifying, and adding vitamins and colour. Hydrogenation can form trans fatty acids, and the EU limit is 2 g per 100 g of fat.
Margarine is made by turning liquid vegetable oil into a spreadable solid fat and mixing it with a water phase. The stages must be written in order.
1. Extract the oil from seeds such as sunflower, rapeseed, soya or palm, then refine it to remove impurities.

2. Hydrogenate it. Hydrogen gas is passed through the heated oil in the presence of a nickel catalyst (a substance that speeds up the reaction), which adds hydrogen at the double bonds and makes the liquid oil a semi-solid fat. The catalyst is then removed.
3. Blend the hydrogenated fat with other oils to give the texture (plasticity) and spreadability needed.
4. Prepare the water phase from water or skimmed milk, salt, colour (carotene), flavour and vitamins A and D. Lecithin is added as an emulsifier, which keeps the fat and water from separating.
5. Emulsify by mixing the fat and water phases, with churning, to form a stable water-in-oil emulsion.
6. Chill rapidly in a votator, a scraped-surface heat exchanger, while working the mixture so that a plastic, spreadable fat forms.
7. Weigh the margarine and pack it in foil-wrapped blocks or plastic tubs. An airtight, light-proof pack protects the fat from oxidation and absorbed smells.
The label tells shoppers what is in the pack and how to store it, and the law sets out what it must show.
The label gives the name and type (margarine or spread), and lists the ingredients in descending order by weight with allergens such as milk and soya highlighted.

It also gives a nutrition declaration per 100 g (energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein, salt), the net quantity, a date mark (best before) and storage instructions, the manufacturer's name and address, and the country of origin and batch (lot) code.

In Ireland, food labelling follows Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 as given effect by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014, with the FSAI giving guidance on food safety and labelling.
Low-fat spreads and functional spreads are different products for different needs. One lowers the fat in the diet, and the other lowers blood cholesterol.
Low-fat spreads have about half the fat of butter and more water, so they are lower in energy and suit a calorie-controlled diet.
Low-fat spreads are made from vegetable oils, water and milk proteins, and are low in saturated fat and high in unsaturated fat.
Low-fat spreads are suitable for spreading on bread but unsuitable for frying or baking because of their high water content.

Functional dairy spreads contain added plant stanol or sterol esters, which block the absorption of cholesterol in the small intestine so that more is excreted. Examples are Benecol (plant stanol ester) and Flora pro.activ (plant sterol).
Functional dairy spreads are made from vegetable oil, buttermilk, plant stanol or sterol ester, water and salt. They contain no hydrogenated fat and virtually no trans fatty acids.
The cholesterol-lowering effect depends on eating the spread regularly as part of a healthy diet, and it lowers blood (LDL) cholesterol.
Data questions give the nutrition figures for several spreads and ask you to judge them. The method is to compare the figures, match them to dietary advice and give a verdict.
Compare the energy value per 100 g or per serving of each spread.
Compare total fat, saturated fat, monounsaturated fat and polyunsaturated fat, and the salt content (and omega-3 where it is given) for each spread.
Lower energy and lower total fat suit weight control, and lower saturated fat reduces the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD).
Higher monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fat, and a lower saturated fat content, suit a diet aimed at protecting the heart. Lower salt suits blood pressure.
Check the water content and whether the spread is suitable for frying or baking.
Compare butter, a spread and a light spread, and state the fat content differences. A lower fat content follows from a higher water content.
Reach a verdict for each product, such as suiting weight reduction or CHD risk reduction, and give a reason for each judgement that refers to the figures.
Vitamins are organic compounds that the body needs in very small amounts. They are grouped by what they dissolve in, and that one difference decides how they are absorbed, stored and lost.
Vitamins are needed for normal growth, health and chemical reactions in the body. The body cannot make enough of most of them, so they must come from food.
There are two classes: fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) and water-soluble vitamins (the B group and C). For example, vitamin A is fat-soluble and vitamin C is water-soluble.

RDA (recommended dietary allowance) is the daily amount that meets the needs of almost everyone in a group. It differs with age, sex, pregnancy and breastfeeding, because needs change at different life stages.
Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat, so they are absorbed together with dietary fat. This also explains why they are stored in the body and why too much can be harmful.
Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed in the small intestine along with dietary fats and are carried in the lymphatic system (the body's drainage network) before entering the blood.
Because they need fat to be absorbed, a diet very low in fat, or a condition that stops fat being absorbed, can reduce vitamin intake.
The liver and fatty (adipose) tissue store fat-soluble vitamins, so the body keeps a reserve between meals and deficiency develops slowly.
Because they are stored, excess intake from supplements or large amounts of liver can build up to toxic levels (toxicity). Water-soluble vitamins are mostly excreted in urine instead.
Excess vitamin A (retinol) is harmful in pregnancy because it can harm the developing baby, so high-dose vitamin A supplements and large amounts of liver are avoided during pregnancy.
Vitamin A comes in two forms: one ready-made in animal foods and one made from a plant pigment. Its main jobs are vision, healthy surface tissues and protection of cells.

Retinol is the active, ready-made (preformed) form of vitamin A, found only in animal foods: liver, fish liver oils, oily fish, dairy products (butter, full-fat milk and cheese), eggs and fortified margarine (margarine with vitamin A added).
Beta-carotene is a plant pigment and a provitamin (a substance the body converts into a vitamin). The body converts it into retinol in the intestine, so beta-carotene is not itself vitamin A.

Good beta-carotene sources include carrots, sweet potatoes, apricots, mango, red and orange peppers, tomatoes and dark green leafy vegetables such as spinach and kale, where the green hides the orange pigment.
Retinol combines with the protein opsin to form rhodopsin (visual purple), the light-sensitive pigment in the rod cells of the retina. This allows vision in dim light.
Vitamin A keeps the cells lining the eyes, mouth, respiratory tract, urinary tract and skin healthy and moist, which protects them against infection.
Vitamin A supports growth, cell repair and a healthy immune system.
Beta-carotene acts as an antioxidant, neutralising free radicals (unstable molecules that damage cells).
Without enough vitamin A, the eye pigment cannot be rebuilt and the body's moist surface linings break down. The eyes show the first signs.
Night blindness is the earliest sign: poor vision in dim light because rhodopsin is not regenerated.
Xerophthalmia: the eyes become dry and damaged, and in severe cases the cornea (the clear front of the eye) is destroyed and blindness follows.
Dry, rough skin and dry, brittle hair, because the skin and other surface tissues are no longer kept healthy and moist.
Poor growth, because vitamin A supports growth.
Lowered resistance to infection, because the mucous membranes (moist linings) dry out, crack and lose their protective role.
In severe cases deficiency causes blindness.

Vitamin D is unusual because the body can make it in the skin when sunlight falls on it, which is why it is called the sunshine vitamin. It is the vitamin that lets the body use calcium to build bones and teeth.
Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) forms in the skin when ultraviolet B from sunlight acts on a cholesterol derivative in the skin. It is also found in animal foods.
Ergocalciferol (vitamin D2) is the plant and fungal form, made when mushrooms and yeast are exposed to ultraviolet light.
Dietary sources include oily fish such as salmon, mackerel, sardines and herring, egg yolk, liver, butter, fortified margarine and spreads, fortified milk and some fortified breakfast cereals.
Vitamin D increases the absorption of calcium and phosphorus from the small intestine, which is why it is the vitamin needed to absorb calcium.
Vitamin D raises blood calcium levels, working with parathormone (the parathyroid hormone) when blood calcium falls, so blood calcium stays at the right level.
Vitamin D supports the mineralisation of bones (the deposit of calcium and phosphorus that hardens them) and the formation of teeth, so it builds and maintains strong bones and teeth.
In Ireland, weak winter sunlight means that dietary sources of vitamin D matter most in the winter months. People who cover up, stay indoors or have dark skin also make less.
Low vitamin D means too little calcium reaches the bones, so they stay soft. The condition has a different name in children and in adults.
Rickets in children: bones soften and bend, causing bow legs, delayed growth and poor tooth formation.
Osteomalacia in adults: bones become soft, weak and painful, and fractures can occur, because they are not properly mineralised.
Low vitamin D lowers calcium absorption, which is a contributing factor in osteoporosis, where bone density falls, and in dental decay.
Vitamin E is the fat-soluble vitamin whose main job is as an antioxidant: it stops oxidation damaging fatty parts of the body's cells.
Tocopherols are the active forms of vitamin E. Alpha-tocopherol is the form the human body uses most, and the main form in the body.
Rich sources are vegetable oils such as sunflower, wheatgerm and olive oil, nuts and seeds such as almonds and sunflower seeds, wholegrain cereals, avocado, green leafy vegetables and egg yolk.
Vitamin E is an antioxidant that protects the membranes of cells and polyunsaturated fatty acids from oxidation (damage by free radicals).
Vitamin E also helps protect the vitamin A and vitamin C in the body, and supports healthy skin and immune function.
Deficiency is rare in healthy people. In people who cannot absorb fat, and in premature babies, it can cause nerve and muscle damage and the early breakdown of red blood cells (a form of anaemia).
Vitamin K is the clotting vitamin: the K comes from the German word for coagulation. It has two forms, one from plants and one made by bacteria in the gut.
Vitamin K1 (phylloquinone) comes from plants: green leafy vegetables such as spinach, broccoli, cabbage, kale and sprouts, and vegetable oils and liver.
Vitamin K2 (menaquinones) is made by bacteria in the large intestine and is also found in dairy products, eggs and meat. The gut bacteria are therefore a second source.
The liver needs vitamin K to make the clotting factors, including prothrombin, that allow blood to clot. This is its primary function.
Vitamin K activates osteocalcin, a protein that binds calcium into bone, so it supports bone formation.
Deficiency impairs blood clotting, causing bleeding and easy bruising. Long courses of antibiotics or poor fat absorption can also reduce vitamin K.

The HSE offers every newborn baby a vitamin K injection within hours of birth, because their gut bacteria are not yet established and they have low stores, so they risk bleeding. It is the parents' choice.
All four fat-soluble vitamins dissolve in fat and not in water, but they differ in what destroys them: heat, oxygen, light or alkalis. Knowing this explains how storage and cooking affect each one.
Vitamin A is insoluble in water but soluble in fats and organic solvents.
Vitamin A is heat-stable in normal cooking but is destroyed by prolonged high temperatures.
Vitamin A is destroyed by oxygen (it is oxidised), so foods kept exposed to air lose it.
Vitamin D is insoluble in water and is relatively heat-stable in normal cooking and storage, so cooking oily fish loses little.
Vitamin E is insoluble in water and heat-stable in normal cooking, but it is destroyed by oxidation, including by rancid fats, by light and air, and by frying at high temperature for long periods.
Vitamin K is insoluble in water and heat-stable in normal cooking.
Vitamin K is destroyed by light (ultraviolet) and by alkalis.
To judge how good a food is as a source of vitamins, use food composition tables and food labels, and think about whether the food is fresh, processed or fortified.
Food composition tables give the vitamin content of foods, usually per 100 g, so fresh and processed foods can be compared on the same basis (like for like).

The mandatory nutrition declaration on a food label lists energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt, under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011. Vitamins appear only when added or when a claim is made, so not listing vitamins does not mean the food has none.
Where vitamins are listed, the label states the amount per 100 g (or per serving) and as a percentage of the reference intake.

In Ireland, the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014 give effect to Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011. The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) advises on food labelling and nutrition in Ireland.
Fortified foods have vitamins added that the natural food does not contain, or that were lost in processing. Examples are margarine with added vitamins A and D and fortified breakfast cereals.
Fresh produce loses vitamin C in storage, while frozen vegetables, blanched before freezing, usually retain more vitamin C than long-stored fresh vegetables.
Canning and prolonged cooking destroy heat-sensitive vitamins, so a processed food may contain less of a vitamin than its fresh form.

Vitamin C, vitamin B12 and folate are water-soluble vitamins, so they behave differently from vitamins that dissolve in fat. Knowing this explains why they are needed every day and why cooking can ruin them.
Water-soluble vitamins (the B group and C) dissolve in water and are not stored in useful amounts in the body. Any excess is lost in urine, so they are needed regularly in the diet.
The exception is vitamin B12, which the liver stores, so a store builds up that can last for several years.
Because they dissolve in water, these vitamins are lost into cooking water and are easily destroyed during storage, preparation and cooking.

The RDA (recommended daily allowance) is the daily amount of a nutrient that meets the needs of almost everyone in a group. It varies with age, sex, pregnancy and breastfeeding, and smokers are advised more vitamin C.
Vitamin C is the most-asked vitamin in the exam, and it comes mainly from fruit and vegetables. Fresh, raw and in-season produce has the most.
Citrus fruit (oranges, lemons, grapefruit), blackcurrants, rosehips, kiwi fruit and strawberries are rich sources of vitamin C.
Peppers, broccoli, sprouts, cabbage, tomatoes, new potatoes and peas are good vegetable sources.
Fresh fruit juices and smoothies, and fortified drinks, also supply vitamin C, and a supplement can too. Any fruit or vegetable is accepted as a source in an answer.
Vitamin C does several different jobs in the body, and exam questions usually ask for two or three of them. The key one is collagen, because so many other effects follow from it.
Vitamin C is needed to make collagen, the protein of connective tissue that gives strength to skin, blood vessels, gums, cartilage, bones and teeth.
By supporting collagen formation, vitamin C speeds up the healing of wounds, because new tissue can be built.
Vitamin C aids iron absorption. It converts non-haem iron (the iron in plant foods) from the ferric form (Fe³⁺) to the ferrous form (Fe²⁺), which is absorbed more readily.
Vitamin C also aids calcium absorption, which marking schemes accept.
Vitamin C is an antioxidant: it neutralises free radicals (damaging particles) and so protects cells from damage.
Vitamin C supports the immune system, helping the body resist infection, and it prevents scurvy.
If the diet lacks vitamin C for a long time, collagen cannot be made properly and the body's tissues start to fail. The deficiency disease is scurvy.
Scurvy develops after a severe and prolonged lack of vitamin C in the diet.
Weak collagen causes bleeding, sore and swollen gums, loose teeth, easy bruising and painful joints.
Wounds heal slowly because new tissue cannot be formed properly.
Reduced iron absorption can lead to anaemia, with tiredness and pale skin.
The body becomes more susceptible to infection because its resistance is lowered.
Vitamin C is easily lost, but the loss depends on method and time. Cooking does not destroy all of it: steaming, microwaving and short cooking keep most.
Buy fresh produce and use it quickly, and eat it raw where possible.
Wash vegetables before cutting rather than soaking them, prepare them just before cooking and cut them in large pieces, so less of the surface is exposed.
Cook in a little boiling water for a short time with the lid on, or steam, microwave or stir-fry, so less vitamin C dissolves or is destroyed.
Do not use bicarbonate of soda or copper pans, which destroy the vitamin.
Serve at once rather than keeping the food hot, and use the cooking water in soups and sauces to recover the vitamin that dissolved into it.
Ascorbic acid is a very unstable vitamin, and its properties explain every rule for keeping it in food. Higher Level answers on vitamin C add these properties to sources, functions and deficiency.
Vitamin C is a white, crystalline, acidic substance with a sweet-sour taste, and it is very soluble in water.
Because it is water-soluble, vitamin C is lost into cooking water when vegetables are boiled or soaked.
Vitamin C is destroyed by prolonged heat, by light, by alkalis such as bicarbonate of soda, and by oxidation in air.
The enzyme oxidase is released when plant cells are cut or bruised and destroys vitamin C, so cut vegetables should be cooked promptly.
Copper and brass pans destroy vitamin C, and it is also lost during long storage and dehydration.
Vitamin C is an antioxidant, which means it acts as a reducing agent (it donates electrons), and this is how it changes ferric iron to ferrous iron.
Vitamin B12 is unusual because only animal foods contain it naturally. Its absorption also needs a helper made in the stomach.
Vitamin B12 occurs naturally only in animal foods: liver and kidney, meat, fish and oily fish, eggs, milk, cheese and yoghurt.
Plant foods contain no natural vitamin B12, so vegans rely on fortified foods such as some breakfast cereals, plant milks and yeast extract, or on supplements.
The lining of the stomach makes intrinsic factor, a protein that binds vitamin B12 so that it can be absorbed in the ileum (the end of the small intestine).
The liver stores vitamin B12, and the store can last for several years, so deficiency develops slowly.
B12 is needed wherever cells are being made or nerves are working, which is why its deficiency affects both the blood and the nervous system.
Vitamin B12 works with folate to form healthy red blood cells.
Vitamin B12 is needed for the synthesis of DNA, so it is needed for cell division, especially in cells that divide rapidly.
Vitamin B12 maintains the myelin sheath, the fatty layer that insulates nerve fibres and keeps nerve impulses working normally, so it keeps nerve cells healthy.
Vitamin B12 is also involved in the body's use of fatty acids and amino acids.
A lack of B12 harms both the blood and the nerves. The cause can be the diet or a failure to absorb the vitamin.
B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia, in which red blood cells are too large and immature and cannot carry oxygen effectively.
Symptoms of this anaemia include tiredness, weakness, pale skin and breathlessness.
Nerve damage causes numbness and tingling in the hands and feet, poor balance and memory problems.
A strict vegan diet without fortified foods or supplements can cause deficiency.
Pernicious anaemia is the form of B12 deficiency caused by a lack of intrinsic factor, often through an autoimmune condition, which prevents B12 absorption even when the diet is adequate.
Failure to absorb B12 can also come from stomach or gut disease, and older people absorb less.
B12 is more stable than vitamin C, but it is not indestructible.
Vitamin B12 is water-soluble, so some is lost into cooking water.
Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline compound that contains the mineral cobalt, which gives it the name cobalamin.
Vitamin B12 is stable to heat in ordinary cooking but is destroyed by light and by strong acids and alkalis.
Folate is the natural form of vitamin B9, and folic acid is the synthetic form. Folate is needed for making new cells, which matters most in early pregnancy.

Natural folate is found in dark green leafy vegetables such as spinach, broccoli, sprouts and cabbage, in pulses such as chickpeas, lentils and beans, and in asparagus, oranges, liver and yeast extract.
Wholegrain and fortified breakfast cereals also supply folate.
Folic acid is the synthetic form used in supplements and in fortified foods such as breakfast cereals. It is not a different vitamin from folate.
Folate is needed to synthesise DNA and RNA, so it is essential for cell division and growth, including the growth of the foetus.
Folate works with vitamin B12 to form red blood cells.

In the first weeks of pregnancy, folate is essential for the formation of the neural tube, the early brain and spinal cord, and it protects against neural tube defects such as spina bifida and anencephaly.
The neural tube forms in the first weeks of pregnancy, before many women know they are pregnant, so folate advice is aimed at women before they conceive.
A lack of folate causes megaloblastic anaemia, with the same large, immature red blood cells as B12 deficiency, and tiredness, weakness, pale skin, breathlessness and a sore tongue.
Neural tube defects, such as spina bifida and anencephaly, can develop in the unborn baby if the mother lacks folate in early pregnancy.
Poor growth is also an effect of folate deficiency.

Women who may become pregnant are advised, in HSE advice, to take a folic acid supplement before conception and during early pregnancy to reduce the risk of neural tube defects, as well as eating folate-rich foods.
Folate is fragile in the kitchen, which is why fortified foods use the more stable synthetic form.
Folate is water-soluble and is sensitive to heat, light and oxygen, so it is destroyed by prolonged cooking and storage.
Folate is lost into cooking water during prolonged boiling.
Synthetic folic acid is more stable than natural folate, which is why it is used in fortification.

The B-complex is a family of separate water-soluble vitamins that often occur together in the same foods. They are named by number or by name, and between them they keep energy release, nerves, skin and blood working.
The family includes B1 (thiamine), B2 (riboflavin), B3 (niacin) and B6 (pyridoxine), plus folate and B12, which also belong to the B complex.

The B-complex vitamins act mainly as coenzymes (helpers that enzymes need in order to work), helping the enzymes that release energy from carbohydrate, fat and protein. They also keep the nervous system, skin and red blood cells healthy.
The B vitamins do not supply energy themselves. The energy comes from the carbohydrate, fat and protein in food, and the vitamins only help release it.

The B-complex vitamins are water-soluble, so any excess is excreted in urine. Most are not stored in the body in useful amounts, so they must be supplied daily in the diet. B12 is the exception, as it is stored in the liver.
Because they dissolve in water, B vitamins are also lost into cooking water and during storage.
Wholegrain cereals, meat, pulses and fortified breakfast cereals are the main dietary sources. Fish, eggs, milk and dairy, nuts, yeast extract and green vegetables also contribute.
White flour and polished rice lose much of their B vitamins in milling (grinding and refining the grain), whereas wholegrain products keep them.

The RDA (recommended daily allowance) is the amount that meets the needs of almost everyone. B vitamin needs rise with energy intake, especially thiamine and niacin, which are closely linked to energy release.
Thiamine is the B vitamin most closely tied to carbohydrate, so the more carbohydrate a person eats, the more thiamine they need. Without it the nerves, muscles and heart suffer.
Thiamine sources include wholegrain cereals and wholemeal bread, fortified breakfast cereals, pork and bacon, liver, pulses (peas, beans, lentils), nuts, yeast extract, eggs and potatoes.
Thiamine acts as a coenzyme that helps release energy from carbohydrate, so the need for it rises with carbohydrate intake.
Thiamine is needed for normal nerve function and keeps the muscles, including the heart, healthy. It also supports appetite.
Beriberi (beri-beri) is the thiamine deficiency disease, with loss of appetite, fatigue, weakness, muscle wasting, depression, irritability and memory loss.
Dry beriberi damages the nerves, causing tingling, numbness, pain, weakness and paralysis. Wet beriberi affects the heart, causing heart failure and swelling (oedema).
Heavy drinkers are at risk of deficiency because heavy alcohol use reduces the absorption of thiamine and the diet is often poor. This can lead to confusion and memory problems.
Riboflavin helps release energy from all three energy nutrients and protects the surfaces of the body, such as the skin, mouth and eyes. Its deficiency shows up mostly in these places.

Riboflavin sources include milk and dairy products (the largest contribution in many diets), eggs, liver and kidney, lean meat, yeast extract, green leafy vegetables, mushrooms and fortified breakfast cereals.
Riboflavin helps release energy from carbohydrate, fat and protein.
Riboflavin helps maintain healthy skin, eyes and mucous membranes (the moist linings of the mouth and other body passages), and it helps growth.
A deficiency causes sore, cracked lips and cracks and soreness at the corners of the mouth, known as angular cheilitis (also called cheilosis or angular stomatitis).
A deficiency also causes a sore, red, smooth, inflamed tongue and skin disorders, such as greasy, scaly skin around the nose.
Deficiency also causes sore eyes that are sensitive to light, and slow growth in children.
Niacin, also called nicotinic acid, is unusual because the body can make some of its own. It helps release energy and keeps three body systems healthy.
Niacin sources include meat (especially liver and poultry), fish, peanuts and other nuts, wholegrain cereals, pulses, mushrooms, eggs, milk, fortified cereals and yeast extract.
The body can make niacin from the amino acid tryptophan, found in protein foods such as milk and eggs. This is why milk and eggs prevent deficiency even though they contain little niacin.
Niacin helps release energy from carbohydrate, fat and protein in the cells.
Niacin keeps the skin, nervous system and digestive system healthy.
Deficiency causes pellagra, remembered as the four Ds: dermatitis (a skin rash in areas exposed to sunlight), diarrhoea, dementia (confusion and memory loss) and, if untreated, death.
Deficiency may also bring tiredness, weight loss and irritability. Pellagra was historically found where maize was the main food.
Pyridoxine is the B vitamin of protein use. It lets the body handle amino acids, build haemoglobin and make the chemicals nerves use to communicate.
Pyridoxine sources include chicken, turkey, pork, fish such as tuna and salmon, liver, eggs, potatoes, bananas, pulses, wholegrain cereals, nuts and fortified breakfast cereals.
Pyridoxine is needed for the breakdown and use (metabolism) of amino acids, so it is central to protein metabolism and growth.
Pyridoxine helps the body form haemoglobin in red blood cells, which is why deficiency can cause anaemia.
Pyridoxine takes part in making neurotransmitters, the chemicals that carry messages between nerve cells, so it supports the nervous system.
Deficiency is rare. It causes skin rashes around the mouth and nose, a sore mouth, confusion, depression, irritability, anaemia, and tingling in the hands and feet.
Exams often give a list of conditions and ask which vitamin is lacking in each. These pairs are worth learning as one set.
Night blindness is vitamin A, rickets is vitamin D and scurvy is vitamin C.
Beri-beri is vitamin B1 (thiamine) and pellagra is niacin (B3).
Neural tube defects are linked to folic acid. Megaloblastic anaemia is B12 (or folate) deficiency, and pernicious anaemia is B12 deficiency caused by a lack of intrinsic factor.

Being water-soluble, most B vitamins are lost into cooking water, and most are also sensitive to heat, light, alkalis or oxidation. Each vitamin has its own main weakness, and niacin and riboflavin are the more stable ones.

Thiamine is destroyed by alkalis (such as bicarbonate of soda) and by prolonged heat, and it is lost into cooking water. It is also destroyed by sulphur dioxide (sulphites) used as a preservative, but it is stable in acid conditions.

Riboflavin is destroyed by light (ultraviolet) and by alkalis, which is why milk in clear bottles loses riboflavin and is better stored in cartons or opaque bottles. Some is also lost in cooking water.
Riboflavin is heat-stable and acid-stable in normal cooking, and it gives a yellow-green colour to solutions that contain it, such as the yellow of some foods and urine.
Niacin is the most stable of the B vitamins. It is stable to heat, light, air, acid and alkali, so little is lost in normal cooking.
Niacin is soluble in water and can be lost into cooking water if the food is boiled and drained.

Pyridoxine is sensitive to light and alkali, and it is lost into cooking water. It is stable in acid conditions and fairly stable to heat in ordinary cooking, but is lost in the processing and milling of cereals.
Minerals are the part of food that is not made by living things at all. The body needs them in small amounts to build structures, run processes and make enzymes and hormones.

Minerals are inorganic elements (not made by living things) that the body cannot make, so they must be obtained from food. They build body structures, regulate body processes and form parts of enzymes and hormones.
Major (macro) minerals are needed in larger amounts, above 100 mg a day. They are calcium, phosphorus, potassium, sodium, chloride, magnesium and sulphur.

Minerals are not destroyed by cooking, because they are elements. They can, however, be lost into cooking water and in the trimming of food. For example, boiling vegetables in a lot of water washes minerals out.
The RDA (recommended daily amount) is the daily intake that meets the needs of almost everyone in a group. It differs with age, sex, pregnancy and breastfeeding, so some groups need more than others.

Phosphorus works with calcium to harden bones and teeth and forms part of ATP (the cell's energy carrier) and cell membranes. Sources are milk, cheese, meat, fish, eggs, wholegrains and nuts, and deficiency is rare.
Calcium is the most important mineral for the skeleton, but it also keeps blood, muscles and nerves working. Because bone is built in childhood and lost in later life, some groups need more of it.
Milk, cheese and yoghurt are the richest dietary sources of calcium. This is why dairy foods matter for bone health.

Canned sardines and canned salmon eaten with their bones, green leafy vegetables such as kale, broccoli and cabbage, calcium-set tofu, fortified plant milks and fortified breakfast cereals are further sources.
Calcium works with phosphorus to form the mineral salts that give bones and teeth their hardness. This is why a diet low in calcium leaves bones weak.
Calcium is needed for blood clotting, normal muscle contraction (including the heartbeat) and nerve impulse transmission. It also activates some enzymes and helps regulate blood pressure.
Rickets in children (soft, bent bones and poor teeth) and osteomalacia in adults result from too little calcium, phosphorus or vitamin D.

Osteoporosis, which develops over years, makes bones thin, porous, brittle and prone to fracture, with loss of height and a stooped back. Other effects of low calcium are tooth decay, slow clotting, and muscle cramps (tetany) and poor nerve function.
Osteoporosis risk is raised by low calcium and vitamin D intake, lack of weight-bearing exercise, smoking, alcohol, the fall in oestrogen after menopause and family history.

Need is highest when bone is being built (childhood, teenage years, pregnancy, breastfeeding) and when it is lost (women after menopause). Bone density peaks in the late teens and twenties, so teenage intake matters.
Iron is needed to carry oxygen, so a shortage leaves the whole body short of energy. It comes in two forms, and the form decides how easily the body absorbs it.
Haem iron comes from animal foods and is absorbed easily. Sources are red meat, liver and offal, kidney, black pudding, poultry and oily fish.

Non-haem iron comes from plant foods and eggs and is absorbed less easily. Sources are eggs, wholegrain and fortified cereals, wholemeal bread, pulses, dark green leafy vegetables, dried apricots and other dried fruit, nuts and seeds.
Iron is an essential part of haemoglobin, the red protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs around the body to all cells.

Iron is part of myoglobin, which stores oxygen in muscle cells, and part of enzymes that release energy from food. It also supports immunity and concentration. This is why a shortage leaves people tired.

Iron deficiency causes anaemia (too few red blood cells or too little haemoglobin). Effects are tiredness, pale skin, breathlessness, dizziness, irritability, poor concentration, feeling cold and reduced resistance to infection.
Causes of iron deficiency are a diet low in iron or poor in vitamin C, blood loss (menstruation, ulcers, operations), high needs in growth spurts, pregnancy and infancy, and poor absorption.

Corrective measures are eating more iron-rich foods together with vitamin C, avoiding tea with meals, and taking an iron supplement on medical advice. This is because vitamin C improves absorption and tea blocks it.

Groups at risk are teenage girls, menstruating and pregnant women, infants and toddlers, people with heavy blood loss, and vegetarians and vegans, who eat only non-haem iron. Children are at risk because of fast growth and low-iron foods. For example, vegetarians miss out on the more easily absorbed haem form.
Trace minerals are needed in only tiny amounts, yet the body cannot do without them. Each has a job that no other mineral can do.

Trace (micro) minerals are needed in only tiny amounts, measured in milligrams or micrograms a day, and the diet must supply them. They are tiny in amount yet essential. For example, zinc and iodine are needed in milligrams or micrograms.
The trace minerals are iron, zinc, iodine, fluoride, copper, selenium, manganese, chromium and cobalt. Iron is a trace mineral by the amount needed, but it is studied in detail at Ordinary Level.
Iron, zinc and iodine each play a specific role in the body that the other minerals cannot replace. Zinc and iodine are set out in the blocks that follow.
Zinc is a trace mineral that works inside enzymes, so it affects growth, healing and defence against infection.
Zinc sources include oysters and other shellfish, red meat, poultry, liver, dairy products, eggs, wholegrain cereals, pulses, nuts and seeds.
Zinc is a component of many enzymes and supports growth and cell division, which is why a shortage slows growth in children.
Zinc supports wound healing and a healthy immune system. This is because new cells must be made to repair the wound.
Zinc contributes to a normal sense of taste and smell, and to healthy skin and hair and reproductive health.
Deficiency causes poor growth, delayed wound healing, dry flaky skin and rashes, loss of taste and appetite, reduced immunity and hair loss.
Iodine is needed to make a hormone that sets the body's pace. Without it the thyroid gland cannot do its job.
Iodine sources include sea fish and shellfish, seaweed, milk and dairy products and eggs. Iodised salt also exists as a source.
Iodine is part of thyroxine, the hormone from the thyroid gland that controls the rate of metabolism (and growth and brain development).
