Deficiency causes goitre, a swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck as it works harder to make more thyroxine. This is because the gland enlarges as it works harder.
Iodine deficiency causes tiredness and sluggishness (lethargy) and weight gain in adults. It causes delayed mental and physical development in children, and in babies of deficient mothers.
Potassium and sodium work as a pair, one inside cells and one outside, to keep fluid, nerves and muscles balanced.
Potassium sources include bananas, potatoes eaten in their skins, tomatoes, dried fruit, orange juice, pulses, green and leafy vegetables, milk, meat, fish and nuts.
Potassium is the main positive ion (electrolyte) inside cells and, with sodium, helps regulate fluid balance in and around cells.
Potassium is needed to transmit nerve impulses and for muscle contraction, including the heartbeat. This is why a shortage causes cramps.
Potassium works with sodium to regulate blood pressure, and a high potassium intake helps lower it.
Deficiency (hypokalaemia) causes muscle weakness, cramps, an irregular heartbeat and tiredness. It is usually caused by severe vomiting, diarrhoea or some medicines rather than by normal diets.
Sodium is essential, and the problem in Ireland is eating too much of it, not too little. Most of it comes from salt, which is sodium chloride.

Sodium is mainly consumed as salt. Table salt, cured and smoked meats and fish such as bacon and ham, cheese, bread, crisps and snack foods, processed and ready meals, sauces, stock cubes and canned foods supply most of it.
Fresh, unprocessed foods contain only small amounts of naturally occurring sodium. This is why processed foods, such as bacon and ready meals, are the main source.
Sodium is the main positive ion (electrolyte) outside cells and, with potassium, regulates fluid balance and blood volume.
Sodium is needed to transmit nerve impulses, for muscle contraction and for enzyme function. It helps the small intestine absorb glucose and some amino acids. This is why a shortage causes cramps.

Excess sodium raises blood pressure (hypertension), which increases the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney problems. Most people in Ireland eat more salt than advised, mostly from processed foods.
To cut salt, cook from fresh food, do not add salt at the table, read labels (salt is on the nutrition declaration) and choose low-salt products.

The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) began a voluntary Salt Reduction Programme in 2003 to cut salt in processed food. Later reformulation work continues under the FSAI-Healthy Ireland Food Reformulation Task Force.
Deficiency is uncommon but causes muscle cramps, headache, nausea and confusion. It can follow heavy sweating, vomiting or diarrhoea.

Absorption is the movement of digested nutrients from the small intestine into the blood. A food can contain plenty of a mineral yet give little of it, because the mineral must be soluble and in the right chemical form to cross the intestinal wall.
Most iron is absorbed in the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine, so this is where the factors that help or block iron absorption do their work.
Absorbed iron binds to transferrin, a protein that carries it in the blood to where it is needed.

Surplus iron is stored in the liver as ferritin. The body has little ability to excrete iron, so absorption is regulated: the body absorbs more when stores are low, for example in pregnancy, growth or heavy blood loss.
Iron is lost in small amounts through sweat, shed skin cells and, in women, menstrual blood.
Iron in food comes in two forms that the body treats very differently. Which form a food contains decides how much iron you actually get from it.
Haem iron is the iron in haemoglobin and myoglobin, so it comes from animal foods such as red meat, liver, poultry and fish. It is already in the ferrous form (Fe²⁺), which is soluble.
Haem iron is absorbed more readily than non-haem iron, and its absorption is largely unaffected by other foods in the meal.
Non-haem iron comes from plant foods, pulses, wholegrain cereals, nuts, seeds, dark green vegetables and eggs.

Non-haem iron is in the ferric form (Fe³⁺), which is not very soluble, so it must be converted (reduced) to the ferrous form before the intestine can absorb it. This makes it poorly absorbed and strongly affected by other foods in the meal.
Eating meat, fish or poultry in the same meal as non-haem iron foods increases the absorption of non-haem iron, an effect known as the meat factor. Chilli with beans and beef is one example.
Vegetarians and vegans have only non-haem iron in their diet, so they need to be more careful, for example by including vitamin C at every meal.
Because non-haem iron is poorly absorbed, the other things in a meal can make a large difference. Some of them help turn ferric iron into the soluble ferrous form.
Vitamin C is a major enhancer of non-haem iron absorption. It acts as a reducing agent on the ferric iron in plant foods, changing it to the soluble ferrous form and keeping it soluble.
Hydrochloric acid in the stomach helps convert ferric iron to ferrous iron, aiding absorption. People with low stomach acid, or who take antacids, absorb less iron.
Eating vitamin C-rich fruit or vegetables with an iron-rich meal increases absorption, for example a glass of orange juice with lentils, peppers or tomatoes with a bean dish, or broccoli with meat.
Meat, fish or poultry in the same meal also raises non-haem iron absorption (the meat factor), and the body absorbs more iron when its stores are low.
Several substances in everyday foods and drinks bind iron in the gut and lock it into forms the body cannot absorb. This is why a meal that looks rich in iron may not deliver much.
Tannins (polyphenols) in tea, coffee and red wine bind iron into an insoluble compound, so these drinks should not be taken with an iron-rich meal. Leave a gap between the drink and the meal.

Phytates (phytic acid) in wholegrain cereals, bran and pulses bind iron, and also zinc and calcium, in an insoluble form, reducing absorption. Soaking, sprouting, yeast fermentation (as in bread) and cooking pulses reduce phytate.
Oxalates (oxalic acid) in spinach, rhubarb and beetroot greens bind iron, reducing its absorption. This is why spinach is a poor iron source despite its reputation.
Excess dietary fibre carries minerals through the gut and binds them, so less is absorbed.
Calcium from dairy products or supplements taken with a meal competes with iron for absorption.
Excess alcohol, a lack of stomach acid and some medicines such as antacids also reduce iron absorption, and very large amounts of protein or alcohol can upset iron and calcium balance.
Two vitamins matter most for absorbing these minerals, and each is linked to one mineral. Mixing them up is the commonest way to lose marks.
Vitamin C helps iron: it converts non-haem iron from the ferric form (Fe³⁺) to the ferrous form (Fe²⁺), which is absorbed more readily.
Vitamin C also aids the absorption of calcium.
Vitamin D helps calcium: it stimulates the production of a calcium-binding protein in the lining of the small intestine, so more calcium crosses into the blood.
Vitamin D increases the absorption of phosphorus, which must be present in a balanced ratio with calcium, and helps lay down calcium in bone.
Where vitamin D is lacking, calcium absorption falls even when dietary calcium is adequate, so bones weaken. Rickets and osteomalacia are the results.
Calcium has to stay dissolved to be absorbed, and the body also adjusts how much it takes in. Several nutrients and hormones push absorption up.
Vitamin D is the main vitamin that drives calcium absorption from the intestine.
Lactose, the sugar in milk, improves calcium absorption, which is one reason milk, cheese and yoghurt are good calcium sources.
An acidic environment in the stomach and the top of the small intestine keeps calcium soluble and easier to absorb. Vitamin C helps too.
Adequate protein provides amino acids that combine with calcium to make it more soluble, aiding absorption.
Phosphorus in a balanced ratio with calcium helps, because the two are needed together for bone.
Parathormone, the parathyroid hormone, raises blood calcium by increasing its absorption from food (through vitamin D activation) and its release from bone.
Oestrogen supports calcium absorption and retention in bone, so the fall in oestrogen after menopause increases the risk of osteoporosis.
Absorption is higher in childhood and pregnancy, and weight-bearing exercise and growth periods increase demand.

Some inhibitors lower how much calcium is absorbed from the gut, while others increase how much is lost from the body. Both are described as inhibiting calcium in marking schemes, so name the mechanism you mean.
Excess dietary fibre reduces calcium absorption by binding calcium and speeding it through the gut.
Excess fat in the diet reduces calcium absorption by binding to it in the intestine, forming insoluble calcium soaps with fatty acids.
Caffeine in tea and coffee increases the loss of calcium in urine.
Excess salt increases the loss of calcium in urine.
Alcohol reduces calcium absorption and increases its loss from the body.
Smoking and nicotine reduce calcium absorption and bone density.
Fizzy drinks containing phosphoric acid are listed as inhibitors, because excess phosphorus upsets the calcium balance.
Tannins in tea and coffee, a lack of stomach acid, falling oestrogen after menopause and old age, when the gut absorbs less, also lower calcium absorption.
Some plant foods that contain calcium also contain substances that lock it away. The calcium is present but the body cannot use it.

Phytic acid, found in the outer layers of cereal grains (bran, wholemeal), in pulses, nuts and seeds, binds calcium to form calcium phytate, an insoluble compound that the body cannot absorb and that passes out in the faeces.
Yeast and soaking break phytate down (using the enzyme phytase), so leavened wholemeal bread is less affected than unleavened.
Oxalic acid, found in spinach and rhubarb, binds calcium to form calcium oxalate, which is insoluble and not absorbed.
Because of its oxalate, the calcium in spinach is poorly absorbed, even though spinach contains calcium. The calcium in milk or kale is absorbed better.
Phytates and oxalates are most damaging when eaten in large amounts at the same meal as calcium-rich foods such as milk or cheese, and when the diet is otherwise low in calcium.

Practical advice: eat calcium foods at a different time from high-phytate or high-oxalate foods, use leavened bread, soak and cook pulses, and take vitamin D. Cooking only reduces phytate and oxalate in part, it does not remove them.
Phytates and oxalates also bind iron and zinc, but calcium is the main case here.

Digestion is the breakdown of large food molecules into small soluble ones that can pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood. It is chemical digestion, carried out by enzymes through a reaction called hydrolysis.
Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts, which means they speed up digestion without being used up.
Each enzyme has an active site (the part where the food molecule binds) whose shape fits one type of substrate (the molecule the enzyme acts on), so an enzyme acts on only one kind of molecule.
Enzymes lower the activation energy of a reaction (the energy needed to get it started), so digestion proceeds at body temperature, about 37 °C.

Each digestive enzyme has an optimum pH, the acidity at which it works best: pepsin works in strong acid, while pancreatic and intestinal enzymes work in the alkaline conditions of the small intestine.
Hydrolysis breaks a chemical bond by adding water: a hydrogen atom attaches to one part of the molecule and a hydroxyl group (–OH) to the other.
Protein is a chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, so proteases (also called proteinases), the enzymes that digest protein, work by hydrolysing these bonds.

As protein is digested the chains get shorter in this order: protein, then peptones (shorter chains), then peptides (shorter again), then amino acids. Only amino acids, and the very smallest peptides, are small enough to absorb.
Diagram: two amino acids joined by a peptide bond, with the water molecule added during hydrolysis labelled.
Examiners ask you to fill in this table, so learn each row as a set of five linked words. The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on and the product is what it is turned into.
Stomach: gastric juice; pepsin; protein; peptones.
Stomach of infants: gastric juice; rennin; caseinogen; casein.
Pancreas (its enzyme acts in the duodenum): pancreatic juice; trypsin (a proteinase); peptones; peptides.
Small intestine: intestinal juice; peptidases (also called erepsin); peptides; amino acids.
Protein digestion starts in the stomach, not the mouth. The stomach uses acid to prepare the protein and then an enzyme to start splitting it.
In the mouth no protein is digested, because saliva contains no protein-digesting enzyme. Chewing breaks food into pieces and so increases its surface area, but this is mechanical only.
Gastric glands in the stomach wall secrete gastric juice, which contains hydrochloric acid and the inactive enzyme pepsinogen.
Hydrochloric acid unfolds (denatures) the protein, exposing its peptide bonds to enzyme action. Acid also kills most bacteria in food.
Hydrochloric acid converts pepsinogen into the active enzyme pepsin, and also gives the acid pH of about 2 that pepsin works best at.
Pepsin hydrolyses protein into peptones, which are shorter chains than the original protein.
Protein-digesting enzymes are themselves proteins, so pepsinogen is made inactive and activated only in the stomach. This is why it does not digest the cells that make it.
Rennin, found in the stomach of infants, clots milk by changing the soluble milk protein caseinogen into insoluble casein (curds), so milk stays in the stomach long enough for pepsin to act on it.
The stomach churns food into chyme, a semi-liquid mixture that passes slowly into the duodenum (the first part of the small intestine).
Peptones leaving the stomach are still too large to absorb. In the small intestine two more enzymes, one from the pancreas and one from the intestinal wall, finish the job.
The pancreas is a gland, not part of the alimentary canal (the tube food passes through), so food never enters it. It secretes pancreatic juice into the duodenum through the pancreatic duct.
Pancreatic juice contains trypsin, which is made in inactive form as trypsinogen so that it cannot digest the cells that make it.
Enterokinase, an enzyme from the lining of the small intestine found in the intestinal juice, converts trypsinogen into active trypsin.
Pancreatic juice is alkaline because it also contains alkaline salts, so it neutralises the acid chyme and gives trypsin the working pH it needs.
Trypsin hydrolyses peptones into shorter peptides, which are still too large to be absorbed.
Intestinal juice is secreted by glands in the wall of the small intestine and contains peptidases (erepsin).
Peptidases hydrolyse peptides into amino acids, the main form in which protein is absorbed. Protein digestion is now complete.
Trace the journey of protein from mouth to liver in order, naming the organ, secretion, enzyme, substrate and product at each stage, then how the products are absorbed.
Mouth: no protein is digested, because saliva contains no protein-digesting enzyme.
Stomach: pepsin acts on the protein (and rennin in infants), and chyme passes into the duodenum.
Duodenum: trypsin and then peptidases complete digestion, and pancreatic juice enters through the pancreatic duct.
Villi of the small intestine: amino acids are absorbed into the capillaries (the tiniest blood vessels) inside each villus.
The capillaries join to form the hepatic portal vein, which carries the absorbed amino acids from the small intestine to the liver.
Liver: processes the amino acids before they enter the general circulation.
Diagram: the digestive system, labelled mouth, oesophagus, stomach, liver, pancreas, small intestine, large intestine and hepatic portal vein, with where protein digestion begins and ends marked.
Absorption is the passage of digested nutrients through the wall of the small intestine into the blood or lymph. The small intestine is built to make this fast.
The small intestine is long, and its lining is folded into villi, finger-like projections whose cells have microvilli (tiny folds on their surface), so the surface area for absorption is very large.
Each villus has a thin one-cell-thick wall, so nutrients have only a short distance to cross, a capillary network, and a central lacteal (a lymph vessel).
Amino acids are absorbed mainly by active transport, which uses energy and carrier proteins and is coupled with the uptake of sodium ions.
Amino acids move through the cells lining each villus into the capillary network inside it. They do not enter the lacteal, which is the route for fat.
Very small peptides (two or three amino acids) may be absorbed too. They are broken down into amino acids inside the cells.
Diagram: cross-section of a villus showing the capillary network, lacteal, epithelial wall (the one-cell-thick lining) and microvilli.
Once absorbed, amino acids are used where the body needs them. The body has no store of amino acids, so any not needed are broken down in the liver.
Body cells take up amino acids from the blood and use them to build body protein for growth and repair, and to make enzymes, hormones and antibodies.
The liver makes plasma proteins, such as albumin, from amino acids and passes the rest on in the blood.
Amino acids cannot be stored, so surplus amino acids are broken down in the liver.

Deamination is the removal of the amino group (–NH₂) from an amino acid. In the liver it is converted to ammonia (a nitrogen-containing compound formed when the amino group is removed from an amino acid), and then to urea because ammonia is toxic.
Urea is carried in the blood to the kidneys, filtered out and excreted in urine.
The remaining carbon part, with its carboxyl group (–COOH), is oxidised to release heat and energy, or converted into glucose or fat. This is why protein is an energy source when eaten in excess.

Food carbohydrates are too big to pass into the blood, so digestion chops them into small sugar units. This is done by hydrolysis, the splitting of the glycosidic bonds (the links) that join sugar units together.

Digestion turns large food molecules into small soluble ones by hydrolysis, using enzymes. Enzymes are biological catalysts, each specific to one substrate, and they work at about 37 °C, body temperature.
Starch is a polysaccharide made of many glucose units joined by glycosidic bonds, so it is a very large molecule that must be broken down before it can be absorbed.
Maltose is two glucose units joined together; sucrose is glucose joined to fructose; lactose is glucose joined to galactose. These three are disaccharides (double sugars).

Hydrolysis adds water across a glycosidic bond, splitting a disaccharide into two monosaccharides or a polysaccharide into smaller units. The end products are the monosaccharides glucose, fructose and galactose, the only forms small enough to be absorbed.
Each carbohydrate-digesting enzyme acts on one substrate, and its name ends in -ase and names that substrate: amylase on starch, maltase on maltose, sucrase on sucrose and lactase on lactose.
Diagram: glucose unit linked to a second glucose unit by a glycosidic bond, with the water added during hydrolysis labelled, giving two monosaccharides.
Carbohydrate digestion starts in the mouth, where chewing and saliva begin to break down starch.
Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces (mechanical digestion), which gives the enzymes more surface to work on.
Organ and secretion: the salivary glands secrete saliva, which contains salivary amylase.
Substrate and product: salivary amylase hydrolyses starch into dextrins (shorter chains of glucose units) and maltose.
Digestion in the mouth is brief, because food is chewed and swallowed quickly, so much of the starch reaches the small intestine undigested.
Diagram: the alimentary canal, with the mouth, salivary glands and oesophagus labelled.
Starch digestion pauses in the stomach, because the conditions there do not suit the enzyme that arrives from the mouth.
The acid of the stomach, hydrochloric acid, denatures salivary amylase (changes its shape so it no longer works) and stops its action on starch.
The stomach secretes no enzyme that digests carbohydrate.
Starch, dextrins and maltose leave the stomach as part of the chyme (the semi-liquid mixture of food and gastric juice) and pass into the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine.
Most starch is digested in the small intestine. Pancreatic juice finishes the starch, then enzymes from the intestine wall split the disaccharides into single sugars.
Organ and secretion: the pancreas, a gland, secretes pancreatic juice, which contains pancreatic amylase. It enters the duodenum by the pancreatic duct.
Pancreatic amylase hydrolyses the remaining starch and dextrins into maltose. It is a different enzyme from salivary amylase but acts on the same substrate.
Pancreatic juice is alkaline, which neutralises the acidic chyme so the intestinal enzymes can work.
The wall of the small intestine secretes intestinal juice from glands in its wall. It contains maltase, sucrase and lactase, which finish the job, and each acts only on its own substrate.
Maltase hydrolyses maltose into two glucose molecules.
Sucrase hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose.
Lactase hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose, so the products of the disaccharidases are not all glucose.
Non-starch polysaccharides (dietary fibre) are not hydrolysed by human enzymes, so they pass into the large intestine. Fibre is the carbohydrate that is not digested.
Putting the stages in order shows how starch travels from the mouth to the blood and on to the liver.
Mouth: salivary amylase begins starch digestion.
Stomach: acid stops amylase action, and food is mixed to form chyme.
Duodenum: pancreatic amylase and intestinal juice complete digestion to monosaccharides.
Villi of the small intestine: monosaccharides are absorbed into the capillaries inside each villus.
Hepatic portal vein: carries all the monosaccharides, glucose, fructose and galactose, from the small intestine to the liver.
Liver: converts fructose and galactose to glucose, and glucose then enters the general circulation.
Diagram: the digestive system, labelled mouth, salivary glands, stomach, pancreas, small intestine, liver and hepatic portal vein, with where each enzyme acts.
Only monosaccharides are small enough to cross the wall of the small intestine. The wall is built to absorb them quickly and has two different ways of moving them across.
The small intestine is very long and its lining is folded into villi, with microvilli on their cells, so the surface area for absorption is large.
Each villus has a thin wall, so sugars cross quickly, and a capillary network that carries them away. It also has a central lacteal, which is used for fat.
Glucose and galactose are absorbed by active transport, which uses energy and carrier proteins and is coupled with sodium ions.
Fructose is absorbed by facilitated diffusion, which moves it down its concentration gradient through carrier proteins without using energy.
Monosaccharides leave the villi in the blood of the capillaries, which join to form the hepatic portal vein. The vein carries all of them to the liver.
Diagram: cross-section of a villus showing the capillary network, the lacteal and the direction of glucose and fructose movement.
Once glucose is in the blood it has several possible fates: it is used for energy, stored, or converted to fat. Two pancreatic hormones keep the blood glucose level steady.
Glucose in the blood is carried to the cells, where cells oxidise it in respiration, releasing heat and energy, some of which is stored in ATP. It is the main fuel for the brain and red blood cells.
Carbohydrate spares protein: because glucose supplies the energy, protein can be used for growth and repair instead.
Surplus glucose is stored as glycogen, a branched polysaccharide of glucose, in the liver and muscles. Glycogen is the animal store, whereas starch is the plant store.
Insulin, released from the beta cells of the pancreas, promotes the uptake of glucose into cells and its storage as glycogen, which lowers blood glucose.
Glucagon, released from the alpha cells of the pancreas, causes the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose, which raises blood glucose.
When glycogen stores are full, the liver converts surplus glucose into fatty acids and triglycerides, which are stored as fat in adipose tissue.
Insulin and glucagon are hormones released into the blood, not digestive secretions, so they are a different job of the pancreas from making pancreatic juice.

Fat is eaten mostly as triglycerides, which are too big to absorb. Digestion is hydrolysis, the splitting of a molecule using water, done by enzymes (specific biological catalysts that work at about 37 °C), and lipase is the enzyme that does this for fat.
A triglyceride is one glycerol molecule bonded to three fatty acid chains by ester bonds, so there are three bonds for the enzyme to break.

Lipase hydrolyses the ester bonds of triglycerides, splitting them into fatty acids and glycerol. Monoglycerides and diglycerides (glycerol with one or two fatty acids still attached) form as intermediate products on the way.

Fats do not dissolve in water, so lipase can act only at the surface of a fat droplet, and a larger droplet surface area speeds digestion. This is why fat must be emulsified (broken into tiny droplets) first.
Diagram: a triglyceride showing one glycerol backbone and three fatty acid chains, with the ester bonds labelled.
Very little fat is digested before it reaches the small intestine, so the early stages of the canal matter mainly for how long fat stays in them.
The mouth carries out little or no lipid digestion.
Gastric lipase (lipase made in the stomach) hydrolyses only a small proportion of the triglycerides.
Fat slows the emptying of the stomach, so it stays there for longer than carbohydrate or protein, which is why a fatty meal keeps you feeling full.
Bile is a digestive secretion that works on fat without being an enzyme. Knowing where it is made, stored and released helps you place it correctly in the sequence.
The liver produces bile, which is stored and concentrated in the gall bladder and released through the bile duct into the duodenum (the first part of the small intestine).
Bile contains bile salts and bile pigments such as bilirubin, and it contains no enzymes, so it cannot chemically digest fat.
Diagram: the liver, gall bladder, bile duct, pancreas, pancreatic duct and duodenum, with the flow of bile and pancreatic juice labelled.
Bile does three jobs, and the most important is preparing fat for lipase. Emulsification is a physical change, not a chemical one.
Bile salts emulsify fat, breaking large fat globules into very small droplets. An emulsion is tiny droplets of one liquid dispersed in another, and no bonds are broken, so this is not hydrolysis.
Emulsification increases the surface area of the fat, so lipase can act on far more of it at once.
Bile is alkaline, so it neutralises the acid chyme (the partly digested food) arriving from the stomach and creates a suitable pH for the pancreatic and intestinal enzymes to work.
Bile also carries waste products such as bilirubin out of the body.
Most fat is digested in the small intestine, where lipase from two sources meets fat that bile has already emulsified.
Pancreas (acting in the duodenum): it secretes pancreatic juice containing lipase. The substrate is triglycerides in the emulsified droplets, and the products are fatty acids and glycerol.
Small intestine: its wall secretes intestinal juice containing lipase, which acts on the same substrate, triglycerides, to give fatty acids and glycerol.
Liver and gall bladder: they supply bile, which has no enzyme and emulsifies fat into droplets.
Lipase hydrolyses triglycerides into fatty acids and glycerol, with some monoglycerides and diglycerides as intermediate products.

The digested fat is absorbed through the villi, the finger-like projections of the small intestine wall. Each villus has a capillary network and a lacteal (a lymph capillary), and the route a product takes depends on its size.

Short-chain fatty acids and glycerol are small and water-soluble, so they pass directly into the capillaries of the villi and do not need to be rebuilt. The hepatic portal vein carries them to the liver.
Long-chain fatty acids and monoglycerides diffuse into the cells lining the villi, where they are rebuilt into triglycerides. Fat is therefore not absorbed as whole triglycerides.
The triglycerides are coated with protein (and other lipids) to form chylomicrons, which are too large to enter the capillaries.
Chylomicrons pass into the lacteals, the lymph capillaries at the centre of each villus.

Lymph carries the chylomicrons through the lymphatic system into the thoracic duct, which empties into the blood near the heart. The fat reaches the general circulation without first passing through the liver; the liver later removes what is left of the chylomicrons from the blood.
Diagram: a villus cross-section showing the capillary network, the lacteal and the two routes.
Tracing a fat molecule from the mouth to the blood brings the stages together in order.
1. Mouth and stomach: little or no lipid digestion takes place.
2. Duodenum: bile emulsifies the fat and pancreatic lipase hydrolyses it.
3. Villi: the products are absorbed. Long-chain fat enters the lacteals, while short-chain products enter the capillaries.
4. Lymphatic system: lymph carries the fat from the lacteals into the thoracic duct and then into the bloodstream.
5. Hepatic portal vein: carries the short-chain fatty acids and glycerol, absorbed directly into the capillaries, to the liver.
6. General circulation: the blood distributes fat around the body.
Diagram: the digestive system, labelled mouth, stomach, liver, gall bladder, pancreas, small intestine and hepatic portal vein.
Once absorbed, fat is moved around the body, broken down again at the tissues and either used for energy or stored.
Lipids travel in the blood as lipoproteins (lipids packed with protein): chylomicrons carry dietary fat, and very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) carry fat made in the liver.
Lipoprotein lipase, an enzyme at the body tissues, hydrolyses the triglycerides in lipoproteins into fatty acids and glycerol, which the cells take up.
Muscle cells oxidise fatty acids in respiration to release energy. Fat is the most concentrated energy source, giving 37 kJ (9 kcal) per gram.
Glycerol is converted into glucose in the liver or enters glycolysis (the first stage of respiration).
Surplus fatty acids are rebuilt into triglycerides and stored in adipose (fat) tissue under the skin and around organs, which gives insulation, protection of organs and an energy reserve.
The liver converts surplus carbohydrate (and protein) into fatty acids and triglycerides, which it exports as VLDL.

Every activity the body carries out, from breathing to running, needs energy, and that energy comes from the food and drink we take in. Knowing what energy is for, and how it is measured, is the starting point for working out how much a person needs.
Energy is what the body needs to carry out every function: breathing, circulating blood, nerve and brain activity, growth and repair, movement and keeping warm.
Energy is measured in kilojoules (kJ) or kilocalories (kcal, often called "calories"). 1 kcal is about 4.2 kJ, and food labels give both units.
The body releases energy from carbohydrate, fat and protein, and from alcohol, through chemical reactions, and uses it for every body function.

Energy not needed straight away is stored, because the body cannot waste it: a small store as glycogen (a stored form of carbohydrate) in the liver and muscles, and the large store as fat in adipose tissue (fatty tissue under the skin and around organs).

Three main functions of energy are basal metabolism (keeping the body working at rest), growth and physical activity. Marking schemes also credit the working of the internal organs and the production of heat to maintain body temperature.

Even when you are lying still, your body is working hard to keep you alive. The energy for this hidden work is called the basal metabolic rate, and it is the biggest part of what most people use each day.
BMR is the minimum amount of energy the body needs to stay alive when completely at rest.
It pays for the functions that continue at rest, such as breathing, the heartbeat and circulation of blood, and the work of the brain, liver, kidneys and other internal organs.
It also pays for maintaining body temperature, and for the continuing renewal of cells.

BMR is measured with the person lying at complete rest and awake, in a warm room, about 12 hours after eating (fasting). These conditions mean no movement, cold or digestion adds extra energy use to the result.
For most people BMR is the largest single part of the energy used in a day, more than the energy used for activity.

Two people lying side by side will not burn exactly the same amount of energy. BMR varies with the amount and type of body tissue a person has and with the hormones controlling the speed of their metabolism.
Age: BMR per kilogram is highest in infancy and childhood because of rapid growth, and it falls with age as lean muscle tissue is lost.
Gender: men generally have a higher BMR than women of the same weight, because men have a higher proportion of lean muscle tissue to fat. Do not say it is simply because they are men.
Body size and weight: the larger the body, the more tissue there is to maintain, so the higher the BMR.
Body composition: lean muscle tissue is more active than fat, so it uses more energy at rest. A muscular person has a higher BMR than a person of the same weight with more fat.

Hormones: the thyroid gland controls the speed of metabolism (the chemical reactions in the body). An overactive thyroid, producing too much thyroid hormone, raises BMR, and an underactive thyroid lowers it.
Health: fever, infection and recovery from injury raise BMR, because the body is working harder to fight illness or repair itself.
Pregnancy and lactation (breastfeeding) raise the requirement, and in a cold climate the body works to stay warm, which raises it too; a hot climate has a smaller effect.
Activity does not change BMR itself. It is a separate part of the total energy the body uses in a day.
Building a new body takes energy as well as nutrients. This is why people who are growing quickly need a lot of energy for their size.
Energy is needed to build new body tissue, especially muscle, bone, blood and organs.
Infants and young children need a high amount of energy for their size because they are growing quickly.
Teenagers have adolescent growth spurts (short periods of very rapid growth) which raise the requirement sharply.
Teenage boys generally need more energy than girls at this stage because of their greater body size and muscle.
After growth stops, adult energy is needed for the maintenance and repair of tissue, not for new growth.
Physical activity is the most variable part of daily energy use, so it is the factor an individual can change most easily.
The energy used in activity depends on the type, intensity, duration and frequency of the activity.
Occupational activity: a manual worker, such as a builder or farm worker, or an athlete uses far more energy than someone in a desk job such as an office worker.
Leisure activity: walking, cycling, gardening and playing sport add to daily energy use.
Sedentary lifestyle (little activity and much sitting) means low energy output, so less food energy is needed to meet the body's needs.

A person's daily energy requirement is more than their BMR. It adds the energy for activity and for dealing with food, and then rises or falls with circumstances such as climate, pregnancy and health.

Total daily energy use is made up of BMR, plus the energy for physical activity, plus the small amount used to digest, absorb and process food (the thermic effect of food). BMR on its own is not the total requirement.
Occupation: manual and athletic work increases the requirement, while sedentary work lowers it.
Climate: in cold conditions the body burns more energy to keep its temperature stable, partly through the muscular work of shivering, so energy needs are higher than in a warm climate.
Pregnancy: extra energy is needed for the growth of the baby and the placenta and for the mother's added tissue, especially in the later months.
Lactation: extra energy is needed to make breast milk.
Health: fever, illness, burns and recovery from injury or surgery raise energy needs. Prolonged bed rest lowers the activity part of the requirement.
The factors examiners list are age, gender, body size or weight, occupation, level of physical activity, climate, pregnancy, lactation, health or illness, growth spurts, sedentary lifestyle and BMR.

When a person is described, such as a teenager who plays sport, a builder, an office worker, a pregnant woman or an older retired person, name the factor, say whether it raises or lowers the requirement, and give the reason.
Your body takes energy in from food and drink and uses it up all day long. Comparing the two tells you whether your weight will stay steady, rise or fall.

Energy input is the energy in the food and drink consumed. Energy output (also called energy expenditure) is the energy the body uses for BMR (the energy needed just to keep the body alive at rest), physical activity, growth and digestion.
Energy balance is achieved when energy input equals energy output. Nothing is left over to store and nothing extra is needed from the body's stores, so body weight stays steady.
Positive energy balance means input exceeds output. The surplus is converted to fat and stored as adipose (fat) tissue, so weight is gained. Note that 'positive' here does not mean good.
Negative energy balance means output exceeds input. The body makes up the shortfall by using its stored glycogen first and then fat, so weight is lost.
Too little energy for a long time (underweight or prolonged negative balance) leads to weight loss, tiredness and poor resistance to infection.
Maintaining energy balance keeps a person at a healthy weight, helps prevent overweight and obesity and the diseases that go with them, and supplies energy for work, study, growth and activity.
If a person is out of balance, there are only two levers: eat and drink less energy, or use more. Most advice combines both.

To reduce energy intake, cut back on sugary drinks, sweets, fried and fatty foods, and check portion sizes. Grilling or baking instead of frying, and avoiding snacking on high-energy foods, also lower intake.
Eating more fruit, vegetables and fibre helps because fibre fills you up, so you feel full on less energy.
To increase energy output, add daily walking, cycling, stairs instead of lifts, active leisure or a regular sport or gym, because each extra activity uses energy that would otherwise be stored.
To reduce time spent sedentary (sitting still), limit television, computer and gaming time and break up long periods of sitting.
A gradual change, sustained over time, is more effective than crash dieting, because it is a habit a person can keep up.
If weight problems continue, a person can return to balance with these changes plus support from a doctor, a dietitian or a weight management programme.
Case studies give a person's lifestyle and daily menu. The answer should analyse the energy balance first and then recommend changes, so work through it in order.
1. Identify the person's energy output: occupation, activity level, time spent sitting, age and any growth or pregnancy needs, because these decide how much energy they use.
2. Estimate the energy input from the menu: note the high-energy items, such as fried foods, cakes, sugary drinks and large portions.
3. State whether the person is in positive or negative energy balance, and what this may do to body weight.
4. Recommend a change to intake: replace the high-energy items with fruit, vegetables, wholegrain foods or lean protein.
5. Recommend a change to output: name a specific activity, how often and for how long.
6. Write a one-day menu that meets the person's energy needs and matches the healthy eating guidelines: breakfast, lunch and dinner, each with two or three items.

Menus may be asked for a person who is obese, a teenager who plays sport, a person with a high energy requirement or a family with young children. A weight-reducing menu uses low-fat milk, grilled or poached foods, wholegrain cereals, vegetables and salad, fruit and water.
Diagram: none is needed. A simple balance diagram, with input on one side, output on the other and a tilt for positive or negative balance, is optional.
Not all energy comes with goodness attached. Some foods give plenty of energy but almost nothing else the body needs.

Empty kilocalories (empty calories) are calories from foods that supply energy but little or no nutritional value, such as sweets, sugary soft drinks, crisps, alcohol, cakes and biscuits, and fried snack foods.

They add to energy intake without supplying protein, vitamins, minerals or fibre, so they can cause positive energy balance and weight gain while the diet is still poor in nutrients. Over-indulgence in sugary food can lead to obesity.
Replacing empty kilocalories with fruit, vegetables, wholegrain foods, lean protein or low-fat dairy gives the same or less energy with more nutrients.
Obesity is a condition of excess body fat that harms health, usually caused by a long-term positive energy balance. Overweight is the milder stage. The causes below are mostly about lifestyle.
Energy imbalance: intake consistently exceeds output, so the surplus is stored as fat.
Sedentary lifestyle: a job or leisure time spent sitting lowers energy output, so more of the food eaten is left over to be stored.
Lack of exercise: regular physical activity is not part of the daily routine, so output stays low.
Psychological factors: depression, boredom and stress can lead to comfort eating, overeating and snacking.
Hormonal imbalance: an underactive thyroid gland slows metabolism and lowers BMR, so the same food intake produces weight gain. This applies to some people only, not as the usual cause.
Unhealthy eating patterns: frequent snacking, skipped meals followed by overeating, and frequent takeaways.
Poor food choices: a high intake of processed foods, sugary drinks and fatty foods. Large portion sizes of energy-dense foods also increase intake without adding to fullness.

In children, causes include sweets and fast food, sugary drinks, too much television and computer time, less outdoor play, advertising aimed at children, and parents using food as a reward. Genetic and family factors may also influence weight, but lifestyle causes are stressed.
Carrying excess fat for years strains almost every system in the body. Exams want each risk with a reason how it happens.
Type 2 diabetes: excess fat reduces the body's response to insulin, so blood glucose rises. It can be caused by a sedentary lifestyle and unhealthy diet.
Coronary heart disease and stroke: obesity raises blood pressure and blood cholesterol levels.
High blood pressure and high cholesterol, both linked to excess weight.
Gallstones: excess body fat increases the risk of gallstone formation.
Arthritis, joint pain and back pain: extra weight puts stress on the weight-bearing joints and the spine.
Breathing difficulties and sleep apnoea, and some cancers, are also linked to obesity. Varicose veins arise because excess weight increases pressure on the veins in the legs.
Depression and poor self-esteem, which can both result from obesity and make it harder to change habits. Difficulties in pregnancy and childbirth, and infertility, are further risks.
Reduced life expectancy, as the combined risks shorten life. Corrective measures are to return to energy balance and get support from a doctor, dietitian or weight management programme.
BMI is a simple measure that relates body weight to height and is used to classify body weight in adults. It is a screening measure, not a diagnosis.
BMI = weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared (kg/m²).
BMI does not distinguish between muscle and fat, so a muscular athlete may score as overweight.
Waist measurement is used alongside BMI, because fat stored around the abdomen carries greater health risk.
Children use age and sex charts, not the adult categories above.
Exams give you weight and height, or a table of results, and ask for a category. Follow the steps in order, and keep height in metres.
Step 1: convert height to metres (for example, 175 cm = 1.75 m).
Step 3: divide weight by the squared height (sample data: 70 kg / 3.06 = 22.9, in the healthy range). Dividing, not multiplying, is what gives the right answer.
Read a BMI table by finding the row for the height and the column for the weight, and matching the result to the categories above.
When comparing groups in data, note which group has the higher share in the overweight or obese categories and link this to diet and activity.

Only three nutrients supply energy in food: protein, carbohydrate and fat (lipid). Each releases a fixed amount of energy, measured in kilojoules (kJ) or kilocalories (kcal), for every gram eaten, and these values are the basis of every energy calculation.

Protein supplies 17 kJ (4 kcal) per gram, carbohydrate supplies 16 kJ (3.75 kcal) per gram and fat (lipid) supplies 37 kJ (9 kcal) per gram. A simple table of these three values is the best way to learn them.
Fat is the most concentrated energy source, giving more than twice the energy per gram of protein or carbohydrate. This is why a high-fat diet is energy-dense and contributes strongly to weight gain.
Vitamins, minerals and water supply no energy, so they are not energy nutrients, even though the body cannot work without them.
Alcohol is not a nutrient, but it does supply energy, at 29 kJ (7 kcal) per gram. It supplies no protein, vitamins or minerals, so it is a source of empty kilocalories (energy with no nutrition).
Fibre is a carbohydrate that the body cannot digest, so it supplies very little usable energy. Do not count it with the starches and sugars, and do not give it 16 kJ per gram.
1 kcal is about 4.2 kJ, so dividing kJ by 4.2 gives kcal. Check: 37 kJ is about 9 kcal, 17 kJ is about 4 kcal, 16 kJ is about 3.75 kcal and 29 kJ is about 7 kcal.

A food's energy value is worked out from how many grams of each energy nutrient it contains. Food composition tables and labels give these amounts per 100 g, so the method is multiply, add, then state the unit.
1. Find the grams of protein, carbohydrate and fat in the amount eaten, from the food label or a food composition table (which gives values per 100 g).
2. Multiply the grams of each nutrient by its energy value per gram: protein by 17, carbohydrate by 16 and fat by 37.
3. Add the three results to give the total energy value of the food.
4. Give the unit, kJ, and convert to kcal if asked by dividing by 4.2.
Scaling to a portion: if the table gives values per 100 g and the portion is 150 g, multiply each per-100 g value by 150 divided by 100 (or 1.5).
Without scaling, the answer is for 100 g, not for the portion eaten.
Seeing the method on sample figures shows where the marks are: each multiplication, the total and the unit. These are invented sample foods, not facts about any named product.
Worked example (sample data): 100 g of a food with 12 g protein, 60 g carbohydrate and 8 g fat gives 12 x 17 = 204 kJ, 60 x 16 = 960 kJ and 8 x 37 = 296 kJ.
These add to a total of 1460 kJ. In kcal this is about 348 (1460 divided by 4.2).
Second worked example (sample data): 100 g of a food with 20 g protein, 50 g carbohydrate and 10 g fat gives 20 x 17 = 340 kJ, 50 x 16 = 800 kJ and 10 x 37 = 370 kJ.
These add to a total of 1510 kJ, which is about 360 kcal.
Percentage contribution: divide the energy from one nutrient by the total energy, then multiply by 100. In the 1460 kJ sample, fat gives 296 out of 1460, which is about 20 per cent of the energy.

Section B data questions give a table of composition per 100 g for several foods, such as protein, fat, carbohydrate, fibre, calcium and iron. The sum is only half the answer, because you must also say what the figures mean for a diet.
To rank foods by energy value, calculate the kJ for each food using the method above, then put them in order and name the highest and the lowest.
A high-fibre food helps bowel health, because fibre adds bulk and keeps waste moving through the gut.
A high-fat food is a disadvantage on a low-fat diet, because fat has the most energy per gram and contributes to weight gain.
A high-carbohydrate food is a good source of energy for the body.
The 2007H bread comparison is an example of this type of question: calculate, rank, then comment on how suitable each bread is for a given diet.
Carbohydrate supplies the largest share of energy in the diet. It is the body's main and most readily available energy source.
Sugars and starches are digested to glucose, which cells use for energy. Any glucose not needed straight away is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles.
Starchy foods such as bread, potatoes, rice and pasta supply carbohydrate together with fibre, vitamins and minerals, so they give energy with useful nutrition. Cereals and fruit are also sources.
Sugary foods and drinks supply carbohydrate with little nutrition, so they are a source of empty kilocalories.
Healthy eating guidelines aim for most energy to come from starchy foods, preferably wholegrain, with less from added sugars.

Fat packs far more energy into each gram than the other nutrients, so it contributes strongly to the energy in the diet even when it is a smaller part of the weight of the food. It is the second largest source of energy.
Fats and oils are lipids, mostly triglycerides, made of glycerol and fatty acids.
Fat supplies the most energy per gram of the three energy nutrients, more than twice that of carbohydrate or protein.
Surplus energy from fat is stored as adipose tissue, an energy reserve, which is why high-fat diets contribute strongly to weight gain.
Saturated fats come mainly from animal foods and some plant oils, such as palm oil. Unsaturated fats come from vegetable oils, nuts, seeds and oily fish.
Sources of fat include butter, oils, fatty meat, nuts, cheese and oily fish.
Protein can supply energy, but this is not its main job. It makes the smallest contribution to the energy in the diet.
Protein is made of amino acids. The body uses it mainly for growth and repair of tissue, but it can also supply energy.
Protein is not stored in the body as protein, so surplus protein is broken down and used for energy or converted to fat.
When carbohydrate and fat are short, protein is used for energy at the expense of its building role.
High biological value (HBV) protein, from meat, fish, eggs, milk and cheese, contains all essential amino acids. Beans are also a protein source.
Protein is not a major energy source in a healthy diet: its value per gram is close to that of carbohydrate, but it is eaten in smaller amounts.
How much each nutrient contributes to a diet depends on how much of it is eaten and on how much energy each gram of the food carries.
Energy density is the energy per gram of a food. Foods rich in fat and sugar are the most energy-dense.
Wholegrain starchy foods, fruit, vegetables and lean protein give nutrients with less energy per gram, so they are a better choice than empty kilocalories.
Healthy eating guidelines aim for most energy to come from starchy foods, preferably wholegrain, with less from fat, especially saturated fat, and less from added sugars.
The typical Irish diet gets more of its energy from saturated fat and from added sugar in drinks and processed foods than the guidelines recommend.
Calculating the contribution of each nutrient: multiply the grams eaten in a day by the energy value per gram, then divide each result by the total and multiply by 100 to give its percentage share.

Dietary guidelines are official advice, based on scientific evidence, on the types and amounts of food that keep a population healthy. They turn nutrition science into practical advice for the general healthy population, and are revised as evidence changes.
Evidence comes from nutrition research, national food consumption surveys (which record what people actually eat) and health data on diet-related diseases.

Expert committees review this evidence and turn it into practical advice on foods rather than nutrients, setting the types of food to eat and the amounts to limit. The guidelines are reviewed as new evidence appears.

The Department of Health publishes the healthy eating guidelines for Ireland and the Food Pyramid, which is one of the tools used to explain them (the current pyramid is called 'Healthy Food for Life', 2016).
The HSE supports the guidelines, and the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) and safefood are other Irish bodies in this field.
The guidelines are written for the general healthy population, so they are not a substitute for advice for individuals with special medical needs.

The aims are to make sure people get enough nutrients, to prevent deficiency, and to reduce the risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, stroke, some cancers and osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones).
One consistent message also helps consumers, schools and food planners, because everyone is working from the same advice.
The Irish guidelines can be given as about eight principles. Together they say which foods to eat most, which to eat in moderation and which to keep small.
Eat plenty of vegetables, salad and fruit: about five to seven portions a day, spread across meals.
Base meals on starchy foods, choosing wholegrain bread, cereals, potatoes, pasta and rice.
Include protein from lean meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans, lentils and nuts, with fish eaten regularly.
Choose milk, yoghurt and cheese in lower-fat forms, as they supply calcium and HBV protein (high biological value protein, which contains all the essential amino acids).
Use fats and oils sparingly, and prefer unsaturated oils such as rapeseed and olive oil.
Limit foods and drinks high in fat, sugar and salt, which are not needed for health and should be occasional.
Drink water as the main drink, and keep alcohol within recommended limits.
Eat regular meals and prepare food with methods that add little fat, such as steaming, grilling and baking.
Each guideline is linked to a health benefit or a health risk. Examiners want the guideline and its reason together.
Fruit and vegetables supply fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants (substances that protect cells from damage), which protect against chronic disease.
Wholegrain starchy foods give more fibre and nutrients than refined white flour products, and promote bowel health because fibre helps prevent constipation and bowel disorders.
Saturated fat raises blood cholesterol, which increases the risk of coronary heart disease.
Excess salt is linked to high blood pressure, which increases the risk of stroke and heart disease.
Sugar adds energy without nutrients, contributes to obesity, and causes tooth decay.
An RDA (Recommended Dietary Allowance) is a planning value: the amount of a nutrient that meets the needs of nearly all healthy people in a group.
An RDA is set for each nutrient and differs by age, sex and life stage, such as growth, pregnancy, lactation (breastfeeding) or adolescence.

RDAs are used to plan menus and to check that a diet supplies enough of each nutrient over the day, by comparing the day's nutrient total with the RDA. They also guide food-labelling and supplement standards and institutions such as schools and hospitals.
An RDA is a guide for a group; it is not a precise target for an individual.
Intake far above the RDA does not give extra benefit and can be harmful for some nutrients, so supplements should be used with care.
Nutrients that are often low in Irish diets, such as iron and calcium, are the ones to check against the RDA when planning a menu.
A food composition table is a reference book of food values. It lets you turn a menu into numbers, so you can check it against the RDAs and the guidelines.
A food composition table gives the nutrient and energy content of a food, usually per 100 g of edible food. Irish tables are produced from national food analysis.
Tables state whether values are for raw or cooked food, so the matching version must be used because cooking changes the nutrient content.
Method: for each food, work out the grams eaten, divide by 100, then multiply by the value per 100 g.
Example (sample data): 150 g of a food with 3 g fibre per 100 g supplies 150 / 100 x 3 = 4.5 g fibre.
Add the results for all foods in the menu to give the day's total for each nutrient and for energy, then compare the total with the RDA. Where a total is low or high, adjust the menu.
A computer nutrition program does the same job as a food composition table, but automatically. It is quick to use, though it is only as good as the information put in.
Nutrition programs contain a built-in food composition database; the user enters each food and the quantity eaten.
The program totals the energy and nutrients for the day and compares them with the guidelines or RDAs.
Check that the portion size entered matches the food as eaten, and that the correct cooking method is selected, because the results depend on correct portions and the right cooking state.
A program shows which nutrients are low or high, which helps the planner adjust the menu.
Advantages are that it is fast and accurate and holds many foods and recipes.

The Food Pyramid turns the healthy eating guidelines into the types and relative amounts of food needed each day. Foods with similar nutrients are grouped on shelves, with the base shelf eaten most and the top shelf least.
The current Irish pyramid has six shelves. At the base are vegetables, salad and fruit, with wholemeal cereals and breads, potatoes, pasta and rice above them.
Next come milk, yogurt and cheese, then meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans and nuts (including lean choices), then a small shelf of fats, spreads and oils, to be used sparingly.
The top shelf holds foods and drinks high in fat, sugar and salt. These are not needed for health, have no recommended servings, and should be occasional. Water is the main drink.

Servings: five to seven servings of vegetables, salad and fruit a day, three servings of milk, yogurt and cheese (five for ages 9 to 18), and three to five servings of wholemeal cereals, breads, potatoes, pasta and rice.

The number and size of servings from the other shelves are adjusted for age, sex, health, activity level and life stage, for example children, teenagers, pregnant and breastfeeding women and older adults.

To plan meals, take most foods from the large lower shelves, some from the middle and very little from the top, and vary the foods within each shelf. Include vegetables or fruit at every meal, and choose wholemeal and lower-fat versions.
Spread the choices across breakfast, lunch, dinner and snacks so the day covers every shelf and matches the person's portions. This supports energy balance and prevents both deficiency and excess.
The pyramid guides what to eat and roughly how much, not an exact diet, and it does not replace advice for medical conditions.
Diagram: draw the Food Pyramid, label each shelf with the main foods on it, and mark the base shelf and the top shelf.
A serving (portion) is a standard measure of food used to plan and count intake against the pyramid. It makes diets easy to compare, because everyone counts in the same units.
A portion is a standard amount of food used for planning, counting and comparing diets.
One piece of fruit, such as an apple, or one serving of vegetables counts as one portion of fruit or vegetables.
One glass of milk counts as one portion of milk, yoghurt or cheese in the dairy group.
Portion size should be adjusted to the person's age and activity: teenagers and active adults need larger portions from the starchy foods shelf than older, less active adults.
Serving sizes and numbers rise for growing teenagers and active people and fall for older, less active adults. Pregnant and breastfeeding women need extra servings of some groups.
Food supplements are concentrates of important nutrients. They can fill a gap in a diet, but they cannot do everything that food does.
Food supplements are concentrates of nutrients such as vitamins, minerals, omega-3 fatty acids (polyunsaturated fatty acids) and amino acids, sold in tablet, capsule or powder form.
They may be used to fill gaps where diet is restricted, where allergies or intolerances exclude foods, or where a person has special needs.
Folic acid prevents neural tube defects (defects of the baby's brain and spine) in a developing baby when taken before conception and in early pregnancy.
Iron supplements can treat anaemia caused by low iron intake, under medical advice.
Older people may absorb nutrients less efficiently, so they may need supplements, particularly vitamin D.

Their popularity is growing for reasons such as busy lifestyles, poor diets, media and advertising, a wish to prevent illness, special needs (vegans, restricted diets, illness), sports performance and convenience.
Supplements cannot replace a varied diet, because food supplies fibre and other nutrients that supplements do not contain.

High doses of some vitamins and minerals can be harmful, especially fat-soluble vitamins, so supplements should not be taken above the recommended levels. They can also cost a lot, so take medical advice.
Healthy eating is only part of staying healthy. The lifestyle guidelines cover activity, mental wellbeing and habits that harm the body.

Regular physical activity: build activity into daily life, such as brisk walking, cycling, sport or active housework, and include muscle-strengthening and weight-bearing exercise (which loads the bones, such as walking or running).

Physical activity improves cardiovascular fitness, maintains muscle and bone, supports weight control and mental wellbeing, and may raise protective HDL cholesterol (the protective form of cholesterol).
Mental health: get adequate sleep and rest, keep a realistic workload, and use stress management, relaxation and social contact.
Avoid tobacco and second-hand smoke, which damage the lungs and blood vessels and greatly raise the risk of cancer and coronary heart disease.
Limit alcohol: it supplies empty kilocalories (energy with no nutrients), harms the liver and judgement, and must never be used to manage stress.
Drink plenty of water and keep a healthy body weight.
Regular health checks and good personal hygiene complete the guidelines.
Together these habits reduce the risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension (high blood pressure) and heart disease.

Before the mid-twentieth century most Irish households ate a simple diet based on home-grown and home-made foods. Knowing what people ate then, and why, is the starting point for judging how the diet has changed.
Potatoes were the staple food (the main food of the diet), eaten in large quantities with milk, butter and buttermilk. This made the diet high in starch.
Oatmeal (porridge) and home-baked wholemeal bread, such as soda bread and brown bread, supplied carbohydrate and fibre, so fibre intake was naturally high.
Vegetables were seasonal and home-grown, such as cabbage, turnips and carrots, while fresh fruit was limited. Eggs and fish were eaten where available, especially in coastal areas.
Meat, especially bacon and salted meat, was eaten occasionally rather than daily, so the diet was relatively low in fat and sugar.
The main meal, called dinner, was eaten at midday, and the family ate together at set times. Food was cooked from raw on an open fire or range.
Processed and convenience foods were largely absent, so meals were prepared from basic ingredients.
The diet was limited in variety, and poorer households could go short of food, so it was not simply 'healthy'.
A typical day's menu then: porridge or bread and tea for breakfast; potatoes, cabbage and bacon or fish for dinner at midday; bread, butter and tea in the evening.
Over the last hundred years the Irish diet has moved from basic, home-prepared food towards processed, imported and ready-made food. Each change affects nutrition, and each has reasons behind it.
Refined white flour and white bread replaced much of the wholemeal bread and oatmeal, which lowered the fibre content of the diet because refining removes the fibre-rich outer layers of the grain.
Rice and pasta partly replaced potatoes, and processed breakfast cereals replaced porridge for many families. The variety of foods and cooking methods increased.
Sugar, sweets, biscuits, cakes and soft drinks increased in the diet, adding empty kilocalories (energy with few nutrients). This made the diet more energy-dense and nutrient-poor.
Fat intake rose, from butter, cream, fatty meat, processed meat, cakes, pastries and fried foods.
Processed, frozen, canned and ready-made convenience foods became common, with microwave cooking, freezers and short preparation times, so fewer meals are prepared from raw ingredients.
Imported fruit and vegetables became available all year round, while home-grown seasonal produce declined. Supermarkets replaced local shops.
Eating out and takeaway meals became more frequent. Holidays abroad, immigration and television cooking introduced new dishes and ethnic foods.

Food labelling, health information and health campaigns gave consumers more knowledge of nutritional value, so low-fat, reduced-sugar, wholegrain, organic, vegetarian and special-diet products became widely available.
Reasons for the changes include rising incomes, urbanisation, women working outside the home, time pressures, food industry growth and advertising, refrigeration, supermarkets and education.
Today's eating patterns are shaped by busy lifestyles, convenience and growing health awareness. These trends are examined separately from the changes in the foods themselves.
Meals are irregular, and many people eat snacks and graze instead of eating planned meals. Meals, especially breakfast, are often skipped.
The main meal is often eaten in the evening rather than at midday, and family members may eat at different times, in front of the television or on the go.
Convenience and ready-made foods are chosen for speed, and microwave and barbecued foods form part of many diets.
Eating out and takeaways are a regular part of many households' diet.
Consumers show more health awareness, reading labels and choosing low-fat, low-sugar, organic, functional and plant-based foods, with allergen and special-diet products widely available.

Television, advertising, social media and food marketing influence food choices, particularly for children and teenagers. Busy work and study timetables, cost, food trends and celebrity chefs also play a part.
Concern for sustainability and locally produced food is growing.
Consequences include more obesity, type 2 diabetes and heart disease, linked to poor diet and inactivity, but also improved choice and food safety.

The Department of Health healthy eating guidelines and Food Pyramid are the benchmark for judging the Irish diet. Compared with them, the typical Irish diet is lower in fibre, fruit and vegetables, higher in saturated fat, and can be too high in salt and sugar.
Fibre: intake is below the guidelines because fewer wholegrain foods, fruit and vegetables are eaten.
Fruit and vegetables: intakes fall short of the five to seven portions a day recommended.
Saturated fat: intake is above the level recommended, from butter, fatty meat and processed foods.
Salt and sugar: intakes can be too high, especially from processed foods, sweets and drinks.
Fish: intake is lower than recommended, particularly oily fish. Many people also eat from the top shelf of the Food Pyramid (foods high in fat, sugar and salt) too often.
Iron and calcium: intakes are relatively low for some groups, especially teenage girls and women of child-bearing age.
Sugary drinks add empty kilocalories, and water is advised as the main drink.
Strengths of the Irish diet: widespread protein intake, the availability of lower-fat products, and a good milk and potato tradition.
Low fibre is one of the four malnutrition concerns the syllabus names. Here malnutrition means an unbalanced diet, not only too little food. Write each concern as cause, effect and correction.

Cause: refining flour removes the bran and germ (the fibre-rich outer layers of the grain), so white bread and rice are low in fibre. Processed and convenience foods and few fruit and vegetables lower fibre, and wholegrain cereals are not eaten.
Effects: constipation, diverticular disease and other bowel disorders, and a higher risk of bowel cancer, because too little fibre slows the movement of waste through the bowel.
Fibre fills you up, so less fullness is linked to overeating and obesity. Low fibre is also linked to higher blood cholesterol and a raised risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.

Corrective measures: choose wholemeal or wholegrain bread and pasta, oats or porridge, brown rice and high-fibre breakfast cereals. Eat fruit and vegetables with their skin where possible, add pulses such as beans and lentils, and use nuts and seeds.
Build up fibre gradually and drink plenty of fluid (water), so that the bowel is not upset.
The Irish Cancer Society gives information on diet, fibre and cancer risk.
Too much saturated fat, the solid fat found mainly in animal foods and processed foods, is the second concern. It is linked to heart disease, so examiners expect effects as well as causes.
Sources: butter, cream, full-fat dairy, fatty and processed meats, pastries, cakes, biscuits, chocolate, fried and takeaway foods, and coconut and palm oil.
Causes: fast food and convenience foods, frying, snacking, large portions of fatty meat, and advertising.
Effects: raised blood cholesterol (LDL), which increases the risk of coronary heart disease and stroke. Excess energy from fat can lead to obesity and type 2 diabetes.
Corrective measures: use lower-fat milk, dairy and spreads, and choose lean meat. Grill, bake or steam instead of frying, and use unsaturated oils such as rapeseed or olive oil.
Replace some meat meals with oily fish, which supplies unsaturated fats. Limit the top shelf foods of the Food Pyramid and read labels.
The Irish Heart Foundation gives information on saturated fat, salt and heart health.
Iron is the third concern, and intakes are relatively low for some groups. Iron makes haemoglobin, so too little iron affects the whole body.
Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, the red pigment in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body.
Sources: lean red meat, liver, eggs, wholegrain and fortified cereals, pulses, dark green vegetables and dried fruit.
Effects: iron-deficiency anaemia, with tiredness, pale skin, weakness and poor concentration. Headaches, breathlessness and poor resistance to infection can also occur.

Causes: low intake of red meat and iron-rich foods, the blood loss of menstruation, and rapid growth in adolescence, which increase the need for iron. Pregnancy, dieting and vegetarian diets without careful planning can also leave intake too low.
Tea and coffee with meals, and phytates (compounds in some plant foods), reduce iron absorption.

Corrective measures: include lean red meat, liver, eggs, wholegrain or fortified cereals, pulses and dark green vegetables. Eat foods rich in vitamin C, such as citrus fruit or fruit juice, at the same meal, because vitamin C improves iron absorption.
Avoid tea with meals, and take supplements only on medical advice.
Calcium is the fourth concern. It does several jobs in the body, so low intake has effects on bones, teeth, muscles and blood.
Calcium is needed for the formation of bones and teeth, blood clotting, muscle contraction and normal nerve function.
Sources: milk, yoghurt, cheese, fortified plant milks, dark green vegetables, nuts and seeds such as sesame seeds, and fish eaten with its bones, such as sardines.
Effects: poor bone growth in children, weak bones and osteoporosis (brittle bones) in later life, dental decay, muscle cramps, and slow or impaired blood clotting.

Causes: low intake of milk, yoghurt and cheese (through dieting, dislike, cost, or replacement by soft drinks), and low vitamin D, which is needed to absorb calcium. Poor sunlight and little oily fish lower vitamin D.

Corrective measures: have three servings a day of milk, yoghurt and cheese (lower fat) or fortified plant alternatives. Eat fish with edible bones, dark green vegetables, nuts and seeds, and add fortified foods.
Get vitamin D from oily fish, eggs and safe sunlight, and do weight-bearing exercise. Take supplements only on medical advice.
A common activity is to compare a typical day's menu from the start of the twentieth century with one from today. The same five steps work for any menu.
Step 1: list every food and drink eaten in the day, with portion sizes.
Step 2: identify the sources of fibre, saturated fat, salt, sugar, iron and calcium in the menu.
Step 3: compare each nutrient with the healthy eating guidelines, saying whether it is too high, too low or about right.
Step 4: recommend specific changes, such as wholegrain instead of white bread, a serving of fish, or a lower-fat dairy choice.
Step 5: rewrite one meal or the whole day to show the changes.
Section B often has a data question on Irish food consumption or the Food Pyramid. A fixed routine lets you pick up the marks for reading, describing, explaining and recommending.
Read the title, the units, the years covered and the groups surveyed before drawing conclusions.

Identify the trend by comparing the first and last data points, noting a rise, a fall or a small change, and any change of direction in between. Compare groups too, such as men and women or age groups.
Quote the figures from the data exactly, and state which food or nutrient they describe.
Compare the data with the healthy eating guidelines and link the difference to a health risk such as heart disease, obesity or anaemia.
Suggest a reason for the trend, such as convenience foods, eating out, advertising, income or changes in family routines, and finish with a recommendation.
Water looks plain, but a handful of its physical and chemical properties explain why the body depends on it. Each property below links to a job water does in the body.
Pure water is colourless, odourless and tasteless.
Water boils at 100 °C and freezes at 0 °C at normal atmospheric pressure. Above 100 °C it changes to steam.

Water is a good solvent (a liquid that other substances dissolve in): it dissolves many minerals, sugars, water-soluble vitamins and gases, which is why it carries nutrients and wastes around the body. It is also why water-soluble vitamins and minerals can be lost into cooking water.
Water absorbs and retains heat well: it takes a lot of heat to warm it and it cools slowly, so it helps keep body temperature steady.
Water is neutral, with a pH of 7 for pure water, meaning it is neither acid nor alkaline.
Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats; water expands when it freezes.
Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium salts, while soft water has little. Hard water is therefore a useful source of calcium in the diet.
Water has no energy value and contains no protein, fat or vitamins of its own, so it is not a source of energy.
Water is a major component of the body and is needed in every body cell and tissue fluid. Because it dissolves so many substances, it is also the body's main transport medium.
Water is an essential component of all body cells.
Water is the main part of blood plasma, lymph and the other body tissue fluids, as well as urine and sweat.
Water is a part of saliva, digestive juices and mucus.
Water lubricates joints and membranes, such as those around the lungs and digestive tract, and the fluid it forms cushions organs, for example around the brain and spinal cord.
Water carries nutrients, oxygen, carbon dioxide, hormones and enzymes around the body in the blood and tissue fluids.
Because water dissolves these substances, they can move from the blood into the cells that need them.
Water is the medium in which the chemical reactions of the cells (metabolism) take place.
The body makes heat all the time and must keep its core temperature steady. Water does this in two ways: it spreads heat around and it carries heat away as sweat.
Water absorbs heat from the body when it evaporates, so sweating cools the body.
Water in the blood and tissues helps spread heat evenly, keeping the internal body temperature near 37 °C.
When the body is hot, more sweat is produced; when cold, less water is lost from the skin, so less heat is carried away.
Cells produce waste that would poison the body if it built up. Water carries these wastes out, mainly through the kidneys.
The kidneys filter the blood, and water carries waste products such as urea out of the body in urine.
Water is also lost in faeces, sweat and breath, and this loss must be replaced by drinks and food.
Adequate water intake keeps urine dilute, so the kidneys can remove waste efficiently.
Digestion breaks food into molecules small enough to be absorbed, and water takes part in the process as well as helping food move along.
Hydrolysis is the breakdown of large food molecules into smaller ones by adding water, and it is needed for the digestion of carbohydrate, protein and fat.
Water in saliva and digestive juices softens food, so it is easier to swallow and digest.
Water keeps faeces soft, so it prevents constipation, especially when fibre intake is high.
Tap and bottled water carry dissolved minerals, so water makes a small contribution to the diet beyond hydration.
Water supplies small amounts of calcium, fluoride and magnesium.
Hard water contains more calcium than soft water, so it is a useful source of calcium in the diet.
Fluoride from water helps to strengthen tooth enamel and protect teeth from decay.
Public water supplies in Ireland are fluoridated under the Health (Fluoridation of Water Supplies) Act 1960.
The body loses water every day and must replace it. Thirst is the first warning that it is falling behind, and dehydration is what happens when it does.
Thirst is the body's signal that its water content has fallen; quenching thirst is one function of water.
Dehydration occurs when water losses are greater than intake. Causes include heat, exercise, fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and not drinking enough.
Signs of dehydration are thirst, dark and small amounts of urine, headache, tiredness, dizziness and a dry mouth.
Severe dehydration can cause confusion, low blood pressure and collapse (shock), so fluids must be replaced promptly and urgent medical help is needed.
Water is the main drink in the diet, and foods such as fruit and vegetables, and soups, also supply water. Water is the main drink advised in the healthy eating guidelines.
