Factors that increase water needs include hot weather, exercise, fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, pregnancy, breastfeeding and high-fibre or high-protein diets.
Many drinks add energy to the diet but water adds none, which is why it is the best choice for staying hydrated.
Water supplies no energy, so it can be drunk freely without adding to energy intake.
Sugary drinks supply energy as empty kilocalories (energy with no useful nutrients), so plain water is the best choice for hydration.
Pregnancy raises the body's demand for water, because the mother must supply the growing baby as well as herself.
The blood volume of a pregnant woman increases, and water is needed to carry nutrients and oxygen to the foetus through the placenta, and to carry waste away.
Amniotic fluid, which surrounds the baby in the uterus and is mostly water, cushions and protects the developing baby and keeps its temperature steady.
Water helps to prevent constipation, which is common in pregnancy.
Breastfeeding women need extra water, because breast milk is mostly water and is produced in large amounts.
Exercise makes the body hot and the body cools itself by sweating, so active people lose water quickly and must replace it.
Exercise raises heat production; sweating cools the body, but sweat contains water and salts, including sodium and potassium, so these are lost too.
Water losses are replaced by drinking before, during and after activity.
Dehydration during sport reduces stamina, strength, concentration and coordination, and raises the risk of cramps, heat exhaustion and heat stroke.
Drinking regularly in small amounts during prolonged or intense exercise is more effective than drinking a large amount at once.

Water is enough for most activity. For prolonged or very intense exercise, isotonic sports drinks containing sodium, potassium and sugar replace the salts and energy lost, but they are not needed for ordinary activity and add empty kilocalories if used unnecessarily.
Diagram: an optional simple water balance diagram, with intake (drinks, food, metabolism) and output (urine, sweat, breath, faeces).
Nobody picks food in a vacuum. A food choice results from several pressures acting together, and each one can be named and explained on its own, with an example.
Culture: the shared customs and traditions of a group decide which foods are normal, acceptable or celebratory, and certain foods are linked with a particular country, tradition or festival.
Travel, television and immigration spread foods from one culture to another, so people often eat dishes that did not belong to their own country's tradition.
Religion: some faiths restrict foods, so a person's beliefs can rule certain foods out. Jews and Muslims do not eat pork, and some Hindus follow a vegetarian diet.
Eating patterns: the number and timing of meals, snacking, eating out and whether the family eats together all shape what is bought and eaten.
Irregular family routines change what is bought and cooked, because people who eat at different times tend to rely on quick foods rather than a shared cooked meal.
Sensory aspects: taste, smell, appearance, texture and temperature decide whether a food is accepted, and unfamiliar flavours are often refused at first.
Likes and dislikes, the way food is presented and early exposure to fatty, salty and sugary food shape preferences, which is why children who grow up on these foods often keep choosing them.
The remaining factors are about knowledge, the body, the shops and the money in a person's pocket. Name each factor, then explain it with an example in a sentence.
Nutritional awareness: knowledge of healthy eating guidelines and of food labels steers people towards lower-fat, lower-sugar and higher-fibre products, while low awareness leads to poorer choices.
Health status: allergies and intolerances, coeliac disease, diabetes, coronary heart disease, high blood pressure and weight management limit or direct what a person can safely eat.
Because of these conditions people buy foods such as lactose-free, gluten-free, low-cholesterol and allergy-safe products.
Availability: seasonal produce, the range stocked by local shops, the distance to a supermarket, access to a car and the foods sold in a school canteen or vending machine determine what is on offer.
Finance: income sets the budget. People with more money buy expensive foods more often, eat out and meet foreign foods on holidays.
People on low incomes tend to buy cheaper and more processed foods, own brands, special offers and inexpensive protein such as pulses, eggs and tinned fish.

Marketing and advertising: packaging, brand image, special offers, shelf placement, endorsements by celebrities or influencers and social media encourage purchases, and advertising to children and teenagers is especially influential.
Two further influences are examined even though they are not separate syllabus factors. They fit under eating patterns, availability, nutritional awareness and culture.
Convenience and lifestyle: lack of time or cooking skill increases the use of ready meals and takeaways, so busy households choose food that is quick to prepare.
Eating food away from home covers restaurants, cafés, hotels, takeaways, delicatessens and pub food. More people do it because they have more money and choice, less time and less cooking skill.
Health and wellbeing: people choose foods for health reasons, such as less fat, salt and sugar and more fibre, which is an example of nutritional awareness at work.

Responsible living: people also choose foods for ethical and environmental reasons, such as organic, Fairtrade, local and seasonal foods, less food waste, animal welfare and sustainability. These choices reflect personal values and culture.
Irish eating habits have changed a great deal over the last century. These changes describe the whole population over time, so they are trends such as more convenience food and less home cooking.
Potatoes and bread have been partly replaced by pasta, rice and a wider range of breads, because a wider food range has become available.
Convenience, ready-meal and processed foods have become more common, bringing more salt, sugar, saturated fat and additives and less fibre into the diet.
Eating out, takeaways and fast food have increased, as has eating on the go. This includes eating food away from home in restaurants, cafés, hotels, takeaways, delicatessens and pubs.
Meals have become more irregular: family members often eat at different times, so the main meal, now in the evening, is less often eaten together.
Foreign holidays, television, the internet, travel, immigration and food bloggers have introduced new cuisines and ingredients to Irish diets, such as ethnic cuisines.
Microwaving, stir-frying and barbecuing are now common cooking methods in Irish homes, and people also have less time for cooking at home.
Greater health and nutritional awareness has encouraged more fruit, vegetables, wholegrain, organic, functional and fortified foods.
Intermittent fasting and plant-based eating are recent trends, reflecting people's interest in health.
Very young children do not choose for themselves. Parents decide, and they weigh up several things.
Parents make most food choices for pre-school children, weighing nutrition and the food pyramid, cost, allergies and health, and the degree of processing.
They also consider a portion size suited to a small child, ease of handling, packaging and labelling, and family habits.
Young children often refuse new foods at first and may need to be offered a food many times before accepting it. This reluctance is called food neophobia.
Involving children in preparation and presenting food attractively encourages them to try new foods, because the food becomes familiar and appealing.
Teenagers start to make their own food decisions, and the influences on them are different from those on young children.
Teenagers' choices are influenced by peer groups, advertising and social media, independence and a wish to eat out.
They have money of their own from pocket money or part-time work, which gives them the buying power to choose for themselves.
Body image, convenience and busy lives also play a part in what teenagers choose.
Many teenagers prefer fatty, salty and sugary foods, which they have often been exposed to since early childhood.
A teenager may choose a vegetarian diet for cultural, religious, moral or ethical reasons such as animal welfare, or for health, environmental, economic or family reasons, or because of peers.
Culture and religion affect young people through foods linked with cultures, religious restrictions, travel, television, immigration and multicultural influences.
Students in school or living away from home share many teenage influences, but time, money and facilities limit what they can choose.
Students in post-primary school choose according to personal preference, cost, nutritional awareness, advertising and peers.
Health status and allergies, and activity level, also affect their choices.
The range sold in the canteen or vending machines, and whether there are facilities to reheat food, decide what is practical.
Students living away or on a budget face the same factors, with limited time, money and cooking skill, so they tend to choose quick, cheap foods.
Higher Level exams give a table or chart and ask you to comment on it. A clear routine earns the marks.
Describe the overall trend first, then support it with specific figures read from the data.
Compare two groups, such as parents and children or boys and girls, by stating which group is higher and by how much.
Suggest reasons for differences by drawing on the factors that shape food choices, because the data only shows what people choose, not why.

Relate the results to healthy eating guidelines, saying whether consumption meets them or falls short, for example whether five or more portions of fruit and vegetables a day (Department of Health Food Pyramid) are being reached.
Comment on what the results mean for planning meals or for health and health education.
These are practical contexts that help you practise applying the factors.
Comparing meal patterns between countries, such as when the main meal is eaten and how many meals are normal.
A theme day or week on the foods of a culture or period, such as a traditional Irish breakfast.
No two people need exactly the same diet. Energy and nutrient needs change with the stage of life and with circumstances, so every meal plan starts from the requirements of the person it is for.
A balanced diet contains all the nutrients in the correct proportions for the individual's needs and good health, so what counts as balanced differs from person to person.
Age: needs change at each life stage, with growth in childhood and adolescence, maintenance in adults and falling energy needs in older age.
Sex: men generally need more energy than women because they have greater muscle mass and a larger body, while girls and women need extra iron once menstruation begins.
Health status: illness, allergy, diabetes or a digestive disorder can change the foods a person is allowed to eat or how well their body absorbs nutrients.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding increase the need for energy, protein, folate, iron and calcium, because the body is building a baby or making milk.
Activity: energy needs rise with physical activity, and active people also need more fluid and carbohydrate. A sedentary adult needs less energy.
Energy balance: energy taken in as food should match energy used by the body; any surplus is stored as body fat.
A baby's first food and a young child's meals are planned around fast growth, a small stomach and teeth that are still forming. Pre-school guidelines are examined as short lists of practical rules.
Breast milk supplies all the nutrients a baby needs for about the first six months.
Breastfed babies, and babies taking little formula, are advised to take a vitamin D supplement from birth to 12 months, because breast milk contains little vitamin D.
Weaning (moving from milk to solid food) begins at about six months, when the iron stored at birth starts to run low. Puréed meat and iron-fortified cereals supply iron.
Salt should be kept low and sugar limited in foods for babies and young children, with none added to baby foods. Sugar harms developing teeth.

Pre-school children have small, variable appetites, so regular balanced meals in small, manageable portions with nutritious snacks between suit them better than large meals. Attractive presentation helps.
Young children need protein for growth, calcium and vitamin D for bones and teeth, iron for blood, and fruit and vegetables, following the Food Pyramid.
Fussy eating is common. Offering new flavours one at a time in small portions, without forcing a child to eat, and involving the child in food preparation, helps them accept new foods.
Sugary foods and drinks should be limited to protect developing teeth.
School-age children need every nutrient in balance, and adolescents need even more during the growth spurt. Teenage eating habits, though, often work against meeting those needs.

Children need every nutrient in balanced proportions, following the Irish Food Pyramid with portions suited to their age and activity. Protein is for growth, carbohydrate and fat for energy, calcium for bones and teeth, iron for blood, plus fibre and water, with nutritious snacks and less sugar and salt.
Ways to include vegetables for children: stir-fries, cut shapes, grated or blended into sauces, smoothies, soups, and vegetables in lunchboxes.
Adolescents go through a growth spurt, roughly between the ages of 12 and 19, which increases the need for every nutrient.

Girls need extra iron once they begin menstruating, because menstrual blood loss depletes iron stores. Fruit and vegetables supply fibre and vitamin C, and vitamin C improves the absorption of iron from plant foods, helping avoid anaemia.
Calcium and vitamin D build bone mass during adolescence, so good intake now builds peak bone mass and reduces the risk of osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) later.

Active teenagers need high-energy starchy foods such as pasta, potatoes, rice and wholegrain cereals. Protein from meat, fish, eggs, dairy and pulses (animal and plant sources) supports growth and repair.

High-salt, high-sugar and high-fat snacks and fizzy drinks add energy but few nutrients, so they should be limited. Irregular meals and skipped breakfasts are common in adolescence and make it harder to meet nutritional needs, so teenagers should eat three varied meals daily and avoid skipping meals, especially breakfast.

Factors making a healthy diet difficult for teenagers: likes and dislikes, early exposure to fatty, salty and sugary foods, convenience and eating on the go, availability, cost, advertising and peers.
Adult bodies are no longer growing, so the aim shifts to maintaining health and weight. The main guideline is to match what you eat to how active you are.
Adults need to balance energy intake with activity to maintain a healthy weight, and to eat a balanced diet with all the nutrients in proportion.
Daily starchy foods, fruit and vegetables supply the fibre, vitamins and minerals that support bowel health.
Protein maintains muscle and repairs tissue, so a protein food is included at each main meal.
Unsaturated oils should replace saturated fats, and sugar and salt should be kept low.
Women of childbearing age need adequate folate and iron, because menstrual losses continue.
A sedentary worker (one who sits most of the day) needs less energy, so should reduce fat and sugar, eat fibre-rich foods, get enough calcium, iron and vitamins, and limit salt.
Older bodies burn less energy but still need nearly as many nutrients, so food must be nutrient-dense. Practical problems with teeth, appetite and money also shape what older people can eat.

Energy needs fall with age because muscle mass and activity decline, so portions should be smaller but nutrient-dense (packed with nutrients per mouthful). Small, frequent, appetising meals suit reduced appetite, and fortified foods help.
Protein remains important for maintaining muscle and repairing tissue, so older people should include a protein food at main meals.
Calcium and vitamin D protect the bones, and calcium absorption decreases with age.
Vitamin B12 absorption can fall in later life, so older people may need B12 from fortified foods or supplements.
Fibre and fluid prevent constipation, which is common among older people who are less active. Iron and vitamin C are also needed.
Salt should be reduced to help control blood pressure, and saturated fat reduced.
Chewing and swallowing difficulties, or dentures, call for soft, moist and easy-to-chew foods. A limited budget and reduced mobility also affect shopping and cooking.
Diet-related conditions common in older people include osteoporosis, diabetes, coronary heart disease, high blood pressure and high cholesterol.

A pregnant woman's diet must feed her own body and build a baby, so the need for particular nutrients rises while food safety matters more. This is the group examined most often, usually as nutrient, reason and food source.

Folic acid (also called folate) taken before conception and in early pregnancy helps prevent neural-tube defects in the developing baby. Sources include green vegetables and fortified cereals, plus a supplement as advised.
Iron supports the extra blood volume of pregnancy and the baby's iron stores; vitamin C eaten at the same meal improves iron absorption.
Calcium and vitamin D are needed for the baby's bones and teeth and to protect the mother's bones.
Protein from lean meat, fish, fully cooked eggs and pasteurised dairy supports the growth of fetal tissue, the placenta and maternal tissues.
Omega-3 fatty acids from cooked oily fish, such as salmon, support the development of the baby's brain and nervous system. Iodine and vitamins A, C, D, K and folate are also needed.

Water is needed for blood plasma and fetal tissues, to carry nutrients and remove waste, and to prevent dehydration and constipation. Fibre also helps prevent constipation, which is common in pregnancy.

Energy needs rise only modestly, mainly in later pregnancy, so a pregnant woman should not double her food intake. She should balance food with activity, follow the Food Pyramid and choose low-GI starchy foods.
Breastfeeding women need extra energy, protein, calcium and fluid to produce milk.
Some foods carry bacteria that can harm an unborn baby, so pregnancy guidelines restrict them. Any menu for a pregnant woman must follow these rules.
Pâté, unpasteurised milk, soft mould-ripened cheese, and raw or undercooked meat, fish and eggs carry a risk of listeria or salmonella (food-poisoning bacteria) and should be avoided.
Alcohol should be avoided in pregnancy, and caffeine and salt should be limited.
Taste changes and morning sickness can be managed with dry toast before rising and small, frequent meals.
A sample one-day menu uses pasteurised dairy and fully cooked foods. Breakfast: fruit juice, porridge made with pasteurised milk and berries, wholemeal toast.
Lunch: vegetable soup, wholemeal bread, yoghurt and fruit. Dinner: well-cooked lean chicken or fish with vegetables and potatoes.
A convalescent is someone recovering from illness. Their appetite is low but their body needs nutrients to repair itself, so food must be light, appealing and nourishing.
Convalescents need small, appetising, easy-to-digest portions, because appetite is often reduced during recovery. Regular balanced meals are important.
Protein from lean meat, fish, eggs and dairy supports tissue repair.
Iron and vitamin C support recovery of blood levels, and vitamin C from fruit and vegetables aids iron absorption. Fibre-rich fruit and vegetables and fluids keep the bowel working.
Lightly seasoned meals are better tolerated; spicy, fried, oily and greasy foods should be avoided.
Active people burn more energy and lose fluid in sweat, so their diet is built around extra fuel and water.
Active people need extra energy, mainly from complex carbohydrates such as wholegrain bread, pasta, rice and potatoes.
Sweat losses mean active people need extra fluid, drunk before, during and after exercise.
Protein supports muscle repair and growth after exercise, and fruit, yoghurt or wholegrain sandwiches supply energy between meals.
Shift work and long or varied days disrupt normal mealtimes. Good planning keeps meals balanced even when no one is home at the usual time.
Irregular shifts disrupt mealtimes, so people often skip meals or rely on fast food and vending machines, which should be avoided.
Planning ahead with a list, and keeping staples and some frozen or prepared ingredients, makes balanced meals easier.
Batch cooking and freezing portions allows balanced meals to be eaten at staggered times without much last-minute preparation.
Soups, casseroles and other reheatable portions suit people eating at different times.
Packed lunches with fruit, wholegrain bread and yoghurt keep nutrition on track during long working days.
Slow cookers and timers allow a meal to cook while the household is out. Portions should stay balanced, following the guidelines.
Obesity develops when the energy taken in as food regularly exceeds the energy the body uses, and the surplus is stored as fat (adipose tissue).
Body mass index (BMI) is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. A BMI of 30 or more in adults is classed as obese, and 25 to under 30 as overweight.
Fatty and sugary foods are energy-dense, which means a small portion supplies a large amount of energy, so it is easy to take in more than the body needs.
Sugary drinks, cream sauces, fried foods, large portions, snacking, late-night eating, too much processed food and a low-fibre diet all increase energy intake.
Not all causes are dietary. Inactivity, heredity, stress and emotional eating also contribute, and a sedentary lifestyle means less energy is used up.
Obesity increases the risk of coronary heart disease, Type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and gallstones, as well as joint strain and arthritis, breathing problems and low self-esteem.
Weight-loss guidance is a balanced low-energy diet: lower fat (especially saturated fat), reduced sugar and salt, extra fibre, fruit, vegetables and water, lean protein and less processed food.

Low-fat cooking methods, removing visible fat from meat, avoiding cream sauces, smaller portions, avoiding alcohol and late-night eating, and regular exercise all help, because they cut energy in and raise energy used.

Coronary heart disease (CHD) happens when the coronary arteries, which supply the heart muscle with blood, become narrowed or blocked by fatty deposits (atherosclerosis), which can cause angina or a heart attack.
Saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol, which is deposited in artery walls and narrows them, so less blood reaches the heart muscle.
Trans fats, found in some hard margarines and in fried and processed foods, raise LDL and lower HDL cholesterol, so they are doubly harmful.
Refined carbohydrates and sugar contribute to raised blood triglycerides (blood fats), reduced HDL cholesterol and weight gain.
Excess salt raises blood pressure, which damages artery walls and makes the heart work harder.
A diet low in fibre, fruit and vegetables offers little protection against CHD, because these foods help lower blood cholesterol.
Other causes are smoking, lack of exercise, obesity, excess alcohol, stress, high blood pressure, heredity, age and gender.

Cholesterol is a soft, wax-like substance found in every body cell. The liver makes most of it, with some coming from animal foods. It forms part of cell membranes and bile, is needed to make some hormones, and helps transport fats in the blood.

LDL cholesterol (associated with saturated fat) deposits cholesterol in artery walls, hardening and narrowing them. HDL cholesterol (associated with unsaturated fat) carries cholesterol away from the arteries to the liver.
Diabetes means the level of glucose in the blood is raised. It happens because of a problem with insulin, a hormone made by the pancreas that lets glucose move from the blood into body cells.

Type 1 diabetes (insulin-dependent): the pancreas produces little or no insulin. It often starts in childhood, adolescence or young adulthood, may be hereditary, is controlled with insulin, diet and exercise, and cannot be reversed.

Type 2 diabetes (non-insulin-dependent): insulin is produced but cells respond poorly to it, or too little is made. It usually develops later in life, although some young people now develop it, and it accounts for about 90 per cent of cases.
Excess weight and inactivity are the main risk factors for Type 2 diabetes. Diets high in sugar and refined carbohydrate, combined with excess weight, raise the risk. Sugar alone is not the cause.
Type 2 can often be controlled with diet, weight loss, exercise and tablets, so losing weight can improve it.
Gestational diabetes develops during pregnancy and usually resolves after the birth.
Symptoms include frequent urination, thirst, hunger, weight loss and tiredness. Long-term complications can affect the eyes, kidneys, nerves and heart.
A diet low in fibre and fluid makes stools hard and dry, and the effort of passing them puts the large intestine under strain. Several bowel problems follow from this in a chain.
Constipation: hard, dry stools are passed with difficulty, usually caused by too little fibre and fluid and too little activity.
Diverticular disease: small pouches called diverticula form in the wall of the large intestine when the pressure from straining pushes the lining outwards.
Diverticulitis: inflamed or infected diverticula cause pain and need medical treatment.
Haemorrhoids: swollen veins around the anus, caused by straining during constipation.
A low-fibre diet also raises the risk of bowel disorders, including bowel cancer.

Prevention: eat wholegrain cereals, brown bread, wholegrain rice, pulses, nuts and seeds, and fruit and vegetables with their skins on, eaten raw where possible, because skins and raw plant foods keep most of their fibre.
Whole fruit and vegetables supply more fibre than juice, and fresh or dried fruit is a better snack than processed alternatives. Plenty of fluid, exercise and regular meals also help.
A high-fibre diet reduces the risk of bowel disease.
Bones are living tissue that is built up in childhood and lost slowly in later life. Osteoporosis is a thinning and weakening of the bone, which becomes porous, brittle and prone to fracture.
Bone mass peaks in early adulthood, after which bone is gradually lost, so building strong bones in childhood and adolescence gives a bigger store to draw on later.
Too little calcium, vitamin D, vitamin C or phosphorus over life raises the risk. Vitamin D helps the gut absorb calcium, and vitamin C is needed for the collagen framework of bone.
Phytates, oxalates, excess fibre and tannins in some foods can reduce calcium absorption, because they bind calcium in the gut.
Excess caffeine and alcohol increase calcium loss, and excess saturated fat can also reduce calcium availability.
Risk factors include older age, the fall in oestrogen after menopause (which puts women at higher risk), smoking and inactivity.
Weight-bearing exercise helps to maintain bone strength.

Prevention: increase calcium, vitamin D, vitamin C and phosphorus in the diet, build bone in childhood and adolescence, take weight-bearing exercise, and limit the inhibitors of calcium absorption listed above.
Teeth are damaged by acid made from sugar in the mouth. Dental caries (tooth decay) and gum disease are separate problems, although both start with plaque.
Bacteria in plaque ferment sugars in the mouth to produce acid, which dissolves enamel and causes dental caries.
Frequent snacking, sticky sweets and sugary drinks keep the mouth acidic for longer, which increases the risk of decay.
Fluoride strengthens enamel and makes it more resistant to acid; fluoride toothpaste is used twice a day.
Calcium, phosphorus and vitamin D support the formation of enamel and dentine, the teeth's hard tissues.
Periodontal (gum) disease is inflammation of the gums and the tissues around the teeth, caused by a build-up of plaque.
Protection: limit sugary food to mealtimes, brush, have dental check-ups, and eat cheese and crunchy fruit and vegetables.
Diet problems rarely come singly. A surplus of one nutrient or too little of another can lead to several conditions, and some conditions lead on to others.
Excess energy leads to obesity, which increases the risk of Type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease and high blood pressure.
Excess salt raises blood pressure, which increases the risk of coronary heart disease.
A diet high in sugar contributes to both obesity and dental caries.
A low-fibre, low-fluid diet can cause constipation, which in turn can lead to diverticular disease.
Too little calcium and vitamin D leads to osteoporosis, and too little iron leads to anaemia.
A poor diet in a teenager can cause several problems at once: overweight, CHD risk, tooth decay, constipation, anaemia, diabetes risk and osteoporosis later.

Coronary heart disease (CHD) is the narrowing of the coronary arteries, the vessels feeding the heart muscle, by fatty deposits. The aim of the CHD diet is to lower LDL cholesterol and blood pressure and to reduce the strain on the heart and arteries.

Replace saturated animal fats with mono- and polyunsaturated oils such as olive, rapeseed and sunflower oil, because saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol, the type that clogs arteries. Use low-cholesterol products where possible.
Choose low-fat dairy products and lean meat, and trim visible fat from meat before cooking. Eat more fish and skinless chicken in place of fatty red meat.
Eat oily fish such as salmon, mackerel and sardines, which supply omega-3 fatty acids.
Increase soluble fibre from oats, beans, lentils, fruit and vegetables, which helps lower LDL cholesterol. Eat more fruit and vegetables in general.
Reduce salt, which helps keep blood pressure down, and use herbs, spices and lemon juice for flavour.
Reduce refined carbohydrate and sugar, such as white bread, sugary foods and sugary drinks, and reduce alcohol.
Use low-fat cooking methods: grill, bake, steam or boil food rather than frying it, avoid creamy sauces, and skim fat from stock and gravy.
A sample day's menu: porridge with low-fat milk and fruit; a wholegrain sandwich with chicken and salad; grilled oily fish with vegetables and potatoes; low-fat yoghurt or fruit.
Cholesterol is the substance behind the CHD diet. The body needs some of it, but the type and amount in the blood decide whether it helps or harms the arteries.
Cholesterol is a soft, wax-like substance found in every body cell, made mainly by the liver and also obtained from animal foods.
Cholesterol forms part of cell membranes and bile, is needed for some hormones, and helps transport fats in the blood.
Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) is associated with saturated fat and deposits cholesterol in artery walls, hardening them. This is why LDL is called the harmful cholesterol.
High-density lipoprotein (HDL) is associated with unsaturated fat and carries cholesterol away from the arteries to the liver.
Lifestyle changes that reduce CHD risk include maintaining a healthy weight, not smoking, avoiding excess alcohol, exercising regularly and reducing stress.
Some foods are designed to do more than feed you. These functional foods can be added to a CHD menu to help protect the heart.
A functional food has health benefits beyond its basic nutritive value, so it does more than supply energy and nutrients.
Plant sterol and stanol spreads, yoghurts, cheese spreads and drinks reduce cholesterol absorption and so lower LDL cholesterol.
Omega-3 enriched eggs and milk supply omega-3 fatty acids.
Prebiotic and probiotic milk and yoghurt improve digestion.
Fortified foods have vitamins and minerals added to them, so they supply nutrients the diet may otherwise lack.
A lacto-vegetarian eats no meat, poultry, fish or eggs, but includes milk and dairy products. Without meat, careful choices are needed to get enough protein, iron, calcium and vitamins.

Protein comes from milk, cheese and yoghurt (high biological value protein), and from pulses, nuts, seeds, soya products such as tofu and textured vegetable protein (TVP), and mycoprotein. Combining plant proteins across the day gives a good range of amino acids.
Calcium comes from milk, yoghurt and cheese, and from green leafy vegetables, sesame seeds and fortified soya products. Vitamin D, vitamin C and phosphorus help calcium absorption.
Iron comes from green leafy vegetables, pulses, wholegrains, dried fruit and fortified cereals; vitamin C from fruit and vegetables at the same meal improves absorption.
Vitamin B12 comes from dairy products, vitamin B group from wholegrains, and vitamin D from fortified spreads and cereals and from sunlight. Omega-3 fats come from flaxseed, walnuts and rapeseed oil.
Some cheeses are made with animal rennet, and some mycoprotein products contain egg white, so labels must be checked.
Eggs are excluded, so the diet relies on dairy and pulses for protein and on fortified foods for nutrients that eggs would normally supply.

Other types of vegetarian: lacto-ovo includes eggs and dairy, ovo includes eggs, and pesco includes fish. Some sources also allow eggs in a lacto-vegetarian diet, but the strict definition is dairy yes, eggs no.

People become vegetarian for religious, cultural, moral, health, economic or environmental reasons. A sample day: orange juice, porridge with milk and wholemeal toast; vegetable soup, brown bread, yoghurt and fruit; vegetarian lasagne or a lentil dish with green vegetables.

A vegan diet excludes all animal-derived foods, including meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, cheese and honey. Because dairy and eggs are gone too, a vegan must plan protein, calcium, iron and vitamin B12 from plant and fortified sources.
Protein comes from pulses, nuts, seeds, soya products, vegan mycoprotein, seitan and tempeh; eating pulses with grains or nuts over the day provides all the essential amino acids.
Vitamin B12 has no reliable plant source, so it must come from fortified foods such as soya milk, cereals and yeast extract, or from a supplement.
Calcium comes from fortified soya milk and flour, calcium-set tofu, sesame seeds in tahini, nuts, vegan cheese, and broccoli, spinach and other dark green vegetables.
Iron comes from pulses, wholegrains, dried fruit, dark green vegetables and fortified cereals; vitamin C from peppers, tomatoes, berries and citrus improves absorption.
Vitamin D comes from fortified foods and sunlight, and omega-3 fats from flaxseed, walnuts and rapeseed oil.

Hidden animal ingredients can turn up in stock cubes, some spreads, some bread and sweets (gelatine) and in cheese made with rennet, so choose labelled vegan products and check for gelatine, milk powder, egg, rennet or honey.
A vegan menu example uses vegan mycoprotein mince, lentils or beans, vegetables and fruit, which excludes animal products and still supplies protein, iron, calcium and fortified B12.
Coeliac disease is a lifelong intolerance to gluten, the protein found in wheat, barley and rye. The only treatment is a strict gluten-free diet.
Gluten damages the villi, the finger-like lining of the small intestine, so food is not properly absorbed and deficiencies of iron, calcium and folate can develop.

Avoid bread, cakes, biscuits, pastries, pizzas and pies made with wheat, ordinary pasta and couscous, seitan, and processed foods such as sausages, some soups, sauces and gravies. Wheat, barley, rye and malt are all sources of gluten.

Build meals around naturally gluten-free staples such as rice, corn (maize), potatoes, buckwheat, soya products and lentils, plus meat, fish, eggs, dairy, fruit and vegetables. Gluten-free versions of bread, pasta and flour are also available.
Check ingredient lists for hidden gluten in stock, sauces, malt products and processed meats, and look for the gluten-free symbol or declaration on products.
A gluten-free claim means the food as sold contains no more than 20 mg of gluten per kilogram (Regulation (EU) No 828/2014, FSAI guidance). Wheat and oats used must still appear in the ingredients.

Avoid cross-contamination in the kitchen, for example by using a separate toaster and utensils, so crumbs of gluten do not reach safe food. Oats are naturally gluten-free but often contaminated, so use only oats labelled gluten-free.
Gluten-free breads and cereals are often low in fibre, so choose brown rice, beans and other high-fibre gluten-free foods.
Replace the iron, calcium and folate normally supplied by wheat products with other naturally gluten-free or fortified sources.

The diabetic diet aims to keep blood glucose stable, maintain a healthy weight and reduce the risk of heart disease. It does not mean no carbohydrate; it means carbohydrate that is low-GI, regular and controlled.
Regular meals and snacks at set times prevent large swings in blood glucose; skipping meals is avoided.
Low-glycaemic-index (GI) carbohydrates such as wholegrain bread, oats, pasta and pulses release glucose slowly, so blood glucose rises gradually. High-fibre foods and plenty of vegetables also help.
Refined sugar, sugar-sweetened soft drinks, sweets and sugar-laden processed foods are avoided or limited, and low-calorie sweeteners can replace sugar.
Fibre-rich fruit and vegetables and low-sugar fruits are chosen, as high-sugar fruit should be limited.
Saturated fat and salt are reduced, and unsaturated oils are used instead, because diabetes raises the risk of heart disease. Keeping a healthy weight and exercising also help.
Insulin dose is matched to the carbohydrate eaten in people using insulin, so meal timing and portions must be consistent.
People on modified diets need suitable foods that are easy to find and easy to use. Manufacturers and retailers both respond to this.
Manufacturers produce specialised ranges such as gluten-free, diabetic, vegetarian and coronary heart disease products.
Manufacturers give detailed labels and packet recipes, and offer smaller portion sizes for people who need them.
Retailers provide specialist shops or sections, designated shelves and wider ranges of special-diet foods, so customers can find suitable products quickly.
Retailers run in-store cookery demonstrations to show customers how to use special-diet products, and provide information and websites.
Labels let people on special diets check quickly whether a food is suitable. What the label shows, and how far it can be trusted, is what exams focus on.
The name of the food and ingredients must be listed in descending order of weight, so the main ingredients are easy to identify.
Under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014, allergens must be highlighted in the ingredient list.
Nutrition information shows the energy, fat, saturated fat, sugar, salt and fibre content of the food.
Symbols and claims show gluten-free, vegetarian and vegan status and whether a food is fortified, functional, low-fat or reduced-sugar, which helps people with specific needs choose.
Labels give cooking and storage instructions, the net quantity, the use-by or best-before date, the origin and any GM ingredients, helping people choose foods safely.
Labels are useful but must be read critically: claims can mislead, small print can hide gluten, and 'may contain' warnings need checking.

Ireland's national guide to healthy eating is the Department of Health healthy eating guidelines and the Healthy Eating Food Pyramid, published under Healthy Ireland. A balanced diet follows the pyramid, so it contains all the nutrients in the correct proportions.
Vegetables, salad and fruit, together with wholemeal cereals, breads, potatoes, pasta and rice, make up the foundation shelves of the pyramid, so these are the foods eaten most often.
Fruit and vegetables: five or more servings a day are recommended, and up to seven, because they supply vitamins, minerals and fibre.
Milk, yoghurt and cheese, preferably the lower-fat versions, supply calcium and protein; three servings a day are given in menu answers.
Meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans, pulses and nuts supply protein; two servings a day, and at least two portions of fish a week are advised, one of them oily fish.
Fats, spreads and oils sit on a small shelf and are used in small amounts, with unsaturated oils preferred to saturated fat.

The top shelf holds foods and drinks high in fat, sugar and salt. They are not needed for health, so they are limited to once or twice a week at most; sugary drinks are limited too, and water is the main drink.
Salt intake is kept low by cooking with less salt and reading labels, and portion sizes are controlled so that energy intake is balanced with activity.
When planning, choose wholegrain, lean meat and lower-fat dairy, vary the foods eaten, and use less salt and sugar.
Good planning starts with who is being fed and ends with a plan for cooking. Meals are then chosen so that the whole day, not just one meal, matches the pyramid.
Planning begins with the people being fed: their ages, health needs, activity, likes and dislikes, any special diets, and the number to feed.
Each meal includes a starchy food, fruit or vegetables, and a protein food or dairy, so that all the pyramid groups are covered across the day.
Breakfast is not skipped, because it supplies energy for the morning, and a packed lunch or snack supplies fruit and wholegrain foods between meals.
Colour, flavour, texture and cooking method are varied, and the same food is not repeated in a day, so that meals are appetising and not repetitive.
Portion sizes are matched to age, appetite and activity, and energy is balanced across the day.
A three-meal menu sets out breakfast, lunch and dinner, often with a drink or snack. Name actual dishes, then show how they meet the person's needs.

The steps in planning are: 1. decide the menus for the week. 2. Check the food and equipment already at home. 3. Write a shopping list. 4. Buy the food. 5. Schedule the cooking order and timing, after checking cooking time, budget and equipment.
When a question names a person such as a pregnant woman, teenager, vegetarian, coeliac or person with CHD (coronary heart disease), apply that group's requirements to the menu.
The cook's own ability decides which meals are realistic. Skill affects both what can be made and how consistent the results are.
A skilled cook can adapt recipes, for example to add fibre, reduce fat or cater for a special diet, and can make dishes from raw ingredients.
A less experienced cook may rely on convenience foods, so simple recipes with few stages suit them.
Following a tested recipe with accurate measures gives consistent results and portion sizes.
Nutrition knowledge, such as reading labels and knowing the guidelines, helps a cook choose healthy meals, and skills can be built by cooking with others.
Time available on the day decides how elaborate a meal can be. Planning ahead lets a busy household still eat well.
Dishes are chosen to suit the time available; quick dishes such as stir-fries, omelettes, soups and grills suit a limited preparation time.
Batch cooking large quantities and freezing portions saves time on later days, because a meal is ready after reheating.
Time can also be saved by preparing ahead, using convenience foods sensibly, and cooking one meal in stages.
For families with irregular routines, keep a shopping list and staple stocks, and use bulk buying and special offers sensibly.

For irregular routines, also keep some prepared or frozen ingredients and reheatable, freezable batches, use a slow cooker or timer, and pack meals, while keeping the diet balanced and portions sensible.
The equipment in the kitchen decides which cooking methods are possible. The right appliances also save both time and energy.

Equipment available decides what can be cooked: oven, hob, grill, microwave, pressure cooker, slow cooker, food processor, blender and freezer. A lack of equipment limits the methods that can be used.
A microwave, pressure cooker, slow cooker or food processor reduces cooking and preparation time; microwave reheating also saves energy.
A freezer permits batch cooking and bulk buying, because portions and large purchases can be stored until needed.
Frozen foods keep their nutritional and sensory quality, and frozen fruit and vegetables are frozen at peak ripeness, retain most of their nutrients and reduce waste.
Frozen foods also save time and money, add variety and out-of-season foods, allow portion control and make emergency meals possible.
Freezers should be kept at -18 °C, and cooked food should not be left between 5 °C and 63 °C, the range in which bacteria multiply quickly.
A limited budget does not have to mean a poor diet if meals are planned before shopping. Low-income families have limited choice, so careful planning matters most for them.
Set a budget, plan menus before shopping, and write a shopping list and keep to it. This prevents impulse buying and waste.
Compare prices, including unit prices, and use special offers sensibly. Bulk buying suits only foods that will be used or frozen.
Seasonal produce is usually cheaper and fresher than out-of-season imports.
Own-brand products are often cheaper than branded equivalents; compare labels and unit prices.
Pulses, eggs and tinned fish are inexpensive sources of protein, as are less expensive cuts of meat, and growing food or batch cooking can also cut costs.
Cheap processed foods are often high in salt, sugar and fat, so budget plans should still include fresh produce, wholegrains and milk.
Foods are chosen for nutritive value, cost, availability and season, suitability for the people (age, health), preparation time and storage, and labels and dates are checked.
Food is stored so that it stays safe and usable: in the fridge, freezer or cupboard, with a vegetable drawer for vegetables, and with stock rotation.
Food that is thrown away is money wasted. Planning, correct storage and understanding dates on packs all cut waste and the food bill.
Plan meals and shop with a list, check what is already at home, and buy only what is needed.
A use-by date relates to food safety and food must not be eaten after it; a best-before date relates to quality, and food may still be safe after it.
Stock is rotated so that older items are used first.
Food is stored correctly, and food that will not be used in time is frozen before its use-by date.
Leftovers are planned into the next day's meals, for example turning a roast into soup or a pie, and the right portions are cooked; scraps can be composted.
Reducing waste saves money and reduces environmental harm, such as landfill and greenhouse gas emissions.

The food industry takes raw produce from farms and fisheries, processes it into finished goods, and distributes and sells them through a service sector. It is organised in three levels, each depending on the one before it: a processor needs farmers' produce, and a retailer needs the processor's goods.

Primary sector: resource-based production, meaning farming, horticulture (growing fruit, vegetables and similar crops), fishing and fish farming (mariculture). It produces raw materials such as milk, cattle, sheep, pigs, poultry, eggs, grain, fruit, vegetables, fish and shellfish.

Secondary sector: manufacturing and processing, which converts raw materials into finished food and drink, such as milk into cheese, butter and milk powder, wheat into flour and bread, carcasses into cuts and meat products, or barley into beer and whiskey.

Tertiary sector: services that move, sell, support and regulate food, including transport, wholesale and retail, catering and food outlets, tourism and hospitality, research, education, advice, marketing and regulation.

Agri-food is one of Ireland's largest indigenous industries (industries that grew up in Ireland rather than being brought in from abroad), and most of its raw material is grown or reared on Irish farms.
The industry matters to the economy because it provides employment, much of it in rural areas, and earns income from export sales.
The UK and other EU member states are the main markets for Irish food overall, and much dairy and beef output is exported.
Besides the three levels, the industry is divided into product sectors. A single sector such as dairy can contain primary, secondary and tertiary activity, so keep the two lists apart.
Dairy and ingredients: milk, cheese, butter, yoghurt, cream and milk powder, plus dairy ingredients sold to other food manufacturers.
Meat and livestock: beef, lamb, pork and poultry, slaughtered and processed in licensed meat plants.
Beverages: beer and stout, whiskey and other spirits, fruit juice and bottled water.
Horticulture: fruit, vegetables and mushrooms, sold fresh or processed.
Seafood: fish and shellfish landed at Irish ports and processed for home and export sale.
Cereals and bakery: flour milling, bread, biscuits and breakfast cereals.
Prepared consumer foods: ready meals, snacks, confectionery and sauces sold in retail packaging.

Ireland produces far more of some foods than its small population can eat, so these are sold abroad. A climate and soil suited to grass means livestock and dairy output is much larger than home demand.
Dairy products, especially cheese, butter, milk powder and infant formula ingredients, are among Ireland's largest food exports.
Beef and lamb are exported to EU and non-EU markets.
Pork, poultry and processed meat products are also exported.
Irish whiskey, beer and stout are exported.
Seafood, including shellfish and farmed salmon, is exported from Irish ports.
Prepared foods and bakery products are sold to retailers and food service companies abroad.

Ireland imports foods it cannot grow, cannot grow all year round, or chooses to buy in for variety and price. Reasons include climate (tropical crops), seasonal gaps, consumer demand for variety and ethnic foods, ingredients for manufacturers and feed for livestock.
Tropical and out-of-season fruit, such as bananas, pineapples, oranges and avocados, which Ireland cannot grow commercially.
Coffee, tea and cocoa, which are grown in warmer countries.
Spices and sugar, which Ireland does not produce in quantity.
Soya and other animal feed ingredients used by Irish livestock producers.
Wine, and some processed foods such as chocolate and confectionery.
Rice, dried pasta, some vegetables and herbs, and sauces are also imported.
Ireland also imports some foods it exports, such as cheeses and meat products, for variety and price, so trade runs both ways.
Ireland is a net exporter of food overall, so the value of exports is greater than the value of imports.
Several State bodies support, develop and regulate the food industry. Each has its own job, so learn each name together with one function.
Bord Bia (the Irish Food Board) promotes Irish food, drink and horticulture at home and abroad, and develops national and international markets for Irish products.
Bord Bia runs quality assurance schemes for food producers, such as the Sustainable Beef and Lamb Assurance Scheme and the Sustainable Dairy Assurance Scheme, shown by a quality mark on pack.
Bord Bia's Origin Green programme records and verifies the sustainability commitments of food and drink companies: companies set measurable targets and their progress is independently verified.
Bord Bia helps Irish food companies with market research, buyer introductions and trade fairs.
Teagasc, the agriculture and food development authority, provides research, advice and training for farmers and food producers, so they can improve what they grow and make.
Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM), the seafood development agency, develops the seafood sector and promotes seafood at home and abroad.
Enterprise Ireland supports export growth and innovation in Irish companies, including food and drink firms.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) sets and enforces food safety standards across the sector.
The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine is the government department responsible for the sector, covering policy and schemes.
A local factory, business or home enterprise can be used to show how a food business fits into the industry structure. Work through the same set of questions for whichever business you choose.
Identify the business's sector, such as dairy, meat, beverages or bakery, and whether its main activity is primary, secondary or tertiary.
Record its raw materials, where they come from, and the finished products it makes.
Note its markets: local shops and customers, other Irish retailers, or export markets.
Assess its contribution to the area through jobs, local suppliers and the income it brings to rural communities, which is why the industry matters locally.
List the careers it offers, such as production operative, technologist, quality staff, chef or sales and marketing roles.

Not every food business is a large factory. Small food businesses produce in small quantities, often family-run and rural, for local or niche (specialised) markets, and a home enterprise is the smallest kind.
A small business produces in small quantities and sells locally or to a niche market, which is why it is often family-run and based in a rural area.

A home enterprise (also called a cottage industry) is a small food business started and run from a domestic kitchen or a small unit near the home, for example making jams, chutneys, baking, chocolate or honey.

An artisan producer makes food in limited quantities by traditional, non-industrial skills and hand methods, such as hand-baked bread, farmhouse cheese or chutneys. Cashel Blue (Co. Tipperary) and Gubbeen (Co. Cork) are Irish farmhouse cheeses.

Speciality foods are produced in small quantities for a particular market by small businesses or home enterprises, often with local ingredients, little or no additives and a traditional or natural image. Examples include cheese, chutney, jam, honey, bread, home baking, smoked fish, chocolate, yoghurt and ice cream.
Speciality foods also include foods made for special diets, such as gluten-free (for coeliacs), vegan or diabetic foods, and organic foods.
Artisan describes how a food is made (by hand, using traditional skills), while speciality describes the product and its market. The two overlap, and neither is a legally protected term.
Small producers often sell through farmers' markets, food fairs, local shops, restaurants and online, and direct to customers.
Many small producers start from a home kitchen and move to a dedicated unit as demand and production grow.
The role of small producers is what they contribute to the food industry and to the country. Each contribution below is a separate point you can develop.
They create employment, often in rural areas where other jobs are limited, which helps keep rural communities alive.
They build a skilled workforce, because staff in small firms often handle every stage of production and so learn every stage.
They diversify the industry by making products that large manufacturers do not produce, and they bring out new exclusive ranges as markets change.
They identify and enter old and new niche markets, meeting consumer demand for local, natural, traditional or special-diet foods.
They use locally produced ingredients, which supports local farmers and suppliers and reduces food miles (the distance food travels from producer to consumer).
They promote quality ingredients and innovation, and work to very high standards of hygiene.
They strengthen Ireland's reputation for high-quality food and drink, and promote the region they are based in.
They support rural communities and farm diversification (farmers earning extra income by making food products rather than selling raw produce only).

Why consumers buy speciality foods is a different question from what small producers contribute to the industry. Features that attract consumers, such as variety, few additives and hand-made quality, are things mass-produced food does not give them.
Consumers want greater product variety and flavour than mass-produced food offers, with recipes that large manufacturers do not make.
There is little or no use of additives, so the foods are seen as natural, less processed or healthier. This is a perception, not a guarantee.
Foods are hand-made with close attention to each batch, using traditional skills, which gives them a quality, premium image and a natural, traditional look.
Many consumers are interested in provenance (where food comes from) and traceability, such as knowing the named farm or maker and the Irish origin of the ingredients.
Consumers want to support local producers and jobs, and sustainability through fewer food miles and organic or sustainable methods, including support for local goods in a recession.
There are more routes to market: farmers' markets, food festivals and food tourism, specialist shops, restaurants, supermarkets that stock local lines, online selling, media coverage and food awards.
There is growing demand for special-diet foods (coeliac, vegan, diabetic), which small producers can supply in small runs.
Changing food culture, through travel and multicultural eating, has increased interest in different and unusual foods.
Small producers rarely start big. They grow step by step, helped by consumer demand and by public bodies that give training and advice.
Rising consumer demand for local, speciality and traditional foods has encouraged new small producers to start.
Farmers' markets and food festivals give small producers a direct route to customers without a large distributor, so they can test products cheaply.

Local Enterprise Offices (LEOs), a network of offices run through the local authorities (31 teams), give start-up and development supports to small businesses: training, business courses, mentoring, advice and networking.
Food supports include the Food Starter Programme for people at the idea stage, and the Food Academy, which gives training and mentoring to new food companies and is run with Bord Bia.
Bord Bia and Enterprise Ireland give food companies, including smaller firms, market development and export advice.
The typical growth path is to start at a farmers' market or from the kitchen, move to local shops, then to supermarkets or export, and move from the home kitchen to a registered unit as demand grows.
Making food at home or on a small scale does not lessen the need for safety. A small producer must follow the same food law as a large company, though the paperwork can be scaled to the business.
A new food business, including one run from home, must register with the competent authority (the official body in charge) before it starts trading.
For most businesses, such as bakers, caterers and jam and chutney makers, the competent authority is the HSE Environmental Health Service, which inspects the premises for food safety and hygiene.

The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine registers premises handling foods of animal origin such as meat, dairy and eggs. Seafood premises are registered with the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority.

EU food hygiene law, Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, is given effect in Ireland by the European Communities (Hygiene of Foodstuffs) Regulations 2006. It requires every food business to operate a food safety management system based on HACCP principles.

HACCP identifies the points in production where food safety hazards could occur and sets controls for each one. For a small producer the system can be simple and proportionate to the size and nature of the business, so the standards are the same but the paperwork is scaled.
Prepackaged food must carry the information required by Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.

The required label details are the name of the food, ingredients with allergens emphasised, the business's name and address, date marking and storage instructions. Small firms follow the same labelling rules.
Traceability means producers must know their suppliers and customers, one step back and one step forward (Regulation (EC) No 178/2002), so that a problem food can be traced and recalled.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) provides guidance, including a guide to food law for artisan and small food producers, and food safety training to small food businesses.

Food reaches us through a chain of jobs, from growing and rearing it, through processing and packing, to testing that it is safe. Each job in the chain has a different focus, so learn what each person actually does.
Primary producers supply the raw food, so they come first in the chain: the farmer, the fisherman or fish farmer, and the horticulturist or grower (who produces fruit, vegetables and plants).
Miller, butcher, baker, confectioner, cheesemaker and brewer or distiller are craft and processing trades, found in small businesses such as retail shops or in food manufacturing.
Production operative: runs and monitors processing and packaging machinery on a food production line, so that products are made and packed to a steady standard.
Food technologist: develops new products and processes, and improves recipes and methods for shelf life (how long food stays safe and fresh) and quality.
Quality control technician: tests raw materials and finished products against specifications (the standards set for the product) and food safety standards.
Food microbiologist: tests food and production surfaces for microbes (micro-organisms) that cause spoilage or food poisoning.

Food engineer and food scientist (for example in process, packaging and research): design, run and maintain processing and packaging plant, and improve products, so that it operates safely and efficiently.
Agricultural scientist and agricultural adviser: research and advise on crop and livestock production, food quality and farm efficiency.
These are the jobs where food is prepared, served and sold to the public. Some work in the kitchen, some face the customer, and some run the business or buy the supplies.
Chef: plans menus, prepares, cooks and presents food in restaurants, hotels, hospitals and other institutions, so chefs work wherever meals are served in volume.
Caterer: plans and delivers food for events, canteens and institutions such as hospitals and schools, so the food is made for a group rather than one table.
Waiter or waitress, bar staff and receptionist: front-of-house service, meaning the staff who deal directly with customers, serving food and drink and taking orders in hotels, restaurants and bars.
Hotel or restaurant manager: runs the business and controls costs, stock and staffing for a food and accommodation business, so the business stays profitable.
Deli counter assistant, retail and sales assistant: serve customers in shops. The buyer sources ingredients, products and packaging from suppliers at the required quality and price.
Food stylist, food writer or journalist, and marketing and sales staff: promote food products to retailers, consumers and export markets (sales abroad).
Some food careers focus on people's health and on keeping the food supply safe and lawful. Two of them, dietitian and nutritionist, are easy to confuse, so note exactly how they differ.

Dietitian: assesses nutritional needs and plans diets for individuals and groups, including people with illness or special needs. It is a protected title, so only people registered with the Dietitians Registration Board at CORU may use it.
The Dietitians Registration Board was set up under the Health and Social Care Professionals Act 2005, and the title dietitian has been protected since 31 October 2016.

Nutritionist: gives advice on healthy eating, often in public health, sport or the food industry, for example advising an athlete on diet. Unlike dietitian, the title is not protected by law in Ireland.

Home Economics teacher: teaches food, nutrition and family and consumer studies in second-level schools, so the career suits someone who wants to pass on these skills. The route is a degree and a teaching qualification, with registration with the Teaching Council.

Environmental Health Officer (EHO): inspects food premises and enforces food hygiene law. EHOs also take samples, investigate complaints and outbreaks, and can serve improvement and closure notices. In Ireland, EHOs working on food are employed by the HSE Environmental Health Service.
Food safety scientist: tests and assesses food safety risks for regulators, producers and retailers. The public analyst does laboratory testing of food.

Veterinary inspectors in the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine carry out official control of meat and dairy. Sea-fisheries inspectors work for the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority and cover seafood.
Food careers are found in many kinds of workplace, and there is more than one way in. Employers range from factories to state bodies, and routes range from apprenticeships to degrees.
Employers include food manufacturers and processors; retailers and supermarkets; hotels, restaurants and caterers; hospitals and schools; schools and colleges; and people who run their own business.

State bodies employ scientists, advisers, inspectors and marketing staff. They include Bord Bia, Teagasc, Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM), the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI), the HSE, and the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine.

Entry routes include apprenticeships (for example chef), further education and training such as PLC and other certificate courses, and third-level degrees in food science, dietetics, culinary arts, Home Economics or environmental health.
Other routes are on-the-job training, where a worker learns the skills while employed, and experience gained through a family business, such as a family bakery or farm.

Most food careers need knowledge of hygiene and food safety, teamwork, communication, attention to detail, and an interest in food. Hygiene knowledge matters because food workers handle food that others will eat.
When studying a local business, list the careers it offers, for example production staff, technician, driver, sales, administrator and chef, and the qualifications each needs.
Meat is not one food but three groups, and each differs in colour, fat and the nutrients it is valued for.
Red meat is beef, lamb, pork and veal, the flesh of mammals, and it is the group most people mean by "meat".
Poultry is chicken, turkey and duck. The breast is paler than the leg or red meat because it contains less myoglobin (the red pigment that stores oxygen in muscle).
Poultry fat is lower than in most red meat, and most of it sits in and under the skin, so poultry is not fat free.
Offal is the edible organs of the animal, such as liver, kidney and heart.
Liver is the richest source of vitamin A, iron and several B vitamins among the offal, which is why offal is valued as cheap, nutrient-dense food.

Nutritive value is about the nutrients meat contains. Meat is valued mainly for its protein, haem iron and B group vitamins, while its fat is mostly saturated and it supplies essentially no carbohydrate.
Protein: meat is a high biological value (HBV) protein, meaning it supplies all the essential amino acids (those the body cannot make) in the proportions the body needs.
Meat is about 20 to 30 per cent protein by weight.
Protein supplies amino acids for growth and repair of body cells and for making enzymes, hormones and antibodies.
Fat: meat fat is mainly saturated, and meat is about 10 to 30 per cent fat, varying with the animal, the cut and whether visible fat is trimmed. Chicken is lower in fat.
Fat gives concentrated energy and insulation, and offal carries fat-soluble vitamins.
Carbohydrate: meat contains essentially none, so it is served with a starchy food such as potatoes, pasta, rice or bread to supply energy and balance the meal.
Besides its macronutrients, meat is an important source of iron and B vitamins, but it is deficient in vitamin C. Water and flavour compounds make up the rest of its character.
Haem iron (the form of iron found in animal foods) is present in red meat, offal and the dark meat of poultry. The body absorbs it more readily than non-haem iron from plant foods.
Iron is used to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood, and myoglobin, which stores oxygen in muscle.
Zinc supports enzyme activity, potassium supports muscle function, and phosphorus supports bones, teeth and energy release. Sulphur is present in the sulphur-containing amino acids.
Sodium is high only in processed meat.
B group vitamins help the body release energy from food. Cobalamin (B12) occurs naturally only in animal foods.
Vitamins A and D are found mainly in liver. Meat is deficient in vitamin C (it is not a source), so serve it with vegetables or fruit.
Water makes up about 50 to 60 per cent of meat. Raw lean meat is about 70 to 75 per cent water, so the figure varies with fat content and cooking.
Extractives are flavour compounds that dissolve out during cooking. They give meat its savoury taste and stimulate digestive juices.
Dietetic value is about how suitable meat is for different people. Some groups gain a great deal from it, while others need to limit it.
Growing children and teenagers need meat protein for growth, and adults need it for repair and maintenance of tissue.
Haem iron is especially important for pregnant women, menstruating women (including teenage girls), children and teenagers, to prevent iron-deficiency anaemia.
Older people and anyone with a poor appetite do well on tender, lean or minced cuts cooked gently, because tough or overcooked meat is harder to chew and digest.

People with raised cholesterol or coronary heart disease, and anyone controlling weight, should limit saturated fat and cholesterol. They choose lean cuts, trim visible fat, remove poultry skin, grill rather than fry and limit processed meats.
Low-income households find cheaper cuts and mince good value protein and iron.
Vegetarians and vegans do not eat meat, so they need other sources of protein of similar quality, iron and B12.

Department of Health healthy eating guidelines and the Irish Food Pyramid place meat in one shelf with poultry, fish, eggs, beans and nuts. They recommend lean and unprocessed choices and advise limiting red and processed meat because of their salt and saturated fat content.
Meat is muscle, and its structure explains how it feels to eat and why some cuts are tougher than others. Muscle is built from fibres, connective tissue and fat.
Muscle is made of long, thin fibres, each a single muscle cell, lying parallel and running in the direction of the muscle's pull.
Groups of fibres form bundles, and the bundles are held together by connective tissue.

Each fibre contains myofibrils made of the proteins actin and myosin, the contractile proteins, which slide past each other to shorten the muscle. The fibre is surrounded by muscle fluid containing water, extractives, soluble protein, vitamins and minerals.
Connective tissue wraps fibres and bundles and attaches muscle to bone through tendons. It contains collagen (white and tough) and elastin (yellow and stretchy).
Fat is found as marbling between and within the muscle fibres, as a layer under the skin or as a covering layer, and around the organs. Marbling adds juiciness and flavour, and fat melts on cooking.
A tougher cut has longer, thicker fibres and more connective tissue.

Diagram: draw a cross-section of muscle showing a bundle of fibres inside a sheath of connective tissue, with one fibre enlarged to show myofibrils (actin and myosin) and a label for fat (marbling). Label connective tissue, fibre, bundle and fat.
Meat contains several different proteins. Some do the work of the muscle, some carry colour and some form connective tissue, and cooking affects each differently.
Myosin and actin are the contractile proteins of the myofibrils and make up most of the fibre protein. They coagulate (set solid) and firm up on heating.
Globulin is a soluble protein in the muscle fluid. It coagulates on heating and is partly lost in drip and cooking juices.
Myoglobin is the red oxygen-storing pigment of muscle and gives raw meat its colour. It denatures (changes shape) on heating, so the meat changes from red to brown or grey.
Collagen is an insoluble connective tissue protein that is tough when raw. It converts to soluble gelatine in slow moist cooking.
Elastin is a springy connective tissue protein in tendons and ligaments. It is very tough and cooking does not soften it, so it is removed or the meat is minced.
Meat spoils quickly, so the first job when buying is to judge how fresh it is. Your eyes, nose and fingers tell you most of what you need to know.

Fresh red meat is a bright, even colour, firm and moist with a fresh smell and little drip in the pack. Grey, brown or green patches, a sticky or slimy surface or a sour smell mean the meat is spoiling.
Fresh poultry has creamy, moist, unbroken skin and no strong smell, because broken skin and odours show bacteria are already at work.
Fat should look white to creamy and firm, not yellow and soft.
Lean cuts show little visible fat, so they suit people limiting fat. Marbling (fine streaks of fat within the muscle) in beef gives flavour and juiciness, which is why it adds to a cut's appeal.
The shape and size of a cut should suit the way you plan to cook it.
Where you buy meat and how you get it home both affect how safe it is, because meat that warms up gives bacteria the chance to multiply.
A butcher cuts meat to order and gives advice. A supermarket sells prepacked meat with a wide choice, all labelled. Farm shops and markets are other sources.
Check that the premises look clean, that meat is kept chilled and that raw and cooked meats are kept separate, so raw juices cannot contaminate cooked meat.
Buy meat last on a shopping trip and carry it home in an insulated bag, so it stays chilled. Refrigerate or freeze it promptly when you get home.

Buy frozen meat in solid, undamaged packs. Ice crystals inside, frost, thaw juice or freezer burn usually mean the meat has been stored badly or partly thawed, and you should not buy above the load line of the freezer cabinet.
Loose meat is cut to order, but prepacked meat carries a label that tells you what you are buying and how to keep it safe. Reading it correctly is an easy source of marks.

A prepacked meat label shows the name of the food, ingredients in descending order of weight (largest first) with allergens emphasised, the net quantity, a date mark, storage instructions, the name and address of the business, origin where required, and a nutrition declaration.

A use-by date goes on highly perishable foods such as raw meat. It is a safety date, so the meat must not be eaten or used after it, because it may carry harmful bacteria even if it looks and smells fine.
A best-before date, found on foods such as frozen or canned meat, is a quality date. After it the meat may be past its best but is not necessarily unsafe.
Frozen and cooked meat products should also be kept to the storage instructions on the pack.
Origin and traceability labelling lets a pack of meat be linked back to the animal and farm it came from, which matters when something goes wrong and meat has to be recalled.

Beef labels show an animal reference code and the origin (the country of birth, rearing and slaughter, or one country) and the slaughterhouse. Origin labelling is also required for fresh, chilled and frozen pigmeat, sheep, goat and poultry under EU origin-labelling rules.
The code and origin let meat be traced back to the farm of origin, so a problem can be found and the affected meat removed.
At Higher Level you must name the law that sets out what a prepacked meat label has to contain.

Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 sets the EU rules on food information, including ingredients listed in descending order of weight and allergens highlighted. It is given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
If meat is faulty or unfit, you have legal rights, and State bodies enforce the rules that stop misleading claims and unsafe food.
Faulty or unfit meat can be returned. The Consumer Rights Act 2022 gives rights for goods: they must be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose and as described.
The Consumer Protection Act 2007 prohibits misleading claims, including misleading food labelling, and is enforced by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC).
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998 and food law prohibit unsafe food.
Two shoppers can stand at the same meat counter and buy very different things. A list of influences, each with a meat example, answers this exam question well.

Price and income: cheaper cuts such as shin, neck, mince, offal and chicken thighs or pieces cost less per portion than prime cuts such as fillet. Special offers, cost per portion, and bulk-buying with freezing also help a budget.

Convenience, time and skills: ready-prepared, marinated and processed meats save time and cooking skill. The cooking equipment at home matters too, such as a cooker, microwave and freezer space, so a household without an oven may buy minced or ready-to-cook meat.

Health: lean cuts, skinless poultry and low-fat, low-salt products suit people controlling fat, salt or weight. Red meat gives iron for those at risk of anaemia, and some people limit processed meat on advice.

Family size, age and likes: portion sizes, children's preferences and tender meat for older people all matter. Religious and cultural rules affect choice, and vegetarians in the household change what is bought.
Quality, appearance and freshness: colour, texture and smell are used to judge quality, and marbling in beef affects its appeal. Traceability and labelling also give confidence.
Origin: many shoppers prefer Irish meat, and the Bord Bia Quality Mark signals assured Irish produce.
Ethics and environment: animal welfare, organic, free-range and assured production, sustainability, food miles and packaging appeal to shoppers concerned about welfare and the environment.
Packaging and portion size: small packs suit single people and reduce waste, while large family packs usually cost less per kilogram.
Advertising, recipes, seasonality and in-store promotions influence choice and encourage shoppers to try new products.
Shoppers cannot check on a farm for themselves, so Bord Bia does it for them. Its quality assurance schemes give buyers confidence that Irish meat meets agreed standards.
Bord Bia is the Irish Food Board, the State agency that promotes Irish food and drink and runs quality assurance schemes. Its Quality Mark shows a product comes from an assured source.

The farm-level scheme for beef and lamb is audited independently, and separate schemes exist for pigmeat and poultry. Meat processors are assured separately under a meat processor scheme, so meat is certified from farm through to processing.

The standards cover animal welfare and care, regulated animal feed, competent herd management, records of veterinary medicines, livestock identification and traceability (each product can be traced back to its farm of origin), pest control, hygiene and the environment.
Farms and processing plants are inspected to check compliance, and non-compliances must be corrected.
