Assured and non-assured product is kept apart in processing, so the assurance claim can be traced.

Consumers gain confidence in quality, safety and welfare. Producers gain market access and sustainability credentials, and Bord Bia advises industry and government and promotes Irish meat to export markets.
Meat is kept safe by controls at every stage, from the farm and abattoir to the shop. Many different bodies share the work.

The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine controls animal health, disease testing, veterinary controls on farms, residue (drug and banned-substance) testing, EU import rules, and approval and supervision of abattoirs.
Veterinary inspectors examine animals before slaughter (ante-mortem inspection) and carcasses and organs after slaughter (post-mortem inspection) in approved abattoirs. Unfit meat is condemned.

Residue testing checks meat for banned substances and for drug residues left by veterinary medicines. Hormonal growth promoters are banned in EU farm animals, and medicines have withdrawal periods before slaughter.
Farmers record the medicines and feed they use. Animals are identified with ear tags and cattle passports, so meat is traceable from farm to pack.

Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 requires food businesses to run HACCP-based food safety procedures (hygiene controls at the steps where hazards could arise). It is given effect in Ireland by the European Communities (Hygiene of Foodstuffs) Regulations 2006.
The Bord Bia scheme adds independent assurance on top of these controls.
At Higher Level you must know the national food safety body and the laws behind meat safety, and who actually carries out inspections.

The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) is the independent national food safety body, established under the Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998 to see that food is safe. It coordinates enforcement, advises and publishes guidance.

The FSAI is not the inspector. Official veterinary staff, the HSE Environmental Health Service and local authorities carry out inspections of food premises under FSAI service contracts, alongside the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine.
Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, the general food law, prohibits placing unsafe food on the market and requires traceability one step back and one step forward in the supply chain.
Regulation (EU) 2017/625, given effect by the European Union (Official Controls in Relation to Food Legislation) Regulations 2020, governs how food premises are inspected.
Raw meat carries bacteria, and these multiply fast in warm conditions. Every storage rule exists to keep bacteria from growing or spreading.
Keep raw meat in the refrigerator at 5 °C or below (the FSAI range is 0-5 °C), because bacteria multiply rapidly between 5 °C and 63 °C, the danger zone.
Store raw meat wrapped or in a covered container on the lowest shelf, away from cooked and ready-to-eat food, so that juices cannot drip onto it.
Use separate chopping boards and knives for raw meat, and wash hands and surfaces, to prevent cross-contamination (spreading bacteria from raw to ready-to-eat food).
Use raw meat before the use-by date on the pack, stored at 5 °C or below. If it has no date, cook or freeze it on the day of purchase.

Minced meat, sausages and offal spoil faster than joints, because bacteria can spread through them over a larger surface area. Poultry often carries Salmonella and Campylobacter on its surface, which are hazards to handle with care.
Vacuum-packed meat stays in its pack until needed and keeps longer unopened in the refrigerator, but once opened it must be treated as fresh.
Freezing lets you keep meat longer, but only if it goes in fresh and is thawed safely. Cooked meat needs its own care because it is often eaten without further cooking.
Freeze fresh meat before its use-by date, in portions wrapped in moisture-proof packaging. Label and date it, and rotate stock so the oldest is used first.
A freezer temperature of -18 °C or colder keeps meat safe, although quality declines the longer meat is kept frozen.
Thaw frozen meat slowly in the refrigerator, on a tray or in a container on the bottom shelf, so juices cannot contaminate other food. Once thawed, cook it fully within the time on the pack.
Do not refreeze raw thawed meat, because bacteria can multiply while it thaws. Cooked dishes made from it can be frozen.
Cool cooked meat quickly, within about 1-2 hours in shallow containers, and refrigerate it promptly, because hot meat left to cool slowly allows bacteria to multiply.
Reheat cooked meat until steaming hot, to a core temperature of 75 °C, and reheat it once only.
Cold storage slows spoilage but does not stop it. Knowing what each method does and does not do explains why dates and handling rules still matter.
Refrigeration slows the growth of micro-organisms and enzyme action but does not kill them, so meat still spoils eventually and use-by dates apply.
Freezing inhibits enzyme activity and microbial growth but does not kill all micro-organisms, so they can regrow once the meat thaws.

Slow freezing forms large ice crystals that damage and rupture cell walls, giving drip loss on thawing and a softer texture. Fast (blast) freezing at about -30 °C forms small crystals and causes less damage.
Drip loss carries away extractives (flavour compounds) and soluble nutrients, mainly B vitamins, so the thawing liquid should be used in cooking.
Freezer burn leaves dry, grey-white or discoloured patches where air reaches the surface of the meat. Fat can also go rancid in poorly stored meat.
Spoilage shows as slime, a sour smell or a colour change. Myoglobin (the red pigment in meat) oxidises to brown metmyoglobin on exposure to air, which is harmless early on but is a quality sign.

Meat is muscle, and muscle is made of fibres held together by connective tissue (the tough, stringy tissue that binds the fibres). How tough a piece of meat is depends on how much of this tissue it has and on what happens to the animal and the meat before and during cooking.

Age of the animal: older animals have longer, thicker muscle fibres and more connective tissue, and the collagen (the main protein of connective tissue) in it is more cross-linked, so the meat is tougher. Young animals such as veal, lamb and chicken are tender.

Activity of the muscle: muscles that work hard, such as the legs, neck, shoulder, shin and flank, have larger fibres and more connective tissue than the little-used loin, sirloin or fillet. This is why the cut of meat decides its toughness.
Treatment before slaughter: an animal that is rested and not stressed gives better meat, while poor rest or stress before slaughter lowers the quality of the meat.

Treatment after slaughter: if meat is not hung long enough, the muscle stays stiff from rigor mortis (the stiffening of muscle after death). Chilling too quickly after slaughter makes the muscle contract (cold shortening), so the meat is tough.
Cooking: high heat, fast cooking or overcooking coagulates (sets) the protein and squeezes out juices, so the meat is dry and tough.
Connective tissue and cooking: collagen is not broken down by quick dry cooking, so tough cuts need slow moist cooking.
Fat content: marbled meat (meat with fine streaks of fat through the muscle) feels juicier and more tender.

Tenderising means making tough meat softer to eat. Each method works by one of four principles: mechanical (physically breaking fibres), chemical (acid or salt), enzymic (enzymes splitting protein) or heat (slow moist cooking).

Hanging (maturing): after slaughter rigor mortis stiffens the muscle. During hanging in a cold room the stiffness passes, glycogen (the muscle's store of sugar) turns to lactic acid, and the meat's own proteolytic (protein-splitting) enzymes break down fibres and connective tissue. Beef is hung for about 1 to 3 weeks.
Mincing: a mincer breaks fibres and connective tissue into small pieces (a mechanical principle), so tough cuts become tender in products such as burgers and bolognese.

Pounding with a steak hammer or mallet, or cutting across the grain, breaks up the long muscle fibres and connective tissue mechanically. Piercing with needles, skewers or forks does the same and lets marinade or brine get into the meat.

Proteolytic enzymes: papain from papaya, bromelain from pineapple, ficin from figs and actinidin from kiwi split the protein bonds in muscle and collagen. They are sprinkled on or injected into the meat before cooking, and act mostly on the surface and as cooking warms the meat.

Acid marinades: lemon juice, vinegar, wine or yoghurt soften muscle protein by acid action and add flavour. A marinade works only on the surface, so it does not tenderise a whole joint or make meat safe.
Brining and curing: a salt solution dissolves some muscle proteins so the meat holds more water and stays juicy and tender during cooking, as in bacon and ham.

Slow moist cooking (stewing, braising, casseroling, pot roasting) converts collagen to gelatine, which softens the connective tissue and separates the fibres. Elastin (another connective protein) is not softened, so trim it or mince it.
Pressure cooking: steam at high pressure and temperature converts collagen to gelatine quickly, so tough cuts tenderise in much less time.
Heat changes the protein, fat, colour, flavour and nutrients of meat all at once. Some changes make meat safe and tasty, and others, if the cooking goes on too long, spoil it.
Coagulation: heating makes the protein denature and set (coagulate), so the meat firms and its fibres harden and shrink. Overcooking makes the protein tough and dry and lowers its digestibility.
Shrinkage: water, juices and melted fat are lost as meat cooks, so it loses weight and size. Lower, slower cooking loses less.
Fat melts during cooking, and in roasting it bastes the meat as it drips. The fat that runs out can be poured away.
Collagen converts to gelatine in moist cooking, which tenderises the meat. Elastin does not change.
Myoglobin (the red pigment in muscle) denatures at cooking temperatures, so red meat changes to brown or grey and the juices turn from pink to clear in well-cooked meat.
Micro-organisms are destroyed, so thorough cooking makes meat safe to eat. Cook to 75 °C at the centre for poultry, pork, mince, sausages and burgers.

Flavour develops: extractives (flavour compounds in the meat) are released, and the Maillard reaction between amino acids and sugars at a high surface temperature browns the surface and gives a roasted flavour. Surface protein coagulates and browns.

Nutrients: correctly cooked protein stays available and is easier to digest. Water-soluble vitamins, especially thiamine (B1), and minerals dissolve into the cooking juices or drip, so use the juices in gravy or sauce. Some B vitamins are destroyed by heat, while fat-soluble vitamins are mostly retained.
Every cooking method works by moving heat into the meat in one of a few ways. Naming the way heat travels is the 'underlying principle' examiners want when you describe a method.
Conduction: heat passes through a solid such as a pan, so frying uses conduction through hot fat.
Convection: heat moves through a liquid or hot air, so stewing in liquid and roasting in a hot oven rely on convection.
Radiation: infrared heat travels directly from the source, so grilling and barbecuing rely on radiant heat.
Microwaves (electromagnetic waves) make the water molecules in the food vibrate, producing heat inside the food. They penetrate only about 2 to 4 cm.
Stewing: meat is simmered in a small amount of liquid at about 80 to 90 °C, which tenderises it and keeps it moist. Heat reaches the meat by conduction through the pot and convection in the liquid.

The best cooking method depends on how much connective tissue a cut has. Tender cuts have little, so they need only quick cooking, but tough cuts have a lot, so they need long, gentle, moist cooking to turn it to gelatine.

Tender cuts such as fillet, sirloin, rump steak, loin chops, lamb cutlets, pork loin and chicken breast suit dry methods: grilling, frying, roasting, stir-frying or barbecuing, which cook them quickly.
Tough cuts such as shin, chuck, brisket, neck, flank, oxtail, stewing steak and chicken legs need slow moist cooking (stewing, braising, casseroling, pot roasting, pressure cooking) or mincing.
Lamb shanks and beef shin become tender when braised slowly in liquid, because the long moist heat turns their collagen to gelatine.
Joints for roasting include leg of lamb, loin of pork, topside and whole poultry. Gammon and ham are boiled or baked, and sausages and burgers are grilled or baked.
Mince is fried and then simmered in dishes such as bolognese and chilli, or shaped into burgers and grilled. It must be cooked through.
Poultry is cooked until no pink meat remains, the juices run clear and the centre is steaming hot (75 °C at the core). It can be roasted whole or in portions, stewed or casseroled.
Liver and kidney are cooked quickly by frying or grilling, or gently braised, because long cooking toughens them, especially liver.
An evaluation question asks you to judge one method of cooking meat, not list several. One well-evaluated method is better than a list.

An evaluation names the method, states its underlying principle (how heat reaches the food), describes its effect on the meat (texture, colour, flavour, nutrient loss, fat), and weighs advantages against disadvantages.

Stewing advantages: it tenderises tough cuts because collagen turns to gelatine, keeps the meat moist, makes use of cheap cuts, and the liquid becomes a sauce so nutrients that leached out are kept. It can be left unattended and uses little fuel, especially in a slow cooker.
Stewing disadvantages: it takes a long time, and nutrients leach into the liquid and are lost if it is discarded, giving a lower vitamin content.
Frying: it is fast and browns the surface, but it adds fat and dries or toughens the meat if overcooked.
Grilling: radiant heat browns tender cuts quickly with little added fat, because the fat drains away, but it can dry out lean meat.
Roasting: dry heat in a hot oven suits tender joints, and fat drips away from a rack.
Microwaving: it is fast and efficient, but it does not brown meat unless combined with a grill, and it can cook unevenly.
Other methods that can be evaluated include boiling, poaching, steaming, braising, pressure cooking and barbecuing. Each needs a name, a principle and an effect on the meat.
A family on a low income can still eat meat if it chooses cheaper cuts, stretches them with other foods and cooks them well. Exam menus ask for a suitable meal with reasons.
Choose inexpensive cuts such as mince, chicken thighs or portions, sausages, liver, shin or stewing steak, and cook them by slow moist methods such as stew, casserole, curry or shepherd's pie.
Stretch mince with vegetables or lentils; a bolognese with carrots, onions and lentils uses less meat without losing flavour.
Starchy foods such as potatoes, pasta, rice or bread complete the meal, make it filling and supply energy.
Cabbage, other vegetables, fruit and potatoes add vitamin C, which meat does not contain.
Meat supplies protein for growing children and haem iron (the well-absorbed form of iron) for teenage girls and pregnant women, so it is worth including in a low-cost family meal.
Stock made from bones, and the cooking juices, make soups and gravies that keep extractives and water-soluble vitamins in the meal.
Batch cooking a casserole and freezing the portions saves fuel and time. Slow cookers and one-pot meals also save fuel.

Give reasons for the menu: cost, nutritive value, ease of cooking, family tastes, skills and equipment, and fuel saving. Examples of two-course menus are spaghetti bolognese with an apple crumble, or vegetable soup followed by spaghetti bolognese.

Fresh meat spoils quickly and the cheaper cuts can be tough. Processing changes meat from its fresh state, usually to make it convenient, to make it keep longer, or to put cheaper cuts and trimmings to use.
Processed meat is meat that has been minced, salted, cured, smoked, cooked, canned, frozen or otherwise altered before sale, for example by adding other ingredients.

Examples include frozen burgers, nuggets and sausages; black and white pudding; rashers, bacon, gammon and cooked ham; luncheon meat, cold cuts and salami; canned stew and corned beef; dehydrated or freeze-dried meat in soups and meals; and ready meals and pies.
Cured meats such as bacon and ham contain salt and curing salts (sodium nitrite), which give them a pink colour and a cured flavour.
Minced products are made from trimmings (small pieces cut off when the carcass is prepared), offal and fat, with seasonings and binders added, so little of the carcass is wasted.
Textured vegetable protein (TVP), a dried soya product, is used as a meat extender, meaning it replaces some of the meat in burgers and stews and makes the product cheaper.

Typical ingredients are minced meat, fat, water, salt, herbs and spices, rusk or breadcrumbs as a binder (to hold the mixture together), and additives such as preservatives (nitrite), colours, flavour enhancers and antioxidants.
Food additives in processed meat must be approved under Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 on food additives, and products list them by E number.

On the label, ingredients are listed in descending order of weight, the meat content is declared where the name stresses meat, and allergens such as cereals containing gluten, soya, mustard and celery are emphasised.
Processed meat is popular because it is cheap, quick and keeps well, but the same processing adds salt, fat and additives. When asked to evaluate it, weigh the benefits against the health drawbacks.
Economy: products are cheap per portion because they can use cheaper cuts and trimmings.
Little waste: all parts of the carcass are used, and portions are uniform in size.
Convenience: products cook quickly and need little preparation, cooking skill or equipment.
Fuel and labour saving: a frozen product often needs only reheating, so less fuel and time are used.
Long shelf life: frozen, canned and cured products keep far longer than fresh meat, and some canned or dried products can be stored for months without refrigeration.
Variety: different flavours, shapes and sizes give choice and appeal to children.

Disadvantages: high salt content can contribute to high blood pressure, and many products are high in saturated fat from fatty trimmings. Health advice is to limit processed meat for its salt, saturated fat and bowel-cancer risk.

Many products contain added water, fillers and additives, so their meat content is lower than the name suggests and their nutritional quality is lower than fresh lean meat. Freezing retains most nutrients, while canning and dehydration lose some B vitamins.
Every process that extends the shelf life of meat works by blocking one of the causes of spoilage, so it helps to know what those causes are.
Meat spoils through micro-organisms (bacteria and moulds), the meat's own enzymes, oxidation of fat (which causes rancidity, an unpleasant stale taste) and drying.
Bacteria need moisture, warmth, air, nutrients and time to grow, so each preservation process removes or controls one of these.
Different processes use cold, lack of air, salt, smoke, heat or dryness to slow or stop spoilage. Extending shelf life means slowing spoilage, not sterilising the meat, except in canning.
Refrigeration (5 °C or below): keeping meat chilled slows bacterial growth and enzyme activity, extending its life by days, but it does not kill bacteria, so meat should be covered or wrapped.
Listeria monocytogenes can still grow at refrigerator temperatures, so ready-to-eat cooked and cured meats need careful hygiene and use-by dates.
Freezing: low temperatures stop microbial growth and enzyme activity, so frozen meat keeps for months.

Vacuum packing: air is removed and the meat sealed in strong plastic, so aerobic micro-organisms (those that need oxygen) cannot grow. The pack is not sterile, so it must be kept refrigerated, carries a use-by date and is treated as fresh meat once opened.

Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP): air in a sealed tray is replaced with a gas mix, usually carbon dioxide, which inhibits aerobic bacteria, and nitrogen, an inert gas that stops the pack collapsing. Oxygen is used for fresh red meat to keep its colour. It needs refrigeration and a use-by date.
Curing and salting: salt, sugar and nitrite draw water from micro-organisms and inhibit spoilage bacteria.

Smoking: after curing, the meat is hung in smoke from burning hardwood sawdust. Smoke compounds (which are antibacterial and antioxidant) and light drying of the surface slow microbial growth and add flavour, and smoking is usually combined with curing.

Canning: meat is prepared, cooked and sealed in cans, then heated to a high temperature under pressure (heat-sterilised), destroying micro-organisms and inactivating enzymes. The airtight seal stops microbes re-entering, so cans keep for years at room temperature.

Dehydration: removing moisture stops microbes growing, since they need water to multiply. Freeze-drying removes water from frozen meat under vacuum. Dried meat is light and long-lasting and is rehydrated in dishes such as soups and ready meals.
Curing is a good process to know in full because it covers the three parts examiners ask for: how it is done, why it works and what it does to the meat.

Method: meat is cooled and trimmed, then rubbed with salt and curing salts, or injected with or soaked in brine containing salt, sugar and curing salts (sodium nitrite), and held in a cool room for several days.
Method: after curing, the meat may be smoked, or sold green (unsmoked and uncooked) as raw cured meat.
Principle: salt draws water out of micro-organisms by osmosis, dehydrating them and reducing the water available for growth.
Principle: nitrite inhibits spoilage bacteria, including Clostridium botulinum (the bacterium that causes botulism), and fixes the pink colour of cured meat.
Effect on meat: there is little loss of nutritive value, but the sodium content rises because of the salt added.
Effect on meat: the meat becomes firmer and drier, and its flavour changes to a salty, cured taste.
Examples of cured products are bacon, rashers, gammon and cooked ham.
Diagram: a flow diagram of curing, from cooled meat to brine or dry salt, a cold room for several days, then smoked or sold green.
Freezing is the cheapest way, along with refrigeration, to keep meat for months. It works by cold rather than by chemicals or heat.
Method: meat is boned, trimmed and portioned, wrapped in moisture-proof packaging, then blast frozen (frozen very fast at about -30 °C) and stored at -18 °C or below.
Principle: low temperatures inhibit enzyme activity and microbial growth, and the water in the meat turns to ice, which is unavailable to micro-organisms.
Principle: fast freezing gives small ice crystals that damage the meat's cells less, and wrapping keeps out microbes and prevents freezer burn.

Effect on meat: colour, flavour, texture and most nutrients are retained, although slight losses of extractives (flavour compounds), B vitamins and minerals occur in drip (the liquid lost on thawing).
Effect on meat: freezer burn (dry, pale patches) and rancidity occur if the packaging fails and the meat is exposed to air.
Diagram: a flow diagram of freezing, from boning and trimming to wrapping, blast freezing and storage.
Canning and dehydration change meat more than chilling or freezing does, which is why their effects on nutrients and texture are worth stating.
Canning: meat is prepared and cooked, packed in cans with brine, sauce or liquid, air is removed, and the cans are sealed and heat-sterilised under pressure.
Canned meat has a shelf life of years at room temperature, and the meat is tender and cooked.
Canning causes a loss of B vitamins, especially thiamine, and changes texture and flavour.
Dehydration and freeze-drying: water is removed using hot air, or by freeze-drying under vacuum, and micro-organisms cannot grow without water.
Dehydrated meat is light and long-lasting, but there is some loss of B vitamins and a change in texture, as in the dried meat found in soups and ready meals.
Fish and shellfish fall into three groups. The groups are based mainly on where the fat is found, and shellfish are then split by the kind of shell they have.
White fish have little or no fat in the flesh, because their fat is stored in the liver (this is why cod liver oil exists). Examples are cod, haddock, whiting, plaice and sole.
Oily fish have fat spread through the flesh. Examples are salmon, trout, mackerel, herring and fresh tuna.
Crustacean shellfish have a hard, jointed outer shell. Examples are lobster, crab and prawns.
Mollusc shellfish have a soft body inside a hard shell with hinged halves that open and close. Examples are oysters, mussels and cockles.

Fish flesh is made of short muscle fibres called myomeres, separated by thin layers of connective tissue (the tough tissue that holds muscle together). With less connective tissue than meat, fish is tender, cooks quickly and is easy to digest.
The flesh of fish is about 65 to 80 per cent water, 0 to 18 per cent fat and 16 to 18 per cent HBV (high biological value) protein.
Water and fat are inversely related: the fattier the fish, the less water its flesh contains.
Fish is valued mainly for its protein, its fat (which differs between white and oily fish) and a wide range of vitamins and minerals. Each nutrient below comes with the fish that supplies it.
Protein: fish is a source of high biological value (HBV) protein, which supplies all the essential amino acids (the ones the body cannot make) needed for growth and repair.
Fat: white fish has almost no fat in the flesh, while oily fish is high in polyunsaturated fat, including the omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA. Fat-soluble vitamins are carried in this oil.
Carbohydrate: fish contains none, so it is best served with a starchy food.
B group vitamins are supplied by all fish.
Vitamins A and D are supplied by oily fish and by fish liver oils such as cod liver oil. Vitamin C is supplied by oysters, but fish is otherwise a poor source of it.
Iodine and fluorine come from sea fish, and phosphorus, potassium and zinc from most fish.
Calcium comes from canned fish eaten with the soft, edible bones, such as sardines and canned salmon, and from shellfish. Iron comes from shellfish and sardines.
Cholesterol is present in shellfish, which matters for anyone on a low-cholesterol diet. Water makes up 65 to 80 per cent of the flesh.
Oily fish is the main food source of these two nutrients, and both do important jobs in the body.
Essential fatty acids are polyunsaturated fatty acids that the body cannot make in the amounts it needs, so they must be obtained from food.
Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated, not saturated, and oily fish is their main dietary source. The types found in it are EPA and DHA.
Omega-3 fatty acids make blood platelets (the cell fragments that help blood clot) less sticky, so fewer blood clots form.
Omega-3 fatty acids reduce the risk of heart attack, stroke and circulatory disease, because fewer clots and less cholesterol mean the blood vessels are less likely to block.
Omega-3 fatty acids reduce the build-up of cholesterol in the arteries and can help lower high blood pressure.
DHA also forms part of brain and eye tissue.
Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin found in oily fish and fish liver oils. It helps the body absorb calcium (and phosphorus), giving healthy bones and teeth.

A lack of vitamin D causes rickets in children and osteomalacia (soft bones) in adults. Vitamin D (the form is D3, cholecalciferol) is heat-stable: it is not destroyed by normal cooking and is not affected by oxygen, acids or alkalis.
Dietetic value means how well fish suits the needs of different people and diets. A good answer links each feature of fish to a person or diet that benefits from it.
Fish is easy to digest, because its short muscle fibres and low connective tissue make the flesh soft. This suits children, the elderly, convalescents and invalids.
Its HBV protein supports growth in children and adolescents and repair of tissue in all age groups, and fish is a good alternative to meat in the main meal.
White fish is low in fat and energy, so it suits low-calorie, low-fat and weight-reducing diets.

Oily fish is recommended for people at risk of coronary heart disease, or with high cholesterol or high blood pressure. Its polyunsaturated fats, including omega-3, are linked to lower blood cholesterol and a lower risk of heart disease.
Shellfish contains cholesterol, so people on a low-cholesterol diet should take it with care.
Fish contains no carbohydrate, so it should be served with starchy foods such as potatoes, rice, pasta or bread. Fish in breadcrumbs, batter or sauce does contain some carbohydrate.
Iodine in sea fish helps prevent goitre (a swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck caused by too little iodine).
Fish is versatile: it can be prepared by many cooking methods and cooks quickly, which saves time and fuel. Canned and frozen fish products make fish available all year, out of season.

The Irish healthy eating guidelines (the Department of Health Food Pyramid, with FSAI guidance) place fish on the shelf with meat, poultry, eggs, beans and nuts, and advise eating fish regularly, including oily fish.
Fish is not a complete food, and some people must avoid it. Eating habits for different fish have also changed over the years for clear reasons.
Fish lacks carbohydrate, and has little iron (except shellfish and sardines) and little vitamin C, so it cannot be the only food in a meal.
Fish, crustaceans and molluscs are each among the allergens that must be highlighted on food labels under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, because they can cause serious reactions in some people.
Salmon and trout consumption rose because of greater awareness of the health benefits of oily fish and the growth of fish farming.
White fish was affected by over-fishing, depleted stocks and fishing laws, although it is still part of a healthy diet.
Shellfish and tuna consumption rose because of foreign travel and eating abroad, trendy recipes, falling cost and farming.

Fish spoils quickly, so you judge it by sight, touch and smell, and by how reliable the seller is. A good buyer checks each sign in turn, because a fish that fails on one is usually failing on others.
Eyes should be bright, clear and bulging (plump); sunken, cloudy or dull eyes show the fish is old.
Gills should be bright red; grey or brown gills show the fish is not fresh.
Flesh should be firm and elastic, springing back when pressed; soft flesh that keeps the dent is stale.
Skin and scales should be moist and shiny, with tight, unbroken scales and no bruising or breaks in the skin.
Smell should be mild and fresh, like the sea; a strong or unpleasant smell means the fish is spoiling.
Shellfish should be alive and heavy for their size. Mussels should be closed, because an open mussel that does not close when tapped is dead and is discarded.
Smoked fish should look glossy; frozen fish should be solid with its packaging intact and no signs of thawing or freezer burn; canned fish should be in an undamaged, undented can within its date.

Buy from a reliable, hygienic retailer where the fish is displayed on ice or refrigerated, check the date on packaged fish, and buy fish in season, when it is better and cheaper. Medium-size fish have the best flavour.
Get the fish home quickly, using a cool bag or ice, and refrigerate it straight away so it does not warm up on the way.
Buyers also rely on official checks on the fish they buy. This is background, not a buying guideline.

The Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority (set up in 2007 under the Sea-Fisheries and Maritime Jurisdiction Act 2006) carries out official controls on fish and shellfish from production to distribution, under a service contract with the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI).

Fish spoils faster than meat, so it must be used or processed as soon as possible after it is caught. Its flesh is soft, high in water and has little connective tissue, and its fat and enzymes act quickly. There are three main causes.
Oxidative rancidity: the fats in the fish, especially the polyunsaturated fat of oily fish, react with oxygen in the air, giving an unpleasant smell and taste.
Bacterial action starts before death: a fish caught in a net struggles and uses up its glycogen stores (the sugar store in the flesh).
When glycogen is present, it converts to lactic acid, which is a preservative. If lactic acid is not present, the fish goes off quickly.
Bacteria work on the flesh and produce trimethylamine, a strong-smelling nitrogen compound, which is what gives spoiled fish its smell.
Enzymic activity: enzymes in the flesh cause deterioration even at low temperatures, so spoilage continues, slowly, even in the fridge.
Storage cannot stop spoilage, only slow it, so fresh fish keeps for a short time only. Good storage keeps it cold and keeps it from contaminating other food.
Chilling slows bacterial growth and enzyme action but does not stop them, so fresh fish is kept chilled, below 5 °C, packed on crushed ice until it is used.
Raw fish is stored on the lowest shelf of the fridge in a covered container, so that drips cannot contaminate other food.
Raw fish is kept apart from cooked and ready-to-eat foods to prevent cross-contamination.
Covering the fish stops it drying out and stops its smell passing to other food.
Fresh fish is used on the day of purchase or as soon as possible after it.
Oily fish deteriorates faster than white fish because its fat goes rancid; this also limits how long it keeps frozen.

Freezing is the best way to keep fish for longer. At freezer temperature the water in the flesh is held as ice, so micro-organisms cannot grow and enzyme action is inactivated. It slows or stops spoilage but does not kill all bacteria, which can grow again after thawing.
Freeze only fish that is very fresh and of best quality; freezing cannot improve fish that is already poor in quality.
Turn the freezer to its fast-freeze setting 3 to 4 hours before freezing the fish, so the fish freezes quickly.
Freeze fish in usable quantities, so that only the amount needed is thawed.
Do not freeze more than about a tenth of the freezer's capacity in any 24 hours, so that the food already frozen stays frozen.
Wrap fish tightly in moisture-proof packaging or vacuum pack it, to prevent freezer burn (dried-out patches) and oxidation, because air in the packaging lets oily fish go rancid.
Label each package with the name of the fish and the date, so you can use it within the time on the pack.
Store frozen fish at −18 °C or below.
Thaw frozen fish slowly in the fridge and do not refreeze it once thawed raw.
Freezing changes fish very little, which is why it is so widely used, but it has costs too.
Colour and flavour are largely unchanged and nutrients are well kept.
Texture may change, and some B vitamins and extractives (flavour compounds) are lost on thawing.
Poor wrapping causes freezer burn, and air in the packaging lets oily fish go rancid.
Advantages: freezing is simple and safe, loses little nutrient, and allows bulk buying and out-of-season fish.
Disadvantages: it needs packaging and freezer running costs.
Fish is prepared according to its shape and type, so that it cooks evenly, looks good and is safe to eat. The steps differ for whole fish, fillets and shellfish.
Whole round fish is scaled, gutted and washed before cooking; the head, tail and fins may be removed or trimmed. Flat fish may be skinned.
Fillets are cut away from the bones. Leaving the skin on helps a delicate fillet hold its shape during cooking, because the skin keeps the flakes together.
Mussels are scrubbed and the beards (the stringy threads that stick out of the shell) removed. Any mussel that stays open when tapped is discarded, because it is probably dead and unsafe.
After cooking, any mussel that has not opened is discarded too. Prawns are cooked until they turn pink, which shows they are done.

Wash and dry fish before cooking, and keep raw fish, and the board and knife used for it, apart from cooked food, so that bacteria from the raw fish do not spread to food that will not be cooked again.
Fish needs less cooking than meat, and the effects of heat are fast and easy to overdo. Examiners ask for a list of four or five effects, so each one below is a separate fact.
Coagulation: the protein in the flesh sets, so raw translucent flesh turns opaque and firm.
Flaking: the thin connective tissue between the muscle fibres changes to gelatine and breaks down quickly, so the flesh separates into flakes. This is why fish cooks fast.
Overcooking toughens the protein and dries out the flesh, because the protein shrinks and squeezes the moisture out.
Micro-organisms (bacteria) and parasites are killed, so well-cooked fish is safe to eat.
Heat changes the protein so that it is easier to digest, and flavour develops during cooking.
Some B vitamins and minerals dissolve into the cooking liquid or are lost by heat. The liquid can be used in a sauce or soup to keep them. Fat-soluble vitamins are mostly kept.
Oily fish loses some fat into the pan or grill, while white fish absorbs fat if it is fried.
Every cooking method moves heat into the food in one of four ways. Knowing which one applies is how you state the underlying principle of a method.
Conduction: heat passes from molecule to molecule through a solid or a liquid in contact with the food, e.g. the pan on the hob, or the fat in shallow frying.
Convection: heat is carried through circulating liquid, steam or hot air, in which the hotter material rises and cooler material falls, e.g. poaching, steaming, baking, stewing and deep frying.
Radiation: infrared heat travels in rays from the heat source straight to the surface of the food, e.g. grilling and barbecuing.
Microwave: electromagnetic waves make the water molecules in the food vibrate, which generates heat inside the food, so cooking is quick.
Poaching is the standard moist method for fish, because the gentle heat cooks the flesh without breaking it up.
How it is done: fish is cooked gently in liquid (water, milk, stock or wine) just below simmering point, about 85 °C (80-90 °C), in a saucepan on the hob or in a covered dish in the oven.
Principle: conduction and convection through the liquid. The gentle heat cooks the fish without breaking up the delicate flesh.
Result: poached fish is moist, easy to digest and keeps its shape, but it may lack flavour, so it is usually served with a sauce.
Poaching is a good method for delicate white fish and for salmon.
Boiling vigorously breaks up the flesh and loses flavour and nutrients, so fish is simmered or poached instead.
Steaming and stewing are two more moist methods. Both keep the nutrients, because they use little or no water that is thrown away.
Steaming: food is cooked by steam rising from boiling water, either between two plates over a saucepan, in a covered bowl standing in boiling water, or in a steamer.
Steaming principle: convection, with the heat released as the steam condenses on the food.
Steamed fish is light and easily digested, has a mild flavour, loses few nutrients and has no fat added.
Stewing or casserole cooking: food is cooked slowly in liquid in a covered container on the hob or in the oven, by convection and conduction.
Stewing suits fish stews, chowders and fish in sauce. The liquid is eaten, so the nutrients that dissolve into it are kept.
Grilling and barbecuing both cook by radiant heat, with no liquid, so they are dry methods that suit fish.
Grilling: food is cooked by radiant heat under the grill. The heat seals the surface, retaining flavour, moisture and nutrients.
Grilled fish is quick to cook and needs little fat, but it is easily overcooked and dries out if left unwatched, so brush it with oil and watch it.
Barbecuing: food is cooked by radiant heat on a grid over burning charcoal or gas flames, which adds a smoky flavour.
Baking and roasting both use the dry heat of the oven, so the principle is convection: hot air circulating around the food.
Baking: food is cooked by the dry heat of the oven, transferred by convection. Fish may be baked whole, in fillets, or wrapped in foil or paper to keep it moist.
Roasting: food is cooked in a little fat in a roasting tin in the oven, by convection. It is suited to firm whole fish or thick pieces.
Frying cooks fish in hot fat or oil. It gives a crisp surface and good flavour, but adds fat.
Shallow frying: food is cooked in hot fat in a pan on the hob, with heat transferred by conduction through the fat. The surface is crisp and cooking is quick, but it adds fat and calories.

Deep frying: food is immersed in hot fat in a deep fat fryer, with heat transferred by convection in the fat. A coating of batter or breadcrumbs seals the fish, keeps it moist and makes it crisp, but the result is high in fat.
Stir-frying: small pieces are cooked quickly in a wok in a small amount of oil, by conduction and convection.
Microwaves cook fish quickly with no added fat. A comparison of methods lets you comment on how palatable the cooked fish will be.
Microwave cooking is quick and needs no fat, but it may cook unevenly, so cover the dish and allow standing time for the heat to spread through the fish.
Grilled fish is quick, low in fat and digestible, but easily overcooked.
Poached fish is digestible and moist, but may lack flavour, so it is served with a sauce.
Fried fish is crisp and flavourful, but higher in fat and less suitable for low-fat diets.
Fish spoils very quickly, so it is processed to make it last longer. Processing works by killing or slowing micro-organisms, slowing enzyme action, or removing the water that micro-organisms need.
The four methods named for fish are freezing, canning, smoking and salting. Each one attacks spoilage in a different way, so the principle must match the method.
Vacuum packing removes air from the pack, so oxygen cannot cause oxidative rancidity (fat going off through reaction with oxygen). It also slows the growth of micro-organisms that need oxygen.
Processing also adds variety and convenience, because it turns fish into products that are ready to cook or ready to eat.
Freezing is the model process to describe in an exam. Fish is frozen in industry at about −30 °C, often on the fishing vessel or soon after landing, and stored at −18 °C or below.
Principle: low temperatures stop micro-organisms from multiplying and inactivate enzymes, so spoilage is halted. Freezing does not kill micro-organisms.
The water in the flesh is converted to ice, so it is not available to micro-organisms, which need liquid water to grow.
Fast freezing, at about −30 °C, forms small ice crystals that cause less damage to the flesh than the large crystals of slow freezing.
Effects: colour and flavour are largely unchanged, and nutrients are well retained, which is why frozen fish is a good nutritional choice.
Effects: texture may change, and some B vitamins and extractives (the flavour compounds in the flesh) are lost, for example in the drip on thawing.
Poor wrapping causes freezer burn (dried, damaged patches on the surface), and air in the packaging allows oxidative rancidity in oily fish, so good wrapping or vacuum packing is used.
Advantages: freezing is simple and safe, loses little nutrient, allows bulk buying and makes fish available out of season.
Disadvantages: packaging and freezer running costs, and the fish must be thawed before use.
Canning gives fish a very long shelf life without refrigeration. It works by heat sterilisation and an airtight seal, not by removing water.
Method: the fish is cleaned, cooked and packed in cans with brine, oil or tomato sauce. The cans are sealed and heated under pressure to sterilise them (commercial sterilisation).
Principle: heat destroys micro-organisms and their spores and inactivates enzymes. The airtight seal prevents micro-organisms from entering after heating, so the contents cannot be re-contaminated.
Effects: canned fish keeps for a long time without refrigeration, and the flesh becomes soft because it has been cooked in the can.
Effects: some heat-sensitive vitamins, such as the B vitamins, are partly lost during heating. Flavour also changes from the cooking and the packing medium.
The soft bones in canned fish such as sardines and salmon are eaten with the flesh, so they supply calcium.
Examples: tuna, sardines, salmon and mackerel, packed in brine, oil or tomato sauce.
Salt has been used to preserve fish for centuries. It removes the water micro-organisms need, so it preserves by drawing water out rather than by heat.
Dry salting: salt is rubbed onto the fish or layered with it. Brining: the fish is soaked in a strong salt solution.
Principle: salt draws water out of the flesh, and out of micro-organisms, by osmosis, so less water is available for them to grow.
Salt also slows bacterial growth and enzyme action, extending shelf life further.
Effects: the flesh becomes firmer and drier, and the fish has a strong salty flavour.
Effects: some B vitamins and other soluble nutrients are lost with the water that is drawn out.
High sodium from salt is linked to high blood pressure, so salted fish should be soaked before cooking and eaten in moderation.
Examples: salted cod and salted herring.

Smoking preserves fish with smoke compounds and with the salting and drying that come before it. Whether the fish is cooked by the process depends on the temperature, which is the difference between hot and cold smoking.
Preparation, the same for both types: the fish is filleted or split and trimmed, brined or dry-salted, rinsed and dried before smoking.
Smoke is produced by smouldering wood, wood chips, sawdust or peat.

Smoke compounds such as phenols, creosote and formaldehyde coat the fish and act as preservatives and antioxidants. They also give colour and flavour, and the earlier salting and drying add to the preservation.
Cold smoking: the fish is smoked at temperatures not exceeding about 27 °C, so the flesh is not cooked by the smoking.
Most cold-smoked fish is cooked before eating, for example kippers (smoked herring) and smoked cod. Cold-smoked salmon is the exception and is eaten as bought.
Hot smoking: the temperature is raised gradually to about 80 °C, so the fish is cooked during smoking and needs no further cooking. Examples: hot-smoked trout and mackerel.
Effects: smoking gives flavour, colour and a glossy surface, and raises the salt content. The shelf life is longer than fresh fish but shorter than canned or frozen.
Examples of smoked fish: smoked salmon, trout, cod and mackerel.
Processing turns fish into ready-made products, and shoppers choose them for convenience as much as for keeping time. Most fall into three groups: frozen, canned and smoked.
Frozen products: fish fingers, fish cakes, fish fillets, breaded or battered portions, fish in sauce and ready fish meals.
Canned products: tuna, sardines and salmon, packed in brine, oil or tomato sauce.
Smoked products: trout, salmon, cod and mackerel.
Ready-to-cook products have no waste, because the bones and skin are already removed, and they save preparation time and fuel.
Ready meals and ready-to-serve products are quick and easy to prepare and can be used as starters or main courses.
Products are good value and versatile, and a long shelf life makes fish available out of season.
Breaded or battered products and fish in a sauce contain extra carbohydrate from the breadcrumbs, batter or sauce, so they add starchy food to the meal.

Fish, crustaceans and molluscs are allergens, so they must be highlighted on labels. The FSAI coordinates food safety enforcement, and the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority carries out official controls on seafood processing.
Milk is a complete food for young mammals, meaning it supports a growing baby animal, and a useful source of most nutrients for people. It is widely available, so it is a staple of the Irish diet.
Water makes up about 87% of milk, so a glass of milk contributes to hydration as well as supplying nutrients.

Protein makes up about 3.5% of whole milk. It is mainly casein, with whey proteins making up the rest, and it is high biological value (HBV) protein, which means it contains all the essential amino acids (the ones the body cannot make).
Protein from milk is used for growth and repair, and for making hormones and enzymes.

Fat in whole milk is about 3.5 to 4%, mostly saturated (fat that is solid at room temperature and raises cholesterol). It is held in small globules, so it is easily digested, and cholesterol is present.
The fat carries the fat-soluble vitamins A and D, so these are highest in whole milk.

Lactose is the milk sugar, a disaccharide (a double sugar) at about 4 to 5%. It is the only significant carbohydrate in milk, it supplies energy, and it aids the absorption of calcium. Milk contains almost no starch.
Minerals: calcium and phosphorus are present in useful amounts for bones and teeth, with traces of magnesium, potassium and sodium. Milk is low in iron.
Vitamins: A and D, and the B group vitamins, including riboflavin (B2) and B12. Skimmed milk keeps the B vitamins but loses A and D with the fat.
Milk supplies energy from lactose and fat, so the more fat a milk contains, the more energy it gives.
Milk is a good source of protein and calcium, but it is not a complete diet for an adult. Knowing what it lacks explains why it must be balanced with other foods.
Milk contains no vitamin C, so it cannot be the only source of this vitamin.
Milk contains no fibre, so it does not help bowel movement the way cereals, fruit and vegetables do.
Milk contains very little starch, so its carbohydrate is almost all lactose.
Milk is low in iron, so it should not be relied on to prevent iron deficiency.
Nutritive value means the nutrients a food contains and what each one does in the body. A good answer names the nutrient, its function and the milk fact.
Protein (HBV) is for growth and repair, and fat and lactose give energy.
Calcium and phosphorus build and maintain bones and teeth, and vitamins A, D and the B group support the body's functioning, while water gives hydration.
Milk lacks vitamin C, fibre and iron, so a full answer also states what it does not provide.
Dietetic value means how milk suits different people and different diets. Each point is strongest when it is given with its reason.
Protein supports growth and repair in children, adolescents and pregnant women, who need extra for their body's needs.
Calcium and phosphorus support bone and tooth development and maintenance, and are needed by older people and nursing mothers.
Lactose and fat give energy for an active lifestyle.
Milk is easily digested, so it suits invalid and elderly diets, and convalescents.
Low-fat milks suit low-cholesterol and weight-watching diets, because less fat means less saturated fat and energy.
Milk is versatile, used in drinks, cereals, sauces, soups, puddings and baking.
Milk is inexpensive, widely available and quick to use with no preparation, and nothing is wasted.
Milk can be fortified (have nutrients added) to add nutrients that are otherwise low.
Milk has real strengths, but there are situations where it is not suitable. State these limits as well as the benefits.
Milk is not suitable as the only food, because it has no vitamin C or fibre and little iron.
Whole milk is high in saturated fat, so it is not ideal for people cutting cholesterol or calories.
Lactose intolerance means a person lacks the enzyme lactase and cannot digest lactose, the sugar in milk. Lactose-free milk exists for them.
Milk allergy is a different condition, a reaction to the milk protein.
Irish healthy eating guidance treats milk and other dairy foods as a food group that should be eaten every day.
The Department of Health healthy eating guidelines and the Irish Food Pyramid place milk in the dairy food group (the milk, yoghurt and cheese shelf), which should be included every day.
Three servings a day are recommended for most adults and five a day for 9 to 18 year olds, because of the calcium and protein needed for growth and bone development.
Lower-fat choices are advised, and cheese in small amounts.
Three servings of milk, cheese and yoghurt are recommended because of the HBV protein, calcium, vitamins A, D and some B, versatility and low cost.
Questions on a teenager's diet ask for several different, practical ways to include dairy, each with a nutritional reason.
Milk can be used on cereal or porridge, in smoothies and milky drinks, in soups, sauces and batters, and in puddings and baking.
Yoghurt can be eaten as a snack, on cereal, in smoothies, or used as a dip or dressing.
Cheese can go in sandwiches, salads, pasta, pizza and soups, or on potatoes.
Cream can be used in soups, mash, sauces and desserts.
Young children are growing quickly, so milk matters more to them than to most adults. The type of milk and what it is eaten with both matter.
Protein is for growth and repair, calcium and phosphorus with vitamin D build developing bones and teeth, and B vitamins and water are also supplied.
Young children need the energy and fat-soluble vitamins A and D that whole milk supplies.
Reduced-fat and skimmed milks have less energy and fewer fat-soluble vitamins, so they are less suitable as a young child's main milk.
Safefood advises full-fat milk for ages 1 to 2, and skimmed milk is not suitable as a main drink under 5.
The HSE advises that cow's milk is not given as the main drink to babies under 12 months, only from 12 months as whole pasteurised milk.

Milk is low in iron and has no vitamin C, so iron-rich foods such as meat, fish, eggs or fortified cereals should be given alongside it, with foods supplying vitamin C and fibre. Too much milk can crowd out other foods.
Milk can be used in young children's diets in cereals, sauces, soups and puddings to add protein and calcium, and it can be fortified.
Milk is sold in several types that differ mainly in how much fat they contain, and so in energy and fat-soluble vitamins. Fortified milk differs by what has been added.
Whole milk is full fat, about 3.5 to 4% fat, with the most energy and vitamin A of the common types, and is the most popular type.
Semi-skimmed or low-fat milk is a reduced-fat milk, with part of the fat removed. Compared with whole milk it has less energy, fat, saturated fat and vitamin A.
Semi-skimmed milk has slightly more protein, carbohydrate and calcium per 100 ml, so it is the milk type higher in calcium, protein and carbohydrate than whole milk.
Skimmed milk has 0.1 to 0.4% fat. Most of the fat is removed along with vitamins A and D, so it suits low-fat and low-cholesterol diets, while the protein, lactose and calcium remain.

Fortified milk has nutrients added to whole, low-fat or skimmed milk, such as vitamins A and D, folic acid, calcium, protein or omega-3 fatty acids. Fortification adds nutrients that are low or were lost in processing, so it can restore vitamins A and D to low-fat milk.
Semi-skimmed and skimmed milk are not fortified unless the label says so.

Other types to name are long-life (UHT), sterilised, evaporated, condensed and dried milk, which are heat-treated or concentrated, and lactose-free milk. Goat's milk and soya (plant) milk are alternatives.
Nutrition labels give values per 100 ml, so different milks can be compared like with like. Use only the figures you are given and link each to a function.
Energy and fat content: a lower-energy, lower-fat milk suits a slimming or low-cholesterol diet, for weight control and heart health.
Protein: needed for growth and repair, so compare grams per 100 ml for growing teenagers.
Calcium: compare the amount per 100 ml, because it is needed for bones and teeth.
Vitamin B12: needed for healthy red blood cells, for making use of folate and fatty acids in metabolism, and for the myelin sheath of nerves.
A fat-free milk compared with whole milk has lower energy and fat, similar protein and vitamin B12, and more calcium, which is the basis for recommending it to a teenager.
Diagram: draw a comparison table of whole, semi-skimmed and skimmed milk (fat, energy, vitamins A and D, calcium) as a revision aid.
Raw milk is a perfect home for bacteria, so it spoils within days and can carry disease-causing bacteria. Manufacturers heat-treat and package it so that it is safe and keeps longer.

Raw milk contains water, lactose (milk sugar) and protein at a neutral pH, which is exactly what bacteria need to grow, so it spoils quickly. It can also carry pathogenic (disease-causing) bacteria such as tuberculosis bacteria, Salmonella, Listeria and E. coli.
Heat treatment destroys pathogenic bacteria and most spoilage bacteria, which makes milk safe to drink and extends its shelf life.

Refrigeration slows bacterial growth but does not destroy bacteria, because bacteria grow fastest in warm, moist conditions and only slow down in the cold. This is why heat treatment is needed as well.

Every heat treatment causes some loss of heat-sensitive vitamins (thiamine B1, B12, folate and vitamin C). The more severe the heat, the greater the vitamin loss and the more the flavour changes, so the process chosen balances safety, shelf life and nutrient loss.
Pasteurisation is the gentlest of the heat treatments. It makes milk safe to drink while leaving its taste, colour and most nutrients almost unchanged, but it does not make the milk sterile.
Milk is heated to 72 to 75°C for 15 to 25 seconds, usually in a heat exchanger (a set of plates) as a continuous flow.
It is then cooled rapidly to below 10°C and packaged. Rapid cooling stops any surviving bacteria from multiplying.
Effect on safety: pathogenic bacteria and most spoilage bacteria are destroyed, but not all, and not bacterial spores (tough resting forms). The milk is therefore not sterile.
Nutritive effect: a small amount of thiamine (B1) and vitamin C is lost, while taste, colour and the other nutrients are little changed.

Because some bacteria survive, pasteurised milk keeps for only a few days. It must be kept refrigerated, and once opened it should be used within a few days. Its shelf life is short compared with UHT milk.
Pasteurisation is also needed for milk that will be made into cream, yoghurt and cheese.
Sterilisation uses stronger heat for longer than pasteurisation, and the heating is done inside the sealed container. The result is milk that keeps for months but tastes different.

The milk is homogenised, filled into bottles, sealed and then heated in the sealed bottle to about 110 to 120°C for about 20 to 30 minutes (approximate figures), then cooled. This is a higher temperature for longer than in pasteurisation.
Effect on safety: all bacteria and their spores are destroyed, so the milk is sterile and safer, and keeps for several months unopened without refrigeration. Once opened it must be refrigerated.
Nutritive effect: more vitamin is lost than in pasteurisation, including thiamine, vitamin C and some other B vitamins, because the heating is long.
Flavour is altered by the stronger heat, giving a creamy colour and a cooked, caramelised taste.
UHT heats milk to a very high temperature for only a moment. Because the heating is so short, the milk is made sterile with less damage to flavour and vitamins than in-bottle sterilisation.
Milk is heated to approximately 132°C for 1 to 3 seconds, by steam injection or in a heat exchanger, then cooled rapidly.
It is then packed aseptically, which means into sterile, airtight cartons in sterile conditions, so that no bacteria can get back in.
Effect: all bacteria are destroyed, giving commercially sterile milk (pathogenic and spoilage micro-organisms are both destroyed).
Unopened UHT milk keeps for several months without refrigeration. Once opened it must be refrigerated and used within a few days.
Nutritive effect: some loss of heat-sensitive B group vitamins and vitamin C. The loss is less than in in-bottle sterilisation because the heating time is so short.
There may be a slight cooked flavour, which is the main disadvantage.
Advantages: long unopened shelf life, no refrigeration needed in the shop or the cupboard, and convenience for travel, holidays and emergencies.
Fat in raw milk floats to the top as cream. Homogenisation changes the texture and appearance of the milk, but it does not make the milk safe.
Milk is forced at high pressure through a very small opening, which breaks the fat globules into much smaller particles that are distributed evenly through the milk.
Even distribution stops the cream rising to the surface, so there is no cream line and the milk stays uniform.
The milk looks whiter and is creamier and smoother in texture.
Smaller fat globules are more easily digested.
Homogenisation is not a heat treatment and does not separate the fat, so it does not destroy bacteria. In production it is usually carried out before pasteurisation or UHT treatment.
Milk goes through a series of stages between the farm and the shop. In order, they make up the production profile of a processed food that has had its shelf life extended.
1. Milk is collected from farms in refrigerated tankers, then tested for quality and bacterial content on arrival, and cooled and stored.
2. Milk is separated where cream is required, and skimmed milk is produced.
3. The fat content is standardised (adjusted to a set level) to make whole, semi-skimmed or skimmed milk.
4. Vitamins or minerals are added if a fortified milk is being made.
5. Milk is homogenised and then heat-treated by pasteurisation, sterilisation or UHT, then cooled.
6. Milk is filled and packaged under hygienic conditions, so that it is not contaminated after heat treatment.
7. Milk is labelled, stored and distributed, with pasteurised milk kept chilled throughout.
Diagram: draw a flow chart of milk from farm to shop, labelling collection, testing, separation and standardising, homogenisation, heat treatment, packaging, labelling and distribution.
Packaging keeps heat-treated milk safe after processing, and the label gives the buyer the information they need and the law requires.
Packaging includes glass bottles, plastic bottles, waxed or plastic-coated cardboard cartons, aseptic cartons for UHT milk, and metal cans for evaporated and condensed milk.
Packaging protects milk from light and contamination, because light destroys riboflavin and vitamin A. It also holds the stated quantity, is hygienic and convenient, and is increasingly recyclable.
Label: the name of the food and type of milk (whole, semi-skimmed, skimmed or fortified), the brand, the name and address of the producer, and the quantity.
Label: nutritional information, including energy, protein, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars and salt.
Label: a date stamp and storage instructions, and allergen information (milk). Pasteurised milk carries a use-by date, whereas unopened UHT milk carries a best-before date.
Labels must comply with Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 on food information to consumers, given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
Milk is the syllabus's example of a food processed to extend its shelf life. Besides heat-treated liquid milk, other processed milks keep for months and are useful where fresh milk is not available.
Evaporated milk is concentrated by removing water by heating. It is canned and sterilised, unsweetened, keeps for months and is used in cooking and drinks.

Condensed milk is concentrated by removing water and is usually sweetened with added sugar. The high sugar concentration helps to preserve it, and it is thick and sweet, used in sweet dishes and confectionery.
Dried milk is made into powder by removing all the water, by spray drying (milk sprayed as droplets into hot air) or roller drying (a film of milk dried on heated rollers), giving a long shelf life.
Dried milk is reconstituted (mixed back up) with water and used in baking, infant formula and where fresh milk is not available.
Processed milks have the convenience of long storage and can be used where fresh milk is not available.
Pasteurisation, sterilisation, UHT, evaporating, condensing and drying all count as processes that extend shelf life. If one is chosen for an answer, give the method, the effect and the labelling.

Cream is the fat-rich layer separated from milk. Because nearly all the fat of the milk ends up in it, its nutrition is very different from that of milk, and its types differ mainly in how much fat they hold.
Cream is high in energy and contributes little protein or carbohydrate, because most of the protein and lactose (milk sugar) stay behind in the skimmed milk.
Its fat is mostly saturated and contains cholesterol, so cream is not suited to low-fat, low-cholesterol or slimming diets and is best used in small amounts.
The fat-soluble vitamins A and D are carried in the cream fat, because these vitamins dissolve in fat rather than water.
Cream contains no vitamin C and no fibre.
Double cream has the highest fat content (about 48%), whips to stiff peaks, pours thick and can be piped, so it suits fillings, toppings and rich sauces.
Single cream has less fat (about 18%), does not whip, and is used to pour over desserts, in coffee and in sauces.
Whipping cream (about 35 to 38% fat) is whipped to a foam by beating air into it, because the fat forms a network that traps the air.
Sour cream is cultured with lactic acid bacteria, giving a tangy flavour used in dips, toppings and baked potatoes. Crème fraîche is another cultured cream.
Cream has to be separated from the milk, made to a set fat level and heat treated so that it is safe and keeps. Take care not to mix up separating cream with churning butter.

Cream is separated from milk by centrifugal separation (a spinning machine called a centrifuge), which spins the milk so the lighter fat rises and is drawn off. This separates cream from skimmed milk.
The fat content of each cream is standardised (adjusted) to the level named on the label, so that single, whipping and double cream are always the same.
The separated cream is then pasteurised or UHT treated, as for milk. UHT (long-life) cream keeps unopened without refrigeration.
After heat treatment the cream is cooled, packaged and labelled.
Cream is a perishable, high-fat food that absorbs smells easily, so choosing and storing it carefully protects its safety and flavour.
Select cream with the fat content stated on the label, which shows whether it is single, double or whipping cream and so whether it will whip or pour.
Check the use-by date and that the carton is intact and sealed.
Refrigerate cream promptly and keep it in its sealed container, away from strong-smelling foods, which it would otherwise absorb.
Once opened, use cream within the period stated on the label.
Whipped cream does not keep and should be used soon after whipping.
Butter is made from cream by agitating it until the fat separates out. Because it is almost all fat, its nutritional profile follows the cream's.
Butter is made by churning (agitating) cream, which breaks down the membranes around the fat globules so the fat clumps together into butter grains.
The liquid left after churning is buttermilk. The butter is then washed, salted if wanted, worked (kneaded) to remove excess water, then shaped, wrapped and labelled.
Butter is about 80% fat (the EU minimum for the name butter) with a small amount of water, and its fat is mostly saturated.
Butter is high in cholesterol and supplies vitamins A and D from its fat. It has no vitamin C or fibre and negligible protein.
Salted butter has salt added for flavour and preservation, so unsalted butter suits those limiting salt.
Spreadable butter is blended with a vegetable oil to soften it. Reduced-fat spreads contain less fat because they are blended with other fats and water, and are chosen to reduce saturated fat.
A product with much less than 80% fat cannot legally be sold as butter, which is why lower-fat products are called reduced-fat spreads or dairy spreads.
Butter is used for its flavour and for the way its fat behaves in cooking. It also picks up other smells easily, which shapes how it is stored.
Shortcrust and other pastry, where the fat is rubbed into the flour to make a crumbly (shortened) texture. Scones are made the same way.
Creaming with sugar in cake making, where air is beaten into the fat to aerate the mixture.
Frying and making sauces, such as white sauce or melted butter sauces, where it adds flavour. Butter burns at a lower heat than oil.
Butter is refrigerated, kept covered, and stored away from strong-smelling foods to prevent it absorbing odours.
Buy butter from a clean shop in intact packs, and use it before the use-by date. It can be frozen for long storage.
Yoghurt is made from milk and so shares milk's nutrients, with the lactic acid making it easier to digest for many people.
Yoghurt supplies HBV protein (high biological value, with all the essential amino acids) for growth and repair.
Yoghurt supplies lactose as an energy source.
Yoghurt is rich in calcium and phosphorus for bones and teeth.
Yoghurt supplies vitamins A, D and B group vitamins.
Yoghurt is about 87% water, with traces of minerals such as potassium.
Full-fat yoghurt contains saturated fat, and yoghurt lacks vitamin C and is low in iron.
Dietetic value: yoghurt suits all ages, is versatile, can be fortified, is inexpensive and is a convenient snack.
Yoghurt is a cream substitute for those limiting cream's fat, and should be balanced with starch, fibre and iron foods, because it provides little of these.

Yoghurt is milk fermented by lactic acid bacteria: the bacteria change lactose to lactic acid, which gives the sharp taste, sets the milk and preserves it. The stages must be learned in order, with their temperatures.
3. Milk is cooled to about 37°C, the temperature at which the culture can work.
4. A lactic culture such as Lactobacillus bulgaricus (usually with Streptococcus thermophilus) is added.
5. The mixture is incubated for 6 to 8 hours. Lactose changes to lactic acid, and the milk proteins coagulate (set) and thicken to form yoghurt.
6. The yoghurt is cooled to about 5°C to halt fermentation.
7. Sweeteners, fruit, nuts, colours, flavours or stabilisers may be added.
8. The yoghurt is weighed, packaged (in sealed plastic pots or cartons) and labelled.
Yoghurt is sold in sealed packs with a legal label, and it comes in several types depending on how it is set and what is added.
Yoghurt is packaged in sealed plastic pots with foil or plastic lids, or in cartons.
The label gives the name and type, brand, ingredients, quantity, nutrition information, allergens (milk, and any nuts), use-by date and storage (refrigerate).
The legal basis is Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
Set yoghurt is incubated in the pot and is firm. Stirred or drinking yoghurt is set in a vat, then stirred and poured into pots.
Greek-style yoghurt is strained and so thicker. Plain (natural) yoghurt has no sugar added.
Bio-yoghurt has an extra live culture added for the consumer's benefit. How and when it is added matters, because heat would kill it.
Bio-yoghurt contains an added live culture such as Lactobacillus acidophilus, and bifidobacteria.
Acidophilus bacteria aid digestion, and help balance the bacteria in the gut.
Probiotic yoghurts contain live bacteria intended to benefit the gut. They must be refrigerated to stay alive.
The culture is added after pasteurisation, because heat would destroy it.
Yoghurt is perishable and used in many ways, so choose and store it well and know a range of uses.
Buy from a clean shop, and check the use-by date and that the lid is sealed and the pot undamaged.
Check the ingredients list for sugar, fruit and possible allergens, and the origin of the product. Check the fat and sugar content on the label.
Refrigerate yoghurt promptly at about 4°C, rotate stock so older packs are used first, and reseal with the original lid. Use it within the time on the label.
Uses: eaten alone or as a drink, in desserts, salads and dressings, and smoothies.
Uses: as a garnish or topping, on cereal, as a dip (such as tzatziki or raita), and in curries, marinades and baking.
Yoghurt may replace cream or mayonnaise in cooking as a lower-fat option, but it curdles if boiled.

Consumers want healthier, more convenient and more specialised dairy foods, so dairy producers change their products and packs. Each product change below answers a reason such as health awareness, convenience or intolerance.
Low-fat and skimmed products, including low-fat cheese and reduced-fat spreads, meet concern about obesity and heart disease.
Fortified products, such as milk with added vitamins, calcium or omega-3 fatty acids.
Functional yoghurts (foods with an added health benefit) with added probiotic cultures or plant stanol or sterol products.
Lactose-free, sugar-free and high-protein yoghurts, for people with lactose intolerance or following healthy eating guidelines.
Convenience formats: individually wrapped cheese portions, drinking yoghurts and frozen yoghurt.
Added-value products such as grated cheese and flavoured spreadable butter.
Extended shelf life through UHT treatment and aseptic packaging.
Resealable packs and varied sizes for family use.

Cheese is made by coagulating (setting) milk protein and draining off the liquid whey. Cheeses are grouped by how firm and moist they are and by how they are ripened, so each class has typical examples that exams ask you to name.
Hard cheese is low in moisture, firm and matured for longer, so it keeps well. Examples are Cheddar, Parmesan, Cheshire and Emmenthal.
Semi-hard or semi-soft cheese sits between hard and soft in firmness. Examples are Gouda, Edam and Halloumi.

Soft cheese is high in moisture. Cottage cheese, cream cheese, feta and mozzarella are fresh (eaten young, with feta also kept in brine), while Brie and Camembert are ripened by a mould on the surface.
Blue-veined cheese is ripened by a mould that grows through the cheese, giving the blue veins. Examples are Cashel Blue (an Irish cheese), Stilton, Roquefort and Gorgonzola.

Processed cheese is natural cheese melted and blended with emulsifying salts and other ingredients, then moulded into a uniform product, so it has a longer shelf life and melts easily. Examples are cheese slices, cheese spreads and processed cheddars.
Smoked cheese is cheese flavoured by smoking, often sold as a processed product, so it is grouped with processed cheese.
Diagram: draw a table with the columns class, description, examples and uses, with one row for each class of cheese.
Cheese is concentrated milk: most of the water and lactose are drained away, leaving the protein, fat and minerals. That is why it is rich in some nutrients and has none of others.

Protein is about 10 to 27% of cheese, mostly casein. It is high biological value (HBV) protein, containing all the essential amino acids (the ones the body cannot make), for growth, repair and the making of enzymes, hormones and antibodies.
Protein content varies by type, because soft cheese contains less protein than hard cheese.
Fat is about 4 to 35%, mostly saturated, with cholesterol, so full-fat cheese supplies concentrated energy. Cottage cheese is about 4% fat.
The more water in a cheese, the less fat it has, and cheese made from skimmed milk is lower in fat.
Carbohydrate is 0 to about 1.5%, because most of the lactose drains away in the whey and the rest changes to lactic acid.
Vitamin A and beta-carotene support healthy skin, vision and membranes. Riboflavin (B2) and B12 are the main B group vitamins supplied.
Calcium and phosphorus support bones and teeth, and some vitamin D is supplied to help calcium absorption. Total minerals are about 1.5 to 4%.
Sodium comes mainly from the salt added during production, so cheddar and processed cheese are high in salt. Cheese is deficient in vitamin C, iron and fibre, and its water content varies by type.
Dietetic value means how suitable cheese is for different people and diets. It has strong points as a food and some limits that matter for health.
Cheese is a relatively cheap protein food with no waste, needs no cooking, and suits packed lunches and snacks.
Protein and calcium support growth in children and adolescents, and are needed in pregnancy and by nursing mothers.
Cheese is a high-energy food because of its fat, so it suits active people.

Cottage cheese and low-fat varieties suit low-kilocalorie, low-cholesterol and weight-watching diets. Full-fat cheeses are high in saturated fat and salt, so people with heart disease or high blood pressure should limit them.
Some cheeses are difficult to digest because they are high in fat.

Pregnant women are advised to avoid mould-ripened soft cheeses such as Brie and Camembert, blue cheeses and soft cheeses made from unpasteurised milk, because of the risk of listeria (a food poisoning bacterium). Hard cheese, cottage cheese, cream cheese and pasteurised processed cheese are considered safe.
Cheese lacks carbohydrate and fibre, so it should be eaten with foods such as bread, crackers, pasta or potatoes, and with vegetables or fruit for fibre and vitamin C.

Cheese is versatile and comes in wide variety, which helps variety in the diet. It sits on the milk, yoghurt and cheese shelf of the Food Pyramid, where it should be eaten in small amounts and in lower-fat forms.
Two ingredients turn liquid milk into cheese: bacteria that sour it, and an enzyme that sets it. Each does a different job, and exams often ask you to keep them apart.
Lactic acid bacteria are added to pasteurised milk as a starter culture. They convert lactose (milk sugar) into lactic acid, which preserves the cheese, adds flavour and helps the curd to form.

Rennet contains the enzyme rennin, which changes caseinogen (the soluble milk protein) into casein (the insoluble form). Rennet traditionally comes from calf stomach, while vegetarian rennet is made from microbes or plants.
The casein coagulates, so the milk proteins bond and set, and the milk separates into curds and whey.
Curds are the solid part. Whey is the liquid part, which holds most of the lactose and water, so little lactose stays in the cheese.
Making cheese follows a fixed order, from adding the bacteria to ripening. Learn the stages in sequence, with what each one achieves.
1. A culture of lactic acid bacteria is added to pasteurised milk, to turn lactose into lactic acid.
2. The milk is heated to about 30°C and rennet is added. Left to stand for about 30 minutes, it separates into curds and whey.
3. The curds are cut or chopped to release more whey, and the whey is drained off.
4. The curds are heated to 35 to 40°C (called scalding), which squeezes out more whey and gives the correct consistency.
5. Cheddaring (for Cheddar and similar cheeses): the curds are cut into blocks and piled on each other, and turned, to complete drainage of the whey.
6. The blocks are milled (cut) and about 2% salt is added for flavour and preservation.
7. The salted curds are placed in moulds and pressed. The moulds may be sprayed with hot water so that a protective rind forms.

8. The cheese is removed from the moulds, date stamped, and stored for about 3 to 12 months to ripen (mature), then graded. Ripening develops flavour and texture, and longer maturing gives a stronger, drier cheese.
