The steps above give a hard cheese such as Cheddar. Ripened cheeses use a mould to get their character, which is the contrast to know.
Blue cheese has a mould added, and the cheese is pierced to let air in, so the mould can grow through it.
Soft ripened cheeses such as Brie and Camembert have a mould growing on the surface.
Packaging protects the cheese, and labelling tells the buyer what it is and how to store it. Both carry marks in the production question.
Cheese is vacuum packed in polythene (plastic) zip-lock bags, which extends shelf life. The pack protects it from mould and drying.
Waxed paper or wax coating and plastic tubs are used, with tubs suiting smaller portions.
The label gives the type of cheese, brand, quantity and nutritional information.
The label also gives the date stamp, storage instructions and allergen information (milk).
Labels must comply with Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
Heat changes both the protein and the fat in cheese. Knowing these changes explains how to cook it well.
Colour changes as the cheese browns.
The fat melts, and if the cheese is overheated the fat separates from it and makes it oily.
Overcooked cheese becomes stringy, tough and hard to digest, and overcooking can carbonise (burn) it.
Little loss of nutrients occurs when cheese is cooked.
To avoid these faults, grate or slice the cheese, cook it at a moderate temperature for a short time, and add it at the end of a sauce.
Cheese is versatile because it can be eaten cold, melted, grated or cooked into dishes. Match the type of cheese to the dish.
Sandwiches and snacks, including cheese slices in sandwiches.
Baking and pastry, such as cheese scones, cheese pastry and cheese straws.
Savoury and sweet fillings, and sauces such as white cheese sauce and macaroni cheese.
Desserts, such as cheesecake made with cream cheese, and cheeseboards.
Main ingredient in pizza, pasta, potato and salad dishes.
Dips, fondue, and toppings and garnishes such as gratin.

Choosing the cheese: Parmesan, a hard cheese, is grated over pasta carbonara; cream cheese is used in lemon cheesecake; cheddar slices are used in a cheese sandwich; mozzarella goes on pizza; grated hard cheese suits toppings that brown.
Irish farmhouse cheese is a speciality (artisan) food that has grown in popularity. Exams ask for reasons, each explained.
Farmhouse cheese is made on the farm in small quantities, mainly by hand, usually from the farm's own cow's, goat's or sheep's milk.
Examples are Cashel Blue (Co Tipperary, blue), Gubbeen (West Cork, washed rind), Durrus (West Cork) and Coolea (Co Cork, Gouda style).
Its distinctive flavours, textures and degrees of maturity differ from mass-produced cheese, and there is a wide variety, including soft, hard, blue, flavoured, organic and reduced-fat cheeses.
It is seen as high quality, hygienic, less processed and more natural.
Consumers value traceable local food, with fewer food miles, and support for local employment and rural family farm businesses.
It is promoted and sold at farmers' markets, specialist shops, restaurants, food tourism, and by celebrity chefs and the media, and it suits the cheeseboard and entertaining.
Awards and quality assurance strengthen its premium image.
The outside of the egg is built to protect the liquid contents while still letting the egg breathe. The air cell inside it is a useful clue to how old the egg is.
Shell: hard and porous, made mainly of calcium carbonate. It protects the contents, and the tiny pores let gases pass in and out.
The outer coating of the shell (the cuticle, or bloom) reduces the entry of bacteria.
Shell colour, white or brown, depends on the breed of hen, so it does not affect the nutritive value.
Shell membranes: two thin membranes, an outer and an inner one, line the shell and help keep bacteria out.

Air cell (air space): a pocket between the two membranes at the blunt, broad end of the egg. It grows as the egg ages because water evaporates through the shell, so a bigger air cell means an older egg.
Water test for freshness: a fresh egg sinks and lies flat in water because its air cell is small, while an old egg floats because its air cell is large.
Diagram: a cross-section of an egg, labelling the shell, shell membranes and air cell.
Inside the shell are two liquid parts, the white and the yolk. Cords and membranes hold the yolk in the centre so it is cushioned from knocks.
Albumen (white): the transparent liquid around the yolk. It is mainly water (about 90%) and protein (albumin, ovalbumin and globulin), and it is fat free.
The albumen has two layers, thick and thin. The thick white is the sign of a fresh egg.
Chalazae: two twisted cords of albumen at each end of the yolk that anchor the yolk in the centre of the egg. They are not the same thing as the germinal disc.
Yolk: the yellow centre, held in the vitelline membrane. It holds the fat, lecithin, cholesterol, protein (vitellin and livetin), the fat-soluble vitamins and minerals, including iron.
Yolk colour depends on the hen's feed, because of carotenoid pigments (yellow-orange colouring) in it.

Germinal disc (blastodisc): a small pale spot on the surface of the yolk. It would develop into a chick if the egg were fertilised, but eggs sold in shops are normally unfertilised. It is not a blood spot or an embryo.
Diagram: a labelled cross-section of the egg showing the shell, outer and inner shell membranes, air cell, thick and thin albumen, chalazae, vitelline membrane, yolk and germinal disc.

An egg packs protein, fat, vitamins and minerals into a small package, but it is missing carbohydrate, fibre and vitamin C. For each nutrient, learn what the egg supplies and what the body uses it for.

Protein is about 13% of the egg. It is high biological value (HBV) with a biological value of 100%, because it contains all the essential amino acids in the proportions the body needs. It is used for growth and repair and for making hormones and enzymes.
White protein is albumin (ovalbumin) and globulin. Yolk protein is vitellin and livetin.
Fat is about 12%, all in the yolk. It is mostly saturated and is in a very fine emulsion because of lecithin (a natural emulsifier in the yolk), so it is easily digested. It gives heat and energy.
The white is fat free, and cholesterol is found only in the yolk. The yolk supplies most of the energy of the egg.
Eggs contain no carbohydrate (0%) and no fibre, so they are served with carbohydrate foods such as toast or potatoes, and with fibre.
Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are found in the yolk. A keeps membranes and eyes healthy, D builds bones and teeth, E is an antioxidant and K helps blood clot.

B group vitamins are found in both the white and the yolk. B1 and B2 help release energy, and niacin and B12 are needed for metabolism. Free-range eggs can contain higher levels of some vitamins, such as niacin and B12, than eggs from caged hens. Eggs lack vitamin C.

Minerals make up about 1% of the egg: calcium and phosphorus for bones and teeth, iron in the yolk for making haemoglobin, and zinc and sulphur. The egg is about 75% water, and the white is mostly water.

Eggs earn their place in the diet because they are cheap, nutritious, easy to digest and easy to cook. Their weak points, saturated fat and cholesterol and the missing nutrients, are dealt with by moderation and by what they are served with.
Eggs are cheap and nutritious, so they suit people on a low budget. They are a protein alternative to meat and fish.
Eggs supply HBV protein for ovo-lacto vegetarians, who eat dairy products and eggs but not meat or fish.
Eggs are easily digested, because the fat is already emulsified and the protein is soft when lightly cooked. This makes them suitable for children, older people, invalids and convalescents.
Their protein supports growth and repair in children, adolescents and pregnant women.

Eggs are quick and easy to cook, which saves fuel, and are versatile in sweet and savoury dishes. They can be eaten alone, or as a meal with carbohydrate such as egg on toast or an omelette with potatoes.
Eggs contain saturated fat and cholesterol, so people with raised cholesterol or heart disease, or anyone limiting cholesterol, should eat eggs in moderation.
Eggs lack vitamin C and fibre, so serve them with complex carbohydrate, vegetables, fruit and wholegrain foods to balance the diet.
Eggs can carry Salmonella (a food poisoning bacterium), so cook them thoroughly for babies, older people, pregnant women and the ill, and wash hands and utensils after handling raw egg.

Eggs are a fresh, perishable food, so choosing well and reading the carton tells you how safe, fresh and traceable they are. Most of what a buyer needs to know is printed on the carton or stamped on the egg.
Choose eggs with clean, unbroken shells from a clean shop, because a cracked shell lets bacteria in. Eggs sold as Class A are not washed.
Eggs are graded by class and by size, which is small, medium or large (and extra large). Shop eggs are Class A.
Check the best-before date on the carton, and use the eggs by it. It is set at no more than 28 days after the egg was laid.
The carton shows the country of origin, and the name, address and registration number of the producer or packer. It also shows the week number (the week the eggs were packed), the class and the size.

The farming method is stated: organic, free-range, barn or caged. Methods differ in animal welfare and price, while nutrition is much the same, though free-range eggs may contain more of some vitamins (B12, niacin).

Each egg is stamped with a producer code, so it can be traced back to its farm and county. The first digit gives the method of production (0 organic, 1 free-range, 2 barn, 3 caged), then IE for Ireland, then a code for the producer.
The Bord Bia Quality Assurance mark confirms that the producer meets its requirements. Many Irish eggs carry it.

Labels must be clear, legible, indelible and not misleading, under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 as given effect in Ireland. Organic eggs come from hens reared to organic standards, with no routine antibiotic or growth-hormone treatment and feed free of artificial pesticides and fertilisers.

Salmonella (a food poisoning bacterium) can be in a hen's gut and, rarely, in the egg itself. Controlling it on the farm lowers the risk of food poisoning, so egg producers follow a quality assurance scheme.
Ireland has an EU-approved national salmonella control plan for laying hens, to keep the national flock healthy and the eggs safe.
Incoming hens (young hens, called pullets) must be certified as salmonella free, so infection is not brought onto the farm.
Laying hens are checked for salmonella each month, so any infection is found early.
All feed for laying hens is heat-treated, which kills bacteria in the feed.
Management systems ensure full traceability of every egg, so a problem egg can be tracked back to its source.
All producers and suppliers are inspected and approved.
Every system is independently inspected before the Bord Bia Quality mark is awarded, so the mark shows the checks have been passed.
An egg's shell is porous and its quality falls as it ages, so good storage keeps it fresh and safe. The rules follow from the shell and the egg's inner structure.
Store eggs in the fridge at 4°C, in the egg compartment rather than the door, because the door is warmer and the eggs are shaken each time it opens.
Store them pointed end down, away from strongly flavoured foods, because the shell is porous and the eggs absorb smells. Keep them away from cooked foods.
Do not wash the shell, because washing removes the protective cuticle (the thin natural coating) and speeds staling.
Use eggs within the best-before date.
Leftover egg white can be kept in a sealed container in the fridge for 2 to 4 days.
Leftover egg yolk can be kept covered with water in a sealed container for up to 4 days.

Wash hands after handling raw eggs. Do not use cracked or dirty eggs in foods that are not cooked, and cook eggs until firm for vulnerable groups, because raw egg dishes such as mayonnaise and mousse carry a risk.
A fresh egg sinks and lies flat in water because its air cell is small, while an old egg tilts or floats. A fresh egg also has a thick white and a high, round yolk.
Coagulation is the setting of egg protein when heated, which thickens and binds food. It is why a runny egg becomes solid when cooked.
Egg white coagulates at about 60 to 65°C; egg yolk coagulates at about 65 to 70°C.
The protein chains untwist, or denature, and straighten, then bond together around small pockets of water, which traps the water so the egg sets.
Overheating makes the protein clump tighter and squeeze out its water, causing curdling and a tough, rubbery texture. Gentle, low heat and stirring give a creamy custard, while high heat curdles it.
Culinary uses, thickening: custards and quiche. Adding egg to a hot liquid slowly prevents lumps.
Culinary uses, binding: burgers, fishcakes, meatballs and stuffings, where the set egg holds the mixture together. Coating: egg and breadcrumbs on fish, and chicken goujons.
Culinary uses, glazing: egg wash on scones, pastry and bread gives gloss and colour. Clarifying: egg white traps solid particles in consommé.
Culinary uses, cooking as a dish: boiled, poached, scrambled, fried and baked eggs, and omelettes. Enriching: rice pudding and mashed potato.
Aeration means trapping air in a food. Eggs do this well, which is how cakes and meringues become light.
Whisking or beating egg, the white especially, traps air as many small bubbles.
The heat from whisking partly unfolds (denatures) the egg protein, which forms a thin film that lines up around each air bubble and sets slightly, giving a foam.

This foam is temporary, so it should not be left standing or it collapses. It is stabilised permanently by further heating, as the protein coagulates in the oven, or by a setting agent such as gelatine. Sugar also helps stabilise it.
Whole eggs and sugar whisked together aerate sponge cakes and Swiss rolls. Egg and fat creamed together also aerate cake mixtures.
Whisked egg whites make meringues, soufflés, mousses, pavlova and the topping on lemon meringue.
For the best foam, use a clean, grease-free bowl and a whisk, because fat or yolk stops the foam forming. Use whites at room temperature and add sugar gradually.
Oil and water do not mix by themselves. Egg yolk can hold them together, which is why it is used in sauces and dressings.
An emulsion is a permanent mixture of two liquids that do not normally mix, such as oil and vinegar, with one broken into tiny droplets spread through the other.
Lecithin, found in the yolk, is a natural emulsifier (a substance that joins liquids that would otherwise separate).
The hydrophilic (water-loving) head of the lecithin molecule attaches to water, and the hydrophobic (water-hating, oil-loving) tail attaches to oil.
This holds the oil and vinegar together and prevents them separating.
To make an emulsion, add the oil drop by drop to the yolk while whisking, because adding it too fast makes it curdle.
Culinary uses: mayonnaise (oil and vinegar), hollandaise and similar sauces (butter and lemon juice), and salad dressings.
Culinary uses: blending the fat and sugar in a cake mixture so the batter does not curdle.
Cooking changes an egg's appearance, texture, safety and nutrients. Some changes are wanted and some are signs of overcooking.
Colour changes: the white turns from transparent to opaque white, as its protein coagulates (sets). The egg white becomes insoluble when heated.
Heat kills bacteria, including salmonella, so thoroughly cooked eggs are safer.
Vitamin B is lost during cooking, though most other nutrients change little.
Overcooking makes eggs tough and rubbery, and harder to digest, because the protein curdles. Digestibility is best with light cooking.
Iron in the yolk and sulphur in the white react to form a green-grey ring around the yolk of an overcooked hard-boiled egg. Cooling the egg quickly in cold water reduces it.
Different cooking methods and times give soft, medium and hard results.

A cereal grain is the seed of a grass, and the wheat grain is the standard example. It has three parts, and its nutrients are spread unevenly across them, so what you eat depends on which parts are kept.
Bran: the outer covering, made of several layers, about 13% of the wheat grain. It is made mainly of cellulose, an insoluble fibre, and it is removed when white flour is milled.

Endosperm: the inner and largest part of the grain. It stores starch, and it also contains most of the grain's protein, which forms gluten when wheat flour is mixed with water. White flour is made from it, and it is the food store for the young plant.
Germ: the small embryo at the base of the grain, about 2% of the grain, which would grow into a new plant. It is rich in vitamin E, unsaturated fat, protein and B group vitamins.
Diagram: longitudinal section (cut lengthways) of the wheat grain, showing bran around the outside, a large endosperm, and the germ at the base. Label all three parts and the crease along one side.
Each part of the grain supplies different nutrients, so you need to name the nutrient and say what it does in the body.

Bran: its cellulose is dietary fibre (roughage), which adds bulk to faeces, absorbs water and stimulates peristalsis (the muscle waves that push food along the gut). This prevents constipation and aids digestion.
Bran also supplies B group vitamins and minerals such as iron, magnesium and phosphorus.

Endosperm: starch is the main carbohydrate in cereals and supplies energy for heat and activity. The protein it contains is of low biological value, meaning it is low in one or more essential amino acids.
Germ: it supplies most of the grain's unsaturated fat, and vitamin E, which acts as an antioxidant (it protects body cells from damage).
Germ: it also supplies protein and B group vitamins such as thiamine (vitamin B1), which are concentrated in the germ.
Refining removes most of the bran and germ, so white flour and refined cereals lose most of their fibre, B group vitamins, vitamin E and minerals unless these are added back.
The nutritive value of a food is the nutrients it supplies. Cereals are mainly a starchy food, with smaller amounts of several other nutrients.
Protein: provides protein for growth and repair of body cells, but cereal protein is of low biological value because it is low in the essential amino acid lysine (an amino acid the body cannot make).
Eating cereals with pulses, milk or eggs improves the protein's value, because the foods make up for each other's missing amino acids (complementary proteins).
Carbohydrate: starch provides energy for heat and activity, and wholegrain cereals also provide fibre.
Fibre: wholegrain cereals provide insoluble fibre from the bran, and oats and barley provide soluble fibre.
Fat: cereals are low in total fat, and the fat they contain is mainly unsaturated and concentrated in the germ.
Vitamins: B group vitamins (thiamine, niacin and riboflavin) and vitamin E, which is found in the germ.
Minerals: calcium, iron and phosphorus, much of the iron and phosphorus being found in the bran and germ.
Water: cereals are dry foods with a low water content, so they keep well when stored correctly.
The dietetic value of a food is how useful it is in the diet, for health and for everyday eating. Cereals score well for cost, fibre and convenience, with a few limits.
Energy: starchy cereals are an inexpensive source of energy and form the staple food (the food a diet is built around) in many countries.
Constipation: the fibre in wholegrain cereals increases stool bulk and stimulates peristalsis, so it helps prevent constipation and bowel disorders.
Blood cholesterol and blood sugar: soluble fibre from oats and barley can help lower blood cholesterol and slows the absorption of glucose after a meal.
Satiety (feeling full): fibre-rich foods give a feeling of fullness, which supports weight control.
Fat: the fat in cereals is unsaturated, so it does not contribute to cholesterol build-up.
Versatility: cereals can be used in sweet and savoury dishes, and they are quick and easy to prepare and inexpensive.
Limit, coeliac disease: gluten, found in wheat, barley and rye, and in oats unless they are labelled gluten-free, cannot be tolerated by people with coeliac disease.
Limit, phytic acid: phytic acid in the bran binds iron and calcium (so the body cannot absorb them) and reduces their absorption.
A wholegrain cereal keeps the whole grain rather than just the starchy centre. This is why wholegrain products are promoted as part of a healthy diet.

A wholegrain cereal product contains all three parts of the grain: bran, endosperm and germ. Examples are wholemeal flour and bread, brown rice, porridge oats, wholegrain breakfast cereals and wholewheat pasta.

Wholegrain products provide more fibre, B group vitamins, vitamin E and minerals than refined products made from the same cereal. They also release energy more slowly and are filling, so their fibre raises fibre intake.
In the Food Pyramid, wholemeal cereals, breads, potatoes, pasta and rice form the second shelf, so wholegrain choices fit into the balance of the whole diet.
Phytic acid in the bran binds iron, calcium and zinc and reduces their absorption; very high fibre intakes can have the same effect.
Beans on wholemeal toast is an example of combining cereal protein with pulses, which raises the biological value of the protein.
A wholegrain label does not cancel excess sugar, fat or salt added to some products, so the nutrition panel must still be checked.
A high-fibre day for a school child could use wholegrain breakfast cereal, brown bread, and brown rice or wholewheat pasta.
Cereals are healthy for most people, but some people avoid or limit them for medical or dietary reasons.
Coeliac disease or gluten intolerance: gluten damages the lining of the small intestine, so gluten-containing cereals must be avoided.
Weight gain: large portions of starchy foods, especially with added fat or sugar, supply more energy than the body uses, so low-carbohydrate or weight-loss diets limit them.
Blood sugar: refined cereals are digested quickly and raise blood glucose quickly, so people managing blood sugar, or following low glycaemic index diets, often choose wholegrain cereals.
Bloating: some people limit cereals because they cause bloating.
Hidden salt and sugar: many breakfast cereals, breads and sauces contain added salt or sugar.
Main sources of cereals in the Irish diet are bread, pasta, rice, breakfast cereals, porridge, biscuits and cakes.

Cereals are the seeds of grasses and are the staple food (the main everyday food) in many countries. Six are eaten as food, and each is made into a range of products, so the cereal named in a product tells you its basic ingredient.
The six main cereals are wheat, rice, oats, maize (corn), barley and rye.
Wheat is made into flours (white, wholemeal, self-raising and strong), bread, pasta, couscous, bulgur, semolina, biscuits and cakes, and into breakfast cereals such as shredded wheat and Weetabix.
Rice is eaten as white and brown rice and in risotto, and is made into rice flour, rice cakes, rice noodles, rice pudding and puffed rice breakfast cereal.
Oats are made into porridge, oatmeal, oatcakes, flapjacks, muesli and granola.
Maize (corn) gives cornflour, cornflakes, popcorn, polenta, corn oil and tortillas. Sweetcorn is eaten as a vegetable, so it is not the product to give for maize.
Barley gives pearl barley (used in soups and stews), barley flakes and barley water, and malt, which is used to make beer and whiskey.
Rye gives rye bread, rye flour and crispbread.
Breakfast cereals are grain products sold ready to eat or ready to cook. They differ in how the grain is processed, and in how much sugar, salt and fat they contain.
Flaked cereals, such as cornflakes, are made from grains that have been rolled flat and toasted.
Puffed cereals, such as puffed rice, are made by heating grains under pressure until they expand.
Shredded cereals, such as shredded wheat, are made from cooked grains formed into shreds and baked.
Muesli and granola are mixes of cereal flakes with nuts, dried fruit and seeds; granola is usually bound with a sweetener and baked.
Porridge oats need cooking in water or milk, while ready-to-eat cereals need no cooking.
Many breakfast cereals are fortified with vitamins and iron.
Sugar, salt and fat levels vary widely between brands, so compare the nutrition panels before choosing.
The ingredients list is in descending order of weight, so a wholegrain cereal should be named first if the product is truly wholegrain.
Fortification is the addition of nutrients (vitamins and minerals) to a food. It is done either to put back nutrients lost in processing or to raise a food above the level it normally contains.
Fortification replaces nutrients lost during processing, such as the B group vitamins and iron removed when wheat is refined.
Fortification can also raise a nutrient above the level normally present, for example vitamins A and D added to low-fat milk.

Folic acid added to some foods helps reduce the risk of neural tube defects (faults in the development of the spine and brain) in a developing baby. Fortifying flour in Ireland is voluntary, so say that some breads and breakfast cereals are fortified.
Iron, folic acid and B group vitamins are the nutrients most commonly added to some flours and breakfast cereals.
Vitamin D and calcium added to foods help address diet-related conditions such as osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones).

Consumption of fortified foods is rising because there is more diet-related illness and fortification tries to address it, it raises the food value of foods, it supports healthy eating, and it is an easy way to raise intake of nutrients people tend to lack.
Fortified products help improve intake of a nutrient, but they do not replace a varied diet, and a fortified cereal can still be high in sugar or salt.
Manufacturers adapt cereal foods for people with particular dietary needs, such as coeliacs, who must avoid gluten (the protein in wheat, barley and rye).

Gluten-free cereal foods are made from rice, maize and other gluten-free ingredients. They are made to avoid cross-contamination (gluten getting in from other foods) and carry a gluten-free declaration.

'Gluten-free' may be used only where the food contains no more than 20 mg/kg gluten as sold (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 828/2014), and oats in such foods must be produced to avoid contamination. The FSAI gives guidance.
Allergens are emphasised in the ingredients list so that people can spot them quickly.
Other lines include high-fibre and wholegrain products, lower-sugar and reduced-salt products, fortified products, vegan products and portion packs.
A special-diet claim does not make a product healthy, because a gluten-free product can still be high in sugar or fat.
Cereal products are dry foods, but they spoil if they are stored badly. Poor storage leads to mould, infestation, staleness, rancid flavour and loss of quality.
Store cereal products in a cool, dry place, because damp encourages mould growth and infestation by insect pests such as weevils.
Once opened, transfer flour, cereals and pasta to an airtight container so that moisture and pests cannot enter.
Use products by the best-before date, after which flour and cereals lose quality and may become stale or infested.
Wholegrain products and wholemeal flour have a shorter shelf life than white products because the unsaturated fat in the germ (the embryo of the grain) can turn rancid.
Cereals absorb strong odours, so keep them away from spices and other strong-smelling foods.
Bread stales faster in a fridge than at room temperature, so store bread in a bread bin or wrapped at room temperature, or freeze it.
The label on a cereal product tells you whether it is fresh, safe and good for you, so read it before you buy.
Ingredients are listed in descending order of weight, so a wholegrain product should name a wholegrain cereal first.
Check the nutrition panel for fibre, sugar and salt, which are usually given per 100 g, so you can compare brands fairly.
Choose products with the best-before date clearly printed, and check the packaging is undamaged and sealed, because damage lets in moisture and pests.

Milling turns the whole wheat grain into flour by separating the bran, germ and endosperm and then grinding the endosperm finely. Each stage has a purpose, and an account of production should give the stages in order with the reason for each.

1. Intake and cleaning: the wheat is sampled, graded and may be blended to give the quality needed. It is then passed through sieves, air currents and magnets to remove stones, dust, chaff and metal, so that none of these end up in the flour.

2. Conditioning (tempering): a controlled amount of water is added and the grain is left to rest. This toughens the bran so it separates in large pieces rather than shattering into the flour, and it softens the endosperm (the starchy centre of the grain) ready for milling.
3. Break rolling: corrugated (grooved) rollers crack open the grain and release the endosperm, while the bran and germ stay in larger pieces because the bran is not crushed.
4. Sifting (plansifting): plansifters, which are stacks of sieves, separate the bran, germ and endosperm particles by size, so each stream can be dealt with separately.
5. Reduction rolling: smooth rollers grind the endosperm repeatedly, with a sieving step after each pass, until it becomes fine white flour.

6. Finishing: flour from different batches is blended for consistent quality, such as gluten strength, and may be treated with permitted improvers. It may be fortified (have extra nutrients added) and is tested for moisture, gluten strength and colour before packing.

Extraction rate is the percentage of the original grain that ends up in the flour. White flour is about 75% and wholemeal flour is 100%, because it keeps all three parts of the grain. Wheatmeal falls between the two.
Stone-ground flour is made by grinding the grain between millstones instead of rollers, and it is accepted as a type of flour.

Diagram: a flow chart of the milling stages in order (intake and cleaning, conditioning, break rolling, sifting, reduction rolling, finishing), with the bran, germ and endosperm streams branching off at the sifting step.
The difference between white and wholemeal flour comes down to how much of the grain is kept during milling. This changes the colour, nutrition, texture of baked foods and how long the flour keeps.
White flour is made from the endosperm only, because the bran and germ are removed. It is lighter in colour and texture, and has about 75% extraction.
White flour has less fibre and fewer B vitamins and minerals than wholemeal, because these are mostly lost with the bran and germ. It has a longer shelf life.
Wholemeal flour is made from the whole grain, with 100% extraction, so it is brown and higher in fibre, B vitamins and minerals.
Wholemeal flour makes denser baked products. It has a shorter shelf life because of the oil in the germ, which goes off over time.
Flours differ in how much of the grain they contain, how much gluten-forming protein they have and whether anything has been added. This decides which job each one does best.
Plain white (cream) flour has a medium gluten content. It is used for pastry, cakes (creamed or whisked), biscuits, sauces and roux, pizza, scones and batters.
Self-raising flour is plain flour with a raising agent, usually baking powder, added, so it is not a different wheat. It is used for cakes, sponges, scones and biscuits.

Strong flour is made from hard wheat and is high in gluten-forming protein. It is used for yeast breads, pizza dough and puff pastry because the gluten traps gas, such as the carbon dioxide produced by yeast, for a good rise.

Wholemeal (wholewheat) flour is milled from the whole grain, so it contains bran, germ and endosperm. It is used for brown bread, scones, muffins and wholemeal pastry, and gives a denser texture because the bran cuts the gluten strands.
Wheatmeal (brown) flour is partly refined, with part of the bran removed. It is used for brown bread and soda bread.
Cornflour is a fine starch made from the endosperm of maize, not a wheat flour, so it does not contain gluten. It is used as a thickener for sauces, custards and gravy.
Rice flour and other gluten-free flours (rice, maize and other blends) are used in baking for people with coeliac disease, who cannot eat gluten.
Gluten is the protein network that gives bread and pastry their structure, and its development is controlled by the way flour is handled.
Gluten forms when the proteins gliadin and glutenin in wheat flour are mixed with water.
Gluten is elastic and stretchy: it traps gas and gives bread its structure.
Kneading develops gluten, producing a strong, elastic dough, whereas rubbing in fat and mixing lightly limit gluten, giving tender pastry.
Strong flour contains more gluten-forming protein than plain flour, so it gives a more elastic dough.

Flour is the syllabus's example of a food that undergoes extensive processing. The grain is cleaned, separated, ground, blended, treated and packed, and the packaging and label then protect and inform the buyer.
Flour is a processed food: milling turns the whole grain into a refined ingredient with a different nutrient profile.
Packaging: flour is packed in strong, sealed, food-grade bags, paper or plastic, that protect it from moisture, insects, contamination and odours, and are easy to handle and store.

Labelling: the label gives the name of the food (the type of flour), the ingredients list, the net quantity, the nutrition declaration, the best-before date, storage instructions and the name and address of the food business. It may also carry cooking or recipe guidance.

Allergens: wheat and gluten must be emphasised in the ingredients list, for example in bold type, so people with allergies or coeliac disease can spot them. This is set by Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011.
Traceability: a batch (lot) code and date mark allow the manufacturer to trace the flour back through production, so it can be recalled if there is a problem.
Fortified flour: any added nutrients are shown on the nutrition declaration.
Labelling also lets shoppers make a safe choice, compare products and follow the storage guidance.

Cereals are mostly starch, with some protein, sugar, cellulose and B group vitamins, and heat changes all of them. The way you heat the cereal, with moisture or without, decides which change is most obvious.
Moist heat (boiling, simmering, steaming) makes starch granules absorb liquid, swell and burst. This is why the cereal softens and thickens the liquid around it.
Dry heat (baking, roasting, toasting) dries the surface and breaks the starch down into dextrins, a change called dextrinisation. This forms a brown, crisp crust.
In frying, the starch also absorbs fat, so the cooked cereal food takes up fat as well as browning.
Dry heat also caramelises sugars in cereal products (heating sugar until it turns brown), adding colour and flavour.
Heat softens the cellulose (the fibre) in the bran and cell walls, so cooked cereals are easier to digest.
Heat coagulates protein (it sets firm), which sets the structure of batters, doughs, baked goods and cooked cereals.
Heat destroys some B group vitamins, and more are lost when cereals are boiled in a large volume of water that is then discarded, because the vitamins dissolve into it.
Overall, the colour, flavour and texture of the cereal all change during cooking.
Gelatinisation is what happens when starch is heated in a liquid: the granules absorb water, swell and burst, and the mixture thickens. It is how flour or cornflour thickens a sauce.
1. Starch granules absorb water from the liquid and swell.
2. Some starch (amylose) leaches out of the swollen granules into the liquid.
3. The liquid thickens as the swollen granules and amylose form a gel-like network that fills it.
4. On further heating the granules burst, and the starch is fully gelatinised.
Heat is essential. Flour left cold in a liquid only forms a paste, so it does not thicken by absorbing liquid alone.
Starch granules must be kept apart before heating, by stirring, by blending the flour with a little cold liquid first, or by rubbing fat in as in a roux. Otherwise they clump into lumps.
Flour or cornflour must be cooked long enough to gelatinise fully, otherwise the sauce tastes floury.
A roux is a cooked mixture of equal weights of fat and flour, used as the base of a sauce. The fat coats the starch granules and keeps the flour from forming lumps when the liquid is added.
Rice shows clearly what moist heat does to a cereal, and the same ideas apply to pasta and oats. The method you choose also decides how many B vitamins you keep.
Rinsing rice removes surface starch, so that the cooked grains stay separate instead of sticking together.
Absorption method: rice is cooked in a measured amount of water, covered, until all of the water is absorbed, and it is left off the heat to finish.
Boiling method: rice is cooked in excess water, which is drained off afterwards.
Moist heat makes rice grains swell, burst and absorb liquid, and gelatinisation gives the cooked rice its soft texture.
Fibre in the grain softens during cooking, making the rice easier to digest. Its colour also changes.
B group vitamins leach (dissolve out) into the cooking water, so use only the water needed, cover the pan, do not overcook, and use the cooking liquid, for example in soups, where practical.
Brown rice takes longer to cook than white rice because the intact bran layer slows water absorption into the grain.

Pasta is boiled in plenty of boiling water until al dente (cooked but still slightly firm). Oats for porridge are cooked in milk or water and stirred as the starch gelatinises, which stops lumps forming.

A raising agent produces or traps a gas (air, steam or carbon dioxide) that expands in the heat of baking. The protein and starch then set around the bubbles and hold the structure, giving a light, risen product.

Air (a physical raising agent) is trapped by beating, whisking eggs, creaming fat and sugar, sieving flour, folding and rubbing in. It expands in the oven, as in sponge cakes, meringues and, slightly, shortcrust pastry.
Steam: water in a mixture turns to steam in the hot oven and expands the product, as in choux pastry, puff and rough puff pastry, Yorkshire pudding and pancakes.

Yeast (a biological raising agent) ferments sugars in warm, moist dough, producing carbon dioxide and alcohol and releasing energy. The gluten (a protein, not starch) traps the gas and the dough rises during proving.
Yeast works best at about 35-40 degrees Celsius and is killed above about 55-60 degrees Celsius, so dough is proved in a warm place, not a hot one. Baking then kills the yeast.

Bicarbonate of soda (bread soda) releases carbon dioxide when it reacts with an acid such as buttermilk, yoghurt, treacle or honey in the presence of moisture and heat. It is used in soda bread and scones.

Baking powder contains bicarbonate of soda with an acid salt and a starch filler. The acid and alkali react when moistened and heated to release carbon dioxide, so it is used in cakes, muffins and scones.
Self-raising flour is plain flour with baking powder already added.

Raising agents for named products: bread uses yeast, bread soda, or air or baking powder; sponge cake uses air, self-raising flour or baking powder; muffins use baking powder or bread soda; lemon drizzle cake uses baking powder or air.
A raising agent only works if the mixture and the oven let it do its job. Small errors in measuring or handling can leave a baked product flat or heavy.
Measure accurately, because too much or too little raising agent gives a poor rise or a coarse texture.
Use the correct oven temperature, so the gas expands and the protein and starch set at the right moment.
Do not open the oven door early, because the cold air can make the risen mixture collapse before it has set.
Handle the mixture correctly, for example folding gently so the trapped air is not knocked out.

Pastries are grouped by how the fat is combined with the flour and how the pastry rises, and this decides the texture of the finished pastry. Knowing the groups lets you name a type, say how it differs from another, and match each to a dish.

Short pastries (shortcrust, sweet shortcrust, rich shortcrust, biscuit and cheese pastry): the fat is rubbed into the flour so that it coats the flour particles and limits gluten (the stretchy protein in flour), giving a crumbly texture.
Flaked or laminated pastries (rough puff, flaky and puff): pieces or layers of fat are folded into the dough, so layers of dough and fat separate and rise, giving a flaky texture.
Choux pastry: a cooked paste of water, fat and flour, with beaten egg added. It contains no rubbed-in fat and is raised by steam into a hollow shell, which is why it suits eclairs and profiteroles.
Filo pastry: very thin sheets of dough layered with fat or oil, which become crisp when baked, as in samosas and strudel.
Suet pastry is a type of its own: the fat is shredded suet, not rubbed in, and it is made with self-raising flour then steamed or baked, as in a steamed pudding. It can also be boiled.

Matching dishes: shortcrust for apple tart, quiche and (as rich shortcrust) mince pies; rough puff or puff for sausage rolls, vol-au-vents and pie toppings; choux for eclairs and profiteroles; filo for samosas and strudel; suet for steamed pudding.

Two types differ in their ingredients, proportions, method, characteristics or appearance. For example, shortcrust has the fat rubbed in while rough puff has the fat left in pieces and folded in, and rough puff uses a higher proportion of fat.

Shortcrust is the most common short pastry and forms the base for sweet and savoury tarts and pies. Rubbing the fat into the flour coats the flour with fat, which limits gluten and makes the pastry short, meaning crumbly.
Ingredients: plain flour, a pinch of salt, cold fat (butter, margarine or lard, or a mix) in roughly half the weight of the flour, and cold water to bind; sugar is added for sweet shortcrust.
Step 1: sift the flour and salt into a bowl, which aerates the flour (puts air into it) and removes lumps.

Step 2: rub the cold fat into the flour with the fingertips, lifting the mixture to add air, until it resembles fine breadcrumbs. Cold fingertips keep the fat from melting, and the fat coating the flour is what limits gluten.
Step 3: add cold water gradually, mixing with a round-bladed knife until the dough just comes together. Too much liquid makes the pastry tough.
Step 4: bring the dough together lightly, wrap and chill it so the gluten relaxes and the fat firms. Heavy handling would develop the gluten and toughen the pastry.
Step 5: roll lightly on a floured surface, line the tin, and chill again before baking so the pastry does not shrink.

Step 6: bake in a preheated hot oven (about 200 degrees Celsius, gas 6) until golden, then reduce the heat if the pastry is browning too quickly. Blind bake a case (bake it empty) when the filling is not cooked, such as quiche, to prevent a soggy base.

Presentation: sweet shortcrust is dusted with icing sugar or glazed with beaten egg or milk; savoury shortcrust is used for quiche and pies, with the edges crimped or fluted. Used for tarts, pies and mince pies, the pastry should be neat, evenly browned, crisp and not shrunk.

Rough puff is a puff pastry in which the fat is left in pieces rather than rubbed in, and the dough is folded in several turns to create layers. It uses a high proportion of hard fat (about three-quarters of the weight of the flour), so it is richer and lighter than shortcrust.
Ingredients: plain flour, a pinch of salt, hard fat (butter or block margarine), and cold water to bind; a little lemon juice is optional.

Step 1: cut the cold fat into cubes or irregular pieces, leave them visible and mix them lightly with the flour, binding the dough with cold water. The lumps of fat must stay, because they make the layers later.
Step 2: roll the dough into a long rectangle, fold the bottom third up and the top third down, then turn the dough a quarter turn.
Step 3: repeat the roll, fold and turn several times, resting and chilling between turns so the fat stays firm and the layers stay distinct.
Step 4: roll to the required thickness and chill before cutting so that the edges stay sharp.
Step 5: bake in a very hot, preheated oven (about 220 degrees Celsius, gas 7 to 8) and do not open the door early.
Why it rises: the water in the dough and fat turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, then the fat melts into the dough and the layers set, so the pastry rises and becomes flaky and light.

Presentation: sausage rolls, vol-au-vents, pie lids and toppings, and Eccles cakes. Glaze with egg wash, keeping it off the cut edges so the layers can rise; the layers should be even and golden, with sharp edges.

Light, crisp pastry depends on keeping the fat solid, handling the dough as little as possible and not building up gluten. These guidelines apply to both types and explain why a pastry turns out tough, shrunk, soggy or heavy.
Keep the ingredients, hands, utensils and kitchen cool so that the fat does not melt before baking.
Weigh ingredients accurately so that the flour-to-fat ratio is correct.
Sieve the flour to introduce air, and rub in lightly with the fingertips.
Add cold liquid gradually; too much liquid makes the pastry sticky or tough and increases shrinkage.
Avoid overhandling: working the dough develops gluten, which makes pastry tough, so handle it as little as possible.
Rest and chill pastry before rolling and baking so that the gluten relaxes and the pastry does not shrink.
Roll lightly in one direction and evenly, and avoid stretching the dough, which causes shrinkage.
Bake in a preheated hot oven, on a hot baking tray, and use blind baking for fillings that are not baked, such as quiche, which keeps the base crisp.
Vegetables are grouped by the part of the plant that is eaten, and this largely determines which nutrients they supply. Learn the nine classes, an example of each and one nutritional note for each.

Roots (carrots, turnips, beetroot, parsnips) are the plant's storage organs, so they supply starch and sugars. Orange varieties such as carrots are rich in beta-carotene (the orange pigment the body turns into vitamin A).
Bulbs (onions, leeks) are layered leaf bases that store sugar, which is why they give flavour. Onions contain small amounts of sugar.
Tubers (potatoes) are swollen underground stems that store starch. Potatoes also supply some vitamin C.
Leafy greens (cabbage, spinach, lettuce, kale) are good sources of folate (a B vitamin), calcium and non-haem iron (the plant form of iron), plus vitamin C.
Flowers (broccoli, cauliflower) are the edible flower buds, and they supply vitamin C and folate.

Pulses (peas, beans, lentils, chickpeas) are the seeds of leguminous plants (plants that carry their seeds in pods). They are richer in protein and fibre than any other vegetable, and examiners often call them pulse vegetables.
Stems (asparagus, celery) are edible shoots and stalks. They have a high water content and little energy.
Fruit vegetables (tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers) are the fruit or seed-bearing part of the plant but are eaten as a savoury vegetable. Tomatoes and peppers supply vitamin C.
Fungi (mushrooms) are not plants. They are a source of riboflavin (B2) and niacin, which are B vitamins.
Fruit is grouped by its structure and type, and each group has a typical nutritional strength. Know the six classes, examples of each and what each is best for.
Citrus fruit (oranges, lemons, limes, grapefruit, mandarins) is among the richest dietary sources of vitamin C.
Soft and berry fruit (strawberries, raspberries, blackcurrants, blueberries, blackberries, grapes) are small and juicy. Blackcurrants and strawberries are high in vitamin C.
Stone fruit (plums, peaches, nectarines, cherries, apricots) has one large stone enclosing the seed. Apricots are rich in pro-vitamin A (beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A).
Pome or hard fruit (apples, pears) is fleshy fruit with a core containing the seeds. The skin and flesh of apples supply pectin (a soluble fibre) and fibre.
Dried fruit (raisins, sultanas, currants, prunes, dates, figs, apricots) is concentrated in sugar, energy and fibre because the water has been removed.
Other, tropical or exotic fruit (bananas, kiwi, pineapple, mango, melon, rhubarb): kiwi fruit is a valuable source of vitamin C, and yellow, orange and red fruit such as mango supply pro-vitamin A.
Nutritive value means what is actually in the food. For vegetables, work through the nutrients in turn: protein, fat, carbohydrate, vitamins, minerals and water, then what each does in the body.

Protein: vegetables contain small amounts, a few per cent of their weight (marking schemes give about 1 to 8 per cent), and it is mainly low-biological-value (LBV) protein. Pulses are the best vegetable source, and soya beans supply high-biological-value (HBV) protein.
Fat: vegetables are generally very low in fat, so they are low in energy. Olives, avocados and soya beans are the exceptions and supply mainly unsaturated fat. Vegetables contain no cholesterol.
Carbohydrate: vegetables provide fibre (non-starch polysaccharides, or NSP), starch in potatoes, root vegetables and pulses, and small amounts of sugar in carrots and onions.

Fibre adds bulk to the stool and stimulates peristalsis (the wave-like muscle movements that push food through the gut), so it helps prevent constipation. It may reduce the risk of bowel disease, such as diverticular disease and cancer of the bowel, and it promotes fullness.
Beta-carotene (pro-vitamin A): dark green, orange, yellow and red vegetables supply it, and the body converts it to vitamin A. Vitamin C comes from green vegetables, peppers, tomatoes and potatoes.

B vitamins and others: pulses and green vegetables supply thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2) and B6, and leafy greens supply folate. Green vegetables also supply vitamin K. Vitamins A, C and E act as antioxidants.
Minerals: non-haem iron (dark green vegetables and pulses), calcium (green leafy vegetables), potassium and magnesium, with traces of zinc and iodine.
Water: vegetables are roughly 70 to 95 per cent water, which contributes to hydration and gives them a low energy density (little energy for their weight).
Fruit is mainly sugar, fibre and water, with a few important vitamins. It has almost no protein or fat, which sets it apart from many other foods.
Carbohydrate: all fruit contains natural sugars (glucose, fructose and sucrose), which provide energy and sweetness.
Underripe fruit such as bananas contains starch, which turns into sugar as the fruit ripens, so ripe fruit tastes sweeter.
Fibre: cellulose in the cell walls is an insoluble fibre, and pectin is a soluble fibre found in the cell walls of fruit.
Fruit contains almost no protein and virtually no fat. Avocados are the exception, supplying mainly unsaturated fat.
Vitamin C: citrus fruit, kiwi fruit, blackcurrants and strawberries are among the best sources. Blackcurrants and kiwi fruit are among the very best.
Yellow, orange and red fruit provide pro-vitamin A (beta-carotene), which the body converts to vitamin A.
Minerals: bananas are a useful source of potassium, while fruit contains only small amounts of calcium and iron.
Fruit has a high water content, which contributes to hydration.
Dietetic value means which diets or conditions a food suits, not what is in it. Fruit and vegetables suit many diets, but they also have limits.
Low energy density, high fibre and high water content make fruit and vegetables filling, so they suit weight control and low-calorie diets.
They are low in fat, with little of it saturated, and vegetables contain no cholesterol, and their fibre helps too, so they suit low-fat, low-cholesterol and heart-healthy diets.
Soya beans and pulses provide protein for vegetarian and vegan diets, and vegetables add iron and folate to those diets.
The antioxidant vitamins A, C and E help protect cells against damage. Vitamin C also supports the immune system and iron absorption, and fibre supports bowel health.
Limits: vegetables do not provide vitamin B12 and are poor in vitamin D, so they cannot meet all nutritional needs alone.
Dried fruit, fruit juice and fruit canned in syrup are high in sugar, so people controlling blood glucose or weight should watch the amount.
Practical value: fruit and vegetables are versatile, available all year (frozen, canned, dried), economical when in season and quick to prepare.
Irish guidelines set a target number of servings, and surveys show many people fall short. You need both the guidance and the skill of commenting on consumption data.

The Department of Health's Healthy Food for Life guidelines and Food Pyramid (2016) make vegetables, salad and fruit the base shelf, the largest shelf of the Pyramid, with 5 to 7 servings a day for adults. HSE and safefood publish the Pyramid material.
Marking schemes phrase the target as 'five portions plus', so you may quote it in that form.
Fruit juice, if drunk, should be unsweetened and counts as at most one serving a day. Whole fruit is better because it gives fibre that juice lacks.
Foods and drinks high in fat, sugar and salt sit on the small top shelf of the Pyramid.
Surveys of Irish people show many do not reach the recommended number of servings.

To comment on a chart, state the share eating none, the share reaching five, and the difference between groups such as adults and children or men and women. Write in full sentences that use the chart's figures.

Exams ask you to suggest ways a named group, such as children, teenagers or men, could eat more fruit and vegetables. Each idea works by hiding, adding or swapping in produce, so give the way and a short reason.
Add vegetables to soups, stews, sauces, curries and Bolognese, and grate or blend them into dishes so that fussy eaters hardly notice them.
Add fruit to breakfast cereals, yoghurt, baking and desserts, or use fruit salads as fillings.
Make smoothies and fresh juices, and add greens such as spinach to smoothies, which adds vitamins without a strong taste.
Use spiralised vegetable noodles or cauliflower rice in place of some starchy carbohydrate foods.
Serve vegetarian main courses, and use vegetables in stir-fries and as toppings on pizza.
For children, cut vegetables into shapes with cutters to make them fun, and try new vegetables and cooking methods.
Pack cherry tomatoes, carrot sticks and fruit pieces for lunch boxes and snacks, and choose fruit instead of sweet snacks.
Grow vegetables at home, so that people are more willing to eat what they have grown.
Shoppers can buy fruit and vegetables in several forms, and each has a place in the diet. The best choice depends on cost, time, storage space and how soon the produce will be used.

Fresh: choose firm produce with no bruising, cuts, mould, wilting or discolouration, because damage shortens keeping time. In-season produce is usually cheaper and has the best flavour; buy usable quantities and shop often for the most perishable items.

Frozen: picked and frozen soon after harvest, so frozen fruit and vegetables retain most of their nutrients. They are convenient, create little waste, are available all year and can be cooked from frozen. Check the pack is solid, undamaged and not frosted, and that it has been kept frozen.

Canned: cooked and sealed in tins or jars, so the product has a long shelf life and is ready to use. Check the liquid: brine adds salt (canned vegetables often contain added salt) and syrup adds sugar, while juice-packed or water-packed options exist. Check cans for dents, bulges and leaks.

Dried: most of the water is removed, so the produce is light and keeps for long periods. Dried fruit such as raisins and apricots is concentrated in sugar and energy, and dried pulses need soaking or cooking.
Other choices also exist: organic, Fairtrade, loose or pre-packed, in-season or imported (out-of-season) produce, and exotic fruit.
Pre-prepared (convenience) produce is washed, peeled, cut or ready to cook, such as salad bags, stir-fry mixes and fruit salad pots. It saves time and skill and leaves little waste.
The disadvantages of pre-prepared produce are that it costs more, has a shorter shelf life once prepared than whole produce, and some vitamin C is lost through cutting.

When buying pre-prepared produce, check the use-by or best-before date, cost and value for money, that the packaging is undamaged and unopened, that there is no discolouration or sliminess, that the quantity suits the household, the storage and cooking instructions, and the nutritional information on the label.
Two shoppers can make different choices from the same shelf, because their circumstances differ. Cost, skills, time and storage space decide how much is bought fresh, frozen or pre-prepared.
Cost: buying in season is cheaper, loose produce is cheaper than packaged, and buying direct from growers or markets can save money.
Buying in bulk only makes sense if there is freezer or preserving capacity, because fresh produce left over will spoil.
Skills and time: the household's cooking skills and the time available decide how much is bought fresh and how much pre-prepared.
Storage space (fridge, freezer, cool dry store) limits the quantity that can be bought and kept in good condition.

Shoppers judge quality by looking, feeling and smelling, and the EU sets grading classes so that buyers know what standard they are getting. Fresh fruit and vegetables sold in the EU must meet marketing standards.

Quality signs when selecting fresh produce: firmness, fresh colour, crispness, no bruising or blemish, no mould or sprouting, uniform size (for even cooking), fresh-looking stalks and leaves, a pleasant smell, and heavy for its size.
Extra class: the best (superior) quality, uniform in shape, size and colour, and free from defects.
Class I: good quality, with minor defects allowed provided they do not affect general appearance, keeping quality or presentation; it is free from bruising and has only slight defects.
Class II: reasonably good, acceptable quality, with more defects of shape or colour allowed, but still fit for consumption. It is sound and good for cooking and processing.
The grading standards are the EU marketing standards for fresh produce, set in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2429.
Fresh produce must show its country of origin under these marketing standards and, where the standard requires it, the class and variety.
Irish produce may carry the Bord Bia quality assurance mark, which shows it has met an assured standard. This mark is a quality assurance scheme and is not the same thing as an EU class.
Fruit and vegetables are still alive after harvest, so they keep changing while they wait to be sold and eaten. This is why storage guidelines exist.
Produce keeps respiring (using up its own food reserves), losing moisture and ripening after harvest, so quality and vitamin C fall with time.
For this reason, buy little and often, use produce soon, and rotate older stock to the front so it is used first.

Fresh vegetables should be refrigerated at about 5 degrees Celsius or below and used as soon as possible, because vitamin C declines during storage. This applies to refrigerated salad and vegetables, not to produce such as potatoes and onions that is kept in a cool store.
Different produce needs different conditions. The aim is to slow moisture loss, ripening and rot without damaging the produce.

Salad and most fresh vegetables: remove any plastic wrapping and damaged items, then store in the refrigerator in the salad or vegetable drawer with air circulating, and use quickly. A sealed bag traps condensation, which speeds rot.

Potatoes: store in a cool, dark, dry, ventilated place such as a vegetable rack or paper sack. Light turns them green and produces bitter solanine, which is harmful, so discard green or sprouting parts or tubers.
Onions and root vegetables: store in a cool, dry, dark, ventilated place, because damp conditions encourage rot. Keep the tops of roots trimmed.
Apples and bananas give off ethylene, a gas that speeds the ripening of nearby produce, so keep them away from other fruit and vegetables.

Bananas and other tropical fruit, and hard fruit, ripen at room temperature, away from ethylene producers. Soft fruit and berries are then refrigerated, and berries are washed only just before eating.
Keep fresh produce away from raw meat and fish to prevent cross-contamination, wash produce before use, and clean the fridge regularly.
Processed produce keeps longer, but only if the storage conditions are right. The rules protect both quality and safety.
Frozen: store at minus 18 degrees Celsius or below, wrapped in moisture-proof packaging, and use within the date. Do not refreeze after thawing.
Canned: keep in a cool, dry place. Once a can is opened, transfer the contents to a covered container in the fridge and use within a day or two.
Dented, swollen (bulging) or leaking cans are discarded, because they may be unsafe.
Dried fruit is kept in a sealed container in a cool, dry place.
Enzymes (proteins in the produce that speed up chemical reactions) stay active after harvest. They cause two kinds of spoilage: ripening that goes too far, and browning of cut surfaces.
Enzymes remain active after harvesting and continue the ripening process until the produce becomes over-ripe, soft and eventually decays.
When cells are cut, bruised or peeled, the enzyme oxidase is released and reacts with oxygen in the air, causing enzymic browning, as seen in apple, potato and banana.
Enzymic browning also destroys some vitamin C and carotene.
Cold slows the enzymes, so refrigeration slows ripening and browning.

Blanching before freezing (brief boiling water, then cold) denatures the enzymes, which means their shape is destroyed so they stop working. Unblanched vegetables continue to deteriorate even in a freezer.
Acid such as lemon juice lowers the pH and slows browning.
Excluding air, for example with water, sugar syrup or wrapping, stops oxygen reaching the cut surface.
Fresh produce is mostly water, so losing it changes how it looks and feels. Loss is fastest in warm, dry, uncovered storage.
Moisture is lost through respiration and evaporation, especially in warm, dry, uncovered storage.
Loss of water causes cells to lose turgor (the firmness that water pressure gives cells), so leafy vegetables wilt, roots shrivel and skins wrinkle.
Produce loses mass and becomes limp, with poorer texture and appearance.
Cool, humid storage such as a salad drawer, and suitable packaging, slow moisture loss.
Covering cut produce and not leaving produce in warm rooms also reduces loss.
Micro-organisms are tiny living things such as bacteria, yeasts and moulds. They use the produce as food, and their growth makes it unfit to eat.
Bacteria, yeasts and moulds come from soil, water, dirty hands and equipment, pests, damaged produce and cross-contamination.
Bruises and cuts give micro-organisms access to nutrients and moisture inside the produce.
Warmth, moisture, food (the produce itself), time and a suitable pH allow micro-organisms to multiply rapidly.
Bacteria cause soft, slimy rot and unpleasant odours; moulds form coloured fuzzy growth, and some produce harmful mycotoxins (poisons).
Yeasts ferment the sugars in fruit, giving a sour or alcoholic smell and bubbles.

Prevention combines good hygiene (clean hands, equipment and surfaces), removing damaged items, separating produce from raw meat, careful washing, refrigeration, correct storage temperatures and prompt use. Washing alone is not enough, because soil-borne contamination can persist.
Other causes of spoilage are physical damage, such as bruising or crushing in transport, and pests.
Businesses that handle produce are bound by hygiene law, and public bodies oversee food safety. Grading is set at EU level.
Food businesses must follow the hygiene rules in Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, given effect in Ireland by the European Communities (Hygiene of Foodstuffs) Regulations 2006.

The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI), established under the Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998, enforces food law through service contracts and gives food safety guidance on handling and storing produce.

Not every nutrient in fruit and vegetables is equally fragile. Some are easily lost in preparation and cooking, and others are hardly affected, so the guidelines are aimed at protecting the fragile ones.
Vitamin C and the B vitamins (thiamine, riboflavin and folate) are water-soluble, so they dissolve into any water the food touches. They are also damaged by heat and by oxygen in the air.
Vitamin C is the least stable of these vitamins, so it is the one the guidelines work hardest to protect.
Minerals dissolve in water too, so they leach out (seep out into the water) when vegetables are soaked or boiled.
Carotene is fat-soluble and stable to heat, so it is not lost into cooking water. This is why you should never say that all vitamins are lost in water.

Nutrients are lost in three ways: by dissolving in water (soaking and boiling), by oxidation (reaction with oxygen in the air, at cut surfaces and by enzymes), and by heat (long cooking). Each guideline prevents one of these.
Most nutrient loss starts before the food reaches the pot. Careful preparation keeps the cut surfaces small, the time short and the contact with water to a minimum.
Use fresh vegetables that have been stored for as short a time as possible, because vitamin C falls during storage.
Eat fruit and vegetables raw where possible, for example in salads and as raw fruit, because there are then no cooking losses.
Prepare vegetables just before cooking and never leave them standing. Cut surfaces are exposed to air and enzymes, so vitamin C is oxidised the longer they wait.
Use a sharp knife or peeler, because a blunt knife crushes cells and releases oxidase (an enzyme that destroys vitamin C). It also removes less tissue and causes less cell damage.
Cut into large pieces rather than small ones, because small pieces expose more surface to air and water. Large pieces lose fewer nutrients.
Peel thinly, scrape, or leave edible skins on, for example on potatoes, carrots and apples, because nutrients (such as vitamin C in potatoes) and fibre lie close to the skin.

Wash vegetables before cutting, never after, because cut pieces would lose soluble nutrients into the wash water. Do not steep or soak them either, because water-soluble vitamins and minerals leach out.
Remove only inedible or damaged parts. Keep the outer green leaves of greens if they are edible, because they contain more vitamin C and carotene.
Once the vegetables are in the pot, the aim is to use as little water, heat and time as possible. Each rule below cuts one of the three routes of nutrient loss.
Cook for the shortest time that makes vegetables tender but slightly crisp (al dente, meaning firm to the bite), because overcooking destroys vitamins and spoils texture and flavour.

When boiling, use the minimum amount of water, bring it to the boil before adding the vegetables, and use a tight-fitting lid. Less water means less dissolving, and the lid keeps steam in and shortens cooking time.

Prefer steaming, pressure cooking, microwaving or stir-frying to boiling, as these cooking methods retain most nutrients. Steaming and microwaving give less contact with water, and pressure cooking, microwaving and stir-frying give a shorter cooking time.
In stir-frying, small pieces cooked quickly in a little oil keep their colour, crispness and vitamins, and fat-soluble vitamins (A, carotene and K) are absorbed better with fat.
Microwaving keeps vitamin C only when it is used with very little water and a short cooking time.
Do not add bicarbonate of soda (bread soda) to keep greens green. It destroys vitamin C and thiamine and makes the texture mushy.
Avoid copper and brass pans, because they speed up the destruction of vitamin C.

Cook frozen vegetables from frozen without thawing, to avoid loss of vitamins in the drip liquid. Serve immediately and do not keep them hot for long, because vitamin C falls on holding, and use the cooking liquid in soups, sauces and gravy so the dissolved vitamins and minerals are eaten.
Cooking costs some nutrients but gives something back. Heat and water remove the fragile vitamins, while the nutrients that survive can become easier to use.

Heat and water destroy or remove vitamin C and the B vitamins (thiamine, riboflavin and folate). The longer the boiling, the greater the loss, because more is destroyed by heat and more dissolves into the water.
Minerals dissolve into the cooking water, which is why the cooking liquid is worth keeping.
Carotene and fibre are kept in cooking, because carotene is stable to heat and fibre is not dissolved by water.
Cooking makes some nutrients more available, because carotene is released from the cell walls and the starch in potatoes and pulses is cooked.

Cooking softens the cellulose and pectin (the materials that hold plant cells together) in the cell walls. Starch in potatoes and pulses swells as it takes up water and softens (gelatinisation). Both changes make the food easier to digest.
Cooking also makes food safer, because it destroys many micro-organisms and denatures (permanently changes the shape of) enzymes.
The colour of a vegetable comes from pigments, and each pigment reacts to heat, acid and alkali in its own way. Knowing which does what explains why some vegetables stay bright and others dull.

Green vegetables owe their colour to chlorophyll. When overcooked or cooked in acid, chlorophyll turns to pheophytin, an olive-green or olive-brown pigment, which is why overcooked cabbage looks dull.
Alkali such as bicarbonate of soda keeps the green colour, but it is harmful to vitamins, so it should not be used.

Orange, yellow and red vegetables such as carrots, peppers and tomatoes contain carotenoid pigments (such as beta-carotene). These are stable in heat, so these vegetables keep their colour when cooked.
Red cabbage contains anthocyanin pigments, which are red in acid and blue or purple in alkaline conditions. Adding vinegar or apple helps to keep red cabbage red when it is cooked.
Cooking changes how vegetables feel and taste. Short cooking keeps both at their best, and long cooking spoils them.
Texture softens as the cell walls (cellulose and pectin) break down and water is lost or taken up. Overcooked vegetables become mushy, while vegetables cooked briefly keep a crisp texture.
Acid keeps fruit and vegetables firm.
Volatile flavour compounds (flavours that evaporate easily) and water-soluble flavours pass into the cooking water or escape in steam, so long boiling loses flavour.
Overcooked cabbage and other brassicas release sulphur compounds, which give a strong, unpleasant smell.
Roasting or frying brings out sweetness and browning, because the natural sugars in onions and carrots brown in dry heat (caramelisation).
Blanching is a quick treatment that stops a vegetable changing, and it is carried out before freezing.
Blanching means putting prepared vegetables into boiling water for a short time (a minute or a few) and then cooling them quickly in cold water.
It inactivates (denatures) enzymes, which would otherwise carry on working and spoil the food in the freezer.
It also fixes the bright colour of the vegetable, and removes some micro-organisms and air from the surface as a small extra benefit.
Blanching is required before home or commercial freezing. Some water-soluble vitamins are lost, which is a necessary cost.
Fruit follows the same rules as vegetables, because its vitamin C is just as fragile. The best fruit dishes are raw ones.
Eat fruit raw wherever possible, because cooked fruit loses more vitamin C than raw fruit.
Leave the skin on if it is edible, as with apples and pears, or peel thinly, because vitamin C and fibre are kept. Wash rather than peel.
Prepare fruit just before cooking or eating, using a sharp knife, to limit the time its cut surfaces are exposed to air.
Stew fruit in as little water as possible, with a lid, for the shortest time, to limit vitamin C loss and keep its texture. Use the juice, so dissolved nutrients are eaten.
Avoid copper pans, do not overcook, and serve promptly.

Cut apples, pears and bananas brown through enzymic oxidation. Lemon juice or another acid, a sugar syrup or cold water slows browning, which is why a fruit salad is dressed with lemon or orange juice.
Fresh fruit and vegetables spoil quickly, so manufacturers process them, often close to the farm soon after harvest. Processing turns a perishable crop into a product that lasts and is easy to use.
Processing changes fresh produce into products with a longer shelf life, greater convenience, availability all year and less waste, or a mixture of these.
The three main commercial methods for fruit and vegetables are freezing, canning and drying (also called dehydration).

Steps common to the methods are sorting, washing, peeling, cutting, blanching or cooking (blanching is a short dip in boiling water or steam), packaging and labelling. Brine, syrup, juice or additives may also be added.

Spoilage is caused by enzymes (natural chemicals in the food that make it deteriorate) and micro-organisms such as bacteria and moulds. Every preservation method works by inactivating, killing or preventing the activity of one or both.

Processed products must be labelled under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 on food information to consumers, which applies in Ireland through the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
Freezing keeps food by cold rather than heat, so the fresh colour and flavour are largely kept. The way the food is frozen decides whether its texture survives.

Process: the fruit or vegetables are washed and prepared, vegetables are blanched, then they are frozen quickly and packed in moisture-proof packaging. They are stored and distributed at -18 degrees Celsius or lower.

Principle: low temperature stops micro-organisms multiplying and slows enzymes, and the water in the food becomes ice, which micro-organisms cannot use. Freezing does not kill them, it only stops their growth and activity.
Vegetables are blanched before freezing to destroy the enzymes that would otherwise keep working and cause deterioration. Blanching does not sterilise the food and does not kill all micro-organisms.
Quick freezing at about -25 degrees Celsius forms small ice crystals, which damage the cell walls very little, so the food keeps its texture.
Slow freezing forms large ice crystals that rupture the cell walls, so the food becomes limp and loses juice (called drip) on thawing.
Air blast freezing blows very cold air through a tunnel over food carried on a conveyor belt.
Plate (contact) freezing presses the food between two cold metal plates, which suits flat items.
Flow (fluidised bed) freezing blows cold air up through a perforated belt so that each piece freezes separately and does not stick together. It suits peas.
Cryogenic freezing immerses or sprays food with liquid nitrogen and suits delicate foods such as strawberries.
Frozen vegetables keep most of their goodness, but a few vitamins are lost along the way. Knowing where they go is a favourite exam point.
Vitamin C and B vitamins are lost into the blanching water and into the drip on thawing, so thaw as little as possible and cook vegetables from frozen.
Colour, flavour and most nutrients are well retained when freezing is carried out properly. Frozen produce can contain more vitamin C than 'fresh' produce stored for several days.
Foods with a high water content and delicate texture, such as lettuce and bananas, do not freeze well because they go soft and mushy on thawing.
Frozen foods are convenient, with little waste and no salt added.
Canning keeps food by heat. The food is sealed in a container and sterilised, so it keeps for a long time with no fridge, but the heat costs some nutrients and texture.

Process: produce is washed, graded, peeled and cut, then blanched or cooked briefly. It is packed into cans or jars with brine, syrup, juice or water, sealed with the air removed, heated in a retort (an industrial pressure cooker heated above boiling point) to sterilise it, then cooled.
Heat sterilisation destroys micro-organisms and enzymes, and the airtight seal stops them re-entering. Canned food therefore has a long shelf life without refrigeration until opened.
Canning causes loss of water-soluble vitamins (vitamin C, thiamine and folate) through the heat and by leaching (dissolving out) into the liquid, so the liquid should be used.
Canning changes the colour, texture and flavour of fruit and vegetables, which become softer and duller.
Canned vegetables contain added salt in the brine, which raises their sodium content. Vegetables in water or with no added salt are lower in sodium.
Syrup raises the sugar content of canned fruit. People controlling their blood glucose should choose fruit in natural juice or water, which has less added sugar.
Fibre, minerals, carotene and protein are well kept in canned foods.
Advantages: long shelf life, ready to use, cheap, available all year, and safe from spoilage if the can is undamaged.
Disadvantages: added salt or sugar, loss of vitamin C and thiamine, and altered texture.
Drying keeps food by taking its water away. Without water, spoilage cannot happen, so dried foods are light, compact and cheap to store and transport.

Process: the produce is washed, cut and usually blanched or treated with a preservative. Most of the water is removed by controlled warm air (hot-air drying), or by sun drying, spray drying or freeze-drying. It is then sealed in moisture-proof packaging.
Removing water leaves none available to micro-organisms and enzymes, so micro-organisms cannot grow and enzymes cannot work. Dried food keeps for months without refrigeration.
Dehydration may reduce B vitamins, vitamin A and vitamin E, and it alters colour, texture and flavour. The food shrinks and becomes chewy.
Vitamin C is lost unless a sulphite preservative is used.
Dried fruit such as raisins, sultanas, apricots and prunes is concentrated in sugar, energy and fibre because most of the water has been removed.
Dried peas, beans and lentils are pulses that keep for long periods and are rehydrated (soaked or cooked) before use.
Other examples are instant mashed potato and dried herbs.
Processing can spoil the colour of produce, let it brown or take out nutrients. Additives are substances added to food to put these right and to help it keep.
Additives improve colour, flavour, texture and keeping quality, replace nutrients lost in processing, and make processing and storage easier. Approved additives are identified by E numbers.
Food additives are approved under Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 on food additives, and the label must list them by function and name or number.
Colourings, in the E100 to E180 range, restore or enhance colour lost during processing, for example in canned peas and other canned vegetables.
