Preservatives prevent micro-organisms from growing. Sulphur dioxide (E220) is used as a preservative in some dried fruit, and sugar and salt also act as preservatives.
Antioxidants prevent browning. Ascorbic acid, which is vitamin C (E300), is used to stop cut or frozen fruit darkening.
Flavourings, sweeteners, acids, firming agents and bulking agents are added to some canned and processed fruit and vegetables, and must be declared on the label.
Nutrient fortification (adding nutrients) improves nutritive value where nutrients are lost in processing.
Processed fruit and vegetables save time and effort, but what is added or taken out during processing changes their nutritional value.

Examples: frozen peas and mixed vegetables, canned beans, tomatoes and sweetcorn, dried fruit, bagged salad and stir-fry mixes, fruit juices, smoothies, fruit salads in juice, fruit yoghurts, jam, vegetable soups, ready meals and sauces with vegetables, and potato products (chips, wedges, crisps, instant mash).
Advantages: they save time, skill and effort, are available all year, have a long shelf life, cause little waste and can be fortified. Some, such as frozen vegetables, retain nutrients well.

Disadvantages: they are often higher in salt, sugar and fat than fresh produce and lower in fibre and vitamins. They are also more expensive, create packaging waste, have lower sensory quality, and can unbalance the diet if eaten too often.
Vegetable crisps and wedges are high in fat and salt, so they are better counted as snacks than as a serving of vegetables.
Vegetables in soups, sauces and ready meals often contain added salt, fat and sugar, which lowers their nutritional value compared with fresh vegetables.

Fruit juice, whether fresh natural juice or made from concentrate, has the sugars of the fruit with little fibre. Juice and smoothies therefore lack the fibre of whole fruit and are not a full replacement for it.
Unsweetened juice counts as at most one serving a day. Check labels for added sugar.

Processed products must carry an ingredients list (in descending order of weight), additives with their functions, net quantity, a date mark (best before or use by), storage instructions, cooking instructions where needed, and nutritional information (energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein, salt).

Allergens must be shown in bold or otherwise emphasised in the ingredients list. The law is Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, in force in Ireland through the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
A physical change alters the size, shape, state, colour or texture of food without forming new substances. Heat usually drives these changes, and each one has a food you can name as an example.

Coagulation: heat unfolds (denatures) egg, milk and fish proteins, which then bond into a set structure. Egg white turns from clear to white and opaque, fish flesh from translucent to opaque, and custard, scrambled egg and omelette set.
Gelatinisation: starch granules absorb water and swell when heated in liquid, and can swell until they burst. This thickens sauces, gravies, custard and porridge.
Tenderising: long, moist cooking converts collagen (the tough protein in connective tissue) into gelatine, so tough cuts of meat become tender.
Shrinkage: meat and fish lose water and melted fat during cooking, so they become smaller and lighter and fat melts out of meat.
Increase in size: dried peas, beans and fruit, rice and pasta absorb water and swell during cooking. Whisked egg foam, sponge and bread also rise and increase in volume.

Colour change: meat turns from red or pink to brown or grey as its myoglobin (the red pigment in meat) is heated. Green vegetables turn olive-brown with prolonged cooking or acid because the chlorophyll is altered, whereas carrots and other orange vegetables stay colourful.
Softening: heat softens the cellulose and breaks down pectin (the 'glue' between cells) in plant cell walls, so vegetables and fruit become tender as cell water is lost.
Increased digestibility and safety: heat destroys most micro-organisms and makes starch and protein easier to digest.
Loss of nutrients, because water-soluble vitamins dissolve in cooking water, is also counted as a physical change.

A chemical change alters the molecular make-up of food and forms new substances with different colours, flavours and textures. Raising agents are a clear example, because they make a new gas that lifts the mixture.
Chemical raising agent: bicarbonate of soda reacts with an acid such as buttermilk and releases carbon dioxide gas, which makes soda bread rise. The same applies in cakes.
Baking powder contains bicarbonate of soda plus an acid, so it releases carbon dioxide when it is moistened and heated.
Biological raising agent: yeast feeds on sugar during fermentation and gives off carbon dioxide (and alcohol), which makes bread dough rise. The gas expands in the oven, and baking kills the yeast.
Tenderising by acid or enzymes, for example in a marinade or with a meat tenderiser, is also accepted as a chemical change.
Browning reactions are chemical changes too, because they make new coloured and flavoured substances: the Maillard reaction, caramelisation and dextrinisation.
Enzymic browning is a chemical change caused by an enzyme in damaged fruit and vegetables. It happens without heat, which separates it from the browning of toast or roast meat.
Cutting, peeling or bruising breaks cell walls, so the enzyme polyphenol oxidase (called 'oxidase' in some marking schemes) meets phenolic compounds in the food.
Oxygen from the air is needed: the enzyme oxidises the phenolic compounds, which then form brown pigments.
Examples: sliced apple, banana, pear, avocado, potato and mushroom turning brown on standing.
Browning spoils the appearance, flavour and vitamin C content of fruit and vegetables. It is wanted in the making of black tea, where it is used deliberately.
To stop oxygen reaching the surface, keep cut surfaces under water, sugar syrup, cling film, a layer of juice or a coating of dressing.
Acid such as lemon juice lowers the pH and slows the enzyme's action. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) reduces the first brown products back to colourless compounds.
Heat inactivates the enzyme, so blanching vegetables in boiling water before freezing, or cooking them, stops browning.
Refrigeration slows enzyme activity but does not stop it. Working quickly and cutting just before serving also limits browning.
A fair test lets you see which treatment slows browning best, by changing one thing at a time and keeping everything else the same.
Aim: to find which treatment best slows enzymic browning on a sliced apple.
Hypothesis: lemon juice will slow browning more than an untreated slice, because acid slows polyphenol oxidase.
Independent variable: the treatment applied to each slice, e.g. untreated (the control), dipped in lemon juice, dipped in sugar syrup, dipped in salt water or cold water.
Dependent variable: the degree of browning, rated on a 0 to 5 colour scale at fixed times.

Controlled variables: the same apple variety and ripeness, slices of the same thickness cut with the same knife, the same dipping time, the same room temperature and the same time after cutting. These keep the test fair, so only the treatment changes.

Method: 1. Wash and dry the apple and cut it into slices of equal thickness. 2. Dip each treated slice for the same time, keeping one untreated slice as the control. 3. Lay all slices on labelled plates and record the colour of each every 5 minutes for 30 minutes.
Safety and hygiene: wash hands and the apple, use a clean board and a sharp knife held with a claw grip, and wipe up any spilled juice.
Expected result: the untreated control browns first and most, while the lemon juice slices stay palest for longest. This supports the hypothesis.
Evaluation: a rating by eye is subjective and apples vary, so repeat the test with several apples and average the ratings.

Non-enzymic browning needs heat and does not involve enzymes. It has three processes, each involving a different food molecule: the Maillard reaction (protein with sugar), caramelisation (sugar alone) and dextrinisation (starch).
Maillard reaction: amino acids from protein react with reducing sugars such as glucose when food is heated in dry conditions, producing brown colour and savoury roasted flavour.
Maillard browning shows on roast meat and poultry skin, roast potatoes, toast and the crust of bread.
Dry heat and a dry surface favour browning, so roasting, grilling, baking and frying brown food.
Little Maillard browning occurs in boiled, steamed or stewed food, because water holds the surface at about 100 °C, too cool for browning, so the food stays pale.
Caramelisation: sugar (sucrose) melts and darkens under strong heat, forming caramel with a sweet, slightly bitter flavour. It needs no protein.
Caramelisation examples: caramel sauce, crème caramel and toffee.
Dextrinisation: dry heat breaks starch down into shorter chains called dextrins, which brown and give a crisp surface.
Dextrinisation examples: toast and the crust of cakes and bread.
Some nutrients dissolve in water or are destroyed by heat and air, so preparation and cooking can lower the nutritional value of food. Knowing why they are lost shows how to keep them.
Water-soluble vitamins, vitamin C and the B group, dissolve into cooking water and are lost when it is poured away.
Vitamin C is also destroyed by heat and oxidation (exposure to air), so the longer vegetables are cooked and exposed to air, the more is lost.
Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are more stable in cooking but drain away with the melted fat from grilled, roasted or fried food.
Soluble minerals such as potassium and some sugars dissolve into cooking water along with the water-soluble vitamins.
Cutting vegetables into small pieces increases the surface exposed to water and air, and soaking them before cooking increases loss. Cooking in a lot of water for a long time has the same effect.
Most nutrient loss can be limited by handling vegetables sensibly before and during cooking.
Peeling thinly or cooking in the skin reduces loss, because nutrients are concentrated just beneath the skin. Peeling thickly increases loss.
Holding cooked vegetables hot for long periods destroys further vitamin C.
Adding bicarbonate of soda to vegetables destroys vitamin C and thiamine, so avoid alkalis and copper pans.

Steaming, stir-frying and microwaving use little water and short cooking times, so they conserve more nutrients. Preparing just before cooking, using a sharp knife, putting the lid on and serving soon after cooking also help.
Cooking liquid from vegetables can be used in soups, sauces or gravies to recover some nutrients.
Cooking is more than making food hot. Heat changes the food in several useful ways, and each change is a reason examiners expect you to give.

Cooking makes food safe by destroying harmful micro-organisms, so food must be heated right through to the centre, because bacteria deep inside a thick piece can survive if the heat never reaches them.
Heat denatures protein (changes its structure), so that digestive enzymes can act on it more easily.
Cooking gelatinises starch (the starch grains swell and burst in water and heat), which makes rice, potatoes and pasta easier to digest.
Cooking softens the cellulose in plant cell walls, so vegetables become tender and easier to chew.
Heat develops flavour and changes colour and texture, which makes food more appetising and gives variety in the diet.
Cooking destroys enzymes and most spoilage micro-organisms, which extends the time food stays fit to eat.
Whatever the method, cooking is heat moving from a source into the food. The cook controls how much heat reaches the food, for how long, and whether moisture or fat is present.

Too low a temperature or too short a time leaves food undercooked and unsafe, because the centre never gets hot enough; too high a temperature or too long a time dries, toughens and burns the surface.
Thickness governs cooking time: thin or small pieces cook quickly and evenly, while a large joint needs lower heat for longer so that the centre cooks before the outside burns.
Moist methods prevent food drying out; dry methods need added fat, basting (spooning hot fat or juices over the food) or a covered dish to keep food juicy.
Food type governs the method: cuts rich in connective tissue need long, slow cooking, while delicate foods need short cooking at gentle heat.
Cooked food must be served promptly or cooled quickly, because the danger zone of 5 to 63 °C is where bacteria multiply fastest.
Conduction is heat transfer through a solid from one molecule to the next, without the material itself moving. It is the way heat passes from a hot pan into the food.
As molecules at the hot end are heated they vibrate faster and pass energy to their neighbours, until the whole piece is hot.

Metals such as aluminium, copper and steel conduct heat quickly, which is why saucepans have metal bases; glass, ceramic, wood, plastic and air conduct heat slowly (they are insulators), which is why handles and oven gloves are made from them.
Pan-based methods begin with conduction: the cooker heats the pan base, which heats the liquid or fat in the pan, and that then heats the food.
Boiling, poaching, stewing, shallow frying and stir-frying all depend on conduction through the pan base.
Searing a steak in a hot pan: heat conducts from the pan surface into the outer layers of the meat and then gradually towards the centre.
Baking trays and cake tins conduct heat into the base of a cake, so the base sets before the top.
A large solid piece of food takes longer to cook through, because the heat has to travel inwards from the surface molecule by molecule.
Diagram: arrows from a gas flame through a pan base into the food, labelled as conduction, with the direction of heat flow marked.
Convection is heat transfer through a liquid or gas by currents. The heated fluid expands and becomes less dense so it rises, and cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place and is heated in turn.
Natural convection occurs in a pot of boiling water, in a stew and in the hot air of a conventional oven, because the heated fluid rises on its own and the cooler fluid sinks.
Forced convection: the fan in a fan oven circulates the hot air, so food cooks faster and more evenly than in a conventional oven.
Deep-fat frying: convection currents in the hot oil carry heat to every surface of the immersed food at once.
Steaming: hot steam rises from boiling water and carries heat to the food, and it also condenses on cooler food, releasing its latent heat (the heat stored in steam) to cook it.
Examples: boiling, stewing, steaming, deep-fat frying, and baking or roasting in an oven.
Diagram: a pot of water with arrows showing hot water rising from the base, cooling at the surface and sinking at the sides.
Radiation is heat transfer by infrared rays that travel in straight lines from a hot source and heat the first solid surface they strike. No solid, liquid or gas is needed to carry it.
The surface struck by radiant heat absorbs it, so browning and crisping happen on that surface while the inside of the food cooks by conduction.
Grilling uses an element or flame above or below the food to heat the surface, sealing and browning it; thin pieces cook quickly because the heat is intense.
Barbecuing and toasting use radiant heat from glowing coals, gas flames or electric elements.
Dark, dull (matt) surfaces absorb radiant heat more readily than shiny surfaces, which reflect it; this is why foil reflects heat.
Radiant heat weakens with distance from the source, so the height of the grill rack is adjusted to control how much heat the food receives.
Diagram: straight arrows from a grill element to the top surface of a piece of food, labelled as radiation.
In practice most cooking uses more than one type of heat transfer at once. Microwave cooking is a special case, because the heat is made inside the food.
Roasting uses radiation from the oven walls and element, convection by the hot air, and conduction inside the food.
Boiling uses conduction through the pan base, then convection in the water, which is at 100 °C when boiling.
In microwave cooking, a magnetron produces microwaves (electromagnetic waves) that make the water molecules in the food vibrate, and this makes heat inside the outer layer of the food.
Once the heat is made in the outer layer, it spreads inwards by conduction.
Each type of food reacts to heat in its own way, so the principles above are applied differently to each one. The right choice gives food that is safe, tender and keeps its colour and nutrients.
Meat: tough cuts, rich in collagen, need long, slow, moist cooking so that collagen converts to gelatine; tender cuts can be grilled or fried quickly.
Fish: its flesh has little connective tissue and sets quickly, so it needs short cooking at gentle heat; poaching, steaming, grilling, baking and frying all suit it.
Eggs: egg proteins set (coagulate) at moderate temperatures, so eggs and custards need gentle heat; high heat makes scrambled egg rubbery and custard curdle.
Vegetables and fruit: short cooking in a little boiling water, or steaming, keeps colour, texture and water-soluble vitamins, which would otherwise dissolve into the cooking water.
Cereals, rice and pasta: starch needs water and heat to gelatinise, so they are cooked in plenty of boiling water or steam.
Milk and cheese: milk scorches on direct heat and cheese turns stringy at high temperatures, so sauces containing them are cooked gently.

Fats and oils: fat overheats, smokes and breaks down if heated too far, so frying oil must be watched, an oil with a high smoke point chosen for deep-fat frying, and it should not be reused too often.
Pastry and cakes: the fat is kept cold when rubbed in, the dry heat of the oven sets the flaky structure, and the oven should not be opened early when baking a cake.
Cooking methods fall into three groups according to what carries the heat to the food. The right choice depends on the food, the eater and the result you want.

Moist methods use water, stock or steam as the medium. Dry methods use hot air or radiant heat (heat given off as rays from a hot element or flame) with little or no added liquid. Fat-based methods use fat or oil as the medium.

The food: tender cuts and delicate foods such as fish, eggs and vegetables suit quick methods, because they need little time to become tender. Tough, fibrous cuts need long, moist methods, which soften the fibres.
Nutrition: steaming, stir-frying and grilling use little or no water and short times, so they conserve water-soluble vitamins. Boiling loses them into the cooking water unless that liquid is used.
Palatability (how pleasant the food is to eat): dry and fat-based methods brown and crisp the surface, adding colour and flavour, while moist methods give a soft, tender texture.
Diet: steaming, poaching, boiling and grilling on a rack add little or no fat, which suits a diet that limits fat. Deep-fat frying adds fat and energy because the food absorbs fat.
Consumer needs: an older person who has difficulty chewing or swallowing needs soft, moist, easily digested food, so a moist method is the better choice.
Time and equipment: a pressure cooker shortens cooking time, while stewing and braising are long, slow methods in a covered pan or oven.
Cost: slow moist cooking makes an inexpensive cut of meat tender and palatable, so you do not have to buy an expensive cut.
In moist methods the food is cooked in water, stock or steam. The temperature of the liquid is what separates them: boiling is hottest, simmering is just below it and poaching is lower again.

Boiling: food is cooked in rapidly bubbling water at boiling point, 100 °C at sea level. It is quick and used for vegetables, pasta, rice, eggs and potatoes, but water-soluble vitamins leach (dissolve) into the water.
Simmering: liquid is kept just below boiling point, with small bubbles breaking the surface. It is gentler than boiling and is used for stocks, soups, stews and stewed fruit.

Stewing: food is cooked slowly and gently in a small amount of liquid in a covered pan or casserole, on the hob or in the oven. It suits tough meat and vegetables, as in Irish stew, a traditional stew.
Stewing keeps nutrients because the liquid is served with the food.

Steaming: food is cooked by the steam from boiling water without touching the water, in a steamer, on a plate over a pan or in a covered bowl in a pan. No fat is added, and nutrients and shape are kept. It suits fish, chicken, vegetables, rice and steamed puddings.

Poaching: food is cooked gently in liquid kept slightly below simmering point, about 85 °C, on the hob or in the oven. It suits delicate foods that would break up or toughen in fiercer heat, such as eggs, fish and fruit like pears.
Braising: tough meat or vegetables are browned in fat, then cooked slowly with a little liquid in a covered dish, in the oven or on the hob. The long, slow, moist cooking tenderises tough cuts.

Pressure cooking: food is cooked in a sealed pan in which steam builds up pressure. This raises the temperature above 100 °C and shortens the cooking time. It is used for stocks, stews, tough meat and pulses.
Dry methods cook food with hot air or radiant heat rather than liquid. They brown the surface, which adds colour and flavour.
Roasting: meat, poultry, potatoes or vegetables are cooked uncovered in the oven in a roasting tin, usually with a little fat. The surface browns while the centre cooks by conduction and convection.

Baking: food is cooked by the dry heat of an oven, mainly by convection (hot air circulating) and radiation. It is used for cakes, bread, pastry, fish, pasta and potato dishes, as with fish pie and lasagne.

Grilling: food is cooked by radiant heat from an element or flame above or below it. The heat seals the surface, so it is a fast method. It suits tender cuts, steaks, chops, thin fish, sausages, rashers, tomatoes, mushrooms, peppers and kebabs.
Barbecuing: this is grilling outdoors on a grid over burning charcoal or gas, using radiant heat, which gives a smoky flavour.
Grilling lowers the fat content of food, because fat drips away from it.
Grilling is fast and the heat is fierce, so food can burn outside while it is raw inside, or dry out. These rules prevent that.
Preheat the grill to the required temperature so that the surface seals on contact.
Oil the grid or the food to prevent sticking.
Use thin pieces, so that heat reaches the centre before the surface burns.
Do not add salt before grilling, because salt draws moisture to the surface.
Turn the food with tongs rather than a fork, so that its juices stay inside instead of running out through holes.
Use the correct cooking time, since grilled food dries out and overcooks quickly.
Fat-based methods, usually called frying, cook food in hot fat or oil. They give a crisp, golden surface, but the amount of fat used varies a great deal from one method to another.
Shallow frying: food is cooked in hot fat in a shallow pan, partly covered by the fat and turned once or twice, giving a crisp surface. It is used for eggs, fish, chops and pancakes.

Deep-fat frying: food is fully immersed in hot oil in a deep pan or fryer, which seals the surface quickly. It is used for chips and fish in batter. The food absorbs some fat, so it is higher in fat and energy than grilled food.
Stir-frying: small, thin pieces are tossed and stirred constantly over high heat in a wok or large pan with a little oil. Because the cooking is so quick, it keeps colour, crispness and vitamin C.
Dry frying: food is cooked in a non-stick pan without added fat, using the fat already in foods such as bacon rashers and sausages.
Pot roasting: meat is cooked in a little fat in a covered pan on the hob, so it cooks in its own juices and steam and stays moist. It is not done in the oven and not uncovered.
A microwave oven is a fast method that suits reheating and cooking small amounts. It works differently from the other methods, so its advantages and limits are worth knowing.
Microwave ovens cook and reheat quickly with little added fat and water, so vitamins are kept.
They do not brown food unless a grill or combination mode is used, so the surface stays pale.
Containers must be microwave-safe, and metal must not be used.
Examiners often ask you to give dishes or foods for a method. These are the examples that are accepted.
Baking: apple crumble, sponge, soda bread, fish pie, lasagne, pizza and muffins.
Grilling: kebabs, chicken satay, burgers, fish, rashers, sausages, tomatoes, mushrooms and bruschetta.
Steaming: fish, chicken, rice, Christmas pudding (a traditional steamed pudding), fruit and vegetables. Roasting: meat, potatoes and vegetables.
Frying has four types: dry, shallow, deep and stir-fry. The moist methods are boiling, stewing, steaming, poaching, braising and pressure cooking.

Classifying methods: moist covers boiling, stewing, steaming, poaching, braising and pressure cooking. Dry covers baking, grilling, roasting and barbecuing. Frying covers dry, shallow, deep and stir-frying.
Steaming is a good choice for an older person because it is simple and gives soft food that is easy to eat. It also has weaknesses, so a full evaluation covers ease, nutrition and palatability.
Ease: steaming needs little attention or equipment, a whole meal can cook in a tiered steamer, and it suits small portions.
Texture: the moist, soft food is easy to chew and swallow, which suits an older person with difficulty chewing or swallowing.
Nutrition: steaming adds no fat, so it suits a diet that limits fat. Because the food does not sit in water, water-soluble vitamins (B and C) are kept.
Palatability: steamed food keeps its colour and moisture, but it can taste bland and does not brown. Overcooking spoils its texture and colour.
Fish, chicken, rice and vegetables suit steaming; steamed puddings are a traditional example.
Herbs, lemon juice and a sauce add flavour without added salt, which suits a diet that limits salt.
Soups are grouped by their thickness and by the temperature they are served at. Knowing the class tells you what the soup is like and how it is made, and each class has typical examples.
Clear (thin) soups are thin and transparent. Consommé is a clear soup made from clarified stock, which is stock cleared of cloudy particles using egg white and minced meat.
Broths are thin, clear soups made by simmering meat or vegetables in water, such as chicken broth or vegetable broth.
Purée soups are thick soups in which cooked vegetables are sieved or blended to a smooth texture, for example carrot, or leek and potato. The vegetables themselves make the soup thick.
Thickened soups are thickened with an added agent such as a roux (a cooked mixture of fat and flour), cornflour, puréed potato, or a liaison, which is a mixture of egg yolk and cream.
Cold soups are served chilled. Gazpacho is a Spanish cold soup of raw tomato, pepper and cucumber.
Stock is the base of most soups. It is a liquid made by simmering bones, meat or vegetables with herbs in water, and it gives the soup its flavour.
To make a good stock, skim off the scum that rises to the surface, do not boil it hard, and strain it at the end so that the finished liquid is clear.
Most soups follow the same order: prepare the vegetables, soften them, add liquid and simmer, then finish. Each step has a reason, which is what examiners look for.
Wash, peel and cut the vegetables into even pieces so that they all cook at the same rate and none is left hard or turned to mush.
Sweating the vegetables means to cook them gently in a little fat in a covered pan until soft, without browning, to release their flavour.
Add the stock or liquid, bring the soup to the boil, then simmer until the vegetables are tender. Boiling hard breaks up the vegetables and loses flavour. Thicken the soup if needed.
Purée soups are sieved or blended until smooth. If using a blender, do not overfill it and hold the lid down, because hot liquid can force the lid off.
After puréeing, reheat the soup and season it. Add seasoning at the end and taste first, because the flavour concentrates as the soup reduces and cooks also season in stages.
Add cream, milk or a liaison (egg yolk and cream) off the boil so that the soup does not curdle. Adjust the consistency at the end too.
For safe practice, cool and chill leftover soup quickly, and reheat it until piping hot.
A soup is served at the right temperature and finished with a garnish, a small decoration added for colour and flavour. The garnish and bowl are chosen to suit the type of soup.
Serve hot soup hot and in warm bowls so that it does not cool quickly. Thick soups are garnished with croutons, chopped parsley or chives, a swirl of cream or grated cheese.
Clear soups are garnished with thin strips of vegetable or chopped herbs, which keep the soup looking light and clear.
Cold soups are chilled thoroughly before serving and garnished with finely diced vegetables or a little cream.
A garnish must be edible, suit the soup and be small. Accompaniments, such as brown bread, are served alongside.
A roux is a cooked mixture of equal amounts of fat and flour (by weight), and the amount of liquid added decides the thickness of the sauce. Changing the liquid, not the roux, gives different sauces.

1. Melt the fat. 2. Stir in an equal amount of flour and cook gently, briefly, to remove the raw flour taste. 3. Add the liquid gradually, stirring or whisking so that the starch disperses without lumps.
4. Bring the sauce to the boil, then simmer it to cook the starch fully. 5. Season.
A roux thickens because the starch granules absorb liquid and swell as the sauce heats, a process called gelatinisation.
A white roux is cooked only briefly, until pale. It thickens most strongly and is used for white, parsley, cheese, mushroom and béchamel sauces.
A brown roux is cooked longer until golden or brown. It thickens less and is used for brown and stewing sauces.

The same fat and flour give thin pouring, thicker coating and very thick binding sauces by using progressively less liquid: more for a pouring sauce, less for a coating sauce, least for a binding sauce (panada).
Béchamel is a white sauce made by infusing milk with flavourings such as onion, bay leaf and cloves. Panada is a thick, roux-based paste used to bind ingredients such as croquettes.
Roux-based sauces accepted as examples are white, parsley, béchamel, cheese, mushroom, curry, stewing, panada and brown sauce.
Besides roux-based sauces, sauces are classified by what thickens or makes them, or by how they are served. Examiners ask for a class with an example, so learn one or two for each.
Roux-based sauces: white, parsley, cheese, mushroom, béchamel, curry and stewing sauce.
Egg-based sauces: custard sets because egg proteins coagulate in hot milk. Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil in egg yolk, and hollandaise is an emulsion of butter in egg yolk with lemon juice.
Sweet sauces: chocolate, toffee, caramel and butterscotch, served with desserts.
Fruit sauces: apple sauce, orange sauce and coulis, a thin purée of raw or cooked fruit, often sieved.
Cold sauces and dressings: mint sauce and French dressing, which are served cold.
Miscellaneous sauces: bread sauce, thickened with breadcrumbs.
Uses: white sauce with fish, cheese sauce with cauliflower, apple sauce with pork, mint sauce with lamb, custard with apple tart and French dressing on salad.
Convenience soups are ready-made soups that save preparation time. They come in five forms, and each is stored and prepared differently.
Dehydrated or packaged soups are dried mixes reconstituted with boiling water or milk. They have a long shelf life.
Cook-chill soups are sold chilled and heated before eating. They have a shorter shelf life than canned soups.
Canned soups are sterilised in sealed tins, which gives a long shelf life, and they only need heating.
Frozen soups are stored at −18 °C and heated after thawing. They keep their flavour well.
Single-portion soups are sold in individual pots or cups that are heated or reconstituted for one serving.
Convenience soups trade cost and quality for speed and ease. Weigh them against homemade soup when you evaluate them.
Advantages: little preparation time, simple skills needed, useful in an emergency, wide variety available, and easy to store. Dried and canned soups also have a long shelf life.
Disadvantages: they can be expensive per portion, are often high in salt, and may contain artificial colours, flavours and additives.
They may also have less fibre and flavour than homemade soup, and you have less choice over the ingredients used.
Adding fresh vegetables, herbs, milk or a topping to a convenience soup improves its flavour and adds nutrients.

Labels let a consumer compare soups and choose for health or allergy needs. Labelling rules for food are set by Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
The label must give the name of the food, the ingredients list, and the net quantity in metric units.
Ingredients are listed in descending order of weight at the time of manufacture, so the first ingredient is the one used in greatest amount.
Allergenic ingredients, such as gluten, milk, eggs, celery and nuts, must be emphasised within the ingredients list so that people with allergies can spot them.
The nutrition declaration gives energy and the amounts of fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt per 100 g or 100 ml.
Cooking instructions, storage conditions and a use-by or best-before date are shown.
The name and address of the food business operator are given, along with the country of origin where it is required.
Labels let the consumer compare soups by salt content, ingredients and allergens, and check that the soup suits their needs.

Good equipment makes cooking easier and safer, but only if it suits the job. Choose for the quantity of food, the cooking method, the type of hob, durability, ease of cleaning and cost, and check how the material conducts heat (passes heat through it).
Buy equipment you will use often and can store easily, because a gadget used once a year wastes money and cupboard space.
A heavy, flat, thick base spreads heat evenly and reduces hot spots that scorch food and make it stick; a thin base heats unevenly.
Aluminium and copper conduct heat quickly and evenly, so they respond fast when the heat changes.
Stainless steel is durable and does not react with acidic foods, but it conducts heat less well, so good pans have a base bonded to copper or aluminium. It is not the best conductor.
Cast iron retains heat well and suits slow, even cooking such as braising, but it is heavy and rusts if left damp. Glass and ceramic dishes suit oven cooking and conduct heat slowly.
A non-stick coating allows frying with little fat, but it is scratched by metal utensils and damaged by overheating, for example heating an empty pan.
A close-fitting lid retains steam, so food simmers with less energy and in less time. The pan base should match the ring size, so that the full base makes contact with the heat source.
Induction hobs heat the pan by magnetism, so they need a pan with a magnetic (ferrous) base; aluminium and copper pans without one will not heat.
Handles should be firm, heat-resistant and fixed securely; plastic and wooden handles are not suitable for the oven unless the manufacturer states it.
A practical kitchen needs a core set of tools, and recipes only work if ingredients are measured accurately.
Pans and dishes: saucepans of different sizes, a frying pan, a roasting tin, a casserole, and baking tins and trays.
Preparation tools: mixing bowls, a sieve, a colander, wooden spoons, a spatula, a whisk, a grater, a rolling pin, a peeler and a tin opener.
Measuring and checking tools: a measuring jug, scales, measuring spoons, a timer and a thermometer.
Weigh and measure accurately with scales, jugs and spoons, because too much or too little of an ingredient can change how a dish turns out.
Ingredients are measured in metric, and spoon measures are level, not heaped, so that every cook gets the same amount.

Knives are the most dangerous everyday tool in the kitchen, so choosing the right one and handling it correctly prevents most cuts. Chopping boards need care too, because they can pass germs between foods.

A cook's knife is used for general chopping, a paring knife for small, detailed work and peeling, a serrated (bread) knife for bread and soft-skinned foods, and a carving knife for carving cooked meat.
A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one because it cuts with less force and is less likely to slip.
The claw grip curls the fingertips of the guiding hand under, so the knuckles guide the blade and the fingertips stay clear of it.
Place the chopping board on a damp cloth or non-slip mat so that it cannot move while cutting.
Colour-coded boards (for raw meat, fish, vegetables and cooked foods) keep them apart, preventing cross-contamination (germs spreading from raw to ready-to-eat food).
Wash boards well after raw meat, and replace badly scored boards because germs can lodge in the cuts.
Carry a knife by its handle with the blade pointing down and away from the body; never leave a knife in a sink of washing-up water, where it cannot be seen.
Store knives in a block, on a rack or on a magnetic strip, so that the edges are protected and the blades are not loose in a drawer.
Most kitchen accidents are burns, scalds, cuts and electric shocks, and most are avoidable with a few habits. Each habit below removes a specific danger.
Hob: turn pan handles inwards over the hob so they cannot be knocked or pulled, use a ring that matches the pan size, and never leave hot oil or fat unattended.
Keep tea towels and flexes away from the hob, where they can catch fire or melt.
Lift lids away from the face so that escaping steam does not scald.
Oven: place the shelves before heating, open the door carefully, and use a stable tray for hot dishes.
Use dry oven gloves or a dry cloth to handle hot dishes; a damp cloth conducts heat and causes scalds.
Electrical: keep the flex of appliances away from hot surfaces and water, never handle an appliance with wet hands, and don't overload sockets.
Switch off and unplug an appliance before cleaning its blades or removing food from them, and do not use one with a damaged flex or plug; it must be repaired or replaced before use.

Pressure cooker: check that the sealing ring and valve are clean and undamaged, never force the lid, and open it only after the pressure has fallen. Microwave: use microwave-safe containers, never put metal in the cavity, and cover and stir food.
Beyond individual appliances, a few habits keep the whole kitchen safe, especially when something goes wrong.
Clean up spills at once, because a wet or greasy floor causes slips and falls.
Keep a fire blanket in the kitchen and know how to use it, so a small pan fire can be smothered quickly.
Never use water on a fat fire, because it causes the burning fat to flare up and spread.
Looking after equipment makes it last longer and keeps food safe. The right care depends on the material, so follow the manufacturer's care instructions.
Wash equipment in hot soapy water or in a dishwasher, then rinse, dry thoroughly and store it clean and dry, so that bacteria cannot grow and metal does not rust.
Do not run cold water into a hot pan; the sudden change in temperature can warp the base and crack a non-stick or ceramic surface. Soak burnt pans before scrubbing.
Cast iron must be dried straight after washing and wiped with a thin film of oil to prevent rust.
Use wooden or silicone utensils on non-stick surfaces, whereas metal utensils scratch them.
Use abrasive pads only on surfaces that tolerate them; stainless steel and cast iron tolerate them better than non-stick coatings.
Wooden items are not left to soak, because the wood absorbs water.
Dishcloths, sponges, tea towels and brushes can carry bacteria and should be changed or washed regularly.
Store knives safely, and stack pans with protection between them so non-stick surfaces are not scratched.
In the practical coursework, equipment is part of what you are marked on, because it shows you can plan and work like a competent cook.
Area B assignments ask you to describe new equipment or a new skill, and the planning section lists the key equipment you will use.
You should be able to name the equipment for a dish, say why it was chosen, and explain how it was used safely and hygienically.

A recipe is balanced when a dish or meal supplies the right proportions of nutrients for the people who will eat it. The Department of Health Healthy Eating Guidelines and the Food Pyramid are the checks a cook uses.

A balanced main meal usually includes a protein food, a starchy food and vegetables, so that protein, carbohydrate, vitamins, minerals and fibre are all present, with little added fat, sugar and salt.
On the Food Pyramid, vegetables, salad and fruit form the base, because they should be eaten most. Next come wholemeal cereals and breads, potatoes, pasta and rice, then milk, yogurt and cheese.

Higher up are meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans and nuts, then a small shelf of fats, spreads and oils, which are used sparingly. Foods and drinks high in fat, sugar and salt sit at the top and are not needed for health.
Wholegrain or wholemeal versions of starchy foods, and pulses, add fibre, B vitamins and minerals to a dish, so they improve balance.
Oily fish, lean meat, pulses and low-fat dairy supply protein with less saturated fat than fatty cuts of meat and full-fat dairy.

Fresh, frozen or tinned fruit and vegetables in a main course or dessert supply vitamin C, folate and fibre, and extra vegetables add vitamins and minerals. Using less fat, sugar and salt also improves balance.
Balance also covers colour, texture, flavour and cost, so that a meal is appealing as well as affordable.
Modifying (adapting) a recipe means changing its ingredients, quantity or method so that it suits the people eating it. There are six main reasons.
To make a dish more nutritious, by adding fibre or reducing fat, sugar or salt, in line with healthy-eating guidelines.
To cater for a person on a special diet, such as a coeliac (someone who cannot eat gluten) who needs gluten-free flour.
To increase or decrease the number of portions, because standard recipes are written for a set number of servings, usually about four adults.
To add variety to a basic recipe, for example by adding nuts to a vegetable stir-fry.
To economise, by substituting an expensive ingredient with a cheaper one, for example margarine for butter in a sponge.
To suit the likes and dislikes of those eating, for example by leaving out an ingredient that a family member avoids.
Making a dish healthier usually means swapping a few ingredients or changing the cooking method. Each change below targets one nutrient.

Reduce fat by grilling, baking, steaming or poaching instead of frying, which adds fat. Also trim visible fat from meat, skim fat from stews, and use a vegetable oil or low-fat spread instead of butter.
Reduce salt by omitting added salt and stock cubes, which are high in salt. Flavour with herbs, spices, garlic or lemon juice instead, and choose reduced-salt products.
Reduce sugar by using less of it, by adding fruit that gives natural sweetness, and by avoiding sugary toppings.

Increase fibre by replacing white flour with wholemeal flour, using brown rice and pasta, and adding oats, pulses and vegetables. Leave the skins on fruit and vegetables, since the skin is a source of fibre.
Other changes alter who the dish suits or how many it feeds. After any change, the result still has to taste right.
Gluten-free cooking replaces wheat flour with a gluten-free flour, such as rice or maize flour, and checks that other ingredients are gluten-free.
Vegetarian versions replace meat with pulses, tofu, eggs or mushrooms, while keeping a source of iron and protein in the dish, because meat is normally where those come from.

Scale a recipe by multiplying or dividing every ingredient by the same factor, so the proportions stay right. Then adjust the tin or dish size and the cooking time, since larger quantities usually take longer, and check the seasoning.
Adapt flavour and texture by substituting herbs and spices, or by using a different fruit or vegetable in season.
Taste and adjust the seasoning after modifying a recipe, because reduced salt or sugar changes the flavour.
Aesthetic awareness is a general reaction to how food looks, smells and feels, not a formal test. Sight, smell and texture help a cook judge food before it is bought and while it is prepared.
Sight judges appearance, colour, size, shape and surface. Colour and appearance show freshness or ripeness, for example a firm, bright, unbruised apple.
Certain colours are linked to flavours, such as yellow with lemon, and people expect particular appearances: mould is accepted on Stilton cheese but not on bread.
Smell detects aroma through receptor cells in the nasal cavity (the nose), which tell us whether food is fresh or rancid (gone off, as fat does).
Texture is judged by mouth feel and by sight, and a variety of textures, such as a crisp salad served with a soft dish, makes a meal more interesting.
The shape and size of cut pieces affect appearance; uniform cuts look neater and cook evenly.

Food that looks and smells good is more appealing and is eaten with more enjoyment. It also helps appetite, which matters especially for children, older people and the ill, and dishes are judged on presentation.
Cut food evenly so it looks neat and cooks evenly. Avoid overcooking, which dulls colour and softens texture; green vegetables cooked briefly in fast-boiling water keep their colour.
A garnish adds colour and contrast, for example parsley on soup, parmesan shavings or grated cheese on pasta, or icing sugar on a sponge or cake.
A garnish should be edible, in keeping with the dish and small enough not to overpower it.
Hot food should be served hot and cold food cold, on warmed plates for hot food and chilled plates for cold food, so the dish stays at its best temperature.
Choose contrasting colours on the plate, such as a red pepper beside green beans, and vary shape and texture.
Arrange food with height and balance, keep the rim of the plate clean and portion each item in proportion to the dish. A neat table setting also adds to the effect.
The same recipe is not right for everyone. The number of people, their ages and activity levels, and the budget all shape what is cooked.
For one person, plan a single-serving dish such as a filled jacket potato, or cook a batch that can be frozen in single portions, which avoids waste.
Someone eating alone, such as an older person or a student, should still make sure the meal supplies enough nutrients.
For a family group, plan meals to suit the ages, tastes, activity levels and budget of the family, use lower-cost cuts and ingredients, and involve the family in choices.
A one-pot or batch dish, such as a casserole, feeds several people at low cost with little washing-up.
Cook a dish in advance and reheat it on a busy day, so that the meal is ready at a convenient time.
Young children need small, soft pieces that are easy to chew, with little added salt and sugar.
Teenagers and active adults need larger portions and energy-rich starchy foods, and teenagers need extra iron and calcium.
Older people often need smaller, nutrient-dense portions (a lot of nutrition in a small amount), with soft textures if chewing is difficult.
A modified diet changes the choice of food and the cooking methods, but the meal must still be balanced and attractive. For each diet, the cook changes particular ingredients.

Coeliac: wheat, barley and rye contain gluten, so gluten-free flours and starches, such as rice and maize, replace them in bread, pastry, sauces and coatings, and labels are checked. Oats must be labelled gluten-free.
Diabetic: carbohydrate portions are controlled and added sugar is reduced, with wholegrain starches and high-fibre vegetables preferred and less fat used.
Low-fat or heart-healthy: lean meat, oily fish and low-fat dairy are used, with grilling, steaming and baking because they need little added fat.
Low-salt: no added salt or stock cubes, processed meats and salted snacks are avoided, and dishes are flavoured with herbs and spices.

Vegetarian and vegan: pulses, tofu, nuts and seeds replace meat, and eggs and dairy foods do so for vegetarians only. Include sources of iron and vitamin B12, use plant-based milks, and check for hidden animal ingredients.
Lactose intolerance: lactose-free milk or a fortified plant alternative replaces milk, and labels are checked for hidden milk ingredients.
High-fibre: wholemeal flour, pulses, vegetables and fruit are used.

The Food Studies practical coursework is worth 20% of the total marks in Home Economics Scientific and Social for every candidate, with the written paper carrying the rest. Each assignment is recorded in the SEC's digital Food Studies Practical Coursework Journal, so you need to know how the marks are split.
Each assignment is recorded under four headings: Investigation, Planning and Preparation, Implementation and Evaluation.
Investigation (the analysis and research) is marked out of 32, the largest share, so it is the part to give most time to.
Planning and Preparation is marked out of 8, for the ingredients with quantities and costing and for the key equipment.
Implementation is marked out of 28, for the procedure followed, the key factors considered, and safety and hygiene.
Evaluation is marked out of 12, for the implementation and for the specific requirements of the assignment.
The four headings total 80 marks for each assignment (32 + 8 + 28 + 12).
For 2027 candidates present two of the five assignments the SEC set, and where more than two are presented the two highest-scoring assignments count. The completion date was 2 November 2026.
The assignment brief still prints the standing instruction to complete four assignments, but the SEC's Assessment Arrangements 2027 override it, so the 2027 number is two of five.
Every assignment falls under one of five areas of practice, and the investigation for that assignment covers the points set for its area.
Area A: Application of Nutritional Principles, such as planning meals for a particular nutritional need.
Area B: Food Preparation and Cooking Processes, involving new skills or equipment, so you learn and use something new.
Area D: Properties of a Food, such as the effect of a marinade.
Area E: Comparative Analysis, including Sensory Analysis.
No Area C assignment was set for 2027, so the five assignments are spread across the other four areas.
The investigation is the biggest part of the marks, and what it must contain depends on the area. In every area, sources of information are cited.
Area A: the nutritional needs being investigated, the appropriate meal-planning guidelines, and suitable or modified dishes, meaning dishes that suit those needs or are adapted to meet them.
Area B: the preparation process, skill or equipment, the key points for success, and dishes that illustrate it, so the research shows why the technique works.
Area C: the processing method and its principles, containers, packaging and labelling, and suitable foods or dishes, for example the container that suits the method.
Area D: the definition of the property, the principles associated with it, and dishes that illustrate it, because the dishes show the property at work.
Area E: the testing technique and its possible outcomes, the foods or products tested, and the conditions that must be controlled so that the test is fair.
The coursework has rules about what you cook, how you work and how you present your written record.
Dishes must meet the requirements of the assignment, so that the dish can earn the marks for it.
A dish may not be repeated, or partially repeated, across assignments, so each assignment needs its own dish.
Fresh foods should be used rather than convenience foods (ready-made or pre-prepared products), so that the cooking is your own work.
Practical work may be done in pairs, or in groups for Area E only.
The written record must be the candidate's own work, even where the practical work was shared.
Every area requires sources of information to be cited, and all sources must be referenced, including AI-generated material.
The SEC set five assignments for 2027. Each links to theory you study elsewhere in the course, named here by subject.

Assignment 1 (Area A): the challenges older people face in keeping a healthy diet; their nutritional needs and meal-planning guidelines; two-course main-meal menus; preparation of one main course. The theory is meal planning for older people and special diets.

Assignment 2 (Area A): the causes and effects of iron deficiency; the nutritional needs and meal-planning factors for reducing the risk; two-course main-meal menus; preparation of one main course. The theory is minerals (iron) and meal planning.
Assignment 3 (Area B): commercially prepared filo and puff pastry, covering brands, forms, ingredients, cost, and sweet and savoury dishes.

Assignment 3 also asks for the key points for success with one of the pastries, preparation of one dish, and evaluation of the advantages and disadvantages of the chosen pastry. The theory is pastry, taught with cereals and grains, and it is the background knowledge the practical rests on.
The remaining two assignments cover the property of a food and a comparison of products by sensory testing.
No Area C assignment was set for 2027.

Assignment 4 (Area D): types of marinade and the dishes that use each; the benefits of marinating and its underlying principles; the key points for success; preparation of one marinated dish; evaluation of whether the marinade achieved its purpose. The theory is meat tenderising.
Assignment 5 (Area E): descriptive rating tests and their use in the food industry; the range of commercial granola, covering brands, ingredients, nutritional content and cost.

Assignment 5 also asks for a descriptive rating test on two similar brands using six agreed sensory attributes and star diagrams, then a comparison of the two sensory profiles. The theory is sensory analysis, taught with food additives and processing.

A processed food is any food changed from its raw state by one or more processes, such as milling, heating, freezing, drying, canning or adding ingredients. Processing makes a raw food safer, longer-lasting, more convenient or more valuable.

Main reasons for processing: to extend shelf life, make food safe to eat, cut down on waste, provide a wide choice of good-quality food all year round and create new food products, which varies the diet.
The range of processed foods includes frozen, canned, dried, instant or ready-to-eat and cook-chill foods, as well as preserved or pickled foods and fortified foods.
Minimal processing includes washing, cutting, bagging salad leaves or freezing vegetables, with no ingredient added, so the food stays close to its raw state.
Extensive processing involves many stages and ingredients, so the finished product is far removed from its raw material.
Flour is the standard example of extensive processing: wheat grain is turned into a fine powder that looks and behaves nothing like the raw grain, and it then becomes the base of many other foods.

Flour is made by cleaning and blending wheat grain, then milling it between rollers (break rolls and smooth rolls) and sieving it. This separates the bran and germ from the starchy endosperm (the white inner part of the grain), and white flour is mainly endosperm.

Removing the bran and germ lowers fibre and some vitamins and minerals, so white flour has fewer of these than wholemeal flour. Nutrients lost in milling, for example B vitamins and iron, may be added back, and flour is a food named as fortified.
White flour keeps longer than wholegrain flour because the germ, which contains oils that can turn rancid (go off), has been removed.
Improvers (additives that help flour perform when baked) or added nutrients may be incorporated at the end of milling.
Flour is weighed into paper bags. The label gives the brand, product name, ingredients, best-before date, quantity, nutrition information and storage.

Flour is then an ingredient in bread, cakes, pasta and breakfast cereals, each of which passes through further stages such as mixing, baking or extrusion (forcing through a shaped opening), then packaging.
Setting: a visit to a local mill shows these stages in practice.

Milk spoils quickly because micro-organisms and enzymes act on it. Preservation methods slow or stop the micro-organisms and enzymes that spoil food, so milk goes through several treatments at the creamery.

A creamery receives milk from farms, tests its quality, cools it, separates cream from skimmed milk, standardises the fat content, pasteurises it, cools it again, packs it and keeps it in chill storage.
Pasteurisation heats milk (to about 72 °C for 15 seconds) to destroy pathogens and most spoilage organisms, then cools it rapidly. The milk still needs refrigeration and keeps for days.

UHT (ultra-high temperature) treatment heats milk to about 135 °C for a few seconds. Sealed in aseptic (germ-free) packaging, it keeps for months at room temperature until opened. Sterilised milk is heated even more severely in the sealed bottle.

Homogenisation forces milk under pressure through tiny openings, breaking fat globules so that cream does not rise to the top. This improves consistency but is not a preservation step and does not kill bacteria.
Canning heats food in sealed containers to destroy micro-organisms; freezing and storage at or below -18 °C stops most micro-organisms from growing.
Drying removes moisture so micro-organisms cannot grow, and vacuum packing removes air to slow spoilage.
Setting: a visit to a local creamery or cheese plant shows milk being pasteurised and separated in practice.

Added value means processing a raw material into a product with greater economic value, not a more nutritious one. The product is worth more to the manufacturer and is better matched to consumer taste, convenience or health.
For example, cook-chill soups and readymade meals, cheese and grated cheese, flavoured yoghurts, sliced cooked ham, herb-flavoured oils and vinegars, jams, pickles and fruit sauces.
Cook-chill foods are cooked, chilled rapidly (to 3 °C within 30 minutes and fully chilled within 90 minutes), stored and transported at 1-3 °C, and reheated thoroughly before serving.
Milk is the raw material for cheese and yoghurt; each involves culturing, coagulating or otherwise changing the milk into a new product with a higher selling price.

Cheese: pasteurised milk is inoculated (given a starter) with lactic acid bacteria, which turn lactose into lactic acid. Rennet coagulates it into curds and whey, the curds are cut and the whey drained, then the curds are heated, cheddared, salted, moulded and pressed.
The cheese is then ripened for months, graded, cut and sealed.
The manufacturer gains a higher selling price, while the consumer gains convenience, taste or a health benefit.
Yoghurt is a worked example of added value: ordinary milk is fermented into a thicker, sour product that sells for more. Follow the stages in order.
1. Milk is tested on reception and its fat content is standardised (adjusted to a set level); milk solids may be added to give body.
2. Milk is homogenised under pressure so that fat globules stay evenly dispersed.
3. Milk is pasteurised to destroy pathogens, then cooled to the temperature the starter culture needs.
4. Lactic acid bacteria, and any probiotic culture, are added and the milk is incubated; the bacteria ferment lactose to lactic acid.
5. The falling pH (it becomes more acidic) coagulates the casein (the main milk protein), giving yoghurt its thick texture and sour flavour.
6. Once the correct acidity is reached, the yoghurt is chilled quickly to slow fermentation.

7. Fruit purée, permitted sugar, stabiliser or flavouring may be blended in; the yoghurt is filled, sealed, coded and kept refrigerated in the chill chain (the unbroken cold storage from factory to shop).
Some foods are chosen for more than their basic nutrients. A functional food has a health benefit on top of ordinary nutrition.
A functional food gives health benefits beyond its basic nutritional value because of an added or naturally present ingredient.
Live yoghurt with probiotic bacteria supports the digestive system, because the added bacteria are the beneficial ingredient.
Plant sterol spreads reduce blood cholesterol, so they are chosen by people wanting to lower it.
Omega-3 enriched foods are promoted for heart health.
Folic acid enriched foods reduce the risk of neural tube defects (birth defects of the brain and spine) in a developing baby.
Fortification is a way of putting nutrients into foods that people eat every day. It is different from food supplements, which are tablets.
Fortification adds nutrients so that their level in the food is higher than the level naturally present.
Fortification replaces nutrients lost in processing, so the food is not poorer, and addresses public health needs.
Breakfast cereals are often fortified with iron and vitamins, fruit juices with vitamin C, and margarine and dairy spreads with vitamins A and D.
Other foods named as fortified include milk, flour, bread and biscuits.
Convenience foods are processed foods that are ready to eat or quick to prepare. They are popular because they solve real problems for busy households.
They save preparation, cooking and cleaning time and need little cooking skill, which suits busy households and people with limited mobility.
Long shelf life gives a wide choice of food all year round, including out-of-season produce.
They give consistent quality, taste and portion size, and clear portions aid meal planning.
Processing reduces waste, so less food is thrown out, and frozen or canned foods keep many of their nutrients.
They are easy to store, so they are useful as an emergency meal.
The same foods have drawbacks for health, cost and the environment, which is why they should not make up the whole diet.
Many are high in salt, sugar and saturated fat and low in fibre.
They are often more expensive per portion than home-prepared food of similar size, because the maker's processing and packaging costs are added to the price.
Many contain additives, a minority of consumers react to particular substances.
Packaging adds waste and environmental impact.
Reliance on ready meals reduces cooking skills, because meals are no longer made from scratch, and can unbalance the diet.
Taste, colour and texture can be inferior to the fresh equivalent, because heating and storage change them.
Ultra-processed foods are at the far end of processing. They are made in factories from refined ingredients and additives rather than from whole foods.
Ultra-processed foods are industrial formulations made largely from refined ingredients and additives, with little or no whole food. They are classed as group 4 in the NOVA system.
Examples, such as packaged snacks, sugary drinks, instant noodles and many ready meals.
They are designed for convenience, palatability (how pleasant they taste) and long shelf life, and often contain flavourings, colourings, emulsifiers and sweeteners that are not used in home cooking.
They are less healthy than fresh food.
Two other labels on food describe how it was produced: genetic modification changes the plant or animal itself, while organic farming limits the chemicals used to grow it.
Genetic modification alters the DNA of a plant or animal to change a characteristic such as size, speed of ripening or resistance to disease.
Soya and maize are examples of crops widely grown as genetically modified varieties.
EU law requires foods containing genetically modified ingredients, including foods made from genetically modified soya or maize, to be labelled.
Organic produce is grown without synthetic chemical fertilisers, pesticides and preservatives.
Organic farming is less intensive, so it gives lower yields, and must follow rules on fertiliser use and on pest, weed and disease control.
Organic certification is given by inspection bodies recognised by the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, and certified products carry the symbol of the certifying body.
Lower yields and more labour make organic food more expensive.
Food packaging is made from six main materials, and each one suits certain foods because of its properties. Knowing a material's strengths tells you what it is used for.

Metals (aluminium and tin) are strong, airtight and can be heat-processed, so they are used for canned fish and fruit, takeaway containers and aerosol whipped cream. Tins are lacquered inside so the metal does not react with the food.

Glass (jars and bottles) is hygienic, transparent, impervious, resealable and reusable, so it is used for beverages, mayonnaise, sauces, preserves and cooking oil. Its drawbacks are that it is heavy and breakable.

Plastics (polythene, PET and similar polymers) are lightweight, flexible, moisture-proof, transparent and can be heat-sealed. They are used for polythene bags, PET soft drink bottles, yoghurt pots, dairy spreads and dried pasta, but are mostly non-biodegradable.
Polystyrene is lightweight, insulating, shock-absorbing, easily moulded and stackable, which suits egg trays and takeaway trays and containers. It is not readily biodegradable.

Paper and cardboard are light, inexpensive, easy to print on and renewable. They are used for cereal boxes, egg cartons and paper bags for bread, cakes, flour and sugar, but they are not moisture-proof unless coated.
Waxed cartons use a wax coating to make the board waterproof, so they are cheap, lightweight, printable and heat-sealable. They are recyclable or biodegradable according to the scheme.
A pack has to do a job for the food inside it, so examiners expect you to list the qualities a good pack needs. Which qualities matter most depends on the food.
Packaging must be strong and durable enough to survive handling and transport, so the food arrives undamaged.
It must be airtight or moisture- and vapour-proof, depending on the food, so the food does not dry out, go soft or spoil.
It must be hygienic and safe, and must not react with or taint the food, so it should be odourless.
It should be easy to open and, where needed, easy to reseal, so the consumer can use it a little at a time.
It should be lightweight, stackable and easy to store, which makes it cheaper to transport and easier to shelve.
It should be heat resistant where the food is heated in the pack, and printable so that labels can be applied.
It should be attractive to the consumer and economical to produce.
Packaging does more than wrap food. It has four jobs that examiners ask for, and a fifth, convenience, is also credited.
Protection: packaging guards food against physical damage and against contamination by micro-organisms and dirt, so the food stays safe and intact.
Containment: it holds the product in the portion size intended for the consumer.
Information: it carries the product name, ingredients, nutrition and storage details, as well as weight, allergens, cooking instructions and branding.
Tamper evidence: a sealed pack shows whether the contents have been interfered with, so the consumer can tell if it has been opened.
Convenience: packs that are easy to open, reseal, store and carry make the food easier to use.

Packaging that protects food can also create waste. How much harm it does depends on whether the material is renewable, biodegradable (breaks down naturally) and recyclable (reprocessed into new products).
Metal and plastic packaging is not biodegradable and is made from non-renewable resources, but both can be recycled.
Glass can be reused and recycled indefinitely without losing quality.
Paper and cardboard are made from a renewable resource, are biodegradable and are widely recyclable.
Polystyrene is bulky and not readily biodegradable, so its environmental impact depends on whether it is collected for recycling.
The impact is reduced by using less packaging, reusing containers and recycling materials.

In Ireland, the Re-turn deposit return scheme supports recycling of plastic drinks bottles and aluminium and steel cans by refunding a deposit: 15c for containers under 500 ml and 25c for 500 ml and over.

The scheme launched nationwide on 1 February 2026 for PET plastic bottles and aluminium or steel cans from 150 ml to 3 litres, under the Separate Collection (Deposit Return Scheme) Regulations 2021 (S.I. 599 of 2021).
Two kinds of packaging answer particular problems: one makes food last longer, the other makes the pack itself break down after use.
Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP): the air is removed and replaced with a controlled mixture of carbon dioxide, nitrogen and oxygen, and the pack is heat sealed.
The gas mixture slows the growth of bacteria, yeasts and moulds, so the shelf life of the food is extended. It also helps keep the food's colour.
MAP is used for fresh meat, fish, fruit and vegetables, baked goods and cheese.
Biodegradable packaging breaks down into the raw materials of nature, with micro-organisms doing much of the work.
Examples of biodegradable packaging: paper bags for bread, cakes, sugar and flour, and cardboard for cereals, takeaway foods and eggs.
Diagram: a labelled sealed pack showing the gas mixture inside the tray and the heat-sealed film lid.
Irish food labels follow Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, and the FSAI coordinates enforcement.

The European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014 (S.I. No. 556 of 2014, in force 13 December 2014) give effect in Ireland to Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, and official agencies working under FSAI service contracts carry out enforcement.
The name of the food must be stated, along with a list of ingredients in descending order by weight, so the main ingredient comes first.

Allergens such as milk, egg, nuts and gluten cereals must be emphasised within the ingredients list, so people with allergies can spot them. The Regulation lists 14 allergens, including cereals containing gluten, milk, eggs, peanuts, tree nuts, fish, crustaceans, molluscs, soya, celery, mustard, sesame, lupin, sulphur dioxide and sulphites.
The net quantity must be stated, and the name and address of the food business operator must appear on the label.

A use-by date is given for highly perishable food and is a food safety date, so do not eat after it. A best-before date (the date of minimum durability) is a quality date, after which the food may still be safe.
Storage conditions and cooking or usage instructions must be given, for example keep refrigerated or stir before use.
The country of origin or place of provenance is given where the law requires it.
Additives are identified by their class name followed by the specific name or E number, for example preservative: E202.
Labels also carry a lot or batch code, which lets a product be traced and recalled if there is a problem.
The nutrition declaration is a standard table that lets shoppers compare foods on the same terms. Claims on the front of a pack are separate, and need careful reading.
The mandatory nutrition declaration gives seven items: energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt.
Values are given per 100 g or 100 ml, which allows fair comparison between products, and often per portion as well.
Claims such as low fat, high in fibre or contains live cultures must be accurate and not misleading, and nutrition and health claims must meet the EU rules, set by Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006.
Low fat does not necessarily mean low sugar, salt or energy, so the full declaration must be read.
A label is the consumer's main source of information at the point of purchase. It helps shoppers choose, stay safe and avoid waste.
Labels allow consumers to compare products on energy, fat, sugar and salt, rather than being guided by brand, pictures or health claims.
Consumers following a low-salt, low-saturated-fat or high-fibre diet can select products by their declared values.
Ingredients and allergen emphasis protect people with coeliac disease, milk, egg, nut or other allergies.
Use-by and best-before dates, storage and reheating instructions protect safety and reduce food waste.
The origin on the label lets consumers choose to buy Irish.
The manufacturer's details and the lot code support traceability and complaints.
Quality assurance (such as the Bord Bia mark), organic, fair-trade and gluten-free marks guide consumers with particular ethical or dietary choices.

A contaminant is an unwanted substance that gets into food by accident, or that is not meant to be there, at any stage from farm to plate. This is the opposite of an additive, which is added deliberately and legally.

Contaminants can enter during primary production on the farm (from soil, water, air, animal feed, sprays and veterinary treatments), during processing, during packaging, during storage and transport, and during cooking in the kitchen.
In processing, the sources include equipment, lubricants and cleaning chemicals, so contamination can happen even when the raw ingredients were clean.

A residue is a small amount of a substance left in food after it was used legitimately, such as a pesticide or a veterinary medicine. Contaminant is the broader word; residue is the case where the substance was used properly.
Foreign bodies such as glass or metal fragments are physical contaminants, as opposed to chemical contaminants such as pesticides, antibiotics and metals.
General food law, set out in Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, requires that unsafe food must not be placed on the market, so a food business is responsible for what it sells.

The Food Safety Authority of Ireland coordinates national enforcement of food safety, including control of contaminants. Official agencies working under FSAI service contracts, including the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, the HSE (including the Public Analyst Laboratories), local authorities and the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority, sample and test food.
Farmers spray crops to protect them, but some of the chemical can stay on the plant and end up on your plate. These leftovers are pesticide residues.
Pesticides are chemicals used on crops: insecticides against insects, fungicides against fungi and herbicides against weeds.

Contamination happens when crops are sprayed, when spray drifts through the air, when it runs off into water, and when plants and soil organisms take it up. Residues can remain on fruit, vegetables and cereals and so enter the diet.
Possible effects on the body include respiratory problems, heart and circulatory problems, damage to the nervous system and birth defects, and some pesticides may cause cancer.
The required wait between the last spraying and harvest is called the pre-harvest interval. Observing it allows residues to fall to a safe level before the crop is picked.
Farmers should use only approved products, at the approved rate. Maximum residue limits are set in EU law, and the limits are checked by testing.
Washing and peeling reduce the amount of pesticide residue on fresh produce, so consumers can lower their own exposure.
Residues are monitored by official testing carried out by agencies under FSAI service contracts, including the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine and the HSE Public Analyst Laboratories.
Animals on farms are sometimes given medicines, and traces can pass into the milk and meat people eat. Antibiotics are the example the syllabus names.
Antibiotics are given to livestock to treat or prevent disease.
For veterinary medicines the required wait before sale is called the withdrawal period. If milk or meat is sold before it has passed, antibiotic residues remain in the food.
Antibiotic residues in milk can prevent the lactic acid bacteria used for yoghurt and cheese from fermenting, so the product fails to set or ripen properly. This is an effect on the food industry.
Antibiotic residues can cause allergic reactions in sensitive people.
Residues may also contribute to the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, which means infections become harder to treat.

Growth-promoting hormones are banned in EU animal production. Residues from legitimate veterinary treatments are controlled by withdrawal periods and monitored in Ireland through the national residue control plan, run by the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine.
Metals such as lead, mercury and cadmium do not break down, so once they get into the environment they can find their way into food. They are a concern because the body cannot easily get rid of them.
Heavy metals such as lead, cadmium and mercury enter food from soil, water and air contaminated by industry or traffic.
Lead can also come from old lead water pipes, and metals can come from food containers and cooking equipment.

Plants grown in contaminated soil can absorb metals, and shellfish filtering polluted water can accumulate them. Mercury in shellfish and large predatory fish comes from industrial pollution of coastal waters.

Mercury accumulates in large predatory fish such as shark and swordfish, a process known as bioaccumulation: the contaminant builds up in an organism over time and is more concentrated further up the food chain.
Because metals build up in the body over time, repeated exposure is a greater concern than a single exposure.
Possible effects on the body include stomach cramps, damage to the kidneys and liver, damage to the nervous system and central nervous system, headaches and effects on the immune system.
Other environmental contaminants include dioxins, and micro-organisms such as bacteria from poor hygiene, undercooked meat or unwashed hands, which cause nausea, vomiting and food poisoning.
Chemicals that belong in a food factory or kitchen, such as cleaners and lubricants, can become contaminants if they get into the food. Packaging can also pass chemicals into the food it holds.
Cleaning agents, lubricants and sanitisers used in food premises can contaminate food if they are not rinsed off or are misused.
Lubricants from industrial waste can cause nausea and central nervous system damage.
Chemicals can migrate (move) from packaging or other food-contact materials into food, particularly fatty or acidic foods.
Food-grade materials (materials made safe for contact with food) reduce the risk of migration.

Pest control chemicals stored near food can contaminate it if the storage is not properly separated, so they must be stored away from food. Separate storage of chemicals from food reduces the risk generally.
No single step can keep every contaminant out of food, so control happens at every level from the farm to the consumer.

Farm level: good agricultural practice, use of approved products only, and observance of the required wait before sale or harvest (the pre-harvest interval for crops, withdrawal periods for veterinary medicines) control pesticide and veterinary residues.
Industry level: food businesses buy raw materials from approved suppliers and test them on reception, so a problem is caught before it reaches the product.
