Traceability records, including lot codes, allow a contaminated batch to be identified and recalled quickly, which limits how many consumers are affected.
Official level: control agencies sample and test food and raw materials to check that the limits on contaminants are met, and unsafe food is recalled.
Consumer level: wash and peel produce, buy from reputable sources and follow storage and cooking guidance.
Varying the diet limits exposure to any one contaminant.

A food additive is a natural or artificial substance added to food during manufacture to improve colour, taste, texture, appearance, keeping qualities or nutritive value, or to aid processing. Because each additive is added for a particular job, additives are sorted into classes by that job.

Additives are grouped into classes by their function: colourings, flavourings (including flavour enhancers), sweeteners, preservatives, antioxidants, nutritional supplements and, at Higher Level, physical conditioning agents.
Each class has natural examples (from plants, animals or minerals) and artificial examples (made by chemical synthesis), and the function of the additive, not its origin, is the basis for its class.
Natural does not mean safer: both natural and artificial additives must be approved before they can be used in food.
Settings: examine a food label to find the additives used, identify the class of each from its name or E number (a code given to an approved additive), and suggest the reason it was added.

Additives have disadvantages: some people react to them (allergy, intolerance, or a hyperactivity warning on certain colours), and they may mask poor-quality food or encourage a diet of processed foods.
Two further disadvantages are specific to one additive each: sulphur dioxide destroys thiamine (vitamin B1), and polyols (bulk sweeteners) can cause diarrhoea if eaten in excess.
Processing, such as heating or canning, can fade or change the natural colour of food, and shoppers judge food by its look. Colourings are added to put this right.
Function: colourings restore colour lost in processing, make food more attractive and give a consistent, uniform appearance from batch to batch.
Natural colourings include caramel (E150), chlorophyll (E140), carotene (E160a), cochineal (E120) and turmeric (E100, also called curcumin).
Artificial colourings include tartrazine (E102), a yellow dye used in soft drinks and sweets.
Colourings are used in foods such as sweets, soft drinks, desserts, baked goods and cheese products.
Tartrazine and some other azo colours (a group of synthetic dyes) must carry a warning that they may affect activity and attention in children, which is one reason some people avoid them.

Some foods taste bland to begin with and others lose flavour during processing. Flavourings put taste back or add it, while flavour enhancers work differently by making a flavour already there seem stronger.
Function: flavourings add flavour to bland food, replace flavour lost in processing, and (as enhancers) strengthen an existing flavour.
Natural flavourings include herbs, spices, sugar and salt, used in foods such as jam, tinned beans, cereals, meat products, sauces, stock cubes, cheese and butter.

Artificial flavourings are chemical compounds made by synthesis, such as esters and aldehydes; ethyl acetate gives a rum flavour, amyl acetate a pear flavour, benzaldehyde a cherry flavour, and maltol is another example. They are used in baked goods and cakes.
Flavour enhancers (in the E600 to E699 range) improve an existing flavour and make it seem stronger; monosodium glutamate (E621) is the most common example.
Monosodium glutamate is used in soups, sauces, stock cubes and prepared meals.
Flavourings in the narrow sense carry no E number, but flavour enhancers do, so do not say that every additive has an E number.
Bacteria, yeasts and moulds spoil food. Preservatives slow this down so that food stays safe and edible for longer.
Preservatives inhibit the growth of micro-organisms (bacteria, yeasts and moulds), which delays spoilage and extending shelf life.
Natural preservatives include salt, sugar, vinegar and smoke, which are accepted as natural preservatives.
Chemical preservatives include sulphur dioxide (E220) and potassium sorbate (E202), used in soft drinks, jams, baked goods, dried fruit and wine.
Sulphur dioxide destroys some thiamine (vitamin B1), so its use reduces the nutritive value of the food.
Sulphur dioxide must be declared on the label as an allergen, because some people react to it.

Sweeteners give a sweet taste, but they fall into very different groups. Nutritive sweeteners supply energy, intense sweeteners replace sugar with almost no energy, and bulk sweeteners (polyols) sweeten while also adding body.
Nutritive sweeteners such as sugar, honey, glucose syrup and fructose supply energy as well as sweetness.
Intense sweeteners (high-intensity, non-nutritive sweeteners) are many times sweeter than sugar, so only a tiny amount is needed and they contribute negligible energy.
Intense sweeteners include saccharin (E954), aspartame (E951), acesulfame K (E950) and sucralose (E955).
Because the quantity used is so small, intense sweeteners do not provide sugar's bulk, browning, preservation or texture, so a bulking agent may also be needed.
Intense sweeteners are used in low-energy and diet soft drinks, tabletop sweeteners, yoghurts, desserts and foods for people reducing their sugar intake.
Products containing aspartame carry a label warning for people with phenylketonuria, as aspartame is a source of phenylalanine (an amino acid they cannot process).

Bulk sweeteners, or polyols, include sorbitol (E420), mannitol (E421) and xylitol; they are less intensely sweet, are used in larger amounts, give bulk and texture, and also act as humectants (they hold moisture in food).
Polyols are found in sugar-free confectionery and chewing gum, and excessive amounts can have a laxative effect (loosen the bowel).
Intense sweeteners are used wherever sugar must be cut, but that does not make the food automatically healthy or suitable for everyone.
Artificial sweeteners are useful in slimming and diabetic products because they reduce sucrose, although the energy and portion size of the whole product still matter.
Sweeteners are not permitted in food for infants and young children.
Fats and oils go rancid (stale and unpleasant-tasting) when oxygen attacks them. Antioxidants take up the oxygen first so the fat is protected.
Antioxidants react with oxygen, so it cannot attack the fats and oils in food, preventing oxidative rancidity.
Natural antioxidants include vitamin C (E300, ascorbic acid) and vitamin E (E306, tocopherols).
Artificial antioxidants include BHA (E320) and BHT (E321).
Antioxidants are used in fats, cooking oils, crisps, biscuits, stock cubes, cheese spread, chewing gum, tinned fish, fruit drinks and jams.
By slowing rancidity, antioxidants extend shelf life and reduce food waste, because less food spoils before it can be eaten.
Some additives are added for nutrition rather than for how the food looks, tastes or keeps.
Nutritional supplements are vitamins, minerals and other nutrients added to food to raise or restore its nutrient content.
They are the additives used for fortification, so the food supplies more of a nutrient than it naturally contains.
Unlike sweeteners, preservatives and colourings, their purpose is nutritional rather than technological.

Physical conditioning agents are additives that change or maintain the physical properties of food, such as texture, consistency, moisture, stability and appearance. Emulsifiers and stabilisers work as a pair to keep mixtures like mayonnaise smooth.
An emulsifier holds two immiscible liquids (liquids that do not mix), such as oil and water, together so that they do not separate.
An emulsifier molecule has a hydrophilic (water-loving) head that attaches to water and a hydrophobic (oil-loving) tail that attaches to oil, so it links the two phases.
Examples are lecithin (E322) and mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids (E471).
Emulsifiers are used in mayonnaise, ice cream, sauces, margarine and chocolate.

A stabiliser prevents an emulsion (a mixture of two liquids that do not normally mix) from separating over time; alginates (E401), carrageenan (E407), guar gum (E412) and pectin (E440) are examples, with stabilisers and thickeners used in ice cream, sauces and desserts.
Diagram: an emulsifier molecule with a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail, shown at the boundary between an oil droplet and water.
These agents protect the texture of food by controlling moisture, lumping and firmness. One function in a single clause is enough when you are asked to name an agent and give its function.
A humectant attracts and retains water, preventing food from losing moisture, drying out and hardening; sorbitol and mannitol are examples.
Humectants are used in marzipan, cakes and sweets, so that they stay soft.
An anti-caking agent prevents lumps forming in dried or powdered foods such as cake mixes and dried milk; polyphosphates (E450 to E452) are an example that also increases water retention.
A setting agent helps a food to set; pectin aids the setting of jams.
A firming agent keeps fruit and vegetables firm during processing.
Some agents control what happens in the pan, in the packet or on the processing line, rather than in the food itself.
Anti-foaming agents prevent scum and froth forming on the surface of food as it boils.
Anti-spattering agents keep water droplets apart in cooking oils, preventing spatter.
Buffers maintain (control) the pH of a food at the level required for processing or taste.
Packaging gases, such as nitrogen, are sealed into sachet foods to replace air and prevent oxidation.
Release agents form a coating, so food does not stick: it stops foods from sticking to each other or to equipment.

Food additives are substances added to food for a technical purpose, such as keeping it fresh or improving its colour. Because they are added on purpose, the European Union controls their use by law under Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 on food additives.
The regulation sets rules for preservatives, colourings, emulsifiers and antioxidants, among other additives such as sweeteners, so every additive group the syllabus names is covered.
As an EU regulation, it applies directly in Ireland, as in every Member State, without needing a separate Irish Act. This is why the same rules apply to a food sold anywhere in the EU.
Its purposes are to protect consumer health, to allow a single market in food, and to make sure additives are used only where there is a technological need and consumers are not misled.
Two related EU rules sit alongside it: flavourings have their own regulation, Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008, and vitamins and minerals added to food are covered by Regulation (EC) No 1925/2006.
The first control is a gate: an additive cannot be used unless it has been checked and approved. This stops untested substances reaching food.
An additive may be used only if it appears on the approved list for the EU (the Union list), and only in the foods and at the maximum levels that the list permits.
Each additive must be tested for safety before it is approved, so every approved additive has been tested.

The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) assesses the safety of the additive and sets an acceptable daily intake, the amount that can be eaten daily without harm. The European Commission then authorises the additive.
Approved additives are re-evaluated as scientific knowledge changes, so an approval is not permanent and an additive can be reviewed again.
Each approved additive is given an E number, a code that shows it has passed the EU approval process. The E stands for Europe, and the number also gives a rough guide to what the additive does.
Each approved additive is assigned an E number, except flavourings, which are not given E numbers.
E100 to E199 are colourings, for example E150 caramel and E102 tartrazine. E200 to E299 are preservatives, for example E202 potassium sorbate and E220 sulphur dioxide.
E300 to E399 are antioxidants, for example E300 vitamin C and E320 BHA; the range also includes acidity regulators.
E400 to E499 are thickeners, stabilisers and emulsifiers, for example E471 mono- and diglycerides and E440 pectin. E500 to E599 are acidity regulators and anti-caking agents.

E600 to E699 are flavour enhancers, for example E621 monosodium glutamate. E900 to E999 include sweeteners and glazing agents, for example E950 acesulfame K, E951 aspartame, E954 saccharin and E955 sucralose.
The ranges are an approximate guide, with exceptions. For example, lecithin (E322) is an emulsifier but sits in the antioxidant range, so the class word on the label tells you what an additive does.
An E number is shown on the label after the class name, for example preservative: E220, or the additive's name can be used instead, for example preservative: sulphur dioxide.
The label tells the consumer what the additive is, what it does and that it is approved. A consumer can also read the label to avoid additives they react to.
Approval is not a free pass. The regulation sets conditions that every additive must meet, and it bans some additives from some foods altogether.
An additive must not present a health hazard to the consumer, because protecting health is the first aim of the law.
An additive must not mislead the consumer about the food, for example about its nature or quality.
An additive must not be used to disguise poor quality or faulty processing, because it must serve a reasonable technological need.
An additive must not reduce the nutritive value of the food.
Each additive must be used in the smallest quantity needed to achieve its effect, so no more than necessary is added.
Colourings are not permitted in fresh fruit, fresh vegetables, fresh meat, poultry or fish, because colour would hide how fresh these foods really are.
Colourings are not permitted in baby food, and sweeteners are not permitted in food for infants and young children. Preservatives, BHA and BHT are also not allowed in baby food.

The label must show the class name of the additive followed by its specific name or E number, for example preservative: sulphur dioxide or preservative: E220. Flavourings are declared by name rather than by an E number.
The EU regulation sets the rules, but Irish bodies make sure they are followed. This is a short section of an answer, but one enforcement sentence can add marks.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI), set up under the Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998, is responsible for the safe use of food additives in Ireland and coordinates enforcement.

Official agencies working under FSAI service contracts check compliance through inspection and sampling. They include the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, the HSE Environmental Health Service and Public Analyst Laboratories, and local authorities.
The FSAI also advises ministers, regulators, industry and consumers.

Evaluation means judging a dish or meal against stated criteria, using evidence from the dish itself rather than just saying whether you liked it. A good evaluation always ends with a reason and an improvement.

Criteria include nutritional value (energy, fibre, fat, sugar and salt), cost per portion, sensory qualities (appearance, aroma, flavour and texture), time and skill required, suitability for the household or special diets, safety and hygiene, and packaging and waste.

Method: 1. State the criterion. 2. Give evidence from the recipe, label or tasting. 3. Make a judgement and give the reason for it. 4. Suggest an improvement. Evidence is what stops a judgement being just an opinion.
Recipes are modified to make them more nutritious, to suit special diets such as coeliac (a condition where gluten must be avoided), to change the quantity made, or to save cost.

Setting: evaluate a family meal against healthy-eating guidelines, such as the Department of Health Food Pyramid, and suggest changes to the portions or ingredients so that it matches the recommended balance.

A home-made dish and its shop-bought equivalent can be compared on the same set of criteria, usually in a table, before you reach an overall judgement. Neither is always better, because the result depends on the dish and the quantities.
Cost: home-made food from basic ingredients is often cheaper per portion, whereas commercial products carry the costs of labour, packaging and distribution.
Nutrition: home-made food lets the cook control salt, sugar, fat and fibre, while the commercial nutrition declaration (the nutrition information on the label) allows products to be compared.
Additives: home-made food usually contains none of the preservatives, colourings or emulsifiers that many commercial products contain.
Time and skill: commercial products need little time or skill, which saves effort, while home-made food needs preparation, cooking and cleaning time.
Sensory quality: home-made food may taste fresher, while a commercial product gives the same taste and texture from one batch to the next.
Shelf life: commercial products are processed to last longer, while home-made food usually needs refrigeration and is eaten within a short time.
Packaging and waste: home-made food made from loose ingredients may create less packaging waste than a pre-packed commercial equivalent, which comes in more packaging.
Method: compare the same product on a set of criteria in a table, then reach a judgement that weighs them up.

Sensory analysis is the scientific evaluation of food using the senses, carried out under controlled conditions. Food companies use it so that decisions about a product are based on what consumers actually perceive, not on guesses.
Product development: testing samples to find which version consumers prefer, and how they respond to a new product, before it is launched.
Modifying an existing product: for example reducing the salt in a product, or changing an ingredient or supplier, with difference tests used to confirm that consumers cannot perceive the change.
Matching an existing product: testing so that an own-label food can be made to taste like the leading brand, copying a well-known brand.
Evaluation and quality control: checking that the final product meets its original specification, such as the shortness of a biscuit.
Comparing an own-brand product with a leading brand, and supporting marketing claims about taste or texture.
The first of three categories of sensory test is the preference test. It asks whether people like a product, not whether they can tell products apart.
Preference tests show whether consumers like or dislike a product, or prefer one product to another.
Paired preference test: the tester chooses the preferred of two coded samples.
Hedonic rating scale: the tester rates how much they like a product on a numbered scale from dislike extremely to like extremely, so it measures liking.
Food action rating: the tester states how likely they are to buy or eat the product, so it measures willingness to eat or buy.
Preference ranking: the tester ranks several samples from most to least preferred.
The other two categories of sensory test ask different questions. Difference tests ask whether people can tell samples apart, and descriptive tests ask what the samples are like.
Difference tests show whether a difference exists between samples and, if so, how noticeable it is, which tells a company whether consumers would notice a change.
Simple difference paired comparison: the tester says whether two coded samples, which may be the same or different, are different.
Directional paired comparison: the tester identifies which of two samples has a greater intensity of a stated characteristic, such as sweetness.
Triangle test: the tester identifies which of three coded samples is different from the other two. By chance one in three would be right.

Duo-trio test: the tester is given a reference sample and two coded samples, and identifies which coded sample is the same as the reference, so the other is different. By chance one in two would be right.
Descriptive tests describe the perceived sensory characteristics of products, such as the effect of processing, packaging or storage on quality.
Descriptive ranking ranks samples by the intensity of a characteristic; descriptive rating scores that intensity on a scale.

The triangle test checks whether testers can detect a difference between two products, for example an established product and a lower-salt version. Each tester gets three samples and must pick out the odd one.
Aim: to find out whether testers can identify the odd sample among three coded samples, and so whether a difference between the two products can be detected.
Independent variable: the samples, two identical and one different.
Dependent variable: the tester's choice of the odd sample.
Controlled variables: temperature, amount, shape, colour and container of each sample, timing of the test and the room conditions, so that only the product itself can explain a correct choice.

Method: 1. Set up a tray with three coded samples (random three-digit codes) in a balanced, randomised order. 2. Each tester tastes the samples in the order given, with water between samples and no discussion.
Method, continued: 3. The tester identifies the sample that is different. 4. Record the responses on a sheet. 5. Reveal the codes and count the correct answers.
Diagram: a tray with three identical, coded containers, one marked as the odd sample for the investigator's records only.

Once the testers have responded, the answers must be read against chance, because a tester who simply guesses will still be right some of the time. The serving order must also be planned so that position does not bias the answers.

Serving order: there are six possible orders (AAB, ABA, BAA, ABB, BAB, BBA, where A and B are the two products), and a balanced or randomised order means no sample is favoured by where it sits on the tray.
Chance: testers guess correctly one time in three, so the number of correct answers is compared with this chance level, using a significance table.
Expected result: if enough testers, compared with chance, identify the odd sample, a difference is detected.
A triangle test shows only whether a difference can be detected. A preference test would then show whether testers like the change.
Sensory tests measure human perception, which is easily disturbed. The room and the testers must therefore be controlled so that the results reflect the food and nothing else.
Location: a quiet, clean, odour-free room with testing booths or enough space between testers, and no talking so that information is not shared and opinions are not influenced.
Lighting and ventilation: bright, even, preferably natural, light so that samples are seen clearly, and ventilation that removes lingering odours.
Timing: mid-morning or mid-afternoon, when taste sensitivity is best, with no strongly flavoured food or drink, smoking or gum for at least 30 minutes before the test.
Testers who are ill should not take part, because illness dulls taste and smell.
Organisers: the people who set up the test should not take part as testers, because they already know which sample is which.
Instructions: clear, identical instructions are given to every tester, and one characteristic is judged at a time.
The samples themselves must be identical in every way except the feature being tested. Otherwise a tester could be reacting to something other than what the test is measuring.
Samples: all samples at the same temperature, of uniform shape, colour and amount, and in identical containers, so that nothing but the product differs.
Number of samples: it is limited so that testers do not become tired or confused.
Coding and sequence: samples are coded so that the codes do not cause bias, and the order of presentation is planned and balanced, as is the set-up of the trays.
Palate cleansing: water, or a dry or plain cracker where suitable, is used for rinsing between samples so that one taste does not carry over into the next.
Hygiene and dietary needs: strict hygiene and food safety are maintained, and special dietary conditions, such as coeliac disease, are catered for.
We choose, cook and eat food with all of our senses, not just taste. Each sense gives information about whether food is fresh, safe and appetising.
Sight: appearance, colour, size, shape, gloss and presentation are used to judge whether food looks acceptable and fresh.
Expectations of colour matter: mould is acceptable on Stilton cheese but not on bread, and lemon is associated with yellow and mint with green.
Smell: aroma and odour help to judge freshness, and a rancid or off smell leads to rejection, while a good smell makes food appetising.
Taste: the taste buds detect sweet, salt, sour and bitter, and umami is the fifth taste, savoury and given by glutamate.
Touch and mouthfeel: nerves in the mouth detect texture (such as crisp, creamy or gritty), temperature (such as ice cream) and chemical heat, such as the burn of chilli.
Hearing: the sound of food, such as sizzling sausages, crunchy vegetables or fizzy drinks, influences choice and eating.
Cooking changes the senses: colour changes, flavours intensify, an aroma develops and textures change, making cooked food more appetising than raw.

Food starts to spoil as soon as it is harvested or slaughtered. Preservation means treating food so that spoilage is slowed or stopped and the food can be kept, moved and eaten later, with colour, flavour, texture and nutritive value as near as possible to fresh.
It reduces waste by keeping surplus produce, such as a glut of home-grown fruit or vegetables, usable for months rather than days, instead of being thrown away.
Because less food is thrown away, preservation also reduces the environmental footprint of food.
It makes food available out of season and over long distances, so perishable foods (those that spoil quickly) can be transported and stored.
It makes food safer by destroying food poisoning micro-organisms or stopping them from growing, and it lengthens shelf life (the time food stays good to eat).
It creates foods with distinct textures and flavours, such as jam, chutney, dried fruit, smoked fish and cured meat, which increases variety and choice.
Spoilage is not caused only by micro-organisms. Several separate processes make food unusable, and each has its own visible effect.

Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions and are naturally present in food. After harvest or slaughter they carry on working, so food ripens, softens, darkens and changes flavour even when no micro-organism is present. Cut apple, banana and potato brown this way.

Micro-organisms (bacteria, yeasts and moulds) grow on food, causing decay, rot, souring, off-odours and slime, and in some cases food poisoning. Moulds give fuzzy growth on bread, cheese and jam; yeasts ferment fruit juice and jam, with bubbling and an alcoholic smell; bacteria cause souring, putrefaction and food poisoning.
Putrefaction is the breakdown of proteins by bacteria, producing foul-smelling products.

Oxidation occurs when oxygen reacts with fats, causing rancidity (an unpleasant, stale taste and smell), and with the cut surfaces of fruit and vegetables, causing browning. Vitamin C is also lost by oxidation.
Moisture loss through the skins of fruit and vegetables causes shrivelling, wilting, wrinkling and loss of weight. It also dries and hardens bread and cheese.
Incorrect storage temperature allows micro-organisms and enzymes to work quickly, because warmth speeds both of them up.
Poor hygiene and careless handling carry micro-organisms from unwashed hands, equipment, pests or raw food onto prepared food.

Chemical contaminants, such as insecticide or pesticide residues, antibiotics, metals and residues from cleaning products, can make food unsafe. Physical damage such as bruising also opens food to spoilage.
Micro-organisms need six conditions to grow and multiply. Every preservation method works by removing or controlling one or more of them.

The six conditions are food (nutrients), moisture (available water), warmth (a suitable temperature), time (to multiply), a suitable pH or acidity and, for aerobic ones (those that need air), oxygen. Most bacteria prefer a neutral or slightly acid pH.

Bacteria that cause food poisoning multiply rapidly in the danger zone of 5 to 63 °C, which is why chilled and hot food is kept outside it. Below 5 °C growth is slowed; above 63 °C it is stopped and most are killed by sustained heat.
Under good conditions one bacterial cell divides about every 20 minutes (binary fission, splitting in two), so numbers rise very fast.
Moulds and yeasts tolerate acid, sugar and low moisture better than most bacteria, so they spoil jam and dried fruit.
Moulds appear as fuzzy colonies or threads; yeasts produce bubbling, gas and a sour or alcoholic smell.
Enzymes work best at a moderate temperature and are destroyed (denatured) by heat or strong acid; cold slows them but does not stop them.
Micro-organisms cannot multiply in food with little available water, which is why drying and concentrated sugar or salt preserve food.
Three groups of micro-organism spoil food, and spores and enzymes also have to be understood. Each acts differently, which is why different methods suit different foods.
Bacteria are single-celled organisms; some cause food poisoning and others spoil food by producing acid and gas.
Yeasts are single-celled fungi that ferment sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide.
Moulds are multicellular fungi that grow as visible threads and spread by airborne spores.
Spores are dormant (resting), resistant forms produced by some bacteria and all moulds; they survive ordinary heat and cold and start growing again when conditions improve.
Enzymes are biological catalysts made of protein, and each one acts on a specific substance in food.

Osmosis explains why strong sugar or salt solutions preserve food. It is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane (one that lets water through but not most dissolved substances) from a weaker solution to a stronger one.
The cell membrane of a micro-organism is partially permeable, so water leaves the cell when the surrounding solution is concentrated.
Loss of water makes the cell shrink and stop growing, and at high concentrations it can kill the cell.

The same process draws water out of food, which is why salted meat and fish and sugared fruit keep. A strong sugar or salt solution outside a microbial cell draws water out, so the cell shrivels and cannot multiply.

Every preservation method works by removing or controlling one or more of the conditions that micro-organisms and enzymes need, and by preventing re-contamination. There are only a few principles, and each method is an application of one or more of them.

Destroy micro-organisms and inactivate enzymes with heat, as in canning, bottling, jam and chutney making, pasteurisation, sterilisation and blanching. Irradiation also destroys organisms and some enzymes.
Slow or stop activity with low temperature: refrigeration slows growth and enzyme action, and freezing makes organisms dormant (inactivated, not killed) and makes water unavailable as ice.
Remove available water: dehydration (drying, freeze drying) takes water away, while sugar and salt tie it up and draw it out of organisms by osmosis, as in jam, salted fish and cured meat.

Alter the pH with acid: vinegar (acetic acid) in pickles and chutney, or acids produced in fermentation, such as lactic acid in yoghurt and sauerkraut and acetic acid in vinegar. This prevents the growth of many spoilage and food poisoning bacteria.
Use chemical preservatives that inhibit organisms: sugar, salt, vinegar, smoke, alcohol and permitted additives such as sulphur dioxide, sorbates, benzoates and nitrite.

Exclude oxygen and prevent re-entry of organisms with airtight packaging, vacuum sealing, sealed hot jars (a vacuum forms as the contents cool) and moisture-proof wraps for the freezer. Removing oxygen also inactivates enzymes.
Prevent re-contamination after treatment, using sterilised jars and lids, clean utensils, good hygiene and sealing straight away.
Most methods combine principles. Jam uses heat, sugar (osmosis), acid and pectin, and a sealed jar; chutney uses heat, vinegar and sugar; smoked fish uses salt, drying and smoke chemicals.
The methods of preservation fall into groups according to the principle they use. Knowing the groups shows the structure of food preservation.
Heat: canning, bottling, jam and chutney making, pasteurisation, sterilisation and blanching.
Water removal: drying and freeze drying, and sugar or salt that bind water.
Chemicals: sugar, salt, vinegar, smoke, alcohol and permitted additives, with sugar, vinegar, salt, smoking and alcohol being the traditional natural preservatives.

Freezing preserves food by lowering its temperature far enough to stop enzyme action and microbial growth, and by turning free water into ice that micro-organisms cannot use. It is popular because no high heat is needed, so food stays close to fresh.
Low temperature slows enzyme reactions (enzymes are the natural chemicals in food that make it spoil or change) and stops micro-organisms from reproducing, but it does not kill most of them.
Frozen food is not sterile: micro-organisms become dormant (inactive) and start growing again when the food thaws, so frozen food is never safe indefinitely.
Turning free water into ice removes the water micro-organisms need, because ice is unavailable to them.
Pure water freezes at 0 °C, but food freezes below this because its dissolved sugars and salts lower its freezing point.
Water expands by about 9 per cent when it freezes, which is why liquids need headspace (an empty gap at the top) in their containers.

Freezing itself does little harm to nutritive value, and colour, flavour and texture are kept better than with most other methods because no high heat is used, except in blanching; most nutrient losses happen during blanching and thawing.
The speed of freezing decides how big the ice crystals are, and crystal size decides how much damage the food suffers. Quick freezing makes small crystals; slow freezing makes large ones.
Quick freezing takes place at about −25 °C (the 2013 Higher Level scheme gives −25 °C to −40 °C) in the fast-freeze section of a freezer, so the food passes through the freezing range rapidly.
Quick freezing forms small ice crystals within the cells, which causes little damage to the cell walls, so there is little drip (juice lost) on thawing.
For this reason quick freezing retains the texture, colour, flavour and nutritive value of food better than slow freezing does.
Slow freezing takes place at a higher temperature than −25 °C, as in an ordinary freezer compartment, where ice forms gradually.
Slow freezing forms large ice crystals, mostly between the cells, that pierce and rupture cell walls, allowing juices to escape.
As a result slow-frozen food is limp and soft when thawed, and it loses colour and flavour and drip containing soluble vitamins B1 and C and minerals.
The fast-freeze setting should be switched on about 3 to 4 hours before food is placed in the freezer, so the freezer is cold enough to freeze the new food quickly.
Diagram: draw two cells side by side, one with small crystals inside an intact cell wall (quick) and one with large crystals and a ruptured wall (slow).
Blanching is a brief heat treatment given to vegetables before freezing. Enzymes keep working slowly even at freezer temperatures, so vegetables would spoil in storage without it.
1. The vegetables are plunged into boiling water for a short, set time that depends on the vegetable.
2. They are plunged immediately into ice-cold water for the same length of time, which stops the cooking so the vegetables do not go soft.
3. They are drained and dried, because surface water left on them would form ice crystals.
Blanching inactivates enzymes that would otherwise cause loss of colour, flavour, texture and nutrients during frozen storage.
Blanching also cleans the vegetable, destroys some micro-organisms on its surface, softens it slightly so it packs well, and keeps its bright colour.

Blanching loses some water-soluble vitamins, particularly vitamin C and vitamin B1, into the water and through heat. Blanch small batches in plenty of fast-boiling water so the water returns to the boil quickly and the timing stays short and accurate.
Fruit is not blanched; soft fruit is open-frozen on trays or packed in sugar or sugar syrup. Some foods, such as soups, sauces and casseroles, are frozen cooked after cooling.
Good results at home depend on following a set of steps, and each step has a reason. Most of them aim either to freeze the food quickly or to keep air and moisture away from it.

Choose fresh, best-quality food in perfect condition and freeze it soon after harvest or purchase, because freezing keeps quality but cannot improve it. Wash, peel, trim or cut as needed, blanch vegetables, and cool cooked food quickly before it goes into the freezer.
Portion food into usable (family-sized) quantities so that only what is needed is thawed.

Open-freeze (tray-freeze) sticky or delicate items, such as strawberries or raspberries, or items to be kept separate, such as sausages and burgers: spread them in a single layer on a tray, freeze hard, then bag them so that they stay separate.

Pack food in strong, moisture-proof and vapour-proof freezer bags, foil or rigid plastic containers, and remove as much air as possible so that the food does not dry out. Leave headspace in containers holding liquids to allow for expansion as the food freezes.

Seal tightly and label with contents and date. Place new packs against the cold surfaces or in the fast-freeze compartment, as the freezer instructs, and keep them apart from already frozen food until frozen, so they freeze quickly.
Do not overload the freezer: freeze no more than about one-tenth of the freezer's capacity in any 24 hours, because overloading raises the temperature and slows freezing.

Store frozen food at −18 °C or colder, using the oldest first. The safe storage time depends on the food: fatty foods and oily fish keep for a shorter period, and fatty foods stored too long can turn rancid.
Foods that freeze well include peas, beans, carrots, broccoli, apples, strawberries, meat, fish, bread, cakes, soups, sauces and prepared meals.

Foods that freeze poorly include lettuce, whole tomatoes and other high-water salad foods, bananas, melons, pears, whole eggs in the shell, low-fat cream and mayonnaise-based foods, which go limp, watery or separate.
Problems with frozen food usually come from air reaching it or from careless thawing. Both are preventable.
Freezer burn shows as dry, discoloured, tough patches where air has reached the surface of the food, caused by dehydration and oxidation, especially in protein foods such as meat and fish.
Airtight packaging with the air removed prevents freezer burn.

Thaw food in a fridge, or cook it from frozen where the food allows, such as vegetables, so that the food stays below the danger zone while it thaws. Thaw meat and poultry fully before cooking unless the pack says otherwise.

Thawed food should be used promptly and not refrozen as it is, because quality declines and micro-organisms may have multiplied. Raw food thawed in the fridge can be cooked and then frozen as a cooked dish.
In a freezer fault or power cut, keep the door closed and do not open it, because frozen food keeps for a time if the cold is held in.

Commercial freezing is faster and colder than home freezing, so ice crystals are smaller and quality is higher. Food is frozen soon after harvesting or catching, often on the farm or on a factory ship. Home freezers are not as cold or as fast, so home freezing does not match these methods.

Air blast freezing: a very cold air stream at about −30 °C is blown over food, often on a conveyor belt or through a tunnel; suitable for most foods, such as fruit, vegetables, meat and bakery products.
Plate (contact) freezing: food is pressed between two hollow metal plates cooled by refrigerant; suitable for thin, flat foods such as fish fillets, flat pieces of meat and burgers.

Flow (fluidised bed) freezing: cold air is blown up through a perforated conveyor belt so that small pieces float and freeze individually, staying free-flowing and not sticking together; suitable for peas, sweetcorn and berries.

Cryogenic freezing: food is exposed to liquid nitrogen or carbon dioxide at extremely low temperature, which freezes it almost instantly; suitable for delicate or high-value foods such as strawberries, prawns and fish.
The cold chain keeps frozen food at −18 °C or colder in cold stores, refrigerated lorries and supermarket freezer cabinets until it reaches the home.
When buying frozen food, check that the pack is intact with no ice crystals or frost inside, that it is below the load line on the cabinet, and take it home quickly in a cool bag.
Freezing helps a household plan meals, save money and cut waste. These benefits are the points examiners expect when they ask about frozen foods in meal planning.
Freezing surplus food before it spoils reduces household waste, and leftovers can be frozen for reuse as ready-made portions.
Bulk cooking and freezing portions saves time and fuel, since a large batch is cooked once.
A freezer stock of meals and ingredients provides emergency food and convenience on busy days, including for households with different eating times.
Buying in bulk or when produce is in season is more economical, and freezing keeps it for a longer period (a longer shelf life).
Frozen foods provide a wide variety of vegetables, fish and fruit all year, including items not available fresh locally.

Freezing retains colour, texture, flavour and nutritive value well compared with heat processing; frozen vegetables keep more vitamin C than canned ones, as one past-paper table shows for peas (25 mg fresh, 17 mg frozen, 8 mg canned).
Fruit and salad foods go soft after thawing because of cell damage, so they suit cooking better than eating raw.
Labelling each pack with contents, date and portion size lets older items be used first, which helps planned menus.

Food spoils because micro-organisms (bacteria, yeasts and moulds) and enzymes (natural proteins in the food that break it down) keep working. Heat processing stops both, and a clean airtight container then keeps new micro-organisms out.

Heat destroys vegetative bacteria (bacteria in their active, growing form), yeasts and moulds, and denatures (permanently changes the shape of) the enzymes that cause spoilage, so the food stops breaking down.
Sealing the food in a clean airtight container while it is hot, or sealing before heating, prevents re-contamination, because otherwise new micro-organisms would simply re-enter after the heating.

Spores (tough resting forms) of some bacteria, such as Clostridium botulinum, are very heat-resistant and survive boiling at normal pressure, so low-acid foods need higher temperatures held for longer, in a pressure cooker or retort (a large industrial pressure cooker).

Acid foods such as fruit, tomatoes and pickles are easier to preserve by heat because acid hinders micro-organisms and their spores. Low-acid foods such as peas, beans, meat and fish need a higher temperature.
Heat also changes the colour, texture, flavour and nutritive value of food, which is why heat-processed fruit and vegetables differ from fresh produce.
Heat-sensitive, water-soluble vitamins (vitamin C and the B group) are reduced by heat processing.

Heat treatments differ in how much they kill. A mild treatment leaves some organisms alive so the food must be chilled, while a severe one kills everything so the sealed food keeps at room temperature.

Pasteurisation is a moderate heat treatment that destroys most food poisoning (pathogenic) bacteria and reduces spoilage organisms, but not all spores, so pasteurised products keep for a limited time and still need refrigeration.
Milk is pasteurised at 72 °C for 15 seconds, then cooled rapidly. Pasteurisation is also used for cream, fruit juice, beer and some canned foods.

Sterilisation uses a higher temperature for longer, for example milk sterilised in the bottle and canned foods. It destroys all micro-organisms including spores, so the sealed product can be stored at room temperature.
The price of sterilisation is that flavour and colour change and vitamin losses are greater than with pasteurisation.
UHT (ultra-heat treatment) heats milk to about 135 °C for a few seconds, and the milk is then packed aseptically (in a germ-free way) into sterile cartons.
UHT milk keeps for months unopened at room temperature, must be refrigerated after opening, and has a slight cooked flavour.
Three processing methods make milk safe: pasteurisation, sterilisation or UHT, and evaporation or dehydration (drying).
Canning seals food in a container and heats it hard enough to sterilise it, so it keeps for a long time without a fridge. Commercial canning in tin cans is different from home bottling in glass jars.
Commercial canning has stages: food is prepared (washed, peeled, trimmed, blanched where needed), packed into cans, covered with brine, syrup or oil, and air is removed (exhausting).
Then the can is sealed with a double seam, heated in a retort at a high temperature for a set time, and cooled quickly. The heat sterilises the contents and the sealed can prevents re-contamination.
Cans are lined with a lacquer, a protective coating, to prevent the metal reacting with the food.
Canned food is shelf-stable, so it keeps at room temperature for a long time without refrigeration, and it can be eaten straight away.
Foods suited to canning include fruit, tomatoes, vegetables such as peas and beans, fish (tuna, sardines, salmon), meat, soup and baked beans.

Low-acid vegetables such as peas, beans and carrots must be processed in a pressure canner (a sealed pot that heats above 100 °C), because boiling water at normal pressure, which is 100 °C, does not destroy Clostridium botulinum spores.

A bulging can end or lid indicates gas produced by micro-organisms. Hissing, leaking, rust, deep dents or an off smell are also warning signs, so the contents must be discarded unopened and never tasted.
The very high temperature and long processing time that make canned food safe also change it. Examiners ask what is lost and what is gained.
Vitamin C is heat-sensitive and water-soluble, so it is lost during high-temperature canning, especially into the canning liquid.
Thiamine (vitamin B1) is unstable at high temperature and is reduced by canning.
Canned vegetables are softer, paler and less bright in colour than fresh or frozen produce, and the flavour changes too.
Canned vegetables gain sodium from added salt (brine), so no-added-salt versions are preferred on a low-salt diet.
Fruit canned in heavy syrup gains sugar, and food packed in oil gains fat, which raises the energy content.
Heat destroys micro-organisms and enzymes in the can, which is the purpose of canning. Minerals and fibre are largely kept, and the liquid can be used in cooking to keep the nutrients it holds.

One past-paper table showed vitamin C in peas falling from 25 mg per 100 g fresh to 8 mg canned, and sodium rising from 1 mg to 230 mg. The reasons were the very high temperature and long time, and the salt used in canning.
Bottling is the home version of heat preservation. Fruit is heated in glass jars so that the contents are sterilised and sealed.

Bottling packs fruit (and tomatoes) into clean sterilised glass jars with sugar syrup or water, seals them, and heats them in a water bath (or oven) until the contents reach a temperature that destroys organisms and enzymes.
The seal closes as the jar cools and a vacuum forms, which holds the lid down and keeps new micro-organisms out.
Jars must be filled hot, leaving headspace, and sealed at once; the contents cool and form a vacuum that holds the lid down.
Jars must be sterilised and undamaged with new or sound lids, and filled leaving headspace (a gap at the top). Hot jars must be lifted carefully.
Label bottled food with the date and store it in a cool, dark, dry place. Discard any jar whose lid is not tight or domed.

Low-acid vegetables and meat should not be bottled in a boiling-water bath at home, because boiling at normal pressure does not destroy Clostridium botulinum spores. They need pressure processing, so home bottling is restricted to fruit and acid foods.
Fruit is routinely bottled in a water bath because acid foods are easier to preserve by heat.
Jam is fruit boiled with sugar until it sets. It keeps because of heat, a high concentration of sugar and a sealed jar, and it sets because pectin, acid and sugar combine.
Heat: boiling at about 100 °C or higher destroys micro-organisms and inactivates enzymes in the fruit. The fruit is first simmered gently to soften its tissues and release pectin.
Sugar preserves by osmosis: at high concentration it draws water out of microbial cells, so they cannot multiply. Sugar also helps the gel to form and gives sweetness.

Pectin is a natural gelling substance, a carbohydrate found in the cell walls of fruit, mostly in the skin and core. It forms a gel with sugar and acid as the jam cools, so the jam sets. Pectin is not a preservative.

Apples, blackcurrants, redcurrants, gooseberries and lemons or other citrus fruit are high in pectin. Strawberries, raspberries, cherries and pears are low, so add pectin-rich fruit or a commercial pectin.

Acid, from lemon juice or the fruit itself, releases pectin from the cell walls and helps the pectin set. It also improves colour and flavour, and lemon juice is added for low-acid or low-pectin fruit.
Choose just ripe, firm, sound fruit. Under-ripe fruit contains more pectin, whereas over-ripe fruit has less pectin and spoils the set.
Sealing: pour the jam hot into clean sterilised jars and cover at once so micro-organisms cannot re-enter. A vacuum forms as the jam cools, and a waxed disc plus cover is the traditional method.
Jam loses some heat-sensitive vitamin C in boiling, its sugar concentration is high, and its flavour and colour change, so it no longer tastes fresh.
A jam method runs in a set order, and each stage protects either the set or the keeping quality. Jam spoils when one of these protections fails.
1. Wash and sterilise the jars, and prepare the fruit. 2. Simmer the fruit in a heavy pan to soften it and release pectin.
3. Add the sugar in the correct proportion, with lemon juice if needed, and dissolve it fully before the mixture is boiled rapidly to setting point.
Setting point is confirmed by the wrinkle test: a spoonful of jam dropped onto a cold saucer wrinkles when pushed with a finger. A sugar thermometer reads about 105 °C (220 °F) at setting point.
4. Skim the scum from the surface with a clean dry spoon. 5. Pot the jam into hot sterilised jars, seal at once, label and store in a cool, dry place.
Jam ferments or grows mould if too little sugar is used, setting point is not reached, jars or lids are not sterilised, the seal fails, or a dirty or wet spoon introduces yeasts and moulds.
Storage in a warm or damp place also spoils jam. Mould on the surface or fermentation (bubbles and an alcoholic smell) is the result.
Dehydration (drying) removes most of the water from food. Micro-organisms and enzymes both need water to work, so taking it away keeps the food from spoiling.
Micro-organisms need available water to grow. With most of the water removed, they cannot multiply, and enzymes (the natural chemicals in food that cause ripening and decay) cannot act either.
Drying to a low moisture level stops micro-organisms growing but does not kill all of them. They are only inactivated, so they can grow again if the food takes in moisture.
Fresh fruit and vegetables contain roughly 70 to 95 per cent water, so they lose most of their weight when dried and become much lighter and smaller.
Dried food is light and compact, which reduces its storage space and the cost of transporting it.
Damp dried food can re-absorb moisture from the air and go mouldy, so it must be stored dry and airtight.

Blanching vegetables (dipping them briefly in boiling water) before drying inactivates enzymes that would otherwise cause darkening and off-flavours during storage. Fruit is treated differently: it is dipped in lemon juice or an ascorbic acid solution, or sulphured, to stop browning.
Home drying uses gentle heat and moving air to carry moisture away from thin pieces of food. The methods differ in how much control you have over temperature and drying time.

Preparation: choose ripe, sound, undamaged produce and wash it thoroughly. Cut it into even, thin pieces so that they all dry at the same rate, blanch vegetables, and arrange the pieces in a single layer.
Oven drying: food is spread in a single layer on trays and dried at a very low temperature, with the oven door slightly open so moisture can escape. It takes several hours.
Electric dehydrator: a fan circulates warm air at a controlled low temperature over trays, so food dries evenly and reliably.

Sun drying: food is laid on trays or racks in strong, dry heat. It is slow and depends on the weather, and exposes food to dust, insects and moisture, so it suits hot, dry countries rather than the damp Irish climate.
Sun drying is common for fruit in hot countries, such as raisins, apricots and sun-dried tomatoes.
Air drying: herbs are tied in small bunches and hung in a warm, dry, airy place away from direct sunlight, which would fade them. Beans and pulses can also be left to dry on the plant.
Food that looks dry may still hold pockets of moisture, and moisture is what lets mould return. So dried food is tested, conditioned and then packed carefully.
Test dryness: dried fruit should be leathery and pliable, with no moist centre or sticky patches, which would let micro-organisms grow.
Dried vegetables should be brittle and snap cleanly when bent.
Condition dried food by packing it loosely in a jar for several days and shaking the jar daily. Condensation on the inside of the jar means the food needs more drying.
Store dried food in airtight, moisture-proof containers in a cool, dark, dry place, since light and moisture reduce its quality and damp lets mould grow.
Many foods dry well, especially those that are mostly water and have a flavour that survives the process.
Fruit such as apples, apricots, pears, bananas and grapes (which become raisins).
Vegetables such as onions, carrots, tomatoes, peas and beans.
Herbs such as mint, parsley, thyme and rosemary, which keep their flavour well when dried.
Pulses and cereals, which are naturally dry foods that keep well.
Meat and fish, which are salted before drying or smoked and dried, as in stockfish (dried fish) and jerky (dried strips of meat).

Factories dry food on a large scale, often by turning liquid foods into powders or flakes. The most advanced method, accelerated freeze drying, gives the best quality but costs the most. Freeze-dried foods keep their shape, colour and flavour better than air-dried foods.

Spray drying: liquid food such as milk, coffee, eggs or soup is sprayed as a fine mist into a stream of hot air. The water evaporates in seconds and the powder falls. It is used for milk powder, instant coffee and infant formula.
Drum (roller) drying: a thin layer of liquid or purée is spread on a heated rotating drum, dries, and is scraped off as flakes. It is used for potato flakes (instant mashed potato) and baby cereals.
Tunnel or cabinet drying: trays or a conveyor belt of food pass through a tunnel of hot air. It is used for fruit and vegetables.

Accelerated freeze drying (AFD): 1. The food is frozen quickly. 2. It is placed in a vacuum chamber and gently heated. 3. The ice turns directly into water vapour without melting, a change called sublimation, and the vapour is drawn off.
4. This leaves a dry, porous food that keeps its shape.
AFD food is packed airtight, often with nitrogen, and is used for coffee, fruit pieces, vegetables in instant soups, camping and ready meals, and herbs.

AFD is valued because the food keeps its colour, flavour, shape and nutrients well (little heat is used, and no liquid water moves to the surface). It rehydrates quickly and fully, is very light, and has a long shelf life.
AFD is limited because the equipment and energy are expensive, so the food costs more.
Diagram: draw AFD in three labelled stages: frozen food; vacuum chamber with ice changing to vapour (sublimation); condenser and dry product.
Drying keeps food safe for a long time, but heat and the loss of water change its nutrients, appearance and texture. These effects are examined, usually with fruit and vegetables.
Water-soluble vitamins, especially vitamin C and the B vitamins, are lost during drying.
Vitamins A and E are reduced, because they are sensitive to heat and oxidation.
Colour darkens or fades, especially in fruit left in the sun, because of oxidation and browning reactions. Vegetables are blanched, and fruit is dipped in lemon juice, to reduce this.
Dried fruit is concentrated in sugar, so a small portion gives much more sugar and energy than the same weight of fresh fruit. Sticky dried fruit can also cause dental decay.
Texture becomes leathery, chewy or brittle, and the flavour becomes more concentrated. Dried food also shrinks and wrinkles.
Minerals and fibre are not destroyed by drying, and protein and carbohydrate are also kept.
Most dried foods must be soaked or cooked in water (rehydrated) before use. Spray-dried and freeze-dried foods rehydrate easily, and the soaking water contains vitamins and can be used.
Advantages: long shelf life without refrigeration, light and compact, no freezer needed, cheap to transport and store, and concentrated flavour.
Disadvantages: vitamin loss, changed colour and texture, slow, needs correct storage, some foods do not rehydrate well, and high sugar in dried fruit.

Micro-organisms (bacteria, yeasts and moulds) need available water, a suitable acidity and working enzymes to grow. Chemical preservatives attack one or more of these, which is why preserved food keeps for much longer.

Some preservatives draw water out of food and micro-organisms by osmosis (water moving out through a cell wall towards a stronger solution), so the organisms cannot multiply. Sugar and salt work this way.
Some lower the pH (make the food more acidic) so that most spoilage and food poisoning bacteria cannot grow. Vinegar and other acids work this way.

Some directly poison or inhibit micro-organisms or their enzymes, such as sulphur dioxide, benzoates, sorbates, nitrite and the chemicals in smoke. Others act as antioxidants (stopping oxygen damaging the food) or inhibit mould.

Sugar, salt, vinegar, smoke and alcohol are the traditional (natural) preservatives. Sugar, salt and vinegar are the traditional home preservatives, and smoke was the traditional preservative for fish and meat.
The permitted additive preservatives are sorbic acid, benzoic acid, sulphur dioxide and sulphites, and nitrites and nitrates.
Many chemical methods are combined with heat, as in jam and chutney, or with drying, as in smoked and salted fish. Using two methods together makes the food safer than either alone.
Fruit can also be preserved in alcohol, for example fruit kept in brandy or rum.
A strong sugar solution holds on to water so tightly that micro-organisms cannot use it. This is why jam keeps in a sealed jar.
At high concentration, sugar binds water and draws it out of microbial cells by osmosis, so the micro-organisms cannot multiply.
Sugar is the preservative in jam, marmalade, syrups, crystallised and candied fruit and condensed milk.
The concentration must be high enough. Low-sugar jam can ferment or grow mould, so a strong sugar solution is essential.
Yeasts and moulds tolerate sugar better than most bacteria, so sugared products still need sealed, clean containers to keep them out.
Sugar also has other roles in jam: it forms a gel with pectin (the setting substance in fruit), and it adds sweetness and colour.

The Department of Health healthy eating guidelines advise limiting foods and drinks high in added sugar, since excess sugar is linked to tooth decay and excess energy intake. Preserves contain a lot of added sugar.
Salt works like sugar, pulling water out of food and out of any micro-organisms on it. It has been used on fish and meat, but it has a health cost.
Salt draws water out of food and micro-organisms by osmosis, and it makes the remaining water unavailable to organisms and to enzyme action.
Dry salting: the food is packed in salt, which draws out moisture. This method is used for salt cod, salt pork, bacon and salted herring.
Brining: the food is immersed or soaked in a strong salt solution, as used for olives, ham, pickled meat and brine pickles of vegetables such as cucumbers.

Curing combines salt with sodium nitrite or nitrate, and sometimes sugar, to preserve meat such as bacon, ham and corned beef. The nitrite inhibits Clostridium botulinum (a dangerous food poisoning bacterium) and keeps the meat pink.
Salt-cured foods must be stored in cool, dry conditions, since moisture in the air can cause surface mould.
Salted foods need soaking or rinsing to remove the salt before they are used.
Excess salt (sodium) raises blood pressure, and salted and cured foods are high in sodium. The Department of Health healthy eating guidelines advise reducing salt in the diet.
Vinegar does not dry food out. It preserves by making the food too acidic for most bacteria to survive, and it adds flavour at the same time.
Vinegar is a dilute solution of acetic acid, which lowers the pH of food and inhibits most spoilage and food poisoning bacteria.

Vinegar pickling: vegetables such as onions, cucumbers, beetroot and red cabbage, and also eggs, are packed in spiced vinegar, which acts as the preservative. It is also used in chutneys, relishes and sauces, sometimes with sugar and spices.
Vinegar also gives sharpness and flavour, and its effectiveness depends on its acetic acid strength. It must be strong enough that the water in the food does not dilute it.
Spiced vinegar, made cold or hot, is poured over vegetables packed into sterilised jars. Malt vinegar is the usual home choice.
Use non-metallic lids on jars of vinegar foods, because the acid corrodes metal and spoils the seal.
Chutney and pickle both rely on vinegar, but they are different products. Chutney is cooked down to a thick mixture, while pickle keeps its pieces whole in a liquid.

Chutney is made by chopping fruit and/or vegetables (apples, tomatoes, onions, marrow, plums) and cooking them slowly with vinegar, sugar and spices until the mixture is thick. It needs no pectin, unlike jam.

Each ingredient has a job. The cooking destroys micro-organisms and enzymes, the vinegar (an acid) and sugar prevent any survivors from growing, and spices such as mustard seed, chilli and ginger add flavour.

Chutney method: 1. Sterilise the jars. 2. Prepare and chop the fruit and vegetables. 3. Cook slowly with vinegar, sugar and spices until thick and no liquid vinegar shows when a spoon is drawn across. 4. Pot into hot jars. 5. Seal with vinegar-proof lids and label.
Chutney is poured hot into sterilised jars, sealed and stored in a cool, dark place, where it matures and improves in flavour after weeks. Once opened it is kept in the fridge.
Pickles are raw, lightly cooked or brined vegetables, eggs or fruit packed whole or in pieces in vinegar or brine. Vinegar pickles are covered with spiced vinegar and sugar and sealed.
Chutney spoils if there is too little vinegar or sugar, if it is not cooked long enough, if jars or lids are not sterile or the seal is faulty, or if a metal lid is corroded by the vinegar.
Smoking preserves food by exposing it to smoke from smouldering wood, and it adds flavour and colour as well. It is used mostly on fish and meat, and also on cheese.

Food is exposed to smoke from smouldering wood (such as oak, beech or hickory) or sawdust. The smoke deposits chemicals (phenols, formaldehyde and organic acids) that inhibit micro-organisms and slow oxidation.
Smoke also dries the surface of the food, which slows micro-organism growth and gives flavour and colour.
Smoking is almost always combined with salting first, by brining or dry salting, because smoking gives limited shelf life on its own. Smoked meat and fish are usually also salted or cured.
Cold smoking is carried out at a low temperature, not exceeding about 27 °C, so the food is flavoured and partly preserved but not cooked and requires further cooking. Smoked salmon is an example.
Hot smoking raises the temperature gradually to about 80 °C, so the food is cooked as it is smoked and is ready to eat, as in smoked mackerel.
Smoking fish, in order: 1. Fillet and trim. 2. Brine or dry-salt. 3. Rinse and dry. 4. Smoke at the chosen temperature. 5. Cool.
Smoked foods have a limited shelf life unless chilled, and they are high in salt. Some smoke compounds (tars) are a health concern if eaten in large amounts.

Besides the traditional preservatives, food manufacturers may add certain chemical preservatives. They are tightly controlled, and each one works best against particular organisms in particular foods.

They are controlled in the EU by Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 on food additives: only listed substances may be used, in listed foods, up to maximum levels. They are given E numbers (E200 to E299 are the preservatives) and are tested for safety by the European Food Safety Authority.
Sorbic acid (E200) and potassium sorbate (E202) inhibit moulds and yeasts in foods such as cheese, baked goods and soft drinks.
Benzoic acid (E210) and sodium benzoate (E211) inhibit yeasts, moulds and bacteria in acidic foods such as soft drinks, pickles and fruit products.
Sulphur dioxide (E220) and sulphites inhibit micro-organisms and prevent browning in products such as dried fruit, wine and fruit juice.
Sodium nitrite (E250) and sodium nitrate (E251) are used in cured meat. Nitrite inhibits Clostridium botulinum and gives cured meat its pink colour.

Under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 on food information to consumers, a preservative in the ingredients list is given with its function ("preservative") followed by its name or E number. Sulphur dioxide and sulphites above the stated level are among the 14 allergens that must be emphasised.

Benefits are longer shelf life, safety, less waste and lower cost. Concerns are that some people react to preservatives (asthmatics may react to sulphites), consumer preference for fewer additives, and high sodium in salt-based preservation.
An E number shows only that an additive is approved, not that it is natural or unsafe.

Fermentation is the controlled breakdown of carbohydrates, mainly sugars, by micro-organisms (tiny living things such as yeasts and bacteria). It produces new substances called by-products, and these give fermented foods their taste, texture and keeping quality.
The micro-organisms used are yeasts, bacteria and moulds, each carrying out a different type of fermentation. Yeast is a fungus, not a bacterium.
Fermentation is usually carried out without oxygen and releases a small amount of energy, which escapes as heat.
Alcoholic fermentation: the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae converts glucose into ethanol (the alcohol in drinks) and carbon dioxide in the absence of oxygen, so this type needs no air.
Chemical equation for alcoholic fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, with energy released. In words: glucose gives ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Lactic acid fermentation: lactic acid bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Streptococcus convert lactose (the sugar in milk) or other sugars, such as those in cabbage, into lactic acid without oxygen.
Acetic acid fermentation: acetic acid bacteria such as Acetobacter oxidise ethanol into acetic acid, the acid in vinegar. Unlike the other two types, this stage needs a supply of oxygen.
Micro-organisms ferment only when their needs are met. Providing or withholding these conditions is how food producers decide whether fermentation happens.

A fermentable sugar (the substrate, the material the organism feeds on) is needed. The sugar is the starting point: yeast does not make alcohol from starch directly, so bread dough gets its sugar from flour and barley is malted first.
Moisture and warmth are needed, because the organisms grow in liquid or moist food and work fastest at their own optimum (best) temperature. Too much heat kills yeast.
Time is needed, and a starter culture (a known culture of the right micro-organism added to the food) is often used.
Alcoholic and lactic fermentations need the absence of oxygen, while the acetic acid stage needs oxygen.
Fermentation is useful because of what it leaves behind. Each by-product has a job in the finished food, so always link the by-product to what it does.
Carbon dioxide is a gas that makes bread dough rise and gives sparkling quality to drinks such as beer and sparkling wine when it is retained in a sealed container.
Ethanol is the alcohol in beer, wine and spirits, and at high concentration it inhibits spoilage micro-organisms. It evaporates during baking, so little remains in bread.
Lactic acid gives a sour taste to yoghurt, sauerkraut, cheese and cultured sour cream, and lowers the pH of the food (makes it more acidic), which helps preserve it.
Acetic acid gives vinegar its sharp taste and also lowers the pH, inhibiting spoilage micro-organisms.
Energy is released as heat during fermentation.
Flavour compounds formed during fermentation give cheese, yoghurt, bread and fermented drinks their distinctive flavours.
Yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, is the micro-organism behind bread, beer and wine. In each, it ferments sugar, but the by-product that matters most is different.
Bread: yeast ferments the sugars present in flour and dough, and the carbon dioxide is trapped in the gluten network (the stretchy protein structure of dough), raising the dough.
Bread: baking kills the yeast, and the ethanol produced evaporates during baking, so little alcohol remains in the loaf.
Beer: yeast ferments sugars (maltose) released from malted barley, and hops are added for flavour. The carbon dioxide produced is kept in the sealed container to carbonate the beer.
Wine: yeast ferments the sugars in grape juice, and fermentation stops when the sugar is used up or the alcohol level becomes toxic to the yeast.
Yeast needs a supply of sugar, nutrients and a suitable temperature to grow and ferment.
Milk is fermented by bacteria and, in some cheeses, by moulds. Here only the fermentation step matters: lactic acid made from lactose changes the milk.

Yoghurt: the starter cultures Lactobacillus bulgaricus (now named Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus, though exams use the older name) and Streptococcus thermophilus convert lactose into lactic acid.
Yoghurt: the lactic acid lowers the pH of the milk, so the milk protein casein coagulates (sets solid) and gives the thick, sour product.
Soya yoghurt is fermented soya milk.
Cheese: starter bacteria produce lactic acid, and rennet, an enzyme, coagulates the milk into curds (solid) and whey (liquid).
Cheese ripening: enzymes and micro-organisms such as bacteria and moulds break down proteins and fats, developing the flavour and texture of the cheese.
Mould-ripened cheese: Penicillium camemberti forms the white rind of Camembert-type cheese, and Penicillium roqueforti forms the blue veins of blue cheese.
Fermentation also produces vinegar, pickled-style vegetables and a meat substitute. Each uses a different organism, so match the organism to the food.
Vinegar is made in two stages: yeast ferments fruit or grain sugars into ethanol, then acetic acid bacteria with air oxidise the ethanol to acetic acid.
The acetic acid stage needs oxygen, so the liquid is left exposed to air.

Sauerkraut (and kimchi): shredded cabbage is salted, so the salt draws out juice and favours the lactic acid bacteria already on the cabbage. They ferment its sugars while many spoilage organisms are inhibited.
Mycoprotein (Quorn): the fungus Fusarium venenatum is grown by fermentation on a sugar-based medium in large vats (fermenters), then harvested and processed into a meat substitute.
Several vegetarian protein foods are made by fermenting soya. Examiners have asked for these by name as fermented products.
Tempeh is cooked soya beans that have been fermented.
Miso is a paste of soya beans with rice, salt and water, which is fermented.
Soya yoghurt is soya milk fermented in the same way as dairy yoghurt.
Fermentation changes food so that spoilage micro-organisms cannot grow in it. The fermented food stays edible longer than the raw ingredient did.
Fermentation preserves food by producing acids, ethanol and carbon dioxide that lower the pH or inhibit spoilage micro-organisms, together with a controlled population of harmless organisms.
Examples are milk turned into yoghurt and cheese, cabbage into sauerkraut, grape juice into wine and wine into vinegar.
Salt used in sauerkraut and other brined foods draws water out of micro-organisms by osmosis.
Fermented foods are not sterile; the controlled micro-organisms outcompete the spoilage organisms that would otherwise grow, and some fermented foods need chilling.
The same organisms can spoil food: a yeast fermenting jam or fruit juice, or a mould spoiling cheese. In food production fermentation is controlled and wanted.
Fermentation has to be steered so that it makes the intended food rather than a spoiled one. Producers control what the organism feeds on, what organism is present and the conditions it grows in.
Substrate: the food must contain fermentable sugar; barley is malted first to release maltose, which yeast can ferment.
Starter culture: a pure culture of known strains is added in a known amount to ensure the intended product forms.
Temperature: each micro-organism has an optimum temperature, and temperatures that are too high kill yeast.
Hygiene: equipment is cleaned and sterilised so that unwanted micro-organisms do not compete with the starter culture, and unwanted organisms are kept out.
Timing: fermentation is stopped when the required acidity, alcohol level or flavour is reached, for example by chilling, pasteurising or removing the yeast.

Irradiation is a physical preservation treatment that exposes food to ionising radiation (high-energy rays that damage living cells). It destroys micro-organisms and pests without heating the food noticeably.
The food is passed, usually on a conveyor, past a radiation source in a shielded chamber for a set time, so that it receives a controlled, measured dose of radiation.
The permitted sources are gamma rays from cobalt-60 or caesium-137, X-rays, or electron beams (streams of high-energy accelerated electrons).
The dose is the energy the food absorbs, not the number of rays. It is measured in grays (Gy), where one gray is one joule of energy absorbed per kilogram of food.
It is a cold process because the food is not noticeably heated, so it is sometimes called cold pasteurisation.
Because there is no heat, it can be applied to food already sealed in its packaging, which prevents re-contamination afterwards.
Irradiated food does not become radioactive at the doses and sources used for food, because the rays pass through it and the food is not in contact with radioactive material.
Ionising radiation damages the parts of a living cell that control growth and survival. How much damage is done depends on the dose, which is why one process can give different effects.
Ionising radiation damages the DNA and cell structures of micro-organisms, insects and parasites, so they cannot reproduce or they die.
It destroys food-poisoning bacteria such as Salmonella, and parasites in food.
It controls moulds on soft fruit, extending their shelf life.
It kills insects and their eggs in grain, spices and other dried foods.
It also inactivates some enzymes, such as ripening enzymes, and stops sprouting by damaging growth tissue.
A low dose delays ripening and sprouting and kills insects. A medium dose destroys most food-poisoning and spoilage organisms and parasites, the pasteurising effect. A high dose sterilises the food.
Bacterial spores (tough resting forms of bacteria) and some viruses are highly resistant, so they need very high doses.
By stopping the causes of spoilage, ripening and sprouting, irradiation lets food be stored for longer. These are effects of the process itself, whichever foods the law allows it to be used on.
It extends the shelf life of fresh and frozen meat, poultry, fish and fruit, because fewer spoilage organisms survive.
It can prevent sprouting in potatoes and onions, so they can be stored for longer.
It delays the ripening of fruit, extending its storage life.
It can be applied after food is sealed in its packaging, which prevents re-contamination.
It reduces the need for chemical preservatives, because the radiation does the preserving.
Because there is no heat, irradiation leaves the look and taste of food largely unchanged. It is not harmless to the food, though, and it has some costs to nutrients and fats.
Colour, flavour and texture change very little at normal doses, because no heat is applied.
Vitamin C and the B group vitamins, such as thiamine, can be partly destroyed.
Free radicals and other reactive molecules (unstable, highly reactive particles) can form in the food during irradiation.
Fatty foods can develop rancidity, a stale or off-flavour, through the oxidation of their fats, so irradiation is unsuitable for high-fat foods.
Evaluation questions want points on both sides, each with a reason. Irradiation is useful for some foods but is not a replacement for good hygiene.
Advantage: no heat is applied, so heat-sensitive foods such as herbs and spices keep more of their quality than they would after canning.
Advantage: it destroys enzymes that cause ripening and spoilage, as well as micro-organisms, and it destroys food-poisoning bacteria and parasites.
Advantage: it leaves no chemical residues in the food, and it reduces the need for chemical preservatives.
Advantage: it can treat food that is already packed, so the food cannot be re-contaminated.
Disadvantage: many consumers reject irradiated food, which limits its commercial use. It may also be used to disguise poor manufacturing or poor hygiene.
Disadvantage: specialised plant and radiation sources are expensive and need strict safety controls and licensing of the facility.
Disadvantage: some micro-organisms (spores and viruses) need very high doses, so the treatment is not effective against all of them and is not a substitute for good hygiene.
Disadvantage: vitamins can be lost and fats can go rancid, so it is not suitable for high-fat foods.
Because many consumers are wary of irradiation, EU law controls which foods may be irradiated and requires them to be labelled. This lets shoppers choose.

In the EU, irradiation is controlled by a framework Directive 1999/2/EC (rules, labelling, authorisation and imports) and an implementing Directive 1999/3/EC that lists the foods that may be irradiated.
At present the only category on the EU list is dried aromatic herbs, spices and vegetable seasonings, with a maximum dose of 10 kilograys (kGy), according to the FSAI.
