Irradiated food, or food containing irradiated ingredients, must be labelled with the words "irradiated" or "treated with ionising radiation" under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011. Consumers can therefore see on the label if a herb or spice product, or an ingredient, was treated.
The Radura, a stylised plant in a circle, is the international symbol for irradiated food. In the EU it may accompany the words but does not replace them.
The FSAI checks food on the Irish market for undeclared irradiation, through official agencies under service contract.
The FSAI reports that no facility in Ireland has been approved for irradiating food, so any irradiated ingredient on sale here would have been treated elsewhere.

A comparative evaluation tests whether one preserved food is better than another. The test must be fair and the criteria must be set in advance, so that the final judgement rests on evidence and not on opinion.
Choose one food that can be preserved by two methods, such as strawberries frozen and strawberries made into jam. Using the same food means the method is the only thing that changes.
Use sound, ripe fruit from the same batch for both methods, prepared equally, so differences come from the preservation method rather than the raw material.

Compare the same criteria for each method: nutritional value, sensory qualities (colour, flavour, texture and appearance), safety and risk of spoilage, storage life and conditions, time, skill, cost and energy, equipment, packaging, convenience and use in meals, and environmental impact.
For the sensory criteria, several tasters rate or rank the two samples on appearance, aroma, flavour and texture, in identical conditions, so the result is not one person's preference.
State the underlying principle of each method (how it stops spoilage) and the risk of spoilage that each carries.
Write the evaluation in order: name of the food, the methods and their main steps, the principle of each, the findings against each criterion, the risk of spoilage, and a conclusion.
A summary table with one column per method and one row per criterion is a clear layout, and a good revision device because every method is set against every criterion.

Conclude by judging which method suits the stated purpose, weighing its advantages against its disadvantages. Choose by purpose, such as long storage without a freezer, nutrient retention, use as a spread or in meals, cost or time, and justify the choice.

Preservation tries to keep colour, flavour, texture and nutritive value as close to fresh as possible. Freezing and canning both change nutrient content, but by different amounts, because canning uses much more heat.
Freezing keeps more vitamin C than canning, because canning uses higher temperatures for longer. Vitamin C is water soluble and unstable at high temperature.
Water-soluble vitamins, such as vitamin C and the B group, leach (dissolve out) into blanching water and canning liquid, and are lost when the liquid is drained away.
Frozen vegetables lose some vitamin C too, because they are blanched (briefly scalded in boiling water) before freezing.
Thiamine (vitamin B1) is lower in canned peas, because the B vitamins are heat-sensitive and the high temperatures of canning destroy much of it.
Sodium is much higher in canned peas than in fresh, because salt (brine) is added during canning. Frozen peas are close to fresh.
In one past-paper data table for peas, vitamin C per 100 g was 25 mg when fresh, 17 mg after freezing and 8 mg after canning.
In the same table, sodium per 100 g was 1 mg when fresh, 3 mg after freezing and 230 mg after canning, because salt is added during canning.
Protein, carbohydrate, vitamin A and minerals show only small changes. Energy values may differ because of water content, not because of the method.
Canning may also add sugar (in syrup), salt (in brine) or fat (in oil), and dehydration may lose B vitamins, vitamin A and vitamin E and gives a product with concentrated sugar.

Strawberries are a good test food because freezing and jam making treat them so differently: one keeps the fruit cold and unchanged, the other cooks it with sugar. The two products look, taste and feel very different.

Freezing: the fruit is washed quickly, hulled, dried and open frozen in one layer, then packed in portions in moisture- and vapour-proof bags with the air removed, sealed, labelled and dated. It is fast frozen at about −25 °C and stored at −18 °C.
The principle of freezing is that low temperature inactivates micro-organisms and slows enzymes, and the water is turned to ice so it is unavailable to micro-organisms.
Frozen strawberries keep their colour and flavour closer to those of fresh fruit.
Thawed frozen strawberries are softer and release juice, because ice crystals have damaged the cell walls.
Jam making: the fruit is simmered, sugar is added, it is boiled to setting point, potted hot and sealed.
The principle of jam is that heat destroys organisms and enzymes, sugar draws water out of organisms by osmosis, pectin and acid set the jam, and sealing stops micro-organisms getting back in.
Jam is sweeter, darker from cooking, with a cooked flavour, and firmer and spreadable in texture.
Jam loses some heat-sensitive vitamin C during boiling, whereas frozen fruit retains more. Jam's high sugar content makes it unsuitable for people restricting their sugar intake.
Neither method makes food completely safe for ever. Each is a barrier to spoilage, and each fails in its own way if it is not done properly.
Frozen fruit is not sterile: freezing only stops micro-organisms growing. If the temperature fluctuates, partial thawing releases moisture, and surviving micro-organisms can grow.
Freezer burn occurs when air reaches the food through loose or damaged packs, causing drying, toughening and discolouration by oxidation (reaction with oxygen).
Thawed fruit should be used promptly and never refrozen, because micro-organisms can multiply once it has thawed.
Jam spoils by fermentation or mould growth when the sugar is too low, setting point is not reached, jars are not clean, or the seal fails.
A bulging lid, gas, mould or an off-odour in a jar means the jam must be discarded.

The practical side often decides which method to use. Equipment, running costs, storage space and packaging all differ between freezing and jam making, and each matters when you make the final judgement.
Freezing needs a continuous electricity supply and freezer space; jam needs no freezer but needs fuel for cooking, jars and time.
Sealed jam keeps well without a freezer and has a long shelf life when stored in a cool, dark place, unopened in a cupboard.
Frozen fruit is versatile, for example in desserts and smoothies, whereas jam suits spreading and baking.
Low-acid vegetables such as peas must be pressure canned, because boiling water does not destroy the spores of Clostridium botulinum (a bacterium whose spores survive boiling).
Glass jars can be washed and reused or recycled, whereas most plastic freezer bags are single-use plastic.
A freezer uses electricity continuously. Reduced food waste is an advantage of every preservation method.
The same approach of setting methods against criteria works for any pair of preserved foods. These short evaluations show the main advantages and disadvantages to weigh.

Freezing against canning (vegetables): frozen food retains more vitamin C, colour and texture. Canned food is ready to eat, needs no freezer and keeps for a long period at room temperature, but loses vitamins and may add salt or sugar.

Freezing against drying: freezing keeps nutrients, colour and texture but needs a freezer and continuous energy. Drying keeps for a long time without refrigeration and is light and compact, but loses vitamins and changes texture and colour, and dried fruit is high in sugar per portion.

Irradiation against heat treatment: irradiation changes colour, flavour and texture little and leaves no residue, but may cause vitamin loss and rancidity and is limited by law and public acceptance. Canning uses heat that changes the food.
Chemical preservation (jam, chutney, pickles, salting) against freezing: sugar, salt and vinegar change the food and add sugar or sodium, whereas freezing does not change the food's content.
Home freezing keeps food by cold, and it works best on fresh, good-quality food frozen soon after it is harvested or bought. Freezing does not improve food, so poor food comes out poor.
Vegetables that freeze well include carrots, peas, beans and broccoli, and fruit that freezes well includes apples and strawberries.
Meat and fish, baked foods, soups, sauces and complete meals can all be frozen at home, so a cook can store prepared dishes as well as raw ingredients.
Bananas and lettuce do not freeze well and are not suitable for home freezing, because they turn soft and limp when thawed.
Melons and pears also freeze poorly.

The principle is low temperature: freezing stops enzyme action and microbial growth (the enzymes and micro-organisms are inactivated), and the water in the food turns to ice, which micro-organisms cannot use.
Quick freezing makes small ice crystals that protect the texture of the food, whereas slow freezing makes the food softer.

Vegetables contain enzymes that keep working in the freezer and spoil colour, flavour and texture. Blanching (a short scald in boiling water) inactivates these enzymes, so it is a key step for vegetables.
1. Choose fresh, young vegetables, then wash them and prepare them by trimming, peeling and cutting them into even pieces so they blanch evenly.
2. Blanch by plunging the pieces into boiling water for the recommended time for that vegetable.
3. Cool quickly by transferring the pieces to ice-cold water for the same time as the blanching, which stops the cooking at once.
4. Drain thoroughly and dry the pieces on absorbent paper or a clean tea towel, so that surface water does not form ice.
Fruit such as strawberries is frozen without blanching. The aim is to keep the pieces separate and whole.
Select sound, ripe fruit, wash it quickly, hull it (remove the stalk and green top) and dry it.
Open-freeze the fruit by spreading it in a single layer on a tray, so the pieces do not stick together, then pack it in portions.
Good packing stops the food drying out and picking up flavours in the freezer, and makes it easy to use later.
1. Cool cooked food completely before packing, because warm food raises the temperature of the freezer.
2. Open-freeze fruit such as strawberries by spreading them in a single layer on a tray, so the pieces do not stick together.

3. Pack the food in usable, family-sized portions in strong, moisture- and vapour-proof freezer bags or rigid containers (rigid plastic containers with tight lids, or foil), so that only what is needed is thawed.
4. Leave headspace in rigid containers, because liquids expand on freezing.
5. Remove the air from bags and seal them securely with ties or heat sealing.
6. Label each pack with its contents, quantity and the date.
Food must freeze quickly and then stay cold. Two different temperatures matter: the fast-freeze figure and the storage figure.
Switch the freezer to its fast-freeze setting 3–4 hours before adding food, so the freezer is as cold as possible when the food goes in.
Add no more than one-tenth of the freezer's capacity in any 24-hour period, because a large load of warm food raises the temperature and slows freezing.
Place new packs against the cold surfaces or in the fast-freeze section of the freezer so that they freeze quickly.
Fast freezing takes food down to about −25 °C, so it freezes quickly.
Store the frozen food at −18 °C or colder.
Rotate stock so older packs are used first, thaw food safely in the fridge, cook it thoroughly, and do not refreeze thawed raw food.
Freezing is one of the best methods for keeping the quality of food close to the fresh product.
Colour, flavour, texture and nutrients are well kept when food is frozen quickly.
Some vitamin C and B1 are lost in blanching and in drip when the food thaws.
Slow freezing softens the food, because large ice crystals damage its structure.
Preparing food for the freezer involves sharp tools, boiling water and electrical appliances, so safe habits protect both the cook and the food.
Use knives, graters and food processors carefully, cutting away from the body, using the guard on the grater and keeping fingers clear of the blades, so that cuts are avoided.
Wash hands before preparation, cover any cuts with a dressing, and tie back long hair, so that bacteria and hair do not get into the food.
Use oven gloves when handling the blanching pan, turn pan handles inward, and do not overfill the pan, so that nobody is scalded.
Avoid overloaded sockets, trailing flexes and wet hands near electrical appliances, to prevent electric shock and fire.
Keep raw and cooked foods separate during preparation and clean surfaces between tasks, to prevent cross-contamination.
Jam keeps because several things work together: heat, sugar, pectin and acid, and a tight seal.
Heat at about 100 °C destroys micro-organisms and enzymes in the fruit.
Sugar preserves by osmosis: it draws water out of any micro-organism, so they cannot grow.
Pectin (a natural setting substance in fruit) and acid make the jam set.
Sealing the jar while hot prevents micro-organisms from getting back in.
Jam is made from fruit that is plentiful. Whether it sets depends mainly on how much pectin and acid the fruit contains.
Use ripe or just ripe, sound fruit that is free from mould and bruising, such as strawberries, raspberries, blackcurrants, plums, gooseberries, apples and blackberries.
Pectin is found mainly in the skin and core of fruit; cooking apples, blackcurrants and citrus fruit are high in pectin.
Strawberries are low in pectin, so lemon juice or another acid is added to help the jam set, and if needed pectin or pectin-rich fruit such as apple.
Sugar is added in the proportion given in a tested recipe and stirred until fully dissolved before the mixture is boiled, because undissolved sugar makes the jam crystallise.
The steps must be in order, and each one has a purpose: sterile jars, soft fruit, dissolved sugar and a fast boil to setting point.

1. Wash the jars and lids and sterilise them (in the oven or in boiling water), and keep them hot until filling, so that hot jam does not crack cold glass. Put a saucer in the freezer for the setting test and weigh the fruit and sugar.
2. Wash the fruit, remove stalks and damaged parts, and cut the fruit as the recipe requires.
3. Simmer the fruit gently in a heavy-based pan, with a little water, until it softens and releases its pectin.
4. Add the sugar and stir until it has completely dissolved, adding lemon juice if needed.
5. Bring to a full rolling boil and boil rapidly until setting point is reached; do not stir after setting point is reached.
6. Test for setting point with a cold saucer, pushing a drop of jam with a finger to check whether it wrinkles, or with a sugar thermometer at about 105 °C.
7. Take the pan off the heat and skim off the scum from the surface with a clean, dry spoon, then allow to cool slightly so the fruit does not float.
8. Pour the jam into the hot sterilised jars, leave a small space at the top, and wipe the rim.
Packaging for jam has two jobs: keeping micro-organisms out and keeping the jam in good condition.
Use clean, undamaged glass jars with new lids (waxed disc and cover, or twist-top lids), and wipe the rim of each jar before sealing.
Seal each jar immediately while the jam is hot, so that a vacuum forms as it cools.
Label each jar with the name of the contents and the date.
Store sealed jars in a cool, dry, dark place, and refrigerate any jar once it has been opened.
A jam that goes wrong can be traced back to a step that was missed.
Failure to set is caused by too little pectin, acid or sugar, or by not boiling long enough.
Crystallised jam is caused by too much sugar or sugar that was not dissolved.
Mould or fermentation is caused by too little sugar, unsterile jars or a poor seal.
Fruit floating is caused by potting the jam when too hot.
Scorching is caused by not stirring or by a pan that is too thin.
Boiling jam is very hot and sticky, so most safety guidelines are about preventing burns.
Hot sugar syrup can cause severe scalds, so do not touch it, and handle the pan with oven gloves and pour carefully from a jug or jam funnel.
Turn pan handles inward and do not overfill the pan, as the mixture foams up and boils over when it is at a rolling boil.
Keep children and pets away from the cooker while the jam is boiling.
Remove scum with a clean, dry spoon, because a wet or used spoon can introduce micro-organisms into the jam.
Use sterilised equipment for food safety.
A second method does not have to be jam. Chutney is an alternative, and a student may name other home methods briefly.
Chutney is made from foods such as apples, tomatoes, plums, onions and marrow, and heat destroys organisms while vinegar (acid) and sugar inhibit growth.

Steps: sterilise jars; chop the fruit and vegetables; cook slowly with vinegar, sugar and spices until thick; pot hot; seal with vinegar-proof lids; label; mature in a cool, dark place; refrigerate after opening. Safety is as for jam.
Chutney is boiled with vinegar and sugar and does not need pectin, whereas jam needs pectin.
Other home methods include drying herbs, apples or tomatoes (oven or dehydrator), bottling fruit and pickling vegetables in vinegar.
Moulds are one of the micro-organisms that spoil food. Knowing what kind of living thing a mould is explains how it feeds and why it grows where it does.
Moulds are multicellular, filamentous fungi: their bodies are made of many cells joined in thread-like filaments.
Moulds are not plants because they have no chlorophyll (the green pigment plants use to make their own food), and they are not bacteria.

Moulds are saprophytes, which means they feed on dead organic matter such as bread, cheese, jam, fruit and decaying plant material. They digest it outside their bodies and then absorb the digested products.
A mould's visible body is built from thread-like filaments. Each part has a name and a job, and the parts are the labels exams ask for on a diagram.
Hyphae (singular hypha): thread-like filaments that grow over and into the food and absorb its nutrients, which is how the mould feeds.
Mycelium: the interwoven mass of hyphae that forms the visible growth, such as the fluffy or powdery layer on bread.
Sporangiophore: an upright hypha that rises from the mycelium and carries a sporangium at its tip, lifting the spores up so they can escape into the air.
Sporangium: a round, spore-filled case at the tip of a sporangiophore; it bursts open when ripe and releases spores into the air.
Conidia: in Penicillium, and also in Aspergillus, spores are borne in chains at the tips of branched conidiophores (spore-bearing hyphae) instead of inside a round sporangium.

Diagram: a mould growing on a food surface, showing the mycelium spreading across the food, a sporangiophore rising from it and a sporangium at its tip; label hypha, mycelium, sporangiophore and sporangium.
Mould spores are almost everywhere, which is why food left out so often goes mouldy. Knowing where they come from shows how they reach food.
Moulds are saprophytes: they feed on dead organic matter, so they grow on decaying food and plant material.
Spores are carried in the air, on dust, on food packaging and on unclean utensils, and they settle on food.
Soil and damp indoor surfaces act as reservoirs (stores) from which spores spread to food.
Already-mouldy food is also a source: a mouldy item releases spores that spread to food stored beside it.
Rhizopus is the common bread mould; it grows on bread, fruit and other moist starchy or sugary foods.
Mould spores only grow into a mould when six conditions are met. Each one gives a way to stop growth, and each has a reason you can give.
Food: moulds feed on the organic matter in food, such as bread, cheese, jam and fruit.
Warmth: most moulds are mesophiles (they prefer moderate temperatures); Penicillium grows best at 20 to 25 °C, and cold slows growth.
Moisture: moulds need moisture to grow, so frozen and very dry foods are less at risk.
Oxygen: moulds are aerobic (they need oxygen), so they grow on the surface of food, such as jam, or through open-textured foods such as bread.
pH: moulds prefer slightly acidic conditions, around pH 4 to 6; strong acids inhibit their growth.
Time: moulds need about 24 to 48 hours to establish visible growth, because the spores must germinate and the mycelium must spread.
Freezing at −18 °C inactivates mould growth, but it does not kill the mould, so growth can start again after thawing.
One type of mould is often asked about in detail. Penicillium is a good choice because its features are easy to remember.
Penicillium is a saprophytic mould with a green-blue, powdery appearance, which comes from its chains of conidia.
It grows on bread, jam, cheese and fruit, and favours temperatures of 20 to 25 °C.
Penicillium reproduces asexually only, by conidia, so it never forms a zygospore.
Heat above 75 °C destroys Penicillium, whereas freezing only inactivates its growth.
Other moulds can be given as your named example. Their differences are in colour, spore structure and whether they reproduce sexually.
Rhizopus (the black bread mould) is saprophytic, with fluffy white mycelium and black pin-head sporangia that hold its spores.
Rhizopus reproduces both sexually and asexually, so it can form a zygospore as well as spores.
Mucor is saprophytic, with white hyphae and grey sporangia, and reproduces both sexually and asexually.
Aspergillus is saprophytic and black or green; it favours 20 to 25 °C and reproduces asexually only, by conidia.
Moulds reproduce by releasing spores, tiny cells that spread through the air. Some moulds can also reproduce sexually, which gives a tough resting stage.
Asexual reproduction, first stage: once the mycelium is established, a hypha (the sporangiophore) grows upwards and its head forms a sporangium, or in some moulds chains of conidia.
When the sporangium ripens it bursts, releasing spores into the air, so they travel to new food.
A spore that lands on suitable food germinates (starts to grow) and develops a new mycelium.
Sexual reproduction (Rhizopus and Mucor): two compatible hyphae grow beside each other and fuse.
The dividing wall between the fused hyphae breaks down and a thick-walled zygospore forms.
The zygospore protects the spores until conditions are suitable; then it germinates, hyphae grow out and spores are released.
Yeasts are single-celled fungi. Each cell is a single oval or round unit, larger and more regular in shape than a bacterium.
Yeast is a eukaryote, meaning its cell has a true nucleus; it is a fungus, not a bacterium.
Cell wall: a rigid outer layer that gives the cell its shape, so it holds together, and protects it.
Cell membrane: a thin layer inside the cell wall that controls which substances pass in and out, so the cell takes in food and keeps unwanted substances out.
Nucleus: a membrane-bound structure containing the genetic material, so the cell is a eukaryote, for example unlike a bacterium.
Vacuole: a fluid-filled storage space within the cytoplasm.
Granular cytoplasm: the jelly-like contents of the cell, containing food reserves stored as granules.
Diagram: a yeast cell labelled cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus, vacuole and granular cytoplasm.
Yeasts live wherever sugar and moisture are found. They reproduce in a different way from moulds, by budding rather than by spores.
Yeasts occur naturally on the skins of fruit, especially grapes, and in soil, in the air, on plant surfaces and on sugary foods.
Yeasts need sugar as food, moisture, warmth and time to grow.
Yeast is facultative, meaning it can do either: it respires with oxygen, or ferments sugar when oxygen is absent.
In fermentation, yeast converts sugar into carbon dioxide and alcohol.
Reproduction is asexual, by budding: a small bud grows from the parent cell, enlarges and breaks away as a new cell.
Yeast spoils sugary foods such as juices, jam and syrups by fermenting them. Baker's and brewer's yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
Bacteria are prokaryotes: single cells with no true nucleus, so their genetic material lies free in the cytoplasm. This is the main contrast with fungi, whose cells have a nucleus.
Cell wall: a rigid layer, made of peptidoglycan, that gives the bacterial cell its shape and protects it.
Cell membrane: controls the movement of substances in and out of the cell.
Cytoplasm: the jelly-like interior where the cell's chemical reactions take place.
Ribosomes: small structures in the cytoplasm where proteins are made, so the cell can build and repair itself.
Flagella: whip-like tails that rotate to move the bacterium; not all bacteria have them.
Nucleoid: the region containing the single circular loop of DNA, lying free in the cytoplasm; plasmids are small extra loops of DNA.
Bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission, where one cell divides in two; under ideal conditions some divide about every 20 minutes.
Diagram: a bacterial cell labelled cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, flagella and nucleoid.

Most bacteria in food are harmless or even useful, so only a few cause illness. Food poisoning is illness caused by eating food contaminated with pathogenic (disease-causing) bacteria or their toxins.
Six environmental factors affect bacterial growth: food, moisture, warmth, oxygen requirement, pH and time. Protein-rich, moist foods are high risk because they give bacteria what they need to grow.
Most food poisoning bacteria favour a near-neutral pH, neither strongly acid nor strongly alkaline.
Under good conditions a bacterium divides by binary fission (splitting in two) about every 20 minutes, so numbers rise very quickly and a few bacteria can become millions within hours.

The danger zone, about 5 to 63 °C, is the range in which food poisoning bacteria multiply fastest. Below 5 °C growth slows down, and above 63 °C most bacteria stop multiplying and thorough cooking destroys them.
Micro-organisms are grouped by the temperature at which they grow best. This explains why the danger zone sits around body temperature.
Psychrophiles grow best at about −5 to 20 °C, in cold conditions such as refrigerated food.
Mesophiles grow best at about 20 to 45 °C. Most food poisoning bacteria are mesophiles, which is why the danger zone is close to body temperature.
Salmonella has an optimum (best) growth temperature of about 37 °C, which is normal body temperature.
Thermophiles grow best at about 45 to 75 °C, in hot environments.
The danger zone, about 5 to 63 °C, is the range in which mesophilic food poisoning bacteria multiply rapidly.
Micro-organisms also differ in their need for oxygen. This decides which foods and storage conditions suit each one.
Aerobic micro-organisms require oxygen to survive and grow; moulds are aerobic.
Anaerobic micro-organisms thrive without oxygen, so sealed foods suit them; Clostridium botulinum is an example.
Facultative micro-organisms adapt to either aerobic or anaerobic conditions, so they can grow with or without oxygen; Salmonella, Staphylococcus aureus and yeast are facultative.
Salmonella is a common infectious food poisoning bacterium, meaning the illness comes from eating the living bacteria themselves.
Structure: a rod-shaped, Gram-negative bacterium that does not form spores (tough resting cells). It reproduces by binary fission.
Habitat and sources: the intestines of humans, animals and birds; faeces; polluted water; unwashed hands, which carry it onto food.
High-risk foods: raw or undercooked poultry, meat, fish and eggs; unpasteurised milk and dairy products.
Growth: needs food, moisture and time, and favours a near-neutral pH. It is a mesophile with an optimum of about 37 °C, and it is facultative.
Incubation period: usually about 12 to 36 hours after eating contaminated food, with a wider range of 12 to 72 hours.
Symptoms: diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and fever.
Staphylococcus aureus is a common toxic food poisoning bacterium. It makes a poison in the food as it grows, and the poison causes the illness.
Structure: a Gram-positive, spherical cell (a coccus) that forms grape-like clusters; it does not form spores.
Habitat and sources: the skin, nose and throat of humans and their hair; infected cuts and boils. It spreads to food by handling.
High-risk foods: cooked meats, poultry, ham, egg products, cream-filled cakes, custard and egg or potato salads made with mayonnaise.
Growth: a mesophile that grows at about 37 °C and is facultative. It tolerates salt and sugar better than most bacteria.
Toxin: it produces an enterotoxin (a toxin that acts on the gut) in food. The toxin is heat-stable, so it is not destroyed by normal cooking.
Incubation period: short, usually about 2 to 4 hours, within a wider range of about 1 to 6 hours.
Symptoms: sudden nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea.
Clostridium botulinum is a toxic food poisoning bacterium that produces a very potent neurotoxin (a poison that attacks the nerves). It is rare but dangerous.
Structure: a rod-shaped, Gram-positive, spore-forming bacterium that is an obligate anaerobe, meaning it can only grow where there is no oxygen.
Habitat and sources: soil and water, from which its spores reach vegetables and other foods.
High-risk foods: home-canned low-acid vegetables, badly processed canned or vacuum-packed foods, cured meats, and honey, which must not be given to babies under one year.
Growth: it multiplies in sealed, low-acid foods where no oxygen is present, because these are the conditions it needs.
Toxin: a neurotoxin that blocks nerve signals to muscles, causing paralysis. The toxin is destroyed by boiling for about 10 minutes, but the spores survive ordinary cooking.
Incubation period: typically 12 to 36 hours after eating contaminated food.
Symptoms: double vision, drooping eyelids, difficulty swallowing and speaking, muscle weakness, paralysis and breathing difficulties; it can be fatal.
A question may ask for any common strain, so it helps to know a few more with one typical high-risk food each.
Listeria is infectious. It is found in pâté, coleslaw, soft cheese and smoked fish, and it grows at fridge temperature. It is serious for pregnant women, newborns and the elderly.
E. coli is infectious. High-risk foods are undercooked minced meat, polluted water and unpasteurised milk.
Campylobacter is infectious. High-risk foods are raw poultry and unpasteurised milk.
Bacillus cereus is linked to cooked rice and reheated rice.
Clostridium perfringens is toxic. High-risk foods are stews, gravies and large cooked joints that cool slowly.

Food poisoning falls into two types, depending on whether the harm comes from the bacteria or from their toxin. Incubation period is the time between eating contaminated food and the appearance of the first symptoms.
Infectious food poisoning: caused by eating food containing large numbers of living pathogenic bacteria, which multiply in the gut.
Infectious food poisoning: the bacteria release endotoxins, which are made inside their cells and released when the cells die.

Infectious food poisoning: endotoxins and bacteria are easily destroyed by proper cooking and reheating, so the risk comes from undercooked food. Incubation is usually more than 12 hours; examples are Salmonella, E. coli, Campylobacter and Listeria.
Toxic food poisoning: caused by eating food that already contains exotoxin, a poison produced by bacteria as they grow in the food.

Toxic food poisoning: exotoxins are hard to destroy and may need boiling for 30 minutes, so cooking may not make the food safe. Symptoms appear quickly, often within 2 hours; examples are Staphylococcus aureus, Clostridium botulinum and Clostridium perfringens.
In one line each: infectious means the bacteria themselves are eaten, onset is slower and cooking destroys them; toxic means the toxin is eaten, onset is fast and the toxin survives cooking.
Outbreaks usually trace back to a few handling failures that let bacteria reach food or multiply in it. Each one links to the growth conditions bacteria need.
Undercooked poultry or minced meat allows surviving bacteria to cause illness.
Cooked food left at room temperature allows bacteria to multiply in the danger zone.
Cross-contamination from raw meat or poultry transfers bacteria to food that is eaten without cooking.
Food handlers with poor personal hygiene or illness, such as not washing hands after using the toilet, transfer bacteria to food.
Contaminated water or unpasteurised dairy products introduce bacteria before any cooking takes place.
Slow cooling of large batches, inadequate reheating and preparing food too far in advance also give bacteria time to grow or survive.
Spoilage is any change that makes food unfit or unpleasant to eat, such as an off smell, taste, colour or texture. Several causes are at work, but micro-organisms are the main one.
Micro-organisms (bacteria, moulds and yeasts) are the main cause of spoilage, and they are the cause this subsection deals with.
Enzyme action (the food's own chemicals continuing to work) causes changes such as browning and over-ripening.
Physical damage and bruising break the surface of food, which lets other spoilage in.
Moisture loss makes food shrink, wrinkle or harden, for example a dried-out piece of fruit.
Rancidity is the going-off of fats, which gives them an unpleasant smell and taste.
Chemical contamination, for example by pesticides, antibiotics or metals, spoils food and can make it unsafe.
Spoilage micro-organisms mainly make food unpleasant, so spoiled food is not always unsafe. Pathogens (disease-causing micro-organisms) can make food unsafe even when it looks and smells normal.
Bacteria are the micro-organisms that spoil most protein and moist foods, and they change food in several ways.
Putrefaction: bacteria break down protein in meat, fish and eggs, producing foul odours and a slimy surface.
Souring: lactic acid bacteria ferment the lactose (milk sugar) in milk, producing lactic acid that curdles the milk.
Bacteria that survive in food can produce toxins (poisons), which can make food unsafe even when the food looks and smells normal.
The foods at greatest risk are high-moisture, high-protein foods such as meat, fish, poultry, eggs, milk and cooked rice, because bacteria find both water and nutrients in them.
Moulds and yeasts spoil foods that bacteria find harder to use, especially acidic and sugary ones.
Moulds grow visibly on food as fluffy, powdery or coloured patches, for example on bread, cheese, fruit and jam, and some produce mycotoxins (poisons made by moulds) that are harmful if eaten.
Mould spores (tiny reproductive cells) spread through the air, which is how they land on food.
Yeasts ferment the sugars in fruit juices, jams, syrups and fruit, producing carbon dioxide, alcohol and off-flavours, and sometimes bubbling or swollen containers.
Mould and yeast growth is mostly on the surface of food, where oxygen is available, but moulds also grow through open-textured foods such as bread.
Acidic, sugary foods favour moulds and yeasts because they tolerate acid better than most bacteria.
Micro-organisms spoil food only when the conditions they need are present. Remove or change one of them and growth slows or stops.
Food: micro-organisms need nutrients, particularly protein and carbohydrate, as a source of energy and for building new cells.
Moisture: their chemical reactions and nutrient absorption take place in solution, so dry foods support little growth and high-moisture foods are high risk.
Warmth: most spoilage and poisoning micro-organisms multiply fastest in the danger zone (5 to 63 °C), while cold slows growth, freezing stops it without killing them, and heat kills them.
Oxygen: aerobic micro-organisms such as moulds need oxygen, while anaerobic bacteria grow in sealed packs from which oxygen is absent, and facultative ones can adapt to either.

pH (how acid or alkaline food is): most bacteria prefer a near-neutral pH, whereas moulds and yeasts tolerate acid. Lactic acid bacteria are an exception because they tolerate acid, but strongly acidic foods are generally safer.
Time: micro-organisms need time to multiply, and some bacteria can double in number in about 20 minutes under ideal conditions (binary fission, where one cell divides into two).

Control of spoilage works either by destroying micro-organisms, keeping them away from food, or restricting one of the conditions they need. The first two principles deal with the micro-organisms themselves.

Heat treatments kill micro-organisms: cooking, pasteurisation, which uses a lower temperature for a set time, and sterilisation, which destroys all micro-organisms and their spores. Canning and bottling also use heat.
Irradiation destroys micro-organisms and parasites in food by exposing it to controlled radiation, without making the food radioactive.
Irradiation can extend shelf life and slow ripening and sprouting in fruit and vegetables, with little effect on colour, flavour or texture.
Preventing micro-organisms reaching the food in the first place uses hygiene, clean equipment, covering food, sealed packaging, sterile containers and separating raw and cooked food.
The other principles leave micro-organisms alive but take away something they need. Most foods use more than one, and applying each to a named food is the usual exam task.
Low temperature: refrigeration slows the growth of micro-organisms, and freezing inactivates them without destroying them, so growth resumes on thawing.

Removing moisture: drying, salting, sugaring and concentrating reduce the water available to micro-organisms. Dissolved salt or sugar draws water out of microbial cells by osmosis, which dehydrates them.
Acidity: pickling in vinegar, or adding lemon juice, lowers the pH to a level that most bacteria cannot tolerate. Chutney and fermentation acids work the same way.
Removing oxygen: vacuum packing and canning exclude air, preventing growth of aerobic micro-organisms, and modified-atmosphere packs replace the air around the food.
Preservatives: chemicals such as sulphur dioxide, benzoates and nitrites inhibit the growth of micro-organisms. Natural preservatives are salt, sugar, vinegar, alcohol and smoke.
Combining principles: jam, for example, uses heat, sugar, acid and sealing together, so several principles protect the same food.
Not all micro-organisms spoil food. Some are added on purpose, because their feeding changes the food in useful ways, and this process is called fermentation.
Fermentation is the breakdown of organic substances, such as sugars, by bacteria or yeast, usually in the absence or shortage of oxygen. It is used to make many foods.

The by-products of fermentation include carbon dioxide, energy, acids (such as lactic acid and acetic acid) and alcohol, which is why fermented foods taste and behave differently from the raw ingredients.
In lactic acid fermentation, bacteria turn sugars such as lactose (the sugar in milk) into lactic acid. This is the basis of yoghurt and cheese.
In alcoholic fermentation, yeast turns sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide. This is the basis of bread, beer and wine.
Milk contains the sugar lactose, which lactic acid bacteria feed on. Their acid changes the milk's flavour and texture, which is how milk becomes cheese or yoghurt.
Starter cultures are lactic acid bacteria added to milk to begin fermentation. They ferment the lactose in milk into lactic acid, giving cheese and yoghurt their sour flavour and texture.
In cheese-making, the lactic acid works together with rennet to curdle the milk and set the curd, so acid on its own is not enough. Ripening by further bacteria or moulds then develops the flavour.

Yoghurt is made by fermenting milk, typically with Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. The lactose becomes lactic acid, so the milk thickens and tastes sour. Some yoghurts add other strains.
Probiotic (functional) yoghurts and drinks contain live bacteria that may benefit the intestinal flora (the helpful bacteria living in the gut) when eaten, so they are examples of functional foods.
Moulds are fungi that grow as fine threads. In a few foods a particular mould is added deliberately, and each gives the food its own flavour.

Blue-veined cheese: the mould Penicillium roqueforti grows through the cheese, producing blue-green veins and a sharp flavour. Cashel Blue, made in Co. Tipperary, is an Irish example; Roquefort and Stilton are others.
Surface-ripened soft cheese: Penicillium camemberti grows on the outside and gives the white rind of Camembert and Brie.
Soy sauce is produced by the mould Aspergillus oryzae, which breaks down the protein and starch in soya beans by fermentation, giving the sauce its savoury flavour.
Yeast is a single-celled fungus, not a bacterium. It ferments sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, and different foods make use of different parts of that result.
In bread-making (including sourdough), yeast ferments the sugars in the dough and produces carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise. This is why yeast is called a biological raising agent.
The alcohol produced in the dough evaporates during baking, so bread is not alcoholic.
In brewing, yeast ferments the sugars in malted barley (barley that has been germinated) to produce alcohol and carbon dioxide, giving beer.
In wine-making, yeast ferments the sugars in grape juice into alcohol. Spirits are distilled from fermented liquids.
Vinegar is made by acetic acid bacteria, such as Acetobacter, which oxidise (add oxygen to) alcohol to form acetic acid.
Micro-organisms are also used in meat products and as foods in their own right. Some provide protein or vitamins rather than flavour.
Salami, pepperoni and chorizo are made by adding bacterial starter cultures to cured meat. The bacteria ferment its sugars to lactic acid, which flavours the product and helps to preserve it.
Quorn is a meat substitute made from mycoprotein, which comes from the fungus Fusarium venenatum grown by fermentation in large fermenters. It is high in protein and fibre and low in saturated fat.
Mycoprotein is a novel protein food, meaning a new kind of food produced by fermentation rather than from animals. It is from a fungus, not from yeast, bacteria or plants.
Mushrooms and truffles are large fungi that are eaten directly as food.
Yeast extracts and yeast-based food supplements are used as sources of B vitamins, and bacteria are also used in food supplements.
Using micro-organisms on purpose gives foods qualities that the raw ingredients do not have.
Fermentation adds flavour and changes texture, for example the sourness of yoghurt, the veins of blue cheese and the rise of bread dough.
Fermented foods can have a longer keeping time, because acids such as lactic acid and acetic acid are produced, for example in salami and vinegar.
Micro-organisms improve nutritional value, since yeast extracts supply B vitamins and mycoprotein supplies protein.
They add variety to the diet, from cheeses, yoghurts and breads to meat substitutes such as Quorn.

Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions, and food is full of them. Plant and animal foods contain their own enzymes, which keep working after harvest or slaughter, so food can spoil without any micro-organisms being involved.
Enzymes occur naturally in fruit, vegetables, fish and meat. Because they keep working after the food is picked or killed, they slowly change its colour, texture and flavour.
Each enzyme has an active site, a shaped region into which its specific substrate (the one substance it acts on) fits to be broken down. This is why each enzyme acts on only one kind of substance.
Enzymes work best in warmth and moisture, so removing water from food leaves them unable to act.
Heat denatures enzymes, which means it changes the shape of the active site so that the substrate no longer fits and the enzyme stops working. Cooking therefore inactivates them.
Low temperatures slow enzyme activity without destroying it, so enzymes resume working when the food warms up again.
Fruit does not stop changing when it is picked. Its ripening enzymes carry on working, and if they are left long enough they turn good fruit into spoiled fruit.
Ripening enzymes continue to act after fruit is picked, converting starch to sugar and softening the cell walls, so the fruit becomes sweeter and softer.
As enzymes change colour, texture and flavour, fruit moves from ripe to over-ripe and then decays, becoming soft and mushy before it rots.
Over-ripening: a hard, under-ripe banana becomes soft and sweet, and then black, as enzymes continue to break it down.
Cut an apple and leave it, and the flesh turns brown. This is enzymic browning, and it needs three things: damaged cells, the enzyme and oxygen from the air.
When the surface of apples, bananas or potatoes is cut, peeled or bruised, enzymes are released from the damaged cells.
Polyphenol oxidase, also called oxidase, acts on phenolic compounds in the presence of oxygen.
The reaction forms brown pigments on the cut surface, which is why cut apples and potatoes discolour.
Browning changes the appearance and flavour of the food but is not a safety hazard.

Enzymes also break down fish, fats and vegetables, even when the food is stored in the cold. The damage shows up as off-odours, rancidity, poor colour and texture, and lost nutrients, and it shortens shelf life.
Lipase in fish and oily foods breaks down fats (triglycerides) into fatty acids and glycerol, causing rancidity (the stale, unpleasant taste of spoiled fat) and off-flavours.
Enzymes in fish continue to break down the flesh even at low temperatures, producing odour.
Vegetables that are not blanched before freezing keep their enzymes active during storage, which spoils colour, texture and flavour in the freezer.
Oxidase in the cell walls of plants is activated by oxygen and can destroy thiamine (vitamin B1), vitamin C and carotene, so some nutritive value is lost.

Control works by inactivating enzymes, slowing their action or excluding oxygen. In other words, enzymes are controlled by destroying them (heat), changing their conditions (acid, cold, dryness) or removing a reactant (oxygen).
Heat: blanching, a brief immersion of vegetables in boiling water or steam followed by rapid cooling, inactivates enzymes before freezing; cooking denatures them.
Acid: adding lemon juice or vinegar to cut apples lowers the pH and inactivates the enzymes that cause browning.
Low temperature: refrigeration and freezing slow enzyme activity but do not stop or destroy it, so enzymes become active again on thawing. This is why frozen vegetables need blanching first.
Sulphur dioxide: used as a preservative in dried fruit and in fruit and vegetable juices, it prevents browning and inhibits enzyme action.
Removing oxygen: vacuum packing, covering cut surfaces with water or sugar syrup, or treating cut fruit with an antioxidant such as ascorbic acid (vitamin C) prevents oxidase from browning the food.
Drying: removing water makes enzymes inactive because they need it to act, which preserves herbs and dried fruit.
Irradiation is also listed as a control for enzymic spoilage.

Almost every rule for handling food comes from two facts about food poisoning bacteria: they multiply fastest in warm food, and they travel easily from one food to another. Knowing these makes the individual rules easy to remember.
Food poisoning bacteria multiply fastest in the danger zone, 5°C to 63°C. This is why safe preparation keeps food cold, hot, or moving quickly through that range.

Cross-contamination is the transfer of bacteria from raw food to cooked or ready-to-eat food, directly or by hands, chopping boards, cloths, utensils or meat juices. This is why raw and cooked foods are kept apart.
Freezing does not kill bacteria, it only stops them multiplying, and thawing lets them start multiplying again. So frozen food must be handled with care once it thaws.
Storage aims to keep food cold or frozen so bacteria cannot multiply, and to stop bacteria passing from one food to another. Short questions usually ask for three to six storage guidelines.
Cover all food and store it in sealed containers, which prevents drying out, odour transfer and cross-contamination.
Keep perishable food (food that spoils quickly) in the fridge at 5°C or below, which slows the growth of bacteria. Check the fridge and freezer temperature with a thermometer.
Store raw meat, poultry and fish on the lowest shelf, on a plate and loosely covered with the shop wrapping removed, so that juices cannot drip onto cooked or ready-to-eat food.
Keep raw and cooked foods apart, covered or in sealed containers, so bacteria cannot pass between them.
Cool cooked food quickly before refrigerating or freezing it, and do not overpack the fridge, so that cold air can circulate around the food.
Check the use-by or best-before date of each food and follow the storage instructions on its label. Use-by is a safety date for highly perishable food, while best-before is a quality date.
Remove fruit and vegetables from plastic wrapping, which encourages mould, and check them regularly for mould.
Store dry foods in a cool, dry, well-ventilated cupboard, in vermin-proof containers, and keep storage areas clean.
Keep perishable food out of the fridge for the shortest possible time while it is being prepared, because food left in warm air soon enters the danger zone.
Freezing keeps food safe for a long time, but only if it is frozen and thawed properly. Bacteria are not killed by freezing, so the care taken when thawing matters.
Freeze food quickly at −25°C, then store it at −18°C.
Defrost frozen food completely before cooking, preferably in the fridge on the bottom shelf, so that it thaws slowly and any drips cannot reach other food.
Never refreeze food that has thawed, because bacteria multiply while it thaws.
Cooking and reheating must heat food right through to kill bacteria, and hot food must then stay hot or be eaten promptly. Otherwise bacteria multiply again in the danger zone.

Cook food thoroughly, using the right time and temperature, and turn or stir it so that heat reaches the centre. Cook meat, poultry and minced meat right through, to a core temperature of at least 72°C for poultry.
Reheat food quickly until it is above 100°C throughout, and reheat it only once.
High-risk foods such as stews and gravies should be brought to boiling when reheated, because their moist, protein-rich nature suits bacteria.
Cover food when reheating. In a microwave, stir or turn the food and allow standing time, so that heat reaches all parts evenly, and follow the appliance's instructions.
Serve cooked food immediately. If holding it hot, keep it above 63°C, because bacteria multiply rapidly between 5°C and 63°C.
Eat food that has been held hot within about 90 minutes (1.5 hours).
Do not keep food in the danger zone. Cool leftovers quickly, refrigerate them and use them soon.

People carry food poisoning bacteria on their hands, hair, skin and clothes, so the person preparing food is a major source of contamination. Examiners usually ask for four to six personal hygiene points.
Wash hands in hot water with liquid soap, and a nailbrush for the nails, before handling food, because hands carry food poisoning bacteria. Dry them on a clean towel or paper towel.
Wash hands after the toilet, sneezing or coughing, changing nappies, handling pets, handling rubbish and handling raw meat.
Keep nails short and clean and remove jewellery before preparing food, because dirt and bacteria collect under nails and around jewellery.
Tie hair back or cover it. Wear a clean apron or clothing, and change it if it becomes soiled.
Cover cuts, boils and sores with a brightly coloured waterproof plaster, so that infection cannot pass to food and the plaster can be seen if it falls into the food.
Do not cough or sneeze over food, and do not taste food with your fingers or lick your fingers.
Do not prepare or serve food for others while suffering from diarrhoea or vomiting, because the illness can pass to the people eating it.
A clean kitchen with sensible habits stops bacteria building up on surfaces and equipment and passing to food. Four kitchen hygiene practices is a common exam question.
Clean and disinfect work surfaces often, and wash equipment in hot water and detergent. Clean as you go.
Use colour-coded chopping boards and separate utensils for raw and cooked foods, to prevent cross-contamination.
Never prepare raw and cooked foods on the same surface.
Handle food as little as possible during preparation, and keep it covered, because every touch can pass on bacteria.
Floors, walls and work surfaces should be easy to clean, and the kitchen should have good lighting.
Effective ventilation reduces condensation, which encourages the growth of micro-organisms.
The kitchen should have a clean water supply and no access for pets or pests.
Keep a covered waste bin and empty it regularly, and change clean cloths and dishtowels often.

Rather than waiting to test finished food, a food business can look for trouble at every step and stop it early. That is the idea behind HACCP, and it comes with a small set of terms that exams ask you to define.

HACCP stands for Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point. It is a preventive system, which means it identifies and controls hazards at each stage from raw material to consumer, before they can reach the consumer, rather than relying on testing the finished product.

A hazard is anything that could contaminate food or harm the consumer. A control measure is an action that prevents, removes or reduces a hazard, such as thorough cooking, which destroys surviving bacteria.

A critical control point (CCP) is a step at which a control measure is essential and can be monitored, for example the cooking step. A critical limit is the value that separates safe from unsafe, for example a minimum core temperature.
Hazard analysis identifies the hazards at each stage of food processing and assesses how likely and how serious each one is, so effort goes where the risk is greatest.
HACCP is used by caterers, restaurants, food manufacturers and food businesses generally.
Hazards fall into three groups depending on what the contaminant is. Naming the type, with an example, helps you decide what control measure fits.
Biological hazards are micro-organisms, such as food poisoning bacteria, moulds and viruses, which can multiply in food and make people ill.
Chemical hazards include pesticide residues, cleaning chemicals, metal residues and allergens, which can get into food during growing, cleaning or processing.
Physical hazards are foreign bodies such as glass, metal, bone, stones, pests and hair, which can injure the consumer or signal poor hygiene.

The seven principles are the steps a business follows to build a HACCP system. They run in a logical order: find the hazards, pick the key steps, set limits, check them, fix problems, prove it works and write it all down.
Principle 1: carry out a hazard analysis at each stage of the process.
Principle 2: identify the critical control points, the steps where control is essential.
Principle 3: set a critical limit for each critical control point, such as a minimum cooking temperature.
Principle 4: set up monitoring procedures to check each critical control point, so you know the limit is being met.
Principle 5: set corrective actions to take when monitoring shows that a critical limit has not been met.
Principle 6: set up verification procedures to confirm that the system is working.
Principle 7: keep records and documentation of the system and its results, which gives written evidence of what was done.
A HACCP answer follows the food from the shop to the plate, giving a hazard and its control at each stage. The first three stages happen before any cooking starts.
Purchase hazards: damaged goods, bacterial or chemical contamination, and pests.

Purchase controls: buy from a reputable shop, and check packaging, use-by dates, temperatures and any signs of pest damage, so unsafe food is never brought home. Keep raw and cooked foods separate in the trolley, and choose foods within date and with quality assurance marks.
Transport hazard: bacteria multiply when food warms up during transport and delays, because warmth lets them grow quickly.
Transport control: carry perishable food in cool bags or refrigerated containers, cover it, minimise the time before it is stored, and store it promptly.
Storage hazards: bacterial multiplication and cross-contamination (bacteria passing from one food to another) of food.

Storage controls: chill perishable food below 5°C, freeze food at −18°C, and keep raw food separate from cooked food, with raw below cooked and covered. Check vegetables for mould, and use clean sealed containers.
Preparation and cooking are where food is handled most and where bacteria can be destroyed. Cooking is the critical control point, because it is the step that kills bacteria already on the food.
Preparation hazards: contamination of food, multiplication of bacteria and cross-contamination.

Preparation controls: wash hands with antibacterial soap and hot water before and after handling food, and handle food as little as possible. Keep perishables chilled until needed, and clean equipment in hot water and detergent.

Use colour-coded boards and separate utensils for raw and cooked meat, and keep raw meat away from cooked meat and ready-to-eat foods, so bacteria from raw meat cannot reach food that will not be cooked again.

Thaw frozen meat or poultry fully, preferably in the fridge on the bottom shelf, before cooking it. Thawing fully matters because a frozen centre may stay too cool to cook through, and the bottom shelf stops drips reaching other food.
Cooking hazard: bacteria that survive cooking, which can cause food poisoning.
Cooking control: cook thoroughly, turning or stirring the food regularly so that it cooks evenly, and use a thermometer to check.

Poultry must reach a core temperature (the temperature at the centre) of at least 72°C to destroy bacteria. In the exam example this is the critical limit, and the current FSAI guidance of 75°C is also correct.
Safe cooking can be undone if food is left standing or reheated badly. The last two stages deal with bacteria that survived cooking and the food that is left over.
Serving hazards: surviving bacteria multiplying in food that is held too long, and cross-contamination from utensils.
Serving controls: serve cooked food straight after cooking, on a clean plate, with clean utensils.
Hold cooked food above 63°C, because bacteria multiply more slowly when it is kept hot, and do not hold it for more than about 90 minutes.
Reheating hazard: food that has been cooled and stored can have bacteria that multiply during storage, or survive.

Reheating control: cool leftovers quickly, cover them and refrigerate. Then reheat food quickly to above 100°C throughout, and reheat it only once. Current guidance of piping hot, about 70 to 75°C at the core, is also correct.
Exams can ask for the HACCP stages of a dish other than a hot main course, such as a barbecue. The stages are the same, with a few extra controls suited to outdoor cooking.
Cook poultry and sausages right through, with no pink or red juices, because pink juices show the centre has not reached a safe temperature.
Do not use the same plate or tongs for raw and cooked food, so raw-meat bacteria cannot pass onto food that is ready to eat.
Keep raw meat separate from salads, which will not be cooked, and keep perishable salads and coleslaw in the fridge until needed.
A marinade used on raw meat must be brought to the boil before it is used as a sauce, otherwise it carries raw-meat bacteria.
HACCP helps both the consumer and the business. It makes food safer and gives the business proof that it took proper care.
HACCP identifies and eliminates or reduces hazards, so food is safer and outbreaks are prevented.
It focuses workers on safety at every step of food preparation.
It meets legal requirements and provides written records as evidence of due care.
Records help a business plan for future safety, time and cost, with less waste and fewer recalls.
It increases consumer confidence, and the system should be reviewed and evaluated regularly.
In a catering business, HACCP helps prevent food poisoning outbreaks by identifying hazards from purchase to serving, controlling them at critical points and monitoring to prevent contamination.
HACCP is not the only system a food business may use. ISO 9000 is a separate, broader approach to managing quality.

ISO is the International Organization for Standardization, which publishes internationally agreed standards. In Ireland the National Standards Authority of Ireland (NSAI) is the national standards body.

ISO 9000 is a family of standards for quality management systems. A quality management system uses documented procedures, records and regular internal review to ensure that products meet customer requirements.
Continual improvement of the system is a central principle of ISO 9000.

ISO 9001 is the standard in the family against which organisations are formally audited and certified. Certification by an independent body shows customers that the business has a consistent quality system.
HACCP is a food safety system that controls hazards, whereas ISO 9000 is a general quality management system for any business and covers safety only indirectly. A food business can use both.

Consumers cannot see how hygienically their food was produced, so the state sets up bodies to check it on their behalf. In Ireland one central body coordinates the system and other bodies do the inspecting.
National agencies protect consumers by setting and enforcing food safety standards, inspecting food businesses, testing food and acting when food is unsafe.
Food businesses must be monitored independently, because a business cannot be relied on to judge its own hygiene and customers have no way of checking it themselves.
An outbreak or contamination can cross counties and countries, so a national system is needed to trace it and respond quickly.
The Irish system has one central body, the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI), which coordinates, and a group of official agencies that carry out the inspecting.
The FSAI is the state body at the centre of food safety in Ireland. It sets the direction and coordinates the work, while others carry out most of the inspections.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) is the state body responsible for food safety in Ireland, established under the Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998.

The FSAI operates under the Department of Health, the government department responsible for health policy. The FSAI advises the Minister on food safety, but the Department itself does not inspect food premises.
It co-ordinates the enforcement of food safety legislation in Ireland, working through the official agencies, and it audits their work rather than inspecting most premises itself.
It protects consumers by ensuring that food is safe to eat and that food information is accurate.

It works with food businesses to make sure food is produced safely, for example through guidance and training on hygiene and HACCP systems (the system of identifying and controlling hazards in food production).
It takes action, through the agencies, when a food premises is in breach of food regulations, because it is the agencies that can inspect and enforce on the ground.
Beyond coordinating enforcement, the FSAI informs the public, handles emergencies and processes applications for new food products. It has one clear limit: it is about safety, not promotion.
It gives consumers and food businesses authoritative advice and publishes food safety information, so that both groups can rely on one trusted source.
It carries out scientific work, which gives its advice and decisions an evidence base.
It processes applications for novel foods and for new methods of food processing, so that new products are assessed before they reach consumers.
It also handles food alerts, product withdrawals and recalls, works with the agencies on traceability and leads on food incidents.
It does not promote Irish food at home or abroad; that is the role of Bord Bia (the Irish Food Board), which is why an exam statement that the FSAI promotes Irish food is false.

The FSAI does not carry out most food controls itself. Official agencies do this work under service contracts with the FSAI, which means the FSAI can coordinate one national system without employing every inspector.
The official agencies are the Health Service Executive (HSE), the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority and the local authorities.
Official agencies carry out inspections, sampling and analysis of food in the places they cover, and they enforce the rules on the FSAI's behalf.
The Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority carries out the official food safety controls on fish and shellfish, from production and landing through processing to distribution, but not retail.
Local authorities carry out food controls under contract to the FSAI in their own areas, mainly veterinary inspections of food premises that handle meat and other animal products.

The HSE is the national health service, and its Environmental Health Service does most of the day-to-day inspection of food premises. Its staff are environmental health officers, who work for the HSE and not for the FSAI.

Environmental health officers (EHOs), working in the HSE's Environmental Health Service, carry out the inspections of food premises, including restaurants, cafés, shops, hospital kitchens, manufacturers and wholesalers.
The service registers new food premises, so that every business handling food is known to the authorities before it starts trading.
It inspects food premises and farms.
It handles hygiene complaints and issues closure orders and enforcement notices where food premises are unsafe, which stops a risky business from continuing to sell food.
It ensures food safety at public gatherings and events.
It monitors compliance with food, labelling, additives and contaminants legislation, and takes samples of food for testing.
It responds to rapid alerts and recalls, and it investigates food poisoning outbreaks.
It educates and advises food businesses on compliance with the law.
Inspectors can see a kitchen, but only a laboratory can tell what is in a food. The Public Analyst Laboratories provide that testing, and they analyse rather than inspect.
The Public Analyst Laboratories are run by the HSE.
They analyse food and water, including samples taken by environmental health officers.
They test food for compliance with food law and labelling law, for example its composition, additives, contaminants and microbiological quality (the bacteria in it).
They test samples submitted by members of the public, for a fee.
Their results help ensure that food sold to consumers is safe and wholesome, and they give the evidence needed for legal action.
This Department looks after food at the farm end of the food chain, where animals and animal products come from. Its controls follow food from the farm to the shop.
It monitors food safety in meat and meat products, milk and milk products, and eggs and egg products.
It monitors the use of pesticides in food production, so that residues (traces left on or in food) do not reach consumers.
It enforces EU controls on the import of animal-based foods from countries outside the EU.
It is responsible for the registration and traceability of cattle, pigs and sheep, so that an animal can be traced if a problem is found.
It ensures correct hygiene procedures are followed from the dairy farm, to the dairy, through to the retailer and the consumer.
Because the inspecting is shared between several bodies, they need common ways of tracking and removing unsafe food. The FSAI coordinates all of these.
The FSAI and the official agencies work together on inspections, sampling, alerts, product withdrawals and recalls.
Traceability allows an unsafe product to be traced back to its supplier (one step back) and forward to the businesses that received it (one step forward).
A product withdrawal removes a product from the supply chain, whereas a product recall also collects it from consumers by asking them to return it.
Rapid alerts pass warnings about unsafe food quickly to the agencies that must act on them, so that action can be taken before more people are harmed.
Food law protects consumers by making sure food is safe and honestly described. It comes from two sources, the EU and Ireland, and the two work together.
An EU regulation applies directly in every member state, so it is not an Irish law. Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 are EU regulations, not Irish Acts.
Ireland also makes national regulations (called statutory instruments) to give an EU regulation effect, which means they set out how it is enforced and which bodies enforce it.
The Oireachtas (the Irish parliament) passes Acts, such as the Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998.
The purpose of all of this law is consumer protection: food that is safe to eat and described honestly.

Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 on the hygiene of foodstuffs is an EU regulation, which applies directly in every member state. It lays down hygiene rules for food businesses at all stages after primary production (the growing or rearing of the raw food). Ireland gives effect to it through national regulations.
The European Communities (Hygiene of Foodstuffs) Regulations 2006, amended in 2009 and 2010, give effect to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 in Ireland.

The Regulations set hygiene standards for food premises, equipment, food handling, water supply, waste and the personal hygiene of food handlers, so that every step where food could be contaminated is covered.
They require food businesses to put in place and operate a food safety system based on HACCP (a system that finds the points where food could become unsafe and controls them).
They require staff to be trained and supervised in food hygiene and to follow hygiene procedures, so that the people handling food know how to prevent contamination.
They require food premises to be registered with the relevant competent authority (the official body in charge of checking them).
They permit authorised officers, for example environmental health officers, to inspect premises, and to close them or have food destroyed where public health is immediately threatened.
How this protects the consumer: food is prepared in clean premises by trained staff under a system that prevents contamination, and unfit food can be taken off sale.

Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 on the provision of food information to consumers is given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014. It applies from 13 December 2014, and the nutrition declaration from 13 December 2016. It lists the information that must appear on pre-packed food, so that shoppers can choose safely.
A label must give the name of the food and a list of ingredients in descending order of weight at the time of manufacture, so the main ingredient comes first.
Fourteen named allergens must be emphasised wherever they appear in the list of ingredients, so that people with an allergy can spot them at once.
A label must give the net quantity of the food, and any special storage conditions or instructions for use where needed.
A label must give the name and address of the food business operator, so the food can be traced to a named business.
Country of origin or place of provenance must be given where leaving it out would mislead the consumer, and for certain meats and fresh produce.
Drinks over 1.2% alcohol must show their alcoholic strength.
A nutrition declaration gives the energy value, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt of the food.
Labelling must not mislead the consumer about the nature, identity, properties, origin or method of production of the food. Nutrition and health claims are regulated separately.
Two parts of the label matter most for safety: the allergens and the date mark. Both help the consumer avoid harm, but they work in different ways.

The 14 allergens that must be emphasised are cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish, peanuts, soybeans, milk, tree nuts, celery, mustard, sesame, sulphur dioxide and sulphites (above a set level), lupin and molluscs.
A use-by date must appear on highly perishable food, because such food can become unsafe to eat. After this date the food must not be eaten.
A best-before date (the date of minimum durability) shows the date until which the food keeps its quality, so food past this date is a matter of quality, not safety.

Alongside the rules on hygiene and labelling, there is a general framework that sets the principles for all food law. In Ireland this is the Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998. Across the EU it is Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, known as general food law.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998 provides the Irish legal framework for food safety. It set up the FSAI and gave it the functions of coordinating food safety law and its enforcement.
The 1998 Act also names the official agencies that carry out controls under service contracts.
Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 sets the general principles and requirements of food law across the EU.
Under general food law, food that is unsafe must not be placed on the market, and responsibility for safety rests with the food business.
Food businesses must be able to trace food one step back to their supplier and one step forward to their customers, so that unsafe food can be found and withdrawn quickly.
General food law set up the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed.

Risk analysis under general food law has three parts: risk assessment (scientific, carried out by EFSA), risk management (decisions by the authorities) and risk communication. The precautionary principle may apply where the science is uncertain.
The result is a common high level of protection of health and consumer interests from farm to fork, with fast withdrawal of unsafe food.

Rules only protect consumers if someone checks that businesses follow them. Regulation (EU) 2017/625 sets out the rules for official controls, which are checks by public authorities that food businesses comply with food law at every stage of the food chain.
Regulation (EU) 2017/625 is given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Official Controls in Relation to Food Legislation) Regulations 2020.
Official controls include inspection, sampling and analysis, and audit (a formal check of a business's records and systems).
Official controls are regular and risk-based, so that higher-risk businesses are checked more often. They are carried out without prior warning in most cases.
Inspectors can take samples of food for testing as part of an official control.
In Ireland the FSAI is the competent authority with overall responsibility. The official agencies (HSE, DAFM, SFPA and local authorities) carry out controls on its behalf under service contracts.
How this protects the consumer: independent checks on all food businesses, with enforcement action such as improvement notices, closure and withdrawal where the law is broken.
Every family has more things it wants to do than it has time, money or energy for. Resource management is how a family decides what to do with what it has.
Family resource management is using the resources a family has wisely and efficiently to achieve its goals. Resource management is the planned use of the resources available.
A resource is anything a family can draw on to meet its needs and wants, such as a parent's time, a cooker or a weekly wage.
Resources are limited, so choices have to be made about how they are used. This scarcity is why management is needed.

Goals are what the family is trying to achieve, and they give management its direction. Short-term goals include this week's meals or a family outing; long-term goals include buying a home, education or retirement.
Managing resources is not only about saving money. The purpose has three parts, and a full answer names all three.
The first purpose is to use available resources efficiently in order to achieve goals, so that the family gets the most from what it has.
The second purpose is to improve the quality of family life, so that home is more comfortable and less stressful for everyone.
The third purpose is to enable each family member to reach their full potential, because well-managed time, money and support leave room for learning, work and interests.
Good management reduces waste of time, money, food and energy, and gets the best value from limited resources.
It also avoids conflict and stress by agreeing who does what, so members know what is expected of them.

Example of efficient management: a weekly meal plan with a shopping list saves money and time and reduces food waste, because the family buys only what it will use. Other examples are budgeting, planned childcare, sharing household tasks, or resolving a conflict by agreeing a timetable.
Families draw on four kinds of resource, and only one of them is money. Naming each type with an example shows you understand what the family has to work with.
Human resources: the time, energy, skills and knowledge of family members, such as one parent's cooking skills or a teenager's free afternoon.
Material resources: equipment, food, ingredients, clothing, furniture and other household goods, such as a washing machine or a freezer.
Economic resources: income, savings and credit available to the family.
Environmental resources: the physical surroundings and community facilities that support family life, such as space, daylight and local services like schools, transport and health care.
Resources other than money matter as much as money. A family with little money can still manage well by using time, skills, knowledge and good planning.
A management system is a planned, step-by-step way of turning a need or goal into a result using the resources available. In other words, it turns what you have into what you wanted.
A management system lets a family decide what needs doing, who does it, when it is done and which resources it needs.

Everyday tasks that use a management system include meal planning, budgeting, housework, childcare and shopping. Money and home management, problem solving and decision-making are also uses of the management process.
One-off events such as a birthday party, a holiday or a house move also use a management system, as does a problem such as choosing an appliance.
Systems work best when the goals, standards and responsibilities are agreed in advance and tasks are shared, so that members know what is expected of them.
Systems are not fixed: they are adjusted when circumstances change, such as a new job, a job loss, a move or the arrival of a baby.
A system is a cycle, not a one-off. The result is checked against the goal, and what was learned improves the next attempt. This checking is called feedback.
When a family uses a management system well, the benefits show up in everyday life: in time, money, workload, relationships and the ability to cope with change.
