Time is used well. Planned routines make sure meals, laundry and school preparation are done on time, with less last-minute stress.
Money is used well. Meal plans and shopping lists reduce impulse buying and the amount of food that is wasted, and budgeting helps the family avoid debt.
Work is shared fairly. Shared tasks spread the workload so no single member carries the whole household, and each member learns skills.
Goals and standards agreed by all members give the family a shared direction, support communication and reduce conflict.
Energy, water and food are used carefully, so the cost of running the home is lower and there is less waste.
Efficient use of time and equipment frees time for leisure, rest and relationships, so quality of life improves.
The family copes better with change and emergencies because it has a plan and some resources in reserve.
The family is a small group that pools, allocates and controls its own resources. Because it sets goals and takes responsibility for results, it acts as a managerial unit.
Each member contributes resources such as earnings, time or skills, and each member benefits from the shared pool of the household.
The family sets goals, makes decisions, allocates resources and takes responsibility for the results.
Adults usually plan, earn and coordinate; children and teenagers take on tasks and share in decisions as they grow older. This means management duties are shared and change over time.
Family goals may be short term, such as a weekly shop or a family outing, or long term, such as buying a home or saving for education.
Management requires balancing individual wants against the needs and goals of the household as a whole, so the unit works best when decisions take everyone's views into account.
Article 41 of the Irish Constitution recognises the family as the natural, primary and fundamental unit group of society.

Inputs are what a family brings into the management process at the start: the demands made on it and the resources it has to meet them. Getting the inputs clear first matters because everything later depends on them.
Needs are necessities that must be met, such as food, shelter, warmth and clothing, so they come before everything else when resources are short.

Wants are things desired beyond necessities, such as a particular brand, a holiday or a new appliance. A want can be postponed or dropped when resources are short, which is the key difference from a need.
Goals are the outcomes the family sets out to achieve, such as a balanced weekly budget or a family meal on the table by six o'clock.
Values are what the family believes is important, and they shape which goals the family chooses.
Human resources are the time, energy, skills, knowledge and people in the family, who make and carry out decisions.

Material resources are equipment, ingredients, food, clothing, furniture and other household goods used in the task. Marking schemes also list economic resources (money: income and savings) and environmental resources (space, surroundings and community facilities).
Inputs are the starting point, so clear goals are the first step: a poorly defined or vague need or goal at this stage leads to a result that does not meet the family's needs.
Throughputs are the actions a family takes to change its inputs into outputs. There are three: planning, organising and implementing.
Planning means gathering information, considering the alternatives, weighing them up and deciding on a course of action.
Organising means allocating tasks and responsibilities (who does what and when), arranging the resources each task needs and communicating with those involved.
Implementing means putting the plan into action, such as booking, buying, cooking or cleaning.
Changes are made during implementing as needs arise, such as an unexpected guest or a shortage of an ingredient, because no plan covers everything.
A plan lists the steps in order and the resources each step needs, so that work can be checked against it.
Decision-making and communication run through all three throughputs, because choices have to be made and shared at every stage.

Outputs are the results produced by the throughputs, and they are judged against the inputs, especially the goals set at the start. Outputs also feed back into the next cycle, so the framework is a loop and not a straight line.
Goals achieved: whether the goals were met and whether needs were fulfilled and wants satisfied.
Changes in values, goals and standards: the experience may change what the family thinks is important or reasonable, or show that a goal or standard was unrealistic and needs to be revised.
Satisfaction: whether family members are happy with the result and whether their needs and wants were met.

Evaluation: an assessment of whether resources were used effectively, whether the task was organised efficiently, and whether time, money and energy were used well and the result met the family's needs.
Effective use of feedback: what is learned is fed back into the system as an input to the next cycle, so that the next round of planning is improved.

The framework can be used to plan any event or task, such as a graduation, a holiday, a party, a meal or a house move. It suits meal planning, money and home management, problem solving and decision-making. A family birthday party is used here as the example.

Inputs: the need is a celebration; the goal is a happy party for a child; the want is a particular cake; the human resources are time and help from relatives; the material resources are food, decorations and invitations; the money available sets the budget.
Throughputs: planning the guest list and the budget; organising who buys food, who prepares the room and who sends invitations; implementing the plan and adjusting for extra guests.
Outputs: whether the goal of a happy party was achieved, whether the money was kept within budget, whether members were satisfied, and what would improve the next event.
Feedback from the outputs is recorded so that the next party is planned more efficiently, which is why the framework is a cycle.

A decision is a choice of one course of action from a set of alternatives. Families make decisions all the time, so a clear method and the involvement of everyone affected make the management process work better.

The sequence of decision-making is: identify the problem or need, gather information, list the options, weigh each option against the goals and resources, choose one and act on it, then review the result.
Review after acting: check whether the decision achieved the goal, and record what should be done differently next time, so that evaluation gives lessons for the future.
Sharing information and ideas before a decision allows the family to allocate tasks fairly and to share values, views and concerns.
Decisions made with the views of all members help to resolve conflict and issues and build commitment to the outcome.
Decision-making helps the family achieve its goals and improves the efficiency of its work.
Discussion gives members a broader view of the issues, because each person sees the problem differently.
Decisions are easier when the family's values and goals have been agreed beforehand, because options can then be judged against them.
Communication is the sharing of information, ideas, values and concerns between family members. Without it, decisions made by one person never reach the people who have to carry them out.
Communication is needed at every stage: agreeing goals in the inputs, allocating tasks in organising, reporting progress in implementing and giving feedback.
Open discussion of what is and is not working provides the feedback that is used to evaluate the outputs.
Practical methods include a family discussion or meeting, notes, a shared written list, a shared calendar and messaging.

Poor communication leads to duplicated or missed tasks, misunderstandings and conflict, because members do not know what has been decided or who is responsible. A decision that is not communicated to every member can lead to duplicated work, missed tasks and conflict.
Families today live in many different ways, so a routine has to be planned around how the household actually works. Sharing the work fairly is what makes a routine last.

Modern patterns of living include two working adults, shift workers, lone-parent households, a parent working from home, and children in childcare or after-school activities, and routines must be fitted around these.
Work sharing: tasks such as cooking, shopping, laundry and cleaning are divided between members, so no one person carries the whole load.
Responsibility for family tasks: each member is given a defined task for which they are accountable, matched to age and ability.
Delegation: an adult passes a task to another member and gives them the instructions, time and resources needed to complete it, and trusts them to do it.
Gender equity: household tasks are shared on the basis of ability, availability and fairness rather than assigned by sex.
Checklists for routines: a daily or weekly checklist lists each task, who completes it and when it is due, so that nothing is forgotten.
Work schedules: a written timetable, such as a weekly cleaning rota or a meal planner, shows the sequence of tasks and who is responsible for each one.
Money is only one resource. Several others help a family run a good management system, and each makes its own contribution.
Time: allows planning and avoids waste; tasks are completed more efficiently when time is scheduled.
People: family members make and carry out decisions and tasks.
Skills and knowledge: support problem solving, healthy meals and budgeting.
Equipment: saves time and energy; a washing machine, for example, replaces hours of hand washing.
Human energy: allows tasks to be completed in an acceptable and harmonious way.

A family passes through a sequence of stages, and at each one its priorities, income and time change. Managing well means adjusting to the stage the family is in, because the same family needs different things as its members age.
The stages include a newly married couple, a family with young children, a family with school-going children, a family with teenagers and an older couple whose children have left home.
Young children need constant care, time, money and space for feeding and supervision, so childcare and daily routines become central to management, and free time is limited.
A parent who works fewer hours to care for young children often brings in a reduced income, which makes money tighter just as costs rise.
School-going children and teenagers raise costs for clothing, books, school costs, leisure and activities, and teenagers also need planning for further education.
Older children can take on tasks and join family decisions, which reduces the workload on parents. In short, as children get older they become part of the decision-making process.
Newly married couples and childless households often have more freedom, more flexible time and more income for leisure than families with young children.
Older people may have a reduced income after retirement and reduced mobility, or greater health needs, which affects choices about food, transport and housing.
Priorities differ for a family with children and a family without, because children add costs, tasks and decisions that a couple alone does not face.

Employment pattern means the number of family members working, whether inside or outside the home, the type of job and the hours worked. It matters because it decides how much money there is to manage and when family members are free to carry out tasks.
A dual-income household (two earners) has more money available but less time for housework and meal preparation.
A single-income household has less money to manage, so budgeting and prioritising essentials are more critical.
Full-time, part-time, job-sharing, flexible and seasonal hours each change when family members are available for tasks, so household work must be fitted around them.
Shift work and night work change meal times and sleep patterns, so family routines must be built around the shifts.
Commuting (the daily journey to work) uses time and money, which affects the family budget and the time left for household work.
Working from home, or a parent working abroad, changes how tasks and childcare are shared between family members.
A dual role means carrying two demands at once. This puts pressure on time and energy, so families need ways of managing it.
A dual role arises when both partners work outside the home, so extra planning is needed for childcare, meals and housework.
A lone-parent household has the extra demand of being both earner and parent, with no second adult to share tasks and decisions.
Sharing and delegating tasks spreads the workload, so no one person is overloaded.
Making a weekly plan or list, such as a weekly planning meeting or a shared calendar, helps the household stay organised and avoid missed tasks.
Using childcare and time-saving equipment frees time that would otherwise go on routine tasks.
Communicating regularly lets family members raise problems early and adjust the plan.
Culture and values both shape the decisions a family makes. Culture is what a group shares, while values are what the family itself believes matters most.
Culture is the shared customs, beliefs and way of life of a group. It affects family management through dress code, the food a family eats, religious practices, and festivals and celebrations.
Culture also shapes expectations of roles, such as who earns income, who cooks, and who cares for children and older relatives.
Culture can affect spending and the use of time, for example around religious festivals and family traditions, when money and time are set aside for them.
Values are a family's beliefs about what is important, such as health, education, family time, faith, sustainability, community or security.
Values determine the decisions a family takes, such as buying local food, choosing organic produce, reducing waste, how much to save, and how money and time are shared.
Values can change when circumstances change, for example after the illness of a family member, so the decisions that follow from them change too.
Standards are the quality a family expects of itself, and sex roles are what is expected of each partner. Both decide how much work there is and who does it.
Standards are the level of quality a family sets for its home, meals, appearance and finances, such as how clean the house is kept or how meals are presented.
Standards decide how much time, money and energy a task takes, because a higher standard means more effort.
High standards can cause strain and overload in a family short of time or money; very low standards can affect health and comfort.
Standards can be reviewed and adjusted when circumstances change, for example lowering a housework standard when time becomes short.
Sex roles (also called gender roles in papers) are the roles and behaviour expected of men and women in the household.

Traditionally men were the earners and women did most household work and caring. Roles are now increasingly equal, with partners sharing earning, childcare, cooking and cleaning, and tasks assigned on fairness rather than sex. Rotating tasks is one way to do this.
Sharing roles reduces overload and gives more equal decision-making. When one partner is expected to carry all household tasks, the workload becomes unfair and management is more strained.

Lifestyle is the way a family lives: its pattern of work, leisure, eating, spending and travel. The syllabus ties it to socio-economic status and family composition, because these shape the resources and needs a family has.

Socio-economic status is a family's position in society, based on income, occupation and education. Socio-economic status affects income, which sets the total resources available to the family and the choices it can make.
Families from lower socio-economic backgrounds tend to emphasise needs such as food, heating and housing, because income is limited.
Families from higher socio-economic backgrounds tend to have more scope for wants, luxuries, leisure and extra services.
Socio-economic group also influences educational opportunity and the type of job available, and so future income.

Family composition is the number of people in the family, the presence of members with special needs, such as a family member with a disability or an older relative needing care, and whether it is a one-parent or two-parent family.
A larger family needs more food, clothing, space and money, so budgets and meal plans must be scaled up.
A family member with a disability or special needs may raise household costs and reduce the time or ability of others to earn.
A lone parent has one income and one adult for all tasks, so management is more demanding.

A household is a group who share a home and make shared decisions about income, spending and saving. It is the basic financial unit of the economy, because everything the economy produces is ultimately bought, taxed or worked for by households.
Households spend on goods and services, which supports the businesses that supply them and the jobs those businesses provide.
Households pay taxes, which fund public services and State welfare payments.
Households buy property, and property purchases generate stamp duty, a tax that is income for the State.
Households supply the workforce: children who grow up in families become the future workers, so families that teach children money management also prepare the next generation.
Families usually run their finances independently, but they may need State aid, such as welfare payments or help from MABS, when income falls short of need.
Households receive money in different forms depending on whether, and how, their members work. The main sources are wages, salaries, pensions and State payments.
Wages: payment for hours worked or output, usually paid weekly or fortnightly, often for manual or hourly work. Because pay follows hours, a week with fewer hours means a smaller wage.
Salaries: a fixed annual amount paid in regular instalments, usually for non-manual or professional work, so the pay is the same each period.
Pensions: income after retirement from an employer's scheme, a personal pension fund or the State. Money paid into a pension while working is a voluntary deduction.
Social welfare allowances and benefits: payments made by the State to people who are unemployed, ill, disabled, caring, retired, widowed or raising children.
Other sources, in one line: profit from self-employment, rent from property, interest on savings, gifts and maintenance payments.
Two households with similar jobs can still have very different incomes. Age, gender, social class, culture and employment pattern all shape how much a household earns and what it must spend.
Age: income tends to rise with experience and promotion, then falls at retirement unless a pension has been arranged.
Age: teenagers can earn part-time income, which eases the financial strain on the family.

Gender: equal-pay law requires equal pay for the same work, but women are still under-represented in senior management, which men hold more of in many sectors. Women are also more likely to work part-time or take career breaks for caring.
Social class: low qualifications or early school leaving can lead to low pay or unemployment, while higher education widens access to better-paid work.
Culture: cultural attitudes shape whether women take paid work, which occupations are seen as suitable, and which spending priorities a household sets.
Employment pattern: the number of family members in paid work, and whether hours are full-time, part-time, job-sharing, flexible or seasonal, all change household income.
Disability, illness or addiction can reduce earning capacity and raise household costs, so income falls while spending needs rise.
The pay a person earns is not the pay they take home, because deductions are taken off first. Knowing which figure is which matters for both exams and household planning.
Gross income is income earned before any deductions are made.
Net income is take-home pay: gross income after deductions have been made.
Compulsory deductions from gross pay are PAYE, PRSI and USC. The law requires them, so the employee cannot choose to avoid them.

Voluntary deductions are chosen by the employee and include union subscriptions, pension contributions, additional voluntary contributions (AVCs, extra payments into a pension), health insurance, savings, social club fees and holiday fund payments.
Budgets are planned from net income, because net income is the money a household actually has to spend and save.
The three compulsory deductions each work differently and each pays for something different. Between them they take money from gross pay for the State.

PAYE (Pay As You Earn) is income tax deducted by the employer from each pay, based on the employee's earnings, and paid to the Revenue Commissioners (the State). It rises with income through a standard rate and a higher rate.
Revenue works out the employee's credits and rate band, and the employer uses these details to calculate the PAYE to deduct.
PAYE and USC go to the State to pay for public services such as health, education, roads and welfare.

PRSI (Pay Related Social Insurance) is a compulsory percentage of pay, so it is related to income. It is paid by the employee, through deduction, and separately by the employer, and it funds social insurance benefits.
Different PRSI classes exist, and self-employed people pay PRSI too. Employees earning below a set threshold are exempt from paying employee PRSI.
USC (Universal Social Charge) is a compulsory charge on gross income, calculated at rates that rise in bands as income rises. It is separate from income tax.
Employees with gross income below a set threshold are exempt from paying USC.
A tax credit lowers the tax bill itself, so it is worth the same as an equal amount of tax saved. It is not a reduction in the pay the tax is worked out on.
A tax credit reduces the amount of income tax a person has to pay. Examples are the personal credit and the employee (PAYE) credit.
Income tax is worked out on gross income first, and the person's tax credits are then subtracted from the tax calculated. A credit does not reduce income before tax is worked out.
Revenue works out the employee's credits and standard rate cut-off point (the income up to which the lower rate applies), and the employer uses them when deducting PAYE.
Tax credits do not reduce the USC, which is charged separately on gross income.
The State pays welfare in two ways. One is earned through PRSI contributions; the other is paid from taxes to people who do not qualify for the first, and it checks their means.
Social insurance payments are paid to people who have made the minimum PRSI contributions, so the person has earned them, and they are not means tested.
Examples of social insurance payments: Jobseeker's Benefit, Illness Benefit, Maternity Benefit, Carer's Benefit and the contributory State pension.
Social assistance payments are paid from taxes to people whose PRSI contributions are insufficient to qualify for social insurance payments, and they are means tested.

Examples of social assistance payments: Jobseeker's Allowance, Disability Allowance, Carer's Allowance and the non-contributory State pension. Carer's Benefit is the PRSI-based alternative to Carer's Allowance.
A means test assesses the claimant's income and capital (usually including a partner's) against a set limit. The payment is reduced or refused as means rise above it.
Some payments follow neither pattern exactly. A universal payment is paid to everyone who meets one condition, without a means test or a contribution record.
Child Benefit: a monthly universal payment for each qualifying child. It is not means tested and does not depend on PRSI contributions.
Working Family Payment: a weekly payment to employees on low pay who have children, and means tested against a family-size income limit. It replaced the name Family Income Supplement.
Supplementary Welfare Allowance: means tested, and paid to people whose means cannot meet their basic needs or those of their dependants.
Supplementary Welfare Allowance can also be a temporary payment for people awaiting another benefit while their claim is being processed.
Maternity Benefit: a social insurance payment for employees on maternity leave.
Other payments a student may name: Carer's Allowance, Disability Allowance, Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance and Fuel Allowance.
There are two State pensions for older people, and the difference between them is the same as the difference between social insurance and social assistance.
The contributory State pension (formerly called the old age pension) is based on the claimant's record of PRSI contributions.
The contributory pension is not means tested, so other income does not normally remove entitlement to it.
The non-contributory State pension is means-tested social assistance for an older person who lacks enough PRSI contributions.
Eligibility for the non-contributory pension depends on means and on residence conditions, including habitual residence in the State (a settled, normal home there).

Expenditure is the money a household spends, and income sets the limit on it. Spending that goes beyond income leads to debt, so spending must be matched to income, and many factors shape how a household divides its money.

Low-income households spend most of their income on essentials such as housing, food and heat, and a larger proportion on food than richer households do, so they have little or no discretionary spending (spending on non-essentials) or saving.

Higher-income households spend more in total and a bigger share on discretionary items such as leisure, holidays and eating out, so they have more discretionary income (money left after essentials) and can also save and pay for credit.
Family size and composition matter, for example the number of children and whether it is a one-parent or two-parent household, because each extra person adds to food, clothing and housing needs.
The stage of the family life cycle changes priorities: young children add costs for food, clothing, childcare and schooling, while teenagers cost more for food, clothing and education.
Once children are independent and at retirement, spending falls and shifts towards health, leisure and heating; older children can also help decide and manage spending.

Employment affects money, travel time and cost, and meal and sleep patterns. Working outside the home adds travel, convenience food and childcare costs, and shift work changes meal and sleep patterns and transport costs.

Urban and rural location change patterns, for example through transport costs and housing costs: rural households depend more on cars, while urban rents and mortgages are higher. Heating costs also differ.

Other influences include socio-economic class and the gender of the earner, personal values and priorities, health or special needs, advertising and peer pressure (the influence of friends and others the same age).
Not all spending is equally urgent. Households divide it into what they must pay to manage family life and what they can choose to spend once the necessities are covered.

Essential expenditure is spending on necessities needed to manage family life, such as housing (rent or mortgage), utilities (electricity, heating), food, clothing, transport, insurance, medical bills, loan repayments and household bills.
Discretionary expenditure is spending on non-essentials, made only after essential expenditure and savings have been provided for.
Examples of discretionary expenditure: holidays, entertainment, alcohol, cosmetics, eating out, leisure and gym membership, and streaming services.
Fixed essential costs stay the same amount at regular times each week or month, such as rent or a mortgage repayment, insurance and telephone bills, so they are easy to plan for.

Irregular essential costs vary in amount or timing, such as clothing, doctor's bills, school expenses and car repairs, so a budget must set money aside for them. Some are also seasonal, such as heating, Christmas and back to school.

Whether an item is essential depends on the household. The same item can be essential for one household and discretionary for another, for example a car for a rural family compared with a city family.
Credit repayments are fixed commitments in the budget, and credit used for essentials adds to future spending because it must be paid back.

A budget is a plan that sets expected net income against planned spending for a period such as a week, month or year. Following a series of steps means essentials are paid first and money is left for savings.
1. List all income, using net (take-home) income, never gross, because net income is the money actually available to spend. Include wages, welfare, maintenance and any other income.
2. List planned fixed, irregular and discretionary expenditure for each week or month, including credit repayments, and choose the time period the budget will cover.
3. Plan essential needs first, such as rent or mortgage and household bills, before any discretionary spending, so the necessities are always covered.
4. Allocate money for short-term and long-term savings, and for emergencies, so unexpected costs do not have to be borrowed.
5. Allow for personal spending and special occasions such as Christmas and holidays, and for changes in circumstances, so these annual costs do not cause a shortfall.
6. Keep bills and receipts, and record one month of actual spending to find where overspending occurs.

7. Compare income with expenditure and adjust. A surplus (income greater than spending) can be saved; a deficit (spending greater than income) means cutting discretionary spending, raising income or seeking advice, rather than borrowing.
8. Review the budget regularly, and change it when family circumstances or income change, so it stays realistic.
When a budget shows overspending or a deficit, a household can cut costs without going without essentials. The savings come from shopping smarter and using less.
Use a shopping list and stick to it, because this avoids impulse buying of items you did not plan to purchase.
Choose own-brand goods and compare prices between shops, since similar goods can cost much less.
Buy second-hand or in charity shops, use sales, and buy food in season, when it is cheaper and plentiful.
Cook from scratch and choose cheaper cuts of meat, because convenience foods and prime cuts cost more.
Cut energy use and switch supplier to reduce utility bills.
Cancel unused subscriptions, such as gym membership or streaming services, so you are not paying for things you do not use.
A budget does more than record numbers. It shows a household where its money goes and helps it avoid problems before they happen.
Budgeting shows where money goes, and identifies overspending and impulse buying before they lead to unplanned debt.
Budgeting reduces reliance on credit and supports a good credit record, because bills and repayments are planned for and paid on time.
A budget gives financial security and reduces the worry and stress caused by unpaid bills, because it ensures bills are paid.
A budget that allows some saving can provide for emergencies and cover unexpected events, such as job loss or an urgent repair.
Budgeting helps a household reach its goals, because money is set aside for them.
Budgeting builds money-management skills that transfer to independent living.

A sample budget shows how a net income can be divided between headings so that every euro is planned. The first sample is a family of two adults and two children with a combined net income of 900 euro a week.
Housing, the largest fixed essential cost, is allocated about a quarter of income (25 per cent): 225 euro.
Food is allocated about a quarter of income (25 per cent): 225 euro, because food needs rise with growing children.
Household bills are allocated about 15 per cent of income: 135 euro. Education is allocated about 10 per cent: 90 euro, to cover school costs.
Clothing, leisure, savings, health and discretionary spending are each allocated about 5 per cent: 45 euro each, with savings kept for emergencies.
A second sample, 800 euro a week for the same type of family, gives 200 euro for housing, 200 for food, 120 for household bills, 80 for education and 40 for each of the five 5 per cent headings.
The totals must add up to the net income, so the plan allocates the full net income, leaves no money unplanned, and is reviewed each month.
The percentages are a planning guide for this sample, not a rule, and should be adjusted to the family's actual fixed costs.
A lower income cannot cover the same percentages, so essentials come first while discretionary spending and savings shrink; a higher income allows more savings.
Households that are in debt, or at risk of it, can get free help from MABS. It advises and negotiates for them but does not lend money or pay their debts.
MABS is a free, confidential and independent service for people in debt or at risk of debt, funded by the State through the Citizens Information Board.
MABS helps a household work out its income and spending, and draws up a realistic budget and repayment plan (schedule) with the family.
MABS negotiates with lenders, including moneylenders and mortgage lenders, on behalf of households in debt.

MABS offers a mortgage arrears service, and advises on personal insolvency (when a person cannot pay their debts) and income maximisation, which means checking and claiming entitlements to State supports.
MABS advises on financial products and interest rates, and points to cheaper sources of credit such as credit unions.
MABS also teaches money-management skills, so households can manage their budgets themselves in future.
A household can pay for what it buys in several ways. Each method moves money differently, and knowing how each works lets you match the method to the purchase.

Cash: immediate payment in notes and coins. It is fast, costs nothing and shows exactly what has been spent, but carrying large amounts is unsafe, it leaves no record, and it cannot be used for online or distance purchases.

Cheque: a written order to the bank to pay a sum from the account to a named person. It requires a current account, takes time to clear, and can be refused if there are not enough funds. Cheques are used less now but are still examined.

Debit card: the amount is taken from the bank account straight away, so spending stays within the balance. It works by contactless or chip and PIN, and can be used online, for cashback and for ATM withdrawals.

Credit card: goods are bought now and paid for later, up to a credit limit. A minimum monthly payment is required, there is an interest-free period if the balance is cleared by the due date, and interest applies to any balance not cleared.
The card issuer may also protect some credit card purchases.
Direct debit: the account holder authorises a company or utility to take money from the account on a due date. The amount can vary, which suits bills such as utilities and insurance.

Standing order: the account holder instructs the bank to make a fixed payment at regular intervals to a named payee, such as rent, savings or loan repayments. The difference from direct debit is that the amount is fixed and the account holder controls the payment.

Online or mobile banking and payment apps: payments, bill payments and transfers made from a bank account through a computer or phone. They are convenient and keep a record, but need internet access and care with security.
Prepaid methods, gift vouchers and store credit are other ways to pay, where the money is paid in advance or held by one retailer.
No single method is best for every purchase. A household compares methods against a set of criteria, then picks the one that suits the item and its own situation.
Cost: whether the method charges fees or interest, since this adds to the price of the goods.
Security: the risk of loss, theft or fraud, and whether the method leaves a record of the payment, which a cash payment does not.
Convenience: speed of payment, the ability to pay at a distance or online, and ease of budgeting.
Availability: whether the retailer or service provider accepts the method, and whether the buyer holds the card or account needed.
Control: whether the buyer can see and limit spending, which is easier with cash or a debit card than with credit, because credit lets you spend money you do not yet have.
Size of purchase: cash suits small everyday purchases, while credit or instalment methods suit large, expensive items the household cannot pay for at once, so the cost is spread.
Credit means obtaining goods, services or money now and paying later, usually with interest or charges. Households can use several different forms, each suited to a different need.
Credit card: a revolving credit facility (borrowing that can be reused as you repay) with a credit limit. It can offer an interest-free period if the full balance is paid on time.
Charge card: the full balance is due each month, and no interest is charged on it because it is repaid in full.
Store card: credit offered by a retailer, usable for purchases in that shop. It is usually costly.
Overdraft: the bank allows the current account balance to go below zero up to an agreed limit, with interest charged on the amount overdrawn. It is short-term and flexible but can be costly.

Personal or term loan from a bank, credit union or other lender: a fixed sum borrowed and repaid in fixed instalments over a set period at an agreed interest rate. It suits one-off large purchases such as a car.
Credit union loan: members can borrow from the credit union, usually after building up a savings record. Credit unions often have lower rates.
Other forms named in marking schemes: a budget account (spreads household bills), a credit sale, a moneylender (a licensed lender, usually very expensive) and a mortgage (a loan for house purchase).
Hire purchase lets a household use an expensive item straight away while paying for it over time. It is different from buying on a credit card, because ownership does not pass to the buyer at once.
Hire purchase combines hiring and buying: the buyer pays a deposit and then instalments over an agreed period, and uses the goods straight away.
The goods belong to the finance company until the final payment is made, so the buyer is only the hirer until then. Ownership passes to the buyer only at the last payment.
Once one-third or more of the total hire-purchase price has been paid, counting the deposit, instalments and the value of any trade-in, the owner cannot repossess the goods without a court order.
Before that point the owner must follow a procedure, including a default notice and time for the buyer to put things right. The buyer may also end the agreement.
Advantages: the goods can be used immediately, repayments are fixed and the cost is spread across instalments, so no large lump sum is needed.
Disadvantages: interest can make the total cost much higher than the cash price, and the buyer does not own the goods until the end.
Missed payments can lead to repossession. The goods may also lose value faster than the debt falls.
Credit nearly always costs more than paying cash. To decide whether it is worth it, a household has to work out exactly how much extra it will pay.
Total cash price: the price of the goods if they are paid for in full at the time of purchase.
Total amount repayable: the deposit plus all the instalments paid under the credit agreement.
Cost of credit: the total amount repayable minus the cash price. It is the extra paid for the convenience of credit, so do not say the cost of credit is the total repayable.
Annual percentage rate (APR): the yearly cost of borrowing, as a percentage, including charges. Because every lender must express cost the same way, it allows different credit offers to be compared.
To compare cash and credit, the household adds all the payments, subtracts the cash price to find the cost of credit, and decides whether the immediate use of the goods is worth that extra cost.
Credit can solve a real problem for a household, but it also carries costs and risks. Exam answers need both sides, each linked to the household.
Advantages: goods are available immediately, and large purchases become affordable because the cost is spread.
Advantages: credit can cover urgent or emergency costs, such as an emergency repair, and avoids the need to carry large amounts of cash, which is safer.
Advantages: loan repayments are fixed over a set period, so the cost is predictable, and a household can take advantage of sales. A good repayment record also helps later borrowing.
Disadvantages: interest makes goods cost more than the cash price, and high interest is charged if the credit balance is not repaid in full.
Disadvantages: credit makes overspending and impulse buying easier, and several credit agreements at once increase the risk of unmanageable debt.
Disadvantages: missed repayments can lead to penalties, repossession or a poor credit record, which makes future borrowing harder.
Before signing a credit agreement, a household should check that the borrowing is sensible and that it can afford it. These are the questions to ask.
Whether the purchase is needed, because credit makes it easy to buy things that are only wanted.
The total cost, the interest rate and the APR, so that the offer can be compared with others and with the cash price.
The repayment amount and the length of the agreement, because a longer period usually means more interest in total.
Fees and penalties for missed payments.
Ownership, and what happens if repayments are missed, for example repossession under hire purchase.
Whether the repayments fit the household budget.
The Consumer Credit Act 1995 (as amended) is the law that protects people who borrow or buy on credit. It sets rules for lenders, so consumers know what they are agreeing to.

The Act protects consumers who buy on credit, including through hire purchase and other credit agreements. It regulates lenders, moneylenders and credit advertising, and the Central Bank of Ireland regulates the sector.
A credit agreement must be in writing and signed, and must set out the APR and the terms of repayment. The consumer must be given a copy.
The consumer has a short cooling-off period of 10 days after receiving a copy of the agreement to withdraw from it in writing.
Credit advertisements must be accurate and must show the APR, so offers can be compared.
For hire purchase, once one-third or more of the total price has been paid, the goods cannot be repossessed without a court order.

Where to get help: MABS (the Money Advice and Budgeting Service) and the Central Bank's consumer hub, the CCPC, and the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman for complaints about a bank or lender.

Saving means setting aside part of your income for future use instead of spending it, and it takes planning, such as a budget or paying yourself first. A household that saves is better prepared for what life brings.
Saving reduces financial worry and gives the household security against unexpected costs, because there is money to fall back on.
A savings fund covers emergencies, such as job loss, illness or an urgent repair, so the household does not have to borrow.
Regular saving allows the household to plan for expensive items or events, such as a holiday, a car, education, a wedding or a deposit for a home, without using credit.
Saving avoids the need for loans and credit agreements, and so avoids the interest charged on them.
Money held in a suitable scheme earns interest (the payment a bank or other institution makes for holding your money) and grows over time.
Saving for retirement means the household has an income to live on once work stops.
Saving sets a good example for children and builds a sound financial reputation for the family, as well as independence.
Teenagers who save regularly gain financial independence, build a habit, gain security, can reach future goals and avoid credit.
How long you plan to save for decides what kind of scheme suits you, because the two aims need different things from an account.
Short-term saving, for an emergency or a planned spend within a year, needs easy access, so the money can be reached when it is needed.
Long-term saving, for retirement or a house, can accept restricted access in return for higher interest, because the money is not needed soon.
Higher interest generally means less access or more risk, so a saver always gives something up for a better rate.
Banks and building societies offer several kinds of savings account. They differ mainly in how quickly you can reach your money and how much interest you earn in return.
A current account is for everyday spending, not for saving.
Demand deposit account: money can be withdrawn on demand (instantly), so it suits short-term saving and an emergency fund, although the interest is low.
Notice account: withdrawals require a set period of notice, and the interest paid is usually higher than on a demand deposit account, because the institution can plan around when money leaves.
Term deposit (fixed-term deposit): money is locked away for an agreed period at a fixed rate, and early withdrawal usually reduces or loses the interest, or is refused.
Regular saver account: a fixed monthly deposit is made into an account that pays a higher rate in return for regular saving.
State Savings products are run by the National Treasury Management Agency and sold through An Post, the Post Office. Because the State stands behind them, they are among the safest places to save.
Instalment saving scheme: a fixed amount is saved each month over a set period, and the money is then left to earn interest for a further period.
Savings certificates: a fixed-term product paying interest higher than an ordinary deposit account, with interest reduced if the certificate is cashed in early.
Savings bonds: a fixed-term product, so the money is tied up for the term in return for a better return. Early withdrawal reduces or removes the interest earned.
Prize Bonds give a chance to win prizes rather than earning interest.
Returns on fixed-term products and instalment savings are not subject to DIRT or income tax, which means the saver keeps the whole return.
State Savings are backed by the State, so there is no loss of capital (the money you put in).
A credit union is a different kind of saving institution, owned by the people who save in it rather than by outside shareholders.
A credit union is a member-owned, non-profit co-operative serving a local or work-based community (a common bond), and its share and saver accounts are run for its members.
Members can usually save small amounts regularly, often by payroll deduction, which suits a low-income family.
Credit union shares earn a dividend, not interest, paid at the end of the year if the credit union can afford it, so the dividend is not guaranteed.
Members with a savings record find it easier to qualify for a low-cost credit union loan.
Credit union deposits are protected by the Deposit Guarantee Scheme.
Money can also go into products that aim for a higher return, but these carry risk and are not the same as saving.
Shares and investment funds, pensions (PRSA, occupational pension, AVCs) and property can give a higher return, but their value can fall.
They are not suited to an emergency fund, because the money may be worth less when it is needed.
Equity-linked products risk loss of capital, whereas savings keep capital safe.
Before choosing where to save, the household needs to know how safe the money is if an institution fails.
The Deposit Guarantee Scheme protects deposits in banks, building societies and credit unions authorised in Ireland, up to a limit of 100,000 euro per person per institution.
State Savings are backed by the State, so their security does not depend on a guarantee limit.
Investment funds and shares in companies are not covered by the Deposit Guarantee Scheme, so they can lose value.
No scheme is best on every count. A saver compares schemes against a set of criteria and picks the one that fits the household's need.
Security: how safe the money is, shown by a State or deposit guarantee, the stability of the institution, and the risk of loss with investments.
Interest: the rate paid, whether it is fixed or variable, and how often it is paid.
The annual equivalent rate (AER) shows the yearly return including the effect of compounding, so different schemes can be compared fairly.
Compounding means interest is paid on earlier interest, so a longer-term deposit grows faster than the simple rate suggests.

Access: how quickly and at what cost money can be withdrawn (instant, notice or fixed term), whether penalties apply, and whether the account is by branch or online, with its opening hours and location.

Tax: Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) is deducted from interest on most bank, building society and credit union deposits before the saver receives it, while State Savings fixed-term products are exempt. Net return matters, not only the headline rate.
Other factors: minimum or regular deposit, fees, convenience, and whether the scheme suits the family's goal and income. A low-income family needs small deposits and easy access.
The criteria only help once they are tied to what the household is saving for, so a good answer links the purpose to a scheme.
Emergency fund: a demand deposit or credit union share account, because money must be reachable at once.
Holiday within a year: a demand or notice account.
Long-term lump sum: a term deposit or State Savings fixed term, because the money can be locked away for higher interest.
Regular small amounts: a credit union, regular saver or instalment savings.
Purpose: short-term access suits emergencies, and longer-term schemes suit planned spending.
Some events, such as a fire or a serious illness, cost far more than most households could pay at once. Insurance solves this by sharing the cost of those events across many people.

Insurance spreads the financial risk of an event, such as death, illness, fire or theft, across many people who each pay a premium. Only the few who suffer a loss are paid, out of the pool everyone has paid into.
The insured (the person covered, also called the policyholder) pays a premium to the insurer, and the insurer pays a stated sum when the insured event occurs.
Cover applies only to the events named in the policy, so an event the policy does not list is not paid for.
Insurance protects a household against a large, unexpected cost that it could not otherwise meet, for example illness, fire, theft or an accident.

Insurance pays the loss and not a profit, and the policyholder must give full and honest information when buying. Reading the policy and comparing quotes before buying helps you choose the right cover.
Exam questions ask you to explain the everyday words of insurance. Each one names a different person or part of the arrangement, so keep them apart.
Premium: the sum paid annually or in instalments to the insurance company to keep a policy in force. It is what you pay in.
Policy: the written document, a contract, setting out the terms and conditions of the cover, including what is covered and what is excluded.
Insurer: the insurance company that accepts the risk and pays claims.

Broker: an agent who advises the consumer on insurance and arranges cover with several insurance companies. A broker is paid by commission or a fee. This differs from an agent of one company, or buying direct from the insurer.
Claim: a request to the insurer for payment after a loss. Excess is the part of a claim that the policyholder pays. The sum assured (or sum insured) is the most the insurer will pay out.

The premium depends on the risk: age, health, claims history, location, the value of what is insured and security measures such as alarms all matter. The cover and excess you choose also change it, and a no-claims bonus lowers car premiums.
PRSI is the State's own insurance scheme. It works like insurance because contributions made while working protect you against losing income later.

PRSI is the State's social insurance scheme. Workers (employees, employers and the self-employed) pay contributions, related to pay, into the Social Insurance Fund. Entitlement to its benefits depends on a record of contributions, not on means.
PRSI is a compulsory scheme set by law, not a private policy chosen by the individual. It is State-run and its benefits are not paid by an insurer, whereas private insurance is voluntary and private.

PRSI-linked payments include Jobseeker's Benefit, Illness Benefit, maternity benefit, Carer's Benefit and the contributory State pension. Others are the widow's or widower's pension and treatment benefit for dental and optical care.
It counts as insurance because contributions pay for protection against loss of income through unemployment, illness, retirement, bereavement or maternity.
Different PRSI classes carry different benefits, and low earners may be exempt from paying.
The public health system is available to everyone, but some people want more choice or quicker treatment. Private health insurance is a voluntary policy that pays towards those costs.
Private health insurance pays towards hospital, consultant and other medical costs, within the terms of the policy. It is voluntary and held alongside the public health system.
Advantages: choice of private or semi-private hospital accommodation, help with consultant fees, and shorter waiting times for some treatment.

Cover can include access to outpatient clinics, day-care, convalescence (recovery time) after treatment, some GP fees, some dental and optical cover, and treatment abroad. It also gives peace of mind.
Premiums may qualify for tax relief at source, which reduces the cost of cover.
When choosing a plan, compare the level of cover, premiums, excess, waiting periods, hospital choice and what is excluded. Compare insurers and plans.
Premiums are set by plan, not by your health (community rating), but joining late costs more.
Providers include Vhi (the largest), Laya, Irish Life Health and Level Health. The regulator is the Health Insurance Authority.
A household faces several different risks: damage to the home, loss of belongings, a car accident, trips abroad. Each has its own type of cover.
Buildings insurance covers the structure of the home (walls, roof, fixtures) against damage such as fire, storm, flood and subsidence. Mortgage lenders usually require it.

Contents insurance covers furniture, appliances, clothes, valuables and personal belongings against loss or damage such as theft and fire. An all-risks extension covers items outside the home, such as phones and bicycles.
Buildings and contents cover can be combined in one household policy, which may also include public liability and temporary accommodation.

Car insurance: third-party cover is required by law before a car is driven on public roads. It covers damage and injury to other people, not the policyholder's own car. Third party, fire and theft adds cover for those events, and comprehensive covers the most.

Travel insurance covers medical costs, cancelled trips and lost luggage abroad. Mobile phone insurance covers loss, theft or damage to a phone. Income protection, holiday, public liability and pet insurance are other types.
Insure for the correct value, because underinsurance means a reduced payout. Keep an inventory and receipts, state security measures, keep the policy up to date and report claims promptly.
Death is certain to happen, so this cover is called assurance rather than insurance. It pays a sum so that dependants are looked after if the insured person dies.
Life assurance pays a lump sum to the insured person's family or beneficiary (dependants) on death, either during the policy term or after it, depending on the type.
Term assurance covers a set period and pays only if death occurs within that period. There is no payout if the insured survives, and it is generally the cheapest type.
Whole-of-life assurance lasts for life, as long as premiums are paid, and pays an agreed sum on death whenever it occurs. It is dearer than term cover.
Endowment assurance pays a sum at the end of a set term or on earlier death, combining cover with saving.

A mortgage protection policy is term assurance taken out with a mortgage. Its sum assured falls with the mortgage balance, so if the insured dies before the mortgage is repaid, the debt is cleared. Lenders normally require it.

Convertible term assurance can be converted into a longer-term policy, such as whole-of-life, during the term without a new health check. Serious illness cover and income protection are related cover.
Benefits of life assurance: financial security for dependants after a premature death, help clearing a mortgage or debts, and peace of mind. Some policies can be cashed in or act as savings.
Every purchase starts with how much a household can spend. Income sets the limit, and it also decides whether a household buys what it needs or what it merely wants.
Household income sets the limit on spending, so a household on a tight budget compares unit prices (the price per kilo or per item), buys own-brand and bulk items, and delays non-essential purchases.

Disposable income is the money left after tax and essential bills. It decides how much is free for discretionary spending (spending that is a choice, not a necessity) such as eating out or branded clothing.
When income rises, households often trade up to branded or higher-quality goods; when it falls, they trade down to cheaper alternatives.
Essential needs such as food, heating and shelter are bought first, and luxury wants are the first to be cut when income falls.
A needs-based decision is guided by necessity and income. A wants-based decision is more open to advertising and impulse buying.
Credit and easy-pay arrangements can allow spending above current income, and the debt they create reduces future choice because part of later income is already committed.
Beyond money, choices reflect who the buyer is, who influences them and what the product offers. For a large purchase such as a washing machine, buyers weigh several of these together.
Personal preference, and values and lifestyle (health, convenience, ethical concerns, and cultural or religious practice), all influence what is bought.
Household composition narrows choice: family size, life-cycle stage and special diets, such as a coeliac or diabetic member or an allergy, determine which goods are suitable.
Time pressure pushes busy households towards convenience foods, takeaway meals and online shopping, because these save time.
Other people influence choice through word of mouth, sales staff, peers and current trends.

For a large purchase, buyers weigh the energy rating, reliability of the brand, ease of use and design, size or capacity for the family, purchase and running cost, quality marks, after-sales service and guarantee, and whether to pay cash or use credit.
The environmental impact of a product or its packaging is a modern factor that some consumers weigh when choosing.

Impulse buying is an unplanned purchase triggered by a display, an offer or an item at the checkout. It results from several of the factors above, such as advertising, values and income, working together.
Shoppers often choose by name rather than by comparing every product. Brands and own-brand goods are the two main kinds of product on the shelf, and they differ in price and in how they are promoted.
A brand is a name, logo or design that identifies a manufacturer's product and distinguishes it from competing goods.
Branded goods are made by a manufacturer and are usually advertised nationally, so they tend to cost more than equivalent goods.
Own-brand goods are sold under the retailer's own name. They are often cheaper because the retailer avoids the cost of national advertising.
Brand loyalty is habitual repeat buying of one brand, which saves the shopper the effort of comparing alternatives.
Advertising is communication that informs consumers about goods and services and tries to create a want for them. It happens mostly outside the shop, in the media a consumer meets every day.
Advertising makes people aware of new products and builds brand loyalty, so that consumers ask for the product by name.
It also informs consumers about features, price and offers.
Media used include television, radio, print, outdoor billboards, websites, social media, and sponsorship of sport and events.
Celebrity endorsement transfers the image or popularity of a well-known person to the product.
Product differentiation: advertising highlights a feature, such as a special ingredient, that sets one brand apart from similar goods.
Advertising can make people feel they need products they cannot afford, and it can encourage impulse buying and the use of credit.
Advertising aimed at children and teenagers is especially influential. It can prompt impulse purchases and family purchases, because young consumers have less experience of judging value.
The advantage to the consumer is awareness of choice and information. The disadvantages are that the cost of advertising is added to the price, claims can exaggerate, and there is pressure to buy.

Merchandising is the arrangement and presentation of goods in a shop to encourage consumers to buy more, and to buy more often. It is what the retailer does inside the shop, in contrast to advertising.

Store layout: goods are arranged in clearly identifiable departments with space to browse, and essentials such as bread and milk are placed at the back so that shoppers pass other products on the way to them.
Route design: aisles are arranged to keep shoppers moving through the store, so that they see more products and spend longer browsing.

Product placement: complementary goods are shelved together, such as biscuits beside tea, so that buying one reminds the shopper of the other. Sweets and magazines are placed at the checkout as impulse items.
Shelf position: premium or luxury goods are placed at eye level, where they are seen first, while cheaper products are often placed on lower or higher shelves.
Special offers displayed at the end of aisles draw attention to promotional stock.
In-store stimuli: background music that slows the pace of shopping, aromas such as freshly baked bread, good lighting and warmth, and colourful displays.
Sampling and demonstrations let shoppers taste or try a product before buying it, which makes a purchase more likely.

Pricing techniques make a price look lower, or make a purchase look more valuable, than it is. Discount offers and discount stores do lower the cost, but the consumer should still compare total value.
Charm pricing: a price set just below a round figure, so that the item appears cheaper than it is.
Multi-buy offers, such as three items for a set price, encourage consumers to buy more than they would at a single-item price.
Clearance and reduction labels suggest extra value and can prompt impulse buying of goods the shopper did not plan to buy.
Loss leaders: a well-known product is sold at or below cost to draw shoppers into the store, who then buy other items at normal prices.
Coupons and money-off vouchers reward a specific purchase and are often distributed through loyalty schemes or advertising.
Discount offers, and discount stores, lower the cost of goods, but a lower price is not always better value, so the consumer should still compare total value.
Loyalty schemes reward repeat custom with points or discounts, and give retailers information about what customers buy. They are one of the shopping systems named in the syllabus.
Customers earn points or tokens for each amount spent. The points are exchanged for money off goods, vouchers or goods after a set period.
Examples in Ireland include the Tesco Clubcard and the Dunnes Stores ValueClub card.
Schemes encourage saving for special occasions, such as Christmas, by building up points over time.
Shoppers may spend more to reach a reward target, and points can take priority over price when they compare shops, so they return to the same shop.
Card use gives retailers data on buying patterns, which helps them target offers and plan stock.
Disadvantages: the scheme discourages shopping around, can lead to unplanned purchases, and ties the shopper to one shop. It also requires the card to be carried.
Easy-pay arrangements spread the cost of a purchase over time, so goods can be bought without paying the full price at once. This is a form of credit, which has both benefits and costs.
Easy-pay schemes: a retailer or utility company lets the consumer pay for goods or a bill in instalments over a set period.
Hire purchase: the consumer uses the goods while paying instalments under an agreement, and ownership passes only when the final instalment is paid.

Hire purchase is governed by the Consumer Credit Act 1995, which requires a written agreement showing the cash price, the cost of credit and the APR (annual percentage rate, the yearly cost of the credit), and gives the consumer a cooling-off period of ten days.
Advantages of credit: goods can be used immediately, the cost is spread over time, larger items become affordable, and essentials can be bought in an emergency when cash is not available.
Disadvantages: the total cost is higher than the cash price because of interest and charges, easy-pay can encourage buying of non-essential goods and overspending, and the debt reduces future choice.
Both allow shopping from home, but the consumer cannot inspect the goods before buying them.
Television buying: goods are demonstrated on screen and ordered by phone or online, often with a limited-time offer that creates urgency.
Mail order: goods are chosen from a catalogue, leaflet or website and delivered by post or courier.
Advantages of mail order: it is convenient for people without time to shop, a wide range is available, there is no travel, and orders can be placed by post or phone.
Disadvantages of mail order: goods cannot be seen, touched or tried on, delivery can take weeks, and postage adds to the cost.

Distance purchases (those made without meeting the seller) carry a statutory right to cancel within a cooling-off period under the Consumer Rights Act 2022, because the buyer could not see the goods before ordering.
Online shopping offers convenience and easy price comparison, but adds risks around payment, delivery and personal data.
Advantages: access at any hour from home, easy comparison of prices across retailers, a wider range, customer reviews, and delivery to the door.
Disadvantages: goods cannot be seen or handled before purchase, and delivery can be delayed or carry extra charges.

Payment risk: card details can be taken through phishing emails (fake messages that trick people into giving details) or fake websites, so pay only on secure sites that show a padlock symbol and an address beginning https.
Keep records of the order, so that there is proof of what was bought and paid for if something goes wrong.
Overspending risk: stored card details and one-click ordering make impulse purchases quick and easy.
Retailers collect data on browsing and buying, which can be used to target advertising at the individual consumer.
Packaging does more than wrap a product. It protects the goods, carries information, and helps to sell the product.
Packaging protects and preserves the product, so food stays safe and goods are not damaged on the way to the shop or home.
It informs the shopper, because the pack carries the name, instructions and other details.
It attracts attention on the shelf and conveys quality through colour, shape and design.
It gives convenience, such as portion size and easy-open features, and it suggests quality.
Care labels and safety or hazard symbols on non-food goods, for example on household cleaning agents, explain how to use the product and prevent accidents.
Labels on pre-packed foods are a legal requirement, so shoppers can choose safely and compare products. The detail is kept short here and is consumer-focused.

Mandatory food labels show the name of the food, ingredients listed in descending order of weight (the heaviest first), net quantity, a use-by or best-before date, storage conditions and instructions for use, and the name and address of the food business.
Use-by dates apply to highly perishable foods and the food is unsafe after the date; best-before dates indicate quality, and the food may still be safe after them.
The 14 major allergens must be emphasised in the ingredients list, for example in bold or capitals, so that people with allergies can spot them quickly.

A nutrition declaration gives energy and the amounts of fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt. The per 100 g (or 100 ml) figure is mandatory, while the per-portion figure is optional.
The country of origin must be shown where the law requires it.
Claims such as low fat, light or high fibre may be made only where the product meets defined criteria.

Quality marks and symbols help consumers choose. The Bord Bia Quality Mark for Irish food shows that a product meets a defined standard, and the gluten-free symbol and allergen emphasis help people with special diets.
EU food information rules are set out in Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
A retail outlet is a business that sells goods to the public. Outlets are grouped into classes by ownership, range of goods and pricing policy, and each class suits a different kind of shopper.

Independent retailer: a single, locally owned shop, such as a butcher, jeweller or boutique, offering personal service and a specialised range. Advantage: personal service. Disadvantage: higher prices and a smaller range.

Chain store (multiple retailer): several outlets under one owner, selling a standard range and buying in bulk, such as Penneys or Dunnes Stores. Buying in bulk lets the owner pass on lower costs to shoppers.

Supermarket: a self-service store (shoppers pick items themselves) selling a wide range of food and household goods, such as Tesco, SuperValu or Centra. Advantage: wide range and one-stop shopping. Disadvantage: it is impersonal.
Department store: a large store divided into departments selling clothing, household goods and cosmetics, such as Brown Thomas or Arnotts. Advantage: range and quality. Disadvantage: higher prices.

Discount store: a store selling a limited range at low prices, kept low by minimal service and fast turnover of stock (goods sell quickly and are replaced), such as Dealz or Aldi. Advantage: low price. Disadvantage: limited choice.

Mail-order or online retailer: sells from a catalogue or website and delivers to the consumer's home, such as ASOS. Advantage: convenience and easy price comparison. Disadvantage: goods cannot be examined first and delivery takes time.
Market stall or farmers' market: small-scale direct selling, often by producers, typically of fresh produce.
Independent retailers compete on personal service and specialist knowledge, while chains and supermarkets compete on range and price.
Buying an appliance such as a washing machine is a big purchase, so the outlet matters as much as the product. A shopper compares outlets on more than the price tag.
Price: compare the cost of the same item in different outlets, since discount and online sellers may charge less than a department store.
Range: a wider range lets you compare several models before you decide.
Advice and demonstration: staff in a shop can explain features and show the appliance working, which an online seller cannot do.
After-sales service: whether the outlet will install, service and repair the appliance, which matters if it breaks down.
Delivery: whether the outlet delivers the appliance, how soon, and whether it charges for this.
Guarantee and returns policy: whether the appliance is covered if it is faulty and whether the outlet takes it back, so you are protected if it is not right.
Retailers design the shopping environment around how people perceive value, risk and time. Understanding these tactics helps a consumer spend on purpose rather than on impulse.
Impulse buying: an unplanned purchase triggered by a display, a special offer or a product seen at the checkout.
Perceived value: shoppers judge a price against a reference price, so a 'was/now' price or a multi-buy makes a reduction seem a bargain even when the saving is small.
Mood and environment: music, aroma, lighting and layout keep shoppers relaxed. Relaxed shoppers browse for longer and so see and buy more products.
Perceived risk: consumers hesitate over unfamiliar products, so a known brand reduces the risk they feel in buying.
Limited time and attention: shoppers rely on quick cues such as brand, colour, packaging and price rather than reading every label.
Scarcity and urgency: labels such as 'limited offer' encourage a purchase now rather than later.
Social proof: displays showing many units, or a 'best seller' label, suggest that other people approve of the product.
Consumer's response: separate needs from wants, then use a shopping list and a budget to reduce impulse spending.
Shopping patterns have changed in response to time pressure, technology and changing values. For each change, be ready to say what changed and why shoppers or retailers changed.
Frequency: many households have moved from a single weekly bulk shop to several smaller top-up trips.
One-stop shopping: large out-of-town centres and retail parks sell food, clothing and services under one roof, alongside local shops.
Extended hours: late-night, Sunday and 24-hour opening give shoppers more flexibility, which suits people with long working hours.
Online, television and social media shopping: consumers order through websites, apps, TV shopping channels and social media, often with home delivery.
Self-checkout and scan-as-you-go systems let shoppers bypass the checkout queue and help retailers cut staff costs. Loyalty apps also record buying habits.
Resale and second-hand trade: charity shops, vintage stores and online resale platforms have grown as shoppers seek value and reduce waste.
Drivers of change: time pressure, working patterns, household structure, technology, budget, health and special diets, and environmental and ethical concern.
How people pay has changed as well as where they shop. Each method can be judged on convenience, security, cost and record keeping.
Cash: widely accepted and carries no interest, but it can be lost or stolen and gives few records of what you spent.
Debit card: contactless and convenient, and it spends funds from your own account without interest, but it depends on funds being in the account and on technology working.
Contactless and mobile payment: tapping a card or paying with a phone app, along with debit cards, has largely replaced cash, because it is quick at the till.
Credit card: lets you buy now and pay later, but the amount spent must be repaid.

Consumer research gathers information about what consumers want, how they buy, and how large a market is. The two types are separated by who collects the data: existing information against new information.
Purpose: research identifies consumer wants and expectations, tests the market before a product is launched or developed, and highlights trends, market size and potential markets.
Desk research uses existing (secondary) information, meaning data someone else has already gathered, such as reports from state agencies, Central Statistics Office data and internet sources.
Desk research is quick to carry out, relatively inexpensive, and can cover a large amount of information.
Desk research may be general or out of date, so it shows what people do rather than why, and it may not answer a specific question about a product.
Field research collects new (primary) information directly from consumers, through questionnaires, surveys, interviews, observation, vox pops, consumer panels and focus groups.
Field research is specific and up to date, showing attitudes, preferences and reasons for buying, but it takes longer and costs more.
A vox pop is a short, informal interview with members of the public in a public place, used to gather opinions quickly.
A consumer panel is a fixed group of consumers who report on products over time; a focus group is a guided discussion with a small group about a product.
Loyalty card data and application forms record buying habits and personal details, which retailers use as a research source.
Research benefits the retailer, the manufacturer and the consumer, because each needs to know what people will buy.
Retailer: research identifies the type of person likely to buy a product.
Retailer: research shows whether a product meets consumer requirements, and shows the size and location of the market.
Manufacturer: research shows what consumers will buy before production is committed, so money is not wasted on products that will not sell.
Consumer: research identifies what consumers need, so that products can be improved in quality and matched to those needs.
A purchase involves several parties, and each has a different relationship to the consumer. Knowing who is who tells you where to go when something goes wrong.
The consumer is an individual who buys goods or services for personal use, not for business, so a shopper buying a kettle for the kitchen is a consumer.
The retailer or trader sells goods or services in the course of business and is the consumer's first point of contact for a complaint, because the consumer's contract is with the seller.
Under consumer law the retailer is responsible for faults in goods, even when the manufacturer made the fault, and must deal with the complaint.
The manufacturer makes the product and is the other party to any manufacturer's guarantee (a written promise to repair or replace a faulty product).
A guarantee is a contract between the manufacturer and the consumer. It is usually offered in addition to the consumer's statutory rights (rights set by law), not instead of them.
The supplier or distributor moves goods from the manufacturer to the retailer, so the consumer rarely deals with this party directly.
Informed decisions rest on reliable information. It comes from the product itself, from the seller and from independent sources, and each should be checked against the others.
Labels, instructions and care labels give the contents or ingredients, how to use and care for the product, and warnings about hazards, so they should be read before buying and using.
Unit pricing shows the price per kilogram or per litre, which allows comparison between different pack sizes.
Advertising and sales material is useful but should be checked against the product label and independent information, because the seller wants to make the sale.
Independent consumer publications and testing reports compare products on quality and value for money. The Consumers' Association of Ireland publishes comparative findings in Consumer Choice.
Citizens Information gives free, confidential information on consumer rights, so a consumer can ask about a problem without cost.
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission publishes guidance on consumer rights and on unfair trading.
