Terms and conditions, the returns policy and guarantee wording should be read before purchase, as they set out what the seller offers.

Marks and symbols are information too: quality marks such as the Bord Bia Quality Mark, the CE mark (the manufacturer declares the product meets EU safety requirements), the energy rating label on appliances, and safety and hazard symbols.
Reviews, word of mouth and online comparison sites are useful but may be biased, so check more than one source.
A consumer's part in a transaction is to be informed, careful and honest. These are the consumer's duties, which are different from the rights the consumer is entitled to.
Know your rights and the laws that protect consumers: the basic rights and remedies under consumer law apply whether or not the seller mentions them.
Be informed about goods and services before buying, and compare value, not only price, by weighing price against quality, durability and the cost of running or maintaining the product.
Read and understand labels and terms before buying, including ingredients, dates, guarantee conditions and cancellation terms.
Follow the manufacturer's instructions and care labels; a fault caused by misuse is unlikely to be the trader's responsibility.
Keep receipts and proof of purchase, since they show when, where and what was bought, and are needed for a claim.
The consumer's duties continue after the sale. A responsible consumer also acts quickly when something goes wrong and plans spending so that problems are less likely.
Report faults promptly, stop using a faulty or unsafe product, and complain where appropriate, as delay can make a problem harder to prove.
Give accurate, truthful information when complaining, including a clear description of the problem and the redress (the remedy) wanted.
Plan purchases and set a budget: check whether a product is needed before buying.
Resist pressure selling and impulse buying, and do not be rushed by sales talk, because a quick decision leaves no time to compare or check.
Check the total cost, including interest and charges, before agreeing to credit or easy-pay arrangements, because the instalments can add up to far more than the cash price.
Use resources responsibly and consider the environment: reduce waste, and reuse and recycle packaging.
Traditional buying principles still shape how a consumer should approach a purchase, even though the law now gives buyers more protection.
Caveat emptor is a Latin principle meaning 'let the buyer beware': it places the duty of checking goods on the buyer, so the buyer had to inspect goods before buying.
Modern consumer law limits caveat emptor by giving statutory rights that apply automatically, but inspecting goods and asking questions before purchase remains the best protection.
A needs-based decision is guided by necessity and income; a wants-based decision is more open to advertising and impulse buying.
Vague claims such as 'the best' or 'new' that lack supporting evidence should be questioned before they influence a purchase, because they sound impressive but promise nothing that can be checked.
Consumer rights are what a buyer is entitled to expect. Papers list them in slightly different ways, so learn the rights below as the common set.
Right to safety: goods and services must not endanger health or life.
Right to honest and truthful information about goods and services, so that buyers can decide on accurate facts.
Right to choice: a range of goods and services is available to choose from.
Right to value for money: goods and services should be of a quality that matches the price paid, and goods should be of satisfactory quality.
Right to redress: a consumer whose goods or service are faulty can seek repair, replacement or a refund.
Right to services completed to a high standard, by a qualified person, using good materials.
There is no right to a refund simply for a change of mind in a shop purchase; a retailer may offer an exchange or a credit note as goodwill.
Rights and responsibilities are linked: each right is only as useful as the consumer's knowledge and action, so a right to information works only if labels are read.

The Consumer Rights Act 2022 gives consumers statutory rights (rights set by law) and remedies when they buy goods, services or digital content from traders. It applies to contracts made on or after 29 November 2022 and replaced the earlier law on sales and services for consumer contracts.
A trader is a person who supplies goods, services or digital content in the course of business, so the Act applies to shops, online sellers and service providers alike.
A consumer is an individual acting for purposes that are not part of their business, so someone buying a washing machine for their home is a consumer.
Statutory rights apply automatically to every contract between a trader and a consumer, whether or not the trader mentions them.
A trader cannot remove statutory rights through terms and conditions, small print or notices; a 'no refunds' sign does not override the Act.

Digital content, such as downloaded software, music or films, is covered by the same standards of quality, fitness and description as goods, because it is bought in the same way and can be just as faulty.
Goods must meet four standards at the time they are supplied, and the consumer is entitled to all of them whatever the trader says.

Satisfactory quality: goods must be of a standard a reasonable person would consider satisfactory, taking account of price and description. This includes being durable, safe, free from minor defects, and having an acceptable appearance and finish.

Fit for purpose: goods must be fit for the purposes for which goods of that type are normally used, and for any particular purpose the buyer made known to the trader, for example asking for a coat that is waterproof.
As described: goods must match any description given by the trader, the label or the advertisement, so a 'leather' bag that is plastic does not meet this right.
Correspond to sample or model: goods must match a sample or model shown to the consumer before purchase.
A fault that is present when the goods are supplied is the trader's responsibility, even if it appears only later.
The retailer is responsible for faulty goods and must deal with the complaint, even if the fault was made by the manufacturer. The consumer approaches the trader, not the manufacturer.
A service is measured against what a competent provider would deliver and against what the trader said or agreed, so the consumer is protected even though there is no physical product to inspect.
Reasonable care and skill: a service must be carried out with the care and skill a competent provider would show, in other words to a high standard by a suitably qualified person.
Materials: any materials used in a service must be of satisfactory quality and fit for their purpose, so a repair using poor parts is a breach even if the work itself was careful.
Time: where no time was agreed, the service must be carried out within a reasonable time, so a trader cannot leave a job half-finished for months.
Price: where no price was agreed in advance, the consumer pays only a reasonable price for the service, which protects them from an inflated bill afterwards.
Matching what was said or agreed: the service must match what the trader told the consumer or agreed with them.
When goods or services do not meet their statutory standard, the remedies are applied in a set order: the consumer starts with the gentlest fix and moves to the next only if that fails.
First remedy for goods: repair or replacement at the trader's cost, within a reasonable time and without significant inconvenience to the consumer.
Second remedy for goods: a price reduction or a refund, where repair or replacement is not possible, is not carried out within a reasonable time, or causes significant inconvenience.

Short-term right to reject: the time limit for rejecting faulty goods outright is 30 days, so they can be rejected within 30 days of supply (delivery) and the consumer receives a full refund, without having to accept a repair first.
Services that are not performed to the required standard must be repeated by the trader, or the consumer can ask for a price reduction.

A manufacturer's guarantee is extra to statutory rights and cannot reduce them. A statutory right is set by law and applies automatically, whereas a guarantee is a voluntary promise from the manufacturer.
The Act protects buyers from faulty goods and services, not from every disappointment, so exam scenarios often turn on spotting when no remedy is owed.

There is no statutory right to a refund merely because the buyer changed their mind or dislikes the colour. Any refund, exchange or credit note in that case is the shop's own policy, a favour rather than a legal duty.
Goods bought in a sale are covered by the same statutory rights as goods bought at full price, so a sale does not weaken the consumer's position.
Exception: a fault that the trader pointed out before the sale is not covered by the statutory rights for that fault.
A consumer who was not told of a fault before purchase keeps the full statutory remedies for it.
Misuse or ordinary wear and tear is not a fault for which the trader is liable, because the goods were not faulty when supplied.
Proof of purchase, such as a receipt, bank statement or order confirmation, is needed to show the goods came from this trader.

The Consumer Protection Act 2007 is about how traders behave in advertising, pricing and selling, rather than what can be claimed for a faulty purchase. It prohibits unfair commercial practices and protects consumers from false and misleading claims, and it replaced the Consumer Information Act 1978.

Misleading actions: giving false or deceptive information about a product, its price, its origin or the trader's identity, which could lead a consumer to buy something they would not otherwise choose.
Misleading omissions: leaving out or hiding material information that a consumer needs in order to make a decision.
Aggressive practices: harassment, coercion, undue influence or pressure that limits the consumer's freedom to choose.
Prohibited practices: a list of practices banned in all cases, such as falsely claiming that a product has an approval it does not have, or using a quality mark without permission.
The Act is enforced by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC), which investigates and can prosecute offences. It does not settle an individual consumer's dispute with a trader.
The consumer benefits from protection against false advertising, honest price information, and a state body that takes action.
Price claims must be accurate, including claims about reductions and comparisons, because a price is often what persuades a consumer to buy.
False or misleading information about the price of goods or services is prohibited.
A claimed previous price or a claimed reduction must be accurate; a false or misleading reduction, such as a 'was' price the item never sold at, is an unfair practice.
A recommended retail price must not be used misleadingly to suggest a saving the consumer would not in fact make.

When something goes wrong as a consumer, there are two kinds of organisation that can help. Consumer protection bodies are either established by law with legal powers, or operate voluntarily through advice, research and self-regulation.
Statutory bodies are established by an Act of the Oireachtas (the Irish parliament) and are funded by the State. They have legal powers to investigate, enforce and, in some cases, prosecute.
Voluntary bodies are independent or industry-based. They advise, research, lobby and handle complaints, but they have no legal powers, so they cannot compel a trader to act.
Self-regulation means an industry sets its own standards. For example, the advertising industry sets its own code, and a voluntary body handles public complaints made under that code.

A consumer with a complaint about a trader should usually approach the trader first, because most problems are settled at that stage. If that fails, use the statutory or voluntary body that fits the problem.

The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) is the state body that enforces consumer law. It was established by statute in 2014 and took over the work of the National Consumer Agency and the Competition Authority.
It enforces the Consumer Protection Act 2007 and other consumer law, so it acts on behalf of all consumers through the law.
It investigates unfair and illegal trading practices, including false or misleading advertising and pricing, such as a price that is not what the trader claims.
It can prosecute offences under consumer law, which is a legal power that voluntary bodies do not have.
It informs consumers of their rights through its website and helpline, and runs consumer information campaigns, including on personal finance.
It enforces product-safety rules for non-food products, which protects consumers from unsafe goods.
It promotes competition and advises government on consumer issues.
It does not resolve individual disputes between a consumer and a trader; it deals with breaches of the law and with information for consumers.
Citizens Information provides free, confidential information and advice on rights and entitlements, including consumer rights. The Citizens Information Board is the statutory body behind it.
The Citizens Information Board is a statutory body that funds and supports (oversees) Citizens Information Centres and services.
Citizens Information Centres are local, independent services that give free, confidential information on consumer issues, so a consumer can get advice face to face.
Services cover consumer issues, social welfare entitlements, housing, health and other rights.
The Citizens Information website and phone service give access to information on rights from anywhere in Ireland, so a consumer does not have to visit a centre.

An ombudsman is an independent official who investigates complaints that have not been resolved directly with the body concerned. Ireland has two that matter to consumers, one for public bodies and one for financial providers.
The Office of the Ombudsman investigates complaints about the administrative actions of public bodies, such as government departments, the HSE and local authorities.
The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (FSPO) investigates complaints about financial service providers, such as banks, insurers, credit unions and pension providers.
The FSPO replaced the Financial Services Ombudsman and the Pensions Ombudsman in 2018, so one office now covers both areas.
Both are a last resort: the consumer must first use the provider's or body's own complaints procedure, and only then go to the ombudsman.
Investigations are free of charge to the complainant.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) protects consumers from food-related risks. It is the body to turn to for unsafe or mislabelled food.
It was established under the Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998, which is why it counts as a statutory body.
It sets and monitors food safety standards and gives consumers advice on food.
It works with official control agencies, such as the HSE and local authorities, that inspect food businesses on its behalf.
Marking schemes accept a few more statutory bodies, each protecting consumers in a particular area. Know the full name and one role for each.
The Central Bank of Ireland regulates financial service providers and protects consumers of financial services.
The National Standards Authority of Ireland (NSAI) sets and certifies standards, so consumers can trust that products meet an agreed standard.

European Consumer Centre Ireland advises consumers on cross-border purchases within the EU, such as faulty goods bought online from a trader in another EU country. It is run by the CCPC as part of an EU network.
The small claims procedure is a court route for settling a dispute, not a consumer protection body, so it is not the answer to a question that asks for a body.
The Consumers' Association of Ireland (CAI) is an independent, non-profit organisation that represents consumers. It was founded in 1966.
It researches and tests goods and services and publishes its findings in Consumer Choice, so consumers can compare products before buying.
It provides objective information and advice on consumer products and services, including a personal advisory service.
It lobbies government on consumer issues, meaning it presses for changes that favour consumers.
It represents consumers on a number of bodies, so consumers have a voice where decisions are made.

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) is a self-regulatory body for advertising, set up by the advertising industry itself. Older material calls it the Advertising Standards Authority for Ireland (ASAI).
It promotes high standards in advertising through a code, requiring that advertisements are legal, decent, honest and truthful.
It investigates complaints from the public about advertisements, such as false claims or offensive content.
Where a complaint is upheld, the advertiser is asked to amend or withdraw the advertisement. The ASA has no legal powers, so it relies on the industry complying with the code.
Some voluntary help comes from industry groups and local services rather than from a single national organisation.
Trade associations look after the interests of their members and may have codes of practice and complaints procedures, so a consumer can complain to the association about a member.
Citizens Information Centres, as local services, are accepted as voluntary in some schemes because they are staffed partly by volunteers.
Exam questions often describe a problem and ask which body helps. Work out whether the problem is about the law, a code, money, public services, food or a purchase from abroad.
A misleading price or advertising claim goes to the CCPC (which enforces the law) or the ASA (which enforces the advertising code).
A complaint about a bank or insurer goes to the provider first, then to the FSPO.
A complaint about a public service goes to the Office of the Ombudsman.
To find consumer information, use Citizens Information, the CCPC or the CAI.
Faulty goods from an EU trader bought online go to European Consumer Centre Ireland.
Unsafe or mislabelled food goes to the FSAI.

A complaint is strongest when it is prompt, documented and specific about the redress (the remedy) wanted. Following the steps in order, from the trader first to outside help last, shows you have tried to settle the matter fairly.
1. Stop using the faulty product, especially if it could be unsafe, and keep it safe so it can be inspected.
2. Return it to the retailer as soon as possible with the receipt, which is the proof of purchase, and speak to the manager or customer service.
3. Describe the fault briefly and state the redress wanted: repair, replacement or refund.
4. Ask for a realistic remedy that matches the problem and the value of the goods, because an unreasonable demand is easier for the trader to refuse.

5. If the retailer does not resolve the matter, complain in writing (a letter or email) giving a description of the goods, where and when they were bought, the fault, a copy of the receipt, the redress sought and a reasonable date for a reply.
6. Keep copies of all letters, emails and replies, and note the dates of phone calls, since they are evidence if the matter goes further.
7. Where the goods carry a manufacturer's guarantee, the manufacturer can also be contacted; the retailer remains responsible for statutory rights (those set by law) even so.

8. If the trader still refuses, seek advice from Citizens Information or the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) before taking further action, and then use the small claims procedure. For a cross-border online purchase, contact European Consumer Centre Ireland.
Services, such as building or repair work, are complained about in much the same way as goods, but the focus is on what was agreed and on timing.
Complain promptly to the supplier, in writing if needed, because delay can make the problem harder to prove.
Describe what was agreed and what was delivered, referring to any quote, contract or written terms, so the gap between the two is clear.
Ask for the service to be carried out again, or for a price reduction, refund or other redress.
Keep receipts, invoices, quotes and any correspondence about the service, because they are your evidence.
If the matter is still unresolved, use the small claims procedure.
Misleading advertising is handled by different bodies from faulty goods and services, so the right body depends on what the problem is.
An advertisement that seems false, misleading or offensive can be reported to the Advertising Standards Authority of Ireland.
Misleading practices, including false price claims, can be reported to the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission.
Keep a copy or screenshot of the advertisement, with its date and where it appeared, because the advertisement may change or be removed.
Complaints about banks or public bodies go to the provider first, then to the relevant Ombudsman if the provider does not resolve them.

The small claims procedure is a special, simple mechanism within the District Court structure for resolving small consumer disputes. Its function is to let ordinary people settle low-value disputes without the cost of a full court case.
It deals with disputes about goods or services bought for private use from a trader, a person selling them in the course of business.
The claim must be within a monetary limit set in law; larger claims go through the ordinary courts.
It is designed to resolve claims quickly, cheaply and without a solicitor.
It is not a separate court building: the marking schemes call it the Small Claims Court, but it is a procedure within the District Court.
Two terms are used throughout: the claimant is the consumer making the claim, and the respondent is the trader answering it.
A claim passes through the Registrar's office (the District Court official who handles it) in stages. The consumer should already have tried to settle the matter with the trader before starting.
1. The consumer completes the claim form at the District Court office, which can be sent or lodged, and pays a small, fixed fee.
2. The Registrar sends a copy of the claim to the respondent, the trader against whom the claim is made.
3. The respondent has 15 days to admit the claim, dispute it or make a counterclaim (a claim of their own against the consumer).
4. If the respondent accepts the claim or does not reply, the claimant succeeds, and the respondent has 28 days to comply.
5. If the respondent disputes the claim, the Registrar tries to resolve the dispute between the parties, which is called a settlement.
6. Claims not settled are referred to a hearing before the District Court judge, where each side presents evidence such as receipts, letters and correspondence.

Scenario questions ask you to apply the procedure to a case, such as a couple whose washing machine breaks down and the shop refuses redress. Each step you have learned becomes a separate point in the answer.
First the couple stop using the machine and find the receipt, then return to the shop and ask for a repair, replacement or refund, because the retailer is responsible for faulty goods.
If the manager refuses, they write to the shop with the details and keep a copy, then seek advice from Citizens Information or the CCPC.
They then complete the small claim form at the District Court office, pay the fixed fee and name the shop as respondent.

The Registrar sends the claim to the shop, which has 15 days to answer; the Registrar then tries to settle, and if that fails the claim goes to a hearing where the couple show the receipt, the letters and the fault.
The procedure suits low-value disputes where the cost of ordinary court proceedings would outweigh the claim. It also has limits, which is why it is not the right route for every dispute.
It is inexpensive, fast and simple, with a fixed low fee, so a consumer can claim without the risk of high costs.
A solicitor is not required, which keeps costs down.
It is available at local District Court offices across the country, so the consumer does not have to travel far.
It resolves disputes about goods and services without the consumer having to go through the full court system.
Claims above the monetary limit set in law cannot use the procedure, and it is not suited to complex disputes.
The consumer needs evidence, such as the receipt and correspondence, because the judge decides an unsettled claim on what each side can show.

A natural resource is a material or energy source taken from the environment, such as fuels, water, minerals, timber, wind and sunlight. Because some resources run out and others do not, what we use and how we use it matters for the future.
Sustainable use means meeting present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs, so resources are still there for the people who come after us.
Resources are classed by how quickly they are replaced: renewable resources are replenished naturally, while non-renewable resources are finite (limited in supply).
Consumers influence resource use through what they buy, how long they keep products in use and how they dispose of them, so everyday choices add up.

Consumers conserve resources by buying only what is needed, choosing durable and repairable goods, and using items fully before replacing them, which means fewer new materials and less energy are used.

A renewable resource is naturally replenished and is not used up by constant use, provided it is used no faster than it is replaced. Each renewable energy source works by turning a natural movement or heat into electricity or heat for buildings.

Solar energy: photovoltaic (PV) panels convert sunlight directly into electricity, and solar thermal panels use sunlight to heat water. Passive solar design, which sites the house and its glazing towards the sun, uses sunlight for heat and light.

Wind energy: turbines convert the kinetic energy (movement energy) of moving air into electricity; wind farms are usually sited on exposed upland and coastal land, or at sea, where the wind is strongest.

Hydroelectric energy: falling or flowing water turns turbines, so the source depends on a steady flow of water and a difference in height. The Shannon Scheme at Ardnacrusha, opened in 1929, is an Irish example.
Biomass: wood, straw, energy crops and plant or animal waste are burned, or converted to biogas, to release heat or electricity.
Geothermal energy: heat stored in the earth's crust is brought to the surface as hot water or steam to heat buildings or generate electricity.
Tidal energy uses the rise and fall of the tides to drive turbines; wave energy uses the motion of waves to drive devices.

Renewable heat in the home comes from heat pumps (which take low-grade heat from the air, ground or water), solar thermal panels, and stoves burning wood from managed forests. Heat pumps count as renewable heat because most of their heat comes from air, ground or water.
Hydrogen can also carry energy, but it is renewable only if it is made using renewable electricity.
Renewable energy is attractive because it does not run out and is cleaner to produce, but it is not free of drawbacks. Exam answers need both sides.
Renewable sources are sustainable: their supply does not run out on human timescales, so a well sited and maintained system can last indefinitely.
Most produce little or no air pollution or carbon dioxide while generating energy, which reduces damage to air and water.
Using renewables reduces dependence on imported fuel, which improves energy security (a dependable supply that does not rely on other countries).
Some renewables can be installed in a home, such as solar panels on a roof or a small wind turbine, so energy is produced where it is used.
Building, maintaining and manufacturing renewable systems creates employment, and running costs are low once the system is installed.
Limitation: wind and solar output varies with weather and daylight, so storage or a backup supply is needed.
Limitation: installation costs can be high, and hydro and tidal systems need suitable sites.
Limitation: wind farms and dams can affect the landscape and habitats.
A non-renewable resource is limited in supply and cannot be replaced within a human lifetime once it is used up. Fuels and minerals dug out of the ground fall into this group.

Fossil fuels are coal, oil, natural gas and peat, formed from the remains of plants and animals over very long periods: peat over thousands of years, coal, oil and gas over millions. Coke and anthracite (a type of coal) are other fuels in this group.

Peat (turf) is cut from bogs for home heating and electricity generation. Bogs regrow far too slowly to count as renewable, so peat is a non-renewable fossil fuel, and bog habitats do not regenerate quickly.
Nuclear energy uses uranium, a mined, finite fuel, so it is non-renewable. Ireland has no nuclear power station.
Iron ore, copper ore and bauxite (the ore of aluminium) are non-renewable mineral resources because they are mined and finite; recycling extends the life of the metal they yield.
For one non-renewable source used in the home, give the source and an advantage: fossil fuels are concentrated, give a lot of heat, and have an established supply and appliances.
The disadvantages are that the fuel is finite, its price rises as reserves fall, burning it causes emissions and extracting it damages the land. For these reasons it is not sustainable.
Using non-renewable resources harms the environment twice: when they are extracted and when they are burned. As they become scarce, the supply itself also becomes a problem.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, the main greenhouse gas (a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere), which contributes to global warming and climate change.
Burning coal, oil and peat releases sulphur dioxide, which forms acid rain.
Mining, quarrying, drilling and peat extraction destroy habitats and landscapes, so the wildlife that lived there loses its home.
Cutting bogs releases stored carbon, which adds to the carbon dioxide in the air.
As reserves fall, fuel becomes harder and more costly to extract, so supplies become less secure.

Consumers are responsible for how they use resources because their daily choices decide how much fuel is burned and how much material is thrown away. Practical steps cut demand for non-renewable resources and support renewable ones.
Reduce energy demand, for example by insulating the home, using appliances efficiently and switching off standby, so less fossil fuel is burned.
Choose a renewable electricity supplier, or install a renewable system such as solar panels or a heat pump, where practical. Smokeless or renewable fuel is also a better choice.
Buy wood and paper products certified by a recognised scheme such as FSC (Forest Stewardship Council) or PEFC, which confirms that the timber came from managed forests.
Reuse and recycle metals, glass and paper so that finite materials are used again.
Choose products made with recycled content, which means less new material has to be mined or felled.

Sustainable waste management means reducing waste first, then reusing, recycling and recovering value, and disposing of only what is left. The waste hierarchy ranks the options from most to least preferred, so that as little waste as possible reaches disposal.
The order of preference is prevention, minimisation, reuse, recycling, recovery (including energy recovery) and disposal. Marking schemes phrase it as reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose.
Prevention and minimisation come first: buying only what is needed and avoiding excess packaging stops waste being created in the first place, so there is nothing to collect or treat.

Reuse means using an item again for its original or another purpose, such as refilling a container, reusing a jar for storage, repairing, donating or buying second-hand. The item stays whole, which is why reuse is not recycling.
Recycling processes used materials into new products, such as paper, glass, metals, some plastics and textiles. It saves raw materials and usually energy, and keeps waste out of landfill.

Recovery means burning residual waste to generate heat or electricity (energy from waste); gas collected from landfill can also be used for energy. Energy recovery is not recycling, because the material is not made into a new product.

Disposal, mainly landfill, is the least preferred option because it uses up land, and food and other organic waste decomposes without oxygen (anaerobically), releasing methane, a potent greenhouse gas.

In Irish law the hierarchy is applied through the Waste Management Act 1996 (as amended). It sets up controls on waste collection and movement, and gives local authorities and the EPA roles in promoting waste reduction, recycling and reuse.
Much household waste is biodegradable, meaning it can be rotted down by living things. Composting turns it into something useful instead of sending it to landfill.

Biodegradable material such as food scraps, tea leaves and garden waste is broken down by micro-organisms into a nutrient-rich soil conditioner called compost. Composting differs from recycling because organic matter rots down rather than being reprocessed into a new product.
Composting keeps biodegradable waste out of landfill, so less methane is produced as it would otherwise rot without oxygen.
Compost returns nutrients and organic matter to the soil, so gardeners need less peat-based compost, and it is cheap for households to make.

In Irish households food and garden waste is collected in the brown bin where a collection is provided. The three bins are green (dry recyclables), brown (food and garden waste) and black (general waste).
Most waste can be cut at home by what a household buys and how it sorts what is left. Each action below moves waste up the hierarchy, away from disposal.
Plan meals and write a shopping list, so food is not bought and then thrown away.
Buy concentrated products, such as concentrated detergents, which need less packaging per wash. Buy in bulk where it cuts packaging per unit, and use refill stations and refillable containers.
Use reusable bags, bottles and containers instead of single-use ones, so fewer items are made and thrown away. Reuse jars, tubs and shopping bags.
Separate waste at home into recyclables, food and garden waste, and general waste, so that each stream can be treated in the right way.
Choose products in recyclable, recycled or biodegradable packaging, and products with the EU Ecolabel. Repair items rather than replacing them.

Take paint and other household chemicals to a civic amenity site (the local authority's recycling and waste centre), not the bin, because they can harm the environment and the people handling waste. Do not put paint, oil, chemicals or batteries in the bin.
Packaging carries symbols that tell the consumer how it can be treated after use. The recycling symbol is the most common, and it says less than many people think.

The recycling symbol (three arrows forming a loop) shows that the packaging is made of material that can be recycled. It does not guarantee that a local collection accepts it, so do not say it is certainly accepted in the household recycling bin.
A percentage inside the arrows shows the proportion of recycled content in the packaging.
A number inside a triangle on plastic is a plastic-type code: 1 is PET, used for drinks bottles, and 2 is HDPE, used for milk bottles and detergent containers.

Two other symbols are often confused with the recycling loop. They tell the consumer about who paid for recovery and about a product's whole environmental effect, not whether the pack can be recycled.
The Green Dot shows that the producer of the packaging has contributed financially to the recovery and recycling of packaging waste.
In Ireland the Green Dot is shown by members of Repak, the packaging recovery scheme, so a producer who pays into Repak can put it on their packs.
The Green Dot does not mean the item itself is recyclable or recycled, which is why it must not be treated as a recycling symbol.
The EU Ecolabel, a flower symbol, is an audited, voluntary label certifying that a product or service causes minimum damage to the environment across its life cycle.
The Ecolabel assessment considers the energy and materials used in making the product, the pollution produced, and how far it can be reused or recycled.

Packaging makes up a large share of household waste, so government, producers, local authorities and consumers all act to reduce it. A strong answer names one initiative and gives two details about it.
The levy on single-use plastic shopping bags, charged at the point of sale since 2002, discouraged their use and increased the use of reusable bags.
The landfill levy is a charge per tonne on waste sent to landfill, which makes landfill more expensive and so encourages recycling and recovery.
Packaging producers must meet national recovery and recycling targets under Irish packaging regulations, and most meet them by funding the Repak scheme (the Green Dot).
Local authority recycling schemes gather glass, cans, paper and plastics through kerbside collections and bring banks or civic amenity centres.

The Re-turn deposit return scheme began on 1 February 2024. A refundable deposit is paid on plastic drinks bottles and aluminium and steel cans, which are returned in shops or to reverse vending machines. Glass and dairy containers are not included.
Consumers can refuse over-packaged goods, choose loose produce and bring their own containers to refill counters.
Manufacturers reduce excess packaging by using less material per product and lighter packaging.
Each packaging material has strengths for the product and a different fate as waste. Knowing both lets you judge how sustainable a material is.
Flexible films are thin plastic films that are light, low in cost, fit the shape of the food closely, can be printed on and can be heat-sealed (closed by melting the edges together).
Flexible films give a good barrier against moisture and gases, which extends shelf life and reduces spoilage, and they are suitable for frozen food.
Their drawback is that many multi-layer films are hard to recycle, so they are often sent to landfill or energy recovery.
Glass can be washed and reused, or recycled repeatedly without loss of quality, but it is heavy and costly to transport.
Steel and aluminium cans are highly recyclable, and aluminium can be recycled repeatedly without loss of quality.
Paper and card are recyclable, though their fibres shorten with each recycling cycle. They also come from a renewable raw material, are biodegradable, are light and take printing well.
Biodegradable packaging breaks down naturally through the action of micro-organisms. Examples are paper or card, and compostable starch-based packaging.
WEEE is waste electrical and electronic equipment, and it is governed by its own collection and take-back rules. It must be kept out of the general bin because of what it contains.

Electrical goods contain hazardous substances such as lead, mercury, cadmium and brominated flame retardants, and also valuable materials that can be recovered, so they must not go into general household waste.
The crossed-out wheeled bin symbol means the item must be collected separately from household waste.
Route 1: repair, sell or donate a working appliance first, because keeping it in use is the top of the waste hierarchy.
Route 2: when a consumer buys a new equivalent item, the retailer must take back the old one free of charge, including on home delivery.

Route 3: a civic amenity site or recycling centre accepts small appliances, batteries and other electrical items. Larger electrical shops must accept very small electrical items without a purchase, and batteries can be returned to shops without buying anything.
Take batteries out of appliances and dispose of them separately before the appliance is handed in. Erase personal data from smart appliances.
Old fridges and freezers contain refrigerant and insulating foam, which must be removed by an authorised treatment facility. Make the appliance safe before disposal.
The legal basis is the WEEE Directive, applied in Ireland by the European Union (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) Regulations 2014.

Pollution is the release of substances or energy into the environment at a rate that harms living things or damages natural processes. It is usually grouped by where the harm happens: in the air, in water or through sound.
Air pollution: gases and particles released into the atmosphere, mainly from burning fossil fuels, industry, traffic and domestic fires.
Water pollution: harmful substances entering rivers, lakes, groundwater or the sea, from sewage, farming, industry and households.
Noise pollution: unwanted or excessive sound from traffic, construction, industry and household equipment.
Litter and land pollution: discarded waste on streets, in the countryside and in water, which harms wildlife and blocks drains.

Most air pollution comes from burning something, whether fuel in a power station, a car engine or a home fire. Each pollutant comes from a particular kind of burning, so it helps to link each gas to its source.

Carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide are released when fossil fuels such as coal, oil, peat and gas are burned for electricity, transport and home heating; sulphur dioxide comes especially from coal, oil and peat.
Nitrogen oxides are produced by vehicle engines and by any high-temperature combustion, because the heat makes nitrogen and oxygen in the air combine.
Carbon monoxide is produced by incomplete combustion (burning without enough oxygen), for example in poorly maintained or faulty boilers, stoves and vehicle exhausts.
Smoke and particulates (tiny solid specks in the air) come from solid fuels such as coal, wood and smoky turf burned in open fires and stoves, and from industry. Smoke and fog together form smog.
CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) released from old fridge refrigerants and foams, and from older aerosol sprays, destroy ozone in the upper atmosphere.
Methane, a greenhouse gas, is released from landfill and from farm animals.
Overuse of chemical sprays and cleaning products, and burning rubbish, add further pollutants to the air.
Air pollutants cause three separate global problems, plus harm to health. Keep each cause with its own effect, because examiners mark the link between them.
Global warming and climate change: carbon dioxide, methane and other greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere, raising average temperatures and sea levels and changing weather patterns and crops.

Acid rain: sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve in rainwater to form acids, which lower the pH of soil and water, harm plants and fish, dissolve limestone and corrode metal and stone buildings.
Ozone depletion: CFCs break down ozone in the stratosphere (the upper atmosphere), so more harmful ultraviolet radiation reaches the earth's surface.
Health: particulates and smoke cause respiratory illness, aggravate asthma and place extra strain on the heart.
Carbon monoxide is a poison that stops the blood carrying oxygen. It has no smell, which is why carbon monoxide detectors are used in homes.
Smog and smoke reduce air quality and visibility.
Water pollution happens when waste from homes, farms and industry reaches rivers, lakes and the sea, often through drains and run-off (rainwater washing material off land).
Untreated or poorly treated sewage is discharged into rivers and the sea.
Fertiliser and slurry (liquid animal waste) are washed off farmland into waterways after heavy rain; together with sewage, these are the main sources of nutrients.
Industrial effluent (liquid waste), chemical waste and pesticides are dumped or washed into water.
Oil leaking from vehicles and heating oil tanks runs off into drains and streams.
Household chemicals, paint and oil poured down drains also reach waterways.
Phosphates in washing powders and detergents once entered waterways through household drains. EU rules now limit phosphorus in these detergents, so they are no longer the main source.
The best-known effect is eutrophication, where too many nutrients set off a chain of events that ends with a lake or river short of oxygen. Other pollutants harm wildlife and people directly.
Eutrophication: excess nitrates and phosphates feed rapid growth of algae, which forms an algal bloom on the water surface.
The bloom blocks light, so submerged plants die; when the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up dissolved oxygen.
Low oxygen levels kill fish and other aquatic life, leaving lakes and rivers depleted.
Toxic substances can accumulate up the food chain, because each animal eats many contaminated ones, affecting fish and birds that feed on contaminated organisms.
Chemical contamination of drinking water sources threatens human health and can leave water unfit to drink.
Noise is sound that is unwanted or too loud. Loud or constant noise damages health as well as comfort.
Main sources: road and air traffic, construction and roadworks, industry, lawnmowers, music systems, televisions and alarms.
Noise is measured in decibels (dB), a logarithmic scale, so an increase of 10 dB represents roughly a tenfold increase in sound intensity.
Effects of persistent noise: stress, tension, headaches, disturbed sleep and insomnia.
Long-term exposure to loud sound causes permanent hearing damage.
Noise reduces concentration in schools and workplaces.
Individual choices add up. Consumers can cut air, water and noise pollution at home, on the road and when shopping.
Air: walk, cycle, use public transport or share car journeys to reduce vehicle emissions.
Air: drive an electric, hybrid or low-emission vehicle, and keep tyres correctly inflated and the engine serviced to reduce fuel use and emissions.
Air: use smokeless fuels or renewable heat, such as heat pumps or solar, instead of smoky solid fuels, and do not burn rubbish.
Air: choose energy-efficient appliances so that less fossil fuel is burned to generate the electricity they use. Dispose of old fridges and freezers properly so that CFCs are not released.

Water: never pour paint, oil or chemicals down drains, use fertilisers and chemicals sparingly, and compost garden waste rather than burning it. Keep boilers and oil tanks maintained so they do not leak.
Noise: keep music and television volumes down, avoid noisy garden work at unsocial hours, maintain equipment, and use double glazing and sound insulation.
General: reduce, reuse and recycle, buy only what is needed, choose biodegradable or second-hand products, and avoid single-use packaging.
Individuals cannot solve pollution alone, so the State uses laws, a regulator and charges that make polluting more expensive.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), set up under the Environmental Protection Agency Act 1992, licenses large industrial and waste activities, monitors air and water quality and enforces environmental law.
The Waste Management Act 1996 (as amended) controls waste collection, movement and disposal, and gives local authorities and the EPA roles in promoting reduction, recycling and reuse.

Solid fuel regulations: the Air Pollution Act 1987 (Solid Fuels) Regulations 2022 ban the sale of smoky (bituminous) coal across the State from 31 October 2022 and restrict the retail sale of turf and of wet wood, to cut smoke and particulates from home heating. Local authorities enforce them.

Levies and taxes make polluting choices dearer: the landfill levy (a charge per tonne of waste sent to landfill, encouraging recycling and recovery), the plastic bag levy (since 2002) and a carbon tax on fossil fuels (introduced in 2010), which encourages energy efficiency and renewable alternatives.
Other clean-green schemes: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle; Green Dot (Repak); WEEE take-back; EU Ecolabel; and, since 2024, the Re-turn deposit return scheme.
Support for renewable energy and home energy upgrades, with grants through the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), reduces the fossil fuel burned.

Everyday household activities use energy, water and materials, and they produce emissions and waste. How big the impact is depends on how much energy an activity uses and which fuel supplies that energy.
Space heating and hot water account for the largest share of energy use in most homes, so savings on heating usually matter more than savings elsewhere.
Electricity used in the home is generated partly by burning fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide at the power station, so using less electricity cuts emissions.
Water used in the home must be pumped and treated, and hot water also needs energy to heat it, so saving water saves energy as well.
Packaging, food waste and discarded appliances all add to the waste that is landfilled (buried in a landfill site) or recovered (reused or recycled).

Heating is the biggest energy use in most homes, so the best savings come from stopping heat escaping and from heating only when and where it is needed. Heat leaves through the roof, walls, floor, windows and gaps.
Insulation laid on the floor of the roof space (attic) is one of the most effective measures for an existing house, because warm air rises and escapes through the roof.
Cavity wall insulation fills the gap between the two leaves of a masonry wall, reducing heat loss through the walls.
Draught-proofing seals gaps around doors, windows, letterboxes and floorboards, which stops warm air escaping and cold air entering. Keep controlled ventilation where fuel is burned.
Double or triple glazing reduces heat loss through windows, and closing thick curtains at night adds a further layer of insulation.
A lagging jacket on the hot water cylinder and insulated (lagged) pipes reduce heat lost while water is stored and moved.
Reflective panels or foil behind radiators on external walls send heat back into the room rather than into the wall.
An annual boiler service keeps combustion efficient and safe, so less fuel is burned for the same heat.
Heating only when and where it is needed saves fuel, and renewable sources reduce reliance on fossil fuels. Controls and cleaner fuels also cut the emissions released when fuel is burned at home.

A room thermostat and a programmer ensure the heating runs only when it is needed, and timers on the immersion heater do the same for hot water. Lowering the set temperature, even slightly, reduces fuel use.
Thermostatic radiator valves control the temperature of individual radiators, so unused rooms can be kept cooler.
Renewable heat sources, such as heat pumps, solar thermal panels and stoves burning wood from sustainably managed forests, reduce reliance on fossil fuels.
Burning fuels at home releases carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and smoke, which harm the environment.
Emissions can be reduced by using smokeless fuel, an efficient boiler, heating controls and renewable heat.
A washing machine's energy use is mostly about heat, so the choices you make about temperature, load size and drying matter far more than the machine itself.
Heating the water accounts for most of the energy used on a hot wash, so lower temperatures save energy.
A cold or 30 °C wash uses far less energy than a 60 °C or 90 °C wash, and modern detergents clean well at lower temperatures, so a hotter wash is not usually needed.
A full load uses almost the same energy and water as a part load, so run the machine only when it is full.
An eco programme runs at lower temperatures or with less water, using less energy per load.
A higher spin speed removes more water before drying, which reduces the time a dryer must run.
A tumble dryer is one of the most energy-intensive appliances in the home, so line drying saves significant energy.
Using the correct dose of detergent avoids residue and reduces the amount of product that enters drains.
Wash clothes only when needed, and repair and reuse them rather than replacing them.
Food has an environmental cost before it reaches the plate and after it is thrown away. Wasting food wastes everything used to produce it and creates a greenhouse gas in landfill.
Food waste sent to landfill decomposes without oxygen (anaerobically) and releases methane, a greenhouse gas.
Food production uses land, water, fertiliser and energy, so wasted food wastes all the resources used to grow, transport and package it.
Plan meals, shop with a list, check dates and stock, and buy only what will be eaten. Use leftovers and freeze surplus food promptly.
Store food correctly: keep the fridge at or below 5 °C and freeze food at -18 °C or below, which slows bacterial growth and spoilage and so cuts waste.
Compost food and garden waste or use the brown bin, so it is not sent to landfill.
What you choose to buy and eat, and how it is packaged and transported, also affects the environment. Small changes in the weekly shop add up.
Vegetables, pulses and cereals generally need less land, water and energy to produce than meat and dairy, so eating more plant-based foods lowers the environmental impact of the diet.
Seasonal and local food avoids the energy used for long-distance transport and for heated or refrigerated growing and storage.
Buy loose fruit and vegetables and products with minimal packaging, and buy in bulk to reduce packaging.
Use reusable bags and containers for bulk and counter purchases, so fewer single-use bags are thrown away.
Buy refills and products in recycled or reusable packaging, and choose products with the Ecolabel.
Cutting the number of shopping trips reduces the fuel used for travel.
The energy label lets you compare appliances before you buy, so you can choose the one that will use the least energy over its life.

The EU energy label rates an appliance from A (most efficient) to G (least efficient) for energy efficiency, and this rescaled scale replaced the older A+++ to D scale in 2021, so do not compare old and new ratings.
The label also shows the appliance's annual or per-cycle energy consumption and its noise level.
For washing machines and dishwashers, the label shows water use as well.
Choose a high rating and the right capacity for the household, because an oversized appliance uses more energy than its load needs.
Other criteria to look for are appliances that are repairable and durable, have little packaging, and offer eco and low-temperature programmes.
Even an efficient appliance wastes energy if it is used badly. Most savings come from small habits, which are easy to name in an exam answer.
Standby is not off: the appliance still draws electricity continuously, so switch appliances off at the socket, or use a switched power strip.
LED bulbs use much less power than incandescent bulbs and last much longer. Older schemes say CFL for the energy-saving bulb.
Use the oven only when needed, avoid preheating for longer than necessary, and use a microwave, slow cooker or air fryer for small quantities. Use lids on pans.
Boil only the water needed in a kettle, so no energy is spent heating water you do not use.
Clogged filters and dirty condenser coils make fridges and dryers use more energy, so keep them clean and keep door seals sound.
A fridge set colder than necessary wastes energy. Keep the door closed and do not overpack it, and a freezer that is not kept full uses more energy to stay cold.
Use full loads and eco or cold cycles in washing machines and dishwashers.
Making an appliance take longer to wear out avoids the energy and materials needed to manufacture a new one. When it is finally finished with, how you get rid of it matters too.
Keeping a working appliance in use through servicing, repair or second-hand sale avoids the energy and materials needed to manufacture a replacement.
Sell or donate a working appliance rather than replacing and discarding it.
Dispose of old appliances through the retailer take-back or a recycling centre, rather than putting them in the bin.
Saving water saves the energy used to pump, treat and heat it. Most savings come from fixing leaks and changing habits in the bathroom and garden.
Showers use less hot water than baths, so short showers save both water and the energy needed for heating.
Turning off the tap while brushing teeth and fixing dripping taps and leaks save water that would otherwise be wasted. Aerator or sensor taps and efficient showerheads reduce flow further.
A dual-flush toilet allows the smaller flush to be used for liquid waste, saving water with each flush.
Collecting rainwater in a butt provides free water for the garden, and grey water (used water from baths, sinks and washing machines) can be reused.
Insulating the cylinder and pipes and timing the immersion save water-heating energy, and solar thermal heating can supply hot water.

Home management means organising time, money, energy and effort to run the household efficiently. Technology contributes by cutting the work, time and energy a task needs and by improving the result, as appliances and home systems take over repetitive tasks.
Washing machines, dishwashers, vacuum cleaners and food processors replace hand washing, drying, sweeping and food preparation, so these tasks are less labour-intensive and take less time.
Because tasks finish quickly, time is freed for family, leisure, study or paid work, which improves the quality of home life.
Automatic programmes and timers let a task run unsupervised, so the household can do other work or rest while it runs.
Steam cleaners clean and sanitise floors, carpets and upholstery with little or no chemical cleaner, helping to remove dirt and bacteria and improving hygiene.
Easy-care products, such as non-iron and stain-resistant fabrics, non-stick surfaces and smooth wipe-clean worktops, need less washing, ironing and upkeep.
Technology can increase the effectiveness of some tasks: steam cleaning lifts dirt that a dry cloth leaves behind, and a dishwasher washes at a higher temperature than hands can bear.
Heating, hot water and appliances are a large part of household running costs. Technology lets the household use energy only where and when it is needed, which lowers fuel bills.
Programmable timers switch heating and hot water on only when needed, reducing fuel use and bills.

Zoned heating uses separate controls (thermostats or thermostatic radiator valves) to heat different parts of the house to different temperatures, so unused rooms are not heated; this gives comfort where needed and lower fuel bills.

Microcomputer chips (microprocessors) in appliances such as washing machines, cookers, microwaves and heating systems sense load, temperature or time and adjust the programme, so the energy and water used are matched to the task.
Microwave ovens heat small and medium portions faster than a conventional oven, so they use less energy for reheating and defrosting.
Appliances with a high energy-label class are cheaper to run. LED lighting and standby-saving features also cut electricity use.
Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity (photovoltaic) or heat water (solar thermal), reducing the household's reliance on mains energy.
Technology protects the home from intruders and its users from accidents, often without anyone having to pay constant attention. This gives security and peace of mind.
Burglar alarms sound on forced entry and can alert occupants or a monitoring service.
CCTV cameras record the outside of the home, deterring intruders and providing evidence after an incident.
Automated security lighting switches on when movement or darkness is detected, making the outside of the home less attractive to intruders.
Entry-phones and video doorbells let residents check who is at the door before opening it.
Electronic gates can be opened and closed remotely, so residents do not have to leave a vehicle to enter the property.
Built-in safety devices such as automatic cut-outs, thermostats, door interlocks and child locks in appliances protect users from hazards without relying on constant attention.
A residual current device (RCD) in the fuse board cuts the power when a fault occurs, and smoke and carbon monoxide alarms warn occupants of danger.
Computers, phones and the internet let a household keep in touch, manage money and find information without leaving the house. This saves travel time and cost.
Mobile phones, email, video calling and messaging keep family members in touch quickly across distances. Social media likewise keeps household members in contact and shares information quickly.
The household can get information and services without travelling, for example recipes, product reviews and consumer information from the internet.
Online and mobile banking let bills be paid and balances checked at any time without visiting a branch.
Budgeting and accounting software or apps record income and spending by category and help the household plan future expenditure.
Internet shopping allows goods to be compared and bought without travelling to shops, and price comparison finds the best deal.
Computers let some members work or study from home, which can reduce commuting time and cost.
Smartphone apps in a smart home can turn lights, heating or appliances on or off, and check their status, from outside the home.
Technology is not all benefit. A balanced answer also weighs what it costs and what can go wrong, which earns extra credit at Higher Level.
The initial cost must be weighed against savings in time, energy and effort over the life of the product. Running costs, repair costs and replacement when machines fail must be added.
Electronic appliances need electricity to operate, so a power cut or breakdown stops the task.
Components of electronic appliances may need a qualified person to repair them, so spare parts and servicing must be available.
Internet-connected devices hold personal data and need secure passwords and regular software updates to resist misuse.
Heavy screen use can reduce the time a family spends together.
Manufacture, energy use and the disposal of electrical waste have effects on the environment.
Questions on this topic ask how technology helps the household run efficiently. The same answer pattern works whether you are asked to state or to discuss.
Use the pattern of a point, a named technology and the benefit, for example timers on heating switch it on only when needed, lowering fuel bills.

Ordinary Level asks you to state three ways, so give any three with a short example, such as appliances saving time and labour, zoned heating, steam cleaners for hygiene, security systems or communication saving time.
Higher Level asks you to discuss, so give five developed points spread across workload, time, quality of life, easy-care products, effectiveness, computer-controlled energy saving and security.
Tie examples to a task such as laundry, cleaning, cooking, heating, security, money or communication.
Before buying, compare the cost, size and capacity of each model against what the household needs. A good choice is value for money, which means quality against price, not simply the lowest price.
Initial cost: compare the purchase price, including delivery and installation, across several shops and brands, so you know the true cost of getting the appliance working in your home.
Running cost: this is the energy and water the appliance uses over its life. Compare it with the purchase price, since a cheap appliance can cost more to run, and the energy label shows this.
Size and space: the appliance must fit the available space and allow room for doors to open, air to circulate (ventilation) and access to plumbing and power points.
Capacity: match it to household size, such as litres of fresh and frozen food for a fridge or kilograms of laundry for a washing machine, and litres for a kettle.
Payment method: compare cash, debit or credit card and credit agreements, and the total amount payable under any credit, because credit adds to the final cost.
Cost and size are not the whole story. A buyer also checks how long the appliance will last, who will fix it, and how easy and safe it is to use every day.
Brand reputation and reliability: established brands with a record of durable products, good reviews and available spare parts are less likely to need early repair.
Guarantee and after-sales service: check the length of the guarantee, what it covers, and how quickly repairs, servicing, spare parts, delivery and installation are available.
Ease of operation and cleaning: clear controls, removable parts and filters, smooth surfaces, dishwasher-safe parts and cord storage reduce the time and effort of use.
Safety features: automatic cut-outs, interlocks, child lock, cool-touch surfaces and recognised safety marks reduce the risk of injury or fire.
Family needs and modern features: choose features the household will actually use, such as programmes, timers and smart controls, rather than paying for extras that stay unused.
The same criteria apply to every appliance, but how much each one matters depends on the size and price of what you are buying. Apply them to one large and one small example.

Large appliances (cooker, fridge, washing machine, dishwasher, tumble dryer) are expensive and long-lived and usually delivered and installed, so cost, energy efficiency, size and servicing weigh most.
Small appliances (kettle, toaster, iron, food processor, mixer) are cheaper and portable, so storage, cleaning and cord length weigh more.
Examples to use for the individual studies: a washing machine, fridge-freezer or dishwasher as the large appliance, and a kettle, toaster, food processor or iron as the small one.
Design is how an appliance looks and works, and construction is what it is made of and how well it is built. Together they decide how safe, durable and easy to clean it is.
Design affects safety, durability, ease of use and cleaning, and how well the appliance fits the style and colour of the kitchen.
Controls should be clearly labelled, easy to reach and simple to read; large, simple controls suit older users and children.
Weight, handles and grip should suit the person using the appliance, so that lifting and pouring are safe, and non-slip feet give stability.

Robust construction and good-quality materials, such as stainless steel for surfaces and blades, increase durability. Other materials used include heat-resistant or cool-touch plastic, glass and enamelled steel.
Smooth, sealed surfaces and removable parts are easier to clean and give fewer places for food and bacteria to collect. Sealed joints and a strong flex and plug add durability.
Design for safety and efficiency: insulation, interlocks, automatic cut-off, energy-saving settings and quiet running make the appliance safer and cheaper to use.
Examples of safe design: an interlock stops a machine working while its door is open, so fingers cannot reach moving parts.
The energy label lets buyers compare the energy efficiency of appliances at a glance, on a common scale. An efficient appliance costs less to run and does less harm to the environment.

The EU energy label rates an appliance from A to G, where A is the most efficient and G the least efficient. This scale applies to fridges, freezers, washing machines, washer-dryers and dishwashers from 1 March 2021, and to tumble dryers from 1 July 2025.

The label is displayed on refrigerating appliances (fridges, freezers and fridge-freezers), washing machines, washer-dryers, dishwashers and tumble dryers. Two named appliances are enough if asked to name two.
A-rated appliances use the least electricity, so they cost least to run and cause the least harm to the environment; G-rated appliances use the most.
The label gives annual energy consumption in kilowatt-hours (kWh), which indicates likely running cost and environmental impact. Washing machine and dishwasher labels give energy per 100 cycles.
It also gives, depending on the appliance, the noise level in decibels, capacity and water use. A refrigeration label shows the fresh and frozen capacity in litres.
The current label carries a QR code that links to the product's entry in the EU product database (EPREL) for more detail.
Energy in kWh equals power in kW multiplied by hours used. Higher Level answers can use this to compare the running costs of two appliances.
Efficiency in use is also the consumer's job: use full loads, eco programmes and lower temperatures, switch off standby, and choose the correct size.
A star rating on a fridge-freezer or freezer tells you how cold the frozen-food compartment is and how long frozen food keeps in it.
The star rating applies to the frozen-food compartment of fridges and fridge-freezers and to freezers, not to the fresh-food section.
One star: the compartment holds frozen food at −6°C for up to one week.
Two stars: the compartment holds frozen food at −12°C for up to one month.
Three stars: the compartment holds frozen food at −18°C for up to three months.
Four stars: the compartment holds frozen food at −18°C to −25°C for up to one year, and fresh food can be frozen in it. Only four stars allows this.
The star rating measures storage performance, not energy efficiency, so the energy label is used to compare running costs.
Marks on an appliance or its packaging tell the buyer that a standard has been met. Each mark means something different, so know what each one does and does not show.
The CE mark is the manufacturer's declaration that the product meets the health, safety and environmental requirements of the European Union. It is not independent testing.

The double insulation symbol, a square inside a square, shows that the appliance has two layers of insulation (a Class II appliance), so it needs no earth wire and its plug has no earth connection. It is common on plastic-bodied small appliances.
The Irish Standard mark of the National Standards Authority of Ireland (NSAI) shows that the product has been certified to a standard.
An ISO 9000 quality mark shows that the maker's quality-management system has been assessed.
Marks should appear on the appliance or its packaging, and a mark that cannot be found on the product does not show certification.
Safety marks show that a product has been tested to a standard, but they do not guarantee its performance or reliability.
A manufacturer's guarantee or a retailer's own-brand label is not an independent mark.
Before buying, a consumer gathers information from several sources. Some are independent, some come from sellers and may be biased, and some are personal experience.
Independent sources: consumer magazines and websites that test and compare products publish independent results on appliance models.
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC), the body for consumer protection and information, publishes guidance for consumers on their rights when buying appliances.

Citizens Information offers free, independent information on consumer rights and on buying goods and services. The European Consumer Centre Ireland helps with cross-border purchases, and libraries also hold information.
Manufacturers' leaflets and brochures give specifications, guidelines for use and guarantee terms, but they are promotional documents.
Product labels and packaging show the energy rating, safety marks, capacity and guarantee details, so you can compare models for example in the shop.
Sales staff can explain features, but their advice may be influenced by the stock and margins of the shop. Advertisements highlight strengths, so check their claims against independent sources.
Word of mouth, online user reviews and in-shop demonstrations reflect other people's experience; read them critically because they can be unreliable.

Benefits of getting information before buying: compare price, installation and running cost; find the most energy-efficient model; compare features, design, size and ease of operation; reduce the influence of advertising; avoid a costly mistake.
An appliance affects the environment at three points: when it is chosen, while it is used and when it is thrown out. A responsible consumer thinks about all three.
Choosing: pick the best energy class you can afford and the correct size, and prefer repairable, durable appliances with eco and low-water programmes and little packaging.
Using: run full loads, use eco and short cycles and lower temperatures, switch off standby, defrost freezers, and do not leave fridge doors open, because each wastes energy.
Maintaining: descale and maintain appliances so that they keep working efficiently.
Disposing: repair, sell or donate an appliance while it still works, so it is not wasted.
Maintaining also helps because limescale and ice build-up make an appliance work harder and use more energy.

Under the European Union (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) Regulations 2014, a retailer must take back an old appliance of similar type free of charge, one for one, when a new one is bought, so old appliances do not end up in landfill.
Collection is on delivery if notice was given, and larger shops must accept very small items without a purchase.
Electrical waste can also go to a civic amenity site. Never put it in the household bin, which the crossed-out wheelie bin symbol warns.
A washing machine shows how the selection criteria apply to a large appliance, where cost, efficiency, size and installation all matter.
Capacity: the drum size, stated in kilograms of dry laundry, should match the number of people in the household.
Spin speed, measured in revolutions per minute (rpm), affects how dry clothes are after washing and so how much drying is needed.
Eco and low-temperature programmes reduce water and energy use, and the energy label shows the rating for the model.
Installation needs: a water supply and drain, a suitable power point, and a level floor must all be available where the machine is placed.
A kettle shows how the criteria apply to a small appliance, where capacity, cleaning and safety features matter most.
Capacity is stated in litres; buy a kettle that holds the amount the household needs, not more, because heating extra water wastes energy.
A concealed element in the base is easier to clean than an exposed element, where limescale collects.
Automatic cut-off switches the kettle off when the water boils, and boil-dry protection switches it off if the water level is too low.

Some appliances exist to make something move, such as a blade, a drum or a fan. They use an electric motor, which turns electrical energy into movement (kinetic energy), rather than a heating element, which turns electricity into heat.

Common motor appliances are the food processor, blender, hand mixer, vacuum cleaner, washing machine, dishwasher pump, extractor fan and the fan in a hairdryer, because each one needs something to spin or move.
Kettles, toasters and irons work differently: they have a heating element that produces heat, not a motor that produces movement.
Some appliances have both, so a washing machine, hairdryer and dishwasher each contain a motor for movement and an element for heat.
Classification check: a food processor has a motor, a kettle has an element and a toaster has an element.

A food processor is a typical motor-driven appliance: the motor sits in the base and drives interchangeable attachments. Each part of its design is there for performance or safety, and exam answers should name the part and its purpose.
The heavy motor is enclosed in a stable base with rubber (non-slip) feet, which keeps the centre of gravity low and prevents the appliance moving during use.
A spindle (drive shaft) transfers rotary motion from the motor to the blade or disc fitted in the bowl, so the attachment turns when the motor runs.

The bowl is transparent and graduated (marked with a measuring scale), so the user can see the quantity and texture of the food being processed. It is made of heat-resistant, impact-resistant plastic or glass.
The lid locks onto the bowl and has a feed tube with a pusher, which keeps fingers out of the tube. A safety interlock stops the motor from starting unless the bowl and lid are correctly fitted.
Further safety features: an overload cut-out protects the motor from overheating, and the blade comes to a stop quickly when switched off.
Interchangeable attachments include the chopping (S-) blade, slicing and shredding (grating) discs, a dough blade and a whisk. Blades are stainless steel, which resists rust and stays sharp.
Controls usually include on/off, variable speeds and a pulse button that gives short, controlled bursts of power.
Removable, dishwasher-safe components and a smooth, sealed base make cleaning easier, and internal cord storage keeps the base tidy.
Diagram: food processor in section, showing the base with motor and spindle (drive shaft), the bowl, the blade, the lid with feed tube and pusher, and the interlock position.

When choosing a motor appliance, some factors matter that do not apply to other appliances. They all come down to whether the machine suits the jobs you will actually do and is safe and easy to live with.
Capacity and motor power (wattage) decide how much food it can handle and how well it copes with heavy tasks such as dough.
Choose a range of attachments you will actually use, because extra attachments add cost and storage problems if they are never needed.
Consider noise, cord length and storage, and how easy it is to assemble and clean, because these decide whether it will be used often.
Look for safety features such as an interlock, and for a guarantee and service availability in case the motor fails.

A food processor has fast-moving sharp blades and an electric motor, so most guidelines prevent cuts, electric shock or damage to the motor. Each guideline is worth stating together with the hazard it prevents.
Read the manufacturer's instructions, assemble correctly and fit the correct attachment before connecting the appliance to the electricity supply, so the machine is used as designed.
Check that the plug, flex and bowl are undamaged, and place the processor on a dry, level surface, away from water and the edge of the worktop so it cannot fall or cause shock.
Lock the bowl and lid before switching on, and never try to defeat the safety interlock, which exists to stop the blade turning while it is exposed.
Cut food into even pieces, do not exceed the maximum fill line, and use the speed recommended for the ingredient, so the motor is not strained.
Do not run the machine for longer than the instructions allow, because the motor can overheat; pause to let it cool.
Feed food only with the supplied pusher, never with fingers, knives or spoons, and keep hands, hair and loose clothing away from moving parts, because the blade can cut or catch them.
Use pulse control to avoid over-processing and to keep control of the texture of the food.
Switch off and unplug before changing attachments, removing the lid, scraping the bowl or cleaning, and wait until the blade has stopped completely, so it cannot start or cut by accident.
Looking after the appliance keeps it safe and working. The rules about unplugging, water and damage matter most.
Lift sharp blades by the centre hub, wash and dry them carefully, and store them safely and out of reach of young children.
Wash the bowl, lid and attachments in warm soapy water, or in the dishwasher if the manufacturer allows it.
