Wipe the motor base with a damp cloth; never immerse it or hold it under running water, because water entering the motor and wiring can cause electric shock.
Wind or store the flex neatly, and do not use the appliance if the plug, flex, bowl or interlock is damaged; have it repaired by a qualified person before use.
Dry your hands before touching the plug, and never overload a socket, because wet hands and overloaded sockets risk shock and fire.

Use the correct fuse in the plug: 3 A for low-power appliances and 13 A for high-power ones, as the manufacturer states. A fuse melts if too much current flows, which protects the appliance and its flex.
Other motor appliances have their own particular hazards, so each has a rule matched to what it does.
Hand mixers: start on the lowest speed to avoid splashing, then increase speed, and switch off before removing the beaters.
Blenders: add liquids first and never run the blender empty. Do not blend hot liquid in a sealed container, because steam pressure can force the lid off.
Vacuum cleaners: empty the dust container or change the bag before it is full, since a blocked airflow strains the motor; clear blockages with the machine switched off.
Washing machines: do not overload the drum, use the detergent amount recommended by the manufacturer, and choose a programme suited to the fabric.
Motor appliances use little energy compared with heating appliances because they run for short periods. Using them well keeps running costs low and saves energy.
Prepare several ingredients in sequence, starting with dry or clean foods, so the appliance is used once for many tasks rather than washed between each one.
Use the appliance only for the job it is designed for, use the right size for the task, and switch it off as soon as the task is complete rather than letting it run on.
Switch off at the socket when not in use, and choose an efficient, correctly sized model.
The cost to run an appliance is its power in kW multiplied by the hours used and the unit price, so a short-use appliance costs very little.
Appliances with a motor that run for long periods, such as the washing machine, dishwasher and fridge, are where the energy label matters. Use eco programmes and full loads to save energy.
A motor converts electrical energy into kinetic energy by using the magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor. Understanding this force explains why a coil of wire can be made to spin.
A wire carrying a current in a magnetic field experiences a force, the motor effect, which is greatest when the wire is at right angles to the field.
The direction of the force is given by Fleming's left-hand rule: the thumb shows the force (motion), the first finger the magnetic field and the second finger the current.

In a simple DC motor, a coil sits between the poles of a permanent magnet or electromagnet. The forces on opposite sides of the coil act in opposite directions, creating a turning effect, so the coil turns.
The commutator is a split ring on the shaft; carbon brushes press on it and reverse the current in the coil every half turn, so the coil keeps turning the same way instead of stopping.
Electrical energy is the input and kinetic energy the output; some is wasted as heat from the resistance of the coil and friction in the bearings.
The shaft's rotation is passed to the blade, drum or fan by a drive shaft, and in some designs by gears or a drive belt.
Diagram: a simple motor showing the magnet poles, the coil, the commutator and brushes, and the supply, with arrows for current direction and the forces on each side of the coil.
Household appliances use different kinds of motor depending on whether they need high speed and light weight or steady, quiet running.

A universal motor (a series-wound motor) is the common motor in small kitchen appliances and vacuum cleaners. It runs on either AC or DC, spins at high speed and is lightweight, which suits portable appliances such as food processors and hand mixers.
The carbon brushes of a universal motor wear and need replacing.
Speed control adjusts the voltage or current supplied to the motor, so a variable-speed controller changes the speed of a universal motor.
An induction motor runs on AC and has no brushes or commutator; the rotating magnetic field of the stator induces currents in the rotor, which turns it.

Induction motors are robust, quiet, long-lived and need little maintenance, which suits uses where steady, quieter running is wanted, such as dishwasher pumps, some older washing machines and fridge compressors.

Some small appliances exist to make heat, and they all do it the same way: electricity is forced through a wire that resists it. Knowing which appliances work like this, and which use a motor, is the starting point for studying one.
A heating element is a coil or strip of high-resistance wire that gets hot when current flows through it, so electrical energy is converted into heat energy.
Examples of appliances with a heating element are the kettle, toaster, iron, electric grill, immersion heater, hairdryer (element plus a fan motor) and oven.
The kettle and the toaster have an element, not a motor, so they have no moving parts driven by electricity. A hairdryer is different because it has both an element and a fan motor.
Heat reaches the water or food in three ways: conduction (through metal in contact), convection (currents in water or air) and radiation (infrared from a toaster or grill element).
A kettle is the usual appliance chosen for a study, so you need to name its parts and say what each one does. The same parts also appear in a labelled diagram of a kettle in section.

The body is made of plastic, stainless steel or glass (cool-touch or insulated, so the outside does not burn the user). The kettle also has a lid, a spout with a filter or limescale filter, and an insulated handle.
A water-level indicator shows the minimum and maximum marks, so the user fills the kettle to a safe level.
The heating element is usually in the base of the water vessel. A concealed or flat-plate element is easier to clean than an exposed coil.
The thermostat (a sensor) or steam switch cuts the power when the water boils, so the kettle does not keep heating. Automatic switch-off and boil-dry protection also stop it overheating.
The on/off switch usually has a light, which shows when the kettle is on.

A cordless (cord-free) kettle sits on a base unit that carries the flex and has contacts, so the flex is not attached to the kettle. This reduces the risk of a trailing flex or of pulling the kettle over, and the 360-degree base lets it be placed either way round.
The plug has a fuse (13 A for a kettle) and an earth wire, unless the appliance is double insulated.
Diagram: a labelled kettle in section showing the element, thermostat or steam switch, spout, level scale, handle, base and flex.
The toaster and the iron also work by heating an element, but each has parts suited to its own job. Both are short study answers, so know the main parts of each.
Toaster: nichrome heating elements sit on either side of the bread slots, so both sides of the bread are toasted at once.

Toaster: a spring-loaded lever lowers the bread, and a timer or bimetallic release lifts it when toasting is complete. A browning control sets how dark the toast is, and a removable crumb tray catches crumbs.
Iron: a sole plate (the flat metal base) is heated by the element, and a thermostat dial lets you choose the temperature for the fabric.
Iron: a steam iron also has a water tank and steam vents, and every iron has a heel rest for standing it safely and a cord guard to protect the flex.
Every kettle guideline protects the user from burns, electric shock or fire, or protects the kettle itself. Examiners want each guideline with its reason, so learn both together.

Read the instructions first, and fill the kettle only between the minimum and maximum marks, never above the maximum. The element must be covered whenever it is switched on, and overfilling can spurt boiling water.
Close the lid, and do not run the kettle empty. Boil only the amount of water you need.
If the kettle is not cordless, switch off and unplug it before filling or cleaning it, so there is no live connection while water is being added.
Use dry hands when handling the plug, and never plug in or switch on with wet hands, because water conducts electricity and could cause a shock.
Never immerse the base or the electrical parts or plug in water; wipe the outside and the base with a damp cloth after unplugging and letting the kettle cool.
Keep the flex away from hot surfaces, out of the reach of children and not trailing over the edge of the worktop. Keep the kettle itself away from the edge of the worktop too.
Do not use a kettle with a damaged flex, plug or body, and do not overload a socket with several appliances. Handle the hot kettle by the handle, and beware of steam from the spout.

Descale regularly with a descaling solution or a vinegar or citric acid solution, rinsed well, because limescale on the element slows boiling and increases energy use. Wash the filter, and do not use abrasives on the element.
Toasters and irons get hot and carry mains electricity, so the safe-use rules are about avoiding shocks, fires and burns. Give each rule with its reason.
Toaster: never put a knife or any metal object into the slots, and unplug the toaster before removing stuck or jammed bread, because metal can touch the live element and give a shock.
Toaster: empty the crumb tray regularly, since crumbs can catch fire or prevent the toaster working correctly.
Toaster: do not use it under a cupboard, and keep it away from curtains, so that nothing can catch fire.

Iron: choose the temperature for the fabric before switching on. Use the lowest setting for delicate fabrics and synthetics, and iron the least heat-resistant garments first while the iron is coolest.
Iron: stand it on its heel rest when not in use, and never leave it switched on and unattended.
Iron: unplug before filling the water tank, and keep the flex clear of the sole plate so it cannot melt. Store the iron only when it is cool.
The element makes the heat, but the heat still has to reach the water, bread or fabric. It does so by three routes, and each appliance uses a different mix of them.
Conduction: heat passes from the element through the metal of the kettle base or iron sole plate into the water or fabric, because metal carries heat well.
Convection: water near the element becomes less dense and rises, while cooler water sinks, so currents circulate heat through the kettle.
Radiation: infrared radiation from the toaster elements heats the surface of the bread directly, with no contact needed.
A kettle is more efficient than boiling water in a saucepan on a hob because less heat escapes. A microwave can also heat small amounts of water, but it is not interchangeable with a kettle.
Heating appliances combine mains electricity with heat and often with water, so several safety devices protect the user. Each one guards against a different fault.

The live wire is fused in the plug, and the earth wire connects the metal body to earth, so a fault current blows the fuse rather than leaving the body live. The 13 A plug fuse is standard for a kettle.
Some appliances are double insulated instead, and these have no earth wire.
A residual current device (RCD), in the fuse board, cuts off the supply quickly when current leaks to earth, protecting the user from electric shock.
A thermal cut-out opens the circuit if an appliance overheats, protecting against fire.
A thermostat switches the element off at the right temperature, for example when the water in a kettle boils.
Heating appliances have a high power, so they use a lot of energy whenever they are on. Small habits therefore make a real difference to how much energy is wasted.
Boil only the water needed, because less water must be heated and less heat is wasted. Keep the lid closed so heat is not lost.
Descale to keep the element efficient, because scale insulates the element, so the kettle takes longer and uses more energy.
Choose a correctly sized kettle with a concealed element and automatic switch-off. Do not leave the toaster or iron switched on when not in use.
Energy in kWh = power in kW x time in hours. As an illustration only, a 2 kW kettle used for 0.1 hour uses 0.2 kWh.
Heating appliances have high power, so they use more energy than motor appliances when switched on.
A heating element converts electrical energy into heat through its resistance to the current.

The heating effect: when current flows through a resistor, electrical energy is converted to heat at a rate equal to I²R, where I is the current and R is the resistance. Power can also be written as V times I.
The element is made of nichrome, a nickel-chromium alloy with high resistance, a high melting point, and does not oxidise quickly when hot.
Resistance depends on the length and thickness of the wire: resistance increases with length and decreases as the cross-sectional area increases.

The thermostat is a bimetallic strip made from two metals that expand at different rates; when heated the strip bends and opens the circuit at a set temperature. In a kettle, steam from the boiling water can trigger a bimetallic strip to switch it off.
As the appliance cools, the strip straightens and closes the circuit, so the temperature is held between two switching points.
The thermostat and the element are connected in series, so the element receives no current while the thermostat is open.
Diagram: a circuit showing the 230 V supply, the bimetallic thermostat in series with the nichrome heating element, and the direction of heat transfer into the water or food.
A refrigerator does not make cold. It removes heat from inside the cabinet and gives it out into the room, and the food left behind is cooler as a result.
A refrigerator keeps food at 0 to 5°C (at or below 5°C), which slows the growth of micro-organisms and the activity of enzymes, so spoilage is slower.
A freezer holds food at -18°C or colder, which stops micro-organisms growing, so food keeps for much longer.
Keeping the cabinet at 5°C or below keeps food outside the danger zone of 5°C to 63°C, where bacteria multiply quickly.
Refrigeration appliances differ in size, layout and whether they include a freezer. In an exam you pick one type to study, so know what sets each apart.
Under-counter fridge (standard): a low unit that fits beneath a worktop and usually has no separate freezer compartment.
Larder fridge: a single-door, all-fridge unit for chilled food, without a freezer compartment.
Fridge-freezer: a combined unit with separate fridge and freezer compartments, each with its own door, and one or two compressors.
American fridge: a tall, wide unit with side-by-side doors, often with an ice and water dispenser in the door.
Integrated model: built into kitchen units, with a door panel that matches the cabinet doors so it blends in.
Upright freezer and chest freezer: freezer-only units, either tall with a front door or a low box with a lid on top.
Retro style: a refrigerator with a classic, old-fashioned look.
A refrigerator is a sealed loop of parts that move a fluid, the refrigerant, round and round. Each part has one job, and examiners ask for these jobs in short sentences.

Compressor: a pump driven by an electric motor, usually at the back or base. It draws in low-pressure gaseous refrigerant and compresses it into hot, high-pressure gas, which also drives it round the loop.

Condenser: a coil of tubing, a black grille at the back or in the walls, where the hot gaseous refrigerant gives out heat to the surrounding air and condenses (changes) into a liquid. It is usually at the back or underneath.
Expansion valve or capillary tube: a narrow restriction that lowers the pressure of the liquid refrigerant before it enters the evaporator.

Evaporator: a coil inside the cabinet, often in the freezer compartment or behind the back panel, where the liquid refrigerant evaporates (changes to gas), absorbing heat from the food compartment so the cabinet cools.
Refrigerant: the fluid that circulates in the sealed system. It evaporates at a low temperature, so it takes in heat from inside the fridge, and it releases that heat when it condenses.

Thermostat: senses the cabinet temperature and switches the compressor motor off when the set temperature is reached and on again when the cabinet warms, holding it at about 5°C or below. The dial is turned to a colder or warmer setting.
Other parts: the insulated cabinet, a door seal (gasket) that keeps cold air in, an interior light that comes on when the door opens, and shelves and drawers.

Diagram: draw a closed loop of compressor, condenser, expansion valve and evaporator, with arrows for the flow of refrigerant and labels for gas or liquid and hot or cold at each part. Each part is also labelled high or low pressure.
The refrigerant passes through the four main parts in a fixed order. Heat is picked up inside the cabinet and released outside it, and the cycle repeats until the thermostat switches the motor off.
1. The motor drives the compressor, which draws in low-pressure gaseous refrigerant and compresses it into hot, high-pressure gas and forces it into the condenser.
2. The hot gas flows to the condenser, where it releases heat to the kitchen air and condenses into a liquid.
3. The liquid passes through the capillary tube or expansion valve into the evaporator, where the pressure is low, so its pressure falls and some of it begins to vaporise.
4. In the evaporator the refrigerant boils at a low temperature, drawing heat from inside the cabinet, so the cabinet and food are cooled. It becomes a low-pressure gas.
5. The gas returns to the compressor and the cycle repeats until the thermostat switches the motor off.
Modern refrigerators use a hydrocarbon refrigerant (isobutane), which does not damage the ozone layer. Older appliances used CFC refrigerants, which are now banned.
A refrigerator moves heat from a cold space to a warmer room, which needs work from the compressor and so a continuous supply of electrical energy.
Heat flows naturally from hot to cold. A refrigerator pumps heat against that direction, from the cold cabinet to the warm room, so the compressor must do work on the refrigerant.
The boiling point of a liquid falls as the pressure on it falls. The expansion valve lowers the pressure, so the refrigerant boils at a low temperature in the evaporator.
Raising the pressure raises the condensing temperature, so the hot gas can release heat to the room air in the condenser.

Latent heat of vaporisation: the refrigerant absorbs a large amount of heat from the cabinet as it evaporates, without a rise in its own temperature. This is how the evaporator takes heat from the cabinet.
Compression raises both the pressure and the temperature of the gas, which is why the condenser is warm. The condenser releases the latent heat as the gas changes back to a liquid.
Heat flows from the warm cabinet air to the cold refrigerant through the walls of the evaporator by conduction.
Where you put a refrigerator and how you load it decide how well it keeps food safe and how hard the motor has to work. Each guideline has a reason, and examiners want the reason with it.

Install the refrigerator on a level surface, away from the cooker, radiators, boiler and direct sunlight, and leave space behind and above it so air can circulate around the condenser and carry heat away.

Keep the cabinet at 5°C or below (0 to 5°C), using a thermometer if necessary, with the freezer compartment at -18°C. This keeps food outside the danger zone of 5°C to 63°C, in which bacteria multiply quickly.
Cool hot food before placing it in the refrigerator, since hot food raises the cabinet temperature and makes the motor work harder.
Cover or wrap food to prevent it drying out and to stop strong flavours passing between foods.
Store raw meat and fish on the lowest shelf, in covered containers and below cooked food and dairy, so that juices cannot drip onto food stored beneath. Keep cooked and raw foods separate.
Do not store opened tins in the tin. Transfer the food to a covered container.
Do not overpack the cabinet, because air must circulate around food for even cooling.
Good habits during daily use save electricity and stop food going off, and regular care keeps the appliance working properly.
Avoid opening the door unnecessarily, and keep it open as briefly as possible, since each opening lets in warm air and makes the motor run for longer.
Use food in rotation, first in and first out, so that items are eaten before their use-by or best-before date.
Thaw frozen food in the refrigerator rather than at room temperature, so the food stays cold while it thaws.
Clean the inside with warm water and bicarbonate of soda, avoid strong-smelling cleaners, and wipe the door seal. Check the door seal regularly, since a damaged seal lets warm air in.
Clean the dust from the condenser grille at the back occasionally, so the condenser can give out heat freely.
Defrost the freezer regularly if it is not frost-free: switch off, unplug, collect the water, and never use a knife or sharp object to remove ice.
In a power cut, keep the doors shut so the cold is held in. If the appliance is left empty for a long time, switch it off and leave the door open to prevent mould.
A refrigerator runs all day, every day, so small habits and a good choice of appliance make a real difference to running costs and to the environment.
Choose a high energy class on the A to G energy label, the scale that rates how efficient an appliance is, and the correct size for the household.
Keep the refrigerator away from heat, keep the door closed as much as possible, and cool food before storing it.
Defrost when needed, clean the condenser, and check the door seal so warm air cannot leak in.
Do not set the cabinet colder than needed, since colder settings make the motor run for longer.
Choose modern features that save energy, such as LED lighting and an inverter compressor.
The star rating applies to the freezer compartment only, not to the fresh-food compartment.
Modern refrigerators add features that make food storage easier and more reliable. Exams ask for about three, so be ready to say what each does.
Automatic (frost-free) defrosting: a fan circulates cold air and a timed heater periodically melts frost from the evaporator, and the water drains away, so no manual defrost is needed.
Zoned refrigeration gives separate areas at different temperatures, such as a chill zone for meat and fish.
Humidity-controlled drawers (crisper drawers) keep fruit and vegetables fresh by controlling the moisture in the drawer.
Gated shelves hold tall bottles securely, and flexible or adjustable shelving fits items of different heights. Bottle or wine racks hold bottles.
A digital display shows the cabinet temperature and allows it to be adjusted, using electronic controls.
A quick-chill, power-chill or fast-freeze setting cools newly added food rapidly, reducing the rise in temperature of the other food in the cabinet.
An open-door alarm sounds if the door is left ajar. A holiday mode is also available.
Other features add convenience, hygiene and lower running costs, and some connect the refrigerator to your phone.
A drinks dispenser in the door, or an internal or external ice maker, gives chilled water and ice without opening the main door. It is usually found on American-style models.
LED lighting uses less electricity than traditional bulbs and gives off little heat into the cabinet.
An inverter (variable-speed) compressor runs at the speed needed, which saves energy and reduces noise.
Antibacterial coatings on interior surfaces reduce the build-up of bacteria.
Smart refrigerators can be monitored and controlled from a phone.

A microwave oven cooks, reheats and defrosts food using microwaves, a form of electromagnetic radiation (energy that travels as waves) made electrically inside the oven. It heats the food, not the air around it, which is why it is quick and uses less energy for small quantities.
A conventional (solo) microwave is the basic type, used for cooking, reheating and defrosting food.
A microwave with a grill adds a grill element, so food can be browned and toasted, which a solo microwave cannot do.
A combination oven joins the microwave with a fan oven and grill, so it can brown, crisp and bake as well as use microwaves.
Each part passes the energy on to the next: mains electricity is stepped up, turned into microwaves, guided into the oven and spread around the food. Learn the parts in that order.
Transformer: increases the domestic mains voltage of 230 V to the much higher voltage the magnetron needs. It changes the voltage, not the frequency.
Magnetron: converts high-voltage electrical energy into microwave (electromagnetic) energy, at a frequency of about 2.45 GHz.
Waveguide: a metal channel that carries the microwaves from the magnetron into the metal cooking cavity.
Mode stirrer (stirrer fan): a rotating metal blade or fan that scatters the microwaves around the cavity, so they are not concentrated in one spot.
Turntable: a rotating glass plate that moves the food through areas of high and low microwave energy, so that it is heated more evenly.
Metal cavity: a metal-lined (enamelled steel) box that reflects the microwaves, so they stay in the oven and bounce around the food.

Door and safety: a glass door with a perforated metal screen, whose holes are much smaller than the wavelength, so microwaves cannot escape but you can see in. A safety seal surrounds the door, and a door interlock (a switch) stops microwave production as soon as the door is opened.

Controls and timer: you choose the power level and cooking time, and the timer stops the magnetron when the time has elapsed. A child lock, an interior light and a ventilation fan that cools the magnetron are also fitted.
Diagram: a labelled cross-section of a microwave oven showing the transformer, magnetron, waveguide, mode stirrer, turntable, cavity and door interlock.
The oven turns electricity into microwaves, delivers them to the food, and the food itself turns them into heat. The working principle follows the parts in order.
1. The transformer raises the mains voltage, and the magnetron converts the electrical energy into microwaves when the oven is switched on.
2. The waveguide directs the microwaves into the cavity, where metal walls reflect them and the mode stirrer or turntable spreads them through the food so it is hit evenly.
3. Glass, ceramic, paper and most plastics let microwaves pass through, food absorbs them (mainly the water, and also fats and sugars), and metal reflects them.
4. The penetration depth of microwaves in food is only a few centimetres, so they heat its outer layers.
5. Water molecules are polar (they have a positive and a negative end), so the rapidly alternating field makes them rotate and vibrate; the resulting friction produces heat.
6. Heat then moves towards the centre of the food by conduction, which is why thick food may not heat through evenly and why standing time is needed.
7. The oven switches off when the timer finishes or the door opens. Food does not become radioactive.

Food does not brown because its surface does not get hot enough: the evaporating water keeps the surface near 100 °C, and browning needs a higher temperature. A grill, a combination mode or a browning dish is needed to brown.
Each guideline exists because of how microwaves behave, so give a reason with every one you write.
Containers: use only containers labelled microwave-safe, such as glass, ceramic, paper or suitable plastic, because some plastics are not microwave-safe.
Never use metal containers, foil or dishes with metallic trim, because metal reflects microwaves and can cause arcing (sparks) and damage the oven.

Pierce the skins of potatoes, sausages, egg yolks, tomatoes and other foods with skins, so that steam can escape and the skin does not burst. Do not cook whole eggs in their shells, because steam pressure makes them burst.
Cut food into even pieces and arrange it in a circle with the thicker parts towards the outside, since the outer parts heat first. Do not pile food up.
Cover food (a lid or microwave-safe film with a vent) to retain moisture and prevent splashing, leaving a gap for steam to escape.
Stir, turn or rearrange food during cooking so that heat spreads evenly through it.
Timing: follow the times in the instructions and start with short times, adding more if needed. Allow standing time after cooking, so that heat continues to conduct to the centre of the food.
Use the defrost setting or a lower power level for thawing frozen food, turn and break up the food, and cook it straight after defrosting.
Check that reheated food, especially poultry, minced meat and other high-risk food, is piping hot throughout, to destroy bacteria.
A microwave is simple and safe when used properly, and it lasts longer when it is kept clean and undamaged.

Safety: never run the oven empty, and do not use it if the door, seal or hinges are damaged. Use oven gloves, open covers away from the face to avoid steam burns, stir liquids before use because they can overheat in the container, and keep children from using it unsupervised.

Care: unplug before cleaning, wipe the cavity, door seal and turntable with a damp cloth and mild detergent after spills, and do not use abrasives. Steam-cleaning with a bowl of water and lemon juice loosens food, and the vents must be kept clear.

When choosing a microwave, consider initial and running cost, wattage and capacity, type (solo, grill or combination), pre-set programmes and features, size and space, ease of cleaning, safety features, and the guarantee and after-sales service.
Modern microwaves add controls that take the guesswork out of power and timing, and extra heating methods that fix the oven's main weakness, no browning.
Variable power settings allow delicate foods to be cooked at reduced power, and allow thawing at defrost power. Inverter technology gives a steady low power.
Auto weight defrost: the user enters the weight of the food and the oven sets the power and time.

Pre-set or sensor programmes for foods such as vegetables, popcorn or reheat remove the need to choose time and power manually. Sensor models detect steam from the food and adjust the cooking time automatically.
A jet power, quick-start or quick-reheat button heats food rapidly at full power.
A temperature probe inserted into the food switches the oven off when the set internal temperature is reached.
A combination oven adds a grill or convection oven, so food can brown and crisp. A crisping dish and, in some models, a steam function are also available.
A child lock stops the oven being started by children, and a keep-warm setting holds cooked food at a low temperature. An interior light and low standby use are also features.

A digital control panel, display, clock, timer, memory settings and recipe memory, plus smart or app control, make the oven easier to operate. Self-cleaning or easy-clean walls make maintenance easier.
Anti-bacterial linings reduce the build-up of bacteria inside the cavity.
A microwave suits modern life because it heats only the food, quickly. It also has limits, and a good evaluation gives both sides.
Microwaves heat the food itself rather than the oven cavity, so no preheating is normally needed.
Cooking time is short, so less heat escapes into the room than from a conventional oven, and less energy is used for small and medium quantities.
A microwave is efficient for small and medium portions, and for reheating and defrosting, which saves time.
A conventional oven may be more economical when several large dishes are cooked together.
Matching the power and time to the quantity of food, and using residual standing heat, reduces energy waste.
Switch the oven fully off rather than leaving its display on standby, and choose a correctly sized, energy-rated model.
Short cooking with little or no added water helps food keep colour, flavour and some nutrients, and no added fat is needed for many foods.

It suits busy lifestyles (reheating, ready meals, defrosting) and is simple and safe to use for children, older people and people living alone. The container can often serve as the serving dish, reducing washing-up.
Limits: it does not brown or crisp (unless combined with a grill), it can heat unevenly and overcook edges, and it is not good for large joints or for baking in the same way.
Microwaves are electromagnetic waves, and the microwave oven relies on electromagnetic induction in the transformer and on the electric field of the waves.

Microwaves have a frequency of about 2.45 GHz, which gives a wavelength of about 12 cm. They are non-ionising radiation, so they do not make food radioactive. The wavelength is the basis of the cavity size and the spacing of the waves in food.

The transformer works by electromagnetic induction: an alternating current in the primary coil induces an alternating voltage in the secondary coil, and the voltage ratio equals the ratio of the turns in the two coils.

It is a step-up transformer, because the secondary coil has more turns. It produces several kilovolts for the magnetron from the 230 V supply, and the high voltage is rectified before it is fed to the magnetron.
The magnetron is a vacuum tube. Electrons moving in a magnetic field set up oscillations in resonant cavities, and the oscillations are output as microwaves.

A polar molecule has a positive end and a negative end. Water, fat and sugar molecules are polar, so the alternating electric field of the microwaves, which reverses billions of times per second, makes them rotate back and forth; friction between them converts this motion to heat.
The metal screen in the door has holes of about 1 mm, much smaller than the wavelength, so the waves are reflected and do not leave the oven while you can still see in.
The door interlock is a switch wired in series with the magnetron, so that microwave production stops when the door is opened.
Diagram: a sketch of water molecules aligning with the alternating electric field, with arrows showing the direction of the field at two instants.
Sociology is the study of how people live together in groups and societies. Its starting point is the society itself, because human life is organised, not random.
A society is a group of people who live in a defined territory and share a way of life, a set of institutions (the established organisations and arrangements of social life) and a sense of belonging.
Social life in a society is organised: people depend on one another and follow common rules, which is why daily life is predictable rather than chaotic.
The term applies at different scales, such as Irish society, a small rural community or Western society, so always be clear which group you mean.
Culture is what makes the way of life of one society different from another. It is much wider than the arts, because it covers almost everything a group of people share and hand on.

Culture is the whole way of life of a society, passed from one generation to the next. It includes language, customs, beliefs, values, norms, mores, music, art, dress, food, religion, technology and objects. Irish culture is a good example.
Culture is learned, not inherited biologically, so a child raised in any society picks up that society's way of life through socialisation (the process of learning how to live in a society).

Material culture is the physical objects a society makes and uses, such as clothing, tools, buildings and housing. Non-material culture is the intangible side: language, beliefs, values, norms, customs and rituals.
Cultures differ between societies, and a culture changes over time. Differences show up in language, dress, food, religious practice, wedding customs and attitudes to age and gender roles.
Members of a society share common symbols and meanings, though not every member values every symbol.

Safe Irish examples of culture include Irish traditional music, the GAA, the Irish language as a cultural symbol, St Patrick's Day, Christmas customs and Irish wedding customs. Symbols like these carry shared meanings for those who value them.

A subculture is a smaller group within a society with some distinct values, norms or styles of its own, such as a youth music scene, a sporting club or a religious minority. It still shares the main culture.

Ethnocentrism is judging another culture by the standards of your own culture. Cultural relativism is understanding a culture on its own terms, by its own standards, rather than by those of another culture.
Every society has rules about how to behave, most of them unwritten. These rules come in different strengths, from everyday habits to rules with serious moral weight.

A norm is an accepted, expected way of behaving in a given situation. It is a rule, mostly unwritten. The standard example is forming a queue; others are greeting people, keeping quiet in a library, turning up on time and dressing suitably for an interview or a funeral.

Norms vary between cultures, between social settings and over time. For example, what is acceptable at a match is not acceptable in church, and what was normal fifty years ago may not be now. Norms about punctuality, personal space and greeting also differ from one culture to another.

Mores (pronounced MOR-ays) are norms with strong moral weight, whose breach is seen as seriously wrong, such as the ban on theft, violence or disrespect to the dead. Breaking a more brings serious disapproval or punishment.

Customs, also called folkways, are everyday conventions and traditional ways of doing things, such as queueing, shaking hands, a birthday custom or a wedding custom. Breaking them is rude, not wrong, and brings only mild disapproval. This helps separate a norm from a more.

Laws are norms that are written down and enforced by the State through officially appointed bodies such as the courts. Some mores become laws, such as the bans on theft and assault, but many norms are not laws, such as queueing.
A norm only works if there is some pressure to follow it. Societies apply that pressure through sanctions, and the result is either conformity or deviance.
A sanction is how a society enforces norms: a reward for conforming to a norm or a penalty for breaking one.
Positive sanctions reward conformity, for example praise, a prize, an award or promotion.
Negative sanctions punish breaking norms, for example a frown, ridicule, ostracism (being left out) or, at the formal end, fines and imprisonment.
Informal sanctions come from family, friends and neighbours. Formal sanctions come from official bodies such as the courts, schools and employers.
Conformity means following norms. Deviance is behaviour that breaks a norm.
What counts as deviance depends on the society and the time, because norms vary between cultures and change over time, so the same behaviour may be deviant in one place and normal in another.
Values sit behind norms. A norm is the specific rule; a value is the broad belief that the rule expresses.
Values are the beliefs and attitudes a society holds about what is right and wrong, good and bad, important and worth striving for.

Values are general, abstract and long-lasting; norms are the specific rules that carry values into everyday behaviour. A value of respect for life lies behind the norm against violence, and a value of honesty lies behind the norm of not cheating in exams.

Examples of values given in Irish and Western societies include family, education, honesty, fairness and equality, respect for others, religious belief, freedom, community and care for the vulnerable. These are examples of values, not a claim about every person.
Core values are held strongly and change slowly; peripheral values are held less firmly and change more readily.
Values are learned from the family first, then from school, peers, religion and the media. They differ between families, groups and generations.
Values change over time, for example attitudes to marriage, gender equality and diversity. The changes feed through into new norms and laws.
Values can conflict, such as personal freedom against duty to family, or career against family time. Individuals must balance them, and societies resolve such conflicts through norms and laws.
The terms in this subsection are not separate lists. They fit together as one system, with culture as the umbrella.
Culture is the umbrella. Values, norms, mores, customs, language, beliefs and symbols are its parts.
Values are the broad beliefs. Norms and mores are the rules that put them into practice.
Sanctions enforce norms and mores, and laws are the formal, written version of them.
A chain to remember: a value of honesty leads to a norm of not cheating, and cheating brings a sanction such as a teacher's disapproval or a penalty.
Exams often ask you to explain four or five terms together, such as culture, norms, values and role. Each term is marked separately, so a clear layout earns the marks.
Give each term its own line or short paragraph so that each one can be credited separately.

Open with a one-sentence definition that uses the correct sociological meaning. Use the wording the schemes credit: way of life of a society for culture, accepted way of behaving for norms, and beliefs about what is right and wrong for values.
Add the point that separates the term from the one most often confused with it, such as folkways from mores or norms from values.
Give a specific example from Irish or everyday life for each term, such as queueing for a norm or Irish culture for culture.

Where a term links to another in the set, say how: for example, values underpin norms, and norms are enforced by sanctions. A three-mark term answer is one definition point, one example or extension point and, where terms are related, a link.
Everyone occupies positions in society, and each position carries a certain standing in other people's eyes. Sociologists call such a position a status, and one person holds several at the same time.

A status is a social position, such as mother, teacher, employee or citizen. One person holds several at once, for example daughter, student, goalkeeper and citizen, so a status describes one part of who a person is, not the whole person.
An ascribed status is given at birth or without choice, for example sex, age, ethnic origin or the family into which a person is born.
An achieved status is gained through effort, choice or ability, for example a qualification, a job or a marriage.

Being a parent or a spouse is usually treated as achieved because it follows from choices a person makes. Social class at birth is ascribed, but class in adulthood is mostly achieved through occupation.
A master status is a status that dominates how others see a person and outweighs the person's other statuses, for example being a serving prisoner.
Status can be based on occupation, education, wealth, family background or achievement. In a society that rewards achievement a person can raise their status, which links directly to social mobility.
Societies that allocate status mainly by birth are described as closed; societies that allocate it mainly by achievement are described as open.
A status tells you where a person stands; a role tells you how they are expected to behave there. Roles are learned through socialisation (the process of learning the ways of a society).

A role is the set of behaviours and expectations attached to a status: the rights, duties and behaviour considered appropriate for a person according to their position in society. Examples include teacher, student, adult, child and parent.

Status and role go together. A teacher (the status) is expected to prepare lessons, mark work and treat pupils fairly (the role). Likewise, the role of a student includes attending class, completing homework and respecting the teacher.
A person plays many roles at once, such as mother, employee, daughter and club member.

Roles change over the life course: a person moves from the role of child to adolescent to adult, and each stage brings different expectations. They also change over time, for example gender roles within the family.
Role conflict occurs when the demands of two roles are incompatible, so meeting one means failing the other.
For example, a parent who is also a manager is asked to work late when a child is ill, or a person is expected to be both a loyal friend and an honest employee.

Role overload occurs when a person has too many roles and cannot meet all the demands placed on them, which reduces leisure time and increases stress. For example, a working parent also cares for an elderly relative.
Role conflict and role overload are most common where people hold several demanding roles at once.
A role model is a person whose behaviour others copy, such as a parent, teacher or sports star.

People in a society are not all in the same economic and social position. Socio-economic groups sort people into categories according to that position, and they show that society is arranged in layers.

A socio-economic group (also called a social class) is a category of people with a similar economic and social position, defined mainly by occupation and linked to income, education, wealth, housing and lifestyle.
Social stratification is the division of a society into layers, a hierarchy of unequal ranks. A socio-economic scheme is one way of describing those layers.

In Ireland the Central Statistics Office (CSO) groups the population into social classes for the census, using the occupation of each person. The groups run from professional workers, managerial and technical, non-manual, skilled manual and semi-skilled to unskilled, with a further group for all others gainfully occupied and unknown.

Occupation, not education, decides which class a person is placed in, so a qualification affects the class only through the job it leads to. Level of education is one of the strongest factors separating socio-economic groups, because it governs access to skilled and professional work.

Examples of occupations, one per group: doctor or solicitor (professional); manager or technician (managerial and technical); factory worker (semi-skilled); labourer (unskilled). Electrician, plumber, carpenter or motor mechanic are skilled manual occupations.
Factors that determine socio-economic group are occupation, income, education level, wealth, housing and family background.

Socio-economic group affects life chances, meaning a person's likelihood of access to opportunities such as educational attainment, health, housing and income. It also shapes housing choices and household expenditure.

Higher socio-economic groups are more likely to complete second level and go on to third level, while lower groups face higher early school leaving and lower expectations. This affects equality of opportunity in education.

People do not always stay in the socio-economic group they start in. Social mobility is the movement of an individual or a group between socio-economic groups, enabled by education, income and occupation. It does not mean geographical mobility, which is moving house or country.
Upward mobility is movement to a higher socio-economic group, for example a labourer's child who becomes a teacher, or a skilled worker who becomes a manager after completing a degree.
Downward mobility is movement to a lower socio-economic group, for example after the loss of a skilled job with no replacement at the same level.
There are two time frames for measuring social mobility. Intergenerational mobility compares a person's position with the position of their parents.
Intragenerational mobility, sometimes called career mobility, compares a person's position at different points in their own working life, for example from apprentice to manager.

Structural mobility is movement caused by changes in the occupational structure, such as the growth of professional and service jobs and fewer farm jobs, so that many people move even when their relative positions do not change.
Exchange mobility is movement in both directions that balances out, so that the overall pattern of relative positions stays the same.

Factors that help people move up include education and qualifications, skills and training, promotion in a job, a good income, free second-level education, access to third level (grants, free fees schemes), equality legislation, ambition and family support. Education is the main route to upward mobility in Ireland.

Barriers to mobility include low family income, poor access to education and third-level education, early school leaving, discrimination, unemployment and living in an area with few employment opportunities.
Social mobility is more likely in an open society, where status is achieved, than in a closed society, where status is ascribed.

A social group is two or more people who interact regularly and share a sense of belonging, such as a purpose, an identity or a place. Groups differ in how close and how formal their relationships are, and a crowd of strangers is not a group.
A primary group is small, intimate and face-to-face, with long-lasting relationships; examples are the family and close friends.
Primary groups meet emotional needs and give a sense of belonging, so they shape a person's personality, values and sense of identity. They are also where primary socialisation mainly happens.

A secondary group is larger and more formal, with relationships that are impersonal and often short-term or limited to a role; examples are a school class, a workplace, a trade union, a sports club and a political party.
Secondary groups are organised around a specific goal, such as completing a course or producing goods. Members often join by choice and leave when the purpose is finished.

To compare them: primary groups are small, close, lasting and personal, while secondary groups are larger, formal, often temporary and purpose-based. A person belongs to both types at once, and some groups, such as a small close-knit club, sit between the two.
An in-group is a group with which a person identifies and feels loyalty; an out-group is a group that members see as different from or opposed to their own.
A reference group is a group whose norms and values (the standards of behaviour it expects) a person uses to judge their own behaviour, even if they are not a member of it.
A peer group is made up of people of similar age and status. It is important in adolescence and can act as a primary or a secondary agent of socialisation, depending on how close its members are.
Kinship is the network of family ties between people who are related by blood, marriage or adoption. It is a relationship, not a type of household, so it includes relatives who live apart.
Kinship means family ties: relationships based on blood (common ancestry or lineage), marriage or adoption.
Consanguineal kin are related by blood, for example parents, children, siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins.

Affinal kin are related through marriage, for example a spouse, a spouse's parents, who are in-laws, and step-relatives. The terms consanguineal and affinal are optional; blood and marriage are enough.
A nuclear family is parents and their dependent children living together as one household.
An extended family includes kin beyond the nuclear family, such as grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins, who live together or keep in close contact.
The family of orientation is the family a person is born into; the family of procreation is the family a person forms through their own marriage or partnership and children.
Kinship is found in every society, which is part of why the family is called universal.
Descent, the line through which kinship is traced, can run through the mother's side, the father's side or both; most modern Western societies trace both sides.
Kin networks matter because relatives are often the first people to turn to when help is needed. They have also changed as society has changed.
Kin networks provide practical and emotional support, including childcare, financial help, care for older members and a sense of identity.
Kinship obligations include mutual support and, in many societies, inheritance rights between relatives.
Kin networks have become looser as families have become smaller and more mobile, but relatives keep in contact through phones and social media.

Socialisation is the lifelong process by which people learn the norms, values, behaviour, roles and skills of their society and so become members of it. Without it a child could not use language or form relationships.
Socialisation is lifelong, so it continues in adolescence and adulthood as well as in childhood.
Primary socialisation takes place in early childhood, mainly within the family, where children learn language, toilet training, manners, self-control, right from wrong and a first sense of identity.

Secondary socialisation takes place later in wider settings such as school, the peer group, the workplace, religious institutions and the media. There people learn the roles and norms of that setting, such as punctuality, rules, teamwork and respect for authority.

Through socialisation the culture of a society is passed from one generation to the next, which maintains continuity over time. It also produces conformity and social order and lets individuals take part in society.

People learn through observation, imitation, rewards and punishments (sanctions), role models and direct instruction. In the family, children learn through observation, imitation and consistent discipline.
Anticipatory socialisation is learning the norms of a role or group that a person hopes to join, such as a student learning workplace norms before starting an apprenticeship.
Resocialisation is learning new norms after a major change in life, such as entering the army or prison, where old habits are replaced.
Agents of socialisation are the people and institutions that pass on norms and values. Each one teaches something different.
The main agents are the family, school, peer group, mass media, religion and the workplace.
School socialises formally through the curriculum and informally through the hidden curriculum, the unwritten lessons taught by its rules and routines.
The peer group becomes an important agent in adolescence, when young people test independence and learn the norms of their age group.
Mass media, including television, the internet and social media, transmit norms and values and shape consumer habits.
Monogamy is one form of marriage; the other forms are classed as polygamy. It describes how many partners a person has at one time.
Monogamy is marriage, or a partnership, with one partner at a time, traditionally one husband and one wife.
Monogamy is the norm in the Western world, and it is the only form of marriage recognised in Ireland. It is not the only form worldwide.
Polygamy is marriage to more than one spouse at the same time; polygyny is one man with several wives, and polyandry is one woman with several husbands. Both are found in some other societies.
Bigamy is entering a marriage while still legally married to another person, without the death or divorce of the first spouse. It is an offence in Ireland.
Serial monogamy is a succession of monogamous marriages, one after another, following divorce or the death of a spouse.
Spouses in a monogamous marriage are expected to remain faithful and loyal to each other, live together, and support one another and their children financially.
Civil and religious marriages are both legally recognised in Ireland, and both are monogamous. Same-sex marriage is also lawful in Ireland and is monogamous, being a marriage of two people.

Every society has basic needs, such as raising children, passing on knowledge and organising work. A social institution is the lasting, organised way a society meets one of them, which is why institutions matter for understanding family life.
A social institution is an established, organised set of norms (accepted rules of behaviour), roles and values built around a basic need of society.
The five main social institutions are the family, education, religion, the economy (work) and government (the State). Health and the media are sometimes added to this list.

An institution is not a building or a single organisation. A school is an organisation within the institution of education, so the school down the road is part of the institution, not the institution itself.

Institutions last across generations, while individual groups come and go. Because they carry norms and values, pass on culture and give structure to social life, each one is an agent of socialisation (a means by which people learn how to behave in society).
Institutions are linked, so what happens in one affects the others. For example, the economy affects family life, and education prepares people for work.
Functionalism is the view that each institution performs functions that help keep society stable. This view describes what institutions do; it does not label any institution good or bad.
A manifest function is an intended and recognised result of an institution, for example the school's function of educating young people.
A latent function is an unintended and often hidden result, for example a school providing supervised care for children while parents are at work.
The family is the first and most basic institution, because it is where every person's care and learning begins. Over time other institutions take over or add to some of its work.
The family reproduces the population and provides for the care of children, older people and dependants (people who rely on others for support).
The family socialises children, passing on language, norms, values and skills, so that children learn how to take part in society.
The family is the basic economic unit of consumption (using goods and services) and provides economic support through shared income and household work.
The family provides emotional security and a sense of belonging and identity.

Other institutions adopt or supplement family functions. Schools take on much of children's education, the State provides welfare and health services, employers provide income, and religious bodies provide moral guidance.

Examples of supplementing a family function: parenting courses support the emotional function, schooling from preschool to third level supports the educational function, welfare payments support the economic function, and medical services support the physical function.
Education is how a society deliberately passes on what it knows, and it also shapes children's behaviour and future work. It works both in the classroom and in the everyday life of the school.
Education transmits knowledge, skills and the culture of a society from one generation to the next. It does this formally through the curriculum (the subjects taught), from primary to third level.
It also teaches informally through the hidden curriculum, the unwritten lessons of school life such as rules, punctuality, respect for authority, sharing and teamwork.

Education socialises children, reinforcing the behaviour and values learned at home. It promotes social cohesion by teaching shared history, language and civic values, such as the Irish language and Irish history in Irish schools.

Education prepares people for work through literacy and numeracy, qualifications, specialist skills and career guidance. Work experience comes through Transition Year, the Leaving Certificate Applied, the Leaving Certificate Vocational Programme and college.

Education sorts and allocates people to positions in the economy by means of qualifications. It can support social mobility (moving to a higher social position) by opening access to skilled and professional occupations.

In Ireland, education runs through primary, post-primary, further and higher education. The Leaving Certificate is the state examination at the end of second level, and most students use it for entry to third-level courses.
Education is meant to give everyone a fair chance, but a family's circumstances can affect how far a child gets. Supports exist to narrow that gap.

Socio-economic status (a family's income, occupation and social position) affects chances in education. Higher-status families often have more educational opportunities and go on to third level more often.
Costs of books, uniforms and equipment can exclude low-income families, because they cannot afford what a child needs to take part fully.
Grants, book rental schemes and allowances help families meet these costs.
DEIS (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools) supports aim to reduce the gap for pupils at risk of being left behind.

Religion is the institution that answers questions about meaning and right and wrong, and it gives people a community to belong to. Describe it neutrally: Ireland has many faiths and people of no religion.
Religion provides a system of beliefs and values that gives meaning to life and explains events that cannot be explained by science alone.
Religion provides moral codes that guide behaviour and reinforce many of a society's norms and values, for example rules against stealing or killing.
Religious rituals mark key stages of life, such as birth, first communion or confirmation, marriage and death.
Religious institutions provide community networks and social support to their members, so people feel they belong.
Churches and other religious bodies have supported education, health care and charity. In Ireland many primary schools still have a religious patron.
The influence of religion on Irish society has changed, with declining influence of the Church, more civil ceremonies and a more secular society (one not guided by religion).
The economy is the institution that decides how a society produces and shares what people need. Work is how most families connect to it, which is why economic change reaches family life.
The economic institution organises the production, distribution and consumption of goods and services.
Employment is the main way the economy allocates status and income to individuals and families, and income decides a family's standard of living.
Economic institutions include businesses, banks, markets and the systems of trade through which goods move between producers and consumers.
Work is where people take on adult roles and learn workplace norms (the accepted behaviour at work).
Economic institutions shape family life, for example by determining whether one or both parents must work outside the home, and so hours of work and childcare needs.
Economic changes affect family income and roles. Unemployment lowers living standards and strains relationships, while growth of service industries creates jobs.
Families are consumers, buying goods and services with the income that work provides.

Government is the institution with the power to make rules for everyone and to provide services that individuals cannot organise alone. Its structure spreads that power so no single body holds all of it.
The political institution, the State, maintains order, makes laws, collects taxes and provides public services, including social welfare, health, education, housing and protection of the vulnerable.
Government is typically divided into three branches: the legislature, which makes laws; the executive, which carries them out; and the judiciary (the courts), which interprets and applies them.
This division is called the separation of powers, and it prevents any one branch from holding unchecked authority.
In Ireland the Oireachtas, the national parliament, consists of the President, Dáil Éireann and Seanad Éireann. The Government is the executive, and the courts are the judiciary.
Local authorities provide local services such as housing, planning and libraries.
Citizens take part in government by voting in elections and referendums, electing representatives to the Dáil in general elections.
The State supports the family in each function: welfare payments for the economic function, health services for the physical function, and schooling for the educational function.
Child protection is part of this support. The State's agency for children is Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, which has exercised the Child Care Act 1991 functions since 2014.
Health services and the media are often added to the five main institutions because they also shape everyday life. Treat them as additions, since the list of institutions is not fixed.
The health institution promotes health and provides care and treatment for illness and injury.
In Ireland the Health Service Executive (HSE) provides public health care.
The media, including newspapers, radio, television and online platforms, inform the public and entertain it.
The media also shape public opinion and attitudes and transmit norms and values, which makes them both an institution and an agent of socialisation.
The legal system (courts and law) is part of government, so it needs no separate institution.

Societies never stand still. Social change is a significant alteration over time in the structures, institutions, relationships, values or behaviour of a society, in other words in the way a society is organised.
In exam terms, social change is change in society caused by law reform, technology or major events. The internet and divorce legislation are good examples.
Change can be gradual, such as the slow shift in attitudes to the role of women or to marriage over several decades, or sudden, such as a new law, a war or a pandemic.
Change can be planned, such as a law or a policy, or unplanned. It happens in every society, but the speed differs from one society to another.

Cultural lag is the gap in time between the appearance of a new material invention and the adjustment of norms, values and institutions to it, because people and organisations take time to catch up. The concept was developed by the sociologist William Ogburn.
Many of the biggest changes come from shifts in how people think and live. These social causes feed one another: more education leads to new attitudes, and new attitudes lead to new family patterns.

Changing attitudes and values: there is more acceptance of cohabitation, separation, divorce, lone parenthood, same-sex relationships and diversity, less stigma attached to children born outside marriage, and the Church has less influence than before.

Greater equality for women through better education, careers, financial independence and legal equality changes gender roles at home. The marriage bar, the rule forcing women to leave their jobs on marrying, ended in the civil service in 1973.
Urbanisation is the movement of people from rural areas to towns and cities. It weakens close kin ties and extended family contact and brings new lifestyles.
Towns have better services and facilities, but also more pressure, traffic and anti-social behaviour. Rural depopulation means rural areas can lose services and older people can become isolated.
Education: more people reach second and third level, which changes attitudes, expectations and the value placed on qualifications. Wider access also links to social mobility.

Demographic change means changes in the make-up of the population: falling birth rates, smaller families, later marriage and parenthood, longer life expectancy and an ageing population. These alter the structure of households and the demand for services.

Migration, the movement of people into and out of Ireland, brings new cultures, languages and religions. Cultural diffusion, the spread of ideas, fashions and practices between societies through travel, migration and the media, has a similar effect.

Globalisation, the growth of economic and cultural links between countries, means events and ideas in one country affect others. Social movements and pressure groups also campaign for change, for example for equality, and gain support for their aims.
Law reform both reflects change in attitudes and drives it, because a new law changes what people may do and what they come to expect of one another.

Divorce: the referendum was held in November 1995 and passed narrowly. The Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 then set up the legal process. Say referendum 1995, Act 1996, not that divorce was available in 1995.
Same-sex marriage was approved by referendum in 2015 and given effect by the Marriage Act 2015.
The Civil Partnership Act 2010 provided civil partnership for same-sex couples. This was the earlier arrangement, because since 2015 same-sex couples can marry.
Other legal changes that alter family life include maternity and paternity leave and equality legislation, which support parents at work and promote equal treatment.
How a society earns its living shapes family life, because work decides who is at home, how much money the household has and where people live.

Industrialisation moved many workers from farms and rural trades into factories and towns. Service industries have since grown, and work patterns have changed to include flexible hours, job sharing and working from home.
Growth of female employment has produced dual-earner households. These have more income but more need for childcare, and can bring role overload and role conflict, which are effects, not causes.

Unemployment, recession, emigration and returning emigrants change family life by splitting relatives apart and bringing them back. High housing costs delay home ownership, marriage and parenthood, while higher standards of living improve comfort.
State welfare: improved social welfare, such as child benefit and pensions, reduces dependence on the family and eases financial strain.
New technology changes daily life faster than norms and institutions can adjust, which is cultural lag in action. Its effects can be positive and negative.

Modern communications technology, including mobile phones, the internet and social media, changes how families communicate, how children learn and how people work, and it changes how people spend leisure time. Examples are children skilled in IT, video calls and apps.
Positive effects include access to information and contact with distant relatives. Negative effects include addiction, cyber-bullying and less face-to-face time.
Labour-saving appliances free time and make shared housework easier, which supports more equal roles at home.
Contraception and medical advances affect family size and life expectancy, because families can plan the number of children and people live longer.
Transport shortens distances, so relatives and workers can live further apart and still keep in touch.
Social change affects the family, institutions and everyday life, and its effects can be both positive and negative.
Changing gender roles: more women take part in paid employment, and household tasks are more often shared between partners, giving more equal roles.
Smaller families: many couples have fewer children or have them later in life, and fewer marriages, and later ones, are taking place.
Changing family structures: lone-parent, blended and cohabiting families have become more common, so family structures are more diverse, and the extended family has declined.
An ageing population increases demand for health and care services and for support for older people, and the roles of older people change. More families use childcare.
Changes in values, such as greater acceptance of diversity, change the norms people expect of one another.

Effects can be positive, such as more choice and freedom, or negative, such as stress and strain, role overload, loss of community and social problems. Rapid change can leave some groups behind, for example people whose skills are no longer needed in changing industries.
Change affects institutions: the Church loses influence, the State takes on more services, and schools adapt to diversity.
Social change can cause tension and conflict between groups that hold different values, for example older and younger generations.
Not everyone welcomes change, and several forces can slow it down or stop it.
Vested interests are groups who benefit from the existing system, so they may oppose changes that would reduce their advantages.
Tradition and religious belief can resist changes in norms and values that conflict with long-held teachings.
Fear of the unknown and uncertainty about the consequences of change make people reluctant to accept it.
The cost of change, in money, time and disruption, can slow or prevent it, and generations may disagree about it.
Ireland has seen rapid change in recent decades, and each example below links a cause to an effect on family life.
Divorce: Irish voters approved divorce by referendum in 1995, and the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 provided for it. Marriage equality followed, with a referendum in 2015 and the Marriage Act 2015.
Women in employment: the marriage bar in the civil service ended in 1973, and more married women have been in paid work since, which changed roles at home.
Migration: the Celtic Tiger, a period of rapid economic growth in the late 1990s and 2000s, brought increased immigration and with it new languages, cultures and religions.
Emigration in earlier decades and in the 2008 recession years, and return migration, moved relatives apart and then back together, affecting families and communities.
Rural depopulation and urban growth shifted people from the countryside to towns, and the influence of the Church has fallen.
Exam questions on social change usually ask for the impact on family life, and marks are given for each cause covered.
Structure a discuss answer by cause (social, economic, technological) and then effect, with one Irish example for each point.
Link each cause to a clear effect, for example urbanisation weakening extended family contact, or dual incomes increasing the need for childcare.
Everyone knows what a family is, but defining it exactly is harder than it looks. The core idea is kinship, meaning the ties of blood, marriage or adoption that link people.
A family is a group of people related by blood (birth), marriage or adoption, and it is the basic social unit of society. It supports its members and passes values from one generation to the next.
Traditional definition: a group related by blood, marriage or adoption, usually living together and sharing responsibility for its members.
Kinship is the tie that makes a group a family: the links of blood, marriage or adoption, or common ancestry (lineage).

George Peter Murdock (Social Structure, 1949) defined the family as a social group with common residence, economic co-operation and reproduction. This is one classic sociological definition among several, and later sociologists criticise it as too narrow.
Article 41 of the Constitution of Ireland (1937) describes the family as the natural, primary and fundamental unit group of society, and protects it.
Article 41.3 pledges to guard the institution of marriage on which the family is founded, so the protection has traditionally been for the family founded on marriage.

A household is people living at the same address and sharing living arrangements. A family can span more than one household, for example when grandparents living elsewhere, a parent working abroad or separated parents remain part of the family group.
Not every household is a family, because a household may contain unrelated people.

Legal definitions are narrower and focus on marriage, blood and adoption ties, because they decide rights such as inheritance and maintenance. Sociological definitions focus on the relationships and functions of the group, so they can include cohabiting couples, lone parents and same-sex parents.
No single definition fits every society or every household. Each criterion used in a definition leaves some real families out, so a good definition combines several.
A definition based only on marriage excludes cohabiting couples with children and lone-parent families, so sociologists usually include the parent-child relationship.
A definition based only on shared residence excludes family members who live apart, such as a parent working abroad.
A definition based only on blood excludes adoptive and step relationships, which is why adoption is included alongside blood and marriage.

Criteria used in most definitions: blood or adoptive ties, marriage or a committed partnership, shared residence, shared economic life (pooling income and sharing expenses), raising children, and mutual support and obligation.
You should be able to build a working definition by combining criteria, for example blood, marriage or adoption plus mutual support.

Universality means a family of some kind exists in every known human society, although its form (structure) differs from one society to another. It does not mean every society has the same kind of family.
Every known society has a family group that raises children and organises kinship relationships.
What is universal: kinship ties, the rearing of children, the care of dependants, and the passing on of values and culture.

What varies: size, structure (nuclear, extended, polygamous and matrilineal forms are all found in different cultures), who lives together, where couples live after marriage, how descent and inheritance are traced, and the roles of members.

The structure of a family is shaped by economic conditions (such as farming or industry), religion and culture, and law and political conditions, so one family type is not found everywhere and no one form is natural everywhere.
The functions of the family, such as raising children and caring for dependants, appear in all societies even where the structure differs.

Sociologists use a small set of terms to describe how families are organised in different societies. Each one answers a different question: how many partners, whose line, where the couple lives and how people are related.

Monogamy is marriage to one partner at a time; it does not mean one partner for life. Serial monogamy is a succession of single marriages or partnerships, one after another, such as remarriage after divorce.
Polygamy is marriage to more than one spouse at the same time. Polygyny is one husband with several wives, and polyandry is one wife with several husbands.

Patrilineal descent traces family and inheritance through the father's line; matrilineal descent traces them through the mother's line. Bilateral descent traces them through both, which is the pattern in Ireland.
Matrilineal is about descent and inheritance, not about who holds political power or who heads the household.

Patrilocal residence means a couple lives with or near the husband's family; matrilocal residence means they live with or near the wife's family. Neolocal residence means the couple sets up a new home of their own, the common modern pattern. These describe where a couple lives, not who inherits.
Consanguineal relatives are related by blood; affinal relatives are related by marriage (in-laws).
The family of orientation is the family you are born into; the family of procreation is the family you form.
Looking at families in other societies shows which features are found everywhere and which change from place to place. This comparison is the evidence for universality.

The Minangkabau of West Sumatra, Indonesia, are a matrilineal society in which descent is traced and family property is passed through the female line. This shows that a family can be organised around women's lines, though it does not mean women rule.
