Kibbutzim in Israel historically raised children in communal children's houses, with parents visiting. This shows that some family functions can be carried out beyond the household, shared with the community while kinship remains. The practice has largely ended.
Other forms include polygamous families in societies where polygyny is accepted, extended households of several generations in many societies, and the nuclear family in industrial societies.

Comparing cases shows which features are universal, such as kinship and child rearing, and which vary, such as residence, descent and household size. The structure varies with the society, but a family group is always present.

You may be given a literature or film extract or a short description of a family in another society. Apply the terms to it by identifying the descent pattern, the residence and the form of marriage, and say what remains universal.
The Irish family has changed a great deal since the start of the twentieth century. It helps to think of the change in three phases, with the 1960s as the turning point.
The first phase is the traditional rural family, lasting until about 1960, when most families lived on and worked farms.

The second phase, about 1960 to 1990, was a period of industrialisation (growth of factories and industry) and rising living standards, which moved families towards the nuclear form (parents and children only).
The third phase is the modern family, from the 1990s onward, shaped by legal change, dual incomes and greater diversity of family types.

In an exam you should be able to give four or five contrasts between past and present: structure and size, authority and roles, work, marriage and relationships, and living standards and State supports.

Summary of past versus present: extended family to nuclear, blended and lone-parent; agriculture to industry and services; high child mortality to improved life expectancy; patriarchal to egalitarian; large to smaller families through family planning; changing roles of men and women; more education; a higher standard of living.
Until the 1960s the Irish family was largely rural, agricultural and organised around the farm as an economic unit. Most features of family life, from size to authority, followed from this.
The extended family (grandparents, unmarried aunts and uncles and children) was the most common type, living in one household or close by, especially in rural areas.
Agriculture provided most employment, so the farm was the family's economic unit: all members worked together on it and shared its income. Farming became less labour-intensive from the 1940s.
Families were large, and high child mortality meant many children did not reach adulthood.
Authority was patriarchal, meaning power was held by the father: he decided matters and controlled the money and land. Discipline of children was authoritarian (strict, with obedience expected).

Gender roles were strictly segregated, with men working outside the home and women responsible for housework and the children. The marriage bar required women in the civil service and public sector to leave their jobs on marrying, until it was lifted in 1973.
The Catholic Church had a strong influence on family life, marriage and morality.

Marriages were often arranged or matched and tied to land and inheritance, so marriage often came late and many people never married, particularly in rural areas. Emigration also took many adult children away.
Rural electrification by the ESB, from the 1940s, eased the workload of mothers by bringing electric appliances and lighting to farm homes. The general standard of living also improved in the 1950s.
Industrial and economic change weakened the rural extended family and moved the family towards the nuclear form. Education, jobs and family planning all changed what family life looked like.
Free second-level education was announced in 1966 and introduced in 1967, so more children stayed in school for longer and were nurtured and educated for longer.

Industrialisation and the growth of services drew people from farms to towns and cities, which loosened links with the extended family. The nuclear family became more common and families became more mobile.
Couples married younger and increasingly married for love rather than for land or money, because more people now earned wages away from the farm.
More women entered paid employment, so both parents could work outside the home, which reduced the domestic role of women.
Wages rose and living standards improved, so families could afford more goods and better housing.

The Health (Family Planning) Act 1979 made contraceptives available on prescription for bona fide family planning (in practice, married couples). Amendments in 1985, 1992 and 1993 widened access, and family size fell as couples chose to have fewer children.
Emigration continued in the 1980s, and many families were separated when adult children left to find work.
The Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989 allowed spouses to separate under a court order.
Changes in the law made separation, divorce and other partnerships legally recognised, which altered family structure.
The Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989 provided for judicial separation, allowing spouses to live apart under a court order on property and maintenance.
Divorce was approved by referendum in November 1995, by a narrow majority, which removed the constitutional ban on divorce.

The Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 set out the conditions for divorce and divorce was available from 1997. The spouses must have lived apart for a set period, there must be no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, and proper provision must be made for spouses and dependent children.
The Family Law Act 2019 amended the living-apart condition to two of the previous three years. More lone-parent and blended families followed once divorce was possible.

Civil partnership was provided for by the Civil Partnership and Certain Rights and Obligations of Cohabitants Act 2010, in force from 1 January 2011. It gave same-sex couples legal recognition and rights similar to those of marriage.
Same-sex marriage was approved by referendum on 22 May 2015 and made law by the Marriage Act 2015, extending marriage to same-sex couples. Same-sex parent families are a recognised family structure.
Economic growth, legal change and the recession after 2008 reshaped family roles and living arrangements. Parents today share roles more equally, with more State support.

Dual-income families became common, with both parents working, and families became smaller. Parents shared decisions and household tasks more equally, so relationships became democratic or egalitarian (shared power and roles).
Some fathers became the main carers at home, a change from the strictly segregated roles of the past.
Standards of living are higher, and State supports for families include welfare, childcare schemes, free pre-school and medical cards.
Lone-parent and blended families grew as separation and divorce became legal options, and same-sex parent families are recognised.

Religious influence has declined and Ireland has become more multi-denominational and multicultural. Couples have children later and have fewer of them, and cohabitation and births outside marriage are common.
Gender equality has advanced through women's education and employment, and the Employment Equality Acts 1998 to 2015 prohibit discrimination in employment.
Two working parents, economic shocks and families spread across countries brought new pressures, and new ways of staying in touch.
Demand for childcare rose as both parents worked, so families relied on creches, childminders and grandparents.
Role overload arose when parents cared for their own children and elderly parents at the same time, which makes it hard to meet every demand.
The recession after 2008 brought unemployment (even among highly qualified parents), mortgage arrears and emigration, and some fathers became the main carers at home.
Family members often live abroad, and mobile phones, email, video calls and social media keep relatives in contact across distances.

A nuclear family is a parent or parents with their dependent children (children who rely on them for support), living together in a self-contained household. It is the standard picture of family in modern Ireland, and each structure has advantages and challenges rather than being better or worse.

Two parents, married or cohabiting (living together without being married), and their dependent children form one self-contained household. Marking schemes also accept the wording 'parent or parents and children'.
The unit is small, and the number of children is usually small too, so the household is easy to manage and to keep running on a modest budget.
It is mobile, so members can move for work, which often separates the family from relatives. The family is independent of relatives day to day, but may lack nearby relatives' support.
Tasks, child rearing and decision-making are usually shared between both parents, and often both parents work.
Children depend mainly on the parents' income and on State supports such as Child Benefit.
Advantages: privacy, independence and mobility, because the household answers only to itself.
Drawbacks: less help with childcare and with the care of ill members, and more pressure on the two adults, because there are few other people to share the load.
A lone-parent (one-parent) family is one parent living with one or more dependent children. It can arise in several ways, and the parent takes on the work that two adults would normally share.
Causes include separation or divorce, the death of a partner (bereavement), desertion, a parent's choice to raise a child alone, and a parent never having lived with a partner.
The lone parent carries the full economic, emotional and practical responsibility, often on one income, which means financial pressure and a heavy workload with little free time.
Most lone parents are women, but fathers can be lone parents too.
Lone parents who work need reliable and affordable childcare, and may depend on relatives, friends or State supports.

The State supports lone parents through social welfare payments and schemes, such as the One-Parent Family Payment (a payment for lone parents) and the Working Family Payment (a payment that tops up low earnings), along with medical cards and childcare supports.
Voluntary organisations also offer lone parents information and support.
Lone parenthood can be temporary, ending when the children grow up or when a new partner joins the household, which creates a blended family.

An extended family is the nuclear family plus wider relatives (relatives beyond the parents and children), often counted in a multi-generation group, and its members stay closely linked and depend on one another. It was the usual form in rural Ireland in the past.
Members include grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins, who live in the same household or very close by. Relatives who live far away and are not interdependent do not make an extended family.

A vertical extended family has three or more generations, for example grandparents, parents and grandchildren. A horizontal one has relatives of the same generation, for example brothers with their wives and children.
Members are interdependent, sharing childcare, housework, income and care of older relatives, so costs and tasks are spread widely.
Members may work together as one economic unit, such as a family farm or family business.

There is a strong family tradition, with respect and values passed between generations. Relationships may be more traditional, and historically roles were segregated by gender and age, with men and women carrying out separate tasks.
Households are larger and more crowded, and grandparents often provide much of the childcare.
Advantages: a wide support network and shared costs. Drawbacks: less privacy, and possible conflict between generations and over the authority of older members.
Extended families are the usual form in many cultures, where grandparents often provide much of the childcare.

A blended (also called reconstituted or step) family forms when a parent with children from an earlier relationship has a new partner, so that two family units join. It begins when the new partner and the children live as one family.
Blended families arise through remarriage or cohabitation, and sometimes after the death of a spouse.

Step-parents, step-siblings (no blood link), half-siblings (one shared parent, when the new couple have a child) and extended step-relatives may all be part of the family, creating new relationships. Children may split time between two households.
A joint child of the new partners creates a sibling group that differs in age and background from the earlier children.
The adults must build new relationships and agree rules and discipline, which can be difficult when children have different expectations and routines.
Children may find it hard to accept a step-parent or step-siblings, and rivalry or jealousy can follow. It takes time and patience.
Parents may have financial obligations to children from an earlier relationship as well as to children of the new union, and there are contact arrangements with the non-resident parent.
Advantages: more adults to share income and care, and new relationships and support.
Blended families have become more common in Ireland since divorce became possible and lone-parent families formed new partnerships.
Beyond the four main types, examiners accept other contemporary family structures, and naming them can earn extra credit when a question asks for contemporary family structures.
Same-sex-parent families have two parents of the same sex and their children, who may come by adoption, fostering, previous relationships or assisted reproduction.
Childless (couple) families are a couple with no children.
Cohabiting-couple families are an unmarried couple, with or without children.
Foster families are children placed in a family's care by the State on a temporary basis.
Irish families can be compared with families in other European countries in three ways. Differences come from culture, religion, the economy and how far the State supports families.
Structure: compare the proportions of nuclear, lone-parent, extended and blended households, using the most recent published statistics from Eurostat and the Central Statistics Office.

Size: compare the number of children and members per family, and how family size has changed since the mid-twentieth century. Ireland has historically had a higher birth rate and larger families than most of Europe, a gap that has narrowed.
Roles: compare who works, who cares for children and who cares for older people.
Roles: Nordic countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Norway provide State-funded parental leave and childcare, which supports shared parenting and mothers' employment.

Roles: in many southern European countries, such as Italy and Spain, the family, including grandparents, often provides much of the childcare and care of older people, and adult children may remain at home longer.
Ireland is a mixture: the nuclear family is the most common household structure, relatives, especially grandparents, are still important for childcare, and care follows a family-based approach.

State support: compare how far each country relies on the State and on the extended family to support parents. In Ireland, State support such as childcare and parental leave has grown but still relies on families and on private spending.

Social changes are shifts in how people live, marry and think. They have altered who forms a family, when families start and how big they are, which is why the Irish family is now more varied than it used to be.

Divorce has been possible since 1997 under the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996. Separation and divorce increased the number of lone-parent families, and new partnerships formed afterwards created blended families, so there are more family types.

Cohabitation (an unmarried couple living together) is now a common alternative to marriage, and a growing proportion of children are born outside marriage. This means marriage is no longer the only basis of a family.
Later marriage and later first births, helped by family planning and by women's choices about education and work, have led to smaller families with fewer children per family.

Same-sex marriage (approved by referendum on 22 May 2015 under the Marriage Act 2015) and civil partnership (under the 2010 Act, in force from 1 January 2011) mean same-sex couples can form families. Adoption by same-sex couples makes same-sex parent families a recognised structure.
Surrogacy and assisted reproduction are also social issues. They give some couples new routes to parenthood.
Changing attitudes to lone parents mean lone-parent families are more widely accepted than in the past, so there is less pressure to marry in order to raise a family.
Other social changes affect how family members share roles, where they live and how long generations stay connected. Each one changes who lives together and who looks after whom.
Gender equality in education and employment has produced more dual-career couples (both partners in a career), more shared household roles and, in some families, a father as the main carer.

Declining religious influence has weakened the Church's influence on decisions about marriage and family life. A more multi-denominational and multicultural society also gives people more choice in how they form families, so a wider range of family types exists.

Urbanisation, the movement from rural areas to towns and cities, loosened links with the extended family (grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins). Fewer relatives live nearby, so households are smaller and more often nuclear (parents and children only).
Children are dependent on their parents for longer because they spend more years in education, so adult children stay at home longer.
Increased life expectancy means more generations are alive at the same time and there are more older people, who need more care from their families.
Addiction, for example to alcohol or drugs, affects family life by causing stress, financial strain and conflict, and can change who takes on caring roles.
Economic pressures shape how many adults earn, where families live and whether relatives share a home. Money and jobs therefore decide family size, location and roles as well as living standards.
The cost of living, housing and childcare has risen, so both parents often need to work (dual incomes). Couples may delay having children or have fewer, which limits family size.

The recession after 2008 brought unemployment, mortgage arrears (missed home-loan repayments) and lower family incomes. Some families moved in with relatives, and adult children stayed at home or returned to it, giving multi-generation households.
Emigration and mobility for work, especially in recessions, mean parents or adult children live abroad, so the family is spread across countries. A parent may also work away from home.
Women's paid employment has increased, so many mothers work outside the home. This increases the demand for childcare and changes who earns and who cares in the family.

Changes in work, such as shift work, part-time work, flexible hours and hybrid working (part at home, part in the workplace), change how caring time is shared. Farming is no longer the main source of income for farm families.
Unemployment, especially long-term, reduces family income. This increases the financial burden and stress, and can bring conflict within the family.

Families on a low income, lone-parent families and the unemployed depend on State support. State supports such as welfare, Child Benefit and childcare schemes affect the choices families make, for example whether a parent stays at home or returns to work.
Technology has changed how families are formed, how housework is done and how members keep in touch. It affects family size, family roles and how family life is lived day to day.
Contraception allows couples to decide whether and when to have children, which affects family size and timing.

Assisted human reproduction, such as fertility treatment, allows some couples who could not otherwise have children to do so. The Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024 regulates it and was enacted in 2024, though only some of its sections are in force so far.

Household appliances such as washing machines, dishwashers, microwaves and smart appliances save time on housework. This frees parents for paid work, leisure and children, and makes shared household roles easier.

Communication technology such as mobile phones, email, video calls and social media keeps family members in contact across distance and time zones. It helps emigrant families and separated parents, but it can reduce face-to-face contact.
Social media and screens also bring pressures, including cyberbullying and pressure on children.

Remote working lets parents work from home, and online services such as banking, shopping, and school and health information save time on household administration. Parents can therefore combine work and care.
Computers and the internet support learning, while screens and games change how families spend time together. Home security systems and monitoring give families safety.
Medical technology and better healthcare lower child mortality and lengthen life, so families are smaller and there are more older family members.
The three kinds of change rarely act alone. Their effects overlap, and together they explain the shape of families today.
High housing costs plus recession: adult children remain in the family home or return to it, creating an extended household.
Emigration plus communication technology: the family is split across countries but can be in daily contact by video calls and messages.
Remote working plus childcare costs: a parent can combine paid work with caring for children at home.
Divorce plus communication technology: separated parents in different households keep shared parenting arrangements going through video calls and messages.
Overall, families are smaller, more varied (nuclear, lone-parent, blended, same-sex and cohabiting) and more mobile, with more flexible roles and more reliance on State and private services.
A family function is something the family does for its members and for society. There are five: physical, economic, emotional, educational and social, and together they explain what a family is for.

The five functions are physical (bodily needs and protection), economic (income and spending), emotional (love and security), educational (passing on skills, language and values) and social (learning how to behave in society).
The emotional function is also called the nurturing or psychological function, and the social function is also called socialisation. The content is the same whichever name an exam uses.
Functions remain constant across societies even when family structures change, because every society still needs its members fed, supported, loved, taught and socialised.
Other social institutions can adopt a function (take it over) or supplement it (help the family with it). The State, through public services and payments, supports the family in each function.
One family activity may serve more than one function, so the categories overlap.
The physical function meets the basic bodily needs of family members and protects those who cannot protect themselves.
The family provides food, warmth, shelter, clothing, rest and a safe environment for its members.
Procreation (reproduction) ensures the continuation of the population and gives children their first physical home.
The family protects dependants who are vulnerable, including young children, older people, the sick and people with disabilities, because they cannot meet their own needs.

Other institutions supplement this function: local authority housing, GPs and the public health service (the HSE and its public health nurses), hospitals, school meals programmes, and foster care and Tusla (the Child and Family Agency, set up in 2014).

The State supports the physical function through the medical card (which helps with health costs for those eligible), housing supports from local authorities, home support services for older people (formerly called home help), public health nursing, Tusla's child protection and family support, and welfare payments towards living costs.
The economic function provides the income that supports dependants and links the family to the wider economy.
Adults earn income to support dependants, meaning children and other dependent family members, because dependants cannot yet or cannot any longer support themselves.
Family members pay taxes and spend on goods and services, which supports the wider economy.
Managing the household budget means planning income and spending, and saving.
Historically, in Ireland and in some societies today, a large family worked together as an economic unit, such as a farm or family business, in which every member worked.
Banks, credit unions and insurance companies supplement the family's money management by offering savings, loans and cover against loss.
The Money Advice and Budgeting Service (MABS) helps families deal with debt and plan their budgets.

The State supports this function through social welfare payments such as Child Benefit, Jobseeker's payments, Carer's Allowance, disability payments, the Working Family Payment (formerly Family Income Supplement) and the State pension.
The State also eases family costs through the Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance, medical cards, free school books and the school meals programme.
The emotional function gives family members love, security and a sense of belonging, so that children grow into well-adjusted people.
A secure, loving home gives children the emotional base from which they develop self-esteem and learn to express emotions and discuss feelings.
Family members learn healthy relationships through daily contact with each other.
Parents act as role models and support each other emotionally, which helps children develop emotionally because they copy what they see.
Other sources supplement the family when it cannot meet emotional needs: school counsellors, youth services, bereavement and relationship counselling, parenting courses, friends and community groups.

The State supports this function through parenting courses and programmes, family support services and psychological services (HSE, Tusla), and by funding voluntary and community groups that provide counselling.
The educational function passes on knowledge, language and values informally from birth and prepares children for formal schooling.
The family is the primary educator (the first and main teacher), passing on beliefs, language, skills and customs through informal learning from birth.
Praise, encouragement and a stimulating environment promote early intellectual development.
Parents support formal school work through help with homework, reading together, educational outings and an interest in school, so that children reach their potential.
Pre-school, primary, second-level and third-level education take over formal teaching as the child grows, supplementing the family.
The State supports this function through the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) free pre-school scheme, free education in recognised schools, and the National Childcare Scheme.

Special needs support in schools includes resource hours, special classes, special needs assistants (SNAs) and exam accommodations. Third-level access schemes such as HEAR and DARE help students who might otherwise miss out.

The social function teaches children the norms (accepted ways of behaving), values and behaviour that allow them to live acceptably in society. This early learning at home is called primary socialisation.
Through observation, imitation and stimulation, children learn the norms, values, language, manners and behaviour that society accepts.
Consistent discipline and fair boundaries help children develop a set of values, self-control and respect for others, because they know what is expected.
Language, manners and social skills are learned at home before children enter school.

Schools continue socialisation (secondary socialisation) through the hidden curriculum, meaning the values and habits learned from school life rather than from lessons, and through SPHE. Peer groups, youth organisations, sports clubs and the media also continue it.

The State supports this function through schools and pre-schools and special provision. If a family fails to socialise a child, the State deals with non-conforming individuals through the justice system.
The family does not carry out every function alone. Some institutions take a function over, and others help the family to carry it out.
To adopt a function is to take it over fully, for example foster care, residential care, boarding schools, and schools taking over formal teaching.
To supplement a function is to support the family in it, as in the examples given for each function above.
Over time, formal education, health care and many economic activities have moved out of the family, while the emotional and social functions remain mainly with the family.

Institutions that help include the State (HSE, Tusla, the Department of Social Protection, the Department of Education), schools, credit unions and banks, voluntary organisations, churches and community groups.
Sorting a week of ordinary family life into the five functions shows that one activity can serve more than one function.
Brainstorming: list each activity a family carries out in a week, then assign each one to a category.
Cooking a meal serves the physical function and also teaches table manners, which serves the social function.
Reading together serves the educational function and also the emotional function, by building closeness and confidence.
Paying bills and budgeting serve the economic function and teach children money management, which is part of the educational function.
Comforting a child is emotional, and teaching manners is social.

A family is not the same from one decade to the next. It passes through stages, and each stage changes who does what and how heavy the workload is. A role is the pattern of behaviour expected of a person in a position such as parent or child, and a responsibility is a duty that goes with that role.
1. Couple (establishment) stage: partners set up a shared home and divide household tasks, often according to paid work, time and skills.
2. Childbearing (expanding) stage: parents take on the provider, nurturing, educating and socialising roles for the first time, and the workload is at its peak.

3. Child-rearing stage (children of school age and adolescents): parents keep these roles while children take on more household tasks and independent responsibilities, and parents move from direct control towards guidance.
4. Launching stage: grown children leave home, so parents' roles change from daily care to advice and support at a distance, and the workload eases.

5. Later life stage (a retired couple, or one partner alone): older members may move from giving care to needing it, and adult children often take on practical, financial and emotional support for them.

Roles are not fixed. They are shaped by the stage the family is in, by each member's age, health, paid work and skills, and by social attitudes. Textbooks label the stages slightly differently, so describe each one as well as naming it.

Parents carry a bundle of different roles at once. These roles can be shared between two parents or carried by one, and they matter because a parent who fills them well, with firm and fair explained rules, gives children the best start.
Provider: supplying food, clothing, shelter and money for the family's needs.
Nurturer: giving love, affection and emotional security, so that children feel safe and valued.
Educator: teaching skills, language, values and good habits through daily routines and example.
Socialiser: introducing children to the norms, beliefs and behaviour expected in family and community, so they learn how to get on with others.
Protector: ensuring safety, supervising children and making decisions in their best interests.
Manager: planning the household budget, meals, schedules and maintenance of the home.
Disciplinarian: setting boundaries and consequences that are explained and applied consistently, because children cope better with rules they understand.

Adolescents are not just receivers of care. As they grow, they take on real roles and responsibilities that prepare them for adult life, and these are best treated as growing responsibility rather than just chores.
Contributing to the household: helping with cooking, cleaning, shopping and minding younger siblings, so the workload is shared and parents have more time.
Managing their own schoolwork, timekeeping and personal belongings, which builds the self-discipline they will need as adults.
Developing independence: making decisions about friends, leisure and part-time work within agreed limits, so freedom grows alongside trust.
Respecting family rules and the privacy of others in shared space, so that everyone in the home can live together comfortably.
Sharing in family decisions, such as holidays or how to spend leisure time, which gives them a voice in family life.
Some adolescents earn money through part-time work, or give informal care to a sibling or grandparent.
Who does what in a family has long depended on whether a person is male or female. These expectations have changed a great deal, but they have not disappeared.

Traditional segregated roles (separate, with each partner's tasks kept apart) assigned men as breadwinners and women as homemakers and primary carers of children. The father earned and the mother ran the home, in contrast to joint roles, where partners share tasks.

Where women work outside the home, they often still carry the larger share of domestic work and childcare, a pattern called the double shift, or second shift (a paid job followed by unpaid work at home).
Men's roles have expanded to include direct childcare, cooking and shared decision-making, and some fathers take the primary caring role.
Gender stereotypes can limit children's roles and experience, for example expecting girls to help in the kitchen and boys to do outdoor jobs.
Sharing household tasks equally reduces overload and resentment, and gives children a model of shared responsibility.
Adult daughters often take on more of the care of ageing parents than sons do.
Family roles have shifted a lot in recent times because society, money and technology have all changed. Each factor below matters because it changes who earns, who cares and who does the housework.
Women's participation in paid employment has increased, so many households depend on two earners and domestic roles have had to be shared. Greater gender equality and changed attitudes support this.
Lone-parent families have increased, so one adult often carries the provider, carer and household roles alone.
Smaller families, by choice or because of later marriage and childbearing, mean each child receives more parental time and money.
Greater acceptance of cohabitation, separation, divorce and blended families has created new parenting roles, such as step-parent.
Weaker extended-family and community support means parents have fewer relatives and neighbours to share childcare and other tasks.

Longer life expectancy means some families care for parents or grandparents while still raising children, a pattern called the sandwich generation (adults caught between caring for children and ageing parents at once).

Rising housing, childcare and education costs make two incomes necessary for many households, shifting the provider role to both partners. Unemployment can also reverse traditional provider and carer roles.

Longer working hours and commuting reduce the time available for family meals, shared activities and housework. Labour-saving appliances cut housework time so tasks can be divided differently, while mobile phones and the internet allow remote working and contact but also blur work and home time.

Role conflict arises when the demands of two or more roles held by one person cannot be met at the same time. It is common in modern families, where one adult may be a worker, parent, partner and carer all at once.
Work-family conflict: a parent is needed at work during the hours a child is ill or has a school event.
Role overload: one person carries too many responsibilities, such as employee, parent, carer and homemaker, for the time available.
Conflict between partners over who does which tasks, or whose career takes priority.
Intergenerational conflict: an adult may have to care for an older parent while still raising children at home.
Consequences include fatigue, stress, less quality time with the family, reduced quality of parenting, tension between partners and guilt.
Reducing conflict: explicit agreement on the division of tasks, flexible working arrangements, shared decision-making and help from extended family or services, such as childcare.

One way to see how roles have changed is a short case study or interview with an older person, asking about family life fifty to one hundred years ago. A planned set of questions gives you something to compare with family life today.
1. Decide who to interview, such as a grandparent or an older neighbour, and agree a time, so they are ready to talk.
2. Ask who earned the money in the family and who cared for the children, to show the provider and carer roles at that time.
3. Ask who did the housework and what tasks children were expected to do, to show how household work was divided.
4. Ask about family size, since the number of children affects how much care and work each person carried.
5. Record the answers accurately in your own notes, and write up only what the person told you, with no invented findings.
6. Compare the answers with family life today, looking for the kinds of change expected: more women in paid work, smaller families, shared tasks, labour-saving appliances and more mobile adolescents.
Young children depend entirely on adults to meet their basic needs for growth and survival. If a physical need is missed, the child's health and development suffer, so each one matters.
Food: a balanced diet in suitable amounts supports growth, and new foods are introduced as the child grows so that the body gets all the nutrients it needs.
Shelter: a warm, dry, safe home protects children from weather and hazards, because young children cannot regulate their body temperature or avoid danger for themselves.
Clothing: suitable clothing protects against cold and injury and allows free movement, so the child can play and explore.
Sleep and rest: regular sleep supports growth, concentration and the repair of the body.
Health care: regular check-ups, immunisation (vaccination against disease) and prompt treatment of illness prevent disease and support healthy development.
Hygiene: washing, care of teeth and toilet training prevent infection, because germs spread easily where hygiene is poor.
Safety and protection: supervision and safe surroundings prevent accidents and abuse, since young children cannot recognise danger.
Children need more than food and shelter. Their emotional and mental needs shape how confident they feel and how well they relate to others, now and as adults.
Love and affection: warm physical and verbal affection helps children feel valued, so they grow up believing they matter.
Security and trust: a dependable, consistent caregiver teaches children that the world is predictable and safe.
Attachment: a strong bond with a consistent caregiver forms the basis for later relationships, because the child learns what a trusting relationship feels like.
Praise and encouragement: recognising effort builds self-esteem (belief in your own worth) and motivation.
Stimulation and learning: play, conversation, reading and exploration develop language and thinking.
Routine and boundaries: consistent limits help children learn self-control and understand expectations.
Social contact: interaction within the family teaches children to form friendships and relate to others.
How well a child's needs are met in the early years affects the adult they become.
When physical and psychological needs are met, children grow into well-adjusted, confident adults who are able to contribute to society.
When needs go unmet, children are more likely to grow up insecure, with poor self-esteem and difficulty forming relationships.
Adolescents are changing quickly in body and mind. They still need care, but they need it in a different form from young children, with more freedom and respect.
Growth: rapid growth (the growth spurt) increases the body's need for energy, protein, calcium and iron, and adequate physical activity supports healthy development.
Sleep: adolescents need extended sleep because they are growing, and changes in their body clock can make early starts difficult.
Independence: adolescents need increasing freedom to make choices, with parents gradually reducing direct control while keeping limits.
Identity and self-esteem: adolescents build a personal identity through relationships, interests and feedback from others.
Peer acceptance: friendships become central, so a safe place at home to meet friends supports them.
Privacy: adolescents need personal space and private time, which parents should respect, because it helps them develop their own identity.
Emotional support: adolescents need to be listened to without judgement when problems arise, so they feel able to turn to parents.
Guidance on risks: adolescents benefit from advice on the risks they meet, so they can make safe choices as they gain independence.
The family is where children's needs are met day to day, mostly through ordinary routines and the way adults behave.
Daily routines: regular meal, sleep and homework times give structure and security, so the child knows what to expect.
Modelling: children learn behaviour, language and values by watching how adults act.
Teaching: parents teach self-care, manners, safety and social skills during everyday activities.
Health monitoring: parents arrange medical care, watch for illness and promote healthy eating and exercise.
Responsiveness: a prompt response to a child's distress builds attachment and trust.
The home is where language, values and early skills are first learned, before formal schooling begins. This first learning within the family is called primary socialisation.
Families do not meet every need alone. The State also helps with the cost and care of rearing children.
Education through schools, for example, gives every child the chance to learn and develop.
Child Benefit is a regular payment to parents for each child, which helps with the cost of rearing children.
Medical cards give access to medical care for families who qualify, so health needs are not left untreated because of cost.
Supports for disadvantaged pupils in school help children from poorer backgrounds to take part and do well.
Child-protection services through Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, protect children from harm.
Children are not just dependants. They have rights, which are things every child is entitled to, and these are linked to the needs children have.
Right to life, and to a name and nationality, so the child has an identity and belongs to a country.
Right to be cared for by parents and to live with them, unless this would be contrary to the child's interests.
Right to protection from abuse and neglect, because children cannot defend themselves.
Right to education and to develop physically, mentally, socially, morally and spiritually.
Right to rest, play, leisure, culture and recreation, because play is how children learn and relax.
Right to protection from discrimination, so every child is treated fairly.
Right to maintenance, meaning financial support from parents. The duty of parents to maintain their children is in the Family Law (Maintenance of Spouses and Children) Act 1976.
Right to express an opinion and be heard in matters affecting the child, in line with age and maturity. Where parents live apart, children also have the right to see both parents.
Children's rights come from international and Irish law, and they are balanced with the duties of parents.
The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted in 1989 and ratified by Ireland in 1992.
The Irish Constitution, since the Children Amendment, states the State's duty to protect children's rights.
Rights come with parents' duties, and the State steps in only where a child's welfare requires it.
The Child Care Act 1991 sets out the State's duty to protect children whose health, development or welfare is at risk.

The Child Care Act 1991 gives the State, through Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, powers to protect children at risk. These include care orders and emergency care orders, which can place the child outside the home, for example with foster carers.
Conflict is common in adolescence because young people are moving towards adulthood while parents are still responsible for them. Most causes come back to the wish for independence.
Adolescents seek independence and may feel their parents are out of touch with them.
Peer and media influence can bring adolescents' values into conflict with the values of their parents.
Adolescents accept adult responsibilities but are not yet allowed adult freedoms, which causes frustration.
Relationships with peers and partners can take priority over schoolwork and family commitments, leading to disagreement.
Parents may struggle to let go gradually and trust young people, such as by allowing more freedom, while still needing to set limits.
Common flashpoints include curfews (a time to be home by), technology and money.
Conflict is easier to resolve when both sides stay calm and work towards a solution together instead of trying to win.
Firm but fair discipline: rules are enforced consistently and, where possible, explained and agreed.
Listening and defining the issue: each side states its view and the problem is named clearly rather than made personal.
Negotiation and compromise: possible solutions are weighed together and reviewed after a trial period.
Home atmosphere: adolescents are more likely to resolve conflict when they feel free to talk to parents.
Parents can draw on their greater life experience while still hearing the young person's view.
Parents need to give trust gradually, so the young person has the chance to show responsibility.
Role-play lets you practise handling a disagreement, such as a curfew, in a safe way.
1. Choose a conflict, for example an adolescent who wants a later curfew, and give one person the part of the adolescent and one the parent.
2. Each person states their view without interrupting, so each side feels heard.
3. Use "I" statements, such as "I feel left out when I have to leave early", so the other person is not blamed.
4. Name the problem clearly and suggest a compromise, for example a later curfew at weekends.
5. Agree a trial period and a time to review it, then discuss how it went.
Communication is how family members share what they need and feel. Good communication keeps relationships strong and helps problems get solved.
Communication lets members express needs, feelings and opinions, so that each person feels heard, valued and secure.
Problems discussed openly are more likely to be solved before they become serious conflict.
Bottled-up feelings, such as anger kept hidden, can lead to resentment, stress and withdrawal.
Discussion of spending, meals, childcare and the care of vulnerable members allows household work to be shared fairly.
Explaining the reasons for rules, rather than simply imposing them, makes them more likely to be accepted.
Children learn language, empathy and negotiation by taking part in conversation with adults.
Older members who encourage and praise achievement build confidence in younger members.
Secrecy or aggressive criticism creates mistrust, loneliness and conflict.
Good communication is a skill, and it can be blocked by everyday habits.
Active listening means listening without interrupting, using calm language and checking understanding before replying.
Taking turns to speak gives everyone a chance to be heard, so no one person dominates.
Family meetings give a regular, planned time to discuss plans and problems, so issues are raised before they grow.
Barriers to communication include lack of time, screens, differences in age and tone of voice.

Independence means an older person keeps control over daily decisions and activities, which supports dignity, health and wellbeing. It is not the same as being alone: it means choosing how to live, with support where it is needed.
Dignity and self-esteem: making their own decisions protects an older person's sense of worth and identity.
Physical health: staying active and managing everyday tasks maintains strength, mobility and balance, so they stay able for longer.
Mental health: making choices and having a purpose reduces the risk of depression and loneliness.
Family roles: an independent older person needs less care, so the load on family members is lighter and shared more fairly.
Living in their own home lets older people keep their routines, friends and community ties.
An older person can be independent and still accept help, such as a home support worker, because independence is about who makes the decisions.
Most older people want to stay in their own community for as long as they can. Small changes to the home, the right housing choice and regular contact with other people all make that possible.

Adapting the home: handrails, ramps, non-slip flooring, good lighting, a level-access shower, and a stairlift or downstairs bedroom, so that stairs and bathrooms stay safe. Local authority housing adaptation grants help older people and people with a disability with the cost.
Sheltered housing: self-contained units with a warden or manager on hand and shared communal facilities, so help is close without giving up a home of their own.
Bungalow living: a single-storey home removes the difficulty of stairs.
Granny flat: a self-contained unit built within or attached to a family member's house, giving privacy with family support nearby.
Downsizing to a smaller house reduces maintenance, cleaning and running costs.
Social contact: active retirement groups, community and voluntary groups, and visits from neighbours and relatives build a social circle and prevent isolation.
Meals on Wheels and similar community meal services deliver meals to the home for older people who find cooking difficult, and home support (home help) assists with everyday tasks.
Personal alarm systems let an older person call for help in an emergency while living alone, which makes living alone safer.
Many older people need some help without wanting to leave home. State and voluntary supports provide that help, and each one protects a different kind of independence.

Home support (home help): the HSE's Home Support Service gives help with personal care and everyday tasks to people living at home, so they can stay in their own home. Home care packages exist for higher needs.
Public health nurses visit older people at home to address minor health problems and advise on care.
A medical card gives free GP visits and subsidised prescribed medicines, with a small charge per item, to people who qualify. It is granted on income (a means test) or on medical need or hardship.
The Free Travel scheme (Travel Pass) makes public transport affordable and allows older people to keep going out, which protects their social life.
The State pension gives a regular income, either contributory or non-contributory (means-tested), which supports financial independence.
Other means-tested social welfare payments provide income support to older people with insufficient means.
Voluntary and community bodies such as Age Action, ALONE, Active Retirement Ireland and Meals on Wheels groups, along with family, neighbours and friends, provide visits, shopping, meals and company.
Where an older person lives affects how independent they can be and how much the family has to do. Each option has advantages and disadvantages, and the best choice differs from person to person.
Remaining in their own home (with adaptations and supports): advantages are familiarity, independence and community ties; disadvantages are maintenance costs, isolation and the cost of adaptations.
Living with a family member: advantages are close support and companionship; disadvantages are loss of privacy, possible generation conflict, growing dependence and strain on the carer.
Granny flat or extension: advantages are privacy with family support nearby; disadvantages are the cost of building and shared space tensions. Planning rules should be checked first.
Sheltered housing: advantages are a self-contained unit, security, contact with neighbours and a warden; disadvantages are communal rules and limited choice of location.
Residential care in a nursing home: advantages are 24-hour nursing and personal care for high needs; disadvantages are loss of the home and of independence, and high cost.
The Nursing Homes Support Scheme, known as Fair Deal and run by the HSE, helps pay for long-term care: the resident contributes according to income and assets and the HSE pays the balance.
The choice depends on health, mobility, finances, family support and, above all, the older person's own wishes.
A real decision about where an older relative should live is best made by gathering evidence and involving the person concerned.
1. Find out the relative's health, mobility, finances and wishes by talking with them.
2. List the options, such as own home with adaptations, living with family, a granny flat, sheltered housing and a nursing home.
3. For each option, record the advantages, disadvantages and cost, including any grants or Fair Deal support.
4. Compare the options against the relative's needs and wishes, and recommend the one that keeps the most independence safely.
Different generations grew up in different worlds, so their attitudes and expectations often clash. This is generation conflict, and it affects families at every stage.
Generation conflict is disagreement between members of different generations because their attitudes, values and experiences differ.
Parents and adolescents disagree over curfews, friends, technology and independence.
Adults and their own parents may disagree over care, living arrangements, spending or the older person's role in the household.
Older people may judge younger generations by their own youth without accounting for social changes such as technology and working life.
Changing moral values and lifestyle choices, such as attitudes to marriage and religion, can divide generations.
When an older person loses independence, decisions made for them can cause frustration and conflict.
Conflict between generations rarely disappears by itself. The aim is for each side to feel heard and to agree arrangements everyone can live with.
Good communication avoids confrontation and lets each generation state its view and listen to the other.
Clear expectations: everyone should know what is expected of them and where the boundaries lie.
Patience and understanding: recognising that values change over time reduces hostility.
Respect for experience: younger people can value the wisdom older generations have gained, and older people can accept change.
Compromise and negotiation: shared arrangements, such as visiting times or care responsibilities, are agreed together.
Early action: problems are addressed before they grow, rather than being ignored.
Regular family meetings create an atmosphere in which family members can talk openly.
Role-play practises these skills, for example a case study of an older person who resists moving into a granny flat.
Grandparents are often an important part of family life. They contribute in many ways, and the family has duties towards them in return.
Childcare: collecting grandchildren from school or minding them while parents work reduces childcare costs for the family.
Emotional support: grandparents listen to and reassure children and adults during stressful times.
Transmitting values: older members pass on values, traditions, culture and family history, giving children identity.
Practical help: grandparents assist with homework, meals and household maintenance.
Financial help: grandparents may help adult children with occasional costs, such as a deposit for a house.
Advice and experience: older people help with decisions and act as positive role models.
Responsibilities: respecting parents' rules and boundaries, communicating honestly and not undermining parental decisions.
As they age, the family has a duty in return to provide transport, care, company, money and emotional support to the older person.
Sharing a home brings grandparents and grandchildren closer, but it also changes family life for everyone.
Advantages: time with grandchildren, relaxed relationships because grandparents do not usually have to discipline, and practical help in the home.
Disadvantages: loss of privacy, differing views on child-rearing, and an extra caring burden as the grandparents age.
A family member has special needs when they need support beyond the usual family routine. The needs can be physical, mental or emotional, and the family's response depends on which kind it is.
Physical needs include limited mobility, sensory impairment (loss of sight or hearing) and long-term illness, so the member may need help with movement, personal care or equipment.
Mental needs include intellectual disability, learning disability, autism and mental health difficulties, so the member may need extra help with learning, communication or daily decisions.
Emotional needs include behavioural or emotional difficulties, so the member may need patient, consistent support from the whole family.
Special needs can be present from birth or acquired later through accident, illness or age, so any family can find itself in this situation.
The member can be a child, an adult or an older relative, so a family may be a parent caring for a child or adult children caring for a parent.
Use respectful language: talk about a member with special needs, and focus on the person and their abilities, not just the condition.
The family responds practically, emotionally and financially, and usually draws on outside services as well. A good answer covers several of these, each with its purpose.
Care at home: family members provide daily personal care, supervision and transport, often reorganising work and routines around the member's needs.
Adapting the home: ramps, wider doorways, grab rails, a downstairs bedroom and special equipment improve access and safety, so the member can move around the house with less help.
Encouraging independence: the family builds the member's skills in self-care, communication, mobility and decision-making, within safe limits, and helps the member to integrate into the community.
Working with professionals and organisations: doctors, therapists, teachers and social workers plan support together with the family, so that care is coordinated.

Claiming assistance: families apply for all the State assistance and grants the member qualifies for, including income support and those for equipment and adaptations, because the costs of care are high.
Emotional support: family members reassure the member, listen to concerns and protect the member's dignity and self-worth, treating the member as a full member of the family.
Siblings also need attention, so that they do not feel overlooked while the family focuses on the member with special needs.
Advocacy: families speak up for the member's rights and lobby (campaign) for better services and State support.

Caring for a member with special needs can put pressure on a family's time, money, health and relationships. Marking schemes credit development, so for each difficulty state the problem and then its effect.
Limited employment and educational opportunities for the member restrict independence and income.
Social isolation and prejudice exclude the member and the family from community life, so they may have fewer friends and less support.
A shortage of help and respite (a short break from caring) leaves carers exhausted.
Limited mobility and inaccessible transport and buildings restrict daily life, so even simple outings need planning.
Stress, fatigue and fear for the future, particularly about who will care for the member when parents can no longer do so.
Gaps in services and the cost of care also affect the household budget and the relationships within the family.
Inadequate State financial support can force a parent to give up paid work to provide full-time care, which means a loss of income.
Insufficient medical, therapy and educational services cause delays in assessment and support, so the member may go without help they need.
The extra costs of care, equipment and transport place strain on the household budget, especially when income has fallen.
Siblings may be given added duties and receive less parental attention, which can strain relationships.
Challenging behaviour in some conditions strains relationships and daily routines.
Statutory services are provided or funded by the State. They are a family's first source of professional help and financial support.

Health, disability and social care services come mainly through the HSE, which offers health, disability and family support services, including physiotherapy, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy, public health nurses, respite and day services, and assessment of need.
The Disability Act 2005 gives the right to an assessment of health and education needs and to a service statement, and families can request this assessment in order to access services.
Education services for children with special educational needs are provided through schools within the State education system, using resource teaching and special needs assistants.

The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) coordinates these supports, under the Education for All Children with Special Educational Needs Act 2004 (the EPSEN Act), the Act on the educational needs of children with special needs.
Social welfare supports include Domiciliary Care Allowance for a child with a severe disability, Disability Allowance for adults, and Carer's Allowance for the person providing care.
The Carer's Support Grant is a yearly payment to carers that may fund respite, giving the carer a break.
A medical card is available for those who qualify, and housing adaptation grants through the local authority help pay for changes such as ramps.
Voluntary organisations are independent, non-profit bodies. They work alongside the State rather than replacing it, and they are funded partly by the State and partly by fundraising and donations.
They provide services, support and advocacy, including respite care, support groups, training, advocacy and information, which statutory services may not provide.
The Rehab Group is a non-profit organisation with service areas: education, training, employment, social care and home services, all to promote equality for people with disabilities.
The National Learning Network is the Rehab Group's training arm, offering training and qualifications for people with disabilities, and Rehab Enterprises provides employment.
Recycling projects and fundraising help to pay for the Rehab Group's work.
Enable Ireland provides services for children and adults with physical and neurological disability, and the Irish Wheelchair Association supports wheelchair users with housing and transport.
Down Syndrome Ireland supports people with Down syndrome and their families, Inclusion Ireland campaigns for people with intellectual disability, and AsIAm supports autistic people.
Voluntary services matter because they fill gaps in State provision, offer peer support from families in similar situations, and campaign for rights.
The syllabus suggests a short case study of a family with a member who has a physical disability, to show how a family uses both statutory and voluntary services.
Choose a family, real with permission or an imagined example clearly labelled as such, and describe the member's needs without medical detail.
Describe how the family responds: care at home, adapting the home, encouraging independence and emotional support.
List the statutory services the family uses, such as the HSE, school supports and social welfare payments, and what each provides.
List the voluntary organisations the family uses and what each offers, such as respite, peer support or training.
Finish with the difficulties the family faces and how services help, because this ties the response to the challenges.
Marriage is both a social institution, recognised by society, and a legal status, recognised and protected by the State. It is a voluntary commitment that is intended to be lasting.

A marriage is a union of two people who freely agree to it, entered into through a civil or religious ceremony that is legally recognised. Because both must agree freely, nobody can be forced into it.
Marriage is a union to the exclusion of all others, so a person may be married to only one person at a time. Marrying again while the first marriage is still valid is bigamy, which is a crime.
Living together as a couple and remaining faithful to each other are part of what marriage involves, and a full definition includes both.

Marriage creates legal rights and duties between the spouses (husband and wife), including inheritance rights and a duty of financial support for the spouse and children. This is why it is a legal status as well as a personal commitment.
The State gives marriage special protection in the Constitution, and the law has changed over time about who can marry and how couples are recognised.

Article 41 of the Constitution (Article 41.3 deals with marriage) pledges the State to guard the institution of marriage, on which the family is founded, with special care, and to protect it against attack.
After the marriage equality referendum on 22 May 2015, the Constitution says marriage may be contracted in accordance with law by two persons without distinction as to their sex.
The Marriage Act 2015 gave this effect, in force from 16 November 2015, so same-sex couples marry on the same legal terms as opposite-sex couples.

Civil partnership, created by the Civil Partnership and Certain Rights and Obligations of Cohabitants Act 2010, gave same-sex couples rights and duties similar to marriage. It is a different legal status, not marriage.
Civil partnership is no longer available to new couples, but existing civil partnerships remain valid. Civil partners who marry each other end their civil partnership.

A marriage can be a civil ceremony (conducted by a registrar or a civil solemniser) or a religious ceremony (by a priest, minister or other person registered as a solemniser). A secular or humanist ceremony is possible with a registered solemniser. Each has the same legal effect once registered.

The law sets conditions so that a marriage is entered into freely, by people who are able to marry, and is properly recorded. A marriage that fails these conditions may be void or voidable, and a court can declare it invalid through legal nullity.
Age: both people must be at least 18. There is no exception for 16- and 17-year-olds, because the minimum age is 18 for everyone.
Free to marry: neither person may already be married or in a civil partnership, because a person can be married to only one person at a time.

Consent: both must consent freely, and consent obtained by force, threat or pressure is not valid. Both must also understand what they are doing, so a person who cannot understand the nature of marriage cannot validly marry (this is called capacity).
Prohibited degrees: the couple may not be too closely related, by blood or, in some cases, by marriage or adoption.

Notice: both must give notice of their intention to marry, in person, to a civil registration service (the registrar of the area) at least three months before the wedding. This applies to civil, religious and secular ceremonies.
They bring the documents the registrar requires with the notice, for example identification and a declaration that there is no impediment (nothing in law to stop the marriage).

Formalities: the ceremony is conducted by an authorised person, a registrar or a registered solemniser. The venue is one the registrar has approved (for a civil ceremony), inspected in advance, or a place suitable for the religion. Two witnesses must be present and the required declarations made.
Place: the wedding must take place in a registered building, such as a register office or registered church, or in an approved venue inspected in advance by a registrar.

Registration: the couple and the two witnesses sign the register at the ceremony, and the marriage is then registered. A marriage certificate can be obtained afterwards. The Civil Registration Act 2004 (as amended) governs notice, solemnisers and registration.
A marriage that breaks the legal requirements is not always treated the same way. The law separates marriages that were never valid from those that are valid until a court ends them.

A void marriage was never valid in law, for example because one person was already married or in a civil partnership, they were within the prohibited degrees, one was under 18, or the formalities were not followed. A court decree is still sought to settle the status.
A voidable marriage is valid until a court annuls it, for example because one spouse did not freely consent, or because one spouse is unable to sustain a normal marital relationship.
A marriage that cannot be consummated (no sexual relations after the ceremony because of an inability to do so) can be annulled.
Only the Circuit Court or High Court can grant a nullity decree, and an agreement between the couple cannot annul a marriage. The court process is called legal nullity.
The arrangements around marriage are not the same everywhere. They differ in who may marry, who chooses the partner and how many partners a person may have.
The minimum age for marriage varies between countries and cultures; in Ireland both partners must be at least 18.

In an arranged marriage, parents or families choose the spouse on the basis of background and suitability, usually with the couple's consent. This contrasts with a marriage freely chosen by the couple themselves.
Arranged marriage is traditional in some communities, for example Sikh, Japanese and Travelling communities, but not for every member of those communities.
Some cultures restrict the choice of spouse by religion, social class or kinship (family relationship), meaning a person may not marry someone from a particular group.
Monogamy, meaning one husband and one wife at a time, is the norm in Western countries, including Ireland, so one marriage at a time is also what the law there recognises.

Polygamy, meaning more than one spouse at a time, is the general term and is not permitted in Ireland. Marrying again without the death or divorce of the first spouse is bigamy, which is a criminal offence.
Polygamy has two forms: polygyny, where one man has more than one wife, and polyandry, where one woman has more than one husband.
Same-sex marriage is legal in some countries, including Ireland since the Marriage Act 2015, and not recognised in others.
The same legal marriage can be celebrated in different ways, depending on the couple's beliefs. The choice of ceremony is one more way marriage varies between people and cultures.
Marriage may be a civil ceremony before a registrar or a religious ceremony; both are legally valid when the marriage is registered.
Some couples choose a secular or humanist ceremony, which has no religious content.

Interfaith marriages join partners of different religions, so the couple must agree how the ceremony and their family's religious life will be arranged, for example which traditions the children will follow.
Weddings are full of customs that carry meaning for the people who follow them. These customs differ by culture and religion, in dress, symbols, venue and the form of the ceremony.
Dress and symbols such as a veil and a wedding ring, and throwing rice or confetti, are wedding customs that have been popular for centuries in many cultures.
Jewish weddings are held under a canopy, which symbolises the couple's future home.
At the end of a Jewish wedding, a glass is broken under foot to recall the destruction of the ancient Temple in Jerusalem.
Quaker couples marry at a public gathering with no priest or official present, because Quakers believe God alone joins a couple as husband and wife.
The ceremony can take place in a church, mosque, synagogue, registry office or other approved location, depending on the couple's religion and the law of the country.
Marriage is more than a private promise. It is a public commitment that carries legal obligations, and couples keep it going through how they live day to day.
Spouses make a public commitment to each other, usually through vows or declarations before witnesses during the ceremony, sealed by registration of the marriage.
Because marriage carries legal obligations, spouses owe each other the rights and responsibilities below, which the law can enforce.
Commitment is maintained, so that the marriage lasts, by working on the relationship, communicating positively and remaining faithful and loyal.
Commitment is also shown through sharing responsibility for the home, money and children, for example through shared finances and a shared home.
A right is something each spouse is entitled to receive from the other because they are married. These rights are the other side of the responsibilities each partner takes on.
Each other's company: spouses are entitled to live together as a couple.

Sexual relations: each spouse is entitled to sexual relations with the other, and consummation is the basis of the marriage. An unconsummated marriage can be annulled (declared never to have been valid) in some circumstances.
Faithfulness: each spouse is entitled to the other's loyalty and faithfulness within a monogamous marriage, because the marriage is a promise to one partner only.
Inheritance: under the Succession Act 1965, a spouse who dies without a will (intestate) leaves the whole estate to the surviving spouse if there are no children.
If there are children and no will, the surviving spouse takes two-thirds of the estate and the children share one-third.

Legal right share: a surviving spouse can claim a share of the estate even where a will leaves them less, so a will cannot cut them out. The share is one half if there are no children and one third if there are children.
Marriage also places duties on each partner, towards each other and towards their children. Some of these are backed by law and some depend on commitment.

Financial support: each spouse must support the other (a dependent spouse) and any dependent children. The Family Law (Maintenance of Spouses and Children) Act 1976 allows a spouse to seek maintenance through the court.

Joint guardianship: married parents are both guardians of their children and share responsibility for their care and upbringing, under the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964 as amended by the Children and Family Relationships Act 2015.
Children's needs: parents must provide for their children's physical, emotional, social, moral, educational and spiritual needs.
Commitment: spouses must work on the relationship, show loyalty and keep their commitment to the marriage.
Positive communication: spouses must talk openly about decisions, finances and family matters to keep the marriage functioning.
Caring for a sick spouse is also a responsibility, since marriage means looking after your partner when they are ill.
A wedding takes a day, but a marriage lasts years. Pre-marriage courses give engaged couples a structured chance to examine what married life involves before they commit.
A pre-marriage course is run before the wedding and helps a couple understand what married life involves and prepares them for it.
Courses explain the expectations and realities of marriage, so couples test their assumptions about married life before the wedding rather than discovering a mismatch afterwards.
Accord, an Irish marriage and relationship support organisation founded by the Catholic Church, provides pre-marriage courses for couples in centres around Ireland. It is not a State body.
Churches and other religious bodies also offer preparation for their own members, and some may require it before a religious wedding. The couple should check the requirements of their own religion.
Courses cover a range of practical and personal topics, so couples can discuss them before the wedding.

Topics include communication, conflict resolution (managing disagreements), relationships, family planning, child-rearing and parenting, financial responsibility and budgeting, and the legal requirements of marriage.
Practical topics include buying or renting a home and managing the household budget as a married couple, so money and housing plans are agreed before they cause disputes.
Couples discuss roles and expectations, such as who will do which household tasks and what each partner expects from the marriage.
Couples examine their own personal qualities that help a marriage, such as honesty, openness, tolerance and commitment, and discuss issues that could harm the marriage.
Courses prompt couples to discuss problems such as addiction (alcohol abuse, drugs and gambling), so they can recognise the warning signs and know where to seek help early.
Exams ask how courses help, not only what they cover. Each benefit below follows from the topics: the course gives couples knowledge, skills and a safe place to talk.
They explain the expectations and realities of marriage, so couples test their assumptions before committing.
They encourage openness and honest communication between partners, so difficult subjects are raised before the wedding instead of after it.
They give couples a forum to discuss shared expectations about roles, money, housing and having children, and to find out whether they agree.
They give practical advice on money, housing, parenting and family planning, so the couple can plan ahead.
They build the skills needed to resolve conflict before it damages the relationship, which reduces the risk of later breakdown, and they show couples where help is available.
Meeting other engaged couples gives support and shows couples that others have the same questions.
Pre-marriage courses are not the only help available. The State, schools, religious bodies and advice services all play a part in preparing people for marriage.
The registrar of the area (the civil registration service) receives the written notice of intention to marry at least three months before the wedding, and the couple supply the required documents.
The registrar also inspects proposed venues, so the ceremony location is approved, and registers the marriage.
Religious bodies may offer preparation for couples before a religious wedding, and the couple should check the requirements of their own religion.
