Schools prepare young people for marriage: Home Economics classes examine the roles and responsibilities of partners in marriage and the laws relating to marriage, and SPHE classes discuss relationships and marriage.

Information and advice services help with specific questions: Citizens Information, solicitors for legal questions such as property and wills, financial advice services such as MABS for budgeting, and the family's own support.

Counselling is the first option for a couple in difficulty. It helps partners talk through their problems while there is still a chance to put things right, so that separation or divorce does not become necessary.
Counselling aims to help a couple resolve their problems before they become grounds for separation or divorce, which is why it is the first step rather than the last.
The service is confidential, so partners can speak openly. They may attend together, separately or, where relevant, with their children.
Several visits may be needed before the couple reach a resolution, because problems built up over time are rarely settled in one session.
The counsellor facilitates the discussion and may offer advice, but does not decide for the couple. The couple work out their own way forward.
Counsellors may refer a couple to a specialist counsellor for a particular problem, such as addiction or difficulties in sexual relations.
Marriage counselling is provided by Accord and by other independent counselling services in Ireland.
Mediation is an alternative to court for a couple who have already decided to separate or divorce. Instead of a judge deciding the outcome, the couple work out the terms themselves with help.

The Family Mediation Service of the Legal Aid Board offers a confidential service to couples who have decided to separate or divorce. It was established in 1986, is State-funded and is free, whereas private mediators charge.
An impartial, trained mediator meets the couple together and helps them negotiate their own agreement. The mediator does not take sides or decide for them.
The issues negotiated include parenting arrangements, custody and access to children, finances and maintenance, and the family home and other property.
Mediation keeps children out of conflict, encourages communication between the partners, and helps them accept the separation.
Mediation is less costly, less adversarial and quicker than court proceedings, which pit the spouses against each other.
The outcome is a written agreement that each partner can bring to their solicitor to be made legally binding.
Legal separation is a legally binding agreement under which spouses live apart but remain married. It lets a couple settle practical arrangements without going to court.
The spouses agree to live apart and set out the terms in a deed of separation, a legally binding written agreement.
Typical terms are living apart, care and access arrangements for the children, maintenance, and what happens to the family home.
A solicitor draws up the deed, and each spouse should have their own solicitor. A mediator may help them reach the terms.
Legal separation can be done without going to court if both spouses agree to the terms.
The spouses are still married, so neither can remarry. Only a divorce or a nullity decree allows that.
Where the spouses cannot agree, a court can grant a judicial separation. This is a court order, so it is different from a deed of separation, which the couple agree themselves.

Nullity and annulment both declare that a marriage was never valid, but only a legal nullity decree has effect in the eyes of the State. Do not confuse either with divorce, which ends a marriage that was valid.
Legal nullity is a declaration by a court (the Circuit Court or High Court) that the marriage was never valid in law. The parties are then free to marry other people.
Couples married in a civil or State-recognised religious ceremony need a legal nullity decree before either spouse can remarry.
A marriage may be void, for example where one party is already married or in a civil partnership, the parties are within the prohibited degrees of relationship, or the formalities were not followed.

Nullity may also be granted for a lack of capacity or free consent, or where a marriage is voidable, for example because one spouse cannot sustain a normal marital relationship, including inability to consummate.
Church annulment is granted by a Church marriage tribunal, which studies the marriage and declares it invalid in the eyes of the Church.
A church annulment has no legal effect in the State, so the couple remain legally married. A civil nullity decree or a divorce is still needed before either can remarry civilly.
Nullity says the marriage never validly existed. Divorce ends a marriage that was valid.
Divorce is a court decree that legally ends a valid marriage. It was introduced in Ireland by the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996, after the 1995 referendum.

The Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 was amended by the Family Law Act 2019, which shortened the living-apart period from four of the previous five years to two of the previous three, and came into force on 1 December 2019.
First condition: the spouses must have lived apart for at least two of the previous three years. The couple can live apart under the same roof, and they do not have to be legally separated first.
Second condition: there must be no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, meaning no realistic chance of the spouses getting back together.
Third condition: proper provision has been or will be made for each spouse and for any dependent children, so that nobody is left without support.
The couple must also have a link to Ireland: either living here permanently, or one of them having lived here for at least one year before applying.

When granting a divorce, the court can make orders on custody and access, maintenance, the family home and other property, and succession rights, which extinguish a spouse's right to inherit from the other.
A decree of divorce is final, and each spouse is then free to remarry.

When a relationship breaks down, one person can be left without money to live on. The Family Law (Maintenance of Spouses and Children) Act 1976 gives a financially dependent spouse and dependent children a legal right to maintenance, which is regular financial support paid by one person for the benefit of a dependant (someone who relies on another for money).
A dependent spouse or civil partner is one who does not have the financial resources to support themselves, so the test for the right is dependency.
A dependent spouse can claim maintenance from the other spouse if the relationship breaks down and no other means of support is available. Spouses owe each other support according to their means.
Maintenance can be sought for the dependent spouse and for the dependent children, which is why the Act protects the whole family, not just one person.
Maintenance is regular support, not a one-off payment or a gift.
Maintenance covers the day-to-day costs of the dependant, such as food, clothing, housing and other necessities.
The amount depends on the means and needs of the people involved: the court considers what the paying person can afford and what the dependant needs.
The Act sets exact limits on which children count as dependent, and these limits are the detail examiners reward. It also says who can be asked to pay and in what circumstances.
A dependent child is under 18, or aged 18 to under 23 and in full-time education, or a child of any age with a disability who cannot support themselves.
The payer for a spouse's maintenance is the other spouse, and for a child's maintenance it is either parent.
Maintenance can be sought whether the couple are living together or apart, so the payer can be ordered to pay even where the parents continue to share the same house after separating.
For a child, the marital status of the parents does not matter, so the parents of a child born outside marriage owe the child support too.
Getting maintenance follows three steps, moving from a private agreement to the courts only if the parties cannot agree.
1. The parties try to reach a maintenance agreement, a written arrangement setting out the amount and how often payments are made. It is a private arrangement between them.
2. If no agreement can be reached, the dependant applies to court. The application goes to the District Court or the Circuit Court.
3. The court hears the application and, if it is granted, makes a maintenance order setting out how much the supporting spouse or parent must pay and how often.
A maintenance order is made by the court and can be enforced by it, whereas an informal agreement is not enforced in the same way, so an order gives the dependant stronger protection.
The court can vary (change) an order if circumstances change, for example if the payer's income falls or the child's needs grow.
A court order is only useful if the money actually arrives. When the payer stops paying, the court has a specific tool to collect it.
If the supporting spouse or parent fails to pay, the court can make an Attachment of Earnings Order.
An Attachment of Earnings Order deducts an amount from the wages of the person who owes maintenance and pays it directly to the dependant.
It matters because the dependant does not have to chase the payer, and the money arrives before the payer can spend it.
An Attachment of Earnings Order is not a fine or penalty. It is a way of collecting what is already owed.
Maintenance owed under a court order is enforceable, so the dependant can return to court if payments stop.
Family breakdown can involve separation or divorce, but the right to maintenance does not depend on which stage a couple has reached. The Act also has a limited job, which is money.
Separation: spouses live apart, either by private agreement or by court order; separation does not end the marriage.
Divorce: a legal process that ends a marriage, governed by the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 as amended by the Family Law Act 2019.
Maintenance can be claimed during a separation or after one, and can exist alongside a divorce, so the dependant's support is protected whatever the legal status of the marriage.
Protection under this Act is available whether the dependant is a spouse, a civil partner or a child, which is why it is described as protection for the whole family.
The Act deals with money (income). It does not deal with the home, violence or children at risk, because each of those has its own Act.

Without this law, a spouse who owned the family home could sell or mortgage it without the other knowing and leave the family homeless. The Act gives the family, and especially the children, security of a home.
The family home is the dwelling in which the spouses ordinarily live together as their home. The Act protects the family from losing it because one spouse deals with it alone.
The spouse who does not own the home, and any dependent children, are the people the Act mainly protects, because they are the ones who would lose their home if the owner sold it.
The Act protects the family home whether it is owned outright or held in only one spouse's name, so whose name is on the title deeds (the documents that show ownership) makes no difference.
A spouse with no legal ownership of the home is still protected. The Act does not make that spouse an owner; it gives a veto, meaning the power to block a sale, lease or mortgage of the home.
The protection depends on marriage and applies while the spouses are married and living together in the home. Unmarried cohabiting couples are not covered by this Act.
The Act is in force as amended by the Family Law Act 1995.
The core of the Act is a consent rule. One spouse cannot deal with the family home alone, and the agreement of the other spouse must be written and given in advance.

A spouse cannot sell, lease (let to someone else for a period) or mortgage (borrow money using the home as security) the family home without the written consent of the other spouse. All three actions are covered.
The consent must be given before the deal (prior consent), so agreement given afterwards does not meet the rule.
Consent must be in writing, so an oral agreement to a sale is not enough. A general written consent given in advance can count as consent for later deals, following the 1995 amendment.
If the required consent is missing, the sale, lease or mortgage is void, which means it has no legal effect, and this is why the rule protects the family so strongly.
Under s.3(8)(b), a dealing without consent is treated as not void unless a court declares it void or the parties state in writing within six years that it is void.
There are limited exceptions to the voidness rule, such as a purchaser who paid full value and did not know it was the family home.
A purchaser or lender should check that the required spousal consent has been given before completing a transaction involving the home, because without it the deal may be void.
The Act works as a sequence of steps, from checking that the home is covered to what happens if the rules are ignored or consent is refused.
1. Establish that the property is the family home, meaning the dwelling where the spouses ordinarily live together.
2. Before any sale, lease or mortgage, the owner-spouse must obtain the other spouse's written consent.

3. If consent is withheld unreasonably, the owner-spouse can apply to the court to dispense with (do without) the consent. The court does so only where it is unreasonable to withhold it, taking all circumstances into account, including the needs of any dependent children.
4. If a transaction goes ahead without the required consent, it is void, because the Act itself says so, and it has no legal effect.

The court can also dispense with or give the consent where the other spouse cannot be found after reasonable enquiries, lacks the mental capacity to consent, or has deserted, so a missing or incapable spouse does not block every deal.
The Act has practical effects on lenders, and it is one of several laws that protect a family when a marriage breaks down.
A lender taking a mortgage over a family home will want the other spouse's written consent before it lends, which is the practical effect of the Act on housing finance.
The protection is in addition to any ownership rights, so it does not depend on whose name appears on the title deeds.
The Family Home Protection Act protects the home during the marriage. On judicial separation or divorce, the court can make orders about who keeps the family home as part of its wider powers.

Under the Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989 and the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996, a court can make property orders that transfer or adjust ownership of the family home between the spouses.
A spouse can register a notice of the marriage against the title of the home, which warns any future buyer or lender that the other spouse's written consent is needed.

The Domestic Violence Act 2018 gives people legal protection from domestic violence and abuse. It lets a court make orders that keep an abuser away from the person they are hurting, and in some cases out of the home.
The Act came into operation on 1 January 2019 and replaced the earlier domestic violence law with a single, modern code.
Domestic violence under the Act includes physical, sexual and emotional or psychological abuse and threats, so the protection is not limited to physical attacks.
The person who applies for an order is the applicant, and the person the order is made against is the respondent.
Applications are normally made to the District Court, the local court that deals with most family matters.
The court can act urgently, including without the respondent being present, where there is an immediate risk, because waiting for a full hearing could leave the applicant in danger.
Each order is made in response to a specific application, and the court can attach conditions to the order.
The barring order is the order that removes the abuser from the home. Because it affects who may live in a property, it is open to fewer people than the other orders.
A barring order requires the respondent to leave the home they share with the applicant (the home the applicant lives in) and to stay away from it.
It lasts for the period the court sets, which is up to three years, and it can be renewed. The court may set a shorter period.
A spouse or civil partner can apply for a barring order, and they do not need to meet the property-interest condition that applies to cohabitants and parents.

A cohabitant (a partner living with the respondent in an intimate relationship) can apply, as can a parent against a respondent of full age who is not a dependent person, such as a non-dependent adult child living in the home.

For cohabitants and parents, the applicant's interest in the home (such as owning or renting it) must not be less than the respondent's. The court cannot make the order if the respondent has an interest and the applicant has none or a lesser one.
This property-interest condition is what keeps barring orders narrower than the other orders.

A barring order protects the applicant, and any dependent children, from further abuse in their own home. It removes the respondent temporarily and does not transfer ownership of the home or end a marriage.

Not everyone who needs protection can get a barring order, and not every case needs the respondent removed from the home. Safety and protection orders protect the applicant while the respondent can stay at home.
A safety order is a longer-term order that prohibits the respondent from using or threatening violence, from molesting or putting the applicant in fear, and from watching or following them.
A safety order does not remove the respondent from the home, so it suits cases where the applicant only needs protection from violence, threats and following.

Safety orders are open to the widest group, including people who have lived together, parents who have a child together but never lived together, parents against an adult child, and adults living together in a non-contractual relationship such as relatives.
A protection order is a temporary order with the same effect as a safety order, made while an application for a safety order or barring order is waiting to be heard.
A protection order protects the applicant in the meantime, so it can be granted quickly, even before the respondent has been heard.
A protection order is available to anyone who could apply for a safety order or barring order.
Sometimes the danger is too urgent to wait for a full barring order hearing. Two short-term versions of the barring order deal with these cases.

An interim barring order is a short-term barring order made where there is an immediate risk of significant harm to the applicant or a dependent person, and a protection order would not be enough to protect them.
An interim barring order lasts until the application for the full barring order is decided, so it covers the gap before the full hearing.
An emergency barring order is for a person who lived with the respondent but could not get a barring order because they have a lesser interest in the home, or none.
Examples are an unmarried partner without ownership of the home, or a parent of an adult respondent.
The test for harm is the same as for the interim barring order: an immediate risk of significant harm to the applicant or a dependent person.
An emergency barring order lasts a very short period, up to eight working days.
Five orders can be made under the Act, and the quickest way to keep them apart is to ask two questions: does the respondent have to leave, and is the order urgent or long-term?
Safety order: prohibits violence, threats and following; the respondent stays at home, so it is the least disruptive order; longer term.
Protection order: the same protection, but temporary, while a safety order or barring order application waits to be heard.
Barring order: the respondent must leave the home and stay away, for up to three years.
Interim barring order: an urgent, short-term barring order that lasts until the full barring order application is decided.
Emergency barring order: an urgent barring order for a person with a lesser or no interest in the home, lasting up to eight working days.
The Act reaches beyond the couple. It protects dependent children, backs its orders with the criminal law and makes controlling behaviour an offence in its own right.
The orders can protect the applicant and also a dependent child or other dependent person, so the court can protect a child who lives with the applicant.
Tusla (the Child and Family Agency) can apply on behalf of a person, including a child, in some cases, for a safety or barring order.
Breaking an order is a criminal offence, so the orders are enforced through the criminal law as well as the civil courts.
The Gardaí can arrest a person who breaches an order, and the respondent can be prosecuted.
Coercive control is a criminal offence under the Act. It means knowingly and persistently behaving in a controlling or coercive way towards a partner or former partner, with a serious effect on them.
Examples of coercive control are isolating a person from family and friends, monitoring them, or controlling their money. It applies to people in an intimate or formerly intimate relationship.
The steps are the same whichever order is needed: apply, get urgent help if there is immediate danger, have the case decided, and enforce the order through the Gardaí if it is broken.
1. The applicant applies to the District Court for the relevant order.
2. If there is an immediate risk, the court can make an urgent order, such as a protection order, an interim barring order or an emergency barring order, before the respondent is heard.
3. At the full hearing, the court decides whether to make a safety order or a barring order.
4. If the respondent breaches the order, it is reported to the Gardaí and the breach can be prosecuted.

When a marriage breaks down and the couple cannot agree how to part, a court can step in. Judicial separation under the Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989, as amended, is a court decree under which spouses live apart with the court's orders in place. It does not end the marriage.
A decree (a formal order of the court) means the spouses are no longer required to live together, and the court sets out the arrangements for their maintenance and property.
Because the marriage continues, neither spouse is free to remarry after a judicial separation. Only a divorce ends a marriage and allows remarriage.
The application is made to the Circuit Court or the High Court, either of which can grant a judicial separation, and it is heard by a judge. It is not made to the District Court.
A judicial separation is a legal status that the court grants, unlike informal separation, which spouses agree between themselves without a court order.
It is needed in particular where the couple cannot agree the terms of separating. If they can agree, they use a separation agreement instead.

A court will not grant a decree just because a spouse asks for one. The applicant (the spouse applying) must prove at least one ground, or reason, set out in the Act. The Act has six grounds, and the respondent is the other spouse.
Adultery by the respondent spouse since the marriage.
Unreasonable behaviour by the respondent that makes it unreasonable for the applicant to continue living with them.
Desertion by the respondent for a continuous period of at least one year immediately before the application.
The spouses have lived apart for at least one year and both consent to the decree being granted.
The spouses have lived apart for at least three years, even if the other spouse does not consent.

The marriage has broken down so that a normal marital relationship has not existed between the spouses for at least one year before the application. This is the ground most commonly used because it does not require either spouse to be at fault.
The applicant must establish one of these statutory grounds (grounds set by law) before the court can grant the decree.
A decree on its own only releases the spouses from living together. The court can add orders that settle money, property and children, so the practical questions are answered at the same time.
Maintenance orders require one spouse to provide financial support (regular payments for living costs) for the other spouse and for the children.
Property orders divide or transfer property between the spouses, including who lives in the family home (property adjustment), and orders can also be made about the use of the family home.
Orders on the custody of children decide where a child lives and who has responsibility for their upbringing.
Access orders set out the arrangements for a parent who does not have custody to see the child.
The court may extinguish succession rights, which means a spouse loses their right to inherit from the other spouse. Without such an order, the right to inherit continues.
A pension adjustment order is also possible.
These orders can be made together with the decree, so that the financial and childcare arrangements are settled at once, which saves the family returning to court.
Maintenance orders made on judicial separation can later be varied by the court if the circumstances of either spouse change, such as a change in income.
Judicial separation sits between informal arrangements and divorce. Comparing it with a separation agreement and with divorce shows who decides in each case and whether the marriage ends.
Judicial separation differs from divorce because divorce ends the marriage and allows both spouses to remarry, while judicial separation does not.
Divorce requires the spouses to have lived apart for at least two of the previous three years (Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 as amended by the Family Law Act 2019), and it ends the marriage.
A separation agreement (a deed of separation, sometimes called a legal separation) is a binding agreement made between the spouses, whereas judicial separation is a decree made by the court.
A separation agreement is drawn up by solicitors and agreed by both spouses, often with a mediator. It is cheaper and avoids court, and it is legally binding.
Judicial separation is used when the spouses cannot agree terms, because the judge decides for them.
In both a separation agreement and judicial separation, the spouses are not required to live together, but they remain married.

The Child Care Act 1991 makes provision for the care and protection of children (a child is a person under 18). It matters because it gives the State, through Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, the power to act where a child is not safe at home.
The Act places a duty on Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, to promote the welfare of children who are not receiving adequate care and protection. Tusla has done this job since 2014.
Tusla's duties include providing child care and family support services and investigating where a child may be at risk, so it helps families as well as stepping in.
A child is at risk where they are assaulted, neglected or sexually abused, or where their physical, emotional or educational needs are not met. Ill-treatment also counts.

Tusla has power to intervene in a family situation where a child is deemed to be at risk. More widely, this means the child's health, development or welfare is likely to be harmed and the child is unlikely to get the care needed without Tusla's help.
Only Tusla, not individuals, applies to the District Court for the orders in this Act, so the agency acts on behalf of the child and the court decides.
Care is not always compulsory: where parents ask for it or agree to it, Tusla can take a child into care without a court order (voluntary care).
The Act balances the family's right to bring up their child with the child's right to protection, so Tusla acts only where a child is at risk and the court decides on the evidence.

The Act's protections support children in the family alongside the protection orders available under the Domestic Violence Act 2018, and Tusla can also apply for protection orders on behalf of a child.

Some children need protection at once, before a court can hear a full case. The Act therefore provides short-term measures, ordered by urgency, which give way to a longer order only if the court decides one is needed.

Where there is an immediate and serious risk to a child, a Garda can remove the child to safety and place them in Tusla's care. Tusla must then seek a court order if it intends to keep the child in care.
An emergency care order is a short-term court order that allows a child to be removed to a safe place where there is an immediate risk. It allows Tusla to take the child into care at once.
An emergency care order can be made without notice to the parents, because waiting to tell them could leave the child in danger.
An interim care order is a court order made while the court considers a full application, so that the child is protected in the meantime.
Emergency and interim orders are temporary, and the court must decide whether a longer order is needed.

A care order is the serious step in the Act: the child is removed from the family home. It is made by the court, not by Tusla itself, and it is for a child who needs care and protection they are unlikely to get at home.
A care order is made by the court on application by Tusla, where a child's welfare requires that they be placed in care.
A care order can place a child in care for a long or short term, away from the family home.
Once a care order is made, Tusla takes responsibility for the child's care until the order ends and decides where the child is placed, such as with foster carers or in a residential unit.
Removal from the family home under a care order is the most serious step the Act allows, so the court must be satisfied that the child's welfare requires it.
Not every child at risk needs to leave home. A supervision order lets the child stay with the family while Tusla keeps a close watch, so it is the less intrusive option.
A supervision order is made by the court on application by Tusla, so that the child can stay at home.
Under a supervision order, Tusla personnel can visit the child in the home periodically to monitor the child's health and welfare.
A supervision order allows Tusla to support the family, and to give support or directions to it, and keep the child at home while monitoring the risk.
A supervision order is the less intrusive option, because the child is not removed from the family home.
The court makes the decision on the evidence put before it by Tusla, including whether the child's welfare requires removal or monitoring.

A will is a legal document, governed by the Succession Act 1965, in which a person (the testator) sets out how their property and money, known as the estate, are to be shared after their death. Making one means your wishes are followed instead of leaving the decision to the law.
Without a will (called intestacy), the estate passes under fixed rules in the Succession Act that set the shares, and these may not match the person's wishes.

Under those fixed rules a spouse with no children takes the whole estate, and a spouse with children takes two thirds while the children share one third. Other relatives inherit only if there is no spouse or children, and the State inherits only if there are no relatives.
A will allows the testator to choose who receives each item of property and in what proportions, so the property passes to the people they want.
A will names an executor (the person who carries out the will), who collects the estate, pays the debts and distributes the property as the will directs.
A will can protect a spouse and dependants, and it can state the testator's funeral or burial wishes.
A clearly drawn will reduces the likelihood of disputes among family members over the estate, and it gives the testator peace of mind.
Parents can use a will to appoint a guardian for young children and to make suitable provision for them.

Divorced parents who make a will can ensure that property passes to their children as they intend, can choose an executor, and can change the will later if circumstances alter, such as remarriage or new children.
Careful planning of a will, with a solicitor's advice, may reduce the inheritance tax burden on those who inherit.
The law sets simple rules so that a will really reflects what the testator wanted. If a rule is broken, the will may not be valid.
The testator must be 18 or over (or be or have been married), because the law treats them as old enough to make this decision.
The testator must be of sound mind, meaning able to understand what a will is and what property they own, so that the will reflects their real wishes.
The will must be in writing, and it must be signed by the testator or by someone signing for them in their presence and at their direction.
The signature must be made, or acknowledged, in the presence of two witnesses who are both present at the same time.
The witnesses then sign the will in the presence of the testator.

A witness, or the witness's spouse, who is also a beneficiary (someone who is given a gift in the will) loses the gift made to them under the will, which is why witnesses should be people with nothing to gain. The executor, however, can be a beneficiary.
Good practice is to date the will, store it safely (for example with the solicitor or in a bank) and tell the executor where it is kept, so that it can be found after the death.
Making a will is a matter of working out what you own and who should get it, then putting that in a form the law accepts. It follows six steps.
Step 1: list all assets, such as property, savings, investments, policies and personal possessions, with their value and location, and any debts or liabilities, so you know what the estate contains.
Step 2: decide who the beneficiaries are, starting with the nearest relatives, and record their full names and addresses and the item or share each is to receive.
Step 3: appoint an executor, a trusted person who is willing to act and who will collect the estate, pay the debts and carry out the terms.

Step 4: decide how the estate is divided, including any specific gifts, provision for children and dependants, any guardian, and any funeral or burial arrangements the testator wishes to make. Check this against the legal restrictions in the Succession Act.
Step 5: have the will drawn up. A person may write their own will, but a solicitor is advised so that it is clear and valid.
Step 6: sign the will before two witnesses, store the signed will safely, and tell the executor where it is kept.
After the death, the executor applies for a grant of probate, which confirms the will and gives the executor legal authority to deal with the estate.
A will can be changed at any time while the testator is of sound mind, because it takes effect only on death. The law allows several ways of changing or cancelling it.
A change to an existing will can be made by a codicil, a short document added to the will, which must be signed and witnessed in the same way as the original will.
A new will that expressly revokes (cancels) an earlier will replaces it entirely.
A will can also be revoked by destroying it with that intention.
A will is revoked by the testator's marriage (or civil partnership), unless the will was made in contemplation of that marriage. This is why remarrying parents must make a new will.
A testator is free to choose who inherits, but not completely free. The law protects a surviving spouse, and it gives the executor a formal step to carry out.
A surviving spouse (or civil partner) has a legal right to a share of the estate that the will cannot remove: one-half where there are no children, and one-third where there are children.

Children cannot be left out without thought: a child may ask the court for fair provision if the parent failed in their moral duty to them. Where there is a will, children have no automatic fixed share.
Executors apply for a grant of probate, which confirms the will and gives the executor authority to deal with the estate.

A household chooses a home by weighing what it needs and can afford against what is available in the place it wants to live. No single factor decides alone, so a good answer shows how several of them pull against each other.

Socio-economic factors include income (which decides whether a household can afford a deposit or rent), employment, household size and the stage of the family life cycle, such as a young couple, young children, teenagers, an empty nest or an older couple whose children have left home.
Each stage of the family life cycle needs a different amount of space, which is why a growing family and an older couple choose differently.
Cost decides the size, type and location of home a household can afford. The deposit and running costs matter as much as the purchase price or rent.

Legal and lender fees, stamp duty, repayments, insurance, maintenance, heating and travel to work must all be counted, not just the headline price. Parental help with a deposit is also an economic factor.
Special needs, such as those of older people or people with a disability, may call for single-storey living, step-free access or a stairlift, because stairs and steps can make a home unusable.
Once a household knows what it needs and can afford, it looks at where homes are, what kinds exist and whether any are on offer.

Location is shaped by proximity to work, schools, shops, childcare, public transport, health services and family or friends. Urban areas offer services and jobs, while rural areas offer space and quiet. Safety, noise and risks such as flooding or pollution also count.
Personal preference covers layout, aspect (the direction the home faces), view, garden size and whether the household wants to own or rent.

Type and size of home: a household chooses between a bungalow, two-storey, detached, semi-detached, terraced, townhouse, duplex, apartment or bedsit. It also weighs room for the family, a possible attic conversion or extension, parking, space to work from home, and energy efficiency, shown by the BER.

Availability, meaning the supply of suitable homes at a given time and place, limits choice. In some urban and commuter areas private supply is short, which raises prices and rents, and social housing waiting lists are long because demand exceeds supply.

Setting: a case study of a student, a young couple or a retired couple, asking which of these factors matters most to them. For example, a student may rank low cost and closeness to college first, while a retired couple may rank step-free access and nearby health services first.
The way new homes are planned and built changes over time. Examiners want you to recognise the current trends and say what each means for households.
Mixed estates plan detached, semi-detached, terraced and apartment or duplex units together, so that different household types live in the same community.

New developments include shared open space and play areas, and in larger estates a crèche or shops, so families have facilities on their doorstep. Many estates and complexes have a gated or controlled entrance.

Refurbishment and inner-city redevelopment bring vacant, derelict and older buildings back into residential use. This includes the restoration of period homes, attic conversions and extensions, which add space without using new land.
Apartment living and higher-density development grow in cities and towns, using less land per household. Townhouses are built on small urban sites for the same reason.

An eco-house (an energy-efficient, environmentally friendly or passive home) is an emerging trend. They have high insulation and renewable heating, and may use timber frame or other modern methods of construction, so they cost less to heat.

Housing development follows employment. Demand rises where jobs grow, which pulls people towards commuter towns and suburbs around cities, and commuting distance becomes a cost to the household. Older marking schemes also name satellite towns and one-off rural houses.
Working from home creates demand for a study or home-office space, which affects the size and layout of home a household looks for.

Housing policy is the government's plan for how enough suitable homes are provided and who is helped. The current national plan is Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025 to 2030, published by the Government in November 2025. It rests on activating supply and supporting people.
Increasing the supply of new homes, with investment in the infrastructure (water, wastewater and roads) that housing needs, because homes cannot be built where these services are missing.
Social housing is built by local authorities and approved housing bodies, and social and affordable housing is delivered by these together with voluntary and co-operative housing organisations.
Affordable homeownership supports include the Starter Homes programme, and cost rental homes are let at rents based on the cost of providing them.
Measures to reduce and prevent homelessness include the Housing First programme, and rented accommodation must be registered, so that rented homes are on a register.
National rent controls protect tenants, and modern methods of construction (factory-built components) speed up building.

Sustainable communities are a policy aim: new housing should be supported by shops, schools, transport, parks and other infrastructure and services. Higher-density living and increased housing supply in urban areas aim to make more homes available at affordable cost.
Energy-efficient homes are promoted through the Building Regulations, BER ratings and SEAI grants for upgrading existing homes.
Accommodation for Travellers is planned by each local authority under a Traveller Accommodation Programme, required by the Housing (Traveller Accommodation) Act 1998.
Policy affects a household's choice because it changes what is built and where, what supports and grants are open to a buyer or tenant, and how much a tenant is protected.
Buying makes the household an owner-occupier. It gives control and a possible asset, but it demands money up front and a long commitment.
Advantage: a home may rise in value, so it can act as an investment, and ownership builds equity (the part of the home's value the owner owns).
Advantage: security of tenure, meaning the right to stay in the home, because an owner cannot be asked to leave by a landlord.
Advantage: freedom to choose the design and type of home, to alter and decorate it, and to decide whether to share it with others.
Advantage: mortgage repayments (the regular payments on a loan taken to buy the home) may cost less than rent over the long term, and grants or other supports may apply to some purchases.
Disadvantage: a large deposit and a long financial commitment are needed before the purchase can be completed.
Disadvantage: legal, lending, valuation and survey fees and stamp duty add to the initial cost on top of the price.
Disadvantage: the owner pays for all maintenance, repairs and insurance, and property tax where it applies, because there is no landlord to carry them.
Disadvantage: the value may fall, leaving the owner owing more than the home is worth, and buying ties the household to one location, so moving is slow and expensive.
A tenant pays a landlord (the owner who lets the home) for the right to live in a property, under a tenancy. Renting asks for little money at the start but gives no ownership.
Advantage: little capital is needed, usually only a deposit and rent paid in advance.
Advantage: mobility, so a household can move when work or family circumstances change.
Advantage: the landlord is normally responsible for structural repairs and maintenance, so the tenant has no repair bills.
Advantage: a wider choice of location and accommodation, from apartments and houses to shared houses and digs.
Advantage: tenants have legal protections, including notice rules before a tenancy can be ended.

Disadvantage: rent paid gives no ownership or return, often described as dead money. The rent can also be as high as a mortgage repayment on a similar home, and there is no long-term security if the landlord sells.
Disadvantage: an agency fee, a deposit and rent in advance add to the initial cost.
Disadvantage: the tenant must insure the contents of the home.
Disadvantage: facilities may be poor or shared, and the tenant has no say over changes to the property.
The private rented sector is made up of homes let by private landlords rather than by the State. Its standards and registration are regulated to protect tenants.

Private rented housing (houses, apartments, flats and rooms) is provided by individual landlords and businesses, mainly in cities and larger towns. Rent depends on demand and supply, location, size, quality and amenities, and quality varies.

Landlords must register tenancies with the Residential Tenancies Board (RTB), which helps the state track rented housing and its standards. The RTB also deals with disputes between landlords and tenants.

Rented homes must meet the minimum standards in the Housing (Standards for Rented Houses) Regulations 2019, enforced by local authorities, who inspect rented homes. The property must be structurally sound and in good repair.
Every room must have adequate ventilation and lighting, hot and cold water must be provided, and there must be heating and fire safety. Gas and electricity supplies must be safe.
Bathrooms, showers and other sanitary facilities must be in good working order and kept in a proper state of repair.

Private renting is popular with students, young workers and people who are saving for a deposit to buy a home. It gives flexibility to people in temporary work or who want to move, and the State helps some tenants with rent through social housing supports.

Few buyers can pay for a home from savings alone, so most borrow. The amount a buyer must borrow is the purchase price minus the deposit, plus any costs of buying that the buyer cannot pay from savings.

The factors that determine the amount of finance required are the purchase price (which depends on the size, type and location of the house, and whether it is new or second-hand) and the buyer's own savings and deposit.
Additional costs of buying add to the total needed, so a buyer must budget for more than the price: solicitor's (legal) fees for the transfer of ownership, and stamp duty, a tax paid on the purchase.

Further costs are the valuation and survey carried out for the lender (to check what the house is worth and what condition it is in), an application or lender fee, land registry fees (to record the new owner), home insurance, and any fitting-out, furnishing or repair costs.

A deposit is the buyer's own money paid towards the purchase price. Lenders require a minimum percentage deposit, set by Central Bank rules, and supply the balance as a mortgage, so saving a deposit is a main barrier for first-time buyers.
A mortgage is a long-term loan to buy property, repaid with interest in regular (usually monthly) instalments over a term of many years. Interest is the cost of borrowing the money.
A mortgage is secured on the house itself, which means that if repayments are not made the lender can take possession of the property and sell it to recover the loan. This is called repossession.
A buyer usually combines several sources of money. Some are the buyer's own, some are borrowed from a lender, and some come from the State or family.
The buyer's own savings are the first source, and they make up the deposit that lenders require before they will lend the balance.
A mortgage from a bank or other lending institution is the main source of finance, because it provides the large sum that savings cannot cover.
A local authority home loan is government-backed and is for people who qualify but cannot get a commercial loan.
A credit union loan is usually a smaller amount, for example to help with a deposit or home improvements.
Help from parents or family, as a gift or a loan, is often used towards the deposit.

State supports for buyers include the First Home shared equity scheme (the State and participating lenders take a share in a new home, which the buyer can buy back), the Help to Buy incentive for first-time buyers of new homes, and affordable purchase schemes run by local authorities.

A lending institution assesses whether the applicant can repay the loan and whether the property is a suitable security for it. Each condition below protects the lender by making sure the loan can be repaid, or the property sold if it is not.

Borrowing limit: the loan is capped at a set multiple of the applicant's gross income (income before tax), so the borrower is not lent more than can be repaid. The multiple is set by Central Bank rules and changes.
Loan-to-value limit: the loan cannot exceed a set share of the property's value, so the buyer must provide the balance as a deposit. The rules differ for first-time buyers and others.
Secure, continuous employment: the applicant must be in stable work so that repayments can be met over the term. The self-employed supply accounts instead.
Proof of income: payslips, a P60 (the yearly summary of pay and tax), and tax and bank statements show the lender what the applicant earns.

Good financial record: a clean credit history with no missed repayments or unpaid debts, a record of regular saving and reasonable spending habits. Existing debts and commitments reduce the amount lent.
Term of the loan: repayments are spread over a long period, but an older applicant is usually offered a shorter term so the loan ends before retirement.

Property: the lender has it valued and surveyed, and it must be in good condition and good value as security. The lender checks the title deeds through a solicitor, and the buyer must have buildings insurance for the term.
Mortgage protection insurance, plus proof of identity and address so the lender can confirm who the borrower is.

A mortgage is a large debt that may last decades, and the borrower could die before it is repaid. A mortgage protection policy is a life assurance policy that protects the lender's loan and the borrower's family if the borrower dies during the term.

Mortgage protection is a term life assurance policy for the length of the mortgage and the amount of the loan. Life assurance means premiums (regular payments) are made and a sum is paid out when the insured person dies.
If the borrower dies during the term, the insurer repays the outstanding mortgage balance to the lender, so the family keeps the home.
Without cover, the remaining debt would fall on the borrower's family, who could be forced to sell the home.
Life assurance in general can run for life, whereas mortgage protection runs for the term only, and the sum insured falls as the loan is repaid (a decreasing term policy).
Under the Consumer Credit Act 1995 a lender must make sure that the borrower has mortgage protection, with exceptions such as where cover cannot be obtained because of age or health.
The borrower may buy mortgage protection from the lender's group scheme, an insurer or a broker, and cannot be forced to buy it from the lender.
Mortgage protection does not pay the repayments if the borrower is ill, disabled or made redundant, because it pays only on death. Income protection is a separate policy.
Annuity and pension-linked mortgages require a mortgage protection policy to be taken out with the loan.
An endowment mortgage does not need a separate protection policy, because its life assurance policy already covers the loan.
Mortgages differ in how the capital (the sum borrowed) and the interest are repaid. Annuity, endowment, pension-linked and tracker mortgages are the main types to be able to describe.

Annuity (repayment) mortgage: each repayment pays part of the interest and part of the capital borrowed, so the amount owed falls over time. Early repayments are mostly interest. It is the most common type, the rate may be fixed, variable or a combination, and it needs mortgage protection.

Endowment mortgage: the borrower pays only interest on the loan, plus a premium on a life assurance (endowment) policy designed to repay the loan when it matures. The policy yield may not fully cover the loan, and no separate protection policy is needed. It is no longer widely available.

Pension-linked mortgage: interest is paid on the loan and contributions are paid into a pension scheme, and the loan is repaid from the pension lump sum on retirement. It needs mortgage protection, is rare today, and was popular with self-employed people because of tax relief on pension contributions.

Tracker mortgage: the interest rate follows a published benchmark rate, the European Central Bank (ECB) rate, plus a fixed margin, so repayments rise and fall with the ECB rate. Trackers are no longer offered to new borrowers, but you may be asked to describe one.
Interest-only mortgage: the borrower pays only the interest for a period, so the capital is still owed at the end of that period. It is rarely offered.
Current account (offset) mortgage: savings held in a linked current account reduce the balance on which interest is charged. It is rarely offered.
Local authority mortgages and loans are also accepted as types of home finance.
Interest is the cost of borrowing, so the rate on a mortgage decides how much the borrower pays each month and in total. A borrower can choose how the rate behaves and how long the loan lasts.

A fixed rate is set for an agreed period of a number of years, so repayments are the same during that period and the buyer is protected from rises. The buyer misses out if rates fall, and ending early may carry a charge.
A variable rate changes with the lender's rate, which tends to follow market and ECB rates, so repayments rise when rates rise and fall when rates fall. This means there is risk for the borrower.
A combination (split) mortgage divides the loan between a fixed portion and a variable portion.
A fixed rate is often higher than the variable rate at the start, because the lender takes on the risk of rate changes.
A longer loan term gives smaller repayments but more interest in total, because interest is charged for more years.
A shorter loan term means higher repayments but less interest paid in total.

Early nineteenth-century housing in Ireland reflected the materials available locally and the wealth of each household. In the countryside the size and roof of a home told you whether the family were labourers, farmers or landowners.
Labourers and small farmers lived in single-storey thatched cottages, usually of two rooms (a kitchen and a bedroom), with solid stone or mud walls, which were cheap and came from the local area.
Cottages had a half-door and a small number of small windows. The half-door opened into the kitchen and could be closed at the bottom to keep animals out and let in light and air.
Thatch was made of reeds, straw or hay, and an open hearth in the main room was used for both cooking and heating, so the kitchen was the centre of family life.
Some cottages had a loft directly under the thatch, reached by a ladder, where children slept. This used the roof space as extra sleeping room without adding to the building.
Prosperous farmers lived in two-storey, slate-roofed houses with several bedrooms and a parlour (a sitting room kept for visitors), showing their greater wealth.
Wealthy landowners lived in large estate houses, with servants' quarters generally in the basement.
Diagram: a thatched cottage in cross-section, showing the thatched roof, the loft reached by ladder, the open hearth and the half-door.
Towns developed their own styles of housing, and the gap between rich and poor was very visible in the streets. Keep these urban types separate from the rural ones, because examiners do.

Georgian terraces in towns (rows of joined houses, for example in Georgian Dublin such as Merrion Square) were two, three or four storeys high, with basements, high ceilings and prominent doors, and were built for the better-off.
The middle classes lived in small terraced houses in the suburbs, away from the crowded town centre.
Shopkeepers often lived above their shops, which kept them close to their business.
Workers lived in small single-storey cottages or, in the towns, in crowded tenements (large buildings divided into rooms let to many families), where space and sanitation were poor.
Better transport in the later nineteenth century changed what houses were built from and how they looked, and it changed who lived where in towns.
Improved transport brought a wider variety of building materials, because heavy goods such as slate could now be moved cheaply over long distances.
Houses became more ornate, with Gothic and Tudor styles.
Two-storey, slate-roofed stone buildings became the most common rural dwelling by the end of the century.
As wealthier families moved to suburban terraced houses, many large Georgian houses in towns were divided and let to poorer families, which added to overcrowding in town centres.
The twentieth century brought new house types and new materials, and for the first time governments played a part in providing and improving homes.
Detached houses (standing alone) and semi-detached houses (joined to one neighbour) appeared, along with council housing (homes built by the local authority) and new housing estates.
Brick with plaster walls replaced stone, and tiles replaced slates; two-storey houses were built where land was expensive, because building up used less land.
Rural electrification in the mid-twentieth century changed rural homes, bringing electric light and power to the countryside.
Government housing grants funded improvements to rural houses.
The slate-roofed bungalow gradually replaced the thatched cottage in rural Ireland.
Later in the twentieth century, housing was built in larger numbers and to higher standards, with new materials that made homes warmer and easier to maintain.
Private estates were built to a common design, while individual private houses varied between classical and modern designs.
High-rise blocks were built in some cities, for example the Ballymun flats in Dublin in the 1960s.
The Building Regulations (legal minimum standards for construction) greatly improved housing standards.
New materials and methods such as double glazing, PVC and fibreglass came into use, which cut heat loss and reduced maintenance.
Indoor sanitation improved, so that homes had proper indoor toilets and bathrooms.
Today's housing is shaped by the cost of land, changing households and concern for the environment, so there is a much wider mix of types than in earlier centuries.
Twenty-first-century estates usually consist of one style but include single-storey detached, dormer and two-storey semi-detached houses, which gives a mix of homes for different households.
Apartments, townhouses and mixed-density schemes (a mix of house and apartment types on one site) are built, including gated complexes.
Old dilapidated buildings and thatched cottages are restored, and custom-designed houses are built on private sites.
Attic space is converted into rooms with Velux roof windows, and extensions, conservatories and sunroom extensions are added to many houses to give extra living space.
Modern homes include home-office space and open-plan living (a kitchen, dining and living area in one space).
Attention is paid to insulation, glazing, security, accessibility and renewable energy, reflecting greater environmental awareness.
Each change in style across the centuries had causes, and naming them turns a list of periods into a developed answer.
Materials and transport: better transport brought slate, brick and tiles to places that once used only local materials.
Rising incomes let more families afford larger and better-built homes.
Population moved from the country to towns, which led to terraces, tenements, suburbs and later apartments.
Government housing policy and grants, and building regulations, led to council housing, rural improvements and higher standards.
Family size and land values: smaller families and expensive land led to semi-detached houses, townhouses and apartments.
Environmental awareness led to a focus on insulation, glazing and renewable energy.
Different styles suit different households, so each is popular for a reason. Tying each style to the type of household it suits is what examiners reward.
Bungalows are single-storey, so they suit older people, people with mobility needs and rural sites, but they need a large site. The dormer bungalow adds bedrooms in the roof space.
Two-storey detached houses suit large families and sites with space for a garden, and give privacy, but they cost more to buy and to heat.

Semi-detached and terraced houses make efficient use of land and cost less; a terraced house loses less heat than a detached house because it shares walls with its neighbours. The drawbacks are less privacy, noise from neighbours and a small garden.

Apartments and duplexes save space and maintenance and are usually in secure complexes with communal space, so they suit first-time buyers, singles, downsizers and city living. The drawbacks are limited space, no private garden and management fees.
Townhouses are multi-storey homes built on small urban sites, with limited outdoor space.
Traditional, neo-Georgian and restored period houses offer proportion and character, while modern minimalist homes are bright and easy to care for.
Custom-designed one-off houses, timber-frame and energy-efficient or passive houses are other styles, and old cottages are kept for holiday and local use in tourist areas.
A home has to work for the people living in it, so the make-up and needs of the household strongly affect the style chosen.
Family size and stage, and the ages of children, decide how many bedrooms and how much space are needed, so a growing family may choose a two-storey house.
Special needs or disability may call for a single-storey home, such as a bungalow, with no stairs.
Some households want a garden or a home office, which rules out styles with no private outdoor space.
Wanting to be near family and community, and the sense of belonging this gives, can affect where and what a household chooses.
Culture shapes what people like and what a place looks like, so it affects both what is built and what people choose to buy.
Personal taste, aesthetics and fashion influence choice, for example a preference for a traditional or a modern minimalist look.
Regional building traditions and local materials, such as stone or slate, shape the look of rural houses in each area.
Respect for heritage and the character of the area leads many people to restore older houses or build in keeping with their surroundings.
Money is often the deciding factor, because it limits what a household can buy or build and what it can afford to run.
Income and the money available decide what a household can afford, so a first-time buyer may choose an apartment or a terraced house.
The price of land affects the cost of any style, which is why cheaper land allows larger, detached houses.
The cost of building and the running costs, such as heating, matter because a large detached house costs more to heat than a terraced one.
Resale value and investment potential matter because a home is usually a household's largest purchase.
A household also decides whether to build, buy new or buy second-hand.
The site and its surroundings affect how comfortable a home is and what may be built on it.
Aspect (the direction a house faces) matters because south-facing rooms gain daylight and solar heat.
Shelter from wind and rain, and exposure to them, affect comfort and heating costs.
The slope of the site affects what style can be built on it.
Energy efficiency through insulation and glazing lowers heating costs and heat loss.
The style must fit the surrounding landscape and neighbouring buildings, and planning rules control scale and materials in many areas.
Setting: a school visit to houses from different periods, or photographs of house styles, can be used to discuss their suitability to their surroundings.
A home that suits one household can be unworkable for another. Each group needs its own mix of space, location, access and services, and in an exam you should say who each requirement serves and why.

Families need enough bedrooms for every member, adequate storage, a well-equipped, ventilated and well-lit kitchen, and a living room for relaxing and watching television, so that everyone has space for their own needs.
A larger family also needs more than one bathroom, and a hot-press (an airing cupboard for the hot water tank and linen) helps with laundry.

Families with young children need a safe, enclosed back garden so the children can play outdoors without danger, and safe stairs. Teenagers need space to study, and families with a car or sports equipment may need a garage or shed.
Families also need to be close to schools, childcare, shops, parks and public transport, which cuts the time and cost of daily journeys for school-going children and working parents.

Single people usually need smaller, affordable accommodation, such as an apartment, bedsit, small townhouse or a room in a shared house, because they have one income. It should be close to work, college or public transport, with privacy, security and space for study.
For these groups the home itself must be adapted, because stairs, steps and standard fittings can make an ordinary house unsafe or unusable.

Older people need single-storey living living, or a ground-floor bedroom and bathroom, or a stairlift where there are stairs, because climbing stairs becomes difficult. They need a level or ramped entrance and non-slip floors with safe lighting to prevent falls.

Older people also need a home that is warm, well insulated and easy to heat, an alarm or emergency call system, and nearness to shops, health services, public transport and community and family support. Sheltered housing (accommodation designed for older people) is one option.

People with disabilities need adjustments that depend on the disability. For mobility: ramps for wheelchair or walking-aid users, wide doorways and hallways, lowered worktops, lowered switches and sockets at reachable heights, a raised toilet with grab rails, an accessible bathroom or shower, and a lift or stairlift.

For a hearing disability, flashing lights are linked to the doorbell and alarms, so the person is alerted without hearing a sound. For a sight disability, audible or tactile alarms and good lighting help, and communication or alarm systems are needed for emergencies.
Homeless people first need somewhere safe to stay tonight, and the aim is then a permanent home with support.

Homeless people need emergency shelter in hostels or emergency bed and breakfast accommodation, ideally regular rather than a nightly queue for a bed, with washing and laundry facilities, privacy and dignity, a safe place to store possessions and a communal space (kitchen or day room) to reduce isolation.
For homeless people the next step is rent-assisted private accommodation or local authority housing, and then a permanent home with support.
Serviced halting sites (sites with water and other services) exist for Travellers who live in mobile homes or caravans.
The State and voluntary bodies provide homes for people who cannot afford to buy or rent privately. Several routes exist, and each works differently.

Local authority housing is rented housing for households on a lower income who cannot afford a home. It is allocated by need through a social housing assessment and a waiting list, with priority given to households unable to house themselves.

Local authorities consider household size, income, current accommodation, age and disability. Families, people with disabilities and older people are often given priority, so single people can wait longer.

Voluntary housing is provided by approved housing bodies (non-profit voluntary organisations), often for specific groups such as older people, people with disabilities or homeless people. The tenant's landlord is the approved housing body.

Co-operative housing is built by a group of members who pool the costs of the site, builder and solicitor, share costs and manage the housing on non-profit principles. A local authority may provide a low-cost site for a co-operative whose members are on its waiting list.

The Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) is a local authority support for private rented housing: the local authority pays the private landlord and the tenant pays a contribution. The Rental Accommodation Scheme (RAS) is where the local authority arranges long-term private rented homes for households with a long-term need.

Cost rental means homes let at a rent based on cost rather than profit, for households above social housing income limits. Do not confuse it with social housing (let at subsidised rent) or with affordable housing (sold below market price).

Shared equity and affordable purchase: under the First Home scheme the State and participating lenders take an equity share in a new home, which the buyer can buy out later. Local authorities also sell affordable homes below market price.

Adaptation grants help older people and people with disabilities to adapt a home so they can stay in it, and specific provision exists for homeless people, older people and Travellers. Demand for social housing exceeds supply, so applicants can wait for a number of years for a home.
Distribution is about where homes are and in what tenure (the way a home is held: owned, rented privately or rented from a social landlord). It is separate from whether those homes meet need.

By tenure, homes are owner-occupied (with a mortgage or owned outright), privately rented or socially rented from a local authority or approved housing body. Owner-occupation is the largest tenure in Ireland, followed by private renting and social housing.

By sector, private housing is built by developers and sold or let on the open market, while social housing is built and allocated by local authorities and approved housing bodies for people who cannot afford a home.
By location, urban areas have higher density, more apartments and greater demand, while rural areas have one-off houses and bungalows and, in some places, vacant homes.

Strong demand in cities and commuter areas pushes up prices and rents, while some rural areas have vacant housing but fewer jobs and services, so empty homes do not solve the shortage where people want to live.
A home can exist and still be a poor place to live. Quality is judged by structure and repair, insulation and heating, damp and ventilation, lighting, space for the household, safety and facilities.
A Building Energy Rating (BER) certificate rates a home's energy efficiency from A, the most efficient, to G, the least efficient, so buyers and tenants can compare running costs.
Older housing stock is often poorly insulated and costly to heat, which can cause fuel poverty (being unable to afford to heat the home adequately). New homes must meet the Building Regulations.
Damp, poor ventilation and inadequate lighting reduce the quality of accommodation and can affect health. Cold and overcrowding also harm health, and school and work performance.
Rented housing must meet legal minimum standards under the Housing (Standards for Rented Houses) Regulations 2019, which local authorities enforce.
Buying and renting both cost money, but at different times and with different returns. Comparing them means looking at initial costs, ongoing costs and what you are left with.
Buying has initial costs: a deposit, legal fees, lender, valuation and survey fees, stamp duty on the purchase, and furnishing.

Buying has ongoing costs: mortgage repayments, mortgage protection and home insurance, property tax, maintenance and repairs, and service charges for apartments. It builds equity (the part of the home you own), may rise in value and gives security.
Renting has initial costs of a deposit (a month's rent is the usual) and rent in advance, and an agency fee where an agent is used. Ongoing costs are rent, contents insurance and utilities.
The tenant has no repair costs but builds no equity, so rent is sometimes called dead money. Renting needs less upfront capital and gives mobility, with lower upfront costs than buying.

In high-demand urban areas, rent can be as high as, or higher than, mortgage repayments on a similar home, so renting for years can cost more than buying, but buying requires a deposit that many people cannot save.
Rural homes are often cheaper to buy than urban ones, but residents may have to travel further to reach schools, shops and jobs.
Adequacy asks whether the housing on offer matches what households need. It goes beyond counting dwellings.
Adequacy means housing must be enough in number, affordable, secure, suitable, accessible, in good condition and near employment, transport, schools, healthcare and shops, for each type of household.

Strengths include a wide variety of house types and tenures, social housing through local authorities, approved housing bodies and co-operatives, cost rental, rent supports (HAP and RAS), supports for first-time buyers, adaptation grants, and better standards through the Building Regulations and the BER.

Weaknesses include high prices and rents in cities, waiting lists for social housing, homelessness, poor access for some people with disabilities and older people, poor stock in places, vacant property, and uneven distribution between urban and rural areas.
Emergency accommodation does not offer the stability of a permanent home, and long stays in it are a weakness.

Low-income families, lone parents, single people (lower priority for social housing), homeless people, Travellers, older people, people with disabilities, students and new arrivals (refugees and asylum seekers) may not get housing suited to their needs.
Local authority building, voluntary and co-operative schemes increase supply, and adaptation grants help particular groups to stay in their homes.
Renovating vacant property and planning mixed, serviced developments are further ways to improve adequacy, along with more social, affordable and cost rental homes and planning for need.
A house is only as useful as what is around it. Amenities and services meet daily needs, and an estate without them isolates its residents.
Schools, childcare and playgrounds serve children and reduce long journeys for families.
Shops, post offices, banks, health services, pharmacies and community centres provide necessities and social contact, which builds a sense of community.
Public transport gives access to employment and services, so a development without transport isolates its residents.
Parks, sports grounds and play areas promote exercise, leisure and community interaction.
Street lighting improves safety, and regular refuse collection keeps the area hygienic.
Accessible healthcare, pharmacies and services for older people or people with disabilities support independence.
Setting: a group housing study of a local area such as a townland, village or housing estate, recording which amenities are present and which are missing.

Where a home is built shapes the household's daily life and costs for years. The choice depends on how suitable the site is, what the household needs and what the site costs. A local authority is the county or city council, and its development plan sets how land in the area may be used.

Urban or rural setting: urban sites give shops, transport, services and jobs, but cost more and offer less space. Rural sites give space, quiet and a lower land price, but may need a private water supply and a wastewater treatment system, and mean longer travel.
Proximity to family, work, schools, childcare, shops, health services and public transport affects the daily time and cost of travel, and the ease of family life.
Ground conditions: a stable soil structure, good slope and drainage and freedom from flood risk are checked by a site survey before building, because a poor site can damage the house later.
Shelter from wind matters, and so does the absence of risks nearby such as pollution, pylons, factories or landfill.
Aspect (the direction the site faces) and orientation of the house determine how much daylight and solar heat it receives. They also affect privacy and views.
Services available: electricity, water, sewerage, gas, broadband and refuse collection, plus the cost of connecting them, which adds to the real price of a site.

Budget and value: the price of the site and the cost of connecting services limit the location a household can afford. Future developments in the area affect the prospects for the value of the property.

Building and planning regulations, including the development plan, can restrict where and how a house may be built. In a case study, apply all these factors to the needs of the family described to choose the location, house design, interior and services.
Once a site is chosen, the style of house must suit the family, the site and the budget. A house that suits one family can be a poor fit for another.
House style is chosen by comparing traditional and modern designs, and bungalow and two-storey layouts, against the family's budget.
The size, stage (age group) and lifestyle of the family determine the number of bedrooms, the amount of living space and the need for storage, because a growing family needs more of each.
Special needs, such as a wheelchair user, may require a single-storey house, step-free access and wider doors so that the person can move around independently.
Potential to convert the attic, extend the house or add a garage must be checked against planning rules for the area, so that future changes are allowed.
Personal taste and the style of neighbouring houses determine whether a design fits its surroundings.

There are two kinds of permission, and they differ in how much detail the applicant must supply and in what each one settles. Outline permission is a first check on the idea. Full permission is the approval needed to build.
Planning permission from the local authority is required for most building work unless the development is exempt under the planning regulations, for example some small extensions.
Outline permission establishes whether the planning authority agrees in principle to a development, before detailed plans are prepared. It is not permission to build.

An outline application needs only a site map showing the location and layout of the proposed house, with basic details of the proposal, not detailed house plans. This saves the cost of drawing full plans for a site that may be refused.
Full permission requires detailed plans and drawings, the site layout, house plans, elevations and finishes, details of water supply and drainage, and the materials to be used in construction.
Full permission also requires the appropriate fee, copies of the public notices (newspaper and site notice) and the position of the site notice.
A person who is granted outline permission must still get full permission (detailed approval) before building.

The procedure for full permission is set in the Planning and Development Act 2024. It follows a fixed order so that the public can see and comment on a proposal before the council decides. Learn the order of the steps.
