The PSO levy is a charge on all customers, set each year by the energy regulator (CRU), that funds support for renewable energy. VAT is added to the bill as well.
A tariff is the pricing plan a supplier uses, and choosing one means matching when you use electricity to when it is cheapest.
A standard tariff charges one rate all day.
A night-rate or day-and-night tariff, also called a time-of-use tariff, charges less for electricity used at night or off-peak, so storage heaters, immersion heaters and dishwashers can be run then.
A smart meter records use in intervals, so it supports time-of-use pricing and helps a household shift use to cheaper periods.

Faults can cause fires or fatal shocks, so each circuit has devices that cut the supply. Fuses and MCBs react to too much current, while an RCD reacts to current leaking to earth, so they do different jobs.

A fuse is a deliberate weak link: a thin wire inside the fuse heats and melts when the current exceeds its rating, breaking the circuit and preventing fire. It breaks once and must be replaced, and is found in plugs and old fuse boards.

A miniature circuit breaker (MCB) is a switch that trips (switches off) when the current exceeds its rating, in an overload or short circuit, or when a fault occurs. It can be reset once the fault is repaired, and is found in the consumer unit.
A residual current device (RCD) compares the current in the live and neutral wires. A difference signals current leaking to earth through a person or fault, and it trips within milliseconds.

Socket circuits are commonly protected by RCDs with a sensitivity of 30 mA, the usual domestic setting, and 30 mA RCDs are required on socket circuits. They can trip before a fatal shock is delivered, protection that fuses and MCBs do not give.
The earth wire, usually green and yellow, is a safe path for fault current to flow to earth, for example if a fault makes the metal casing of a kettle, cooker or washing machine live.
The surge of current along the earth wire blows the fuse or trips the MCB, so the metal casing cannot stay live to shock the user.
Appliances with double insulation have a plastic casing, shown by the symbol of a square within a square, and no earth wire, so the appliance cannot become live through a metal part.
Each circuit has its own protective device in the consumer unit, so a fault on one circuit disconnects only that circuit.
A ring circuit is a single circuit that supplies many sockets in a room or floor from one protective device.
The live, neutral and earth conductors run from the consumer unit, out through each socket in turn, and return to the same breaker in the consumer unit, forming a continuous loop.
Each socket is supplied from two directions, so the current divides between two paths and the cable can be smaller than a single radial cable (one run out to the sockets) carrying the same load.
Many sockets can be added to the ring, and a fault cuts off only that ring.
Upstairs and downstairs ring circuits are often wired separately, usually one ring per floor, so a fault on one floor does not disconnect the other. Lighting and the cooker are on separate circuits.
A spur is a short branch from a socket in the ring, which can supply one additional socket or one fixed appliance.
The ring has its own protective device, an MCB or fuse, in the consumer unit, which trips if the total current on the loop exceeds its rating.
Diagram: a wiring circuit showing the consumer unit, live, neutral and earth conductors forming a loop, sockets along the loop and one spur labelled.
These guidelines each remove one danger: water near electrical equipment, damaged flexes or appliances, and overloaded sockets.

Never mix water and electricity: do not handle electrical equipment with wet hands, and keep water and electricity apart in the bathroom and kitchen, because water conducts current through the body. Bathroom switches are pull-cords, and the only appliance normally used there is a shaver socket.

Do not overload sockets or use multiple adaptors or long extension leads; each plug and socket should be used within its rating, because too much current overheats the wiring and starts fires. Avoid trailing flexes.
Check flexes, plugs and sockets regularly for damage, replace damaged flexes, and never pull a plug out by its flex.
Unplug appliances before cleaning or repairing them, and never repair an appliance yourself while it is connected to the supply.
Keep flexes away from hobs, sinks and heat sources, and never cover a heater or drape clothes over it.
Use only appliances with a recognised safety mark, fit the right fuse and follow the instructions. Do not use portable heaters in bathrooms.
Electric blankets should be checked for damage and wear, and not folded or left switched on under a sleeping person.
Outdoor sockets and appliances need an RCD and weatherproof fittings; repairs and new circuits must be carried out by a qualified, registered electrician.
Unplug all appliances, except a fridge or freezer, before going to bed to reduce the risk of an electrical fire, and fit smoke alarms.
Gas can leak, and burning it in the wrong conditions makes a poisonous gas. Safe use means knowing what to do about a leak, about carbon monoxide, and about ventilation and servicing.

Natural gas and LPG are odourless without the added odorant, so a gas smell is an emergency. The three immediate actions are to turn off the gas supply at the meter, open doors and windows, and not use switches, matches or other flames.
Then call the gas emergency number, or leave the house and call from outside.

Carbon monoxide is produced by incomplete combustion, when gas, oil or solid fuel burns without enough air, for example from a blocked flue or a faulty boiler. It has no smell and causes headache, dizziness and nausea.
A carbon monoxide alarm gives early warning of the gas, and should be fitted in rooms containing fuel-burning appliances.
Gas appliances need adequate ventilation for the air needed to burn the gas, so they must not be blocked by furniture or closed vents, and flues and vents must be kept clear.
Do not use a cooker or oven to heat the room.
Gas appliances should be installed by a registered installer (on the Register of Gas Installers of Ireland) and serviced at regular intervals so the flue and burner stay safe and efficient.
Electrical services must match the use of the room, and the layout must keep sockets and switches safe and convenient.
Lighting: plan layers of light, with ambient lighting from ceiling fittings, task lighting over work areas and accent lighting for display.
Switches should be placed at the door, within easy reach, and sockets at a safe height and away from water sources.
Heating options: electric storage heaters charged on night rate, panel heaters on a thermostat, or electric underfloor heating, each controlled by a thermostat or timer.
Ventilation: a fan with a timer or humidity switch, fitted in a kitchen or bathroom, removes moisture and cooking smells from the room.
Circuits and sockets: enough double sockets on the ring or a separate circuit so no extension lead is needed for regular appliances.
Safety: the fittings for a bathroom must suit its zone rating, and any new work must be done by a registered electrician and certified.

Water for the public mains is taken from rivers, lakes or underground sources, and it is not safe to drink as it comes. It is treated at a treatment plant in stages, each removing a different problem. Today the public water service is run by Uisce Éireann (formerly Irish Water, renamed from 2023).
Stage 1, screening: water passes through coarse and fine screens that remove floating debris such as leaves and twigs, and large solids, so they do not block or damage the later stages.

Stage 2, coagulation and sedimentation: chemicals are added to bind fine dirt into larger clumps, which sink to the base of the tank and are removed, because very fine particles would otherwise stay suspended.
Stage 3, filtration: water passes through filter beds of sand, gravel and stones to remove the remaining small particles.
Stage 4, chlorination (disinfection): chlorine is added to kill bacteria and other micro-organisms. A small amount stays in the water to keep it safe as it travels through the pipes.
Stage 5, fluoridation: fluoride is added to many public supplies to help protect teeth from decay. It is carried out under the Health (Fluoridation of Water Supplies) Act 1960.
Once treated, water must be checked and held safely until it is needed. It then reaches houses through mains pipes.
Stage 6, testing: samples are tested regularly for quality and purity before the water is released, so any fault is caught before it reaches homes.

Stage 7, storage: treated water is held in a covered, high-level reservoir so it cannot become contaminated and so that pressure is available for distribution, because water from high ground flows down with force.
Distribution: clean water flows from the reservoir through a mains pipe to houses, with manholes or valves at regular intervals for inspection and repair.
Not every home is on a public main. Rural homes can get their water in three ways, and the choice affects how safe the water is.
Rural homes may use the public mains, a group water scheme, or a private well or spring.
Private supplies need to be protected from contamination, filtered and treated, and tested, because nobody else is treating or checking the water before it reaches the tap.
Water travels from the public main to the attic through a chain of pipes with a valve to control it. Each part has its own name and job.
Mains pipe: the public pipe under the road, which carries clean water from the public main to the area.
Service pipe: connects the mains pipe to the house, so it brings water into the house.

Stop cock (stop valve): a valve on the service pipe, outside the house near the boundary or under the kitchen sink, that turns the water off at the main. A second stop cock may be found inside the house.
The stop cock is closed to isolate the supply, for example in a burst pipe, during a repair or when the house is left empty.
Rising main: a pipe that carries water from the stop cock up to the cold water storage tank in the attic.
Drinking water tap: the kitchen cold tap is usually fed directly from the rising main, so drinking water is fresh from the main and does not pass through the storage tank.
The attic tank stores water and keeps it under control, so the house has a supply even when the mains is busy. Two safety parts stop it from over-filling.

Cold water storage tank (cistern): a tank in the attic that stores water for the bathroom taps, the WC cisterns and the hot water cylinder. It is placed high so that gravity gives pressure, and it is covered and insulated. Its water is not for drinking.
Ball valve (ball cock, float valve): a float on an arm closes the inlet when the water reaches the set level, so the tank is not over-filled. The same valve is in the WC cistern.

Overflow pipe (warning pipe): leaves the tank and goes through the wall to outside, carrying water away if the ball valve fails. It also warns that something is wrong and stops flooding of the attic and ceilings.

Distribution pipes: carry cold water from the tank to the bathroom taps, the WC cistern and the feed to the hot water cylinder. The cylinder is fed from the tank and heated by the boiler or immersion.

Diagram: a labelled cold water system showing the mains pipe, service pipe, stop cock, rising main, attic tank with ball valve and overflow, distribution pipes, taps, WC, hot water cylinder and kitchen tap.
Putting the parts together, the system fills and delivers water automatically with no pump, using height and a float valve.
1. Water enters through the service pipe, passes the stop cock and rises through the rising main into the attic tank.
2. The ball valve closes when the tank reaches its set level, so the tank is never over-filled.
3. Water is stored in the tank and flows out by gravity to the taps, cistern and cylinder when a tap is opened or a cistern refills.
4. The ball valve then opens as the level drops and refills the tank.
Water pressure depends on the height of the tank above the outlet, so a tank in the attic gives enough pressure at lower-level taps without a pump.
If the ball valve fails, water leaves through the overflow pipe, which carries it outside so that it does not damage or leak into the ceilings below.
Water expands when it freezes, so cold weather can split pipes and tanks. The damage often shows only when the thaw comes and the water starts to leak.
Water freezes at 0 °C and expands as it turns to ice, so pipes and tanks in cold spaces such as the attic and external walls can split.
Lag the cold water storage tank with an insulated lid or jacket, and lag the pipes in the attic and in external walls with pipe insulation, because these are the coldest places.
Keep the heating on at a low setting in very cold weather or when away, rather than switching it off, so the building remains warm.
Keep the attic hatch closed and repair draughts near pipes, so that cold air does not reach them.
Open the doors of cupboards containing pipes on external walls so that warm air reaches them.
In severe frost, allow a tap to drip or run slowly, because moving water is less likely to freeze.
Know where the stop cock is, so that you can turn the water off quickly if a pipe bursts.
A frozen pipe is a warning sign. The aim is to thaw it safely before it splits, and to avoid causing a fire or a burst.
Turn off the water at the stop cock, so that nothing floods if the pipe has already split.
Open the nearest tap, so that melting water and pressure have somewhere to go.
Thaw the pipe gently from the tap end with a warm cloth or a hot water bottle; never use a naked flame or a blowtorch, because they can damage the pipe and start a fire.
After thawing, check the pipes and joints for leaks before turning the water back on.
Water is a finite resource, and treating and pumping it uses energy, so saving it cuts costs and emissions. Each saving method works because it stops water being used or wasted.
Bathroom: take a short shower instead of a bath, because a shower uses far less water than filling a bath. Water-saving or aerated showerheads cut the flow further.
Turn off the tap while brushing teeth and shaving, because running water is wasted when nothing is being washed.
Fit a dual-flush WC cistern so that the half-flush can be used for liquids, and fit cisterns with reduced-volume flushes or a cistern displacement device where possible.
Kitchen: wash vegetables and small amounts of dishes in a basin or a plugged sink rather than under a running tap.
Laundry: use washing machines and dishwashers only on full loads, or on economy programmes for lightly soiled items, so that fewer washes are needed.
Do not overfill the kettle, since only the water needed should be heated, which also saves energy.
Repair leaks and dripping taps promptly, because a constant drip wastes a large volume over a year. Check the overflow pipe for dripping.

Garden and reuse: collect rainwater from the roof in a butt for watering plants and washing outdoor surfaces. Rainwater harvesting for flushing toilets, grey-water reuse, and sensor or aerator taps also save water.
Hot water costs both water and the energy to heat it, so cutting hot water use saves twice.
Heating less hot water saves both water and energy, for example by timing the immersion, using solar heating and insulating the hot water cylinder.
Shorter showers and full washing loads also use less heated water, so they reduce fuel costs as well as water use.
Heat is a form of energy that always moves from warmer places to cooler ones. It does so in three ways, and every heating system and control in this topic relies on one or more of them.

Conduction: heat passes through a solid because vibrating particles pass energy to their neighbours. Metals conduct well, so they feel cold and carry heat away quickly; air, wool and polystyrene conduct poorly, so they are used to keep heat in.

Convection: in a liquid or gas, the warmed part becomes less dense and rises, and cooler fluid moves in to replace it. This sets up a circulating current, which is how warmth spreads through room air or water.

Radiation: heat travels as infrared waves, which need no material to carry them. The waves pass through air without heating it and warm the objects they hit, so a bar fire or a sunlit wall heats whatever it faces.
A radiator heats a room mainly by convection, because the air beside it warms and rises. Some heat is also given off by radiation from its surface.
Solids, liquids and gases expand when heated, and different metals expand by different amounts. This is the basis of the thermostat and of the expansion tank in a central heating system.
Thermal comfort is the feeling that the temperature of a room suits the people in it, their clothing and what they are doing. Heating a home well means controlling more than the air temperature.
Six factors determine thermal comfort: air temperature, the temperature of surrounding surfaces (walls, windows, floor), humidity, air movement (draughts), clothing and activity level.
A cold wall or single-glazed window makes a person feel cold even when the air temperature is correct, because the body loses heat by radiation to cold surfaces.
Each room needs a different temperature because people do different things in it: living spaces need more warmth than bedrooms, where people are under bedclothes.
Recommended temperatures: sitting room 19 to 23 °C, living room 17 to 21 °C, kitchen 15 to 19 °C, bathroom 16 to 19 °C and bedroom 10 to 16 °C.
Babies, older people and people who are ill need warm rooms with a steady temperature, and older people need at least 20 °C.
Thermal comfort is kept steady by heating that suits the house, by controls that switch it on and off, and by reducing heat loss.
A heating system sized to the house gives enough heat without wasting fuel, because too small a system never warms the rooms and too large a one overheats them.
Zoning gives each area its own control, so rooms are heated only when and to the level they are needed.
Timers, thermostats and thermostatic radiator valves control when heat is supplied and how much.
Insulation, draught proofing and controlled ventilation reduce heat loss and cold surfaces without creating draughts.
Clothing is also a control, since adding or removing layers changes how warm a person feels without changing the heating.
A thermostat is a temperature-sensing switch. It turns a heat source off at a set temperature and back on as it cools, so the temperature stays steady without anyone watching it.
Its working part is a bimetal strip, made of two metals, brass and invar, bonded together so they cannot slide apart.
Brass expands much more than invar when heated, so the strip bends away from the contact and breaks the electric circuit, switching the appliance off.
As the strip cools it straightens and reconnects the circuit, switching the appliance on again.
Diagram: a bimetal strip with brass on one side and invar on the other, shown curved when hot and straight when cool, with the contacts that make and break the circuit.
The same bimetal principle is used wherever a temperature must be held steady, and in heating there are different thermostats for different jobs.
Bimetal thermostats operate kettles (each with its own control), irons, ovens, immersion heaters, electric blankets, refrigerators and freezers, and electric showers.
A boiler thermostat stops the boiler when the water reaches its target temperature and restarts it when the water falls.

A room thermostat senses air temperature and switches the boiler or heating circuit on or off to keep the room at its set level. It is placed in a main living area away from direct heat, so a nearby fire does not give a false reading.
A cylinder thermostat keeps the stored hot water at its set temperature.
A thermostatic radiator valve (TRV) is fitted to one radiator and opens or closes to control the flow of hot water into it, so each room can have its own setting.
Controls make sure heat is supplied only when and where it is needed. This saves fuel and keeps a home comfortable.

A programmer (timer) switches heating and hot water on and off at preset times, such as before the family wakes and before they return home, so rooms are not heated when empty. It may be mechanical, electronic or smart.
Timers and thermostats used together prevent heating empty rooms and overheating, so less fuel is burned and bills are lower.
Zoning gives each area its own timer and thermostat, so bedrooms, living spaces and unused rooms can run at different settings.
Smart controls allow a household to change heating schedules from a phone when its plans change.
Heating options are first described by how much of the dwelling they heat. The four types are easily confused, so learn what makes each one different.
Full central heating: one boiler heats water that is pumped to radiators throughout the whole dwelling, and it can also supply hot water.
Partial central heating: radiators heat only some rooms, usually the main living areas.
Background heating: a low, steady level of heat is supplied to the whole house, with local heaters used for extra warmth.
Local heating: individual room heaters, such as electric fires, gas heaters or stoves, heat only the room they are in.
Systems also differ in how the heat is made and delivered. Some heat water, some use electricity directly, and some draw on renewable sources.

Storage heating (a dry system, with no water): electric elements inside thermal blocks of fireclay or concrete are charged on off-peak night electricity and release heat through the day, often with an afternoon boost.

Underfloor heating: pipes (water) or electric cables beneath the floor warm the floor, which then heats the room by radiation and convection. It leaves walls clear and works well with low-temperature heat sources.
Ground-source heating: pipes buried in the ground collect heat, and a heat pump raises it to a temperature suitable for heating the house.

A heat pump (ground-source or air-source) uses a refrigerant to take heat from the ground, air or water, and a compressor raises its temperature before the heat passes to the heating water. It runs on electricity but delivers more heat than the electrical energy it uses.
Heat pumps work best in a well-insulated house with underfloor heating or large radiators, and they qualify for SEAI grants.
Passive solar heating: large south-facing windows admit winter sunlight, which the walls and floors absorb and release as heat.
Active solar heating: solar collectors absorb sunlight and heat a fluid, which transfers the heat to water stored in a cylinder.
Biomass boilers burning wood pellets or wood chips are another low-carbon option.
No single system suits every home, so a choice weighs cost, the house and the people who live in it. Examiners ask for these factors as a list, each with a reason.
Installation, running and maintenance costs must all be considered, not only the purchase price.
Fuel price and availability differ between oil, gas, solid fuel and electricity.
Energy efficiency: an efficient system uses less fuel for the same heat output, and a condensing boiler recovers heat from its flue gases.
Environmental impact: fossil fuels release carbon dioxide, while wood and solar energy are renewable sources.
Heat output must match the house: floor area, insulation, number of occupants and hot-water demand decide the size of system needed.
Family needs: households with babies, older people or illness need reliable and precise control of warmth.
Beyond cost and efficiency, a system has to fit the home, be safe to live with and be easy to run.
Convenience and control: timers, thermostats and smart controls make a system easier to run economically.
Safety: radiator surfaces and any open flame need consideration where young children are present.
Space and appearance: boilers, tanks, fuel storage and radiators take up wall or floor space, while underfloor systems leave walls clear.
Hot water needs and available grants also affect the choice.
A wet system heats water in a boiler and circulates it round a closed loop of pipes to radiators. It is the usual system to describe in an exam, because it shows all three kinds of heat transfer.
Parts: boiler, circulating pump, small-bore pipes (flow and return), radiators, a feed and expansion tank with an overflow pipe, and a hot-water cylinder with a heat exchanger coil.
The boiler burns oil, gas or solid fuel, or uses electricity. Solar collectors feed a cylinder rather than the boiler.
Water heated in the boiler expands, becomes less dense and rises up the flow pipe to the radiators by convection.
A pump drives the water round the closed loop, so the system works in long pipe runs where natural convection would be too weak.
Each radiator warms the air beside it by convection and gives off heat from its surface by radiation.
The cooler water returns through the return pipe to the boiler to be reheated.
Diagram: plan of the closed loop showing the boiler, pump, flow and return pipes, radiators, expansion tank in the roof space and hot-water cylinder, with arrows showing the direction of water flow.
Water that is heated must have room to expand, and the same boiler can also heat the water used at the taps.
As water heats it expands. The expansion tank, usually in the roof space, takes up the extra water, tops up the system, and acts as an overflow for steam and excess water through its overflow pipe.

The hot-water cylinder transfers heat from the circulating water to the stored domestic hot water through the heat exchanger coil. The cylinder is heated indirectly, so the water in the loop and the domestic hot water do not mix.
The thermostat and timer control the boiler, and a room thermostat, TRVs and a cylinder thermostat control the heat further.
A condensing boiler recovers heat from its flue gases, and an annual service keeps the boiler running efficiently.
One boiler supplies heat for the whole house and hot water.
The impact of a heating system depends mainly on its fuel, and this is a part of any exam answer on central heating.
Burning fuel gives off carbon dioxide, so fossil fuels add to emissions. A flue removes the gases from the house, and a boiler needs ventilation so it has air to burn the fuel.
Renewable options, such as heat pumps, solar heating and biomass, lower emissions.

New dwellings are built to a near-zero-energy standard under Part L of the Building Regulations. Its performance requirements have effectively phased out fossil-fuel boilers as the main heating in new homes.
A warm house loses heat to the cold outside all the time. Insulation does not make heat; it slows the escape of heat, so less fuel is needed to keep the house warm.

Heat leaves a house in four ways: by conduction through solid parts such as walls and glass, by convection (warm air rising and leaking out), by radiation (heat given off as rays), and by air leakage through gaps. Insulation reduces these losses, so less fuel is needed.

Insulating materials are poor conductors of heat. Still air is a very poor conductor, so poor conductors such as still air, polystyrene, fibreglass, mineral wool, sheep's wool, cellulose and foam trap air in small pockets, which reduces heat transfer by conduction.

Fibre and foam insulation holds air in small cells that are too small for convection currents to form. Because the air cannot circulate, it cannot carry heat by convection, which is why a big open gap is not insulation.
Reflective foil and low-emissivity (low-E) coatings (thin coatings that give off little heat) reflect radiant heat back, so they reduce heat loss by radiation.
Draught proofing stops heat leaving in moving air, because it seals the gaps around doors, windows and floorboards where air leaks.
Insulation also keeps a house cool in hot weather, because it slows heat moving in as well as out.
Warm air rises, so the roof is a main route of heat loss. Insulating the attic is the cheapest and most effective place to start.
Fibre blanket or quilt: strips of mineral or glass fibre, or wool, are laid between and over the ceiling joists (the beams that carry the ceiling).
Loose fill: pellets of polystyrene or vermiculite are poured between the joists.
Sprayed or foam insulation: foam is applied between the roof rafters (the sloping beams that hold the roof), where it expands and sets into a solid layer.
Blown fibre: cellulose or mineral fibre is blown into the roof space to cover it evenly.
Rigid boards are fitted between the rafters in a converted attic, where the roof space is used as a room.
Once the attic floor is insulated, the attic becomes colder, so lag the cold water tank and attic pipes to stop them freezing. Insulate and draught-proof the hatch, and keep the eaves ventilated.
Diagram: cross-section of a roof showing the joists, the ceiling below and an insulation layer laid between and over the joists, with the roof space above.
Walls are a large surface through which heat escapes. The method depends on whether the wall has a cavity (a gap between two layers of wall) or is solid.

Cavity wall insulation: a cavity wall has an outer and an inner leaf (layer) with a gap between them. The cavity is filled with polystyrene beads, foam or mineral wool blown in through small holes, and even an unfilled cavity holds some still air.
Internal dry lining: insulated plasterboard is fixed to the inside face of the wall, which adds insulation on the room side. It reduces room size and takes time to fit, but needs no scaffolding.

External insulation: boards of polystyrene or mineral wool are fixed to the outside of the wall and finished with reinforced, waterproof render. This keeps the wall itself warm and avoids thermal bridges (cold spots where heat escapes), but needs planning checks.
Solid walls have no cavity, so they can only be insulated from the inside (dry lining) or the outside (external insulation).
Diagram: cross-section of a cavity wall showing the outer leaf, the insulation in the cavity, the inner leaf and an internal dry lining.
Heat also escapes through floors, glass, gaps around doors and bare pipes. Each has its own simple method.

Floors: seal the gaps between floorboards, add insulation between the joists on suspended floors, and lay a carpet with underlay. Rigid insulation goes under a new concrete floor. All of these reduce heat loss through the floor.

Double glazing: two panes are separated by a sealed gap of air or argon (a gas used instead of air in some units). The trapped gas is a poor conductor and cannot circulate, so conduction and convection across the gap are reduced.
Triple glazing adds a third pane and a second sealed gap for further insulation.
Low-E glazing: a thin coating on the pane reflects radiant heat back into the room.
Secondary glazing (an extra window fitted inside the existing one), heavy lined curtains and blinds close to the glass, and shutters trap a layer of still air against cold glass.

Doors and gaps: draught excluders, brush strips on doors, a letterbox flap, keyhole covers and sealing strips around windows and floorboards stop air leaking in and out. A porch adds a buffer of still air.
Lagging: an insulating jacket or factory-fitted foam on the hot-water cylinder and sleeves on exposed pipes save heat and help prevent pipes freezing.
Insulation reduces condensation, because warm inner surfaces stay above the temperature at which moisture condenses. However, an airtight, well-insulated house needs controlled ventilation.
Examiners often ask for the benefits of insulation. Each one follows from less heat escaping.
Lower heating bills, because less heat escapes and the heating runs for shorter periods.
Comfort: a steadier indoor temperature with no cold surfaces and fewer draughts.
Less noise, because insulation absorbs sound from outside and between rooms.
Less fuel burned, so lower carbon dioxide emissions and less use of fossil fuel, which makes a more sustainable house.
Less condensation and damp, because inner wall and window surfaces stay warm. This means healthier air and less mould.

A better Building Energy Rating (BER), which rates a dwelling's energy performance on a scale from A (most efficient) to G (least efficient) and is run by SEAI. A better BER can also raise the value of the property.
SEAI grants may help with the cost of insulating.
You may be asked to assess the insulation in your own home and suggest improvements. The method is to inspect, rank the problems and justify each recommendation.
Inspect the attic for the depth and coverage of insulation. Check whether joists are left uncovered and whether the tank and pipes are lagged.
Check doors and windows for draughts by feeling for cold air around the frames on a windy day, and note the type of glazing.
Find out the wall type (cavity or solid) and check whether the hot-water cylinder has a jacket.
Note cold rooms, cold surfaces and any signs of condensation or damp.
Recommend improvements in order of cost and effect: draught proofing and attic insulation first, then a cylinder jacket and lined curtains, then wall insulation and glazing.
Justify each recommendation by the heat it saves and its cost, and mention SEAI grants and the BER.

Ventilation is the continuous replacement of stale indoor air with fresh air. A well-ventilated home stays healthy and dry, and it does this without causing a draught or lowering the room temperature much.
Ventilation supplies fresh air (oxygen) for breathing and for the combustion (burning) of fuel in open fires, stoves and gas appliances, because a flame needs a steady air supply.
It removes stale air, carbon dioxide and impurities, together with moist air and cooking smells, so rooms stay fresh and the spread of infection is reduced.
It controls humidity (the amount of water vapour in the air) and temperature, so rooms do not become hot, damp and stuffy.
It prevents condensation, mould and damp, which damage the fabric (the structure and finishes) of the house and can aggravate asthma and bronchitis.
Modern airtight construction, insulation, double glazing, tight-fitting doors and windows and sealed fireplaces reduce natural air flow, so artificial methods are often needed.
Part F (Ventilation) of the Building Regulations requires adequate ventilation in new homes.
Fresh air should be introduced without causing a draught or lowering the room temperature, because the aim is controlled air change and not lost heat.

When stale air cannot escape, moisture, heat and smells collect indoors. The most obvious results are stuffy rooms and condensation, and the longer-term results are damp, damage to the house and health problems.
Air becomes stale and stuffy, with high humidity and lingering smells, because nothing is replacing it.
Condensation forms on cold surfaces such as windows, external walls and room corners, which leads to damp, mould and mildew, peeling paint and wallpaper, rotting wood and rusting metal.
Persistent damp causes structural damage to walls, ceilings and window frames, and wet insulation insulates less well.
Respiratory conditions such as asthma and bronchitis, and allergies, get worse in damp, mouldy air.
Kitchens and bathrooms suffer steam, heat, grease and smells, which collect and create overheating and slippery floors.
Gases can build up as a secondary effect: carbon dioxide rises and the oxygen supply falls, causing headaches and tiredness.
Combustion appliances that are not properly vented are starved of air and burn incompletely, which can produce carbon monoxide.

Air only moves when something drives it. Two forces do this in a home, and the principle you give must match the method you name. A flue is a third idea, because it carries waste gases away from burning fuel.
Convection: warm air is less dense (lighter), so it rises to high outlets, while cooler fresh air enters through low openings to replace it, producing a circulation that exchanges the air.

Suction (a pressure difference): an extractor fan lowers the air pressure inside a room, so stale air is drawn out and fresh air enters through openings such as vents and gaps under doors to replace it.
Wind and cross-ventilation: wind moving across the outside of a building creates pressure differences, so air enters on the windward side and leaves on the opposite side.
Combustion appliances need a steady air supply, and a flue (a chimney or pipe) carries their waste gases up and out of the house by convection as the hot gases rise.
Natural methods use openings in the building and the movement of air through them, so they need no electricity. They are simple, but they depend on conditions outside.
Windows and doors are the simplest method: a window open at the top and bottom gives convection, and opening windows on opposite sides of a room gives cross-ventilation and the greatest air change.
Air bricks and wall vents are openings in external walls that let air into and out of a room. High and low openings give an exchange of air, and they must never be blocked.
Trickle vents are small adjustable slots in window frames that let fresh air in continuously at a low, slow rate, so rooms are ventilated without opening a window.
Chimneys, fireplaces and flues: an open fire draws air into the room and carries smoke up the chimney as the hot gases rise.
Natural ventilation depends on the weather, wind and season, so the air change is not constant, and it can cause draughts and heat loss. It cannot be relied on to give a steady air supply.
Diagram: cross-section of a room showing warm, stale air rising out of a high vent and cooler fresh air entering through a low air brick.
Artificial methods use electric fans, so they give a more reliable air change in places where moisture and smells are made. Modern airtight homes need them because natural air flow is limited.

Extractor fan: an electric motor turns the blades, which create suction and draw out stale air, steam and smells. Shutters open when the fan runs and close when it is switched off, and fresh air flows in through gaps, under doors or through vents.

Extractor fans are fitted high on an external wall, in the ceiling or in a window, and are placed in kitchens, bathrooms and toilets, where moisture and smells are produced. They can be controlled by a switch, pull cord, timer or humidity sensor.
Ducted cooker hood: a motor drives a fan that draws air up through grease filters and expels it outside through a duct, so it removes steam and heat as well as grease.

Ductless cooker hood: filters trap grease and fumes, and the cleaned air is recirculated into the room. It does not remove moisture or heat, so it does not reduce steam. Filters need cleaning or replacing.

Mechanical ventilation system: a duct system in the ceiling or floor, in which fans blow fresh air in and remove stale air. Heat-recovery versions warm the incoming air using heat from the outgoing air, and the system suits airtight houses.
Air conditioning is an alternative that also controls humidity and temperature, but it is unusual in Irish homes.
For a kitchen, recommend an extractor fan or a ducted cooker hood plus a window or trickle vent, giving the principle of suction and the replacement of air.
Diagram: an extractor fan in an external wall with shutters, and a ducted cooker hood with its duct running to the outside.
Condensation is the most common ventilation problem in homes. It is not caused by damp walls: it is water vapour from the air turning to liquid on a cold surface.
Warm air holds more water vapour than cold air, so when warm, moist air touches a cold surface it cools and its water vapour turns to liquid water.
Everyday sources of moisture are cooking, kettles, bathing and showers, drying clothes indoors, breathing, and unflued gas or paraffin heaters.

Effects include damp patches, mould growth on walls and ceilings, peeling paint and wallpaper, rust, rotting wood and window frames, musty smells and respiratory problems. Damp insulation also loses its effect.
Prevention: ventilate with extractor fans, trickle vents and open windows, and keep lids on pots so less steam escapes.
Dry clothes outdoors or in a well-ventilated room, and keep the heating steady so surfaces do not get cold.
Insulation and double glazing keep surfaces warm, so water vapour has no cold surface to condense on. Wipe off condensation and keep furniture away from walls.
You may be asked to judge how well a room is ventilated and to recommend improvements. Look for the signs of poor air change first, then check what is provided to deal with it.
Assess ventilation by noting smells, stuffiness, condensation on windows and any mould or damp in corners.
Check which vents, air bricks and extractor fans are present and whether they are working and not blocked, because a blocked vent gives no air change.

Recommend improvements such as an extractor fan or cooker hood over the cooker, trickle vents in windows, keeping the kitchen door closed while cooking so steam does not spread, and moving clothes drying indoors to a ventilated space.

Light is a form of energy that travels in straight lines as waves, and white light is made of the colours of the spectrum. How a surface or material treats light decides how a room looks, so each property has a practical use in the home.
Materials treat light in three ways: transparent materials let light through, translucent materials scatter it, and opaque materials block it.

Reflection: light rays bounce back from shiny surfaces such as mirrors, glazed tiles, gloss paint and white ceilings, which brightens a room and makes it look larger. Fitting reflectors behind lamps use the same idea.
Refraction: light rays bend as they pass into thick or ridged glass, such as glass bricks or cut crystal, which spreads light through a room and gives decorative effects.
Diffusion (scattering): light scatters when it passes through translucent material such as frosted glass, net curtains, fabric or opal shades, so the light is soft and glare is reduced.

Absorption: dark, matt surfaces take in light rather than reflecting it, so a room with dark walls looks darker, appears smaller and cosier, and needs more light. Pale surfaces absorb less, so choose wall, ceiling and floor colours with the light level in mind.
Dispersion: a prism or crystal splits white light into its component colours, as in a crystal chandelier.
Colour of light: warm light is yellowish and cool light is bluish, and this is described by the lamp's colour temperature. Coloured surfaces and shades also change how colours look in a room.
Good lighting is planned, not added at the end. A plan matches the light to how each room is used, mixes natural and artificial light, and keeps the system safe and easy to look after.
Plan the lighting at the design or building stage, so that outlets, switches, wiring and fittings are positioned before construction begins, which also keeps the cost lower.

Match the lighting to the function of the room and its users: a kitchen and a study need bright task lighting at work surfaces, a living room needs a softer, flexible mix of light, a bedroom needs general and bedside light, and a bathroom needs safe, moisture-protected fittings.
Think about who uses the room, such as children, elderly people, reading or homework, because their needs decide how bright and how safe the lighting must be.

Combine general (ambient) light for the whole room, task light for an activity such as reading, cooking or desk work, and accent light to highlight a picture or feature. Use one or more focal points to set the atmosphere.

Balance natural and artificial light. The aspect of the room (a south-facing room gets most daylight) and the size and position of its windows decide how much daylight it receives. Daylight saves electricity and helps wellbeing.
The colour and size of the room matter: pale walls and ceilings reflect light while dark colours absorb it, and the size and shape of the room decide how many fittings are needed.
Once the right light is chosen for each room, the plan must also be comfortable to live with, safe and easy to look after.
Avoid glare and shadows by placing fittings away from the normal line of sight (for example TV and screens), using shades or indirect light that spread the light, and using several light sources.
Allow flexibility and mood with dimmers, timers, movable lamps, switching in groups and two-way switches on stairs, so the light can suit different activities and times of day.

Safety: use the correct voltage and fuse rating, have fittings installed correctly by an electrician, leave adequate space between the bulb and the shade, avoid trailing flexes, and choose bathroom fittings suited to the zone.
Maintenance: fittings should be easy to clean, bulbs and any replaceable parts should be easy to reach and replace, and switches in sensible places.
Daylight is free and pleasant, so a good plan makes the most of it before adding lamps. A room gets the most daylight when light can enter easily and reflect around it.
Use large windows, skylights and glass bricks, which let in more daylight, and keep clear glass in windows because frosted glass scatters light.
Leave out net curtains and heavy blinds, cut back trees outside the window, and place furniture so it does not block the light.
Use pale colours and mirrors, which reflect daylight deeper into the room.
Fittings are grouped by the job they do. Name the type of lighting first, then give a fitting that does that job.

General lighting lights the whole room: central ceiling fittings such as pendants, semi-flush and flush fittings, chandeliers, rise-and-fall fittings, recessed downlights, and track lights and spotlights.

Task lighting lights a specific activity: table and desk lamps, floor lamps with a pivot or flexible stem, under-cabinet and under-counter lights, pelmet lighting, and recessed downlights over a work area.
Accent lighting highlights a feature or focal point: picture lights, wall brackets, uplighters and downlighters, swivel lights, track lights and spotlights.
Outdoor fittings include sensor lights, solar lights, and column, step and decking lights.

A lamp is energy efficient when most of the electricity it uses becomes light rather than heat. To explain this, compare the old filament bulb with the compact fluorescent lamp (CFL) and the light-emitting diode (LED).

A filament bulb produces light when current heats a tungsten filament until it glows. Most of the energy it uses is given off as heat, not light, so it is inefficient, and it has been phased out of sale in the EU under efficiency rules.
CFL principle: electric current heats electrodes at each end of a coiled (looped) glass tube containing argon gas and mercury vapour. The mercury vaporises and the gas gives off ultraviolet light.
A phosphor coating on the inside of the CFL tube converts the ultraviolet light into visible light.

CFLs use much less energy and last much longer than filament bulbs, but they cost more to buy, are slow to reach full brightness, may cause glare without a shade, and contain mercury, so they must be recycled and disposed of safely.
The EU exemption that allowed mercury in compact fluorescent lamps ended on 24 February 2023, so CFLs are being phased out in favour of LEDs.

LED principle: electricity passes through a semiconductor chip, and electrons combine with gaps called holes and release energy as light, a process called electroluminescence. The colour depends on the semiconductor material.

LEDs use far less electricity than filament bulbs, start at full brightness instantly, give off little heat, have a very long life and come in many shapes and colours. They can be dimmable with a compatible dimmer, and although they cost more to buy, they save money on bills.
Energy-saving use: dimmers, timers, motion sensors, task lighting instead of lighting a whole room, using daylight and switching off unneeded lights reduce the energy used by any lamp.
When you buy a lamp, the watts on the box do not tell you how bright it is. Several labelled details help you choose well.
Brightness is measured in lumens, not watts. Watts measure the power a lamp uses, so a lower-wattage LED can be as bright as a higher-wattage filament bulb.
Check the colour temperature, to get warm (yellowish) or cool (bluish) light that suits the room.
Check that the lamp is compatible with the fitting and with any dimmer, and check its life.
Look for a high rating on the energy label. The EU energy label for light bulbs has used an A to G scale since September 2021.
Modern lighting is smaller, smarter and more efficient than older types, and developments are often judged on energy saving, convenience and mood.
LED strips, bulbs, rope lights and compact fittings come in many colour temperatures, can be dimmable, have a long life and give off little heat, and they can be fitted into small or awkward spaces.
Sensor or motion-activated and timer lighting switches on only when someone is present, saving energy and improving security in halls, stairs, porches and outdoor areas.
Smart lighting can be controlled from a phone, app or voice assistant to set schedules, dim the lights or change their colour.
Solar (photovoltaic) outdoor lights use a small panel to charge a battery during the day for garden and path lights, which light up at night.
Colour-changing LEDs and LED rope lighting create ambience and can be used as accent lighting.
Recessed and under-counter lights suit kitchens, and low-voltage and fibre-optic lighting are further developments.
Dimmable LEDs need a compatible dimmer, and cheap LED lamps may flicker or give poor colour rendering (colours looking unnatural).
This practical work builds the skill of judging lighting for a real room, using examples you collect yourself.
Collect examples of contemporary lighting from magazines, brochures and shop visits, and record the type of fitting and its lamp, such as LED or CFL.
For each example, note whether it provides general, task or accent lighting, and what its packaging states about brightness and colour temperature.
Evaluate each example for energy efficiency, safety, maintenance and suitability for a named room.

A textile is a material made from fibres or yarns (the threads spun from fibres) that has been woven, knitted or otherwise made into fabric. Textiles are a household resource, like food or fuel: they are bought, used, cared for and eventually replaced.
Textiles serve household purposes, such as bedding, curtains, carpets, towels and upholstery, and clothing purposes.
Because textiles cost money and need care, choosing well saves money and effort over the life of the item.
Most household textiles do several jobs at once. A curtain, for example, gives privacy, decoration and some warmth.
Textiles are used throughout the home for practical and decorative purposes, often several at once. Examiners often ask for a list of functions, so learn each one with its example item.
Warmth and insulation: blankets, duvets, throws and thick curtains trap still air within their fibres and layers, reducing heat loss from the body.
Sound absorption (sound insulation): carpets, rugs, curtains and upholstery absorb sound and reduce echo in a room.
Privacy and light control: curtains, net curtains and blinds screen the room from view and control the light entering it.
Comfort: cushions, mattress covers, bed linen and upholstery give softness and support.
Protection: oven gloves and aprons protect the user from heat and spills, carpets protect floors from wear, and mattress protectors protect the mattress.
Absorbency: towels, tea towels, dishcloths and bath mats take up water from the body, from dishes or from the floor, which makes washing and drying easier.
Decoration and aesthetics: curtains, cushions, wall hangings, bedspreads and rugs add colour, pattern and texture to a room.
Hygiene: washable textiles can be laundered to remove dirt and micro-organisms. Safety is a further function, because fire-resistant finishes make textiles safer.

A textile is chosen by weighing the properties of the fabric against the job it has to do, the money available and the household's preferences. Examiners often ask for three or four of these criteria, each with an explanation.
Fitness for purpose: the fabric's properties must suit its job, for example a towel needs absorbency and a curtain needs to drape well and resist fading.

Suitability in use: the fabric must withstand the wear, washing and conditions of the room it is used in, such as a kitchen, a living room or a child's bedroom. Purpose is the job; use is the wear and conditions, and both come under fitness.
Cost: the price must fit the budget and the expected life of the item, so a durable fabric can be better value. Wool and silk cost more than most other fibres.
Personal choice: likes and dislikes, colour and style, comfort, a preference for natural or easy-care synthetic fabrics, and current trends.
Aesthetic appeal: appearance, drape, weight, texture, lustre, colour and pattern, because the textile must look right in the room.
Care and cleaning: whether the fabric is washable or dry clean, how much ironing it needs, and its fade resistance, stain resistance and shrinkage, which affect how practical it is for the household.
Safety: a flame-retardant finish or fire-resistance label is wanted, and a loose or pile surface is avoided because it burns more easily.

In a longer Higher Level answer, durability (how long the fabric lasts), finishes (treatments added to improve a fabric) and sustainability (the environmental effect of the fabric) are also accepted, with one developed line on each.
Each property below describes how a fabric behaves in use. Define each in plain words and give an example fabric, since examiners ask what a property means and which fabric has it.
Absorbent: the fabric takes in and holds moisture. Cotton and linen are absorbent, which makes them suitable for towels, and an absorbent fabric also takes up dye easily.
Flammable: the fabric ignites and burns readily when exposed to a flame, creating a fire risk. Cotton burns easily, so flammability is not wanted in household textiles.

Crease-resistant: the fabric resists wrinkling in wear and washing and returns towards its smooth shape, so less ironing is needed. Polyester and wool resist creasing, but cotton and linen crease unless finished.
Colourfast: the colour resists running in water and fading in light, so it stays bright after washing, because the dye is fixed firmly to the fibres.
Durable (hard wearing): the fabric resists abrasion, tearing and wear over a long period of use.
Drape: the way a fabric hangs in folds. A good drape suits curtains and loose clothing.
Other properties examiners accept as desirable are warm, strong, washable, easy to dye, shrink resistant, stain resistant, quick drying and resilient (springs back into shape).
Static: synthetic fibres build up static electricity, so the fabric clings, and fabric conditioner reduces this. Wool can shrink in hot washing.
Choosing a fabric means matching its properties to the job of the item. When you recommend a fabric for a stated item, give the fabric and a reason from its properties.
Cotton towels: absorbent, strong when wet and able to withstand hot washing.
Linen tea towels: absorbent, strong and quick drying, but they crease easily unless treated.
Polyester curtains: drape well, resist fading, wash easily, dry quickly and resist creasing.
Cotton curtains: easy to launder and dye, with a crisp appearance and strong when wet, but they shrink if not pre-shrunk.
Wool blankets: warm, insulating, absorbent and elastic (resilient), but they can shrink and felt (the fibres mat together) if washed at high temperatures or carelessly.
Carpets in nylon or wool: strong, hard wearing and resistant to abrasion from foot traffic.
Bed linen in cotton or polyester-cotton: washable, strong and easy to iron.

Household textiles such as curtains, bedding and sofas can feed a fire, so fire risk is a key safety check when buying. How likely a textile is to catch light depends on the structure of the fabric, the fibres in it and the filling inside it.
Loosely spun yarns (yarns twisted only lightly, so they trap plenty of air) ignite very easily, so loosely spun fabrics are a poor choice where fire risk is high.
Fabrics with a raised pile or nap (a fluffy surface of upstanding fibres) ignite more easily than smooth, tightly woven fabrics, because flames can run quickly across the loose surface fibres.
Blends of man-made and natural fibres can burn more quickly than either fibre on its own, so a blend is not automatically safer than a single fibre.
Foam and other fillings in cushions and upholstery burn fiercely and give off toxic fumes when they burn, so check what the filling is and whether it is fire resistant.

Flame-retardant treatment lowers the risk of ignition. Inherently flame-retardant fabrics keep their resistance because the fibre itself resists ignition, while coated or finished fabrics rely on a treatment applied to the fabric.

Read the labels for fire-resistance information, for example a statement that the materials meet the requirements for resistance to cigarette and match ignition. Read the care label too, so that a flame-retardant finish is not damaged by washing or cleaning.
Higher-risk items in the home are children's nightwear, upholstered furniture, curtains near heat and protective workwear. Keep textiles away from heaters and cookers.
A flame-retardant finish is a chemical treatment that reduces how easily a fabric ignites and burns. Proban is one such finish; Pyrovatex is another.
Identification: Proban is used on cotton, linen and other cellulosic fabrics (fabrics made from plant cellulose).
Phosphorus and nitrogen compounds are fixed within the fibre structure, so the protection is built into the fibre rather than sitting on the surface as a coating.
You cannot tell by looking or touching whether a fabric has the finish. Its presence is shown on the product label or in the manufacturer's information.
Effect 1: it reduces the flammability of the fabric, which lowers the risk of ignition.

Effect 2: when taken away from a flame the fabric self-extinguishes (goes out by itself), because an insulating char forms around the fibres instead of the fabric burning on. The fabric neither melts nor keeps burning once it is taken away from the flame.
Drawback 1: the finish may cause an allergic reaction in some people.
Drawback 2: the fabric may need special care in cleaning, so follow the care instructions to avoid damaging the finish by washing or cleaning.
Uses: children's nightwear, protective workwear, upholstered furniture, military clothing and curtains, all items where a fire would be particularly dangerous.
Upholstered furniture is sat on every day, so its fabric has to cope with constant use while staying comfortable and safe.
Durable and hard wearing: the fabric resists abrasion and rubbing from constant use, so it keeps its appearance and does not wear through or tear.
Resilient: the fabric springs back after being sat on, so cushions keep their shape. Wool is resilient, while cotton loses its shape more readily.
Comfortable: the fabric has a pleasant handle (the feel of the fabric) and is not harsh against the skin.
Stain resistant: spills are less likely to soak in and wipe off more easily. Fabric that is also fade resistant and easy to clean stays looking good for longer.
Fire resistant: the fabric and the filling should resist ignition, and this is shown on a label.

A label stating that the materials meet the requirements for resistance to cigarette and match ignition tells the consumer that the covering has been tested and resists catching fire from a lit cigarette or a match.

The rules on the fire safety of domestic upholstered furniture changed in July 2026. The Irish fire safety order for domestic furniture that the syllabus names was revoked (by S.I. 357/2026), and these products now fall under EU product-safety law.
From July 2026, the fire safety requirements for domestic upholstered furniture are those of the EU General Product Safety Regulation (GPSR), Regulation (EU) 2023/988.
The GPSR is an EU regulation, so it applies directly in Ireland without needing an Irish Act, and it has applied since 13 December 2024.
Its core duty is that only safe products may be placed on the market. Producers must assess the risks of their products, and sellers, including online sellers, must not supply unsafe goods.

In practice, furniture that meets EU product-safety requirements may be sold to consumers in Ireland. The separate Irish fire label is no longer a legal requirement, though consumers can still look for fire-resistance information from the supplier.
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) is the Irish body for consumer information and complaints (ccpc.ie).

A fibre is a hair-like strand, the raw material that is spun into yarn and then made into fabric. Fibres are grouped by where their raw material comes from and how the fibre is formed, which gives three classes: natural, regenerated and synthetic.

Staple fibres are short, such as cotton, wool and linen, so they must be twisted together to make a yarn. Filaments are continuous and very long, such as silk and all man-made fibres as they are extruded (pushed out).
Natural fibres are obtained directly from plants or animals and need only cleaning and processing before they are spun into yarn, which is why they are the simplest class.

Natural fibres of plant origin are made of cellulose (the plant material that forms cell walls), and are called cellulosic: cotton, linen, and also hemp and jute. Natural fibres of animal origin are made of protein: wool and silk.

Regenerated fibres are made by dissolving a natural polymer (a long chain molecule), usually cellulose from wood pulp, and forcing the solution through a spinneret (a plate with fine holes) so that it reforms as a fibre. Examples are viscose (rayon), acetate and triacetate.

Synthetic fibres are made entirely from chemicals: small molecules called monomers, derived from coal or petroleum, are built into polymers. Examples are nylon (polyamide), polyester, acrylic and elastane (Lycra).
Regenerated and synthetic fibres together are called man-made (manufactured) fibres.
Diagram: a classification tree branching from textile fibres into natural (plant and animal), regenerated and synthetic, with one named example at the end of each branch.

Each natural fibre comes from one plant or animal source, and that source decides what the fibre is made of and what it is used for. Learn one source, one use and one property for each of the four main fibres.
Cotton: a cellulose fibre from the seed hairs of the cotton plant (the boll); used for shirts, jeans, T-shirts, towels, bed linen and curtains. It is absorbent and cool to wear.
Linen: a cellulose fibre from the stem of the flax plant; used for tea towels, tablecloths, summer clothing and bed linen. It is strong and absorbent, so it suits cloths that must dry dishes.
Wool: a protein fibre from the fleece of sheep; used for jumpers, knitwear, tweed, suits, blankets and carpets. It is warm and resilient (springs back into shape).

Silk: a protein filament from the cocoon of the silkworm (the caterpillar of the silk moth, fed on mulberry leaves); used for scarves, ties, formal and evening wear, lingerie and luxury bedding. It is smooth, drapes well and is absorbent.
Cotton and linen absorb moisture readily and are cool to wear; wool and silk are warm because they trap air in their structure.

Natural fibres are popular for household textiles because they are absorbent, comfortable, durable, washable, and accept dyes and finishes well. They come from renewable sources, and many people simply prefer natural fabric.
Regenerated fibres start from cellulose that already exists in a plant. The cellulose is dissolved and re-formed as a long filament, which is why they are called regenerated.

Viscose (rayon): cellulose from wood pulp is treated with chemicals, dissolved and forced through a spinneret into a chemical bath, where the fibre reforms. Rayon and viscose are the same fibre family, not two different fibres.
Viscose is absorbent, soft, drapes well and dyes well, but it is weak when wet, so it needs gentle handling. It is used for dresses, blouses, linings and soft furnishings.
Acetate: cellulose is chemically combined with acetic acid, dissolved and extruded to form a fibre with a silky, lustrous appearance. Triacetate is a related fibre.
Acetate drapes well, so it is used for linings, blouses and evening wear. It is also used for ties.
Lyocell is a newer regenerated cellulose fibre made by dissolving wood pulp in a solvent; it is absorbent and soft, much like other cellulose fibres such as cotton.
Regenerated fibres start from a plant-based raw material, wood pulp cellulose, so they are classed apart from synthetics, which start from coal or petroleum chemicals.
Synthetic fibres are built from chemicals rather than grown, so their properties can be designed. Each one has a typical strength that decides where it is used.
Nylon (polyamide): made from chemicals derived from coal or petroleum; very strong, elastic, light, abrasion resistant and low in absorbency. Used for hosiery, swimwear, jackets, carpets and ropes.
Polyester: made from petroleum-based chemicals; strong, crease resistant and quick drying. Used for shirts, fleece, curtains and bed linen, and often blended with cotton.
Acrylic: made from a polymer of acrylonitrile; it resembles wool, being soft, warm and light, so it is used for knitwear, socks and blankets.
Elastane is a stretch fibre; Lycra is a brand name for it. It is usually blended in small amounts with other fibres, for swimwear, sportswear and hosiery.
Synthetic fibres can be produced in a range of thicknesses and lustres by changing the spinneret holes and the amount of drawing.

Both are man-made and both are extruded through a spinneret, but they begin with different raw materials and behave differently. Compare them point by point: source, process, moisture, heat and an example.
Source: regenerated fibres begin with a natural polymer, cellulose from wood pulp; synthetic fibres begin with small molecules, called monomers, made from coal or petroleum.
Process: regenerated fibres are dissolved and reformed from an existing natural polymer; synthetic fibres are formed by linking monomers into a polymer, then extruding it.
Moisture: regenerated fibres such as viscose absorb moisture like cotton and drape well; synthetic fibres such as polyester absorb little moisture, so they dry quickly and resist creasing.
Heat: nylon and polyester melt at high temperatures, because they are plastic-like polymers, whereas viscose chars and burns like cotton.
For example, regenerated fibres include viscose and acetate; synthetic fibres include nylon, polyester and acrylic.
Example in use: a viscose blouse is more absorbent and comfortable next to the skin; a polyester blouse resists creasing and dries more quickly.
Regenerated and synthetic fibres are made in the same basic way: a thick liquid is pushed through tiny holes and hardened into long filaments. The steps below apply to both.
1. A thick liquid, either a molten polymer or a polymer solution, is forced through a spinneret, a metal plate with many fine holes.
2. The emerging streams harden: by cooling in air (melt spinning), by setting in a chemical bath (wet spinning), or by warm air evaporating the solvent (dry spinning).
3. The filaments are drawn, or stretched, so that their molecules line up, which makes them stronger.
Diagram: a spinneret cross-section showing polymer pumped through holes, forming filaments that are drawn onto a winding bobbin.

A profile follows one named fabric from its fibre to its end use, with the evidence used to identify it. Examiners ask for it under set headings, so knowing the structure lets you collect marks heading by heading.
Name the fabric and its fibres first, for example woven cotton or knitted polyester, because older marking schemes gave a mark for the name alone.
Fibre production: how the fibre is obtained from its raw material, or made from a polymer (a long chain of repeating units).
Yarn production: how the fibres become a yarn, either by spinning staple fibres (short fibres) or by twisting filaments (continuous fibres).
A yarn is fibres or filaments twisted together, and a fabric is made by weaving or knitting yarns, so keep these three terms apart.
Properties: give two or three properties, each linked to the fibre structure or the yarn, so the property has a reason behind it.
Identification: give the burning test result and the microscopic appearance of the fibres.
Uses: give suitable household or clothing uses, each with a reason based on the properties.
Other headings seen in past questions are fabric construction technique and fibre composition, so answer exactly the headings the question lists.
Cotton is the usual natural fabric to profile. Its production is a sequence of stages, and each stage has its own job, so learn them in order.
1. Harvest: the bolls (seed pods) on the cotton plant open when the plant matures, and the fibres are picked by hand or machine.
2. Ginning: machines separate the fibres from the seeds and remove large impurities, so that only clean fibre goes on to be made into yarn.
3. Baling and grading: the fibres are baled and graded by length, fineness and colour, so that similar fibres are used together.
4. Cleaning and blending: fibres are cleaned and opened, and mixed so that the yarn is uniform.
5. Carding: fibres are combed into a loose web and drawn into a continuous sliver (a loose rope of fibres).
6. Combing (optional): combing before spinning removes short fibres, which gives a finer, smoother yarn.
7. Spinning: the sliver is twisted into yarn, because the twist is what holds the short fibres together.
Cotton's properties come from its fibre structure, and the same structure shows up in the burning test and under the microscope.
Properties: cotton is absorbent, strong and stronger when wet, cool and comfortable to wear, washable and dyes well, which is why it suits everyday clothing and household textiles.
Weaknesses: cotton creases easily unless treated, so it often needs ironing; it also shrinks, burns easily, may mildew and has little elasticity.
Burning test: cotton burns quickly with a steady yellow flame, keeps burning when removed from the flame, smells of burning paper and leaves a soft grey ash.
Microscope: each fibre is a flat, twisted ribbon with natural twists (convolutions), and a central canal (lumen) is visible.
Uses: shirts, jeans, towels, bed linen, curtains and T-shirts, where absorbency and washability matter.
A profile of any natural fabric is accepted, so you can write about wool, linen or silk instead of cotton. Each needs only a few points under each heading.
Wool production: shearing (clipping the fleece from the sheep), grading, scouring (washing out grease and dirt), carding and spinning.
Wool properties: warm, resilient and absorbent, but it shrinks and felts, so it needs careful washing.
Wool burning test: burns slowly with a smell of burnt hair or feathers and leaves a black, crushable ash.
Linen production: it comes from the flax stem, which is retted, scutched, combed and spun.
Linen properties and test: strong, absorbent and creases easily, so it often needs ironing; it burns quickly with a paper smell, like cotton.
Silk production: it comes from the cocoon, with the continuous filaments reeled off.
Silk properties and test: smooth, so it drapes well; it burns slowly with a burnt-hair smell and leaves a crushable black bead.
Manufactured fibres are made from chemicals rather than harvested. Nylon is the usual example, and its production turns small molecules into a long chain, then into filaments.
1. Polymer: two chemicals (monomers), joined in equal proportions and heated, link up to form a long nylon polymer.
2. Extrusion: the molten polymer is forced through a spinneret, a plate with many fine holes, to form filaments.
3. Cooling: the filaments solidify and harden as they cool.
4. Drawing: the filaments are stretched to line up their molecules, which increases their strength.
5. Winding: the filaments are wound on bobbins, ready to be made into yarn.
Yarn production: the continuous filaments are twisted together into a filament yarn, which can be textured to add bulk.
Nylon's long, aligned molecules and smooth, non-absorbent filaments explain both its properties and what it does in a flame.
Properties: nylon is very strong, elastic, light, abrasion resistant (it resists rubbing and wear), low in absorbency and quick drying, and it resists creasing.
Weaknesses: nylon builds up static, may feel hot to wear because it absorbs so little moisture, and is flammable, melting when it burns.
Burning test: nylon melts and shrinks away from the flame, forms a hard bead and gives off a chemical smell.
Microscope: nylon appears as smooth, even, round rod-like filaments with no scales or twists.
Uses: hosiery, swimwear, lingerie, jackets and carpets, such as in tights and swimsuits, where strength, stretch and quick drying matter.
Polyester and viscose are also accepted as the manufactured fabric in a profile, and they are made in different ways.
Polyester production: a viscous liquid is extruded through a spinneret and solidifies in cold air.
Polyester properties: strong, crease resistant and non-absorbent, so it dries quickly.
Polyester burning test: it burns and melts, with a sweetish smell, and leaves a hard bead.
Viscose production: cellulose is treated and dissolved, then forced through a spinneret into a bath.
Viscose properties and test: it is weak when wet, so it needs gentle handling, and it burns like cotton because both are cellulose.

A blend combines two or more fibres in one yarn, or different yarns in the warp and weft, to get the best properties of each. This is different from joining two separate fabrics, because the fibres are combined in the yarn or in warp and weft.
Examples of blends are polyester-cotton, wool-nylon, cotton-Lycra and linen-cotton.
Production: each fibre is produced separately, with cotton harvested, ginned and cleaned and polyester extruded and cut into staple (short) lengths.
Yarn production: the staple fibres are blended before or during carding, then drawn and spun into one yarn.
A blend can also be made by using one fibre yarn for the warp and another for the weft.
Properties: cotton gives absorbency and comfort, while polyester gives strength, crease resistance and quick drying.
Compared with pure cotton, the blend dries faster, is easier to iron and is cheaper; in the same way, linen-cotton is cheaper than pure linen.
Burning test: the results are mixed, because the blend burns like cotton and melts like polyester, so the test is indicative only.
Microscope: both fibre types are visible in the same sample, with cotton's twisted ribbon beside polyester's smooth filaments.
Uses: shirts, school uniforms, bed linen and curtains, because easy care and comfort both matter there.

Modification changes a yarn or filament to improve the properties of the fabric made from it. Filament modification changes a continuous filament yarn so that it is bulkier, softer or stretchier, without changing the polymer. Examiners ask for two examples, so know several and what each achieves.
Modification examples in marking schemes include blending, crimping, twisting, mercerising, brushing, flame or stain resistance and water repellence.
Crimping and texturising: the filaments are crimped, looped or curled, trapping air so the yarn is bulkier, warmer and softer, as in textured (bulked) polyester.
Air-jet texturing: compressed air loops the filaments, giving bulk without mechanical crimping.
Heat setting: a textured yarn is heated under tension so that it keeps its crimp or loops in the finished fabric.
Twisting: more twist gives a stronger, smoother yarn, and ply yarns are made by twisting yarns together.
Mercerising: cotton under tension is treated with caustic soda, which gives extra lustre, strength, absorbency and a better affinity for dye.
Brushing raises the surface of the fabric, trapping air and giving a warmer, softer fabric.
Textured or slub yarns have uneven thick and thin sections, or loops added to the yarn, to create surface interest in a fabric.
Fibre identification is an investigation in which a known control sample is compared with an unknown sample. Two tests are used together because one alone can mislead.
Aim: to identify an unknown fabric sample from its burning behaviour and its microscopic appearance.
Burning method: hold a small fibre sample with tongs or forceps, remove any finish where possible, and bring it slowly towards a flame held over a non-flammable surface.
Observations: record how the fibre behaves as it approaches the flame, as it burns and when removed from the flame, whether it melts, the smell and the appearance of the ash or residue.
Control: so the unknown has something to match, test a known sample of cotton, wool or nylon under the same conditions, and compare the results, so the unknown has something to be matched against.
Microscope: mount a few fibres on a slide, in water, examine them under magnification and compare their shape (twist, scales, rod or ribbon) with reference images.
Safety: ventilate the room, keep water and a fire blanket nearby, use small samples, tie back hair and do not breathe in fumes from the burning sample.
Limits: finishes and dyes change the results, and blends give mixed results, so use both tests together.
Conclusion: the fibre is identified when both the burning result and the microscopic appearance match a known fibre.

Woven fabric is made by interlacing two sets of yarns at right angles on a loom (the frame that holds the yarns). The way the yarns cross each other decides how firm, smooth or hard wearing the fabric is.
Warp yarns run lengthways and are held under tension on the loom; weft yarns are passed across them at right angles, over and under the warp.
Plain weave: each weft yarn passes alternately over and under each warp yarn. It is the simplest and most stable interlacing, so it is firm and hard wearing, as in calico and cotton shirting.

Twill weave: each weft passes over two or more warp yarns before passing under one, and the pattern shifts each row, forming diagonal lines. Twill is more drapable and hard wearing than plain weave, as in denim.

Satin weave: long floats (stretches of yarn lying loose on the surface) cross with few interlacings, giving a smooth, lustrous face. Because the floats are long, satin is less durable and more prone to snagging.
Plain, twill and satin are the three basic weaves.
Selvedges: the tightly woven edges formed where the weft turns back. They resist fraying, so the edges of the fabric do not unravel.
Diagram: interlacing grids for plain, twill and satin weaves, marking the warp and weft yarns that pass over or under at each crossing.
Knitted fabric is formed from a series of interlocking loops of yarn, made by hand with needles or by machine. Loops can open and close, so the fabric stretches and recovers its shape.
