Weft knitting: loops are formed across each row, so usually one yarn can make the whole fabric. Warp knitting is machine-made, with the yarn zigzagging along the length of the fabric.
Plain (jersey) knit: loops are formed in one direction on each row, giving a smooth face and a looped reverse. It stretches across the width and is used for T-shirts.
Rib knit: knit and purl columns alternate, typically 1 by 1, giving elasticity in both directions, so it suits cuffs and waistbands.
Purl knit: loops are pulled to the reverse side, producing the purl face of a fabric, the reverse of a plain knit. Purl is a looping method, not a different kind of fabric.
Double knit: two sets of needles make a double-thickness fabric that is warm and reversible.
Knitted fabric is stretchy and flexible, with the amount of stretch depending on the yarn used and the looping structure. It is also comfortable and drapes well.
Knitted fabric is warm because its loops trap air, and it can be knitted into shaped pieces or garments with few seams, or none. It may snag, sag or shrink.
Uses include jumpers, hats, scarves, socks, T-shirts, blankets and throws.
Fabric does not always need yarn. Fibres can be locked together directly, which gives a third construction technique beyond weaving and knitting.
Felting: wool fibres are matted together by heat, moisture and agitation (pressure). The scales on each fibre interlock, so no yarn is needed.
Non-woven bonding: fibres are fixed into a web using adhesive, heat or needle punching, forming a fabric without weaving or knitting.
Needle punching: barbed needles push fibres through a web, interlocking them mechanically.
Felt is used for hats, interlinings and insulation; bonded non-woven fabrics are used for interlinings and disposable items.
Crochet, lace and macramé are other constructions that appear in marking schemes.

A finish is applied after weaving or knitting to change the fabric's appearance, handle (how it feels) or performance. Finishes are used to prevent creasing and shrinkage, add water repellence or stain resistance, increase durability and safety, improve wear and prevent loss of colour.

Crease-resistant finish: a resin cross-links the cellulose in cotton and linen so the fabric resists wrinkling, which means less ironing, for example on a linen skirt. It can slightly reduce strength and absorbency.
Water-repellent finish: a silicone coating makes water bead on the surface and run off, as on raincoats and tablecloths.
Stain-resistant finish: spills sit on the surface so they can be wiped away before they soak in, as on jackets, upholstery and tablecloths.
Anti-static finish: applied to synthetic fibres, or added at home through a fabric conditioner, to reduce static build-up and cling, for example in dresses and linings.
Flame-retardant finish: reduces how easily the fabric burns, so it is used on household textiles and nightwear.
Mercerising: cotton is treated with caustic soda, which makes it stronger, lustrous and more absorbent, as in bed sheets and jeans.
At Higher Level you must know a third finish. Either of these two will do.
Calendering: fabric is passed between heated rollers under pressure, flattening the surface to give a smooth, glossy or embossed finish.
Shrink resistance: a finish or controlled pre-treatment reduces the shrinkage of cotton and wool during washing, so the garment keeps its size.
Colour is applied either by dyeing or by printing a design onto the surface. Dyeing colours the fibre, yarn or fabric, and the dye must be matched to the fibre type.
Reactive dyes form strong chemical bonds with cotton and linen, giving bright, washfast colour. Cotton takes reactive dyes, not acid or disperse dyes.
Acid dyes are used on protein fibres such as wool and silk, and on nylon, in an acidic dye bath.
Disperse dyes are used on polyester and acetate, applied as fine particles dispersed in water.
Yarn dyeing: yarn is dyed before weaving or knitting, so it produces stripes, checks and tweeds.
Piece dyeing: the finished fabric is dyed in one plain colour after it has been constructed.
Printing places colour on the surface of a made fabric in a pattern, while resist methods block dye from parts of the fabric so those parts stay undyed.
Screen printing: a stencil on a fine mesh screen blocks off the areas that should not print, and ink is pushed through the open mesh with a squeegee. Each colour needs its own screen.
Roller printing: engraved rollers, one for each colour, print the fabric continuously and quickly, so it suits long runs.
Stencilling: a cut stencil and sponge are used, which is simple and suits children's clothing.
Transfer printing: the design is printed on paper, and heat transfers it to polyester.
Resist dyeing: wax (batik) or tying (tie-dye) stops dye reaching parts of the fabric, leaving a pattern.
Diagram: cross-section of a screen-printing stage showing the screen, stencil, squeegee, ink and the fabric beneath on a padded table.
Design is applied to a fabric by adding decoration once the fabric has been made. Each technique gives a different look and suits different garments.
Appliqué: a shaped piece of fabric is attached to a background with stitching, with raw edges turned under or satin stitched, as for logos and jackets.
Embroidery: decorative threads are stitched onto the fabric surface by hand or machine, for example cross stitch or chain stitch.
Quilting: a top fabric, wadding and backing are stitched together through all layers, trapping the wadding in a pattern.
Patchwork: pieces of fabric are sewn together to form a design, often combined with quilting.
Smocking: fabric is gathered and held in pleats by stitching in a pattern, giving stretch and decoration, often on children's clothing.
Embossing: a heated, patterned roller presses a raised design into the fabric surface.
Beading and sequins: small pieces are sewn on by hand or machine to add sparkle and texture.
Printing (screen, roller, stencil, transfer) also counts as design application in marking schemes.
Performance tests compare fabrics under identical conditions to judge their suitability for a particular use, such as a school jacket or uniform.
Fair test: samples are cut to the same size with the grain in the same direction, conditioned in the same room, and tested under the same load and time. This way only the fabric differs.

Crease-recovery test: a sample is folded in half, placed under a set weight for a set time, then released and left to recover. The angle between the two halves is measured with a protractor, and the angle closest to 180 degrees shows the best recovery.
Another crease method is to crumple equal samples in a closed fist for one minute, release them and compare on a five-point scale.
Absorbency test: a set volume of water is dropped onto the fabric and the time it takes to soak in is recorded. A fabric that absorbs quickly is suited to towels.

Colourfastness test: a sample is sewn between white fabrics and washed in a detergent solution. The change in colour of the sample and the staining of the white fabrics are compared with a grey scale.
Shrinkage test: a sample is measured, washed at a set temperature, dried and measured again, and the percentage change is calculated.
Repeat each test and calculate an average so that a single result does not mislead.
Other tests named in schemes: abrasion, insulation, stretch, pilling or snagging, tearing, water resistance and flame resistance.

A garment's care label is not arbitrary: a fabric's properties come from its fibres, its yarn and its construction, and these decide how it reacts to water, heat, friction and detergent. Knowing the fibre family tells you how to wash, dry and iron it safely.

Natural cellulose fibres (cotton, linen) absorb water readily, swell when wet and are strong when wet, so they can be washed hot and often. They also crease easily and tend to shrink on first washing.

Protein fibres (wool, silk) absorb moisture but are damaged by alkaline detergents and high temperatures, so they need a mild or wool-specific detergent, a low temperature and gentle action. Wool is washed cool, about 30 °C, as the label states.
Wool can felt or shrink when agitated in hot water, which is why hot, rough washing ruins it.

Manufactured fibres such as polyester and nylon absorb very little water, dry quickly, keep their shape and resist creasing. They can attract static, and they melt or glaze under a hot iron or high tumble-dry heat.

Blended fabrics combine the care needs of both fibres, so the more sensitive (most delicate) fibre sets the washing temperature and ironing heat. For example, a wool/polyester mixture is washed and ironed as wool.

Fabric construction matters too: a tightly woven fabric resists water and wind more than a loosely knitted one, because the gaps between yarns are smaller. Knitted fabric stretches and can sag or shrink.
Shrinkage is a permanent reduction in a fabric's length or width after laundering. It happens in three different ways, and the cause decides how to prevent it.
Relaxation shrinkage happens because fibres stretched during spinning, weaving and finishing relax back to their natural length in water. It is most marked in cotton, linen and viscose.
Felting shrinkage happens to wool when the scales on its fibres interlock under heat, moisture and agitation. The fabric thickens and shrinks, and this cannot be reversed.
Heat shrinkage occurs when a fabric is washed or tumble dried hotter than it can tolerate, especially in knitted and thermoplastic fabrics (those that soften with heat).
Percentage shrinkage = (original length − new length) ÷ original length × 100.
Prevention: follow the care label, wash at the stated temperature and avoid hot tumble drying, because heat is a common cause.
Pre-shrunk fabric or a shrink-resistant finish reduces shrinkage in garments that will be laundered often. Washing a test sample of fabric before cutting out a garment shows how much it will shrink.
Water repellence is how well a fabric resists wetting. It matters for rainwear and for choosing the right fabric for a garment.

Three things give a fabric water repellence: a close weave or tight knit, so the gaps between yarns are too small for water to penetrate; a fibre that absorbs little water; and a water-repellent finish.
Fibres that do not absorb water, such as polyester and nylon, shed water more readily than cotton or linen. Cotton and wool absorb water, so they are not naturally repellent.
A water-repellent finish coats the surface of the fabric with a chemical so that water forms beads that roll off.
Washing and wear reduce a finish, so a repellent garment may need re-proofing.
Water-repellent (showerproof) fabric resists wetting but will let water through in heavy or prolonged rain.
A waterproof fabric (coated or laminated, with sealed seams) stops water passing through entirely.
Breathable fabrics let perspiration vapour escape while keeping rain out, so the wearer stays dry inside as well as outside.
Crease recovery is how well a fabric springs back to its smooth state after being folded or crushed. It decides how much ironing a garment needs.
A crease forms when fibres are bent and the bonds between them shift, holding the fabric in the folded position.

Cotton, linen and viscose have poor recovery, so they crease easily and need ironing. In cotton and linen, cellulose chains form hydrogen bonds that break and re-form when the fabric is wet and dried.
Wool recovers well because its fibres are elastic, and creases hang out or can be relaxed by steaming.
Polyester and nylon have good crease recovery because their fibres spring back to shape once the folding force is removed.
Crease-resistant finishes, such as resin finishes on cotton or linen, improve recovery and cut down ironing. Blending with polyester also helps.
Care link: damp garments can be shaken and hung to reduce creases, and ironing temperature must match the fibre.

Care labels use a fixed set of symbols so that anyone can read how to launder a garment safely, whatever language the label is in. Reading the label before buying and before washing helps you avoid shrinkage, colour loss and damage.
The symbols are international (standard ISO 3758; GINETEX is the European association behind them) and appear in a fixed order: washing, bleaching, drying, ironing, then professional care.
Wash: a washtub means the garment may be machine washed, and the number or dots in the tub give the maximum water temperature. Bars under the tub mean gentler action.
A hand in the tub means hand wash only, usually at a low temperature with gentle action. A cross over the tub means do not wash in water.
Bleach: a triangle means bleach may be used; a crossed-out triangle means do not bleach.
Drying: a square containing a circle means tumble drying is allowed, with dots showing the heat setting; a crossed tumble-dry symbol means do not tumble dry.
A square with a horizontal line means dry flat; a square with one vertical line means line dry. Drip dry means hang the wet garment to drip without wringing.
Iron: one dot means a cool (low) iron, two dots a warm or medium iron and three dots a hot iron; a crossed iron means do not iron.
Dry cleaning: a circle shows dry cleaning is allowed, and the letters inside tell the cleaner which solvent process to use. A crossed circle means do not dry clean.
Diagram: draw and label the washtub (with 30 or 40 or dots), hand wash, triangle with a cross, tumble dry, dry flat, iron with two dots, and circle (dry clean).
A modern laundry detergent contains several components, each with a specific job in removing soil from the fabric. Choosing a detergent to match the fabric depends on knowing what each does.

Surfactants reduce the surface tension of water, so the water can wet the fibres thoroughly. One end of a surfactant molecule attracts water and the other attracts oil and grease, so they lift oily and greasy soil away and break it into small particles.
Surfactants hold the loosened soil suspended in the wash water, so it is rinsed away and does not redeposit on the fabric.

Enzymes (in biological detergents) are proteins that act as biological catalysts, speeding up the breakdown of stains: protease breaks down protein stains such as blood and egg, amylase breaks down starch stains and lipase breaks down fat stains.
Enzymes work best in warm, not hot, water and are damaged or destroyed by very high temperatures.
Fluorescent whitening agents (optical brighteners) absorb ultraviolet light and re-emit it as blue-white light, which makes white and light fabrics look brighter and whiter.
Fluorescent agents do not clean or remove stains; they only change how the fabric reflects light.
Match the detergent to the fabric: use a mild detergent for wool and silk. A biological detergent is not for wool or silk, because enzymes can attack their protein fibres.
Simple tests let you compare how different fabrics behave, using their general properties of shrinkage, water repellence and crease recovery. They only give useful results if the test is fair.
Shrinkage test: mark and measure a square on each sample, wash and dry under identical conditions, remeasure and calculate the percentage shrinkage.
Water-repellence test: place drops of water on each sample (flat or on a slope) and time or observe whether the drops bead and roll off, or soak in and darken the fabric.
Crease-recovery test: crumple equal-sized samples in a closed fist for one minute, release, and compare how smooth each is after a set time.
Fair test: use equal-sized samples, the same conditions and the same timing, so that the only variable is the fabric. Name the fibre or fabric of each sample.
Repeat the test on several samples of each fabric to give reliable results, note any variation, and record the results in a table.
Draw a conclusion on how suitable each fabric is for a garment, using your results.
Clothing requirements are the needs an outfit must meet, and they vary between people and situations. Working out which needs matter most is the first step in choosing what to buy.

Function: clothing must protect the body from weather, provide the movement an activity needs and be safe for the wearer's work or play. For example, a waterproof jacket needs a close-weave, water-repellent fabric so rain cannot soak through.

Climate and season decide the weight of fabric, the amount of covering and the need for waterproof or insulating layers, because the clothing has to keep the body comfortable in the weather it will meet.

Cost versus money available: a buyer weighs the price of a garment against their budget, and the purchase cost is balanced against durability and the number of times it will be worn, which is why a dearer, hardwearing garment can be better value.
Availability: clothing can only be bought if it is stocked in the shops or online in the right size, colour and style, so what a person wears is limited by what they can actually find.
Personal taste and body shape guide the choice of style, colour and fit, because people want clothes that suit them and feel comfortable.
Occasion and activity define the level of formality, such as a school uniform, work wear, sportswear or a wedding outfit.
People do not choose clothes in isolation. The culture, beliefs and groups around them shape what feels right to wear.

Culture shapes modesty and dress codes, and it inspires designs, because each culture has its own standards of what is suitable to wear. Traditional dress such as the sari and pashmina shawl, and traditional embroidery motifs, are examples.
Religious and national traditions influence the clothing worn for ceremonies, festivals and rites of passage (the key events in life, such as a wedding or graduation).
Peer groups influence teenagers, who often adopt the styles and brands their friends wear to gain acceptance.
Status: clothing signals a person's rank, wealth or profession, so what someone wears tells others about their position.
Identification: uniforms show that a person belongs to a group or holds a role, such as the uniform of a nurse. The principle is that a uniform signals role.
Most people see what is fashionable long before they see it in a shop. The media, admired public figures and designers decide which styles spread.
Magazines, newspapers, television, film and advertising popularise fashion by showing what is worn, so people see new styles and want them.
Young people copy the clothes worn by actors, presenters, musicians and sports stars they admire.

Trendsetters are individuals or groups whose choices are copied by others, and they set the direction for the mass market. Examples are James Dean (jeans, white T-shirt, black leather jacket), Jackie Kennedy (A-line suit and pillbox hat) and Princess Diana.
Fashion houses and designers launch collections at seasonal shows, which are then copied by high street retailers.
Fashion is the currently accepted style, and it changes over time, so clothing that was fashionable in one decade can look dated in the next.
Trendsetters are people, fashion is the accepted style and a trend is a short-lived direction, so keep the three terms apart.
Social conditions change what people want to wear, so designers and makers change the garments they produce.
Social conformity, the wish to fit in with a group, drives demand for common styles, because people buy what others around them are wearing.
Changes in women's status and in male roles have altered the silhouettes and tailoring that designers offer, so garments such as women's trouser suits became common.
Money decides both what consumers can spend and what it costs to make a garment, so the economy shapes design and construction.
Prosperity encourages consumers to spend on fashion, including power dressing and luxury items, because they have more money to spare.
In a downturn, consumers buy simpler, more sombre and lower-cost clothing, and manufacturers use cheaper materials to keep prices down.
Production costs, including raw materials and labour, set the price a garment must be sold at.
Technology changes how garments are designed and made, and how quickly new styles reach buyers.
Computer-aided design (CAD) allows designers to develop patterns and styles on screen before production, so ideas can be tested without making a sample.
Advanced sewing machines, computerised cutting and mass production make garments faster and cheaper to make.
New and high-tech fibres and blends, such as stretch fibres and microfibres, create fabrics with new properties.
Media and communication allow new styles to reach markets around the world very quickly, for example through fashion shows and images shared by phone.

A trend is recognised by the features it repeats across many garments and outfits. The elements of design (colour, shape, line, proportion, pattern and texture) give you the words to describe those features, and the examples below are only examples, because the trend shown in an exam may be any current one.
Colour: bright, fluorescent or tonal colour schemes, colour panelling and monochrome outfits make a trend easy to spot from a distance.
Shape and silhouette: oversized or boxy shapes, high-waisted trousers, and tailored coats or capes. Cropped tops are another example of a current shape.
Line: exaggerated vertical lines add height, horizontal lines widen and shorten the look, and diagonal lines give contrast and movement. This is why a trend can be described through its lines.
Proportion: for example a short jacket worn over a long dress, or a deep cropped top with wide trousers.
Pattern: geometric prints and bold retro statements. Retro patterns are old designs revived by designers, so name the pattern and say it is a revival.
Texture: shiny finishes reflect light, while matt fabrics absorb it. Embroidery, sequins, beads and distressed or frayed surfaces add surface interest.
Accessories: belts, large bags, statement jewellery and hats, which can carry a trend on their own.

Seasonal examples are examples of their year, not fixed lists: summer 2024 gave light leggings, loose T-shirts, crochet knits, denim jackets, cut-outs, cargo trousers and oversized jackets. Teenage trends gave ripped denim, bomber jackets and chunky jewellery. Casual wear showed neon and panelled colour and geometric prints.
Trends do not appear by accident. Several forces decide which colours, garments and styles become popular, and exams ask you to outline or evaluate these influences.
Social media spreads a fashion image internationally within hours, and repeated exposure can turn a colour, garment or vintage look into a trend. This is why trends also increase sales.
Influencers and bloggers display outfits and styling videos, give samples and feedback, and their endorsements can encourage or discourage a purchase.
Celebrities, musicians and athletes are photographed in specific designers' clothes, and fans copy their style. Music and dance styles, sports and world events also shape what people wear.
Designers and fashion houses define the season's direction through seasonal collections and fashion weeks. Ready-to-wear (mass-produced) clothing then copies the runway looks.

Environmental concern has created demand for sustainable or circular fashion (clothing kept in use for as long as possible). This favours durable natural or recycled materials, repair and upcycling, and fast fashion is criticised for waste.
Trends are also shaped by travel and by culture, including global and ethnic styles from other countries that become popular at home.
Past decades return: retro and vintage styles and bold retro patterns are revived by designers and high street brands.
Athleisure (also called leisure wear) is sportswear styling worn for everyday life, not sportswear for playing sport. It has become a major trend because it puts comfort first.
Typical items include leggings or joggers, hoodies, zipped jackets and trainers, worn for work, school and leisure.
Stretch, breathable and easy-care fabrics give comfort and freedom of movement, and they wash easily, which suits busy everyday use.
Its strengths are comfort, versatility, durability, affordability and adaptability to many occasions. It is casual and trendy and is promoted by influencers.
Athleisure can support activity and posture and a healthy active lifestyle, since clothing that is comfortable to wear makes it easier to exercise and move.
It works as a wardrobe staple (a basic item worn again and again) when the pieces are neutral in colour and can be combined with smarter items.
Its weaknesses are that it can look too informal for some workplaces and occasions, and that tight leggings and tops do not suit every body shape.
Another weakness is that it may encourage a casual dress code to become the default in everyday life.
Buying older or second-hand clothes has moved from a bargain habit to a fashion statement. The two terms are different, and both are examined.
Vintage clothing is older clothing from a past era, often a previous decade. Pre-loved clothing is any second-hand clothing, so all vintage is pre-loved but not all pre-loved is vintage.
Both are bought in charity shops, vintage or second-hand shops, online marketplaces and swaps.
Pre-loved clothing extends the life of garments already made, which reduces the demand for new production. This is why it is linked to sustainability and the reaction to fast fashion.

Reasons for its popularity: it is cheaper than new, it gives a unique, individual look because fewer people wear the same piece, and influencers and celebrities promote it. The economic climate also encourages it.
Distressed looks, such as frayed edges, grated patches and bleached areas, take inspiration from the vintage punk look, along with studs, sequins and embroidery.

Retro statements, such as bold patterns and bright colours from earlier decades, are revived by designers and high street brands. They are eye-catching because they stand out from plain everyday wear.
Upcycling changes an old garment into a new one, for example by adding patches, embroidery or appliqué (fabric shapes sewn on), dyeing, shortening, or customising denim with studs.

To restyle a garment to follow a trend, add belts or embellishment, alter the hem or trouser length, add layers or shoulder pads, crop or deconstruct a jacket, distress or recolour jeans, or change the buttons, patches or linings.
Accessories are the items added to an outfit rather than the main garments. They are often the quickest way to show a trend.
Examples include belts, bags, scarves, hats, gloves, jewellery, sunglasses, footwear, ties, cufflinks and pocket squares.
Accessories complete an outfit and create a focal point (the place the eye goes first), drawing attention to a feature of the look. A belt, for example, shows off the waist.
They add colour and contrast, and they tie an outfit together by repeating a colour from another garment. A colourful scarf brightens a plain outfit.
Accessories can change the formality of a basic outfit, for example a scarf or hat that makes a plain outfit look smart or casual. They also help balance colour and proportion.
A vintage look can be created with items such as retro sunglasses, large brooches and patterned scarves.
Footwear contributes to the overall look, complements the outfit and can create a focal point.
Accessories are often the cheapest way to follow a trend, as one item can update or modernise an existing outfit.
A critical evaluation weighs the advantages and disadvantages of a trend rather than simply describing it. Describe the trend first, then judge it under the headings the question gives.
Advantages: a trend can express identity, create employment in the fashion sector and bring new ideas to design.
Disadvantages: fast fashion encourages frequent buying, leading to waste and to garments of low quality that wear out quickly.
Cost: following trends can be expensive, and garments may date quickly once a trend passes.
Comfort and function: a trend should be judged on whether the garment is comfortable and suits the wearer's activity.
Suitability: a trend may not flatter every body shape, so a critical evaluation considers who it suits and who it does not, and the occasion it is worn for.
Other headings the exam may give include colour, pattern, line, shape, proportion, texture, accessories, aesthetic appeal and influences.
Elective questions ask you to sketch and describe an outfit built around one current trend, so you need to show the trend and explain your choices.

Diagram: draw a front view of the outfit (add a back view if needed) and label the design features, such as line, shape, proportion and harmony. Give the colour and fabric, and say which trend it follows and why.

Fabric reasoning: choose for a reason, such as absorbent, breathable, stretch, easy-care or shape-retaining. Cotton-elastane jersey suits fitted tops because it stretches, and polyester/cotton suits durable jackets and joggers.
Aesthetic appeal: explain how colour, line, balance and emphasis work together, and how the outfit suits the wearer and the occasion.
The elements are the visual building blocks of a garment, and each can be changed to alter the look of the outfit. There are five: line, shape, colour, texture and pattern.

Line: a visible edge or direction in a garment, created by seams, necklines, hemlines, trims, pleats, fastenings and pattern. Where the eye is led along a line, the garment seems to go in that direction.
Shape: the outline of a garment or of an area within it, such as a neckline, sleeve or pocket. The outline of the whole garment is its silhouette.

Colour: hue (the actual colour), tone (how light or dark it is) and intensity (how bright or dull it is). Warm colours such as red and orange appear to advance, while cool colours such as blue and green appear to recede.
Colour schemes can be monochrome or tonal (one colour in different shades), contrasting or complementary. Colour should also suit the wearer's skin, hair and eye tones.
Texture: the surface quality of a fabric, which can be smooth, rough, shiny or matt, and which can be seen or felt.
Pattern: the repetition of line, shape or colour over a surface, such as stripes, checks, herringbone, zig-zag, polka dots, florals or geometric prints.
Because the eye follows lines, the direction of the lines in a garment changes how tall, wide or soft the wearer appears. Designers use this to flatter the figure.
Vertical lines give the impression of length, so they make the figure look slimmer and taller.
Horizontal lines draw the eye across the body, which makes the figure look wider and shorter.
Diagonal lines add contrast and movement, and they lead the eye across the garment.
Curved lines soften an outfit and add a feminine feel, such as the curve of a rounded neckline.
A princess seam runs from the shoulder or armhole to the hem. It shapes the garment to the body without a waist seam, and the long unbroken line also helps the wearer look taller.
Colour and texture change how much light a garment reflects or absorbs, and that changes how big the wearer appears. Remember that these are effects on appearance only.
Dark colours appear to reduce the size of the figure because they absorb light, while light and bright colours appear to enlarge it. Dark navy and black also define and slim the silhouette.
One colour worn from head to toe, or tonal shades of one colour, creates a longer, unbroken line, so the figure looks taller. Tonal shades also add depth.
Contrasting or complementary colours at the top and bottom divide the outfit and can balance the shape of the figure, for example when the shoulders and hips are different widths.
Shiny fabrics reflect light and increase the apparent size of the figure, while matt fabrics absorb light and reduce it.
Rough, thick or heavily textured fabrics look bulkier, while smooth fabrics give a neater, more streamlined finish.
Pattern and shape work in the same way as line and colour: they decide where the eye goes and how wide or narrow the figure looks.
Small patterns suit small figures, and a larger figure can carry a large pattern well.
Vertical stripes add height, and horizontal stripes add width and draw attention to the middle of the figure.
A patterned area draws the eye to the place where it is worn, for example near the face or neckline for the upper body or at the hem.
Narrow rectangular shapes slim the figure, while triangular or A-line shapes widen the hem or shoulders and so can balance the hips or shoulders.
A fitted bodice with a full skirt gives an hourglass shape, and a fitted top with straight trousers gives a streamlined shape.
The principles describe how the elements are arranged to create a unified garment. There are five: proportion, balance, emphasis, harmony and rhythm.

Proportion: the relationship between the sizes of the parts of a garment, to each other and to the wearer, such as pockets sized to the garment, a collar sized to the neckline, or jacket length to skirt length.
Balance: an even distribution of visual weight. It can be vertical, symmetrical (both sides match) or asymmetrical (the sides differ but still feel even).

Emphasis: a centre of interest that draws the eye to one area, created by a brooch, contrasting trim, a belt, a bright accessory, a bold hemline or a neckline. There should be only one centre of emphasis in an outfit.
Harmony (unity): the sense that all parts of a design work together and complement one another, for example colours, fabrics and style that suit each other, or one colour repeated.
Rhythm or repetition: the repeated use of a colour, line or shape, such as a repeated button or stripe, which moves the eye through the garment.
Diagram: when asked to sketch an outfit, label the elements and principles used, such as line, shape, proportion, harmony and emphasis.

Choosing the elements well lets a wearer look taller, slimmer or better balanced, and draw attention to a feature or away from one. This is the use of the elements that exam questions ask about directly.

To look taller or slimmer, use vertical lines, one colour head to toe or tonal shades, dark colours such as navy and black that absorb light, V-necks, princess seams, a single long line from shoulder to hem and narrow shapes.
To balance or add width, use horizontal stripes, light or bright colours and bulky textures. Contrasting top and bottom colours balance the shoulders and hips.
To draw attention to a feature, put pattern or a bright colour near it, such as near the face for the upper body, or use a belt to define the waist.
To draw attention away from an area, wear dark colour over it, because dark colours appear to reduce size.
Colour also flatters the wearer's hair, eyes and skin; for example, blues can brighten the complexion.
Shape, fit and proportion matter too: choose lines that suit the figure. A short jacket with slim trousers lengthens the leg line.
The way a garment is made creates its line, shape and emphasis. Here the focus is on the effect of each feature on the design.
Seams join the parts of a garment, and their placement creates line and can add shaping to the body.
Darts remove excess fabric to shape a garment around the bust, waist or hips. Pressing defines the darts.
Princess seams shape the garment without a waist seam.
Pleats, tucks and gathers add fullness and movement, and are used at the waist, sleeve or skirt, where they can add visual interest.
Pockets, collars, buttons, trims and fastenings add line and emphasis, and they must be positioned in proportion to the garment.
Fabric choice affects the finished design: crisp fabrics hold a shape, as in tailoring, while soft fabrics drape. The fabric's texture and pattern must also suit the design lines.
Design and colour can be applied to fabric by dyeing, screen, roller, stencil or transfer printing, embroidery and appliqué (fabric shapes stitched on).
A garment is evaluated against three criteria: how well its design serves its function, its comfort and its aesthetic appeal. Examiners often set these as headings for an outfit shown in a picture.

Function: the garment must suit the purpose, activity, climate, weather and occasion it is intended for, such as freedom of movement for sport. Durability, easy care, useful pockets and fastenings that work also count.
Comfort: the fabric (soft, absorbent, breathable or stretch), fit and ease of movement, weight, versatility in different weather and footwear determine whether the wearer is comfortable.
Aesthetic appeal: the colour scheme, line, shape, texture, proportion, balance and emphasis, and any accessories, must work together to produce an attractive and pleasing overall look.
A well-designed garment shows a clear relationship between its design features and the function they serve, for example a drawcord hood, reflective trim or a zip opening.
Using colour and design to flatter the body: choose colours and lines that emphasise the wearer's best features and balance any areas they wish to de-emphasise.
Other headings that appear are shape, proportion, design features, current fashion trend, lifestyle, cost, care and suitability for the occasion.
Method: for each heading make a point from the picture, then give the reason, such as the fabric, cut or colour.

Making a garment well starts long before the first cut. The design process is a fixed sequence of seven stages that takes you from the brief (the task you are set) to a finished garment that has been judged against that brief.
1. Define and analyse the brief: identify who the garment is for, its purpose, the occasion, the budget and any constraints, so you know exactly what the garment must achieve.
2. Investigate and research: gather ideas from magazines, fabric samples, pattern books and observation of current trends, so your design is informed rather than guessed.
3. Generate possible ideas: sketch several designs, varying line, shape, colour and pattern, so you have real choices to compare.
4. Present the ideas: a labelled fashion sketch and a short written description show the chosen design features and why that design was chosen.
5. Refine the design: adjust the chosen design, the fabric and the trimmings (the decorative extras) until they meet the brief.
6. Implement: plan the work, select fabric and pattern, cut, construct and finish the garment.
7. Evaluate: assess the finished garment against the brief for fit, finish, comfort, function and appearance, and note improvements for next time.

The design specification is a list of what the garment must be and do: the wearer, its use, fabric needs, size and fit, care, cost, time and key features. It turns the brief into a checklist you can design and evaluate against.
A design has to be communicated before it is made. A fashion sketch shows what the garment will look like, and a written description spells out the details a sketch cannot.
A fashion sketch shows the garment's line (the direction of its seams and edges), shape, proportion (how the parts relate in size) and harmony, and it can show colour and fabric.
The front view and, where needed, the back view show the design features, and the sketch must label them so the maker can see what is intended.
The written description covers colour, design, line, proportion, shape, pockets, seams, neckline, sleeves, fabric and finishes, and accessories.
Each design feature named in the description must be visible in the sketch, so the two match and nothing in the description is left unexplained.
Diagram: a labelled front-view fashion sketch, with the features (neckline, sleeves, pockets, seams, fabric) labelled.

The fabric decides how a garment looks, hangs and wears, so it must suit both the purpose and the design. Fabric tests help you decide, and the notions (the small items used to make up a garment) must suit the fabric too.
Fabric is chosen for its suitability to the purpose: its absorbency, shrinkage, water repellence and crease recovery. Tests on these properties inform the choice.
A fabric test sample is washed and dried to check shrinkage before cutting, so the finished garment still fits after laundering.

Fabric choice must match the design: a soft drape suits a flowing skirt, while a crisp fabric holds the shape of a tailored jacket. Stretch suits fitted or sportswear, and easy-care fabric suits everyday wear.
The fabric must also fit the wearer's budget.
Notions such as zips, buttons, interfacing, lining, thread, elastic and trims should be chosen to match the fabric's weight, care needs and colour.
Interfacing (a layer sewn or fused inside to stiffen the fabric) gives body and support at collars, cuffs, waistbands and buttonholes, so these areas keep their shape.

A commercial pattern is a full-scale tissue paper pattern sold in a sealed envelope. Choosing the right one, and reading what is on the envelope, saves money and mistakes. This applies at both levels.
Choose by skill level: a beginner needs a simple pattern with few darts and seams, and a pattern from an easy-sew range (a range of simple patterns) where one is offered.
Also choose by the design and purpose, by the buyer's preference, by the availability of suitable fabric, and by cost and the value it offers for the number of garments it can make.
Choose the size from body measurements: skirts and trousers are sized by hip measurement; dresses, shirts, coats and jackets are sized by bust or chest measurement. Waist is not the sizing measure.
The envelope gives the standard body measurements and the finished measurements of the garment, which show how much ease (room to move) the garment has.
The envelope lists the fabric quantity needed for each size and style, which stops you over- or under-buying, and whether the fabric should be plaid or diagonal-matched.
The envelope lists the notions needed, such as buttons, zips, interfacing, lining and trimmings, and the number of pattern pieces, so you can buy everything at once.
The envelope shows front and back views and suitable fabrics, which helps you avoid an unsuitable fabric, and it may include advice on the layout and construction order. It also gives the size range.

Pattern size is chosen from your measurements, so they must be accurate. Take them over light clothing, with the tape level and comfortably snug, not pulled tight, then compare them with the pattern's measurement chart to choose the size.
Bust or chest: measure around the fullest part of the bust or the chest.
Waist: measure around the natural waistline, with the tape held comfortably, not pulled tight.
Hips: measure around the widest part of the hips, keeping the tape level all the way round, because a tilted tape gives a false reading.
Nape to waist: measure from the most prominent bone at the base of the neck down to the waistline.
Inside leg: measure from the crotch down the inside of the leg to the required hemline. Shoulder is measured where needed.
Where and how the pieces are placed on the fabric decides how the finished garment hangs and looks. Accurate layout and cutting prevent twisted seams and wasted fabric.
Follow the pattern instructions and pin the pattern pieces to the fabric with the fabric folded as directed.
Place the straight grain of the pattern (the grain line marked on each piece) parallel to the selvedge (the finished edge of the fabric), so the garment hangs correctly.
Pattern pieces to be placed on a fold must sit exactly on the fold line, so the garment is symmetrical when opened out.
Take account of the nap, or direction of the pile, and of any pattern or print on the fabric, so that all pieces face the same way. Match checks and stripes at the seams.
Keep the fabric flat while pinning and cutting, and cut accurately around the pattern edges, then transfer the markings.
Diagram: pattern pieces on fabric showing the grain line parallel to the selvedge and a piece placed exactly on the fold.
A plan of work puts the making in the right order so each step prepares the next. Evaluation follows once the garment is finished, as the last step of the design process.
Stage 1: lay out and cut the pattern pieces.
Stage 2: transfer markings and pin and tack (sew with temporary long stitches) the pieces together to check the fit.
Stage 3: machine sew and assemble the garment, joining darts and seams in the order the pattern gives, pressing as you go.
Stage 4: insert fastenings, attach facings and collars, add trimmings and complete the hems and edges.
Stage 5: press the seams and the finished garment, which removes creases and sets the shape, then evaluate the fit and finish and note any changes needed.
Pressing removes creases, defines darts, flattens seams and prevents puckering, so the garment looks professional.
Careful finishing means neatening seam allowances, clipping curves and trimming corners, so edges lie flat and do not fray.
A commercial pattern is made for a standard figure, so it is often changed to suit a particular person. Check any modification on the pattern before cutting.
A pattern is modified when the buyer's measurements differ from the size chosen, when the design needs a different length or width, or for a different style or preference.
Lengthen a pattern: cut through the alteration lines, spread the pieces, insert tissue paper and redraw the seam and fitting lines.
Shorten a pattern: fold along one of the alteration lines by half the amount to be removed, and redraw the seam and fitting lines.
Alteration lines are marked on the pattern, showing where the length can be changed.
Similar adjustments can change the width of the waist, hip, bust or sleeve by folding along the marked lines or cutting them.
Check the modification on the pattern, matching seams and keeping the grain line, before cutting the fabric.
Elective 2 includes coursework in which you design and make a garment. These are the facts of the 2027 brief and how it is marked.
The coursework is worth 100 marks, or 10 per cent of the total marks: a design folder (25 marks) and a garment (75 marks).
The 2027 brief: design and sketch an outfit suitable for a young person to wear on holiday, expressing values, interests and personality; the outfit may be knitted, crocheted or machine stitched.
The candidate sets out the design specifications for the outfit, then makes and evaluates one garment from it.
The garment must include two of three processes: buttons and buttonholes; darts or shaping; a pocket.

Design folder marks: analysis and research 15, implementation 4, evaluation 6. The folder covers requirements, constraints, theme, sketches and justification, then the work sequence, then evaluation of the garment against the brief.
Garment marks: design aspects 15, skills and processes 50, finish 10.
The work must be the candidate's own, done under the teacher's supervision, with every source referenced, including any AI-generated material; the completion date is 6 April 2027.
The garment must include two of three processes: buttons and buttonholes, darts or shaping, and a pocket. Each is made in a set order, and each is reinforced where it takes strain.

Buttonholes: mark the position and length (the button's diameter plus its thickness) on the right front for a woman's garment (left for men), at right angles to the edge for a horizontal hole, then reinforce with interfacing.
Buttonholes are worked by machine with a buttonhole foot or by hand with buttonhole stitch, and cut the opening last, without cutting the stitching.

Buttons: sew on to match the buttonholes, marked through the buttonhole position, with a thread shank (a short stem of thread) so the fastened layers lie flat; reinforce on fine or loosely woven fabric.

Darts (folded wedges that shape fabric to the body): transfer the dart markings from the pattern with tailor's chalk or tacking, fold right sides together matching the marks, stitch from the wide end to the point, and tie off or backstitch at the point.
Press bust and waist darts flat, then towards the centre or downward; the direction depends on the dart type and fabric.
Other shaping: gathers, pleats, tucks, princess seams and elastic also shape a garment to the body.
Patch pocket: mark the position, neaten and turn down the top edge as a facing, press under the seam allowances, and topstitch to the garment, reinforcing the top corners so they do not tear.
In-seam pocket: the pocket bag is stitched into a side seam so the opening is hidden.
Each process is interfaced or reinforced where it takes strain, and is pressed as it is made.

The clothing and textile industries cover the design, manufacture, distribution and sale of clothing, textiles and accessories. Each stage passes the product on towards the consumer, and the whole sector is market-driven, so it depends on skill, imagination and creativity to keep up with what customers want.

The parts of the industry are designers, who create ranges (collections of garments), manufacturers of clothing and of textiles, distributors, and retailers such as shops, department stores and online sellers.
Manufacturers produce menswear, womenswear, children's wear, knitwear, sportswear, accessories, lingerie and footwear, so the industry covers almost everything people wear.
Designers create ranges that are made by manufacturers and sold through their own shops or through retailers.
Distributors and retailers move the finished goods from the factory to the consumer, through shops, department stores and online sales.
The industries provide employment in manufacture, distribution and sales, and they earn export income because Irish designers sell their work abroad.
Irish designers sell under their own label and also produce ranges for high street stores, which gives their designs a much wider customer base.

Local Enterprise Offices (the county and city enterprise support bodies that replaced the Enterprise Boards in 2014) give small firms and designers advice, training and grants, so they can grow their businesses.

A cottage or home-based industry is a business run in or near a person's home, often by one or a few people making a product by hand and selling to craft shops or directly to customers. Small firms like these are especially important in rural areas.
Start-up costs are low, so a business can be set up without a large investment in premises or machinery.
The work can be fitted around family life, which suits people who cannot work fixed hours.
Cottage industries provide employment in rural areas and so help keep people in their communities.
Some work is subcontracted (given out by a larger business) to local people who do it at home, for example Aran knitting.
They keep traditional skills and crafts alive, such as hand-knitting, weaving, lace-making and crochet.
Small businesses can develop distinctive products that stand out from mass-produced clothing, and a successful one can grow into a larger business.
Hobbies can turn into businesses, especially when the economy is poor and people look for another source of income.
Cottage industries are often promoted through craft shops and design centres, which sell the work of makers directly to the public.
Their weaknesses are small scale, limited marketing and finance, and an income that can be low.
Knitting, stitching and similar crafts have become popular again. Several different reasons explain why, and an exam answer needs a few of them.
Socialising: people join knitting and stitching clubs to meet others.
Learning traditional skills, which many people want to pass on or take up for the first time.
Saving money, because making or mending an item yourself can cost less than buying it.
More free time, which gives people the chance to take up a craft.
Start-up businesses, because a craft can be turned into a small business with little money.
A desire for original items that are not mass-produced.
The social influence of celebrities who knit or wear handmade items.
Irish designers draw on traditional crafts for ideas and materials. This links modern fashion to Irish heritage and gives Irish design a recognisable identity.
Hand-knitting and hand-weaving inspire coats and coatigans (a long knitted jacket) that use Aran stitches, the textured stitches of Aran knitting.
Irish linen, woven from flax, is used for products ranging from light tops and skirts to heavy coats and jackets.
Lace and crochet work feature in wedding dresses and other occasion wear.
Hand-weaving produces textured fabrics that designers use in contemporary clothing.
Tweed, Aran sweaters and hand-weaving are recognised Irish products that link design to Irish heritage.
These traditional crafts contribute to the identity of Irish design, which designers use to market Irish fashion abroad.
John Rocha used Irish fabrics and Celtic influence to create unique designs.
Irish designers show that fashion can be a successful business in Ireland. Learn one or two designers well enough to name them and give two or three points about their work.
John Rocha and Simone Rocha are Irish designers whose work is sold internationally, and John Rocha uses Irish fabrics and Celtic influence in his designs.
Philip Treacy is a contemporary Irish milliner (hat designer) from Ahascragh, County Galway, known internationally for couture hats.

Philip Treacy studied fashion at NCAD in Dublin, then took a master's degree in millinery at the Royal College of Art in London, and he built an international career creating hats for couture, royalty and celebrities.
Lainey Keogh is known for knitwear, and Louise Kennedy is known for detailed work and designed for a previous president.
Other Irish designers include Paul Costelloe, Carolyn Donnelly, Sybil Connolly and Orla Kiely, who is Irish-born.
Irish designers have created clothing and accessories for royalty, celebrities, world leaders and major events.

Designers contribute to the industry by creating employment in manufacture, distribution and sales, exporting menswear, womenswear, children's wear, knitwear and accessories, and promoting Irish design at home and abroad.
Irish fashion needs publicity and support to reach customers at home and abroad. Several routes help a designer or maker become known.
Local Enterprise Offices support small designers and makers with advice, training and grants.
Shops and design centres sell Irish design, for example Kilkenny Design Centre, a craft and design centre in Castle Yard, Kilkenny.
Designers produce ranges for high street stores, so their work reaches a wide public.
Irish designers show their collections at fashion weeks and international fashion shows, which gives them exposure to buyers and the press.
Press coverage and public figures wearing Irish designers' clothing create publicity for the designers.
Fashion blogs and social media promote Irish designers to a wide audience at home and abroad.
The Irish clothing and textile industries face strong pressures. Most of them come from competition on price and from the small size of the home market.
Imports made in low-wage countries with cheaper and faster labour mean Irish producers find it hard to compete on price.
Discount stores sell clothing at low prices in high volumes, which pressures Irish firms that make smaller runs of higher-quality garments.
The industry is labour-intensive (it needs many workers), so high labour costs for skilled workers push up the price of Irish goods.
A global recession leaves people with less disposable income to spend on clothes.
A small home market limits the number of customers available to Irish designers, so growth depends on export sales.
Firms must adapt to new shopping patterns such as online and mobile shopping, and keep up with trends and technology.
Small firms and cottage industries have limited funds for marketing, equipment and expansion.
A shortage of skilled workers means that keeping them and training new ones is a continuing challenge for manufacturers.
The industries offer jobs for creative, technical, presentation and retail talents. Exams ask you to name one career and give details of it, so know what each person does.
Creative careers include fashion designer (creates the range), milliner (makes hats), stylist and fashion journalist or writer.
Technical careers include tailor, machinist (sews garments in a factory), clothing manufacturer, factory worker and fashion buyer.
Presentation careers include model and photographer, and fashion advertising and blogging.
Retail careers include retail sales assistant.
To answer a career question, name one career and give two details, such as what the person does, the skills or qualities needed, where they work, and the training route.

A settlement pattern is the way a population is spread across the land, in scattered rural homes and farms, villages, towns and cities. Over the last century Ireland's pattern shifted towards towns and cities, so a rising share of the population lives in urban areas while the countryside loses people.
Rural means countryside, farms and small villages; urban means towns and cities, where jobs, colleges and services are concentrated.
Urbanisation is the growth in the proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities. It is about a rising share, not just population growth.

Rural depopulation is the fall in the number of people living in the countryside, through migration to towns or abroad. Moving within Ireland is internal migration, while leaving the country is emigration; both can cause rural decline.
Rural depopulation is most marked in remote areas and where farm employment has fallen, because larger and mechanised farms need fewer workers.
Young adults are the group most likely to leave rural areas for education and first jobs, so many villages are left with an older population and fewer children.
Rural areas that lose population also lose local services such as post offices, Garda stations and schools, which makes rural life less attractive.

The movement is not one-way or uniform. Towns, commuter belts (the areas around cities where people live and travel to work) and some rural areas have grown while remote areas lost people, so the overall picture is mixed.
People move to towns and cities because that is where most opportunities are. Examiners want each reason explained, so give the reason and then say why it draws people.

Employment: towns and cities contain most of the jobs in manufacturing, services and office work. Larger, mechanised farms need fewer workers, so farm jobs fell, and the children of small farms could not all inherit land.
Education: third-level colleges and specialist schools and courses are concentrated in urban centres, so many young people move for college and do not return.
Services and infrastructure: hospitals, shops, public transport, entertainment, leisure facilities and fast broadband are more available, and better, in towns and cities.
Housing: towns offer a wider choice of rented and owned accommodation, including apartments for people without land.
Family and social ties: moving closer to friends, relatives, a partner or a partner's workplace draws many people into towns, and towns offer a bigger social life for young adults.
Young adults are the group most likely to leave, so the countryside is left with an older population and fewer children.
Living in a town or city changes how a family spends its time, money and support. There are gains and losses, and a good answer gives both.
Urban families have easier access to childcare, schools, health care, shops and entertainment, which can improve quality of life.
A wider choice of jobs means both parents can more easily find work, and there are more leisure facilities for the family to use.
Long commutes from suburbs to city workplaces reduce the time parents spend at home and add pressure to family routines.

High housing costs and high rents (because heavy demand meets limited housing) can delay marriage and the birth of children until young couples can afford a home, squeeze family budgets and cause overcrowding.
Urban neighbourhoods can face congestion, noise and air pollution, and crime and antisocial behaviour in some areas.
Families in cities are often farther from grandparents and extended family, so there is less daily childcare and practical help.
There is often less community spirit in cities, with neighbours who do not know each other, so families have less informal support.

When people leave the countryside, the families who stay feel it in their relationships and in the services they depend on. The loss feeds on itself, because fewer people mean fewer services, which makes the area less attractive to the next generation.
Older people living alone in rural areas can become isolated and lonely when younger family members move away, because fewer relatives are nearby for daily support.
Children in depopulated areas may attend smaller schools with fewer classmates, and grandparents are less available for childcare.
Teams and clubs struggle to field players, so children have fewer chances to take part in local activities.
Rural decline can cause whole family units to emigrate, weakening the local network of family and neighbourly support.

Withdrawal of services such as shops, post offices, banks, public transport, Garda stations and schools makes daily life harder for families who remain in the countryside. With fewer customers these services close, which makes the area less attractive to the next generation, a cycle of decline.
Family farms may have no heir, because the younger generation has moved away.
There are positives for those who stay: lower housing costs, a strong sense of community, lower crime and pollution, more space and safer play for children, and a slower pace of life.

Rural depopulation is not the whole story, because some rural areas have gained people. Better connections and lower costs have made country living workable for families who would once have had to move to a town.
Better roads and transport let people live in the country and commute to work in towns and cities.
Cheaper housing and living costs make the countryside attractive to families, especially compared with high urban rents.
Lower crime and pollution make rural areas appealing places to raise children.
Improved local services, leisure and community facilities mean country life no longer means going without.
Broadband and working from home allow people to keep a job in a town or city while living in the countryside.
Rural resettlement and local-authority housing moves have brought families into some rural areas.

Governments and state agencies have used job creation and infrastructure to slow rural depopulation. People stay where they can earn a living and where services remain, so most initiatives aim to create local jobs or make country living practical.
Redeployment (decentralisation) of government departments and state agencies to rural and regional towns creates public-sector jobs outside the cities and Dublin.
Rural resettlement schemes help families, including city families, move to and settle in the countryside, which helps keep rural communities viable and schools and services open.
IDA Ireland is the agency responsible for attracting investment from overseas companies. It encourages foreign firms to locate in regional towns as well as the cities, creating jobs.
Enterprise Ireland helps Irish firms to start, grow and export, including firms outside Dublin, so jobs are created locally.

Local Enterprise Offices, one in each local authority area, give advice, mentoring, training and small grants to micro and small businesses. Local people can then create their own jobs, for example in cottage industries, craft and food businesses and tourism.
Údarás na Gaeltachta is the regional authority responsible for the economic, social and cultural development of the Gaeltacht areas, encouraging enterprise and jobs there.
LEADER is the EU-funded rural development programme that supports community-led local projects such as village renewal, tourism and enterprise.

Investment in roads, public transport, electricity and telecommunications, especially broadband (the National Broadband Plan, which aims to bring high-speed broadband to areas the market did not serve), makes rural living and remote or hybrid working practical, and remote-working hubs in towns support this.
Community employment and training programmes, for example in childcare, horticulture and caring, give rural people skills and work experience.
A good way to understand settlement change is to compare family life a hundred years ago with today, and to ask someone who lived through it.
Compare who lived on the land, the size of families, school attendance and leisure then and now.
Interview an older relative or community member about when people left the area, why they left, and what changed.

The standard working week has shortened over the last century, and regular overtime has become less common for many workers. This has changed how families divide their time, and the law now sets limits on how much an employee can be asked to work.
Working hours fell as the standard working week was shortened and regular overtime (extra paid hours beyond the normal week) became less common for many workers.

The Organisation of Working Time Act 1997 sets an average maximum working week of 48 hours, a minimum daily rest period, rest breaks during the working day, a weekly rest period, paid annual leave and public holiday entitlements.
Because these limits are set by Irish law, an employee cannot lawfully be required to work beyond them, which protects workers' health and their time with their families.

Part-time and flexible hours let some parents work around school hours and be at home earlier in the day. Other flexible arrangements include job-sharing, flexitime, term-time working, compressed hours, and remote and hybrid working.
The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 gives employees a right to request flexible and remote working, for example so they can care for a child or relative.
Shift work and extended opening hours in retail and services mean that some family members work evenings or weekends, so families must plan time together.

Shorter hours give families more time for shared meals, homework, household tasks and outings, and mean more time at home to care for children and for older relatives. They also bring a better work-life balance and less stress.
Not every effect is positive: long commuting and irregular hours cut time together, and technology means work can follow people home, for example emails received out of hours.
Shorter working hours and easier housework left families with more free time than earlier generations had. That free time changed what families do together, with benefits and some drawbacks.
Paid annual leave gives employees a set number of holiday weeks each year, which made family holidays a regular feature of family life.
Labour-saving appliances such as washing machines, dishwashers and microwaves, and convenience foods, cut the time spent on housework and cooking, releasing time for leisure.
Weekends became the main block of free time for most workers and their families.
Rising household incomes increased spending on leisure, including cinema, sport, holidays, travel and eating out.
Home entertainment such as television, radio, computers, the internet, streaming and gaming changed how families spend evenings, often indoors.
Community sport and clubs, such as GAA, soccer, swimming and dance, give children and parents structured leisure outside the home.
Shared activities strengthen family relationships and communication, support children's physical, social and emotional development, and relaxation reduces stress.
Leisure also has downsides: screen-based leisure can separate family members, and because leisure costs money, some families cannot afford it.
As the economy became more productive, pay rose, and the law now protects the lowest earners. Higher pay changes what a family can afford.

Real pay (pay after allowing for price rises) rose as productivity and living standards increased, giving families more disposable income to save, buy a home, and pay for education, holidays and leisure.
The National Minimum Wage Act 2000 sets a legal minimum hourly rate of pay, protecting low-paid workers and their families.
The Payment of Wages Act 1991 sets the rules on how wages must be paid and on what deductions an employer may make.
Higher incomes let families move to larger or better housing, buy household goods and build savings, and financial security reduces stress and arguments in the home.
Better pay and the cost of housing mean many families now need two incomes, which links to the growth in women's paid work.
Employees can now take time off for children, illness and holidays without losing all of their income.
Statutory paid annual leave means every employee is entitled to paid holidays, which is why family holidays became regular.
Maternity leave and maternity benefit come under the Maternity Protection Acts 1994 and 2004, so a mother can take time off for childbirth without losing all of her income.
Paternity leave comes under the Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016 and lasts two weeks, so a father can be at home after the birth.

Parental leave under the Parental Leave Act 1998 is unpaid time off to care for a child, while Parent's Leave and Benefit under the Parent's Leave and Benefit Act 2019 gives each parent leave with a benefit payment.
Statutory sick leave under the Sick Leave Act 2022 lets employees take paid time off for illness: 3 days in 2023, 5 in 2024, 7 in 2025 and 10 days a year from 2026.
Time off for children and illness lets parents care for their families without losing all their income.
Alongside pay and leave, employees gained legal protection against unsafe workplaces and unfair treatment, and a way to bargain together.
Employees are entitled to written terms of employment, so both sides know the job, pay and conditions.
The Unfair Dismissals Acts protect employees from being dismissed without a fair reason, and redundancy payments compensate workers whose jobs are cut.

The Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 requires employers to provide a safe workplace and reduce the risk of workplace injury, and the Health and Safety Authority enforces it. Healthier, safer work lowers the risk of injury that would cut family income.

Grievance and disciplinary procedures give employees a route to challenge poor treatment or unfair conditions, and complaints can be taken to the Workplace Relations Commission, which hears employment complaints.
The Protection of Young Persons (Employment) Act 1996 is a law that protects young workers.

Trade unions negotiate pay and conditions on behalf of their members through collective agreements (agreements between unions and employers covering a group of workers). ICTU is the national body for Irish trade unions.
Some of the biggest gains for families are not in the weekly pay packet but in the benefits that come with a job.
Occupational pension schemes (pensions arranged through an employer) provide retirement income, reducing the need for adult children to support retired parents.
The My Future Fund scheme began on 1 January 2026 and automatically enrols employees aged 23 to 60 who earn over EUR 20,000, so more workers build up a pension.
In My Future Fund the employee, the employer and the State all contribute, which means the worker does not carry the whole cost.
Other benefits of a job can include canteens, health insurance, bonuses, training and career breaks.
Taken together, shorter hours, more leisure and better pay and conditions have changed family life, with benefits and strains.
Higher incomes let families move to larger or better housing and buy household goods.
Reduced hours and more leisure can strengthen family relationships through shared activities.
Long hours or shift work can cause tiredness and strain, and reduce time spent with children.
When both parents work full-time, there may be less time for family meals and supervision of children.
Comparing family life a hundred years ago with today shows the changes in work directly. An interview with an older relative gives first-hand evidence.
Interview an older relative about the hours worked each week, the holidays taken each year and the leisure activities they had as a young adult.
Record the same three measures for a present-day family and note the differences in working hours, holidays and leisure.
Compare the two answers to show how changes in work have altered who has time for leisure and when it is taken.

Access to education has widened across generations, so more children and adults now complete school and continue into further study. A hundred years ago many children left school at primary level, and second-level and university education were mainly for those who could pay.
Today every child has free primary and second-level education and a wide choice of routes after school, so schooling no longer depends on what a family can afford.

Free second-level education was announced in 1966 by the Minister for Education, Donogh O'Malley, and has been in effect since 1967. It removed the fees that had kept many children from completing school.
School attendance is compulsory from age 6 to 16, or until three years of second-level education have been completed (Education (Welfare) Act 2000).

Third-level tuition fees for eligible full-time undergraduates were abolished from 1996 (the free fees initiative), widening access to colleges and universities. A student contribution (registration charge) remains.
Grants to meet living and other costs at third level are paid by SUSI (Student Universal Support Ireland) and are based on means, so students from lower-income families receive more help.

The free pre-school programme, the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) programme, began in 2010 and now provides two years of free pre-school before primary school, for children of the eligible age.
Post Leaving Certificate (PLC) courses, further education, apprenticeships and adult and community education give adults a second route to qualifications for work or further study.

Free fees alone do not keep every child in school. Further supports help pupils who need extra help, who are at risk of leaving early, who come from disadvantaged areas, or who want a different route.
Special needs assistants and resource teaching, for example, support pupils with special educational needs within mainstream classes, so these children can learn alongside their classmates.
The School Completion Programme targets students at risk of leaving school early, through extra supports such as homework and out-of-school activities, which helps them stay on to finish.
The DEIS programme (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools) supports schools in disadvantaged areas, because pupils there face more barriers to staying in school.
Leaving Certificate Applied is a modular, practical programme assessed over two years, so it suits students who learn by doing, preparing students for work and adult life.

Transition Year and Youthreach offer practical, work-based and personal development learning to young people in different circumstances. Youthreach is for early school leavers, so it gives them a second chance.
The Back to Education Allowance is an income support, not a course. It helps people on certain social welfare payments to take approved courses at second or third level.

The Higher Education Access Route, HEAR, improves third-level access for socially disadvantaged students, and the Disability Access Route to Education, DARE, does the same for students with disabilities.
Education changes what parents can do for their children and what a family can earn. Most effects are positive, but there are costs as well.
Better-educated parents are better able to help with homework and to encourage children's progress and achievement.
Educational attainment affects job prospects and earnings, so better qualifications raise the family's standard of living.
Women's education has increased their financial independence and their participation in paid employment, because qualifications open up better-paid jobs.
Adult education lets parents return to work after raising children, adding a second income to the household.
As education widens choices, families tend to be smaller and people marry later, and there is less poverty across generations.
Negative effects include the cost of books, uniforms, transport and college living away from home, and exam pressure on students.
Children may leave the area for college or work.

Social welfare is income support from the State, through the Department of Social Protection, to people who cannot earn enough: those who are unemployed, ill or disabled, retired, widowed, parenting alone, caring for others or on low pay. It is funded from taxes and PRSI (pay-related social insurance) contributions.

Social insurance payments (contributory) depend on PRSI contributions paid while working and on a record of those contributions. Examples are Jobseeker's Benefit, the contributory State pension and maternity benefit.

Social assistance payments (non-contributory) are means-tested, meaning they depend on an assessment of household income and savings, so they are targeted at households in need and paid from taxation.

Examples of means-tested payments are Jobseeker's Allowance, the non-contributory State pension, Supplementary Welfare Allowance, One-Parent Family Payment, Disability Allowance and Carer's Allowance.
Universal payments are paid to everyone in a category regardless of income. Child Benefit is the main example, paid for each child regardless of parental income.
Several payments are aimed at families with children, because children are costly and parents with the main responsibility for them may have low or interrupted incomes.
Child Benefit is a monthly payment for each child, paid up to age 16, or up to 18 where the child is in full-time education. It is universal. It was called Children's Allowance until it was renamed.
The Working Family Payment (formerly Family Income Supplement) supports employees on low pay who have children, making work more worthwhile.
One-Parent Family Payment supports parents who have the main responsibility for children on their own.
The Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance is paid once a year, means-tested, to help families on low incomes meet the cost of school clothing.
Maternity, paternity and parent's benefits support workers who take leave to care for a child, so they do not lose all income while away.
Medical cards (and GP visit cards) give eligible families free GP visits and free or low-cost prescribed medicines. They depend on means or age.
Other supports are the Fuel Allowance, the Household Benefits Package and the free travel pass for older people.
Welfare payments give families a safety net, but they also have drawbacks and a cost. A good answer weighs both.
Welfare payments reduce child poverty by giving families a regular income when a parent is out of work, ill or on low pay, so children can stay in school and have more activities.
Old age pensions give older people financial independence, so they do not depend on their adult children.
Carer's payments allow a family member to care for an elderly or disabled relative at home, for example without giving up all income.
Lone-parent families can support their children because of payments such as One-Parent Family Payment, which replace part of a second income.
