Conditions attached to payments, such as job-seeking and activation requirements for jobseekers, means tests and contribution records, aim to avoid long-term dependence on welfare.
Criticisms are that payments can be low relative to living costs, that people can become dependent on welfare, and that extra earnings can reduce payments, a trap called the poverty trap.
Critics argue that welfare can discourage people from taking up low-paid work, which is why work incentives form part of many schemes.
Some people feel stigma in claiming, and welfare is a cost to taxpayers because it is funded from taxes and PRSI.
Comparing who attended school a hundred years ago with today shows how education has changed within a family's own history.
Ask an older relative how many years they attended school, how many children were in their class and whether they stayed on after the minimum school-leaving age.
Record the same details for a present-day young person and compare the answers.
Note which supports, such as special needs assistants, the School Completion Programme and free pre-school, were not available to the older relative.

A few generations ago, marriage was expected of everyone and was the only accepted basis for living together and raising a family. Pressure from society, family and the Church has fallen, so people now treat marriage as a choice.
Couples now tend to marry later, often after completing their education and establishing a career. Some do not marry at all, because social, family and Church pressure to marry young has fallen.
Cohabitation, living together without being married, has become common and is widely accepted, because marriage is no longer seen as the only acceptable basis for a couple's life together.
Marriage is no longer seen as the only acceptable basis for a family, so many children are born to parents who are not married.
Legislation recognises cohabiting couples through the Civil Partnership and Certain Rights and Obligations of Cohabitants Act 2010. Cohabitation still gives fewer legal rights than marriage.
Children born outside marriage are no longer treated differently in law, under the Status of Children Act 1987. In this way the law reflected, and helped to change, attitudes.
The 2015 marriage referendum allowed same-sex couples to marry, under the Marriage Act 2015, reflecting wider acceptance of different types of family.
Divorce only became possible in Ireland after the 1995 referendum. Attitudes changed, and the law followed, so married couples now have two legal routes when a marriage breaks down.

Divorce became legal in Ireland after a referendum in 1995 (carried narrowly, after an earlier referendum in 1986 had rejected divorce). The Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 sets out the conditions for granting one.

Under that Act, a divorce may be granted only where three conditions are met. First, the spouses have lived apart for two of the previous three years, a period set by the Family Law Act 2019, in operation from 1 December 2019.
Second, there is no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, meaning the couple are unlikely to get back together.
Third, proper provision has been or will be made for the spouses and dependent children, so that nobody is left without support.
Judicial separation, provided for under the Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989, as amended, allows spouses to live apart under a court order that deals with maintenance and property.
Judicial separation does not end the marriage, so neither spouse can remarry. Divorce does end the marriage.
Changed attitudes to marriage, cohabitation, separation and divorce have changed what families look like and how they feel to live in.
There are more lone-parent, blended (reconstituted, where partners bring children from earlier relationships) and cohabiting families, so family structures show more variety.
Families are smaller and first births come later, because couples marry later and plan when to have children.
There is more family breakdown, but also greater freedom to leave an unhappy or abusive marriage.
Children may live in more than one household when parents separate.
Family relationships are now chosen rather than expected, because people are less bound by duty to follow one set pattern.
There is less stigma (social disapproval) for lone parents than there once was.
Parenting has moved from strict authority towards partnership with children, and from mothers alone towards both parents and wider carers.
Parenting has become more child-centred, with greater emphasis on children's views, rights and wellbeing, open communication and negotiated rules instead of strict obedience.
Children's rights are recognised in the Constitution, through the Thirty-first Amendment (Children) 2012, which inserted Article 42A and was signed into law in 2015.
Physical punishment of children by parents is prohibited by Irish law: the Children First Act 2015 removed the defence of reasonable chastisement, so smacking is no longer lawful discipline.
Attitudes moved towards explaining, praising and setting limits. Child protection is the State's concern, carried out by Tusla, the Child and Family Agency.

Smaller families are now more common, as contraception and family planning let couples choose the number and timing of their children. The cost of rearing children and women's work also play a part, and each child gets more attention and money.

Mothers and fathers increasingly share childcare, and fathers are more involved in caring and housework. Paternity leave (the Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016, two weeks) recognises the father's role.

Parental leave (the Parental Leave Act 1998) allows parents to take unpaid time off work to care for children. Paid Parent's Leave and Benefit (the Parent's Leave and Benefit Act 2019) recognises both parents' role, and some men are the main carers (house husbands).

Grandparents often take on regular childcare, particularly where both parents work outside the home. Paid childcare (childminders, creches and after-school services) and pre-school education are also widely used.
A more open and shared style of parenting brings benefits, but it also puts new pressures on parents and changes the way children fit into the family.
Relationships are closer and more open, and decisions are more equal, because children's views are heard.
Children have greater independence, because they are given more say and more responsibility.
Working parents feel more pressure and guilt, a state sometimes called time poverty (never having enough time for everything).
Childcare costs money, which adds to the strain on family budgets.
There is less respect for traditional authority, because rules are negotiated rather than simply obeyed.
Children may take on more responsibility for chores, or for the care of younger siblings.
Who earned, who cared and who decided used to be settled by gender. Attitudes have shifted towards sharing these jobs, which is the biggest change in everyday family life.

Traditional roles assigned the male as breadwinner (earner) and head of the household, and the female as homemaker and carer, with responsibilities kept largely separate. Children obeyed and helped, and older children minded younger ones.

Egalitarian roles (equal, shared roles) are now more common. Partners share earning, finances, housework, childcare, discipline and decisions, and both partners often work, which is the dual-earner family.
Men take a greater part in housework and childcare, while women take a greater part in paid work and decision-making.
A man taking on the role of house husband or primary carer, and a woman as main earner, are now socially accepted.
The decline in the influence of the Church lessened expectations about marriage, sexuality and parental roles.
Household tasks are shared with children, and older children may look after younger siblings.
Family diversity means that nuclear, extended, lone-parent, blended, cohabiting and same-sex-parent families are all recognised as families.
Shared roles bring clear gains, but they also create new tensions that families have to manage.
Relationships between partners are more equal, because tasks and decisions are shared.
Families have more income when both partners work.
Women gain greater independence, because earning their own money reduces reliance on a partner.
Role overload and role conflict (the strain of balancing work and home duties), time pressure and stress can follow when both partners work and also care for the family.
There can be arguments about sharing tasks, because the old rules about who does what no longer apply.
Some men feel a loss of status, because the breadwinner role is no longer theirs alone.
Attitudes did not change by accident. Several developments in education, law, work and communication made new choices possible and acceptable.
Improved education, particularly for women, has widened choices about careers, marriage and having children.
Contraception and family planning allowed couples to control family size and plan or delay childbearing.
Women's participation in paid work, and equality legislation, gave women financial independence.
The decline in the influence of the Church and of tradition (secularisation) means that marriage, sexuality, cohabitation and divorce are now seen as personal choices.
Urbanisation (growth of towns and cities) and greater mobility loosened the influence of the extended family and the local community.
Media, travel and international influences, and communications technology, introduced new ideas about relationships and family life.
Greater personal freedom and individual choice came to be valued over duty to family or community. Higher living and housing costs now often require two incomes.
Legislation and referendums both reflect and speed up change: a law can follow a shift in attitudes and then help to make the new attitude normal.
Mobile phones, social media and video calls have changed how family members stay in touch and how they spend time together, with gains and losses.
Mobile phones, social media and video calls keep the extended family and emigrants in contact, so distance matters less to family relationships.
These technologies also allow remote working, which can give parents more flexibility.
Screen time can reduce face-to-face time, because family members may spend time together while each looks at a device.
Parents may find it harder to supervise children, because much online activity is private.
Cyberbullying and online safety are concerns for families.
A direct comparison of the past and the present is a good way to see how attitudes have changed.
Compare roles, the number of children and attitudes to marriage a hundred years ago and today.
Interview an older relative about who earned, who cared and who made decisions in their childhood home.

The share of women in paid work has risen steeply since the early 20th century, and the number of married women in work is far higher than in the past. Women's participation in paid work now forms a large part of the workforce. Several changes in education, family life, the economy and the law together explain this.
Education: more girls complete second level and third level, which gives them the qualifications for professional and managerial posts and raises their expectations of a career.
Contraception, smaller families and later marriage: women can plan when to have children and return to work after childbirth, or stay in employment, and they have fewer years of child rearing.

Economic need: the cost of housing, mortgages, rent and education means many families need two incomes, and some couples want a higher standard of living. Lone parents must earn because there is no second income.

Changing attitudes: work outside the home is now accepted for married women and mothers, equal opportunity is expected, and financial independence, job satisfaction and a career valued for its own sake are goals in themselves.

Equality legislation removed barriers: equal pay and equal treatment laws, and maternity leave with protection from dismissal. The marriage bar (the rule that women had to leave public-service jobs on marriage) was removed in 1973.

Childcare and supports: creches, childminders, pre-school and after-school services, and the free pre-school programme make it possible for parents to work outside the home. The National Childcare Scheme subsidises the costs.

Flexible work: part-time work, job-sharing, flexitime, term-time working and remote working help women combine work and family. The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 gives a right to request flexible working.

Labour-saving appliances and convenience foods cut housework time, and the service sector grew, with more jobs in offices, health and education that suit women. Jobs have also become less gender-specific: women work as engineers, doctors and lawyers, and men work as nurses and childminders.

When women move into paid work, the way a household earns money, shares tasks and cares for children changes. Examiners expect both the gains and the pressures, and a few effects reach beyond the family to society.
Dual-earner households (where both partners are in paid work) often have higher household incomes and a higher standard of living, and there is more security if one partner loses a job.
Women gain financial independence and self-esteem, so economic independence also gives them more choice about whether to remain in an unhappy marriage.
Women's employment has changed the division of housework and childcare, so many couples now share these tasks more equally and children see equal roles.

Combining a paid job with most of the housework and childcare creates role overload (too many roles to manage) and time pressure, especially for lone parents and parents of young children. This brings stress, tiredness and sometimes tension about sharing tasks.

The need for childcare means many families rely on grandparents, relatives or paid childminders, and childcare costs are a major expense. Children may be in care for long hours, and there is less time with children and less family time together.
Career moves can require relocation, so women's jobs can influence family decisions about where to live.
Effects on society: a bigger labour force and more tax revenue, smaller families, and more demand for childcare, convenience foods and services.
Laws exist so that women are not paid less or held back at work because of their gender. In Ireland the main law is the Employment Equality Acts 1998 to 2015, which cover every stage of employment.

The Employment Equality Acts 1998 to 2015 prohibit discrimination in employment on nine grounds: gender, civil status, family status, sexual orientation, religion, age, disability, race, and membership of the Traveller community.

They cover recruitment and advertising, access to training and promotion, pay, terms and conditions of work, harassment and dismissal. This means women and men have equal access to benefits linked to work.
Equal pay: men and women must receive equal pay for like work, meaning work that is the same, similar, or of equal value. An employee may claim equal pay on any of the nine grounds.
Equal opportunity: employers cannot refuse to hire, train or promote because of gender or marital status. An exception exists where a gender is a genuine occupational requirement.
Family status ground: this protects employees who are parents of children under 18, or carers of a person with a disability who needs care, against discrimination.

Pregnancy and maternity: the Maternity Protection Acts 1994 and 2004 give the right to maternity leave and protection against dismissal and loss of rights. Dismissal because of pregnancy is unlawful and is also treated as gender discrimination.
Maternity leave is a right to time off with job protection. Maternity benefit, the payment during leave, is a social insurance payment from the State, in most cases not from the employer.
Enforcement: complaints are made to the Workplace Relations Commission, with appeals to the Labour Court. The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission promotes equality and can assist.
Two further laws sit alongside the Employment Equality Acts. One makes pay differences visible and the other covers areas outside the workplace, so it is important to know which law applies where.

The Gender Pay Gap Information Act 2021 requires larger employers to report the difference between men's and women's average hourly pay and to explain the gap. The size of employer covered has been widened in stages.
The Equal Status Acts 2000 to 2018 cover discrimination in goods, services and education, not employment, which is why employment complaints rely on the Employment Equality Acts.
Equality laws have opened the workplace, but women and men still do not have the same experience of work. Higher Level answers need to show what still holds women back.
Women are more likely than men to work part-time, often because of caring duties.
A gender pay gap persists in many sectors, partly because women and men are concentrated in different jobs.
Women are under-represented in senior management, a pattern known as the glass ceiling (an invisible barrier that stops women reaching the top posts).
Career breaks for childcare reduce pension entitlements and promotion chances, because time out means fewer years of contributions and less experience.
Affordable childcare is hard to find, and women still do most unpaid housework and caring, which limits the hours and posts they can take on.
Women's working lives have changed greatly, and the best way to see this is to compare the past with today.
Compare women's employment and options a hundred years ago with today, for example the marriage bar and the range of jobs open.
Interview an older woman about her working life, and whether she left work on marriage.
Being without a job is not the same as being unemployed. The word has a precise meaning, and the effects that follow depend on how long a person is out of work and why.

Unemployment means being available for and willing to work, and actively seeking work, but having no paid job. Students, full-time carers and retired people are not counted as unemployed because they are not seeking work.
Long-term unemployment means being out of work for 12 months or more. The longer it lasts, the more damaging it becomes, because savings run out and skills fade.
People lose work for different reasons, for example when a business closes, an industry declines or work is only available at certain times of year.
Unemployment black spots are areas where many people are out of work for a long time, often after a major employer closes, so whole communities feel the loss together.
Unemployment is not all of one kind. Economists group it by what causes it, and the type matters because each one needs a different response.
Frictional unemployment is short-term and occurs while people move between jobs, for example while they apply and attend interviews.
Structural unemployment results from lasting changes in the economy, such as technology replacing workers or the decline of a whole industry, so the old skills are no longer wanted.
Cyclical unemployment rises during recessions, when demand for goods and services falls, so firms produce less and recruit fewer workers; recovery usually reverses some of it.
Seasonal unemployment occurs in industries that depend on the time of year, such as tourism or construction, so the same workers may be out of work every off-season.
A job gives a person income, status, routine and company. Losing it can damage all four, and the harm usually grows the longer the person is out of work.
Financially, loss of income means a lower standard of living and difficulty paying for food, clothing, heating, and rent or mortgage, which can lead to debt.
Psychologically, losing a job can mean losing status, identity and daily routine, so a person may suffer low self-esteem and confidence, boredom and a sense of failure.
Unemployment is linked with stress, anxiety and depression (mental health problems), especially when money worries and rejected job applications build up.
Health and behaviour can suffer: physical health may be poorer, and some people turn to alcohol, drugs or gambling to cope, which adds to financial and health problems.
Socially, a person loses workplace contacts and friends, and has less social life because going out costs money, so isolation and loss of motivation can follow.
Skills become out of date, and a gap in the CV makes employers less likely to hire, so long-term unemployment feeds on itself and makes finding work harder.
Young people lose the chance to gain work experience, which delays independence: they may stay living with their parents and find it hard to move out.
Young people may be tempted to emigrate to find work, and some are at risk of antisocial behaviour when they have no job or routine.

When one person loses their job, the whole household feels it. Money, relationships, roles and children are all affected, though how badly depends on how long the unemployment lasts and how much support the family has.
Lower income means a reduced standard of living, cuts to savings, holidays, clothes and activities, and debt, with mortgage or rent arrears that can put the home at risk.
Families may rely on credit or moneylenders, social welfare payments and help from MABS to manage, but borrowing can make the money problem worse.
Financial strain causes arguments between partners and can lead to relationship breakdown, because stress and tension build up, and in some families to violence or addiction.
Roles can reverse: a parent who loses the job may become the main carer at home, which can reduce their status and authority in the family.
The other partner may have to work longer hours or take work they would not choose, to make up the lost income.
Children may have a poorer diet, miss school trips, school costs, activities and leisure, and show stress and behaviour problems because of the tension at home.
Older children may leave education early or choose a college by cost rather than by what they want to study.
Children in long-term unemployed households may lack working adults as role models, which makes it harder for them to see work as normal.
Unemployment can pull a family apart physically, as people leave to find work, though it can also give some families more time with one another.
Family members may emigrate or move to find work. This splits families, leaves older relatives without support and reduces the population of the community they leave.
More time together can be a positive effect, since a parent at home can spend more time with the children and do household tasks, but this is usually outweighed by stress.
Unemployment is not only a private problem. When many people are out of work, the State, the local economy and the community all pay a price.
The State spends more on social welfare while it collects less income tax and PRSI, because fewer people are earning, so there is less money for public services.
Households with less income spend less, so local shops and businesses suffer and more jobs can be put at risk.
Loss of skills and productive effort reduces output and economic growth, and emigration of skilled people (brain drain) takes talent away from the country.
Concentrations of unemployment cause social exclusion and unemployment black spots, where people are cut off from the opportunities most others have.
Poverty, crime, vandalism and antisocial behaviour can increase in areas of high unemployment.
High unemployment puts strain on health, mental health and other services, and contributes to family breakdown and homelessness.
Emigration can cause depopulation of areas, and a weaker community spirit follows when people, clubs and services leave.
Statutory schemes are run by the State and paid for by taxes. They replace some lost income and help people get back to work.
The Department of Social Protection runs the income supports and operates its public employment service as Intreo.

Jobseeker's Benefit is a social insurance payment based on PRSI contributions, paid for a limited period. Jobseeker's Allowance is means-tested, meaning it depends on the person's income and resources.
Supplementary Welfare Allowance meets urgent needs, and the Working Family Payment tops up the income of low-paid workers with children.
A statutory redundancy payment is paid to eligible employees who are made redundant, under the Redundancy Payments Acts.
The Back to Education Allowance gives income support to people on certain social welfare payments while they take approved second or third level courses.

SOLAS (which took over from the earlier training body in 2013) and the Education and Training Boards provide further education and training, and Springboard+ offers courses to help people return to work.
Community Employment and Tús are temporary work placements in communities that give work experience, and Youthreach helps young early school leavers.
Not all help comes from the State. Free advice services and charities support unemployed families, often with the practical problems that the payments do not cover.
Citizens Information is a free, impartial information service that tells people what payments and services they are entitled to.
MABS, the Money Advice and Budgeting Service, gives free, confidential help with debt and household budgeting, so families can manage on a reduced income.
The Society of St Vincent de Paul (SVP) is a voluntary charity with local conferences and charity shops. It helps with bills, food, school costs and housing, and visits families.
The Irish National Organisation of the Unemployed (INOU) is a national network that gives advice, advocacy and information to unemployed people.
Local community and family resource centres also offer support close to home.
Voluntary work benefits the unemployed person by giving structure, skills, contacts and confidence, and it benefits the community through the help given.
Exam questions often describe a family and ask you to apply what you know, so practise working through each member in turn.
Start with the parent who lost the job: loss of income, status and routine, stress, and the risk of skills becoming out of date.
Then the partner, who may work longer or take work they would not choose, and the couple, whose relationship is under financial strain.
Then the children, who may miss trips and activities, have a poorer diet and feel stress at home.

Finish with the supports the family could use: a Jobseeker's payment through Intreo, MABS for money problems, Citizens Information for entitlements, the SVP for practical help, and the Back to Education Allowance or a training course for a route back to work.

Socialisation is the process by which a person learns the norms (accepted rules of behaviour), values, beliefs, language and behaviour of their society so that they can take part in it. The family is the first agent of socialisation, and school is a second, major one.

Formal socialisation is the planned, stated part of school: the curriculum, timetable, school rules, uniform, codes of conduct, sanctions and rewards. It teaches punctuality, respect for authority, following instructions and responsibility, because pupils must keep to these every day.

Informal socialisation is the unplanned part, called the hidden curriculum (what pupils pick up without being taught it directly): peer groups, playground rules, friendships, school routines, the school's ethos (its character and values) and the example set by teachers.

The hidden curriculum teaches sharing, taking turns, cooperation, teamwork and how to get on with others. Remember that it is not the written curriculum: rules and timetable are formal, while peer groups and playground life are informal.
School is an early and long experience of a group outside the family, so children learn to share, take turns and cooperate with others who are not relatives.
Education transmits (passes on) the culture of a society, including its language (English and Irish), customs, history, shared values, and the rights and duties of citizens.
School brings together children from different backgrounds, which helps them fit into wider society.
Through school, pupils learn to accept responsibility, follow rules and respect the rights of others.
Physical development is how the body grows stronger, more skilled and healthier. School supports it through activity, practical work and teaching about health.

Physical education, games, sport and dance develop gross motor skills (large body movements) such as running, jumping, balance and co-ordination, as well as strength, fitness and general body development.

Practical subjects such as Home Economics, Art, Construction Studies, Engineering and Science develop fine motor skills (small, precise hand movements), manual dexterity and hand-eye coordination. In early years, play with building blocks, jigsaws, drawing and writing does the same.
Regular physical activity strengthens muscles and bones and builds cardiovascular fitness (a healthy heart and lungs).
Lessons on nutrition, hygiene, safety and health (in SPHE, Home Economics and PE) give pupils the knowledge to look after their physical health.
Physical education and school sport can establish exercise habits that a person keeps into adult life, so the benefit lasts beyond school.
Emotional development is learning to understand and manage feelings and to get on with other people. School gives children many situations that call for this.
Starting school moves a child towards emotional independence from parents, because they meet other adults and peers outside the home, cope with separation and learn to depend on themselves.
Group work and class discussion develop empathy, the ability to understand and respond to the feelings of others, and help pupils express their own feelings appropriately.
Education helps a young person form healthy relationships and friendships.
Coping with success and failure in tests, sport, performances and tasks builds resilience (the ability to recover from setbacks), confidence, self-esteem and maturity.
Praise and encouragement from teachers strengthen self-worth.

The Social, Personal and Health Education (SPHE) programme teaches emotional literacy (recognising and naming feelings), relationships, coping skills and personal safety. It continues into senior cycle as a non-exam programme.
Guidance counsellors and pastoral care (support for pupils' wellbeing) give extra help.
Moral development is learning the difference between right and wrong and acting on it. School teaches this through its rules, its subjects and the people in it.
The ethos of a school sets out its values and the behaviour it expects from pupils.
School rules, sanctions and rewards teach pupils to distinguish right from wrong, fairness and accountability for their actions, because actions have consequences they must accept.
Religious education and SPHE address moral questions such as honesty, fairness, respect and tolerance, and subjects such as History and English raise the same questions.
Moral development is also shaped by teachers as role models and by the example of the peer group.
Pupils learn to respect the rights, property and opinions of others and to accept responsibility, so becoming responsible citizens.
Intellectual development is the growth of knowledge and thinking skills. A school's curriculum and assessment are built to promote it.
A broad curriculum develops literacy, numeracy, languages, scientific reasoning, creativity and artistic skills, and builds knowledge across many subjects.
Subjects that require analysis, argument and problem solving, and research, develop critical thinking and the ability to apply knowledge.
Concentration and memory are trained through homework, revision and classroom tasks, because they require pupils to practise focusing and recalling.
Examinations and continuous assessment (work marked throughout the year) measure learning and progress, and give motivation, goals and a sense of achievement.
Competition in class, sport, quizzes and extra-curricular activities challenges students to extend their abilities.
Education also builds curiosity and a habit of lifelong learning.
Most people spend much of their lives working, and school is where the groundwork is laid. Education gives skills, qualifications and habits that employers look for.
Literacy, numeracy, communication and computer or ICT skills are basic skills that employers expect in almost every job.

Qualifications such as Junior Cycle and the Leaving Certificate, and Post Leaving Certificate, further education and third-level awards, show employers what a person has learned and open doors to jobs and higher-paid work.
Higher levels of education are linked with better employment prospects.

Punctuality, good attendance, respect for authority, reliability, trustworthiness, responsibility, self-discipline and teamwork are taught through daily school routines and group tasks. Social skills are learned by working with others.

Work experience (in Transition Year, the Leaving Certificate Vocational Programme (LCVP) and the Leaving Certificate Applied (LCA)), career guidance and subjects chosen for a career help students connect school with the world of work.
Vocational and practical subjects such as Business Studies teach skills used directly in employment.

Education matters more as industry changes, because technology and a service-based economy raise the education required for employment. It also prepares people to retrain throughout their working life.

Achievement is the result of a student's ability combined with the effort, attitude and health they bring to learning. Ability is only one factor among several, so two students of equal ability can get very different results.
Intellectual ability (intelligence) affects how quickly a student learns and the level at which they can perform, but ability alone does not decide results, because work and support matter too.
Learning difficulties, such as dyslexia (a difficulty with reading and spelling), can lower achievement if the student is not supported.
Work ethic, meaning commitment to homework, revision, attendance and class participation, has a direct effect on results because learning builds up through regular practice.
Attitude and motivation matter: a student who values learning and sets personal goals tends to achieve more, while one who sees school as pointless will often disengage.

Poor health, including illness, tiredness, lack of sleep and poor nutrition, reduces concentration and attendance, so the student misses or fails to take in lessons. Mental health and stress matter too.
Choosing subjects and a level that match a student's interests and abilities improves engagement and results. At third level, choosing the wrong course can lead to poor results or dropping out.
Part-time work during term time (at second and third level) reduces study time and can leave a student tired in class.
A student's family shapes their expectations, their resources and the conditions in which they study. Some of these influences come from the family's attitudes, others from money and circumstances.
Parental attitude: parents who value education, take an interest in homework and school, and have high expectations tend to raise their child's achievement.
Parents' own level of education shapes the expectations they hold for their children, their understanding of the school system and how much help they can give with schoolwork and choices.
Family size: in larger families, parents' time, attention and money for each child are often more limited, and older children may have caring duties.

Family finances and socio-economic background affect access to books, uniform, a computer, extra tuition, school trips and activities. They can also decide whether a student must work part-time or leave school early.

Home environment: a quiet place to study, books, a computer and internet access, a routine for homework and the absence of overcrowding all support homework and revision. Without them, study is difficult.
Family circumstances such as separation, bereavement, illness, addiction in the home, conflict or unemployment cause stress that can lower concentration and attendance.
A cycle of poverty and low expectations can pass down through generations, because children who see little value in education may carry the same expectations into their own lives.
Students spend much of the day with people their own age, so the peer group (the friends and classmates a student mixes with) has a strong influence on how they behave in school.
Positive peers encourage effort and study, because students tend to copy the behaviour of the group they belong to.
Negative peer pressure encourages truancy (staying away from school without permission), disruption and early leaving, so a student can disengage in order to fit in.
Bullying damages self-confidence and can cause a student to miss school or stop engaging with learning.
The school a student attends affects what they can learn and how they feel about learning. Both the atmosphere of the school and the resources it has to work with count.

School attended and environment: the school's ethos (its values and outlook), discipline, atmosphere and expectations of its pupils, together with the range of subjects offered and whether it is single-sex or mixed. A supportive, safe environment helps achievement.
Teacher expectations shape pupils' attainment, because low expectations of a student can limit the goals they set themselves. Teacher quality also affects how well students learn.
School resources, including class size, access to technology and equipment, laboratories, libraries and a guidance counsellor, affect what students can learn.
Supports such as learning support teachers, special needs assistants (SNAs) and exam accommodations help pupils with special needs to achieve.
Where a school is, how often a student attends, and the supports on offer all affect results. Poor attendance in particular leaves gaps that are hard to close.
The locality of a school matters: schools in socially disadvantaged areas often face higher rates of early school leaving, fewer after-school facilities and less access to resources.
Students may also live far from school or lack transport, which can hurt attendance. Good local amenities, libraries and community supports help.
Poor school attendance leads to gaps in learning and lower attainment, and it is linked with early school leaving.

Programmes and supports can raise achievement for students who might otherwise drop out: Transition Year, LCA, LCVP, JCSP, work experience, access routes to third level (such as HEAR and DARE) and exam accommodations (RACE).
Many of the same factors apply to students in college, though the details change because students are older and often live away from home.
Correct choice of course matters, because the wrong course can lead to poor results or dropping out.
Cost of fees, accommodation and travel, together with family situation, can limit what a student can afford, so working part-time may be needed, which cuts study time.
Home and college environment affect study: a student needs a suitable place to work and a college that supports them.
Positive or negative peers influence a student's effort, and parental attitude still affects their motivation.
Locality and distance from home affect travel time and cost, and college supports help students who are struggling.
Ability and work ethic remain key, because college students must study independently.

Pre-school (early childhood) education is provided by private, community and voluntary services before a child starts primary school. It is not compulsory, but it gives children a head start, so the State funds some of it.

The Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) scheme provides a free pre-school year to children before they enter primary school, delivered through approved providers. It is a government scheme, so it costs families nothing.

Early Start is a one-year preventative pre-school programme for three- and four-year-olds, run in selected primary schools in disadvantaged areas. It aims to give children a positive start and prevent later school failure.
Early Start is staffed by primary teachers working with a child care assistant, so the programme is led by trained teachers.
The Access and Inclusion Model (AIM) supports children with disabilities to take part in the free pre-school programme, so they are not left out.
Naíonraí are pre-schools where children learn through the Irish language.
Montessori schools, which are generally privately run, use trained teachers and encourage children to learn through play at their own pace.
Playschools give children of a similar age the opportunity to play together and learn to share, take turns and follow group rules.
Pre-school builds language, social skills and the routines a child needs for the transition to primary school, so children settle in more easily when they start.
Primary school is the first stage of compulsory education. Exams ask for the ages involved, the types of school to choose from and the alternatives open to parents.
Children may enrol in primary school from age four and must begin by age six, because school is compulsory from six.
Primary education is an eight-year cycle, from junior infants to sixth class, and most pupils finish between the ages of 12 and 14.

Primary schools are state-funded or private. A state-funded school is paid for by the State but run by its patron (the religious body, Educate Together or other group that runs it), so it is not state-run and not private.
State-funded schools may be religious, multidenominational or non-denominational. Educate Together is an example of a non-denominational school, and it is not a private school.
Specialist types include Educate Together schools, Gaelscoileanna (Irish-medium schools, where subjects are taught through Irish), Montessori schools and single-sex schools.
Parents may educate a child at home instead of enrolling them in a school. Home-educated children are registered with Tusla.

Second-level education follows primary school and is made up of several programmes. Each has a set length, a particular kind of curriculum and its own form of assessment, which is how exams ask you to describe them.

Junior Cycle is a three-year programme that uses classroom-based assessments and ends with a state examination at the end of third year, marked by the State Examinations Commission. Its award is the Junior Cycle Profile of Achievement, which replaced the old Junior Certificate.

Transition Year is an optional year between Junior Cycle and Leaving Certificate with no state examination. It focuses on personal development, work experience and self-directed learning (students taking charge of their own learning).
The Leaving Certificate Programme is a two-year programme that ends with state examinations at the end of sixth year.
Leaving Certificate subjects are offered at higher and ordinary level, and foundation level exists only in Irish and mathematics. Grades are converted to points for third-level entry.

Leaving Certificate Applied (LCA) is a two-year modular programme (made up of separate units) with practical, written and oral assessment. It suits students who prefer practical learning and can lead to Post Leaving Certificate courses.
The Leaving Certificate Vocational Programme (LCVP) has two link modules: Preparation for the World of Work and Enterprise Education. Work experience is part of Preparation for the World of Work.
Work experience is a placement in a workplace. It lets a student try out working life while still at school, and the benefits are a common exam question.
Work experience is part of the Leaving Certificate Vocational Programme (inside the Preparation for the World of Work link module) and is a standard element of Transition Year.
A placement lets students test their career preferences and see what a job actually involves, so they can make a better choice about their future.
Students learn workplace co-operation and how working life differs from school.
Work experience develops communication, teamwork, planning, organisation, punctuality and problem solving.
Students learn the expectations of a workplace, including timekeeping, appearance and health and safety.
Completing a placement builds confidence and responsibility, and gives the student a work record for a curriculum vitae.
Third level is education after second level. It includes degree courses in colleges and further education courses, and students need a way in and a way to pay.

Third-level institutions include universities, technological universities and institutes of technology, which offer full-time degree and diploma courses. TU Dublin, created under the Technological Universities Act 2018, is an example of a technological university.
Most full-time undergraduate places are allocated through the Central Applications Office (CAO) using Leaving Certificate points, which are based on the grades a student earns.

Post Leaving Certificate (PLC) courses are full-time further education courses, usually delivered by Education and Training Boards in second-level schools and colleges. They provide training with work experience and can give access to third-level courses.
The Student Universal Support Ireland (SUSI) scheme provides means-tested grants (based on family income) towards the costs of approved third-level courses.
The Free Fees Initiative pays tuition for eligible undergraduates, so students pay only a student contribution.

The Higher Education Access Route (HEAR) and the Disability Access Route to Education (DARE) are reduced-points entry routes for students from disadvantaged backgrounds or with disabilities, so these students can enter with fewer points.
Adult and second-chance education lets people return to learning at any age, whatever their earlier educational level.
Adult education courses are available full-time, part-time, modular, day, evening and weekend, and by distance learning, so adults can fit study around work and family.
Second-chance education gives people who left school early a route to qualifications, such as Youthreach.
Education and Training Boards (ETBs) run adult, community and further education courses; they replaced the Vocational Education Committees in 2013.
SOLAS, the Further Education and Training Authority, funds and co-ordinates further education and training programmes across the country.
Adult literacy schemes provide basic reading, writing and numeracy courses for adults.
Adult education builds skills for work, supports career change, and helps adults keep pace with new workplace technology.
Students with special educational needs are supported through a combination of planning, specialist staff and school settings. The aim is that each student gets the help that suits their need.
An Individual Education Plan (IEP) sets out the goals, teaching approach and supports for a student with special needs, drawn up with the school and the parents.
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) plans and co-ordinates special educational provision, and Special Educational Needs Organisers allocate supports to schools.
Special Needs Assistants (SNAs) provide care and support in class for students who have care needs or who need help to take part in lessons.

Special education teachers (formerly called learning support and resource teachers) give withdrawal teaching, taking students out of class individually or in small groups, to students with learning difficulties.
Special classes in mainstream schools, such as autism classes, have a reduced number of pupils per teacher, so each pupil gets more attention.
Special schools provide for students with significant general or specific learning difficulties, physical disabilities, or sensory impairments.
Visiting teachers advise and support students who are blind or vision impaired, or deaf or hard of hearing, and the teachers who teach them.
Assistive technology, such as text-to-speech software, helps students with reading or writing difficulties.
Beyond the school, specialist professionals assess needs and provide therapy, and the examinations themselves are adjusted for students who need it.
Educational psychologists assess students' needs and recommend supports, which helps the school decide what help to give.
The Health Service Executive (HSE) provides speech and language therapy and occupational therapy to children with special needs.

The State Examinations Commission provides reasonable accommodations in state examinations, such as a reader, a scribe or extra time, so that a student's disability does not stop them showing what they know.

Equality of opportunity means every student has a fair chance to access, take part in and benefit from education, whatever their background. It is about the chance, not about guaranteeing that everyone ends up with the same result.

Equal access means every student can enrol and attend; equal outcomes means students finish with similar results. The two are different, because equal access does not automatically lead to equal outcomes.
Every person should have a fair chance to enter, take part in and progress through education, whatever their gender, family background, income, ability, disability, ethnicity or where they live.
Students begin school from different starting points, so equal treatment alone may not give equal opportunity.
Equity means giving extra support in proportion to need, so that students at a disadvantage can reach the same level of achievement as others.

Free education helps: the State funds primary and second-level education, and the Free Fees Initiative pays third-level tuition for eligible undergraduates. Even so, some groups still have lower participation and results, so the State adds targeted supports.
Barriers to equality of opportunity include gender, socio-economic status, disability, family background and location.

The Equal Status Acts 2000 to 2018 prohibit discrimination in education, in schools, colleges and access to courses, on grounds that include gender, civil status, family status, age, disability, race, religion, sexual orientation and membership of the Traveller community. There is an exemption for single-sex schools.

The Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018 bars schools from using religion as a selection criterion when they are oversubscribed (the minority-faith-school exception remains). The Education Act 1998 sets out equality of access as a goal of the system.
Gender inequity in education has changed direction over time. Girls once had fewer opportunities, but today the inequity lies mainly in the subjects students choose and the careers that follow.

In the past girls had fewer opportunities, for example fewer girls stayed on to the Leaving Certificate or went to third level. Today girls' participation and attainment at second and third level are, on average, higher than boys'.

Boys are more likely than girls to leave school early, to have lower literacy levels at second level and to achieve lower grades on average. Reasons include peer pressure against being seen to work hard, lower expectations and less engagement with some subjects and teaching methods.

Subject choice can be gendered: fewer girls than boys take subjects such as Physics, Engineering, Construction Studies, Technology and Design and Communication Graphics, and fewer boys take subjects such as Home Economics, Languages and Art.
Single-sex schools can limit the subjects on offer, for example a girls' school without technical subjects or a boys' school without Home Economics, so students may not get the chance to choose them.
Subject choice affects later course and career choices, which is why there are fewer women in engineering and IT and fewer men in caring and teaching roles at primary level.

Teacher and parent expectations can differ by gender, and stereotypes held by parents, teachers and peers, textbooks, career guidance and a lack of role models can influence the subjects and courses students consider.
Schools can widen opportunity by encouraging students to choose subjects on the basis of ability and interest rather than gender stereotypes.

Other responses include less stereotyped textbooks and resources, mixed-gender access to subjects, encouragement into non-traditional subjects (for example promoting STEM for girls), gender balance in career guidance and equality legislation.

Socio-economic status (SES) is a family's position based on income, occupation and education, also called social class. It shapes a student's chances because it affects what a family can pay for, what it expects and what support it can give.

Students from higher groups (professional, managerial) are more likely to complete second level and go on to third level. Students from lower socio-economic groups are more likely to leave school early and less likely to progress to third level, so they are under-represented at third level.
School costs such as books, equipment, uniforms, trips, subject charges, school bags and technology, transport and, at third level, accommodation and living costs can exclude low-income families.

Partial relief comes from the back-to-school clothing and footwear allowance, book rental schemes and grants, school meals and school transport schemes, free fees and SUSI grants, and the Back to Education Allowance with its Cost of Education Allowance add-on for participants with dependent children.
These supports reduce costs, but they do not remove the wider gap in resources between families.

Higher-status families usually offer higher expectations and aspiration, more help with homework and course choices, a quiet place to study, grinds and extra-curricular activities, and social contacts and knowledge of the system, so their children start with advantages.

Parents with higher levels of education are more likely to have high expectations for their children and to be able to help with schoolwork. Lower-status families may face a cycle of poverty and low expectations, poor housing or crowding, and pressure to earn.

School factors add to this. Some schools use streaming (grouping students by ability), and students in lower-status groups may be placed in lower streams or sets, which can limit the subject level, grades and courses open to them.
Teacher expectations and the locality of a school (a disadvantaged area, with fewer resources and more early leaving) can reinforce the effects of socio-economic status.

Responses include DEIS (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools), which gives extra support to schools in disadvantaged communities, HEAR, which gives reduced-points third-level entry to students from disadvantaged backgrounds, and the financial supports above.

A disadvantaged student is one at risk of low achievement because of several causes working together, not just low income. Knowing who is at risk, what holds them back and what helps lets you answer both the short and the long questions.

Groups at risk of educational disadvantage include students from low-income and unemployed families, Travellers, Roma, students from migrant, asylum-seeking or refugee families, students with disabilities or special educational needs, homeless young people, young people in care, those in disadvantaged areas and lone-parent households.
Students from migrant families may need language support in English or Irish (English as an additional language), and their qualifications from other countries may not be recognised.
Students living in disadvantaged areas may face poor housing, poor health, lack of study space and limited access to after-school activities, which makes it harder to study and take part.
Other barriers are poverty, discrimination, low expectations, lack of role models and, in some communities, negative experiences of school. These lead to low attendance and early leaving.

The DEIS (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools) programme identifies schools serving disadvantaged communities and gives them extra staffing and supports. These include the school completion programme, homework clubs, mentoring, school meals, home school community liaison and enhanced book grants.

Other responses to name are language support, learning support and special needs assistants (SNAs), Traveller and Roma education supports, grants and allowances, school meals and transport, and the Home School Community Liaison scheme.
Leaving school early closes doors that are hard to reopen. Knowing who is at risk, why students leave and what follows explains why the State invests in keeping them in school.
An early school leaver is a young person who leaves school before completing senior cycle, that is before the Leaving Certificate or an equivalent programme.
Early school leaving is more likely among students with poor attendance and truancy, low literacy and numeracy, or learning difficulties, because they fall behind and lose interest.
Bullying, family problems, poverty and the cost of staying on, and negative peer pressure all increase the risk of leaving school early.

Other causes are a cycle of poverty and low parental expectation, living in a disadvantaged area, dislike of school or a lack of suitable programmes, the pull of jobs, pregnancy, and health or addiction problems.
Leaving school early means few or no qualifications, which limits access to further and third-level education and training and to skilled employment.
Later in life early school leaving is linked with unemployment or low-paid unskilled work, welfare dependence, poverty, low self-esteem, poor health, social exclusion and a higher risk of crime.
The effects spread: the next generation is also affected through the cycle of poverty, and the State loses skills and pays more in welfare.

Responses include the School Completion Programme, the Home School Community Liaison scheme, DEIS, the Educational Welfare Service of Tusla (which deals with school attendance), JCSP and LCA, Youthreach, the Back to Education Allowance and VTOS.

The normal points system can shut out students whose circumstances have held back their results. Access routes give these students another way to reach third-level courses, and extra help once they arrive.

HEAR (Higher Education Access Route) is a CAO route that gives reduced-points entry to Leaving Certificate school leavers from socially and economically disadvantaged backgrounds who meet set indicators, such as family income, social welfare or medical card, parental occupation and area.
Meeting the HEAR criteria does not guarantee a place, and the points reduction varies by course and year. The participating colleges run HEAR together.

Students admitted through HEAR receive support services in college once they have started their course, so they are helped to stay and succeed, not just to get in. The supports depend on the institution.

DARE (Disability Access Route to Education) is a CAO route for school leavers whose disability has affected their second-level education, such as dyslexia, autism, a sensory or physical disability, a mental health condition or a learning difficulty. It gives reduced-points entry because of the disability.

Students admitted through DARE receive ongoing support in college, such as assistive technology (equipment or software that helps them study), exam accommodations and study skills help. Students apply through the CAO with supporting documents.

Post Leaving Certificate (PLC) courses at QQI Levels 5 and 6 are a route into higher education for students who did not progress directly from second level, through the Higher Education Links Scheme. Level 7 courses in institutes of technology and technological universities are a separate route.

Springboard+ (previously Springboard) is a State-funded scheme of part-time or full-time higher education courses at Levels 6 to 9, managed by the Higher Education Authority. It is free for unemployed people and returners to the workforce and part-funded for others, to improve employability.

Other routes and supports are mature student entry, apprenticeships, the Free Fees Initiative, SUSI grants (means-tested, towards the cost of an approved course), distance learning such as the Open University, and scholarships.
Students from disadvantaged areas are more likely to fall behind or leave school early. These schemes put extra help into schools and homes so that young people stay in education and do well in it.

DEIS (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools) is an action plan launched in 2005. It identifies primary and second-level schools in disadvantaged communities and gives them extra support, aiming to reduce early school leaving and improve attendance, attainment and progression.

DEIS supports include an improved teacher ratio in some schools, the school meals programme, enhanced book grants, literacy and numeracy supports, the Home School Community Liaison scheme, the School Completion Programme, homework clubs, after-school supports and mentoring programmes.

The School Completion Programme (SCP) is a targeted programme of local projects, run through Tusla Education Support Service, for children and young people at risk of leaving school early. It is part of DEIS and aims to reduce the number leaving early.
SCP offers homework clubs, mentoring, and after-school and holiday activities, and eases the transfer from primary to second level, so students are supported through the change of school.

The Home School Community Liaison (HSCL) scheme is school-based and also run through Tusla Education Support Service. A coordinator links the school with parents and the community to build partnership between home, school and community.
HSCL helps parents support their children's learning, for example through courses for parents and home visits, and it identifies students who need financial or learning support.

The Junior Certificate School Programme (JCSP, now often called the Junior Cycle School Programme) was introduced in 1996 for students most at risk of leaving school early. It makes Junior Cycle more accessible through short, achievable learning targets and literacy and numeracy support.
JCSP certifies the skills students attain and the subject statements they complete, so a student who might not do well in an exam still has achievement recognised in a profile.
Not every student is best served by the standard academic course. Alternative programmes, welfare follow-up and practical and inclusion supports remove other barriers to staying in school.

Leaving Certificate Applied (LCA) is a two-year modular programme for students who prefer a practical or work-related approach. It has continuous assessment, practical, oral and written examinations, in four half-year sessions with credits. It ends in a certificate graded Pass, Merit or Distinction and leads to PLC courses.

The Leaving Certificate Vocational Programme (LCVP) adds vocational link modules, Preparation for the World of Work and Enterprise Education, to the Leaving Certificate. It is assessed by a portfolio and a written exam and counts for CAO points.
Transition Year gives students an extra year for maturity and career exploration before the Leaving Certificate cycle.

The Educational Welfare Service (Tusla) enforces school attendance, follows up non-attendance and supports families, under the Education (Welfare) Act 2000, so that a student who stops attending is followed up.

Financial and practical supports cut the cost of school: the Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance (Department of Social Protection), book rental schemes and grants, the School Meals Programme, school transport (including special transport), free exam fees for medical-card holders, and laptops and ICT for pupils with special needs.

Inclusion supports help students with particular needs: learning support and special education teachers, SNAs (special needs assistants), language support for English as an additional language, language assistants in Gaeltacht schools, visiting teachers, special classes and assistive technology.
Reasonable accommodations in exams (RACE) adjust how an exam is taken for students who need it, so the exam tests what they know and not their disability.
Youthreach and VTOS give early school leavers and unemployed adults a second chance at training and qualifications, with an allowance during the course.

Youthreach is an integrated education, training and work experience programme for early school leavers aged 15 to 20 without qualifications. It runs for up to two years through Education and Training Boards (ETBs, which replaced VECs in 2013) in Youthreach centres, including community training workshops.
Youthreach centres are located throughout the country.
Youthreach participants get a weekly training allowance and a nationally recognised QQI award, so they gain both income and a qualification.

VTOS (Vocational Training Opportunities Scheme) offers full-time education and training courses, of up to two years, designed to meet the educational needs of unemployed adults aged 21 and over. Courses are run through ETBs and cover personal development, business and computer skills.
VTOS pays a training allowance in place of the welfare payment during the course, similar to social welfare entitlements, so unemployed people can study without losing their income.
Adults who return to learning can use the Back to Education schemes, adult literacy courses and advocacy bodies to study and to get support.

The Back to Education Allowance (BTEA, Department of Social Protection) helps people getting certain social welfare payments to attend an approved full-time second-level or third-level course and keep an allowance. An annual Cost of Education Allowance add-on, introduced in Budget 2017, is available to participants with dependent children.
The Back to Education Allowance (BTEA) helps people on social welfare payments to attend approved full-time or part-time education courses.
The Back to Education Initiative (BTEI) offers part-time further education courses run by ETBs, so adults, including those with low qualifications, can study around work or family.

Community education and adult literacy schemes, run by ETBs, provide adult literacy and other community-based courses in local settings. NALA (the National Adult Literacy Agency) supports literacy and numeracy tuition.

Aontas, the Irish National Association of Adult Education, promotes the development of adult learning through advice, support, research and advocacy. SOLAS (the Further Education and Training Authority, set up in 2013) funds and coordinates further education and training through ETBs, including apprenticeships.
Initiative questions reward a precise, well-matched answer. Choose a scheme that fits the group in the question and give its details, not a list of several.

For a question asking you to name and give details of one initiative, name it first, then add two or three points of detail: the target group, what is provided, who runs it and the benefit. Giving three schemes for a one-scheme question wastes time.
To evaluate a scheme, say how it helps, then give a limit: it does not reach everyone, it depends on funding, or it depends on a student's disadvantage being identified.
Match the scheme to the group: DEIS, SCP and HSCL for disadvantaged schools, JCSP, SCP and LCA for students at risk of leaving, and Youthreach, VTOS and BTEA for early school leavers.
For third-level access, use HEAR, DARE, SUSI and free fees. For adults, use BTEA, BTEI, Springboard+, community education and Aontas.

Work is any activity that produces goods or services, using a person's time and effort. It is not only paid: it falls into three types, which differ in whether it is paid, who it is for and whether it is chosen.

Paid employment is work done for financial gain (a wage, salary, fees or profit), usually under a contract of employment between employer and employee. It may be permanent, temporary, full-time, part-time or contract-based.

Self-employment is also paid work, not a fourth type: the worker earns income directly from their own trade, business or profession and carries the financial risk, because there is no employer to pay them if business is poor.
Paid employment carries entitlement to PRSI-based social insurance (cover built up through PRSI contributions) and, in many jobs, a pension, sick pay and paid holidays.

Unpaid work in the home is done without financial reward, mainly for the household: housework, cooking, cleaning, laundry, shopping, child care and care of elderly or disabled relatives. It is done out of duty or family commitment.
Home-related activities such as DIY, home maintenance, gardening and household budgeting are also unpaid work, because they keep the home running without anyone being paid.

Voluntary work is unpaid work done freely, by choice, for people or causes outside the household, usually through a charity, community group or organisation, to help others and improve the community. Volunteers may receive expenses but no wage.
Examples of voluntary work include St Vincent de Paul, charity shops, fundraising and helping at local sports clubs.

In one line each: paid work brings income; unpaid work in the home is a household duty with no income; voluntary work is chosen, for the wider community, with no income. Work placements and work experience are unpaid but are not the same as voluntary work.

The distinction matters because paid work brings income and entitlements, while unpaid and voluntary work are not counted in earnings. They still use a person's time, which is also a resource, so work affects the time and money available for family life.

Job satisfaction is how fulfilled and content a person is in their work. It comes from two sources: rewards that surround the job (extrinsic) and the task itself (intrinsic). A worker usually gets a mix of both, and occupations differ in the balance.

Extrinsic satisfaction comes from rewards linked to the job rather than from the task itself. Sources are pay, bonuses, pension, paid holidays and leave, job security, promotion prospects, working conditions, and company benefits such as a car or private health insurance.
Repetitive, uninteresting work, such as assembly-line production, may leave pay as the main source of satisfaction, because the worker works 'for the money'.
Satisfaction is also gained by spending income on goods, leisure and socialising outside work.
Extrinsic rewards can sustain a worker in a job, but on their own they bring less pride and self-esteem, because they do not come from the work itself.

Intrinsic satisfaction comes from the work itself: the fulfilment, pleasure and creativity it offers. Sources are challenge and variety in tasks, autonomy and responsibility, the chance to use skills, pride in a finished task, achievement and feeling useful.
Work builds self-esteem, confidence and independence.
Work can confer status and respect in the community and a personal identity, such as being a nurse or a teacher, which meets social and psychological needs.
Intrinsic satisfaction is strongest when a job matches a person's skills and interests, because the worker enjoys and takes pride in what they do.
Work ethic is the attitude a person brings to work. Work attainment is about getting and achieving the kind of work a person is aiming for.

Work ethic is a person's commitment to working hard and doing a job well. It is shown through punctuality, good attendance and low absenteeism, reliability, effort, honesty, commitment to tasks, pride in the work, and respect for authority, colleagues and employer.
Employers value a strong work ethic, and it helps a worker to keep a job, be promoted and get good references. A positive attitude makes a worker more likely to be trusted with responsibility.
Work ethic is influenced by upbringing, education and the example of family and peers.

Work attainment is getting and achieving the kind of work a person wants. How far someone attains the work they aim for is affected by education and qualifications, social group, ambition and aspirations, family expectations, and the availability of jobs.
People who have high aspirations (goals they set themselves) and are encouraged at home are more likely to attain work in a desired field.
A person's attitude to work, positive or negative, is shaped by their background, their circumstances and what the job is like. Each factor can raise or lower how a worker feels about their job.
Upbringing and family attitudes to work, together with education and qualifications and earlier work experience, shape expectations before a person starts a job.

Social group, ambition and economic situation: children from higher socio-economic groups tend to have higher educational aspirations and long-term goals, and a person's financial situation affects how much they need the job.
Financial reward: fair pay and benefits encourage a positive attitude, while poor pay discourages it.
Fulfilment and personal identity: some occupations confer status in the community, which can encourage a positive attitude to work, and a worker who feels fulfilled has higher self-esteem.
Social contact: a workplace meets social needs through friendships, and peer pressure influences how seriously a worker takes the job.

Working environment and conditions: a good atmosphere and a supportive supervisor produce a positive attitude, whereas poor conditions, a long commute and unsociable hours produce a negative one. Part-time work, job-sharing, flexitime and working from home make work-life balance easier.
Changing gender roles affect who works and in what jobs, and so change attitudes to work.
Occupations differ in the mix of intrinsic and extrinsic satisfaction they offer, so workers in different jobs often feel differently about their work.
Professional and creative occupations, such as teaching, medicine and design, often give high intrinsic satisfaction through responsibility, autonomy and recognised expertise.
Repetitive manual and production jobs, such as assembly-line work, tend to depend more on pay, job security and working conditions, because the task itself offers little interest.
Shift work and unsocial hours can reduce satisfaction in occupations such as nursing, emergency services and hospitality unless flexibility is offered.
Self-employed workers often report high intrinsic satisfaction because they control their own hours and methods, but they bear greater financial risk and have less security.
Occupations that have status in the community encourage a positive attitude to work.
A job description sets out what a post involves. In a case study it is the basis for judging how satisfying the work is likely to be.
A job description usually states the job title, main duties and responsibilities, working hours, place of work, pay and the qualifications or skills needed.
Duties involving planning, decision-making or creativity suggest scope for intrinsic satisfaction.
Routine, repetitive duties with a fixed pay scale suggest that satisfaction depends mainly on extrinsic rewards.
Flexible hours, job-sharing or home working in a description indicate conditions that can improve work-life balance.
Method: list the duties, mark each as offering intrinsic or extrinsic satisfaction, judge how satisfied the worker is likely to be, then suggest one or two improvements.
Satisfaction can be judged by checking both sources of satisfaction and the factors that undermine them. Once the weak points are found, they suggest what to improve.

Questions to ask: is the worker paid fairly, is the employment secure, is effort recognised, does the worker use their skills, and is there social contact? Then balance the intrinsic and extrinsic answers.
Variety in tasks, training, more responsibility and clear routes to promotion increase intrinsic satisfaction, because the work becomes more challenging and the worker sees a future.
Taking part in decisions, teamwork and a safe, pleasant workplace raise satisfaction, as do better relationships with management, because the worker feels valued and comfortable.
Fair pay and secure employment improve extrinsic satisfaction, because the worker is rewarded for effort and need not worry about losing the job.
Flexible hours and leave arrangements help workers balance work with family life, so work causes less strain at home.
Regular feedback and recognition reward performance and reinforce commitment, because workers who are told they do well keep up the effort.
New technology changes how work is organised, how many workers are needed and which skills are in demand. Some effects are gains for workers and some are losses, and exam answers need both.
Automation (machines and robots taking over repetitive production and processing tasks) means fewer workers are needed for the same output, because the machines do the routine work.
Increased output with fewer workers reduces working hours in some industries, which gives people more leisure time, but it also removes jobs at the lower-skilled end.

Computers and electronic communication change office work. They create new skilled jobs to design, install, maintain and operate the technology, so jobs shift towards programming, supervising and maintaining.

Electronic communication allows home working (teleworking), which suits some people. The downside is that it makes it harder to switch off from work, and it reduces face-to-face social contact at work.
Technology also makes work safer and cleaner in some settings, because dangerous and dirty tasks are carried out by machines. This means fewer injuries and healthier workplaces.
Workers whose skills become out of date, or who lose unskilled and manual jobs, need retraining. Companies can also relocate production to low-cost countries, which removes jobs at home.
Technology has also changed office and service work: banking, shopping and booking online mean fewer counter and clerical jobs and more technical ones.
Employment has moved from extracting and manufacturing towards services. To describe the shift you first need to know the three kinds of industry.
Primary industry extracts resources from the land and sea: agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining or quarrying (such as peat).
Secondary industry manufactures and processes primary raw materials into finished goods, for example food processing, clothing, engineering and construction.

Tertiary (service) industry provides services such as tourism, leisure, healthcare, transport, media, retail, education, banking and finance, hospitality and IT. Note that tertiary means services, not third-level education.

Automation and mechanisation reduced the number of manufacturing and farming jobs because machines do more of the work. Service industries expanded and absorbed many workers as incomes rose and demand for services grew.
Companies relocated production to lower-cost countries, causing job losses in manufacturing in Ireland. Growth of tourism, finance and technology firms added service jobs.

The effects on people were that manual and unskilled workers were displaced and rural areas lost jobs, while urban areas gained service jobs. Service work brought more part-time and shift work and a new demand for qualified workers.
