Setting: compare Ireland's current occupational structure with that of fifty years ago, noting the shift from farming, factory and other manual work to service and professional work. Describe the pattern without figures.
As jobs have shifted towards services and technology, employers increasingly expect higher qualifications. Education has become the way into work and the way to move up within it.
Service and technology jobs need literacy, numeracy, computing and communication skills, which are developed through education.

Employers use qualifications to select between applicants, so a larger share of applicants now hold them. The Leaving Certificate is the minimum for many jobs, and many need a further education or higher qualification.
Qualifications widen employment options and allow career advancement, because they show an employer what a worker can do.
Early school leavers and unskilled workers find it difficult to acquire work, as many jobs require a minimum level of education. They are most at risk of unemployment and low pay.
Continuing education, such as evening courses, distance learning and part-time courses, allows adults to gain qualifications, keep pace with technology, improve promotion prospects or change career.
Upskilling programmes (courses that build on skills a worker already has) also let adults keep their skills up to date.
Reskilling (training in new skills) allows workers whose jobs have disappeared to move into new occupations.
Many more women, including married women and mothers, are now in paid work than in the middle of the twentieth century. The causes are social and economic, and each one needs a short reason.
Women are better educated than in the past, and qualifications open access to professional and skilled work.
Equality legislation removed barriers: the Civil Service (Employment of Married Women) Act 1973 removed the marriage bar (the rule forcing married women to leave civil service jobs).
The Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 first legislated for equal pay for equal work. Both Acts are now covered by the Employment Equality Acts 1998 to 2015.
Income from paid work gives women financial independence, self-esteem, status and a stronger personal identity, as well as social contact outside the home.
The growth of service industries and part-time work created many jobs that suited women's skills and flexible hours.
Rising living, housing and child care costs, and the need for a second income, encourage women into paid employment. More marital breakdown and lone parenthood also make earning necessary.
Flexible hours, job-sharing, term-time work, maternity and parental leave and career breaks make it possible to combine paid work with home and family responsibilities.

More child care facilities, labour-saving appliances and smaller families free up women's time, and changing attitudes make work more accepted. The result is financial independence for women and more dual-earner families (both parents earning).
Pay, safety and time off have all improved, which made paid work more attractive. These improvements also enabled women to take part in the workforce more fully.
Better pay, including the introduction of the minimum wage, plus pension entitlement and paid holiday arrangements, make paid work more attractive.
Statutory protections for workers (those set down in law) cover health and safety, pay and working time. Employment is protected by legislation, as are equal pay and equality law.
Safer and cleaner workplaces, made possible by technology, reduce risk of injury and illness. Working hours are also shorter than in the past.

Statutory leave includes maternity leave, parental leave and force majeure leave (urgent family reasons). Parental leave and career breaks let workers take time away for family reasons and return to their job.
Facilities for working parents, such as crèches and breastfeeding breaks, make it easier to stay in work after having a child.
Improved conditions have enabled many women to return to the workforce after raising children, because work no longer has to be given up for family life.
Working time is now arranged in many ways other than the traditional full-time, fixed-hours week. These arrangements let workers fit paid work around family life.
Flexitime: employees choose their start and finish times within agreed core hours, when everyone must be at work.
Job-sharing: two people share one full-time post, dividing the hours, pay and duties between them.
Part-time and term-time working: reduced hours, or work arranged around the school year, which suits parents of school-age children.
Compressed or reduced working weeks, such as working longer days across fewer days, and teleworking: working from home or another remote location using electronic communication.
Career breaks: an agreed period of unpaid leave, after which the worker returns to their job.

Parental leave: under the Parental Leave Act 1998 (as amended), parents are entitled to unpaid leave to look after a young child, currently 26 weeks per child for a child under 12 (longer if the child has a disability or long-term illness).
It is taken in one block or in agreed blocks, and it is not paid by the employer by right.

Related leaves exist under other laws: maternity leave (Maternity Protection Acts 1994 and 2004), paternity leave (Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016), parent's leave (Parent's Leave and Benefit Act 2019), carer's leave (Carer's Leave Act 2001) and force majeure leave.
The law now gives employees a right to ask for flexible hours or to work remotely. The employer does not have to agree, but must handle the request fairly.
The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 provides these rights, and the flexible and remote working provisions commenced on 6 March 2024.
Parents and carers of children up to 12 (or up to 16 if the child is disabled or long-term ill), and carers, can request flexible working. Any employee can request remote working.
The employer must consider the request and reply in writing within set time limits, giving reasons for any refusal, so workers get a clear answer.
The Act also provides paid domestic-violence leave (5 days, from November 2023) and unpaid medical care leave (from 3 July 2023).
Taken together, the changes in technology, industry, education, women's work and working hours affect individuals and families in both helpful and difficult ways.
Workers displaced from manufacturing may need retraining before they can find work in services, so the availability of work changes for individuals.
Flexible working helps parents plan childcare and family life more smoothly. It means more time with children, less stress and an easier balance of work and family.
Blurred boundaries between work and home can increase stress and make it harder to switch off.
Flexible working can also mean lower income, slower promotion, a shortfall in pension and resentment from colleagues.
Families in which both parents work gain income but may face role overload and role conflict, because family tasks still have to be done.
Employers gain access to a wider, more skilled labour pool and can keep staff by offering flexible arrangements.
Unpaid work is the work done in and around the home without any wage. It keeps households running and spares families the cost of paying for services.
Unpaid work covers child care, housework, cooking, laundry, caring for an elderly parent or a person with a disability, gardening, household management, and DIY and home maintenance.
It is done mainly within the household, without financial reward and often out of family duty, so it is not a free choice in the way voluntary work is.
It keeps households and the community functioning and supports the paid workforce, because children and workers are cared for and fed. In this way it makes family life possible.
Because it is unpaid, it saves families the cost of paying for these services themselves, such as child care or home help.
It is not counted in measures of national paid output and has no wage, pension entitlement or sick pay of its own, so its contribution is often overlooked.
Unpaid work can be monotonous, and it often falls unequally on women within the household.
Carers can become isolated or stressed, because looking after a relative can take up most of the day.
Many people look after a relative at home. They are unpaid carers, and the care they give matters to both families and the State.
Unpaid carers look after relatives at home, such as an older person or a person with a disability. They are often helped by State supports such as carer's payments.
They save the State and families large costs, because the care would otherwise have to be paid for through nursing homes, home help or hospital services.
They give care in a familiar home setting, which is often more comfortable for the person being cared for.
Voluntary work is unpaid work done freely, by choice, for people or a cause outside the household, usually through an organisation.
The volunteer gets no wage, sick pay or pension, but expenses for travel or training may be repaid.

Voluntary work is carried out through charities, community groups, sports clubs, schools, parish and church groups, youth organisations and local development groups. St Vincent de Paul is one example: a national voluntary agency using church-gate collections, charity shops and local visiting.

Typical activities include running charity shops, fundraising, providing meals on wheels and transport for older people, visiting the housebound, and mentoring and coaching young people as club coaches or youth leaders.
Other activities include running local events, community clean-ups, first aid and emergency or rescue services, and community care and support groups.
Environmental volunteering includes litter clean-ups, tree planting, conservation work and local recycling projects.
Volunteers need training, and Garda vetting through the organisation for work with children or vulnerable adults, so that those they help are protected.
Both kinds of work are unpaid and neither is employment, but they differ in why, for whom and how they are done.
Unpaid home work is largely a duty within the family, whereas voluntary work is chosen freely.
Unpaid home work benefits the household, whereas voluntary work benefits people and causes in the wider community.
Voluntary work is usually organised through an organisation, whereas home work is usually carried out individually.
Volunteers give their time without pay, but they gain a great deal themselves. These benefits are personal, practical and social.
Skills and experience such as teamwork, communication, organisation and leadership, plus training, can be listed on a CV and used for a reference.
Confidence and self-esteem grow as the volunteer contributes to something valued, giving a sense of purpose and achievement.
Social contact and friendships bring a feeling of belonging and reduce isolation, particularly for people who are retired, unemployed or new to an area.
Volunteering gives people a sense of purpose and fulfilment, and a chance to develop their potential.
Volunteering can lead to paid employment, or to expertise in a particular area, as it builds experience and references in that field.
Empathy and insight into the lives of others develop through helping people in need, such as older or vulnerable people.
Volunteering keeps people active and healthy, and is a good use of free time for people who are retired or between jobs.
The community gains services, support and a stronger sense of belonging from the people who give their time. These benefits are separate from what the volunteers themselves gain.
Services that would otherwise be unavailable or unaffordable can be provided, such as meals for older or housebound people, transport, youth clubs, sports coaching and support groups.
Support for vulnerable groups, including older people, people with disabilities, lone parents, the homeless, people at risk of poverty and new arrivals, reaches those who might otherwise be missed.
Volunteers build community spirit and social cohesion by bringing people from different backgrounds together around a shared purpose.
Where young people are involved in clubs there is less crime and vandalism, because they have something positive to do.
Local facilities such as halls, pitches and parks are built, maintained and improved through volunteer effort and fundraising.
Volunteering saves the State and local bodies money and complements paid services, though it does not replace them.
Volunteers raise awareness of local issues and encourage participation (civic participation) and active citizenship in decisions that affect the area.
Volunteers do more than provide services. Their work changes how a community lives and how it treats its surroundings.
Social change: volunteers campaign for services and for the rights of groups, and help people to claim the supports they are entitled to.
Social change: volunteer-run projects build inclusion by supporting people with disabilities, minorities, Travellers and migrants to take part in community life, and they reduce isolation.
Environmental change: litter picks, clean-ups of rivers and beaches, tree planting and conservation work reduce litter and protect habitats such as woodland, river banks and coastline.
Environmental change: community gardens and growing schemes, recycling projects and local heritage projects change local habits and reduce waste.
The Tidy Towns competition is a well-known example of a community improvement effort driven by local volunteers.
Long-term change comes from volunteers passing on their knowledge and skills to others, so the work continues beyond any one project.
Voluntary work depends on people's goodwill and spare time, which creates some limits.
Volunteers can experience burnout when a few people carry a large share of the work.
Groups depend on continued volunteer commitment, which can be hard to sustain as people take on paid work or family responsibilities.
Volunteers can face out-of-pocket costs for travel, equipment or training that are not reimbursed.
Volunteers are not employees, so they have no pay, sick pay or pension.
Volunteers need training, and Garda vetting for work with children or vulnerable adults.
Volunteering is helped along by national organisations and by ways of encouraging people to take part.

Volunteer Ireland is the national volunteer development organisation, supporting Volunteer Centres and running National Volunteering Week. The first national strategy, the National Volunteering Strategy, was published by the Government in December 2020. Its period ended in 2025, so a successor may exist.
Volunteering can be encouraged through training, recognition and repaying expenses, which helps to remove the out-of-pocket costs that put people off.

Young people are easily exploited at work and can lose out on school if they work too much. The Protection of Young Persons (Employment) Act 1996 sets limits so that work does not harm a young person's health, safety, education or development.
The Act sets a minimum age for work, limits on working hours, rules on breaks and rest, and limits on night work, which stops employers exploiting young people and protects their schooling.
The Act splits young workers into two age groups, because the rules differ for each: a child is under 16, and a young person is 16 or 17. Use the phrase 'under 18' only for the two groups together.
The Act also sets out what employers must do before employing a young person, and what records they must keep.
The Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) inspectors enforce the Act. Employers who break it commit an offence and can be prosecuted and fined.
Employers are expected to know the Act's rules. The Act also applies in most cases to work done for family employers, with some limited exceptions.
The younger the worker, the tighter the limits. The Act uses age to decide whether a person can work at all, and what kind of work is allowed.
It is an offence to employ a child under 16 on a full-time basis, because full-time work would interfere with schooling.

Children under 14 may not be employed at all, apart from licensed work in cultural, artistic, sporting or advertising settings, such as film, theatre, modelling or sport. These need authorisation from the relevant Minister, with conditions, in individual cases.
Children of 14 may do light work during school holidays and approved work experience. Children of 15 may do this and also light work during the school term.
Light work means work that is not harmful to health, safety or development and does not interfere with schooling.
Employers must not give children work that is unsuitable or dangerous, because children are less able to judge risks.
Limits on hours stop work from crowding out school and rest. The limits depend on age group and on whether it is school term or holiday time.
During school holidays, 14- and 15-year-olds may do light work only, for a maximum of 7 hours in a day and 35 hours in a week.
During the school term, only 15-year-olds may do light work, for a maximum of 8 hours a week. 14-year-olds cannot work during term, apart from approved work experience.
Approved work experience as part of a school programme (at 14 or over), and approved training or work experience (at 15), allows up to 8 hours a day and 40 hours a week.
During the summer holidays, a child must have at least 21 days free from any work, so that they get a proper break.
16- and 17-year-olds may work up to 8 hours a day and 40 hours a week.
Young workers are still growing and studying, so the Act guarantees time to rest during the working day, between shifts and across the week.
Children (under 16) must have at least 14 consecutive hours' rest in every 24 hours, and two days off in every seven, so that they can sleep and recover.
Children must get a break of at least 30 minutes after 4 hours' work, so that they do not work for long stretches without rest.
Young persons (16 and 17) must have at least 12 consecutive hours' rest in every 24 hours.
Young persons must have two days off a week, consecutive where practicable, so that they get a proper rest.
Young persons must get a 30-minute break after 4.5 hours' work. Breaks are unpaid.
The Act bans work late at night and early in the morning, because tired young people cannot work or study safely.
Children may not work between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m.
Young persons (16 and 17) may not work between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.
A later window of 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. applies only in prescribed limited cases, and never before a school day during term.
The Act puts responsibility on the employer to check the worker's age, get the right permission and keep proof that the rules were followed.
Before employing anyone under 18, the employer must see a copy of their birth certificate or other satisfactory evidence of age, so that the right rules are applied.
Before employing a child (under 16), the employer must have the written permission of a parent or guardian.
The employer must keep a record (register) of each young person's name, date of birth, daily start and finish times and pay, and must keep it for at least three years.
Employers may be inspected, and must give inspectors access to the records, so that inspectors can check the rules are being followed.
Employers who break the Act can be prosecuted and fined.
A part-time job brings benefits, but it also carries risks, and the Act aims to keep the balance in the young person's favour.
Advantages of part-time work are income and experience, for example money of their own and skills for later jobs.
Disadvantages are tiredness and an effect on study. The Act's hour, rest and night-work limits exist to reduce these risks.

The Act is one of several laws that protect workers (five areas of wider employment protection). The Organisation of Working Time Act limits adults' hours, whereas the 1996 Act protects under-18s, so keep the two separate.

Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005: employers must provide a safe workplace, assess risks, supply safety training and equipment, and have a safety statement. Workers have duties too, such as following safety rules, and the Health and Safety Authority (HSA) enforces it.
National Minimum Wage Act 2000: sets a minimum hourly pay rate, so that no worker is paid below it. Reduced rates apply to young workers.

Employment Equality Acts 1998–2015: prohibit discrimination in employment on nine grounds: gender, civil status, family status, age, disability, sexual orientation, race, religion and membership of the Traveller community.
The Employment Equality Acts cover access to work, pay, conditions, training, promotion and dismissal, so discrimination is banned at every stage of a job.
Organisation of Working Time Act 1997: limits weekly hours, sets rest breaks and daily and weekly rest, and gives paid annual leave and public holidays. It also has Sunday and night work provisions.

Other examples: the Unfair Dismissals Acts 1977–2015 (protection against unfair dismissal), the Maternity Protection Acts 1994 and 2004, the Parental Leave Act 1998, and the Terms of Employment (Information) Acts (written terms of employment).
Disputes go to the Workplace Relations Commission. Trade unions also represent workers and negotiate pay and conditions.

Reconciling paid work with family life depends on how a household divides its roles and tasks between its members. Over time, the roles people expect of men and women have changed, and that change shapes how dual-earner families run.
A dual-earner family (also called a dual-career family) is one in which both partners are in paid employment, so the household has two incomes and two sets of work demands.

A role is the set of behaviours and responsibilities expected of a person in a position such as parent, employee, partner or homemaker (the person who runs the home). Sex roles, also called gender roles, are the tasks and behaviour expected of men and women.
Traditional sex roles gave the man the main earning role, as breadwinner, and the woman the main responsibility for childcare and home care, as homemaker.
Sex roles have loosened as more women take up paid work and more men take an active part in childcare and housework, so tasks are increasingly shared rather than fixed by sex.
Fathers can now take paternity leave and parent's leave, and some families have a stay-at-home father, which shows that caring is no longer seen as only a woman's job.
The change is real but not complete: attitudes have changed, yet women on average still do more of the household and caring work.
Children learn sex roles from the way tasks are shared at home, as well as from school, peers and the media, so what they see their parents do shapes what they expect for themselves.
When both partners work, someone still has to do the childcare and the housework. Role overload is what happens when one person is asked to do too many of these jobs at once.

Role overload occurs when one person tries to perform several roles at the same time, for example employee, parent, homemaker and carer, and cannot meet the demands of all of them. It is about too many roles to cope with at once.
Effects on the individual: less leisure and rest time, tiredness, stress and poorer health, with a risk of burnout (complete exhaustion from long-term stress) if the load continues.

Effects on work: difficulty finding time for training, extra hours or promotion, and less energy for them, because the person has little left after the demands of home. There may also be pressure to take work home.
Effects on the family: tension between partners and other family members, less time with children, and neglect of family and household tasks that no one has time to do.
Vulnerable members, such as young children, an elderly relative or a family member who is ill, may have no one available to care for them.
Women often carry a larger share of the strain because they usually remain the main carers at home, so they end up doing a full job and then the home tasks as well.

Overload can be reduced by sharing tasks, using labour-saving appliances, buying in outside help such as a cleaner or childcare, keeping routines simple, planning meals, and using leave and flexible work arrangements.
Role conflict is a different problem from overload. Here a person may be able to manage each role, but two roles pull in opposite directions at the same moment and a choice has to be made.
Role conflict arises when the expectations of one role clash with the expectations of another, so that both cannot be met and one has to give way. It is two roles pulling in different directions.
Example: a child becomes sick and needs a parent at home while a work deadline or meeting requires the same parent to be at work.
Priority choice: a parent must decide which role to put first at a given moment, and that decision often causes guilt about the role that lost out.
Conflict between partners: one partner may not support the other's employment, or the couple may compete over career priorities, so each feels the other is getting in the way.
Conflict with the employer: an employer may expect availability, such as late meetings or travel, that clashes with school hours and childcare arrangements.
Effects include stress, guilt, and tension and arguments between partners. Employment may suffer through absence or missed promotion.
Outcome for the family: children may feel lonely or neglected, and the family may need outside help to resolve the conflict.
Every household has two sets of jobs: caring for the children and caring for the home. How a dual-earner couple divides them decides whether the family copes or falls into overload and conflict.

Parental responsibilities include feeding, dressing, supervising, school runs and collections, helping with homework, health care, emotional support, discipline and play, and transporting and supporting children.
Home-care responsibilities include cooking, cleaning, laundry, shopping, budgeting, bills, repairs, the garden and maintaining the home.
Fair sharing: in the modern pattern, partners agree which tasks each one owns, so that tasks are not done only when one partner asks for help. Fathers are more involved in childcare.
Labour-saving appliances, such as washing machines, dishwashers, microwave ovens and slow cookers, reduce the time needed for home-care tasks, which frees time for the family.
Outside help, such as paid childcare, a childminder, cleaning services, or grandparents and other relatives, takes over some parental and home-care duties.
Older children can take on age-appropriate tasks, such as tidying their rooms or setting the table, which builds independence.

Benefits of sharing: less overload, stronger parent-child bonds including father-child bonds, and fairer family relationships. When both parents take an active part in care, children see shared parenting as normal, which models gender equality and shows that men and women have equal roles.

Drawbacks if tasks are not shared or are poorly managed: resentment and arguments, one partner carrying a double shift (a full day of paid work followed by the home tasks), and children given too much responsibility.
Having two earners changes family life in both good and bad ways. The balance depends on how tasks are shared, how childcare is arranged and how flexible the employers are.
Positive: a second income raises household living standards and reduces financial worry, and it gives security if one job is lost.
Positive: both partners gain independence and self-esteem, and parents gain wider social contact through work.
Positive: children may become more independent when they take on responsibilities, and they see their parents working, which gives them a role model for work and equal roles.
Positive: when parents share tasks, children learn that care and housework are shared responsibilities.
Negative: less time for shared family activities, conversation and leisure, and tiredness and stress, which can weaken family relationships. The couple may also have less time for each other.
Negative: children may feel lonely, neglected or left out, especially at times such as after school or when they are ill.
Negative: extra responsibility falls on older children, who may become carers for younger siblings. Less time for home tasks can also mean meals eaten out or convenience foods.
Negative: childcare costs can absorb a large part of the second income, and the family may face role overload and role conflict.

Employers and employees use working arrangements that give more control over when and where work is done, and families add supports at home. Together they make it easier to hold a job and care for a family.
Flexitime: the employee chooses start and finish times within agreed limits, so that the working day can fit around school hours.
Job-sharing: two employees share one full-time post, dividing the hours and responsibilities between them.

Parental leave: unpaid leave taken to care for a child, which may be taken in blocks or spread over an agreed period. Under the Parental Leave Act 1998 (as amended) it is 26 weeks unpaid leave per child under 12.

Other leave arrangements are provided under the Maternity Protection Acts 1994 and 2004, the Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016, the Parent's Leave and Benefit Act 2019 and the Carer's Leave Act 2001, and force majeure leave covers family emergencies.
Career break: a temporary period of unpaid leave that allows the employee to return to the same job later.
Teleworking: working from home reduces commuting time and lets a parent be available around the home.

Part-time and term-time work: reduced hours allow the employee to be at home during school hours or school holidays. Compressed working week: longer working days over fewer days free up time for family commitments.

At home and at work: help from childcare, after-school care and relatives, sharing housework, labour-saving appliances, planning such as meal planning, shopping lists and online shopping, and family meetings to share the load. Employers can help with flexible hours, crèche facilities and understanding about family emergencies.
A class survey shows how real households divide tasks and whether traditional sex roles still hold. This investigation uses a questionnaire about twenty home tasks.
Aim: to find out how male and female family members share twenty named home tasks in a sample of households.
Method step 1: list twenty home tasks, such as cooking, ironing, grocery shopping, car maintenance, paying bills, childminding, gardening, cleaning the bathroom and DIY.
Method step 2: design a questionnaire that asks who usually does each task: mainly male, mainly female, shared or someone else.
Method step 3: survey a sample of students, or their parents, and ask respondents to answer about their own household.
Method step 4: keep responses anonymous, so that no family or individual can be identified and people can answer honestly.
Analysis: count the answers in each category for each task and express each category as a percentage of the total answers, so you can find which tasks are mostly male, mostly female or shared.

Conclusion: the results show whether the sample's home tasks are still divided on traditional sex-role lines or are shared. Compare the results with traditional roles and link them to dual-earner households.
Limits: a small sample, bias in who answers and how honest the answers are can all weaken the conclusions.
Choosing child care starts with the family, not the service. A family's working pattern, support network, budget and school calendar decide which options are even possible.
Working pattern: whether both parents, or a lone parent, are in paid work, and how many hours each works. Shift work or irregular hours need a more flexible carer than a regular nine-to-five job.
Support network: whether grandparents, other relatives or friends are available and willing to mind the child. If they are, the family may need little or no paid care.
Cost: what the family can afford to pay, which may limit the options available. Some families qualify for a State subsidy towards the cost of registered child care.
After-school and holiday cover: school closing times and school holidays create gaps that the family must fill, because school usually finishes before work does and the holidays are long.
Once the family's situation is clear, it must be matched to what a service can actually offer. These requirements test whether an option is practical, reliable and right for the child.
Availability and convenience: the option must have a place free and be open at the times needed, and be reachable without a long journey.
Hours and flexibility: the option must cover the parents' hours, including early starts, late finishes and changing shifts.
Proximity: a service near home, school or work reduces travel time for the child and the parent.
Child's age or special needs: the option must suit the child's stage of development and any additional care needs, including health needs.
Reliability: the option must stay open during staff illness and closures, so that the parent is not left without cover if the carer is ill or the service closes.
Quality: safety and hygiene, staff qualifications, the activities provided and the ratio of staff to children all matter, as do the parents' trust in the carer and whether the child is happy there.
Some options care for children for the whole working day. They differ in who the carer is, where the care happens and who employs them.

Crèche or day nursery: a centre with trained staff that cares for children in groups during the working day, usually open all day, in premises used for that purpose, with structured routines and play.

Childminder: an adult who minds one or a small number of children in the minder's own home. The setting is a home, the attention is personal and the hours are often flexible. A childminder is self-employed.
Nanny: a carer employed by the family, who usually looks after the children of that one family in the family home. The family is the employer.

Au pair: a young person, often from abroad, who lives with the host family and provides childcare and does light household duties in exchange for board and pocket money. An au pair is not a trained carer or nanny, works limited hours and suits older children or extra support.

Relative or friend: a grandparent, aunt, uncle or friend who minds the child informally. This is usually low cost or free and familiar and trusted, but it depends on the helper's health and availability.
Employer or workplace crèche: care provided at or near the workplace by the employer, which saves the parent a separate journey.
Other options fill part of the day. After-school groups cover the gap when school ends, while pre-school services give younger children a few hours of play and learning.
After-school group: a service that collects children from school and cares for them until a parent finishes work. Some also run holiday or summer camps and may offer homework help and activities.
Playschool or playgroup: a sessional service (one that runs in set sessions) for pre-school children, mainly play-based, usually for a few hours in the morning or afternoon.
Montessori: a pre-school method, following the educational ideas of Maria Montessori, that encourages self-directed learning through structured materials and activities.
Naíonra: an Irish-medium pre-school (naíonraí is the plural), where the children learn through the Irish language by play. Naíonraí are supported by Forbairt Naíonraí.

Pre-school under the national free pre-school scheme (ECCE): State-funded pre-school hours in the year or years before primary school, in registered services, so the family does not pay for the funded sessions.
Parents hand their children to carers they do not supervise, so the State regulates child care. Knowing who registers and inspects a service tells parents what to check before they choose.

Early years services (crèches, playschools, Montessori schools, naíonraí and after-school services) must be registered with Tusla, the Child and Family Agency. Tusla's early years inspectorate inspects them under the Child Care Act 1991 (Early Years Services) Regulations 2016.
This is why parents should check that a service is registered and read its inspection reports. Staff-to-child ratios are set by regulation.

Childminders: the Child Care (Amendment) Act 2024 and the Child Care Act 1991 (Early Years Services) (Childminding Services) Regulations 2024 bring childminders into Tusla registration. Registration opened on 30 September 2024 and is currently voluntary, with mandatory registration due after a transition period.

Registered childminders can take part in the National Childcare Scheme. Parents should ask whether a childminder is registered, has training, Garda vetting (a police check), references, insurance and emergency cover.
The National Childcare Scheme (NCS) is the State's scheme that subsidises the cost of registered child care according to the family's circumstances.
Pre-school is more than minding children while parents work. It is the first place many children learn to mix with others and begin to learn, which prepares them for primary school.
Children become more socially aware by playing and interacting with other children.
Children form relationships outside the home and learn to share and take turns.
Children become more independent and confident when they are cared for away from their parents.
Intellectual development is supported through activities that build language, number, listening, problem-solving and creativity skills, which also prepares children for primary school.
Physical development is supported through games and active play, which build coordination and fine motor skills (the small, precise movements of hands and fingers).
Emotional development: children learn to separate from their parents, which builds self-esteem.
Pre-school also helps working parents, because the child is cared for in a safe, structured setting.
A crèche suits parents with regular hours who want trained staff and structure. Its strengths come from being a larger, organised centre, and its weaknesses come from the same thing.
Advantages: fixed daily opening hours, which suit parents with regular working patterns and make the service reliable.
Advantages: several staff care for a group of children, so cover is available when one staff member is absent.
Advantages: structured activities and peer play (play with other children) support the child's social and intellectual development.
Advantages: staff often hold early-childhood qualifications and work to a written programme, and the service is registered and inspected.
Disadvantages: fixed hours give little flexibility when a parent's shift changes at short notice, and travel must happen at set times.
Disadvantages: group care exposes young children to infections, so they may be ill more often.
Disadvantages: fees are often charged by the session or by the week, and can be a significant cost for the family.
Disadvantages: the child gets less individual attention and may be unsettled by a large group.
A childminder offers a small, home-like setting, which many parents prefer for babies and young children. The trade-off is that everything depends on one person.
Advantages: care is given in a home setting with a small group, which suits very young children and babies.
Advantages: childminders are often able to offer flexible or extended hours.
Advantages: the child receives individual attention and the minder may collect children from school.
Advantages: a childminder is often cheaper for a family with several children.
Disadvantages: the service depends on one adult, so illness, holidays or an emergency can leave the family without cover.
Disadvantages: the range of planned educational activities may be narrower than in a larger centre, and there are fewer facilities.
Disadvantages: quality depends on the minder, so the family must check registration with Tusla, experience, training, vetting, safety and insurance before making a decision.
To judge any option fairly, a family uses the same set of criteria each time. These criteria come straight from the family's requirements.
Cost: the total weekly cost, including fees, extras such as meals or outings, and the cost of travel.
Hours and location: whether the opening hours and the journey time fit the parents' working day.
Hygiene and safety: cleanliness of premises, safe equipment, secure entry and a safety policy.
Staff qualifications and training: the level of early-childhood training held by the staff, and the ratio of staff to children.
Staffing cover: what happens when a staff member is ill or on leave.
Activities and learning: the play, learning and outdoor activities provided for the child's age.
Suitability for the child: whether the option meets any additional needs and whether the child is happy there.
Investigating the options in your area: research each option's type, cost, hours, registration and activities, then compare them in a table.

An evaluation compares each option with the family's requirements, then weighs its advantages against its disadvantages. Any two options can be chosen, but a crèche and a childminder is the usual pair.
Step 1: identify the two options and the family requirements they must meet, such as hours, cost, reliability and the child's age.
Step 2: test each option against each requirement, rating how well it meets it.
Step 3: compare the options point by point; a crèche offers fixed hours and cover for absent staff, while a childminder offers flexibility and a home setting.
Step 4: identify which requirement decides the choice; for a family whose hours change often, flexibility may outweigh a crèche's structure.
Step 5: state the conclusion, showing which option suits which family and what the family must check before choosing.
Other pairs work too. An au pair is low cost and flexible in the home but untrained and short-term, while an after-school group is structured and registered but only covers after school.
A playschool, Montessori school or naíonra is educational and sociable, but runs only a few hours each day, so another arrangement is needed to cover the working day.
Leisure is time, not an activity. An activity counts as leisure when the person chooses it freely in time left over after necessary tasks.
Leisure is the residual time (the time left over) after essential activities have been completed.
Essential activities include paid work, travel to work, school and study, sleep, meals, personal care, household tasks and caring for dependants. These come first, so they are not leisure.
The individual chooses how to spend leisure time, for ease, relaxation or enjoyment. Because it is freely chosen, leisure is not the same as free time spent on chores.
Leisure pursuits are the activities a person chooses within leisure time, such as sport, music, reading, hobbies, crafts, gardening, socialising, drama, games, cinema and travel.
The same activity can be work for one person and leisure for another, for example gardening or cooking, depending on whether it is chosen and enjoyed.
Leisure can be active (sport, walking, dance) or passive (reading, TV, listening to music), and can be done alone, with friends or with family.
Sport is only one form of leisure, so do not treat leisure and sport as the same thing.
Leisure does more than fill spare time. It gives individuals, families and society a set of benefits, which matter more today because many jobs are sedentary and pressured.
Relaxation: leisure relieves the stress and fatigue that come from paid work, study and daily demands, so people recover and cope better.
Physical wellbeing: active leisure improves fitness, weight control, heart health and strong bones and muscles, and helps prevent illness. This matters more as many jobs involve sitting.
Skill development: leisure allows people to learn and practise new skills, from swimming to a musical instrument.
Challenge: competitive and creative pursuits give a sense of achievement and personal growth.
Social interaction: leisure brings people together, forming friendships and wider social networks and community involvement, which reduces isolation.
Family bonding: shared leisure builds relationships, communication and shared memories between family members.
Modelling: parents who use free time constructively are role models, showing children how to do the same.
Work-life balance: leisure offsets the demands of work and helps people sustain their working lives, staying productive and avoiding burnout. It also gives enjoyment and gratifies the senses.
Leisure benefits the wider community as well as individuals, because what people do in their free time adds up across a whole society.
A healthier population results when many people take part in active leisure, which reduces demands on health services.
Tourism and sport industries grow from people's demand for leisure activities and travel, which provides jobs and activity in the economy.
Community spirit is strengthened when people join clubs, teams and local events together.
Leisure can be pursued by a person on their own or shared by a household. Each kind gives different benefits, and families need to balance both.
Individual leisure: a person chooses and pursues an activity alone or with a group that is not their family, such as a solo hobby, running or a club.
Family leisure: members of one household take part together, such as family outings, walks, cycling, picnics, meals out, board games, cooking, holidays, sport or games at home.
Family leisure builds bonds, communication and a shared identity, and gives children common experiences and memories.
Family leisure needs activities suitable for all ages and a cost the family can manage, so everyone can take part.
Individual leisure allows a person to develop personal interests, independence and identity, which can benefit the whole family.
Leisure helps people develop in different ways. Physical and social development are two of the areas examiners name, so give each its own heading in an answer.
Physical development: sports and active pursuits build muscle tone, improve fitness and increase energy levels.
Physical development: coordination is developed through activities such as ball games, dance and gymnastics, and skills such as swimming are learned.

Physical development: weight-bearing activities, such as walking, running and dancing, help reduce the risk of osteoporosis (a condition where bones become weak and brittle) and help with weight control.
Social development: team sports require co-operation, communication and sharing of responsibility.
Social development: winning and losing teach people to cope with success and failure, which they meet in wider life.
Social development: joining a club or team helps a person make new friends, expand their social circle and feel they belong to a community.
Social development: leisure can develop leadership skills, for example through captaining a team or running a club.
Leisure also shapes how people feel and think. Examiners sometimes add intellectual development to physical, social and emotional development.
Emotional development: competitive activities can improve self-esteem and confidence, and give a sense of achievement.
Emotional development: relaxing pursuits such as yoga, reading or gardening reduce stress and support mental wellbeing.
Emotional development: being part of a team or community gives a sense of belonging, and coping with success and failure builds resilience.
Emotional development: fun and enjoyment encourage positive emotions and a positive outlook.
Intellectual development: card games, bridge, chess and puzzles develop concentration, analysis, problem solving and planning.
Intellectual development: debating and drama develop listening skills, argument and self-expression, and creative pursuits such as art encourage creativity and learning.
What people do in their free time is shaped by the society and culture around them, not only by personal taste.
Social group: a person's socio-economic group affects which activities are available and affordable.
Local factors: the clubs, facilities and transport in a person's area shape which activities they can join.
Trends: popular activities, such as skateboarding, spread through peer groups and the media, and greater access to foreign travel has made it a common leisure choice.
Technology, social media and education also shape leisure choices, because they change what people know about and can do.

Culture: traditions tied to a country or region, such as hurling, Gaelic football, camogie, Irish music and Irish dancing in Ireland. The GAA (Gaelic Athletic Association) is the national amateur sports body.
Religious and community traditions, and a family's ethnic and cultural background, also influence the activities people take up.
Family traditions: activities handed down through families, such as music or sport, shape a person's leisure from childhood, so children often take up the leisure activities their parents enjoy.
A person's job decides how much time and money they have for leisure, and even the kind of leisure they want.
Disposable income: the money left after essential spending determines how much can be spent on leisure.
Cost of leisure: membership fees, joining fees, pay-as-you-go charges and special clothing or equipment, plus travel, all add to the cost.
Low-cost choices: people with little disposable income often choose free or inexpensive activities, such as walking, the library or the park.
Working hours: long or irregular hours reduce the time available for leisure.
Type of work: a sedentary (desk-based) worker may choose an energetic activity, and an active worker may prefer a quiet pursuit, so leisure balances the job.
Leisure can be an extension of work, for example when a person's job involves sport or the arts, or when colleagues' clubs lead to a new pastime.
Part-time work, job-sharing and career breaks create more time for leisure.
Recession: a fall in income reduces spending on costly activities such as foreign holidays, while people spend more time on free or home-based activities.
Leisure changes as a family moves through the life cycle (the stages from young adults, to parents of young children, to retirement). The stage a person is at matters more than their age alone.
Young people have fewer commitments and more time for leisure, and teenagers often prefer to spend leisure time with their peers.
Couples with young children usually have the least time and disposable income for leisure, because childcare takes both.
Families with school-going children often have leisure built around school sport, clubs and outings.
Retired couples usually have more time and often more money for leisure.
Older people may have physical limits that restrict them to less strenuous or sedentary pursuits.
Some activities are regarded as too dangerous for young children, so families choose age-appropriate pursuits that are suitable and safe for them.
Gender can affect which leisure activities people choose and how much time they have for them.
Some activities are male- or female-dominated, which can affect whether a person feels welcome to take part.
Gender affects the time available for leisure, because household and caring duties still fall mainly on women in many families. Traditionally women had less time for this reason.
Changing gender roles have reduced the strength of traditional divisions in leisure choices, and many sports and activities are now open to everyone, though some differences remain.
Two further factors affect what a person can do in their leisure time.
Health and ability limit or shape the activities a person can take part in.
The facilities available locally decide which activities are within reach.
This practical shows how much of a day is really leisure and what leisure costs. It also lets you compare families at different stages of the life cycle.
Aim: to find out how a person spends their day and how much of that time is leisure.
Method step 1: keep a record of each hour of a typical day, noting each activity.
Method step 2: sort each entry into essential activities (sleep, personal care, paid work, household tasks) and leisure.
Method step 3: add the hours in each category and express the leisure time as a percentage of the day.
Method step 4: list each leisure pursuit and cost it, including membership fees, equipment, travel and pay-as-you-go charges.
Method step 5: list the physical, social, emotional and intellectual benefits of each pursuit beside its cost, so that value can be judged.
Case study method: compare the time-use records of families at different life-cycle stages, such as a young couple, a couple with young children, teenagers and a retired couple.

Leisure facilities in a community come from three kinds of provider: public bodies, commercial businesses and voluntary groups. Each is paid for and run differently, and that shapes the cost, range and condition a user can expect.

Public facilities are often provided or part-funded by local authorities (councils). They include swimming pools, leisure centres, libraries, parks, playgrounds, sports pitches, walking and cycling trails, community halls and arts centres.
Commercial facilities are private businesses run for profit, such as gyms and private health clubs, cinemas, bowling alleys, golf clubs, cafés and entertainment venues.
Commercial facilities depend on fees from users for their income, so the fee charged must cover running costs and make a profit.

Voluntary and community facilities are run by non-profit groups and volunteers. They include GAA clubs, soccer and tennis clubs, youth clubs, active retirement groups, drama and musical societies, and community centres.
Voluntary facilities are funded by membership fees, fundraising and grants, so they are not free: clubs usually charge a membership fee.
Voluntary facilities depend on volunteers and member subscriptions, so their range and condition vary from club to club.

Some facilities suit particular groups. Retired people, for example, often use golf, bingo, gym or leisure centre classes, library and book clubs, the swimming pool, the cinema, a choir or musical society, a drama group and card games.

An evaluation judges a facility against fixed criteria, so that two facilities can be compared on the same basis. A list of features is not an evaluation: you must weigh strengths against weaknesses for a particular user.
Cost: the fees charged, judged against what the user can afford, including membership and joining fees, pay-as-you-go charges, class fees, equipment, clothing, travel and concessions.
Value for money: the benefit the user gains, judged against the cost. It depends on how often the facility is used and whether it suits the user.
Location and accessibility: the ease of reaching the facility and using it, including distance, transport, parking and access for people with disabilities.

Range and quality: the number and variety of activities, such as pools, classes, courts or equipment, and the condition of the equipment. Classes should suit different ages and abilities, and there should be family provision.
Convenience: whether the opening hours and booking arrangements suit the user's working and family pattern. Crowding, waiting time and childcare on site also matter.
Safety, hygiene and staffing: clean changing rooms and equipment, qualified instructors and lifeguards, supervision during sessions, first aid, security and emergency procedures.
Atmosphere and suitability: whether the facility suits the user's age, gender, interests and ability, and whether it suits individual or family use.
Benefits: social (the chance to meet people and join groups, classes or teams), physical (fitness), emotional (relaxation) and intellectual (skill).

A facility is only useful if the person can reach it and use it at a time that suits them. Accessibility is about getting there and getting in, and convenience is about fitting the facility into daily life.
Location: a facility close to home or work reduces travel time and cost, so it is more likely to be used regularly.
Transport: the availability of buses or trains and the provision of parking affect how easily a user can get there.
Access for people with disabilities: ramps, lifts, accessible changing rooms and pool hoists allow people with mobility difficulties to use the facility.
Opening hours: early, late and weekend hours suit people who work or attend school during the day.
Booking systems: online booking and advance booking of classes make it easier to plan use, while queues and walk-in only systems can discourage use.
Family access: facilities that allow children and adults to use the same area together make family leisure easier to organise.
On-site childcare, short waiting times and uncrowded sessions also make a facility more convenient to use.
The price on the door is only part of what a facility costs. To judge it fairly you need to add up every kind of cost the user will meet over a period such as a year.
Membership fee: a regular fee, usually paid monthly or yearly, that gives unlimited or extended use of the facility.
Joining fee: a one-off payment made when a person first becomes a member of a facility.

Two types of charge a facility makes: fixed charges, such as a membership or joining fee, do not change with use, while variable charges, such as pay-as-you-go, class and equipment fees, rise with each visit.
Pay-as-you-go charge: a fee paid each time the facility is used, which suits people who visit only occasionally. Membership suits regular users.
Class and course fees: extra charges for instructor-led sessions, which are often separate from the basic entry or membership fee.
Concessions: reduced fees for students, children, older people, unemployed people and families, which lower the cost for these groups.
Hidden costs: travel, equipment, clothing, locker or towel hire, parking and refreshments add to the total cost of using a facility.
Total annual cost: the sum of membership or joining fees, pay-as-you-go charges, class fees, extras and travel for one year.
Cost is not the same as value. A low price does not make a facility good, because value compares what the user gains with what the user pays.
Value is the benefit a person gains from a facility, measured in fitness, enjoyment, social contact and skill.
Value for money is the benefit gained for each euro spent, so a cheap facility that is rarely used may offer poor value.
A facility offers more value when its range of activities matches the user's interests, and when the user actually uses those activities.
Cost per visit is found by dividing the total annual cost by the number of visits made in the year.
A low cost per visit shows that the facility is used often, which generally means better value for regular users.
Value depends on the user: a person who uses only the pool may find a high-fee gym poor value, even though it offers more activities.
A dearer facility used often may give better value than a cheap one used rarely, so value depends on use.
The syllabus asks for a cost and value comparison of two facilities. Follow the same steps each time so that the comparison is fair and ends in a justified conclusion for a named user or family.

Step 1: select two facilities that serve the same community and are used for the same purpose, such as fitness or swimming, for example a local authority leisure centre and a private gym, or a community club and a commercial club.
Step 2: find each facility's fees: membership, joining, pay-as-you-go and class fees. To investigate, list the facilities, visit them or check their websites, and collect the fees.
Step 3: calculate the total annual cost of each facility, including the travel cost of getting there.
Step 4: estimate the number of visits per year for the user, and divide the total annual cost by that number to find the cost per visit.

Step 5: list the benefits each facility gives the user, including fitness, social contact, relaxation and skill, and compare them with the cost. Also compare location, access, hours, range of activities, condition, safety, staffing and atmosphere.
Step 6: state which facility gives better value for the user, and say what would change the conclusion, such as a change in visits or income, or a different household member.
An evaluation ends in a judgement, not a list. You weigh each facility's strengths against its weaknesses for a particular user, then suggest how the facility could do better.
An evaluation weighs the strengths of each facility against its weaknesses, then reaches a judgement for a named type of user.
A facility with low fees but few activities may suit a student who wants cheap exercise, but not a family wanting varied activities.

When you name a facility, give two developed points, each a strength or a limit. For example, a swimming pool gives low-impact exercise and social contact for retired people, but may involve travel and set sessions.

Improvements a facility could make include extended opening hours, reduced fees or concessions for families and older people, better access for people with disabilities, and more classes for older people or families.
Improvements to booking and information, such as online booking and online timetables, make a facility easier to use and so raise its value.
Being out of work is not the same as being unemployed. Unemployment is being without paid work while being willing and able to take up work, and statisticians apply a strict three-part test.
Three conditions must all be met: the person has no paid employment, is available to start work, and is actively seeking work. Missing any one of them means the person is not counted as unemployed.
Paid work is the test, so unpaid work such as volunteering or caring at home does not make a person employed.
Available for work: the person could start work within a short period, normally within two weeks, so someone who could not take a job for months is not counted.

Actively seeking work: the person has taken specific steps to find work, such as applying for posts, answering advertisements, contacting employers or registering with Intreo, the Department of Social Protection's public employment service. Registering is one such step, not proof on its own.

Students, people in full-time home duties, retired people and those unable to work through illness or disability are not counted as unemployed, because they are not available for work or are not seeking it.
A person in part-time work who wants more hours is counted as employed in the standard measure (such a person is underemployed).
To judge how serious unemployment is, a count of unemployed people has to be set against the number of people who could be working. That is what the unemployment rate does.
The labour force is the number of people in employment plus the number of unemployed people.
The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people divided by the labour force, multiplied by 100.
A rate is more useful than a raw total when comparing periods or areas, because the size of the labour force changes over time.

The Central Statistics Office (CSO) measures unemployment in Ireland using the definition set by the International Labour Organization (ILO). Its Labour Force Survey is a household survey that gives the standardised unemployment rate, the official measure, published monthly and quoted seasonally adjusted.

The Live Register is the Department of Social Protection's count of people claiming jobseeker payments (signing on), mainly Jobseeker's Benefit and Jobseeker's Allowance. It includes some part-time, casual and seasonal workers, so it is not the official unemployment figure.
Unemployment is also described by how long it lasts, because a short gap between jobs is a very different problem from years without work.
Short-term unemployment is a brief spell out of work, usually between jobs or after leaving education.
Frictional unemployment is short-term unemployment caused by the normal time workers take to move from one job to another, for example while applications are made and interviews arranged.
Long-term unemployment is being out of work for one year or more.
Long-term unemployment is harder to escape because skills, habits and confidence erode with time, which makes re-entry to work harder.
Young people have tended to have higher rates of unemployment than older workers, especially in downturns.
The extent of unemployment means how many people are unemployed, as a rate and as a number, and how that changes over time. It follows the economic cycle: it rises in recession and falls in growth.

The Labour Force Survey, a household survey by the Central Statistics Office, produces the standardised unemployment rate. The Live Register, kept by the Department of Social Protection, counts people claiming jobseeker payments, including some part-time workers, so it is not the standard measure.
Unemployment was low in the boom years of the 2000s, then rose sharply after the economic downturn that began in 2008, with construction and related professions worst affected.
Retail and service industries also shed jobs during the downturn as consumer spending fell.
Unemployment peaked at roughly 15% in the early 2010s and then fell steadily as the economy recovered and jobs returned in construction, retail, services and multinational firms.
Emigration rose during the downturn. It held the measured rate down, because people who left are no longer in the labour force, so the rate alone understates the damage.
Unemployment is not spread evenly. It is higher among young people and among people with few or no qualifications, and rates differ between regions.

Unemployment black spots, areas that lost their main employer, tend to keep higher rates for longer than areas with plenty of work. Long-term unemployment forms a hard core that remains when the overall rate falls.
The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 caused a sudden temporary rise in joblessness, and the State paid a temporary pandemic unemployment payment.

These causes come from when and where work is available rather than from the workers themselves. Some jobs exist only at certain times of year, and some regions simply have far fewer jobs than others.

Seasonal unemployment means jobs that depend on the time of year, for example in construction, farming, fishing, tourism and hotels, which slow down in winter because of weather and fewer visitors. It is predictable and temporary.
Seasonal workers in these industries are often laid off each winter and re-employed in spring or summer, so they are out of work only in the off-season.

Geographical unemployment means jobs are concentrated in certain regions, usually the larger cities and their commuter areas, so people living far from employment centres are more likely to be out of work.
Moving to where the jobs are costs money and means leaving family, which is why many people stay out of work in areas with few vacancies.
Unemployment black spots are areas that lost their main employer, such as a factory closure, and keep high unemployment for many years.
When a local firm closes, job losses spread to suppliers, shops and services that depended on its workers' spending, which adds to the unemployment.
Outward migration (rural depopulation) is when young and skilled people leave rural areas to find work. Shops, schools, post offices and services then close, so fewer local jobs remain.
Rural depopulation is both a cause and a result of unemployment: people leave because there is no work, and their leaving removes more jobs.
Changes in production methods and in the structure of industry reduce the number of jobs available, and workers whose skills are out of date are the first to lose out.

Technical (technological) unemployment happens when machines, automation, computers and robots replace workers, for example automated production lines and robots in manufacturing, self-service checkouts, and self-service and online banking that reduces the number of bank tellers.
Difficulty adapting means workers whose skills no longer match industry needs struggle to find new work, particularly older workers and those with few qualifications, because retraining is hard.

Ireland's economy has shifted away from primary industries such as agriculture and fishing, and secondary industries such as manufacturing, which employ fewer people than in the past, towards services, information technology and pharma/science, which need new skills.
Globalisation (the global economy) means manufacturers may relocate production to countries with lower labour costs, removing jobs from Ireland.
A world recession also cuts demand for Irish exports and so jobs, because Ireland is an open economy that depends on world trade and foreign investment.
Rising educational requirements mean many jobs now require qualifications, so people with few or none are excluded from applying.
Firms hire workers to meet demand for what they sell. Unemployment rises when demand falls, because firms cut output and staff.

A recession reduces consumer spending, so firms reduce production and make workers redundant. National and international recession was the main cause of the rise in unemployment after 2008, and economic growth reverses it.
Cheaper imported goods reduce demand for Irish-made products, and the firms producing them cut jobs.
Online shopping from abroad and cheaper foreign holidays move spending away from Irish shops and tourism businesses, so those businesses lose sales and jobs.
Unemployment reduces household income, which reduces spending further and causes more job losses in local shops and services. This is a downward spiral.
High wage and other costs can reduce the competitiveness of Irish firms against rivals abroad, leading to lost sales and job losses. High wages are one factor, not the only cause.
Residual unemployment is the hard core of people who stay out of work even when the economy is growing and vacancies exist.
Causes include poor skills or education, a long time out of work, ill health or disability, age, discrimination, and living in an area with few jobs or far from jobs.
Residual unemployment persists during economic growth, so growth alone does not bring unemployment to zero.
Long-term unemployed people make up much of the residual group, because time out of work makes employers less willing to hire them.
Some groups face barriers in addition to the general level of demand for labour. Each group has its own typical reason for higher unemployment.
Travellers and ethnic minorities can face discrimination in recruitment and may have lower qualifications.
Asylum seekers may face restrictions on the right to work while their application is decided. Refugees and migrants may face language barriers and non-recognition of foreign qualifications.
People with disabilities or long-term ill health may be excluded because employers doubt their ability to do the work, and access and transport barriers can also keep them out.
Homeless people lack an address, clothing or hygiene facilities, which makes applying for and keeping a job very difficult.
People with criminal records face employers' mistrust.

Homeless people, people with criminal records and early school leavers face employers who are unaware of their abilities, and often lack skills or qualifications; early school leavers may lack qualifications and literacy.
Long-term unemployed people may have out-of-date skills after time out of work.
Residents of unemployment black spots face few local vacancies and may need to travel or move to find work.

Work gives a person income, purpose and a place in society, so losing it hits a person's money, status and wellbeing at the same time. These are individual effects, felt by the person who lost the job.
Financial insecurity: lost income forces people to cut spending and lower their living standard, and to rely on savings, credit or welfare payments, which are lower than a wage.
Debt: unpaid bills and loans build up, which can lead to mortgage or rent arrears (payments missed) and, in serious cases, repossession of the home or homelessness.
Loss of identity and status: work gives identity, purpose and social standing, so unemployed people may feel undervalued, worthless, a failure or guilty, and lose self-esteem.
Stress, anxiety and depression: long-term unemployment can create feelings of hopelessness, and stress and depression can in turn affect a person's health.
Social isolation: losing work removes daily contact with colleagues, and having less money for leisure reduces participation in social activities.
Loss of daily routine can lead to boredom.
Addiction: some people turn to alcohol, drugs or gambling to cope, which adds to their difficulties.
Loss of skills over time and falling confidence make it harder to get a job, so a person can slip into long-term unemployment.
Young people who cannot find work are at the start of adult life, so unemployment delays the steps that normally follow a first job.
Delayed independence: without a wage, a young adult may have to remain at the parental home instead of moving out.
Delay in starting a family or buying a home, because there is no steady income to save or borrow against.
Risk of emigrating in search of work, which takes the young person away from family and friends.
When an adult loses a job, the whole household feels it. These are family effects, felt by the people who live together and share the household income.
Reduced income lowers the family's standard of living, so it may struggle to afford food, clothing, heating and other household bills, and it relies on welfare payments.
Debt and housing risk: arrears on rent, mortgage or utilities build up, and families that fall behind on rent or mortgage repayments face a risk of losing the home and of homelessness.
Financial pressure, changed roles within the household and the stress of one or both adults being at home cause arguments and strain relationships.
Relationship strain can lead, in some cases, to separation or family breakdown.
Children may have to give up activities such as sports, music lessons or school trips, and may feel different from classmates or be teased.
Family members may emigrate for work, which breaks up the family's support network.
Reliance on welfare payments can shape family finances for long periods.
Children grow up in the household, so the effects of unemployment can follow them into school and into their own working lives.
Children's educational opportunities suffer when a family cannot pay for books, technology or a quiet place to study.
Children of unemployed parents have fewer working role models (people whose working life they can copy), which can lower their expectations of work.
Intergenerational unemployment: children raised in a household with no one in work may come to expect unemployment, so the disadvantage is repeated when they reach working age.
Financial pressure at home can lead to early school leaving, which reduces the qualifications children take into the labour market.
Unemployment is also a cost to the whole community and the State, because jobless people stop paying into the system and start drawing on it. These are society effects.
Cost to the State: higher spending is needed on social welfare payments and related supports such as medical cards, fuel and housing supports, and taxes may have to rise to pay for it.
Loss of income tax and social insurance (PRSI) income means less money for public services.
Loss of production and skills: the economy's output falls and unused skills are wasted.
Crime, antisocial behaviour and vandalism can follow in areas with high long-term unemployment. This is an association with those areas, not a rule about unemployed people.
Emigration of working-age and skilled workers reduces the population, the skills base and future tax income.
The black economy grows, as unpaid or undeclared work avoids tax and PRSI, so the State loses that income.
Social exclusion and inequality: people cut off from work, income and social networks become harder to reintegrate, and the gap widens between those in work and those without.
Pressure on health and community services: more people use mental health, addiction and counselling services, and local authorities, voluntary bodies and community groups take on more work.
A black spot is an area of very high unemployment. When many people in one place lose their jobs, the effects feed on each other and the whole area declines.
Falling local spending closes shops and services, which causes further job losses in the area.
Population loss reduces the number of users of local schools and transport, making services harder to keep open, because people move away in search of work.
Black spots acquire a poor reputation, which deters investment and new businesses.
People still in work feel it too: they face job insecurity and fear of redundancy, and where an area empties there is less local demand for their products and services.
The levels are connected, and an answer is stronger when it shows how one effect leads to the next.
Effects chain from one level to the next: lost income (individual) leads to arrears and strain (family) and, multiplied across a town, to closed shops and falling tax income (society).

The same effect can sit at more than one level, but give it once, at the level the question asks about. For example, depression is an individual effect, while the cost of treating it falls on society.
Marks go to answers that cover every level the question names, with each effect named and explained.
Cover each level asked for: at least one effect for the individual, the family and society, then further effects.
Give each point a name and a short explanation of why it follows, for example lost income, so debt.
Poverty is more than having a low income. It is a lack of the income and resources needed for basic needs and for normal participation in society, and it is examined through two concepts.
Poverty means being without enough income and resources (material, cultural and social) for an acceptable standard of living.
It means inadequate food, clothing, shelter and warmth, because there is not enough income or resources to pay for them.

It also means being unable to take part in socially acceptable activities that most people take for granted, which is why poverty brings social exclusion (being shut out from ordinary community life).
Poverty includes the lack of opportunities, comforts and self-respect that other people enjoy, so it cannot be measured by income alone.
Poverty is examined through two concepts: absolute poverty and relative poverty.
Absolute poverty is the most severe form: a person cannot afford the things needed to stay alive and healthy.
Absolute poverty is income too low to meet basic physical needs for food, clothing, warmth and shelter, so health and survival are threatened.
The standard is a fixed minimum, set regardless of how other people in society live. It does not change with the living standards of the surrounding society.
Absolute poverty is rare in a developed country like Ireland, but homeless people, and people living without proper housing, clothing or medical care, may experience it.
In Ireland the main concern is relative poverty rather than absolute poverty.
Relative poverty is judged against the living standards of the society in which a person lives, so it exists even in a wealthy country.
