A person in relative poverty lives below the standard of living that society regards as basic, so cannot take part in activities that are normal for others.

The poverty line is the level of income below which a household is counted as poor: the estimated minimum income for basic food, clothing and shelter and an acceptable standard of living. A household below it is at risk of poverty.

In Irish official statistics the Central Statistics Office (CSO) sets the line at 60% of median equivalised household income. The median is the middle income, and equivalised means adjusted for household size and composition.
Because the poverty line moves as incomes change, relative poverty can persist even when incomes rise.

Examples of relative poverty: being unable to afford a warm waterproof coat, two pairs of strong shoes, adequate heating for the home, or a meal with meat, chicken or fish (or a vegetarian equivalent) every second day.
Photographs of the same type of home or setting from different times and places show that the accepted standard of living changes, which is why poverty is relative.
A child's clothing or a family's home in a photograph from another time or place may look very different from today's norm, yet be an ordinary standard for its own society.
Governments need numbers to track poverty. Two official measures are used, and the second is stricter than the first.
The at-risk-of-poverty rate is the share of people whose income is below the poverty line (60% of median income). It is another way of describing relative poverty.
Enforced deprivation means being unable to afford basic items that most people regard as normal, such as those in the examples of relative poverty. It is not by choice.
The CSO counts a household as deprived if it lacks two or more of 11 listed items.
Consistent poverty means being both below the poverty line and in enforced deprivation, lacking at least two of the 11 items.
Consistent poverty is narrower and more severe than the at-risk-of-poverty rate, because it counts only people who both have a low income and cannot afford the basics.
The CSO publishes these measures every year from the Survey on Income and Living Conditions (SILC), an EU-wide household survey. Social Justice Ireland also publishes a count of people in poverty.
The level of poverty in Ireland has followed the economy and unemployment. It is also not spread evenly across the population.
Poverty fell from the 1960s and 1970s onwards as living standards rose, but rose again during the recession of the 1980s, when unemployment was high.
Poverty fell during the Celtic Tiger period of economic growth in the 1990s and early 2000s, because employment grew.
Poverty rose again after the 2008 downturn as unemployment soared and living costs rose, and rose further with high housing and living costs.
The COVID-19 pandemic increased the risk of poverty for people who lost work or income.
Today poverty is a real problem for a sizeable minority of people, with children and some adult groups at higher risk.
Poverty is not spread evenly. Risk differs by household type, by labour-market status, by region (urban black spots and some rural areas) and by age.
Some groups face a higher risk of poverty because of low income, limited skills, or caring responsibilities. Each group below has its own reason for being at risk.
Lone-parent households, particularly those without paid work, because they have one income and childcare costs make it hard to work.
Unemployed people and long-term unemployed people, who depend on welfare or low-paid work; welfare payments are lower than wages, so they may be too low for their needs.
Low-paid workers (the working poor), including those on the minimum wage who may not qualify for state supports, and people in insecure or part-time work.
People with disabilities or long-term illness, who may be unable to work or face extra costs.
Older people, especially those living alone on a State pension in poorly insulated or substandard homes that are costly to heat, which can lead to illness.
Large families, because there are more children to feed and clothe on one income.
Travellers and other ethnic minorities, who face discrimination, lower education and employment, and poorer accommodation, including in the labour market.

Homeless people, who face isolation and poor health; asylum seekers, who have a restricted right to work while awaiting a decision; and refugees, who may have low income and language barriers and lack skills and qualifications.
Education and opportunity also shape who is at risk. Two further groups are linked to low qualifications and low pay.
Early school leavers and people with few qualifications are at risk because they face low pay and poor job prospects.
People in households in a cycle of deprivation lack education and opportunity, so low income passes from one generation to the next.

Poverty persists where income from work is low or missing and where the costs of living absorb whatever income there is. The reasons fall into economic ones, about money and jobs, and social ones, about family, health and society.

Unemployment: a household with no earned income depends on State payments, which are normally lower than wages, so it has less to live on. Recession and high unemployment are the usual first reason given.
Long-term unemployment erodes skills, work habits and confidence, which makes re-entry to the labour market (the pool of available jobs) harder the longer it lasts.
Low pay: unskilled and minimum-wage work, and part-time or insecure work, often leaves full-time workers unable to afford an acceptable standard of living. These are called the working poor.
Limited education: early school leavers and people with few qualifications or skills are concentrated in low-paid and insecure work, or in no work at all.
Lone parenthood and large families: one income must cover food, housing and childcare for several people, and childcare costs can stop a lone parent working at all.
High housing and living costs: rent, mortgage repayments, a shortage of affordable housing, energy, transport and childcare take a large share of low incomes, so little is left for other needs.

Social problems: addiction and gambling divert money from essentials and lead to debt, for example when spending on alcohol, drugs or gambling replaces spending on food or heating. Ill health and disability can also stop people working.

Economic change: recession and industrial decline mean the closure of a major employer removes jobs and the local businesses that depended on its workers' spending. Globalisation (production moved abroad) and automation (production mechanised) reduce demand for unskilled labour, mainly in manufacturing.
Inequality in society: wealth and power are unequally shared, and some groups face discrimination, which limits their access to jobs, housing and services.

Disadvantage is passed from one generation to the next, so poverty repeats itself unless something interrupts the pattern. The cycle of poverty is poverty handed from parents to children through limited education, work and income.
Children raised in low-income households often have less access to good education, health care and social networks than children from better-off families, as well as poorer housing and diet.
Disadvantage such as poor study conditions, low expectations and financial pressure can lead these children to leave school early with few qualifications, and then into unemployment or low-paid work.
Their own children are then born into the same financial conditions, so the pattern repeats across generations.
Each stage reinforces the next: low income means poorer housing and diet, which affect health and school attendance, which in turn limit qualifications and later earnings.
Breaking the cycle requires action at a weak point where it repeats, for example early-years education, family support and access to training and employment.
Social policy is the set of State decisions on welfare payments, housing, education, health, minimum pay and employment. These decisions affect how many people are poor and for how long.
These decisions determine who is poor and for how long, because they set the income, housing and training available to each household.
Policy can reduce poverty through welfare payments, the national minimum wage, free or subsidised health care, housing supports and education measures for disadvantaged areas.
A minimum wage sets a legal floor for pay, so it directly determines what a full-time low-paid worker earns.

Policy can also keep people poor if it is inadequate or badly designed. Critics argue that welfare payments set below the cost of basic needs keep recipients in poverty, and that a gap between welfare and wages is a problem.
Social policy can perpetuate poverty where losing benefits when a person takes a job makes low-paid work financially unattractive.
Other critics argue that generous payments reduce the incentive to seek work and so sustain dependence on the State. This is a contested view, so present it as a criticism.

Housing policy affects poverty directly: the supply and cost of social and private rented housing decide how much of a low income is left after rent, and a failure to supply affordable homes keeps people poor.
Support that is poorly targeted or changes often leaves gaps, so families move in and out of poverty rather than escaping it.

Deprivation is the lack of resources, services and opportunities that are normal in society. The cycle of deprivation is the way deprivation across several areas of life together, income, education, housing, health and services, reinforces itself and is passed on.
In families, low income, low education and ill health limit the support parents can give children for learning, and children inherit the same limits.
Children in such families often have little contact with people in employment, so they grow up with few examples of working life and low expectations, and repeat the pattern.

In geographical areas, unemployment, welfare dependence and poor housing are concentrated in the same place, creating employment blackspots, often after a major industry closes. Some disadvantaged urban estates and some rural areas are examples.
Services in those areas, such as shops, buses, schools and health centres, close as spending falls, and the area gets a poor reputation, making it less attractive to employers and families.
Deprivation reinforces itself: an area losing population, employers and skilled workers loses the tax base and local spending that could sustain new employment.
Responses must work on the place as well as the household, for example community development, community education, transport, local training, job creation and local services.
The poverty trap is a situation in which taking up work brings little or no gain in net income, so a person stays on welfare. It is a problem of benefit withdrawal.

A person on welfare who takes a low-paid job loses benefits or supports, and may pay tax and PRSI, so net income (what they keep) rises little or not at all, and may even fall. They can be no better off than on welfare.
Supports often withdrawn as earnings rise include housing assistance, a medical card and, in some cases, child-related payments.
The costs of working, such as transport, childcare and work clothing, reduce the gain further.
When welfare is financially more rewarding than low-paid work, people have little incentive to take employment, which keeps them dependent on welfare.

Payments reduced gradually as earnings rise, rather than withdrawn all at once, lessen the trap. In-work payments such as the Working Family Payment, a tax-free weekly payment for low-paid working parents, are designed to help low-paid working families.
Poverty affects a person's mind, health and place in society, and these effects can then make it harder to escape poverty.
Stress, worry and fear about money can lead to depression and poor mental health.
Loss of status and self-esteem, and a feeling of worthlessness, can reduce confidence to seek work or training.
Social isolation and exclusion, because the cost of leisure, travel and social activities is beyond reach.
Poor diet, and poorly heated or damp housing, increase the risk of illness, and ill health can prevent people from working.
Some people turn to alcohol, drugs or gambling as a means of escape, which adds to debt and poverty.
When a household cannot meet its basic needs, the strain falls on the whole family, and children can carry the effects into adult life.
Families may be unable to afford adequate food, clothing, heating and housing, and fall into rent, mortgage or utility arrears and debt. In the worst cases, they lose their home and become homeless.
Financial pressure increases conflict and relationship strain, and can contribute to family breakdown.
Children may be unable to take part in school trips, sport, clubs or activities their peers attend, which leads to embarrassment and affects belonging and self-esteem.
Children without a quiet place to study, books or internet access may fall behind in school, and poor diet and health can affect their concentration.
Children growing up in poverty are more likely to leave school early with few qualifications, which limits their later earnings and risks poverty as adults, the cycle of poverty.
Poorer diet and access to health care can affect children's physical health and development.
Loss of a home forces children to move school and loses the stability that supports their learning.
Poverty does not stay within households. Where it is concentrated, it affects whole neighbourhoods and the public finances.
Higher demand for welfare, health and housing services increases the cost to the State.
Concentrated poverty can contribute to crime, anti-social behaviour and vandalism in an area.
Falling spending in poorer areas leads to shop closures and fewer local services, which reduces jobs further.
Poverty reduces the skills and productive capacity available to the economy, because people who are unemployed or poorly educated cannot contribute fully.
The State pays income support to unemployed people through two routes, and the route decides what a claimant has to prove. All social welfare payments come from the Department of Social Protection.
Social insurance payments (also called benefits) depend on a record of PRSI contributions paid while in work, and they are not means-tested. They are funded from those PRSI contributions.

Social assistance payments are means-tested, which means the household's income and savings are assessed, and no contribution record is required, because they are paid on the basis of need. They are funded from general taxation.
Jobseeker's Benefit is the main social insurance payment for an unemployed person who has enough paid PRSI contributions, so the claimant's own contributions earn the right to it.
Jobseeker's Allowance is the main social assistance payment for an unemployed person who does not qualify for Jobseeker's Benefit or whose benefit has ended, so it acts as a safety net.

A Jobseeker's Allowance claimant must be unemployed, capable of work, available for full-time work and genuinely seeking employment. This shows the payment supports people who want work, not people who have chosen not to work.
Supplementary Welfare Allowance is a means-tested payment for people with no or very low income whose basic needs are not met. It also pays exceptional needs.
Families with children face extra costs, so several payments are aimed at them. Some reach every family, and others are limited to low-income households.
Child Benefit is paid for each qualifying child regardless of the parents' income. It is universal, not means-tested, so it reaches families on every income level.
Payments for lone parents are means-tested, because they are aimed at those in need, and recognise that one adult is carrying the full cost of the household.

The Working Family Payment (formerly Family Income Supplement) is a tax-free, means-tested weekly payment for low-paid workers who have a dependent child. It is an in-work payment, so it makes work pay and eases the poverty trap.
Means-tested payments are reduced as income rises, so the household gains less from extra earnings than the wage itself.
The Fuel Allowance is paid weekly to qualifying low-income households during the winter season to help with heating costs, which rise in cold weather.
Besides cash payments, the State lowers the cost of essentials such as health, school, housing and childcare for families on low incomes. Each scheme either pays for something or removes a cost.
Medical card: gives free GP visits and access to many health services, run by the HSE. Eligibility depends on income and, in some cases, health needs.

Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance: a once-yearly payment, because the cost falls at the start of the school year, that helps qualifying families meet the cost of school uniforms and shoes.
Household Benefits Package: help with electricity or gas and a free television licence for qualifying older people and people with certain disabilities or long-term illnesses.

Housing supports: local authority (social) housing is let at rents related to income. The Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) is paid through the local authority to help households pay rent in the private rented sector, and the tenant's rent contribution is based on income.

Education supports: the school meals programme and free school book schemes ease the cost of school, and the free pre-school place (ECCE), an early-learning place before primary school, reduces childcare costs.

Money Advice and Budgeting Service (MABS): a free, confidential, State-funded service, working under the Citizens Information Board, that helps people in debt, mainly low-income households, to budget and deal with creditors.
These initiatives work through training, business supports and job creation rather than income support alone. A statutory body is one set up by law or run by the State.
SOLAS is the State further education and training authority. It funds, plans and coordinates further education and training through the Education and Training Boards (ETBs).
SOLAS supports apprenticeships, vocational courses and literacy, numeracy and digital training, and it provides skills training and upskilling, matching the skills of unemployed people to vacancies.
Enterprise Ireland is the State agency that helps Irish-owned companies increase sales, exports and employment through grants, market advice and training. More sales and exports create jobs.
Local Enterprise Offices (LEOs) in each county are the first stop shop for people starting or growing small businesses, giving training, mentoring, advice and grants and encouraging job creation.
Intreo is the Department of Social Protection's public employment service. It gives job-seekers advice, job-matching and referral to training, so unemployed people can be linked to vacancies.
Work-based learning and CV and job-search preparation give unemployed people the experience that employers ask for, which makes them more employable.

Community Employment (CE) offers temporary part-time work placements on local community projects for long-term unemployed and other eligible people. It is a Department of Social Protection scheme, not a SOLAS one.

Other schemes that support a return to education and training are the Vocational Training Opportunities Scheme (VTOS), the Back to Education Allowance and Youthreach, an ETB programme for early school leavers.
Foreign direct investment (FDI) is investment by an overseas company that sets up or expands operations in Ireland. The State encourages it because it creates jobs, but it also brings risks.
IDA Ireland is the State agency responsible for attracting overseas companies and for helping foreign companies already here to expand, through grants, site selection and advice.
A low corporation tax rate is a key incentive for multinational companies to locate in Ireland: 12.5%, and 15% for the largest multinational groups.
Other attractions are a young, skilled, flexible, educated and English-speaking workforce, grant assistance, good telecommunications and access to the European Union's single market.
Foreign investment, for example a new plant, creates direct jobs in the foreign firms and indirect jobs in suppliers and services, so it reduces unemployment.
It also brings tax revenue and new skills and technology into local labour markets, so workers can move on to other employers.
Dependence on a few large multinationals is a weakness: if a parent company closes or moves a plant, a local area can lose many jobs at once.
Multinational employment tends to be concentrated in larger towns and cities, so rural areas benefit less from it. IDA Ireland aims to spread investment to regions outside the main cities.
When a family loses its income, the State is not the only source of help. Voluntary organisations are non-profit bodies set up to meet a social need, and they step in where people are struggling.
A voluntary organisation is a non-profit group run largely by volunteers, often with some paid staff. Because it is independent of government, it can respond quickly and locally.
Many receive some State funding, but they are still not State bodies. Statutory (State-run) bodies such as SOLAS, MABS and the Department of Social Protection are a different thing.
They are funded by donations, fundraising, charity shops and State grants, so they can keep helping people without charging them.
Unfunded services, such as volunteer-run listening services, fill gaps that statutory services do not cover, for example by giving someone a friendly person to talk to.

The Society of St Vincent de Paul (SVP) is the standard example of a voluntary organisation that supports people at risk of poverty or unemployment. Its strength is that help comes from neighbours who know the local area.
SVP works through local volunteer groups called conferences. They visit households in their own area, in confidence, and assess the help needed, so families are not shamed by asking publicly.
It gives practical help: food or fuel vouchers, help with essential household bills, school books and uniforms, furniture and advice, and also emergency accommodation.
It also runs hostels and housing, homework clubs and education supports, so it helps with long-term needs as well as emergencies.
SVP raises its funds through charity shops and public and church collections, such as church-gate collections, rather than relying only on the State.
Several other voluntary organisations work with particular groups. Each has a clear role you can state in one line.
Simon Community provides support and emergency accommodation to people who are homeless or at risk of homelessness, with housing and outreach (going out to meet people on the street).
Focus Ireland works to prevent and end homelessness. It provides accommodation, training in personal and life skills, and information on job opportunities, as well as housing, support and advice.
Barnardos supports children and families, and Age Action supports older people, so each targets a group that is at particular risk of poverty.
Rotary and Lions clubs give local fundraising and practical support, and Men's Sheds give men a place to meet and work together, which reduces isolation.
When the main earner is unemployed, a family needs more than money. Voluntary organisations meet several different needs, and they also work on behalf of everyone affected.
Financial or material help: vouchers, help with bills, clothing and food, so the family can cover essentials while income is low.
Advice, information and advocacy (speaking up for someone): they direct clients to State entitlements, MABS and Citizens Information, linking people to services they are entitled to.
Coping and skills classes, and a friendly visit and someone to talk to, which ease the stress and isolation that unemployment brings.
Voluntary organisations act as pressure groups: they gather evidence on local need and campaign and lobby the Government for changes in public policy.
Voluntary work benefits the individual through purpose, skills, confidence and friendships, and it may lead to a job.
It benefits the community through quick, low-cost local services that complement State services and build community spirit.
Community initiatives are locally run responses to unemployment and early school leaving, often funded by the State. They work because they are close to the people they help.
Community-based projects build confidence, work experience, skills and social networks, which help people move back into paid work.
Community education centres offer adult literacy and numeracy classes and personal development courses, often for people who left school early.

Education and Training Boards (ETBs) provide adult and further education, and many community courses are delivered through them. Youthreach is for early school leavers and the Vocational Training Opportunities Scheme (VTOS) is for unemployed adults.
Community training centres and local training projects offer practical and vocational skills, often with a route to a recognised qualification. They are funded through SOLAS and the ETBs.
Local groups identify training needs in their area, such as skills gaps in the local economy, and design courses to meet them, so training leads to real jobs.
Some schemes give people paid work in their own community, so they keep working habits and earn while they look for a job. These are State-funded employment schemes run locally.

Community Employment (CE) provides part-time temporary paid work on local community projects for long-term unemployed people, in areas such as the environment, heritage, sport, tourism and community services.
Tús gives temporary work placements in local communities through local development companies.
The Rural Social Scheme gives income support to low-income farmers and fishers for community work.

Local development companies deliver the Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP 2024-2028). It is funded by the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht, with EU funding through the ESF+.
SICAP aims to reduce poverty and social exclusion by supporting communities and individuals, with courses, job-readiness and help starting a business.
A co-operative is a business owned and democratically controlled by its members, who pool resources, skills and knowledge to meet their needs and share its surplus.
Each member has one vote regardless of how much they have invested, and members elect the board. This is why no wealthy investor can take control.
The surplus (profit after costs and reserves) is shared among members in proportion to their use of the co-operative or reinvested in the business, rather than paid to outside shareholders.

Types include agricultural co-operatives (farming, dairy, fishing), housing co-operatives (owned by their members, who build or manage homes), and worker co-operatives (owned by their employees) and consumer co-operatives (owned by their customers).
Credit unions are member-owned co-operatives where members save and borrow at fair cost. They offer savings accounts and affordable loans, a key service for low-income households.
A community co-operative can run a shop, a childcare service or local transport where no private business will, creating local jobs.
Co-operatives respond to poverty and unemployment because profits stay with members and the local area rather than leaving the community with outside owners.

Optional international principles: voluntary and open membership, democratic member control, member economic participation, autonomy and independence, education and training, co-operation among co-operatives, and concern for community.

A cottage industry is small-scale production by an individual or family, usually at home or in a small workshop, using traditional or craft skills. It is a separate idea from a co-operative, which is a member-owned business.
Irish examples are hand-knitted Aran jumpers, hand-weaving including Donegal tweed, Carrickmacross lace, pottery and other handmade crafts, often sold to local and tourist markets.
Artisan food producers and farmers' markets are also accepted as community initiatives.
They give families an extra or sole source of income, especially in rural areas where other employment is limited, and they keep traditional skills alive.
They need little capital, because the equipment is simple and production takes place at home.
Limitations include seasonal or irregular income, small output, difficulty in marketing and competing with mass production, limited marketing reach, no employment benefits and reliance on tourism.
Local Enterprise Offices can help producers with training and grants to develop craft businesses.
In the clothing and textile industry, cottage firms supply handmade clothing and textiles.
The Combat Poverty Agency is a past tense topic: it was a State body, not a voluntary one, and it has been closed. Answer about it in the past tense.
The Combat Poverty Agency was a State body that researched poverty, advised government and funded local anti-poverty projects.
It was dissolved on 1 July 2009 and its work merged into the Social Inclusion Division of the Department of Social Protection (then the Department of Social and Family Affairs).

It no longer exists as an independent agency, so current answers should name the bodies and organisations that carry out this work today, such as the Department's Social Inclusion Division and the Roadmap for Social Inclusion, SICAP, and voluntary organisations such as SVP.
